This patent application describes transistors with metal gates having reduced resistivity. Polysilicon gates suffer from a poly depletion effect, which metal gates can solve. However, tungsten metal gates require a tungsten nucleation layer for adhesion, and this nucleation layer has high resistivity that degrades transistor performance at small dimensions. The application proposes using a metal-containing layer comprising cobalt and/or a metal silicide (such as cobalt silicide) over a metal nitride barrier layer (e.g., titanium nitride) in the gate electrode, source/drain contact plugs, and/or gate contact plug. The metal-containing layer may be a homogeneous cobalt layer, a homogeneous metal silicide layer, or a composite with a lower layer (e.g., cobalt silicide) and an upper cobalt layer. The deposition can involve physical vapor deposition and chemical vapor deposition using cobalt-containing and silicon-containing precursors, with temperature adjustments to vary silicon content. Cobalt and metal silicides offer low resistivity, good adhesion to the barrier layer, and resistance to acid corrosion during etching processes. The method includes forming a replacement gate stack by depositing a gate dielectric, work-function layers, a titanium nitride barrier layer, and the cobalt-containing layer, then planarizing. Contact plugs are similarly formed with a barrier layer and the metal-containing layer.

Small-body populations in planetary systems exist as remnant reservoirs after gas disc dispersal, and understanding them is necessary to infer the origin, composition, and thermal history of exocomets. In the Solar System, reservoirs range from Ayló'chaxnim asteroids interior to Venus, near-Earth asteroids, the main belt (2–3.5 au) with compositional mixing and Kirkwood gaps, co-orbitals and Trojans for most planets, Hildas, Jupiter Trojans, irregular satellites, Neptune Trojans, and the trans-Neptunian region. The latter includes the cold classical Kuiper belt (42.5–47.5 au) and dynamically excited populations (resonant, hot classical, scattered disc, detached disc, extreme TNOs), totaling >10^6 objects, with icy surfaces containing H2O, CO2, CO, CH4, CH3OH, and organics. Centaurs and Jupiter-family comets are temporary populations from the scattering disc. The Oort cloud, with ~10^11 objects >0.3 km beyond ~1000 au, is the most distant reservoir. Star formation in dense molecular clouds leads to protostellar discs that evolve through Class 0 to III stages; Class II discs are planet-forming sites with ALMA-detected substructures. Most stars form in clusters, where stellar flybys and radiation can truncate discs, reducing planetesimal-forming material. External photo-evaporation dominates in massive long-lived clusters with OB stars, while flybys dominate in low-mass short-lived clusters. Protoplanetary discs have high dust-to-gas ratios; dust masses vary widely. Thermal conditions set snowlines: CO snowline at ~20–30 au, water at ~1–2 au for solar-mass stars, farther for more luminous stars. Planetesimal composition is icy beyond the water snowline. ALMA reveals CO depletion and gas-phase C/O>1 anomalies, explained by UV/cosmic-ray destruction and differential freeze-out of O, C, N into ices. Exocomets require a source population and massive bodies to drive nuclei inward. Wide-orbit giant planets are detected around ~10% of B stars, with a positive correlation with stellar mass; lower-mass planets may be preferred drivers but are hard to detect. Debris discs are the primary exocomet source, more common around younger and earlier-type stars, though all main-sequence stars likely have some debris. Dust growth from µm to km sizes faces a bouncing barrier for silicates; icy particles may not have this barrier. Growth timescales are long in outer discs, so planetesimals likely form via gravitational collapse of pebble clouds reaching Hill density. The streaming instability (SI) amplifies dust-to-gas ratios, but super-Solar metallicity is needed to trigger collapse. SI simulations yield shallow mass distributions favoring large planetesimals. In the Solar System, asteroids and cold classical KBOs should form with ~100 km diameter, supported by primordial asteroids, Arrokoth, high binary fraction, and orbital inclinations. Around other stars, planetesimal mass scales with stellar mass, so typical diameters ~100 km. Protoplanetary disc lifetimes depend on stellar mass: A stars 1–4 Myr, M/K stars 5–10 Myr. After gas dispersal, debris discs form; cold debris discs are detected around ~20% of AFGK stars, diverse in structure, with features suggesting planetary interactions that could drive exocomets. Dust masses are 10^-3–1 M_earth; total masses extrapolated to 0.3–300 M_earth. Collisional grinding depletes material over time, so exocomets may be preferentially detected in younger systems. Solar System small-body orbital distributions are well characterized except the Oort Cloud. TNO orbits and dynamical properties constrain early Solar System evolution and stellar environment. Surface colors of TNOs, Centaurs, and Trojans are bimodal, probing primordial disc composition. JWST reveals distinct spectral groups among TNOs, suggesting formation locations relative to sublimation radii. Cometary outgassing and in-situ missions (Hayabusa2, Rosetta) provide detailed composition, though D/H ratios are challenging to interpret. The Oort cloud has inner and outer regions; ~1–3% of ejected planetesimals remain bound. Its existence is inferred from a spike in 1/a0. Formation timing is open; the Sun likely formed in a cluster, leaving signatures in minor planets. Non-native planetesimals may be captured. Cluster flybys reduce Oort cloud content but increase short-term exocomet influx. Exo-Oort clouds are theoretically possible but unobserved. Open questions concern natal environment, binary hosts, self-consistent models, planetesimal formation differences, dominant exocomet sources, planet requirements, non-local fractions, debris disc masses and formation, diversity of shapes, Kuiper belt analogy, LSST, and implantation timing. In conclusion, small-body reservoirs are a probable outcome of planetesimal formation at any young star, with complex possibilities for exocomets depending on planetary architecture and mixing history. Solar System details combined with exoplanetary diversity will improve understanding, aided by future facilities.

The Boston Zone Offense, developed by Tom Davis at Boston College, features players staying in one position and flipping sides rather than interchanging, allowing efficiency. It emphasizes a strong low post attack and uses a dribble entry, making it suitable for up-tempo play, and combines overloading and spreading principles. The alignment: point guard (O1), baseline runner (O3), low post (O5), shooting guard (O2) at top, weakside rebounder (O4). O1 initiates with dribble penetration. Continuity relies on sharp passing, moving the ball sideline to sideline, using skip passes, post feeds, and pump fakes, while avoiding forced passes and dribbling. Ball reversal to O2 triggers O4 stepping to the wing and O3 running the baseline. When the wing passes to the corner, a give-and-go basket cut occurs; if covered, O4 empties weakside, O5 flashes, and O1 breaks to the ballside wing. Post feeds are crucial: the post reads the defender's position (behind, high side, baseline side, fronting) to seal and receive passes, and when the zone collapses, outside shooters get open. The baseline runner creates matchup and vision problems; on ball reversal, a passing lane opens to the cutter, forcing defensive dilemmas that create open corner shots or post opportunities. Against overplay, skip passes are used; denied passes lead to skip passes to the top, cross-court "X" passes, or back cuts. Extended zone pressure opens the middle for post isolation or dribble penetration, with kick-out passes for open shots if defenders help. It includes reads and counters for 2-3, 1-2-2, and 1-3-1 zones.

The Turnaround Tuesday effect is a market tendency for price reversals from Monday's close to at least Tuesday's close. Backtesting on SPY from inception with 0.03% commissions and slippage shows that buying on a weak Monday—where the close is at least 1% lower than Friday's close—and selling at Tuesday's close has been a profitable strategy for about 30 years. Buying at the Monday close yields twice the return of buying at the Tuesday close, and other days are even less profitable. The strategy works only on weak Mondays; buying on strength on Monday is not effective. Adding filters like Intraday Breadth Strength can improve performance. An example is Black Monday 1987, when the market rebounded 5.3% on Tuesday and 9.1% on Wednesday.

This study uses femtosecond noise correlation spectroscopy (FemNoC) to investigate ultrafast magnetization fluctuations in the canted antiferromagnet Sm₀.₇Er₀.₃FeO₃. By varying temperature across the spin reorientation transition (SRT) and applying external magnetic fields, the relationship between spin fluctuations, the free energy landscape, and quasi-ferromagnetic (qF) magnon properties is examined. Temperature scans show that qF magnon fluctuation variance sharply increases near the lower critical temperature of the SRT, accompanied by softening of the qF mode frequency; both effects are suppressed by external magnetic fields. Atomistic spin model simulations reproduce these trends. Monte Carlo simulations of a magnetization vector in a Landau-type free energy potential demonstrate that fluctuation enhancement arises from softening of the potential landscape, and random telegraph noise emerges when energy barriers between degenerate minima are small. Field scans reveal that an applied magnetic field along the c-axis reduces qF mode variance and increases its frequency, consistent with field-induced stiffening of the free energy potential. The results indicate that ultrafast spin fluctuations are governed by the free energy curvature and can be tuned by external fields, and that FemNoC can map magnetization potentials.

The passage describes a camera module and its molded circuit board assembly and molded photosensitive assembly, along with manufacturing methods. The molded base has a light window with an inner side surface that is at least partially inclined. Specifically, a first inclination angle α (3°–30°) is formed between a first portion inner side surface and the optical axis, and a third inclination angle β (3°–30°) may be formed between a third portion inner side surface and the optical axis. An outer side surface may have a second inclination angle γ (3°–45°). These acute angles facilitate demoulding, reduce friction, prevent damage, and reduce stray light reaching the photosensitive element. The light window forming block of the molding mould has a trapezoidal or multi-step trapezoidal cross-section with diameters increasing from bottom to top. Manufacturing methods involve placing a circuit board (with or without a photosensitive element) in a mould, filling liquid molding material into a base forming guide groove around the light window forming block, solidifying, and demoulding. Joint board array operations can produce integral pieces of molded circuit board assemblies or molded photosensitive assemblies, which are then cut into individual units. The molded base may also include a top groove for an optical filter, lens actuator pin grooves, and a lens mounting portion.

David Hardt, co-lecturer, presents a mechanical engineering perspective on manufacturing process control, building on prior lectures. He focuses on processes as geometric change of an object, driven by a directed energy exchange between equipment and material. The output geometry is a function of input process parameters. Energy sources can be mechanical, electrical, thermal, or chemical. A taxonomy for control classifies processes by geometry change mode (removal, addition, deformation, formation) and by interaction type: serial (localized energy applied over time via trajectory) or parallel (energy distributed simultaneously over the entire area, often via tool shape). Examples include turning, injection molding, rolling, CVD, stereolithography, and 3D printing. The taxonomy helps understand flexibility, rate, cost, and quality. Serial removal processes tend to be most flexible; parallel processes offer high speed.

Process parameters are divided into equipment states (transient energy variables like forces, velocities, temperatures), equipment properties (inherent characteristics like stiffness, thermal expansion), material states (transient conditions like temperature of the material during processing), and material properties (constitutive properties like yield strength, elasticity, dimensions). Equipment states are typically well-controlled and are the primary variables manipulated for control. Material properties are often a major source of variation and uncertainty, while equipment properties can degrade over time. Material states are variable and harder to know. The lecture emphasizes that understanding these distinctions helps identify and address sources of process variation.

The study examined the potentiality and apprehensions of AI in education from the perspectives of 63 academic staff and administrators at Kuwait University’s Faculty of Education, using a cross-sectional survey with three published instruments. Results indicated medium acceptance of AI (overall mean 3.37), with high consensus that AI will benefit humankind (mean 4.03). Most participants (58.7%) had no prior AI teaching experience. Linking educational aspects to AI was moderate (mean 4.21), with data analysis, machine learning, and natural language processing rated most important. A majority acknowledged a desire for explicit AI integration into curricula. Student empowerment requirements were moderate (mean 4.36), emphasizing the ability to determine AI use cases and evaluate AI intelligence. Challenges and difficulties in using AI were high (mean 4.83), particularly the lack of suitable teaching materials and required expertise. Scenarios for education using AI scored high (mean 4.82), notably personalized intelligent teaching and smart schools. No statistically significant differences were found by gender, academic degree, or academic department, except for challenges and difficulties between males and females (p=.067). The study concluded that both potential and apprehensions are high, and reforms are needed to align AI with education.

The lecture discusses interactions between neutral atoms. Classically, neutral atoms have no dipole moment and no attraction, because creating a fluctuating dipole costs more energy than the dipole-dipole interaction gains. In quantum mechanics, zero-point fluctuations give a non-zero expectation value for the squared dipole operator, enabling a van der Waals potential. One derivation uses second-order perturbation theory, yielding a 1/R⁶ potential. Another interpretation treats the atoms as coupled LC circuits, where the ground-state zero-point energy of the coupled oscillators gives a 1/R⁶ contribution. A third picture involves spontaneous dipole fluctuations on one atom inducing an aligned dipole on the other, leading to a 1/R⁶ interaction.

Considering vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field, long-wavelength fluctuations induce correlated dipole moments in two atoms, producing a 1/R⁷ potential (Casimir-Polder). The dominant contribution comes from virtual photons with wavelength approximately equal to the interatomic distance R. The short-range 1/R⁶ potential assumes instantaneous electrostatic interaction without propagation effects; the long-range 1/R⁷ potential includes retardation. The crossover distance is the wavelength of the atomic transition.

A diagrammatic approach using fourth-order perturbation theory describes the interaction as exchange of virtual photon pairs. Two classes of diagrams are compared: one where the intermediate state has two atomic excitations, and another where it has two photonic excitations. At short range (photon frequency larger than atomic resonance), the first class dominates; at long range (atomic frequency larger), the second class dominates, introducing an extra factor of 1/R and changing the power law from 1/R⁶ to 1/R⁷.

This lecture introduces risk preferences from the perspective of expected utility theory. It covers how economics assumes people make choices involving risk, how to measure risk preferences, and the model's implications and limits. The expected utility model evaluates risky options by defining utility over final outcomes, weighting those utilities by their probabilities, and summing them. Key assumptions are that only final outcomes matter and that probabilities are treated linearly. Risk aversion is modeled solely as diminishing marginal utility of wealth, captured by a concave utility function.

The lecture presents three stylized facts: people are risk averse (e.g., buying insurance), risk reduction has a price (people accept risk for higher expected returns), and people sometimes take on risk for its own sake (e.g., casinos, lotteries) despite negative expected value. Measures of risk aversion include the coefficient of absolute risk aversion and the coefficient of relative risk aversion (gamma). These can be estimated using certainty equivalents, choices between gambles, or real-world insurance choices.

A central problem is that expected utility cannot reconcile small-scale and large-scale risk aversion. Large-scale choices suggest gamma is between 0 and 2, while rejecting small gambles (e.g., a 50-50 bet to win $11 and lose $10) implies gamma greater than 18. Rabin’s calibration argument shows that under weak concavity, rejecting such small gambles leads to absurd implications for larger gambles, such as turning down a bet with infinite gain. The marginal utility of money would have to decrease extremely rapidly.

The lecture then discusses Justin Sydnor’s study using home insurance deductible choices to estimate risk aversion. The data include menus of four deductibles with associated premiums and actual choices. Claim rates are very low. By comparing chosen deductibles to available options, one can bound gamma. The lecture notes that this will be explored in more detail next time.

In Shircliff v. The State, the Indiana Supreme Court affirmed a conviction for conspiracy to bribe a township trustee. The indictment charged that Shircliff and O'Connor conspired to corruptly influence trustee Valentine Strange by offering money to employ O'Connor as a teacher, with Strange retaining $50 of the wages. The court held the indictment valid under sections 2139 and 2009, R.S. 1881, even though it did not allege a school vacancy, because employing teachers is a matter that may legally come before a trustee. The court declined to consider alleged errors in overruling a continuance motion and admitting evidence, because the bill of exceptions was filed after the term without an extension, so it was not part of the record. The affidavit for continuance was also not in the bill. The discharge of O'Connor as a witness under section 1804 was not objected to at trial, so the issue was waived. After verdict, the defendant absconded, and at the next term, the original special judge was absent. The regular judge appointed one special judge, then later the same day appointed another, who rendered judgment. The court presumed the first appointee was absent or unable to preside, making the second appointment proper. The judgment was affirmed with costs.

U.S. objectives for dependent areas included promoting advancement through international collaboration, encouraging self-governance, safeguarding security, and applying non-discriminatory treatment. A March 9, 1943 draft declaration proposed placing mandated territories under international trusteeship, establishing regional commissions, and granting colonial peoples timed independence. British objections were noted at subsequent conferences, and the plans were refined. The chapter on international trusteeship was deleted from the American Tentative Proposals at the Joint Chiefs of Staff's request before the Dumbarton Oaks Conversations, so dependent territories were not discussed there, though the issue was understood to be considered later. The British government later accepted the President's proposal on Security Council voting. A memorandum from the Secretary of War argued against raising any territorial questions during the war, warning such discussions would risk controversies and jeopardize unified war prosecution.

Turing GPUs introduce RT Cores that accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, offloading the SM and enabling real-time ray tracing when combined with advanced denoising filtering. Far fewer rays per pixel are needed with RT Core acceleration and denoising. Real-time ray tracing of selected objects can achieve cinematic-quality reflections, shadows, and ambient occlusion on a single GPU. Turing also includes Tensor Cores for AI-based features via NVIDIA NGX, such as Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) which uses a neural network trained on 64x supersampled images to produce high-quality output with reduced shading work, and DLSS 2X mode for near-64xSS quality. Other NGX features include InPainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez. New shader stages—Task and Mesh Shaders—enable more flexible geometry processing, eliminating CPU draw call bottlenecks and supporting efficient level-of-detail and culling. Variable Rate Shading allows shading rate to vary per 16x16 pixel region, enabling content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering optimizations. Texture Space Shading decouples shading from screen space, storing results in texture space for reuse and temporal stability. Multi-View Rendering supports up to four views per pass for efficient stereo and multi-instance rendering. Turing GPUs also feature hardware support for USB Type-C/VirtualLink, and VRWorks Audio accelerated by RT Cores. The TU104 GPU contains 48 SMs, 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores; TU106 has 36 SMs, 2304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores. A workload-based RTX-OPS metric combines Tensor, FP32, RT, and INT32 operations according to typical frame time distribution. Ray tracing basics, BVH structures, and denoising are described, along with examples of ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections in games.

The ambassador pattern uses an ambassador container to broker interactions between the application container and the external world. It provides modularity and reuse. Examples include client-side sharding via a proxy that routes requests to appropriate shards, service brokering where the ambassador handles service discovery so the application connects to localhost, and request splitting where a fraction of traffic is redirected to an experimental service.

The adapter pattern modifies the application container’s interface to conform to a predefined interface. It is used for monitoring (e.g., adding a Prometheus exporter container to adapt Redis), logging (using fluentd to normalize different log formats to a common structure), and health checks (an adapter container runs diagnostic queries for MySQL, exposing an HTTP health check).

Replicated load-balanced services consist of identical stateless replicas behind a load balancer. Readiness probes indicate when a replica is ready to serve. Session tracked services use consistent hashing to route a user’s requests to the same replica. Application-layer replication can add a caching layer (e.g., Varnish) deployed as a separate replicated tier to improve hit rate, and an SSL termination layer (nginx) for HTTPS.

Sharded services split data across shards, each handling a subset of requests. A sharded cache increases the fraction of the dataset that can be stored. Sharding functions use hashing and modulo, requiring determinism and uniformity; key selection must group identical responses without being too specific. Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping when resharding. Hot sharding handles uneven load by scaling individual shards.

The scatter/gather pattern parallelizes requests by sending them to all leaf nodes, each performing part of the work, and the root combining results. It can be used for document search. When data is too large for a single machine, leaf sharding distributes different data subsets across leaves. The straggler problem (overall latency determined by the slowest leaf) limits gains from increased parallelism. Replicating each leaf shard improves reliability and allows upgrades under load.

Functions and event-driven processing (FaaS) simplify deployment and scale automatically but force strong decoupling, complicating debugging and monitoring. FaaS is poorly suited for background processing or applications needing to hold large data in memory.

On January 16, 1945, the Yalta Briefing Book was completed. A memorandum records Leo Pasvolsky's second conversation with the Soviet Ambassador on Dumbarton Oaks proposals. Before leaving for Moscow, the Ambassador sought clarification. He was puzzled by a reference to Chapter VIII, Section C, paragraph 1 about the Council encouraging regional peaceful settlement, and found it logical. A voting formula discussion yielded no new points; he wanted to fix the arguments. He considered the Court matter settled, with details studied in Moscow. The dependent areas discussion was lengthy. He noted Soviet interest and favorable view of Hull's Moscow memorandum, despite no colonies. Pasvolsky outlined problems: trust vs. colonial areas, general principles, trusteeship machinery, regional commissions, accountability, and relation to the international organization. He said their thinking followed Hull's memorandum and the Philippines example. He stated only international trusteeship belongs on the UN Conference agenda; colonial problems should be addressed separately. The Ambassador asked if colonial discussions would involve only colonial powers or others, and suggested the future international organization could arrange it. Pasvolsky said any of these procedures was possible.

The President submits to Congress a letter from the Creek Indian agent seeking U.S. protection of Creek treaty rights and territory (treaty ratified April 22). Georgia surveyors are surveying Creek lands; some may have been arrested by Indians. The Indians' forbearance may prevent violence.

The 1802 act prohibits surveying Indian lands, with penalties. It provides two enforcement processes: military apprehension in Indian country, or civil arrest and trial if the offender is found within a State, with military aid if needed. The President chose the civil process, directing prosecution of the surveyors in Georgia and assuring the Indians of protection while urging their forbearance.

He avoided military force because the surveys were under Georgia state authority, and using federal force risked a state-federal conflict. He states that Georgia's actions violate the treaty and Constitution. He warns that if Georgia persists, the Executive will be compelled to use all force, including military, but only after other legal means fail. He asks Congress to consider further legislation.

A retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 290 patients (aged 41–80 years, 84.14% male) who underwent CABG surgery at Mordovian Republic Hospital between 2017 and 2021. The study examined the role of shunt number and internal thoracic artery (ITA) use in postoperative complications. Most patients (95.86%) had on-pump surgery. Preoperative risk factors included diabetes mellitus (22.76%), dyspnea (18.97%), arrhythmia (23.79%), progressive angina (38.62%), and post-myocardial infarction sclerosis (61.38%). Postoperative complications included arrhythmia (10.73%), psychosis (4.95%), stroke (1.41%), myocardial infarction (0.71%), hydrothorax (12.01%), re-sternotomy (3.18%), sternal wound infection (2.40%), and dyspnea (3.89%). Mortality was 1.72%.

Statistical analysis showed that elderly patients had higher risk of postoperative arrhythmia, psychosis, stroke, and longer ICU and total hospitalization days. Hydrothorax was associated with low BMI, longer aortic cross-clamp time, and longer cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time. Progressive angina and post-myocardial infarction sclerosis were linked to a higher number of complications. No statistical significance was found between number of shunts or ITAs used and number of complications. Direct correlations were observed between age and ICU/total hospitalization days/complications; number of complications and age/CPB time/aortic cross-clamp time/ICU days/total days; total hospitalization days and ejection fraction/ICU days; aortic cross-clamp time and CPB time; and BMI and ejection fraction. The study concluded that elderly patients are at higher risk for psychosis, arrhythmia, longer hospitalization, and stroke; hydrothorax is seen with low BMI and long aortic cross-clamp time; and progressive angina and post-myocardial infarction sclerosis increase postoperative complications, particularly hydrothorax.

The author believes national legislators should soon enact a graduated inheritance tax, with rates increasing based on the amount inherited and the remoteness of kin, to place a growing burden on large fortunes while keeping taxes low on moderate amounts to encourage thrift. Progress should be gradual. The U.S. has previously imposed temporary graduated inheritance taxes in 1797, 1862, and 1898. The Supreme Court has upheld such taxes as constitutional excises, not direct taxes. An income tax differs, as it does not address the perpetuation of unhealthy fortunes. The 1894 income tax was ruled unconstitutional, but the court's hesitation suggests a constitutional income tax might be devised. Amending the Constitution is difficult and should be a last resort; legislation should first be attempted for inheritance tax and for national control over corporate wealth in interstate business, with constitutional amendment as a final alternative if legislation fails.

Lewis Roberts sued Prosser and King for false imprisonment after being arrested on an execution against his person. The arrest arose from a judgment in a prior suit where Roberts, as an assignee for creditors, was sued by a creditor for an accounting and distribution of assigned assets. The court considered whether that prior action was “for money received … in a fiduciary capacity” under Code § 179 subd. 2, which would permit arrest. The court held it was not. The prior action sought more than mere recovery of money received; it required a judicial determination of the net amount chargeable to the assignees, including money they should have received, and a distribution among creditors. The statute’s phrase “action for money received” means an action primarily and simply for the recovery of money, like money had and received, and does not extend to suits against trustees for an accounting where multiple beneficiaries are interested. Therefore, the execution against the person was unauthorized, and the judgment for the plaintiff in the false imprisonment action was affirmed.

The President expresses gratitude for reelection and the confidence it shows, pledging to merit continued good opinion. He considers himself an instrument of the union displayed in the election, attributing it to the strength and stability of the Union. He states the propriety of a reelected President reviewing the past term's events to guide future policy.

The previous term began just after the War of 1812 ended, which had driven commerce from the sea, caused frontier invasions, immense loss of life, and added $120,000,000 to the public debt. In response, the nation reduced the land force to a peace establishment and provided for coastal fortifications and naval augmentation under laws of 1815 and 1816. A report shows these works would save expenses in the event of invasion by allowing a small regular force to detain an enemy at fortified points while militia collected, avoiding the need to spread forces along the entire coast. These measures, supported by the Navy, would present an armed front from St. Croix to the Sabine, protect the coast and interior, and preserve peace and order during other powers' wars. They were dictated by love of peace, economy, and a desire to save lives, and are believed to prevent war. Considerable progress has been made.

Regarding foreign powers, Europe had concluded peace after long wars, and U.S. peace with its former adversary was also concluded. The only remaining conflict was between Spain and its South American colonies. The predecessor considered this a civil war, granting equal rights in U.S. ports to both parties, a decision in accord with the law of nations. Congress maintained strict neutrality, affording no aid or exclusive privilege to either, and enforcing laws against illegal equipments equally. Public vessels of both were received on the same footing, and citizens traded equally with both. The President opines that neutrality should continue, though a change in Spain's government and ongoing negotiations may settle differences. Should war continue, the U.S. can adopt measures as honor and interest require.

After the general peace, adventurers engaged in buccaneering, evidenced by events at Amelia Island in 1817 and other parts of Florida in 1818. A decisive course was necessary. Many culprits were condemned to death for piracy. The Executive pardoned those led astray by ignorance, allowing the law to take effect only where no extenuating circumstances existed.

The late treaty with Spain, ratified by both parties, places relations on a basis of permanent friendship. It provides for citizens' claims and settles the western boundary. The acquisition of Florida is highly important: it secures valuable territory, opens river passages to the ocean for neighboring states, secures against Indian tribes, provides Gulf harbors for large warships, and covers the Mississippi and other waters, protecting Western produce.

A treaty with Britain in October 1818 revived and continued the commerce convention of 1815 for ten years, and adjusted differences under the treaty of Ghent regarding fishing rights and other interests. No agreement has been reached on commerce with British West Indies and continental dominions; restraints remain in force. Negotiation with France for commercial regulation has been transferred to Washington and will be pursued with conciliation. Relations with the Barbary Powers are maintained as before, with a squadron in the Mediterranean since 1801, except a short interval. Naval force is also maintained in the Pacific for commerce and fisheries, and used to suppress the slave trade and piracy.

The nation's resources and revenue are gratifying. Nearly $67,000,000 of public debt has been paid, and progress made in defense and improvements, all without burdening the people, as the direct tax and excise were repealed after the war. Resources remain untouched. However, a depression of prices has diminished revenue, compelling Congress to authorize loans for the last and present year. The President had recommended repeal of internal taxes in 1817, pledging to recommend their recurrence if exigencies required. If the revenue deficiency continues and appears permanent, the course is obvious: generally, current year demands should be met by current year revenue. Internal duties and excises, with corresponding imposts, could enhance prices, promote manufactures, and augment revenue without serious burdens.

Regarding Indian tribes, they have been treated as independent nations, which flattered pride, retarded improvement, and led to destruction as settlements pushed them westward. They have claims on the nation's magnanimity and justice. The President proposes that their sovereignty over vast territories cease, with each individual secured a competent portion of soil, and tribes granted reasonable equivalents vested in permanent funds for civil government, education, instruction in husbandry, and sustenance. He hopes Congress will digest a plan on these principles.

Europe is unsettled with increasing war prospects. The U.S. is unconnected with the causes and in amity with all powers. It will remain neutral in any contests, but will maintain neutral rights and seek redress for injuries in amity. Preparation for dangers is advisable, as peace is the best season for it.

Domestically, since independence forty-four years ago, the nation has realized favorable anticipations. The system of government has avoided defects of ancient republics: there is but one order, the people, whose power is transferred through representation to elected bodies and officers, with complete sovereignty in the people. No serious conflict has arisen between National and State Governments; defects have been remedied by argument and appeal to good sense. The system is expected to attain high perfection. Physical attainments include acquisition of the Mississippi and its tributaries, Louisiana, and the Floridas, giving uninterrupted sovereignty from St. Croix to the Sabine. New States have been admitted equally, population has augmented, and the nation comprises the dimensions and faculties of a great power with a government incapable of oppressing the people.

The President enters office with satisfaction in the assistance of enlightened citizens from the preceding term, confidence in the people's candor, and reliance on Almighty God.

This protocol describes a systematic review to assess the relationship between viral burden measures (e.g., serial rt-PCR Ct values) and the presence of replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 in viral culture among immunosuppressed solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients. The review will search LitCovid, medRxiv, Google Scholar, and the WHO Covid-19 database from November 2019 to December 31, 2021, using specified terms. Four reviewers will independently screen titles/abstracts and full texts. Included studies must report serial Ct or other viral burden data from nasopharyngeal specimens alongside viral culture results from transplant patients. Studies using only post-mortem or non-respiratory samples, or lacking viral culture, will be excluded. Data extraction will be performed in duplicate, and quality will be assessed using five criteria covering case diagnosis, patient characteristics, follow-up, PCR methods, and culture methods. Due to laboratory variability, data will not be pooled; a narrative synthesis with a summary estimate is planned. The review is funded by the NIHR Evidence Synthesis Working Group and the University of Calgary. Author competing interests are disclosed.

The speaker honors the murdered President's memory and pledges to profit by his example. The country enjoys prosperity, a fixed fiscal policy, and peaceful foreign relations. A 245-million-year-old fossil of a pregnant Dinocephalosaurus, a long-necked marine reptile, was unearthed in southwestern China. It shows the creature gave live birth, making it the first known viviparous archosauromorph, a group including birds, crocodilians and dinosaurs. The fish-eating reptile was about 13 feet long with a 5.5-foot neck, paddle-like flippers, and large canines. Its embryo, curled and facing forward, indicates it was not swallowed prey. Live birth allowed it to remain fully marine, avoiding land predators. It determined offspring sex genetically, like mammals and birds.

North Korea's defaulted debt, once seen as a turnaround opportunity, may become even less tradable after new sanctions. The country has around $1 billion in syndicated loans in default since the 1980s, repackaged in 1997 into NK Debt Corporation securities. Total debt including interest was estimated at $3 billion in 2013. Trading occurred from 2000, with prices rising to 14-18 cents on the dollar after Kim Jong-il's death in 2011, but the market froze in 2013 due to UN sanctions. Exotix Capital has not seen trades in three to four years. This week, fresh UN sanctions ban North Korean exports like coal and seafood, potentially cutting export revenue by a third. The Franklin Emerging Markets Debt Opportunities Fund held $15.5 million principal of the zero-coupon bonds, valued at $830,000 in 2013 after being acquired for over $3.1 million. Other frontier markets such as Cuba and Iran have also faced setbacks. Expert Charles Blitzer estimates interest arrears at 4-5 times principal and says North Korea has shown little interest in dealing with private creditors.

Researchers developed a modular, open-source framework for AI-driven, multi-modal synchrotron experiments, enabling synchronous X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) measurements across multiple beamlines. The system uses an ensemble of AI agents for data processing, dimensionality reduction (e.g., K-means clustering), Gaussian process regression, and Bayesian optimization to suggest measurements. Human-controlled adjudicators mediate agent requests, ensuring safety and user autonomy. The framework leverages Bluesky, Tiled, and queue-server infrastructure at NSLS-II. A digital twin of the diffraction workflow was created using a simulated Al-Li-Fe oxide combinatorial library. In silico campaigns showed that AI-driven mapping surpassed conventional geometric series and random sampling, achieving 98.9% model accuracy after collecting 5% of total possible measurements, compared to 95.9% and 96.6%, respectively. AI-driven measurements prioritized phase boundaries and rapidly changing regions. Real-world synchronous experiments on identical Al-Ni-Pt thin film combinatorial libraries at the PDF and BMM beamlines demonstrated successful inter-beamline communication, real-time data processing, and adaptive switching between autonomous and grid-based acquisition. Post-experiment analysis extracted composition from EXAFS and phase information from XRD, revealing FCC and FCT phases with compositional gradients. The framework supports collaborative human-AI operating modes, is extensible to other techniques, and aims to increase facility throughput for spatially heterogeneous samples.

Farmers State Bank of Craig sued Samuel J. Lydick on a $3,000 promissory note due six months after March 17, 1920. Lydick alleged the note was partial payment of a prior $5,000 note, that he received no consideration, and that he was fraudulently induced to buy stock in Missouri Valley Cattle Loan Company. He claimed Everett J. Martin, cashier and later president of the bank, participated in the fraud. The bank and Martin filed separate defenses. The trial court directed a verdict for the bank on Lydick’s cross-petition for affirmative relief. The jury found the bank was a holder in due course—purchaser for value, without notice, before maturity, in good faith—and returned a verdict for the bank. The jury also found for Martin on the fraud claims. A second count regarding a later stock purchase was withdrawn for lack of evidence. On appeal, the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed. It held the withdrawal of issues was proper, evidence supported the verdict, and instructions were correct. The main appellate argument was that the bank, as payee of a note made directly payable to it, could not be a holder in due course. The court rejected this, citing Bank of Commerce & Savings v. Randell, which held a payee who receives a negotiable instrument in good faith, for value, before maturity, without notice, from a holder not the maker, is a holder in due course. The court noted the jury found Martin was not a party to the fraud, so the bank lacked knowledge. The judgment was affirmed.

A federal judge ruled the 1991 Nirvana album cover of a naked baby is not child pornography. Spencer Elden sued; Judge Olguin found only nudity among factors like sexual suggestiveness, calling it akin to a family bathing photo. The suit was dismissed.

A Florida Museum of Natural History study found that blood-sucking lice that parasitize primates and humans have continuously hosted their vitamin-producing bacterial symbionts for at least 20–25 million years, aligning with the common ancestor of great apes and old world monkeys. The bacteria, which supply essential B-vitamins missing from blood, live in specialized cells and are passed from female lice to offspring. Researchers sequenced symbiont genomes from human, chimpanzee, gorilla, and red colobus monkey lice, revealing tiny genomes (530,000–570,000 base pairs) with extensive remodeling that clustered genes critical for symbiosis. The findings illuminate coevolution of lice, bacteria, and primates, and provide insights into bacterial genome evolution and mutualistic relationships.

This study investigated whether resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the nucleus accumbens (NAc) could predict the course of ADHD symptoms in 54 newly diagnosed adult patients. Baseline resting-state fMRI and clinical assessments using the Wender-Reimherr-Interview (WRI) were conducted at diagnosis (t1), with a follow-up approximately three years later (t2). Change in WRI scores (Δ WRI) was correlated with baseline NAc-FC. Medication status at t2 was also examined: 34 patients continued stimulant treatment, while 20 had discontinued due to non-response.

Results showed that higher symptom severity at t1 was associated with lower FC between the NAc and the right paracingulate gyrus. Long-term symptom improvement (Δ WRI) correlated with lower FC between the NAc and the right anterior insular cortex. When considering medication, a significant interaction emerged: in the treated group, higher FC between the NAc and the right posterior insula predicted better outcome, whereas in the non-responder group, higher FC predicted worse outcome. No significant motion differences were found between groups.

The findings suggest that FC patterns between the reward system and default mode and salience networks are linked to ADHD symptom course and medication response. Limitations include small sample size and the need for replication with task-based paradigms.

Let’s Grow Kids was a Vermont advocacy organization founded in 2015 by philanthropist Rick Davis with a planned 10-year sunset. Its goal was to create a permanent child care infrastructure and provide quality child care for every child. Davis recruited Aly Richards as leader, emphasizing the time-limited nature. The organization raised over $70 million, grew to 40 staff, and built momentum that supported Act 76, a 2023 law creating a near-universal child care program. Since the law, over 100 new child care programs opened, adding over 1,000 spaces, 230 educator jobs, and 4,000 more children qualified for tuition assistance. Let’s Grow Kids officially sunset on Oct. 3, 2024. Leaders said the deadline sharpened focus, accountability, and fundraising, enabling one-year capital gifts and faster pace. The sunset strategy prompted building infrastructure and partnerships for transition. Permanent organizations now handle financing, workforce, data, and advocacy. Staff dispersed to roles at First Children’s Finance, Vermont’s NAEYC, the state’s Child Development Division, and the new Let’s Grow Kids Action Network, a 501(c)(4) protecting Act 76 funding. Despite progress, child care is not fully universal; 80-90% of families are subsidy-eligible, and some still face hardship. Richards has been contacted by other states interested in replicating Vermont’s approach, and she emphasizes the sunset provision’s importance. Richards will chair the Action Network board after a break.

The Aedes aegypti mosquito, which spreads Zika, also caused a deadly yellow fever epidemic in Philadelphia in 1793. Hot, dry conditions and an influx of Caribbean refugees led to an outbreak. Symptoms included fever, pain, and jaundice, often fatal. Doctors like Benjamin Rush advised fleeing; about 5,000 people (over 10% of the population) died. Treatments like bloodletting and quarantines failed. Over a century later, the mosquito was identified as the vector. Public health measures and sanitation improvements followed, with the last North American outbreak in 1905. Today, yellow fever prevention advice resembles Zika recommendations: avoid standing water and mosquitoes. Brazil has faced a severe yellow fever outbreak since December 2016, with 326 confirmed cases and 220 deaths, threatening major cities. A highly effective (99%) vaccine, available since 1939, is recommended for endemic areas and travelers. Brazil requested millions of doses. Researchers at Penn are using the yellow fever vaccine as a foundation to develop Zika and Dengue vaccines, with DNA and mRNA candidates in trials. WHO recommends the yellow fever vaccine for travel to Brazil.

QoCGM is an open-source MATLAB tool for comprehensive continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data analysis. It processes preprocessed CGM data from CSV files containing timestamps and glucose values. The tool operates in two stages: preprocessing (removing duplicate timestamps, identifying missing periods using a tolerance around the expected sampling frequency, and interpolating gaps with Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomial) and deriving metrics. Users specify sampling frequency, tolerance, end-of-night hour, unit conversion flag, plotting flag, and missing data handling method (interpolation or removal). QoCGM outputs a CSV file of derived metrics.

Metrics are grouped into domains: basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, SD, CV, IQR, percentiles), time-in-range metrics (TIR 70–180 mg/dL, TITR 70–140 mg/dL, TBR1, TBR2, total TBR, TAR1, TAR2, total TAR), glycemic risk indicators (GRI Hypo, GRI Hyper, overall GRI, LBGI, HBGI, GRADE and its components), glycemic variability metrics (CONGA at 1h, 2h, 6h, 24h; MAGE; Mobility; Distance Traveled per Minute; day-to-day SD of mean glucose and TIR), glycemic control indicators (fasting glucose proxy, glucose management indicator, hypoglycemia events), and entropy/complexity (Multiscale Entropy, Multiscale Complexity Index). Basic statistics and TIR are calculated for whole day, daytime, and nighttime; other metrics use the complete signal. Day-to-day variation is provided for selected variables.

An example analysis used 7-day CGM data from 324 insulin-treated type 2 diabetes patients. Median glucose was 162 mg/dL, TIR 65%, CV 24%. Coefficient of determination (R²) analysis showed many metrics overlap, but some (day-to-day SD of TIR and mean, MCI, Mobility, DTpM) had low R² with others, indicating they capture unique information. Diurnal and nocturnal TIR metrics differed significantly. The tool is available on GitHub and aims to facilitate identification of clinically relevant CGM metrics.

Gulf Island Fabrication (GIFI) builds offshore platforms, offshore support vessels, wind turbine pedestals, and other complex steel structures through three divisions: Fabrication, Shipyards, and Services. The offshore support vessel market in the Gulf of Mexico is oversupplied, with 196 OSVs and only 21 active floaters, limiting new contracts. The company reported a fourth-quarter loss of $24.3 million on revenue of $37.3 million, driven by a $23.9 million loss from technical problems on two MPSVs built for Hornbeck Offshore, delaying delivery to 2019. Gulf Island had $43 million in outstanding billings and about $40 million in remaining costs for these vessels. A prior issue with two unaccepted OSVs was resolved. The company has drawn $10 million under a $40 million credit facility and describes its position as “no debt.” Its backlog includes the two MPSVs, eight brown water tugs, a research vessel, and an icebreaker-class vessel. It was selected as prime contractor for the SeaOne Caribbean Fuels Supply Project, expected to start mid-2018, and received a memorandum of understanding from EEW for an offshore wind project. Following a share price drop, market capitalization fell to roughly $120 million. Gulf Island is selling non-core Texas facilities: a purchase option agreement with Buckeye Pipe Line for the South Yard at $55 million, with due diligence ending no later than April 25, 2018, and the North Yard also for sale. The book value of these facilities and equipment is about $100 million, implying the remaining business is valued at approximately $30 million.

Sarasota County petitioned for a writ of certiorari to review a declaratory statement issued by the Department of Administration. The County had sought to have a proposed crude oil splitter in Manatee County considered a development of regional impact (DRI) under Chapter 380, the Florida Environmental Land and Water Management Act of 1972. The Department’s declaratory statement concluded that the DRI definition is limited to projects described in Florida Administrative Code Rule 22F-2, and the splitter was not among those presumed to be a DRI. The court denied the petition, holding that Sarasota County lacked standing to seek judicial review. The majority opinion found that the County is not among the entities authorized to initiate the DRI process under Chapter 380—it is not a developer, regional planning agency, appropriate local government, or state planning agency. The court noted the County could petition those entities. Chief Judge Boardman concurred specially, suggesting the County could proceed through its regional planning agency or under the Florida Environmental Protection Act. Judge Scheb dissented, arguing the declaratory statement was final agency action subject to review and that the Department’s interpretation unduly restricted the legislative intent by limiting DRI determinations to the listed presumptions.

A model of immune waning and boosting was inferred directly from clinical endpoints by fitting to national-level vaccine effectiveness estimates from England for Delta and Omicron variants. Immunity level (IL) over time was modeled as a biphasic exponential decay, and a logistic function related IL to protection against mild disease, hospitalization, and death. Data covered AZD1222, BNT162b2, and mRNA-1273 vaccines in adults >65 years. A 6.5-fold (95% CrI 4.8–8.9) reduction in IL against Omicron relative to Delta was estimated. The initial fast decay half-life was 33 days (95% CrI 29–37), and the subsequent slow decay half-life was 580 days (95% CrI 415–755). At 180 days post-boost, estimated effectiveness against Omicron hospitalization was 49.5% for AZD1222, 69.8% for mRNA-1273, and 63.7% for BNT162b2; at 365 days, 38.9%, 60.0%, and 53.3%, respectively. Using immunogenicity data, a bivalent vaccine (mRNA.1273.214) showed a 1.61-fold increase in neutralizing antibody titres against BA.1, yielding predicted hospitalization effectiveness of 77.9% at 365 days versus 60.0% for the original mRNA-1273. Applying fold reductions from immunogenicity data to the earlier Khoury et al. model gave more pessimistic predictions than fitting to clinical data, possibly due to broader immune responses. Limitations include inability to separate infection- and vaccine-induced immunity, absence of direct immunological measurements, and challenges in attributing hospitalizations/deaths to COVID-19.

A survey of 2,000 British adults by Tweak Mattress found the average Brit wakes three times a night, with one in ten waking 7-10 times. Top reasons for sleep disruption include needing the toilet (47%), snoring (41%), being edged out by a partner (25%), discomfort (19%), bad dreams (11%), tossing and turning (10.5%), bedroom talk (10%), phone light (10%), anxiety (6%), and a partner watching TV/reading (4.6%). Psychologist Robert Stewart attributes sleep quality to sleep hygiene (avoiding food/drink before bed, consistent sleep times, no screens in bed) and sleep cycles, noting REM sleep is the lightest stage. He recommends a comfortable environment, such as earplugs or a good mattress.

Rachael Caplan, 29, suffers from Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), a rare disease causing constant excruciating pain that leaves her bedridden and confined to her parents’ home; she hasn’t been outside since August 2016. Previously athletic with a law degree, she worked in family law before CRPS spread. Dr. David Shulman, a pain specialist, says CRPS begins like an autoimmune disease and after six months becomes a neurological condition with nerve injury, causing burning, shooting, or tingling pain like a constantly banged funny bone. It affects over 9,000 people annually in Canada, over half in Ontario. Helen Small founded PARC in 2002 to promote awareness and reduce isolation. Symptoms include intense pain spreading from a hand or foot, swelling, temperature/colour changes, brittle bones, altered hair/nail growth; triggers include trauma, injury, stroke, infection, or casting. Her symptoms began seven years ago with a hip injury, worsened after acupuncture, and took 1.5 years to diagnose; Dr. Shulman diagnosed her on her 26th birthday in June 2013. Early diagnosis is critical: 80–90% treatment success in first three months, possible reversal within six months, afterward only symptom management. Prognosis is poor: constant pain causes insomnia, memory loss, depression, disability, and shortened lifespan. A severe case, Caplan found physiotherapy and opioids worsened her pain; she consulted about 60 providers and traveled to the U.S. Green light therapy recently alleviated head pain and allowed up to nine hours of sleep. Despite her condition, she remains positive with family and friends’ support. Friends run a Facebook page and launched an ice-water challenge with hashtag #AceThisFire to mimic CRPS pain, gaining over 20,000 views. Caplan hopes sharing her story leads to quicker diagnoses, more treatments, or a cure, and she aspires to remission and simple pleasures.

Larry Connors’ R3 strategy, from his 2009 book 'High Probability ETF Trading,' is a mean-reversion strategy. Its rules: close above 200-day MA, 2-day RSI drops three consecutive days with first drop from below 60, enter when 2-day RSI <10, exit when >70. Backtesting on ETFs from inception to Dec 2020 could not fully replicate Connors’ results (fewer fills). About 50% of strategies performed worse in the last 12 years. SPY had a 90% win ratio over 79 trades since 1993. A portfolio of all 25 ETFs (2000–2020, max 5 positions, 20% equity each) produced 992 trades, 75% win ratio, 0.68% avg gain, profit factor 2.08, max drawdown -16% (Aug 2011), CAGR 6.47%. A Nasdaq/S&P 500 portfolio (50% each) had profit factor 3.37, CAGR 2.69%, low market exposure 4.5%. The R3 strategy still works, best on equity markets, and may be improved.

Despite a Western military decision, the disputed belt will likely remain within German lines. Germany's Near East supremacy is her victory, and the Reichstag Resolution's acceptance rests on this. The blockade is a difficulty; the Near East, even with Russia, is an inchoate empire needing a generation of peace. Two German imperialist schools, the Fatherland Party and Kühlmann-Helfferich groups, both seek eastern domination and outer supplies, but disagree: Kühlmann favors Western accommodation, the Fatherland Party demands military force and retention of Belgium. Belgium is the pivot; controlling it would leave France at Germany's mercy by preventing English landings.

A study investigated the effects of COVID-19 mRNA booster vaccination (BNT162b2) on glucose control and insulin sensitivity. In a longitudinal clinical trial, 155 adults who had received two prior doses were assessed before and two weeks after a booster. Diabetic and pre-diabetic subjects exhibited similar immune responses (SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, IgG antibodies, neutralizing ability) to healthy controls. However, pre-diabetic and diabetic patients showed exacerbated risks of glucose intolerance and insulin resistance after the booster, with significant elevations in HbA1c, HOMA-IR, triglyceride, and TyG index. Fasting blood glucose and insulin levels did not change significantly. About 61.1% of diabetic subjects had impaired insulin sensitivity per HOMA-IR, and 66.7% had increased cardiovascular risk per TyG. HOMA-IR positively correlated with immune response markers.

In mice, weekly mRNA vaccination for four weeks led to impaired glucose tolerance (OGTT) and reduced insulin sensitivity (ITT), with decreased insulin-induced Akt phosphorylation in liver and muscle. Serum triglyceride increased, but fasting blood glucose, insulin, and body weight were unchanged. Metformin, administered at a clinically relevant dosage, alleviated vaccine-induced insulin resistance in mice, improving OGTT and ITT indexes and rescuing insulin signaling, without affecting SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, spike IgG, or neutralizing antibody levels.

The discussion notes that booster shots weakened insulin sensitivity in pre-diabetic and diabetic patients, providing a causal link between COVID-19 vaccines and insulin resistance. Potential mechanisms include spike protein affecting insulin signaling via TLR4 and ER, and systemic immune responses. The study suggests that individuals with impaired glucose tolerance should monitor blood glucose after vaccination, and that metformin may serve as an adjunctive treatment to maintain glucose control post-vaccination.

Six Texas public university systems are reviewing curricula, syllabi, and course descriptions after conservative politicians targeted faculty teaching gender identity. Following criticism of a children's literature lesson on gender identity, Texas A&M's flagship campus audited all courses, and the system's Board of Regents extended the audit systemwide for legal compliance. The University of North Texas system ordered an expedited syllabus review due Jan. 1 to ensure compliance with laws and executive orders. The University of Texas system is reviewing all gender-identity courses for alignment with regents' priorities and law. System leaders cited an executive order declaring only two sexes, though no laws prohibit teaching transgender identity. The University of Houston system is reviewing general education courses under a five-year review law, and Texas Woman's University is reviewing all programs, with oral policies limiting gender-identity instruction and erasing transgender topics. It is unclear whether courses will be censored or removed. Faculty representatives argue political dictation harms education and teaching gender requires acknowledging diverse identities. Conservative politicians used public syllabi to target professors. Many institutions use Simple Syllabus; Texas law requires public syllabi with certain details, so some universities allow public viewing. A UH lecturer was targeted after a conservative site found his courses via Simple Syllabus keyword search. While privacy features exist, faculty are now encouraged to detail syllabi thoroughly to avoid complaints.

A prospective study compared 101 cardiomyopathy patients (43 with dilated cardiomyopathy, 58 with other cardiomyopathies) to 101 healthy controls. Blood concentrations of C-reactive protein (CRP) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) were significantly higher in cardiomyopathy patients. In these patients, TNF-α showed positive correlations with glutathione peroxidase (GPX) and malondialdehyde (MDA). NT-proBNP was positively associated with MDA and GPX activity. Interleukin-6 did not significantly correlate with GPX. The findings indicate correlations between inflammatory and oxidative stress markers in cardiomyopathy patients, suggesting cross-talk between these processes in late-stage cardiomyopathy.

Sheikh Humaid bin Rashid Al Nuaimi issued a decree reducing Ajman's tourism tax from 10% to 7% for hotels and tourism companies, effective immediately until December 31, to promote tourism and improve investment.

This statistical analysis plan describes a multicenter study comparing dasiglucagon 0.6 mg versus placebo, with GlucaGen® as a reference. The primary endpoint is time to plasma glucose recovery (≥20 mg/dL increase from baseline within 45 minutes without rescue IV glucose). Sample size: 20 patients randomized to dasiglucagon, 10 to placebo, and 10 to GlucaGen, providing 90% power for a log-rank test at a 2-sided 5% significance level.

Analyses will be performed using SAS 9.4 or higher and Phoenix WinNonlin for PK/PD. The primary efficacy analysis uses the full analysis set (FAS) with a stratified log-rank test (age group and injection site as strata). A hierarchical testing procedure controls multiplicity for primary and secondary endpoints. Secondary endpoints include recovery rates at 10, 15, 20, and 30 minutes and plasma glucose changes from baseline at those times, analyzed via Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel tests and ANOVA. Sensitivity analyses include alternative censoring rules and linear interpolation of recovery times. A Cox proportional hazards model is used descriptively.

Safety analyses are based on the safety analysis set (all randomized patients receiving at least one dose). Treatment-emergent adverse events are summarized by MedDRA system organ class and preferred term. Other safety assessments include local tolerability, laboratory parameters, vital signs, ECG (including QTcF categorical analyses), and immunogenicity (ADA incidence). Pharmacokinetic parameters (Cmax, AUC, etc.) are derived by non-compartmental analysis. Pharmacodynamic analysis includes AUE0-30min. Data handling rules for concentrations below LLOQ are specified. All statistical tests are 2-sided at the 0.05 level. No interim analyses are planned. The SAP also details conventions for tables, listings, figures, and programming quality control.

At Huntington University Hospital (HUH), approximately 71% of patients undergoing aortic valve replacement (AVR) or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) received blood transfusions between 2011 and 2013, exceeding the national average of 48.9%. Transfusions were associated with reduced long-term survival. Dr. Frank Young, who joined HUH in 2011, proposed a blood conservation project to cut blood product use by two-thirds within one year, aiming to reach the national average, save $2.5 million annually, and save 125 lives over 10 years. Challenges included physician autonomy, Young’s newcomer status, and a complex organizational structure: surgical team members (nurses, perfusionists, anesthesiologists) reported through separate chains, giving Young no formal authority. HUH, a major teaching hospital, had a Center for Cardiac Medicine with seven surgeons performing over 900 heart surgeries yearly. In 2013, a Committee for Operational Excellence was formed to improve quality and reduce costs under value-based purchasing. Young chaired a sub-committee that found 51% of cardiac patients had bleeding complications, and AVR/CABG transfusion rates averaged 65% in 2013. Direct bleeding-related costs were nearly $8 million, half from cardiac surgery. Young identified techniques like autologous blood harvest and retrograde autologous priming. The Chief Medical Officer appointed Young to lead the project. Supporters included an ICU director and various staff; skeptics were veteran surgeons reluctant to alter routines. Young faced decisions on how to persuade colleagues and sustain changes.

The speaker emphasizes drawing on experience from past big games, maintaining good habits and work ethic, and playing the same way despite higher stakes. Phlogopite, a dark mica with a layered monoclinic structure, is susceptible to ionizing radiation and used in geological dating and studied for radionuclide waste storage. The hybrid code XTANT-3, combining tight-binding molecular dynamics, transport Monte Carlo, and Boltzmann collision integrals, simulates its response to electronic excitation. Simulations with a 92 eV, 10 fs laser pulse reveal damage thresholds: at ~0.17 eV/atom (Te~11,000 K), hydrogen detaches and migrates, matching experimental β/γ irradiation damage at ~0.2 eV/atom. Nonadiabatic electron-phonon coupling increases the damage threshold compared to Born-Oppenheimer simulations. At ~0.4 eV/atom, Mg atoms diffuse while other sublattices remain solid, forming a superionic state. At ~0.5 eV/atom, the entire lattice disorders; at ~0.9 eV/atom, the bandgap collapses, producing a metallic liquid. At ~2 eV/atom, nonthermal acceleration selectively heats K and O on femtosecond timescales. The study identifies various transient states and provides damage threshold fluences for future X-ray experiments.

The lecture covers utility from beliefs, focusing on anticipatory utility and its influence on information acquisition. People may avoid negative information (e.g., Huntington’s disease risk) to maintain positive beliefs, as utility can be derived from looking forward to good outcomes. A model with correct beliefs conditional on information shows that the shape of the utility-from-beliefs function determines information aversion (concave) or love (convex). If beliefs could be freely chosen, individuals would set the probability of being healthy to 1, but reasons to resist overoptimism include the need for optimal actions when outcomes are belief-dependent, potential disappointment when reality contradicts high expectations, and the trade-off between current happiness and future letdown.

Evidence of overoptimism includes Weinstein’s study, where students rated positive life events as more likely and negative events as less likely for themselves than for peers. Other examples: couples underestimate divorce, business owners overestimate success, smokers exempt themselves from health risks. Overconfidence in abilities is widespread (e.g., 99% of drivers, 94% of professors). MIT students, however, show under-confidence, especially women, possibly due to frequent feedback or motivation from worry. Ego utility—feeling good now—also drives inflated beliefs. Positive illusions may promote mental health, while “depressive realism” could be harmful. Biases are larger for personally important traits, reduced by objective feedback, and increased by ambiguity, perceived control, and expertise without clear feedback.

Lab experiments (Eil and Rao) show asymmetric updating: people incorporate positive feedback about IQ or attractiveness roughly Bayesianly but discount negative feedback, and they pay more for information expected to be positive. Memory favors positive signals (Zimmermann). Real-world evidence includes excessive trading by overconfident investors (Barber and Odean) and value-destroying mergers by overconfident managers (Malmendier and Tate).

Bayesian updating is hard, so people use heuristics. Three systematic deviations: gambler’s fallacy (expecting reversal after a streak in independent draws), hot-hand fallacy (expecting streak continuation), both explained by belief in the law of small numbers; and base-rate neglect (underweighting prior probabilities, as in the HIV test problem). Two-dimensional learning (assessing information and source accuracy) is even harder; attention matters more than partisanship for fake news discernment.

Kahneman and Tversky’s heuristics include representativeness (conjunction fallacy in the Linda problem) and availability (judging frequency by ease of recall, e.g., overestimating homicides vs. suicides). Different sources of misinformation—limited attention, wrong theories, motivated beliefs, faulty updating—imply different policies. Making information salient helps if people overlook it; correcting theories aids if they misunderstand. But if people derive utility from biased beliefs, providing information may be ignored or reduce welfare, as it could diminish happiness without enabling beneficial action.
