In Phase 1, some participants had a temporary drop in lymphocytes 1–3 days after Dose 1 of BNT162b1 or BNT162b2, which returned to normal by 6–8 days; no low lymphocytes were seen 6–8 days after Dose 2. Injection site reactions (redness, swelling, pain) and systemic events (fever, tiredness, headache, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle/joint pain) within 7 days were common, mostly mild or moderate, and well tolerated. Pain was the most common injection site reaction; tiredness and headache were the most common systemic events. Within 1 month after Dose 2, most medical problems were mild or moderate. In Phase 1, no single medical problem occurred in more than 2 participants per dose group; BNT162b1 100 µg was stopped after Dose 1 due to injection site reactions or systemic events. BNT162b2 30 µg was selected for Phase 2/3. In Phase 2/3, fewer than 1% of participants left due to medical problems (32 of 21,926 BNT162b2, 36 of 21,921 placebo). Commonly reported medical problems included nausea (1% BNT162b2, <1% placebo). Serious medical problems were infrequent. In Phase 1, two BNT162b2 recipients had serious problems (inflamed appendix, inflamed nerves) not attributed to the vaccine. In Phase 2/3, a few serious problems were considered possibly related to BNT162b2 (e.g., numbness/tingling, portal vein clot, mini stroke). No single serious problem occurred in ≥1% of any group. Deaths in Phase 2/3: 85 of 23,141 in the BNT162b2 group, 62 of 21,371 in placebo-then-BNT162b2, and 23 of 23,141 in placebo-only; none were attributed to the vaccine. No deaths occurred in Phase 1 or among BNT162b2SA recipients.

Researchers have developed a topological insulator laser that overcomes common laser problems such as efficiency loss from defects and the emergence of unwanted colors or beam distortion at higher power. The concept originates from topological insulators, where electrons in surface states are protected from scattering because their spin is locked to their direction of motion; reversing direction requires a spin flip, which is energetically difficult in an insulator. This allows electrons to flow with minimal resistance along the surface despite defects. Applying this idea to lasers, the researchers constructed a photonic topological insulator using rings of optical waveguides made from a material that emits light when excited. By exciting only the outer rings, light is forced to travel along the edge. The protected state is created through the precise arrangement of intermediary rings that shift the phase of light as it leaks between waveguides, ensuring that light can only be scattered out if it changes color. Unprotected light is quickly scattered away, leaving only the protected light to be amplified by the gain material. Experimental comparisons between lasers with protected and unprotected edge states showed that the topological insulator laser remains operational even when rings are removed, is more efficient, and maintains a single color and beam profile as power increases, unlike the unprotected version. Accurate modeling and tight fabrication tolerances were essential to the design. These lasers, with their stable, well-defined wavelength and spatial profile, are critical for applications such as 5G networks and space-based interferometers and may soon transition from the lab to high-end use.

The lecture discusses neutral particle diagnostics for measuring the ion distribution function in the core of a tokamak, where ions are confined and cannot be directly sampled. Existing diagnostics like electron cyclotron emission, laser-induced fluorescence, and Thomson scattering provide electron temperature or distribution, not ion information. The proposed solution is to exploit core ions that spontaneously become neutrals, which then escape and can be detected, carrying information about the original ion distribution.

Two main challenges are addressed: neutral production and neutral transport. Neutral production can occur via charge exchange with edge neutrals (passive) or with an injected neutral beam (active). Radiative recombination is negligible because rapid re-ionization keeps the steady-state neutral fraction extremely low. Neutral transport involves re-ionization processes—electron impact ionization, ion impact ionization, and charge exchange with ions—that attenuate the escaping neutrals. For a 10 keV neutral in a dense plasma, the mean free path is about 10 cm, so the diagnostic requires a low line-integrated density (below 10^19 m^-2) for neutrals to reach the detector.

Passive charge exchange with edge neutrals yields a line-integrated measurement of the core ion energy distribution. A stripping cell and magnetic spectrometer produce an energy spectrum; the Maxwellian slope gives the ion temperature, and deviations at high energy reveal fast-ion tails.

Active charge exchange using a neutral beam localizes the measurement to the intersection of the beam and detector sightline. This enables charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) on impurity ions: the beam donates an electron to fully stripped impurities, which then emit characteristic photons. From the line intensity, shift, and broadening, one obtains localized impurity density, flow velocity, and ion temperature. Beam modulation helps separate the signal from Bremsstrahlung background.

Beam emission spectroscopy (BES) observes collisional excitation of the neutral beam atoms. The emitted line intensity is proportional to local electron density, so fluctuations in intensity reflect density fluctuations, providing a localized measure of turbulent transport, though beam attenuation must be accounted for.

Finally, the motional Stark effect (MSE) uses the electric field (V × B) experienced by fast beam neutrals to split energy levels. Measuring the splitting and polarization of Balmer-alpha transitions yields the magnetic field magnitude and direction, enabling reconstruction of the poloidal field and current profile.

In late 2004, Walt Bernstein, director of production control for Toyota Motor Manufacturing’s Macon, Georgia (TMMGA) operation, was frustrated with supplier ChassisCo's Athens plant. The plant was producing rear suspension cradles for the new Suprima crossover vehicle at barely 60% of the standard production rate, with frequently nonconforming parts and insufficient problem-tracking ability, despite Toyota deploying extensive support resources.

The 2003 Suprima launch represented a significant increase in responsibility for ChassisCo compared to the 1997 model, including sourcing all 85 parts and managing incoming logistics. The new cradle was more complex, and automation increased from 13 to 102 robots. ChassisCo faced internal challenges, including a decentralized organization that dissipated experienced staff, an unprecedented number of global launches that stretched engineering resources thin, and a lack of project management skills and processes. ChassisCo did not communicate that Toyota's aggressive target price was unrealistic, leading to decisions like accepting low bids from inexperienced parts suppliers and underestimating logistics costs.

Toyota personnel later realized they had underestimated the capability gap and failed to recognize how much more support ChassisCo needed, particularly with parts and tool tuning processes and second-tier supplier development. The launch proceeded on time in September 2003 despite the Athens plant failing the required high volume production trial three times. Throughout 2004, quality concerns persisted, with assembly-critical weld problems and a significant increase in external defects reaching TMMGA. The Athens plant manager stated the plant was "bleeding money" and needed a price increase, while Bernstein insisted the underlying quality problems had to be fixed, noting that TMMGA's resources were taxed to the limit.

Radiotheranostics enables personalized cancer treatment, but current regimens are often standardized. Computational nuclear oncology (CNO) uses theranostic digital twins (TDTs) and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models to enable personalized, dosimetry-driven planning. PBPK models incorporate patient physiology and drug properties to estimate pharmacokinetics and absorbed doses. The reliability of these models depends on rigorous verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ). Verification ensures the model is built correctly. Validation, including internal goodness-of-fit assessment and external prediction evaluation, confirms the model describes patient biokinetics for its intended use. Uncertainty quantification characterizes prediction variability. Extending PBPK models to dynamic TDTs introduces further VVUQ challenges due to continuous data integration. Establishing clear VVUQ frameworks is needed to support regulatory approval and clinical translation of PBPK models in radiopharmaceutical therapies.

The Clock offense is a simple 1-3-1 free lance passing attack with basic rotation rules, effective against both person-to-person and zone defenses. It emphasizes sharp ball movement to create outside shots, basket cuts, and post rolls. The name comes from outside players' clockwise and counterclockwise rotations.

On a corner pass, the wing cuts to the basket for a return pass; if the defender helps, the corner feeds the post. Ball reversal involves swinging the ball quickly to attack the weakside, with options to hit the cutter or post. The dribble clear option allows the wing to dribble to the corner while the corner back cuts, exchanging roles. Continuity: the wing can pass to the corner and cut, dribble clear, or make a reversal pass; the baseline shooter may cut to the opposite corner.

Against a 1-3-1 zone, the offense exploits baseline weakness with the same corner pass and ball reversal reads. Against a 1-2-2 zone, it attacks the vulnerable middle and corners. When double-teamed in the corner, the "Cat" counter rotates into a 2-1-2 alignment with sharp passes, and rules include the post rolling to the basket on a baseline corner pass and baseline corners back cutting on a middle entry. Crunch time specials: "Vegas" uses a double screen away for a skip pass shot, and "Back" is a weakside lob play with a back screen.

The Turing TU102 GPU is the highest-performing Turing GPU, featuring 6 GPCs, 36 TPCs, and 72 SMs. Each SM contains 64 CUDA Cores, 8 Tensor Cores, 256 KB register file, 4 texture units, 96 KB configurable L1/shared memory, and one RT Core for ray tracing acceleration. TU102 includes 12 32-bit GDDR6 memory controllers (384-bit), 96 ROPs, and 6144 KB L2 cache. It also has 144 FP64 units (two per SM) for FP64 code compatibility. Two second-generation NVLink x8 links provide 100 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth.

The Turing SM supports concurrent execution of FP32 and INT32 operations, independent thread scheduling, and is partitioned into four processing blocks, each with 16 FP32 Cores, 16 INT32 Cores, two Tensor Cores, a warp scheduler, dispatch unit, L0 instruction cache, and 64 KB register file. The unified L1 data cache/shared memory can be configured as 64 KB L1/32 KB shared memory or vice versa. Turing adds a parallel integer execution unit, yielding approximately 36% additional floating-point throughput. L2 cache capacity is doubled compared to Pascal, and memory compression improvements deliver a 50% effective bandwidth increase. GDDR6 memory operates at 14 Gbps with 20% power efficiency improvement over GDDR5X.

Turing Tensor Cores add INT8 and INT4 precision modes for inference. TU102 contains 576 Tensor Cores; each performs up to 64 FP16 FMA operations per clock, with INT8 at double that rate. The Tesla T4 (TU104) includes 2,560 CUDA Cores and 320 Tensor Cores, delivering up to 130 TOPS INT8 and 260 TOPS INT4, with up to 40X higher inference performance and 50X energy efficiency versus CPUs.

The display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, 8K at 60 Hz with DSC 1.2, HDR, and tone mapping. The NVENC encoder adds HEVC 8K encode at 30 fps with bitrate savings; the NVDEC decoder supports HEVC 4:4:4 and VP9 10/12-bit. VirtualLink provides a single USB-C connector for VR headsets, carrying power, display, and data. NVLink replaces MIO/PCIe for SLI, enabling two-way SLI and advanced display topologies.

RT Cores accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, offloading the SM and enabling real-time ray tracing. Hybrid rendering combines rasterization and ray tracing. Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) uses Tensor Cores to infer high-quality images from lower sample counts, improving performance. NGX Neural Services provide AI-based features including InPainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez.

Mesh Shading introduces task and mesh shaders with a cooperative thread model, reducing CPU draw call bottlenecks and supporting dynamic level-of-detail. Variable Rate Shading (VRS) allows per-16x16-pixel region shading rate control for content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering. Texture Space Shading (TSS) decouples shading from screen space, storing results in texture space for reuse and temporal stability. Multi-View Rendering (MVR) supports up to four views per pass, expanding Pascal’s Simultaneous Multi-Projection for VR and cascaded shadow maps. Resource binding supports bindless Constant Buffer Views and Unordered Access Views (Tier 3) and resource heaps (Tier 2).

TU104 GPU has 6 GPCs, 48 SMs, 8 memory controllers (256-bit), 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, and one NVLink x8 link. TU106 GPU has 3 GPCs, 36 SMs, 8 memory controllers (256-bit), 2304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, 36 RT Cores, and no NVLink. The RTX-OPS metric combines peak operations of Tensor, FP32, RT, and INT32 units weighted by typical hybrid rendering workload distribution. Ray tracing overview describes reverse ray casting, BVH acceleration structures, and denoising. Ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections provide physically correct effects, overcoming limitations of traditional techniques.

This paper proposes a theory-driven framework for evaluating and improving the persuasive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), grounded in Bayesian persuasion. It conceptualizes LLM persuasiveness as a Sender's ability to strategically reveal information to shift a Receiver's beliefs favorably. The authors repurpose human-human persuasion datasets to create environments where both Sender and Receiver are LLMs, validated by a human study with 45 participants. Experiments with frontier models show that stronger models like DeepSeek-R1 achieve higher persuasion gains and exhibit adaptive information revelation. The paper also uses reinforcement learning to train LLMs for strategic persuasion, finding that even small models can be trained to match large models, with improvements transferring across Receiver architectures. Key contributions include a principled measurement framework, concrete evaluation and training environments, and empirical evidence that frontier models possess strong persuasive capabilities that can be enhanced via reinforcement learning. The paper also provides background on Bayesian persuasion, defines persuasion gains and signals as metrics, and develops a benchmark for opinion-change tasks.

A variable multiplexer for vehicle communication bus compatibility is disclosed. Vehicles use a communication bus (e.g., CAN bus) with a data link connector for external devices. Although the connector is standardized, pinout configurations (pin-to-function mappings) vary among manufacturers, necessitating different cables. An external device includes a variable multiplexer that can be electronically configured to a desired pinout configuration, allowing a single cable to be used across vehicles. The device determines the pinout configuration by: (1) sending a vehicle identifier (e.g., VIN) to a remote computing system that uses a vehicle data index to return the configuration; (2) entering a listening mode to gather bus data, then comparing received data at each pin to known pinout configurations to identify a consistent one, including determining enabled/disabled pin sets and, if multiple matches, analyzing a pin with differing functions; or (3) using checksum values transmitted with data blocks—generating a checksum from received data using the same algorithm and comparing it to the transmitted checksum for various known configurations until a match is found. The device has a connection detection component, a pinout configuration determination component, and a pinout configuration modification component that commands the variable multiplexer to adopt the determined configuration.

The passage describes patterns for building distributed systems with containers, emphasizing modularity, reuse, and shared vocabulary. Single-node patterns group containers on one machine: the sidecar pattern augments an application container (e.g., adding HTTPS, configuration synchronization, monitoring); the ambassador pattern brokers interactions between the application and external services (e.g., sharded service access, service brokering, request splitting); the adapter pattern standardizes interfaces (e.g., monitoring, logging, health checks). Multi-node patterns include replicated load-balanced services for stateless services, which can incorporate session tracking, caching layers (Varnish), and SSL termination (nginx). Sharded services address stateful services where data exceeds a single machine’s capacity, using sharding functions to map requests to shards based on a key; key selection must balance grouping identical requests without over-generalizing. Hands-on examples deploy these patterns using Kubernetes.

A defensive wall in soccer is a shoulder-to-shoulder line of defenders placed 10 yards from a free kick to block part of the goal, typically when the ball is near the penalty area. It becomes important around age 12 when players can shoot accurately. The wall blocks roughly half the goal, cutting the near-side angle while the goalkeeper covers the far side, increasing reaction time.

Law 13 governs free kicks: the ball must be stationary and kicked to be in play; defenders must be at least 10 yards away unless on the goal line. Attackers may take a quick free kick (QFK) immediately; if they choose a ceremonial free kick (CFK), they may ask the referee to move the wall back. Referees are not obligated to allow time to build a wall and should caution players who delay the restart. When three or more defenders form a wall, attackers must stay at least 1 yard away.

The goalkeeper decides whether to build a wall, based on ball location and personal judgment, and calls the number of players. The number depends on distance and angle: closer and more central spots require more players (two near the end lines, up to five or more directly in front). The first player, the anchor, positions on an imaginary line from the near post to the ball, 10 yards out. The goalkeeper (or a designated wall setter positioned beyond the ball) directs the anchor left or right by steps until centered, then says “hold.” Other wall players fill in shoulder-to-shoulder by height, facing the ball, with no gaps wider than a ball. Players may protect genitals or breasts, jump vertically, but must not turn, rush, or handle the ball. A defender may lie behind the wall to block low shots.

A non-traditional method uses a wall setter beyond the ball to position the anchor, freeing the goalkeeper to watch the ball and prepare for a quick kick. In the rare case of an indirect free kick less than 10 yards from goal, defenders stand on the goal line between the posts; the tallest faces the ball, others fill to the near post. Coaching tips include using a rope to demonstrate angles, keeping the wall just large enough, warning against delaying tactics, and practicing against set plays.

The Reverse Action Offense was introduced by Hall of Fame Coach Pete Newell in the late 1950s. It features a basic guard around continuity that is difficult to defend due to precise execution and footwork. The most recognizable option is the weakside wing's rub cut off a post screen to the basket, but the offense also provides a strong post-up game, a two-player guard around isolation, and numerous quick-hitting counters against defensive overplays.

In the basic continuity, O1 passes to wing O3 and cuts to the corner. If no shot is available, weakside wing O4 makes a rub cut off O5 to the basket. O2 moves to the center for a possible reverse pass. If O4 does not receive the ball, O3 reverses to O2, who passes to O5 stepping out. O5 and O2 execute a guard around cut, O1 moves to the center, and O3 rubs off O4's screen. Continuity continues with a reversal pass to O1.

The key is patience and execution of off-ball post screens, requiring the passer, screener, and receiver to function as one unit with proper footwork, timing, and non-verbal communication. Reads for the reverse action cut: if the defender plays low, the cutter fakes low and cuts over the top; if the defender plays high, the cutter fakes high and cuts baseline; if the post defender shows and recovers, the screener pops; if the defense switches, the screener dives.

Entries do not rely on a single pass. Weakside entries initiate guard around action from O4 or O3 stepping out. Strongside entries use a guard around cut to initiate sideline triangle action, with a reversal pass if no shot. Dribble clear entry uses a back cut when the wing is overplayed. Back door entry involves a flash to the middle and back cut, with a lob pass option if denied.

Guard around action is a two-player game with reads: if the defender chases over, drive; if weakside defenders sag, drive and kick; if the defender goes under, pull-up jumper; if the defender cheats over early, drive opposite; if defenders switch, roll and post up; if the defense shows and recovers, slip.

Sideline triangle action creates post isolation and options: lob pass against a fronting defender, high post feed, post split (baseline cut and tight cut off the post), post split corner feed, post split screen option, high post split, post isolation with clearing cuts, post sag counter (wing drives), double team counter (weakside dive and kick-out).

Post isolation requires reading the defender's position relative to the "line of deployment." High side denial: power lay-up or corner feed. Baseline side denial: baby hook or point feed. Behind: turn and face triple threat (jump shot, pump fake and drive, step back). Front: lob or ball reversal. Double team: pressure release to elbow or short corner.

Overplays are countered with back cuts: wing back cut, back door cut with flash, lob pass, skip pass, and corner give-and-go. Corner pass reads mirror guard around reads with drive, kick-out, pull-up, drive opposite, roll, and slip options. Crunch time specials include weakside screen and roll, double screen, and back screen lob.

The reverse play is a deceptive football trick play where the ball is run in one direction, then handed to a player running the opposite way. In a traditional reverse, the quarterback hands off to a running back or receiver moving behind him, who then tosses the ball to a wide receiver crossing in the opposite direction, often starting late to disguise the play. An example from the 2018 Panthers vs. Buccaneers shows Cam Newton tossing to DJ Moore, who then handed to Curtis Samuel running full speed the other way, gaining 15 yards and eventually a touchdown, aided by offensive linemen forming a seal. The fake reverse variation, demonstrated by the 2020 Cardinals, involves Kyler Murray faking handoffs to a running back and a motioning receiver before running the ball himself, exploiting safeties who bit on the motion. The reverse screen, used by Purdue in 2021, features a handoff, a reverse toss to a receiver, then a toss back to the quarterback, who throws a screen to the initial running back, with linemen forming a wall for a touchdown. The reverse pass play adds another twist: after the reverse, the quarterback becomes a passing option, catching a throw from the receiver for a touchdown.

Charles W. Parker, administrator of Melvin Douglas's estate, appealed a district court ruling that Farmway Credit Union could exhaust its security interest in the decedent's personal property without filing a claim in estate proceedings or a foreclosure action. Before his death, Douglas had defaulted on a $111,290.17 debt secured by farm equipment, crops, and livestock. He and his wife orally agreed with Farmway to a public sale of the collateral. After Douglas died, his heirs cooperated, and Farmway repossessed and sold the collateral (equipment, wheat, and cattle) after providing notice. The administrator, appointed after the death, took no steps to halt the sales and later sought a declaratory judgment that he had sole right to the property. The district court granted summary judgment for Farmway, finding no conflict between the administrator's right to possession under K.S.A. 1985 Supp. 59-1401 and Farmway's self-help repossession right. On appeal, the court affirmed. It held that an administrator's right to a decedent's property is not absolute and is affected by the decedent's lifetime contracts. Citing In re Estate of Dahn, a secured creditor may exhaust security under K.S.A. 59-1303 without judicial foreclosure. The uncontroverted facts showed Farmway had a security agreement granting possession upon default and that the decedent and heirs had agreed to the disposition. Thus, Farmway had the contractual right to exhaust its security. The court did not decide whether self-help repossession is allowed absent a specific agreement. Regarding the premature summary judgment claim, the court found that because the existence of the security agreement and the pre-death agreement were uncontroverted, no material facts remained to be discovered, so summary judgment was proper.

The Counter play is a run scheme that fakes Power in one direction before the runner goes opposite. The backside Guard pulls to kick out an edge defender, and a Fullback inserts through the lane to block an Inside Linebacker. Its main strength is exploiting quick, aggressive defenses that over-pursue the Power action, giving the offense more blockers at the point of attack while the defense is a step behind. Its main weakness is a longer development time, making it susceptible to defensive penetration, especially in the open B gap vacated by the pulling Guard. Defenses often combat Counter by spilling it, forcing the ball carrier laterally into pursuing Linebackers and Safeties. The passage details assignments for Counter Trey against 3-4 and 4-3 fronts. Variations include Singleback GT Counter, where the backside Tackle replaces the Fullback as the insert blocker and the Fullback secures the backside edge, and Gun Split GT Counter Triple Option, which adds triple option reads for the Quarterback on the backside edge defender and alley defender.

This paper introduces a mathematical framework to investigate cubic-to-tetragonal (CT) phase coexistence in ferroelectrics using high-resolution X-ray diffraction 3D reciprocal space mapping. The model extends the adaptive state (AS) concept, describing CT coexistence via a periodic assemblage of tetragonal domains without requiring domain miniaturization. The work catalogs 24 variants of mismatch-free connections between the cubic phase and tetragonal domains, deriving analytical expressions for the orientation relationships and predicting the resulting splitting of Bragg peaks in reciprocal space. The predictions are compared with experimental results from high-resolution reciprocal space mapping of a PMN-35PT single crystal at the phase transition, and the comparison supports the formation of an AS-like state without domain miniaturization.

The study examines the SARS-CoV-2 BA.2.86 (Pirola) lineage and its descendant JN.1, which contain over 30 spike mutations relative to BA.2. A reverse mutational scanning approach was used, creating a library of 33 single reversion mutants on the BA.2.86 background to identify epitopes contributing to immune escape. Neutralization assays with sera from 30 healthcare workers before and after BNT162b2 XBB.1.5 booster vaccination showed that BA.2.86 and JN.1 efficiently escaped antibodies induced by pre-XBB immunogens, with JN.1 escape more pronounced. Mutations ins16MPLF, K356T, N460K, V483Δ, A484K, F486P, and S621P were found to contribute to this escape. The XBB.1.5 adapted booster substantially increased neutralization titers against both variants, eliminating the difference between them. Post-booster, reversions of ins16MPLF, Y144 deletion, K544E, S621P, and K484A improved neutralization to BA.2 levels. The results demonstrate the utility of reverse mutational scanning for mapping polyclonal antibody escape epitopes in variants with many simultaneous mutations.

The lecture discusses Langmuir probes, noting the instructor's personal confusion and the need for sheath theory. References are made to Hutchinson's and Lieberman and Lichtenberg's textbooks, with a warning about differing notations. A Langmuir probe is a conductor inserted into a plasma, causing a sheath to form. Initially, electron flux dominates due to higher electron velocity, charging the probe negatively until it reaches a floating potential where net current is zero. The floating potential differs from the plasma potential. By biasing the probe and measuring current, an IV curve is obtained, showing electron saturation current at plasma potential, ion saturation current at sufficiently negative bias, and a transition region. Sheath theory is required to relate probe-surface quantities to bulk plasma parameters. Key sheath concepts include the Debye length as the shielding distance, allowing a quasi-planar assumption for small Debye length relative to probe size. The sheath forms when probe potential is less than minus Te/(2e). With cold ions, continuity and energy conservation give ion flux at the sheath edge in terms of bulk density and temperature. Electrons are treated with a Boltzmann factor. The total current equation (Hutchinson's equation) combines ion and electron contributions. For interpretation, a single probe is swept near the floating potential. The electron temperature is found from the slope of the I-V curve after subtracting ion saturation current, and density is then obtained from the ion saturation current. Limitations include risk of drawing large currents and melting the probe, and sweep time limiting temporal resolution. A double probe uses two probes biased relative to each other, with current limited to the ion saturation current. The I-V characteristic follows a hyperbolic tangent, and temperature and density are extracted from the slope at zero bias and the saturation current. This design prevents accidental large currents but still requires sweeping. A triple probe adds a floating probe to a double probe, measuring three points on the IV curve simultaneously without sweeping, enabling fast time resolution. However, it assumes the IV curve model is accurate. Adding more probes can reproduce the curve instantaneously but risks presheath interference. Complications include magnetic fields, which alter particle orbits and make presheath size difficult to calculate, and collisions, which modify particle flux and require rederivation of results. Hutchinson's and Lieberman and Lichtenberg's books are recommended for these advanced topics.

In 1911, the city of South Bend passed an ordinance to fill low lands and tide lands, creating an improvement district and estimating the cost at $9,500. The city planned to use material from federal dredging of the Willapa River at nominal cost. The federal government later decided to deposit all material within a 1,500-foot limit, increasing the fill depth there from 18 to 36 inches and leaving the area outside unfilled. The city council, partly on its own initiative and partly on petition of some property owners, contracted with a dredging company to fill the outside area. The actual cost borne by benefited property became $89,199.92. The assessment roll was confirmed based on this actual cost. Appellants challenged the assessment, arguing the ordinance was void for indefiniteness and that the assessment was invalid because it greatly exceeded the preliminary estimate. The court held that under Rem. & Bal. Code § 7974, the preliminary estimate is solely for the council's guidance in deciding whether to initiate the improvement. Section 7983 allows the assessment roll to reflect the actual bona fide cost, with notice and hearing if the estimate is too low. The assessment was not invalidated by the increase, as it did not exceed the actual cost and the excess was explained by changed conditions. The ordinance was not void for indefiniteness; it followed statutory requirements and contained all material provisions. The evidence on benefits, though conflicting, preponderated in favor of the assessment. The court found all proceedings regular and affirmed the judgment confirming the assessment roll.

This document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP encrypted virtualization. The GHCB is a 4KB decrypted page that mirrors the VMCB save state area, allowing guests to selectively share register state with the hypervisor during Non-Automatic Exits (NAEs). Version 2 introduces hypervisor feature advertisement and initial SEV-SNP support. Revision 2.01 updates the Secrets Page for 64-bit sequence numbers and adds an error code for malformed input. Revision 2.02 adds the VLEK certificate GUID and expands error code usage in SW_EXITINFO2. Revision 2.03 adds support for APIC ID list retrieval, multiple VMPL levels, and page state change notification. Revision 2.04 documents the SEV-SNP Confidential Computing Blob EFI protocol. Additional changes include AP reset hold via MSR protocol, CPUID request/response protocol, NMI handling updates, termination request via VMGEXIT, and various clarifications on NAE events, GHCB layout, and exclusive access.

A study surveyed 106 nurses at the University of Iowa Health Care to evaluate the perceived usefulness of a Patient Report Template (PRT) designed to improve nursing handoffs and reduce electronic health record burden. The PRT integrates established handoff frameworks (SBAR, I PASS the BATON) and includes sections: Patient Profile, Review of Systems, Situation, Safety, Background, Actions, Timing, Ownership, and Next. Nurses rated each component on a 5-point Likert scale. Patient Profile and Safety sections received high average ratings (above 4, “Very Useful”), with Patient Name, Code Status, and Allergies among the highest. Review of Systems ratings varied; Chief Complaint averaged 4.40, while Eyes averaged 3.73. Situation section ratings were mixed, with Level of Uncertainty averaging 3.25. Background section’s Current Medications averaged 4.29, Family History 3.36. Actions, Timing, Ownership, and Next sections were generally rated useful (averages 3.71–4.19). Regarding artificial intelligence, nurses reported low comfort (mean 2.38) and trust (mean 2.5) but moderate expected utility (mean 3.0). Respondents represented diverse departments, with over half having 0–10 years of experience. The study concludes that the PRT shows potential to streamline handoffs but requires real-world testing and validation of AI-generated report accuracy.

The turn of the month trading strategy involves going long at the close on the fifth last trading day of the month and exiting at the close of the third trading day of the next month, resulting in being invested approximately 33% of the time. The end-of-month effect (also called the Ultimo Effect) is known to spill over into the first three days of the next month, making “turn of the month” a more accurate name. The strategy has performed well in most markets, frequently beating buy and hold with lower drawdowns. For the S&P 500, it has worked since at least 1960, delivering a CAGR of 7.1% with smaller and shorter drawdowns compared to buy and hold. The effect is likely caused by structural forces such as increased capital inflows or fund rebalancing, though the exact cause is uncertain.

Backtests were conducted on various markets using ETFs or Fidelity fund quotes as proxies. Emerging markets (EEM), healthcare (XLV), gold mining (GDX), high yield (HYG), real estate (IYR), consumer staples (XLP), Brazil (EWZ), Japan (EWJ), Bitcoin, commodities (DBC), utilities (XLU), and energy (XLE) all showed positive turn of the month effects, often outperforming buy and hold. Gold (GLD) showed a low to non-existent effect. Tech stocks (XLK) exhibited a more erratic effect. The Indian Nifty Fifty was also tested. An optimization of entry days from the 1st to 7th last trading days of the month, exiting at the close of the last trading day, showed positive average gains since 1960. The last trading day of the month was the worst among those seven days. The last calendar day of the month (day 31) had an average gain of 0.1%, better than a random day’s 0.04%, and better than the last trading day. Calendar days and trading days are not the same, requiring careful coding.

The strategy is believed to be structural and likely to continue working in the future, given its consistent performance over 60 years. The article provides Python code originally written for seasonal effects of long-term Treasuries, which may be helpful but is explicitly not for the turn of the month strategy; no responsibility is taken for it. The Ultimo effect is similar to the end-of-month effect, emphasizing the last trading day or very last few days of the month, often attributed to institutional buying, dividend reinvestments, or monthly fund inflows.

The PATCH model extends the Barabási-Albert network growth model by incorporating triadic closure, homophily, and preferential attachment. Simulations with a minority group (fmin=0.2) show homophily drives network segregation, preferential attachment drives degree inequality (Gini coefficient), and homophily drives inequity (Mann-Whitney statistic). Unbiased triadic closure moderates segregation and inequity, while biased triadic closure can exacerbate degree inequality. The advantaged group always exhibits higher within-group degree inequality. Likelihood-free inference applied to empirical scientific collaboration (APS, DBLP) and citation (APS-CIT) networks from 1970–2010 identifies the model variant where both global and triadic closure links are biased by preferential attachment and homophily (PAH,PAH) as best reproducing observed gender inequalities, with inferred moderate gender homophily and triadic closure tendencies. The findings suggest that reducing inequalities requires simultaneous reduction of all mechanisms.

Researchers discovered a structural quirk in dandelions that helps seeds catch upward gusts and avoid downward flight. Measurements show that pulling seeds slantwise upward requires an order of magnitude less force than pulling downward. Microscopic imaging revealed an off-center tether surrounded by a horseshoe-shaped shield. When wind tilts the seed toward the shield's open side, it detaches easily; force in the opposite direction causes the taller barrier to grip the seed. This directional release mechanism allows the plant to selectively disperse seeds in favorable winds.

CMD6, introduced in Physical Layer Specification Version 1.10, is mandatory for SD memory cards of that version or higher. The host must check the SD_SPEC field in the SCR register or bit10 of CCC in CSD before use. CMD6 is valid only in Transfer State. It returns an R1 response on the CMD line and 512 bits of status on the DAT lines, with a 100 ms timeout. After the status data end bit, a switching period of 8 clocks is required before new functions (e.g., changed clock frequency) can be used. A power cycle, CMD0, or CMD6 with Mode 1 and Function 0 in each group returns all functions to default. CMD6 supports six function groups, each with sixteen functions; Function 0 is the default. Mode 0 (Check function) queries which functions a card supports and the maximum current/power consumption under selected functions. Mode 1 (Set function) switches functionality. Selecting 0xF keeps the current function. If a function selection is invalid, the response returns 0xF and no change occurs. Function Group 1 is Access Mode (Bus Speed Mode). Function Group 2 is Command System. Function Group 3 is Driver Strength for UHS-I modes (1.8V signaling). Function Group 4 is Power Limit, defining total card power consumption. Default Power Limit is 0.72W. In UHS-I, after selecting SDR50, SDR104, or DDR50, the host must change Power Limit to enable higher performance. UHS-II also requires Power Limit setting after initialization. Removable cards are allowed up to 1.80W; UHS-I cards up to 1.44W. The switch function status data block is 512 bits, containing support bits for each function group, function selection results, and maximum current/power consumption. Busy status bits indicate if a function is busy; Mode 1 can only be applied to ready functions. High-Speed mode (25 MB/sec) is achieved by setting the clock to 50 MHz via CMD6. This study used 7 tesla magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to measure brain metabolite concentrations in occipital cortex (OCC) and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) in people with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP), first-degree biological relatives, and healthy controls. Six metabolites were examined a priori: GABA, glutamate, glutamine, glutathione, NAA, and NAAG. In OCC, NAA levels were significantly lower in both PwPP and relatives compared to controls. In PFC, NAAG levels were lower in PwPP relative to the other groups, but this difference was not significant after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. Post hoc analyses revealed significantly higher glucose levels in PFC in PwPP versus controls, with relatives showing intermediate values; a similar trend in OCC did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Hierarchical clustering showed that glucose levels in OCC and PFC clustered with psychiatric symptom measures and visual task performance, indicating higher brain glucose was associated with greater impairment. Longitudinal data from a subset of participants showed fair to excellent reliability of metabolite measurements over several months. The study employed an ultra-short echo time (8 ms) STEAM sequence, accounted for macromolecules in the basis set, and used a rigid baseline without soft constraints to minimize quantification errors. The findings suggest metabolic dysfunction in psychosis, with lower NAA and higher glucose possibly reflecting impaired neuronal metabolism, and lower NAAG potentially linked to glutamatergic abnormalities. The inclusion of relatives allowed examination of genetic liability, with NAA reductions in OCC possibly related to genetic risk.

The Tenth Circuit affirmed the INS's reinstatement of a 1996 exclusion order against Alejandro Mendez Suarez, a Mexican citizen. Suarez was excluded and deported after attempting entry with counterfeit documents, illegally reentered in 1999, and was taken into INS custody following a 2002 domestic-violence arrest. The district court transferred his habeas petition to the Tenth Circuit as a petition for review. The court held the transfer was proper. It declined to address due process claims related to his state criminal proceedings because its jurisdiction was limited to reviewing the removal order. The court rejected the argument that reinstatement under INA § 241(a)(5) was improperly retroactive, as his unlawful reentry occurred after IIRIRA's effective date. It found him ineligible for adjustment of status under the LIFE Act due to a prior misrepresentation. The court did not reach the merits of his due process challenge to the reinstatement procedure because he failed to show prejudice, given that he did not contest the factual prerequisites for reinstatement. The INS decision was affirmed.

This study estimated the direct healthcare-related economic burden of mental health (MH) disorders associated with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in the United States. A systematic review and meta-analysis of published controlled studies through July 2021 identified 25 eligible studies. Meta-analyses using random effects models yielded pooled prevalence ratios (PRs) for anxiety (PR 1.42, 95% CI 1.32–1.52), depression (PR 1.65, 95% CI 1.44–1.89), and eating disorders (PR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06–2.05) in women with PCOS compared to controls. Postpartum depression showed a non-significant increase (PR 1.20, 95% CI 0.96–1.50) and was excluded. Based on a PCOS prevalence of 6.6% (NIH criteria) and cost data adjusted to 2021 USD, the excess annual direct healthcare costs were $1.939 billion for anxiety, $1.678 billion for depression, and $0.644 billion for eating disorders, totaling $4.261 billion. Combined with prior estimates, the total excess economic burden of PCOS exceeds $15 billion annually, with MH disorders accounting for approximately 28%. Other components include reproductive endocrine morbidities (29.5%), obstetrical/pregnancy complications (15.1%), type 2 diabetes (10.1%), strokes (16.1%), and initial diagnostic evaluation (1.1%).

The study examines the separation of the Druze school system from the Arab education system in Israel, initiated in 1976, and its impact on matriculation certificate eligibility and higher education achievements. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with nine Druze high school principals, supervisors, and trainee principals, and analysis of matriculation results from 1976 to 2020.

The literature review notes that Druze education was part of the Arab school system until the 1970s, when Druze leaders sought separation to emphasize ethnic consciousness and heritage. The Israeli Ministry of Education established a separate Druze education unit, developing unique curricula, textbooks, and heritage studies. The system aimed to shape an Israeli-Druze identity, loyalty to the state, and connection to Druze heritage. The separation also involved replacing Arab teachers with Druze teachers and introducing the subject “Druze heritage.” The study’s point of departure is that matriculation eligibility opens access to academia and quality employment.

Interview analysis generated eight themes:
1. Overall satisfaction with Druze students’ achievements, especially rising matriculation eligibility rates, with principals expressing pride.
2. A desire to continue excelling, with principals emphasizing the need for ongoing improvement, investment in human capital, and addressing weaker areas like Hebrew proficiency.
3. Similarity and uniqueness of the Druze study program: core subjects are identical to those in the general system, while uniqueness lies in Druze heritage, history, and language studies.
4. The contribution of the teaching staff as a key factor in student success, including quality of teachers, management, and professional supervision.
5. Liberal-modern trends as an important factor, with sociocultural changes enabling more Druze women to pursue education and work, raising overall education rates.
6. Identity issues: some principals see the separation as accelerating development and achievements, while others view it as a government tool for “reeducating” the Druze population rather than directly causing academic success.
7. The connection between separation and achievements: opinions are divided; some attribute improvements to focused supervision and resource allocation, others to internal community efforts and sociocultural changes.
8. The school as an academic advocate: principals recognize the importance of preparing students for higher education but note insufficient resources and programs for this purpose.

The discussion highlights that principals’ satisfaction is linked to continuous educational efforts from preschool onward. The cultural-religious uniqueness coexists with shared professional-pedagogic content, making achievements comparable. Principals stress that maintaining success requires constant effort, quality teaching staff, and adaptation to liberal trends. The separation’s role is contested; many principals attribute achievements to internal community actions rather than the structural separation. The study also identifies a gap between high matriculation results and students’ sense of academic preparedness, recommending intervention programs to improve readiness for university.

The study’s contribution includes being the first to examine the long-term effects of the Druze school system’s separation. It notes that Druze matriculation eligibility reached about 89% in 2022, among the highest in Israel. Limitations include convenience sampling, non-representative samples, and reliance on subjective qualitative data. The study suggests that other school systems could adopt positive features of the Druze model, such as increased supervision, and considers the possibility of a uniform state school system that accommodates cultural uniqueness.

The study evaluated testing and isolation protocols in France, Belgium, and Italy for winter 2022/2023 using a multi-country survey (4,594 participants) and a mathematical model of Omicron subvariants. Survey results showed booster willingness among the elderly varied (France 72.5%, Belgium 93.9%, Italy 86.4%). Adherence to testing if symptomatic was high (92.7% France, 91.2% Belgium, 97.3% Italy), lower if asymptomatic. Introducing a test cost (<20 Euros) reduced testing adherence substantially in France and Belgium but less in Italy. Compliance to isolation recommendations was high.

Modeling with R=1.6 and 75% isolation effectiveness predicted the French protocol reduced R by 18.4%, Belgian by 17.2%, and Italian by 24.4%. None brought R below 1. If tests were not free, effectiveness dropped by approximately 60%. The Italian protocol’s greater effectiveness came with longer average isolation (11 days vs. 6 days for France/Belgium) and a lower fraction released while still infectious (8% vs. ~60%). The Belgian protocol required fewer tests per infected person (0.7) compared to France (1.0) and Italy (1.2) while achieving similar transmission reduction to France. Simpler isolation guidelines could reduce testing resources without compromising performance. Booster vaccination remained critical; low uptake would compromise control. Limitations included lack of age stratification and fixed isolation effectiveness assumptions.

The professor discusses a Porter article on CSR strategy, arguing that four common justifications for CSR—moral obligation, license to operate, reputation, and sustainability—are insufficient because they lack measurable trade-offs, disconnect from business capabilities, lack proven business value, or are too vague. Porter proposes a framework where companies categorize social issues into generic social impacts, value chain social impacts, and social dimensions of competitive context, leading to responsive CSR (mitigating risks) and strategic CSR (creating competitive advantage by integrating issues into core business). The professor stresses the importance of a life cycle view, measurement, and setting goals tied to operational metrics. Examples from companies like Starbucks, Unilever, Nestle, Ford, and Toyota illustrate how strategic CSR can involve deep supply chain engagement or focusing on product use-phase impacts. The session concludes with advice on embedding sustainability into procurement scorecards, first by asking suppliers to measure and report, then eventually making it a mandatory selection criterion.

Alcoa reported a big fourth-quarter loss but investors are looking at adjusted earnings. Two Motley Fool contributors offer opposing views. Rich Duprey argues Alcoa is a buy, noting shares have gained 68% since the Arconic spinoff and 36% in 2017. He highlights a significant expected increase in bauxite production (47.5-48.5 million bone dry metric tons vs. 45 million last year) and new bauxite supply contracts worth nearly $600 million in revenue over 2016-2017. Alcoa, the world's largest bauxite producer, expects to double EBITDA to $2.2 million if guidance holds. Jason Hall sees potential value but remains on the sidelines. He notes Alcoa's book value fell from over $49 to $42.13 per share due to facility closures and an impairment. The stock rose on expectations of infrastructure spending and 'America first' policies, but aggressive trade policies could harm Alcoa, which relies on foreign raw materials and global sales. Aluminum prices remain near multi-year lows, and the company's profitability is still unclear after only a few quarters as a standalone business.

This paper introduces a bound-preserving technique for coupling cell-centered finite volume (CCFV) and discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for steady convection-diffusion problems. The approach targets spurious oscillations in high-order DG regions by adaptively reverting to CCFV in a neighborhood of cells where DG cell averages violate bounds, aiming to obtain bound-preserving cell averages without postprocessing; standard slope limiters can then be applied. The method leverages hp-adaptivity and does not modify the underlying CCFV or DG schemes. The model problem is a convection-diffusion-reaction equation with Dirichlet and Neumann conditions. The domain is partitioned into FV and DG subdomains with a matching interface, using TPFA-admissible meshes in the FV region and higher-order polynomials in the DG region. Notations for jumps and averages across interfaces are defined for the coupled discretization.

A Metrocosm animation shows city growth from Eridu (c. 3000 BC), using earliest recorded population figures and dot sizes. Urbanization rose from 34% in 1960 to 54% today, projected 75% by 2030. The lecture introduces a course on building secure systems, co-taught by James Mickens, with four TAs. The course uses research papers for discussion and lab assignments in various languages, starting with a buffer overflow exploitation lab. Security is defined as achieving a goal despite an adversary, comprising policy (the goal), threat model (assumptions about the adversary), and mechanism (the enforcing software/hardware). Security is difficult because it is a negative goal and requires iterative refinement.

Examples of policy failures include account recovery questions weakening authentication (e.g., Sarah Palin’s Yahoo account) and multi-system interactions enabling compromise (Mat Honan’s Gmail accessed via Amazon and Apple). Threat model failures involve relying on human behavior (weak passwords, clicking links), outdated assumptions (Kerberos’s 56-bit keys becoming brute-forceable), and trusting all certificate authorities in SSL. Mechanism failures include missing rate limiting on iCloud’s “Find My iPhone,” Citibank’s URL-based access control flaw, an Android Bitcoin app’s unseeded random number generator, SSL certificate name encoding mismatches allowing null byte injection, and buffer overflows.

A buffer overflow demonstration shows how the `gets()` function can overwrite a stack’s return address, allowing redirection to arbitrary code. Defenses like non-executable stacks can be bypassed via return-to-libc attacks. The lecture notes that minimizing the trusted computing base helps reduce mechanism bugs.

The passage critiques Keith E. Whittington's argument that professors should self-censor to protect academic freedom. It states Whittington is wrong to claim professors must limit classroom speech to only what is germane and competent, calling that standard too restrictive. It notes that many professors expressed sadness about Kirk's assassination without facing punishment, while only a few critical of Kirk (mostly outside class) are investigated, indicating viewpoint discrimination. Whittington fears offending powerful people will undermine legal protections, but the author argues academic freedom is a fundamental right justified by free expression, not by professors' inoffensiveness. The passage disputes Whittington's interpretation of the AAUP's 1940 statement, noting it never used 'discretion' and that later comments embraced controversy. It concludes that demanding discretion destroys academic freedom, and that the response to repression should be fierce support for the right, not self-censorship.

The study investigates WSe₂/CrI₃ van der Waals heterostructures using quasiparticle self-consistent GW with ladder diagrams (QSGŴ) to understand proximity effects on excitonic properties. Crystal structures for bilayer and trilayer (ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic) configurations were optimized with DFT-PBE including van der Waals corrections. A 2×2 WSe₂ unit cell is stacked on CrI₃ with C1 stacking. At the LDA level, a type II band alignment is predicted with a 0.77 eV gap, but QSGW and QSGŴ yield a type I alignment with both band edges of W-d character at the K point. The band gap increases to 2.33 eV (QSGW) and 2.21 eV (QSGŴ) for the bilayer; similar values are found for trilayers. The change arises because self-energy corrections shift Cr-d and I-p states upward more than W-d states. The type I alignment preserves the A and B Wannier-Mott excitons of WSe₂, with binding energies consistent with pristine WSe₂. Additionally, Frenkel-like magnetic excitons of CrI₃ appear at 1.45, 1.85, and 2.1 eV, localized within a few angstroms, while WSe₂ excitons extend over tens of nanometers.

A key finding is the emergence of interlayer excitons between the A and B excitons, with significantly enhanced brightness—oscillator strength roughly twenty times that of intralayer CrI₃ Frenkel excitons—due to interlayer dipole effects. These interlayer excitons are robust across all layered and magnetic variants, with binding energy around 400 meV. The A₂ₛ exciton is also observed near 1.83 eV, close to an interlayer exciton at 1.84 eV, but their primary dipoles have different polarization directions. Magnetic proximity from CrI₃ induces spin splittings of A and B excitons. The largest splitting (~1000 GHz) occurs for the B exciton in the ferromagnetic trilayer, attributed to the proximity of Cr-d electron-like states to the WSe₂ conduction states. In bilayer and antiferromagnetic trilayer configurations, splittings are smaller (tens to 100 GHz). Even the AFM trilayer shows finite spin splitting despite zero net magnetization. The interlayer exciton wavefunctions reveal finite WSe₂-CrI₃ dipole elements in the FM trilayer but nearly zero in AFM. The study notes that magnetic splittings are sensitive to band alignments and can vary significantly with factors like interlayer spacing, strain, and phonon coupling. The interlayer excitons combine bright dipolar character with on-site magnetic character, making them attractive for photonic and spintronic applications. The authors suggest that similar principles apply to other TMD/magnet combinations, with expectations of different behaviors for CrBr₃ due to more ionic bonding and deeper valence states.

Using effective Hamiltonian molecular dynamics simulations, this work investigates topological textures in Zr-substituted BaTiO₃ (BZT). In pure BaTiO₃, the rhombohedral phase hosts antiskyrmions with topological charge −2, composed of six −1/3 topological quarks. The study extends to BZT because the rhombohedral phase can be stabilized above room temperature for 10–15% Zr. A 12.5% ordered superlattice with a doubled unit cell along [111] is constructed. At 1 K, induced nanodomains exhibit alternating topological charge along the nanodomain axis: one half of the doubled cell contains a −2 antiskyrmion (six −1/3 quarks), the other half a +4 skyrmion (six +2/3 quarks). The two textures share the same vortex skeleton, with an integer offset of +1 per vortex attributed to the chemical sublattice modifying local anisotropy. An alternative field-theoretic picture interprets this as a binary background imposing a sign flip. For diameters above ~4.5 nm, further quark splitting occurs.

Randomly substituted BZT (0–12.5% Zr) also supports nanodomains at 1 K. Increasing Zr concentration distorts the textures: at 2% Zr, a positive hotspot reduces the plane charge to −1; at 6%, threefold symmetry is locally broken and charge fluctuates; at 12.5%, a patchwork texture retains a recognizable six-vortex framework but with reduced correlation length. Topological charge varies along the axis, indicating a disorder-pinned skyrmion-glass-like state.

Thermal stability was assessed by heating simulations. Critical temperatures for pure BT range from ~65 K (3.5 nm diameter) to ~110 K (6.5 nm). Random Zr substitution lowers the critical temperature, with a minimum near 6–8% Zr and partial recovery at 12.5%. The 12.5% superlattice shows less diameter dependence. At 12.5% Zr and 6.5 nm, the random composition slightly outperforms the superlattice. Nontrivial topology persists up to nearly 100 K.

Near room temperature, the 12.5% superlattice remains rhombohedral (transition ~320 K cooling, ~345 K heating). Without an external field, nanodomains are not retained at 293 K. Applying a local electric field of 350 kV/cm along [111] stabilizes cylindrical nanodomains with a uniform topological charge of +4 on every (111) projection, with no −2/+4 alternation. In contrast, the 12.5% random composition under the same field destabilizes a single-domain state and nucleates multidomains. Thus, room-temperature topology is field-stabilized and volatile in the ordered case, while disorder causes fragmentation in the random case.

The study concludes that BZT is a versatile platform for ferroelectric topology, hosting fractionalized quarks, alternation in ordered superlattices, and disorder effects. Future stabilization strategies include strain, electrostatics, and compositional patterning.

The reproduction number (R) is a common measure of pathogen spread but does not account for the time-varying quantity of diagnostic tests, which affects the number of known cases. The acceleration index (ε), introduced in prior work, measures the proportional responsiveness of cases to tests as an elasticity, defined as the ratio of the growth rate of cases to the growth rate of tests. This paper shows that the reproduction number is a special case of the acceleration index. A derived relationship, ε = R × (A/B), decomposes the ratio into infectivity intensity (A) and test intensity (B). When test intensity exceeds infectivity intensity, R overestimates viral acceleration relative to ε; when infectivity intensity exceeds test intensity, R underestimates it. The acceleration index equals R only if the infectivity function is specified to incorporate testing. Empirical analysis for France (May 2020–October 2022) reveals substantial differences: R often underestimates viral spread compared to ε, notably during the Omicron wave and the second lockdown, because it ignores test volume variations. Similar discrepancies appear in five other countries. The authors conclude that tracking viral acceleration accurately requires either the acceleration index alone or the reproduction number combined with test and infectivity intensities, but the acceleration index is more parsimonious and avoids bias from time-varying tests.

Michael Liersch, head of goals-based advice and strategy at JPMorgan, offers five tips for investors. First, make a plan by creating a budget to see where your money goes and adjust allocations. Second, reframe decisions by viewing investing as future gain rather than current sacrifice, and market declines as buying opportunities. Third, stay the course by being patient and not trying to time the market. Fourth, don't go it alone; seek a partner with a different mindset to challenge your views. Fifth, take small steps first, such as paying down a credit card or contributing a few dollars to an IRA, and automate savings.

The lecture introduces a class on geometric folding, covering the mathematics and algorithms of folding and unfolding geometric objects. The instructor, Erik Demaine, outlines the class structure: mandatory lectures, problem sets, and a project with a presentation. Projects can involve sculpture, algorithm implementation, solving open problems, or surveys. The textbook is *Geometric Folding Algorithms* by Demaine and Joe O'Rourke.

Applications include robotics (programmable matter, transforming robots), computer graphics (character animation), mechanics (historical linkages), manufacturing (sheet metal, nano-manufacturing), optics, medical (stents, drug delivery), aerospace (deployable structures), biology (protein folding), sculpture (origami design), and architecture (reconfigurable buildings).

The class studies three main geometric structures: linkages (1D rigid bars with hinges), paper (2D, no stretching, tearing, or cutting, only folding), and polyhedra (3D or 2D surfaces in 3D). Mathematical questions are categorized as foldability (given a structure, how does it fold?) or design (given a goal, how to fold to achieve it?). Results fall into three types: universality (everything can be folded with an algorithm), decision (fast algorithm decides foldability), or hardness (computationally intractable).

For linkages allowing intersection, a historical motivation was converting linear to circular motion, exemplified by Watt's parallel motion and Peaucellier's linkage. A universality result shows a linkage can trace any piecewise polynomial curve (e.g., sign your name). An open problem is whether this is possible without crossing bars. Rigidity (whether a linkage folds at all) is easy to decide in 2D but open in 3D.

For linkages forbidding intersection, reconfiguration between two configurations is computationally intractable in general. Special cases include chains and trees. In 2D, chains can fold from any configuration to any other (universality), but some trees have locked configurations that cannot reach others. In 3D, chains are not universal; an example is the "knitting needles" where long bars prevent untying a knot-like structure. In 4D and higher, everything is easy. Locked trees exist; the smallest known has 8 bars and was found in a previous iteration of the class. An open problem is characterizing which 3D chains and 2D trees have locked configurations. Proteins are modeled as 3D trees or chains; they fold reliably despite theoretical hardness, possibly due to uniform bar lengths.

For paper foldability, determining whether a crease pattern folds flat is NP-hard. However, flat-foldability around a single vertex is well understood. An open problem is deciding flat-foldability for a 2×n map with given mountain-valley assignments.

For paper design, a universality result shows any shape (polygon, polyhedron, two-color pattern) can be folded from a square, but the method is impractical. The Origamizer algorithm can fold any 3D polyhedron from a square and is practical, though its efficiency is unproven. The tree method (implemented in TreeMaker) designs origami bases with specified limb lengths; finding the most efficient square usage is NP-complete, but heuristics work well in practice. The folding cut problem states that folding a paper flat and making one straight cut can produce any collection of polygons. Curved creases allow self-folding origami and sculptures, some in the MOMA collection. A self-folding sheet with rubber hinges and muscles can fold into a boat or airplane via electrical signals, illustrating programmable matter. A universal hinge pattern (box pleating) can fold any 3D shape made of cubes. Most results assume zero thickness; the only thickness analysis is by Britney Gallivan, who computed the paper length needed to fold in half many times.

For polyhedra, edge unfolding convex polyhedra (cutting along edges to get a single non-overlapping piece) is an open problem dating back to Dürer in 1525. Non-convex polyhedra can fail to have an edge unfolding. General unfolding (cutting anywhere on the surface) is always possible for convex polyhedra; for non-convex, it is open, but orthogonal polyhedra (made of cubes) always work. This study examined the intentions of Ethiopian national education policy documents and the conceptualizations of secondary school principals and teachers regarding curriculum differentiation (CD). Two schools were selected via purposive sampling, and data was collected through document analysis of three national policies and interviews with two principals and 17 teachers.

The findings show that the Education and Training Policy (ETP) and the General Education Curriculum Framework (GECF) conceptualize CD in terms of separate tracks, including school types, fields of study, and streams. Conversely, the National Guideline for CD and IEP emphasizes differentiating curriculum components (content, instruction, assessment, learning environments) within inclusive classrooms. Principals' and teachers' conceptualizations of CD varied across five themes: CD as gifted programs, as student placement into subjects/streams/schools, as a special curriculum for student groups, as identification and accommodation of gifts and talents, and as curricular planning and teaching strategy. These conceptualizations ranged from a lack of awareness to alignment or divergence with policy intentions. The study concludes that there is a lack of coherent policy guidance on CD, and that the practice of differentiation by school type does not adequately correspond to variations in subject difficulty, implying a need for policy alignment and a more flexible, diverse secondary school curriculum structure.

The bark Cape Horn Pigeon, on a whaling voyage since December 7, 1891, was in the Okhotsk Sea on September 10, 1892, whaling on the high seas. That day, the vessel was seized by an armed Russian navy vessel on the open sea and taken by force to Vladivostok, despite protests; the crew was compelled to navigate the Russian vessel. The lecture covers financing sustainable real estate at the portfolio level, following a prior session on asset-level financing. It first addresses equity through Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). REITs are publicly traded companies that primarily invest in income-generating commercial real estate, enjoy pass-through tax benefits, and must distribute 90% of income while holding 75% of assets in real estate. Compared to direct real estate investment, REITs offer greater liquidity, diversification, and lower capital requirements but less control. The US is the birthplace of modern REITs, and other countries have adopted them, often triggered by financial crises (e.g., China launched infrastructure-focused REITs during the pandemic recession to raise funds, later expanding toward commercial real estate).

The lecture then discusses green REITs. Over 60% of REITs by equity market size have net-zero carbon targets, driven largely by institutional investors (especially European and Canadian pension funds) that allocate capital based on ESG performance. Research indicates that REITs with higher shares of green-certified properties show better return on equity, return on assets, and lower risk. Ongoing research aims to distinguish “green talking” from “green doing” and measure stock market responses.

The debt side is covered through green bonds. Bonds are fixed-income instruments issued by governments or companies. Green bonds are designated for green investments (e.g., renewable energy, green buildings) and can lower the issuer’s cost of capital, as investors may pay a premium for them. REITs like Boston Properties issue green bonds to obtain cheaper capital. Fannie Mae also issues green bonds backed by pools of green mortgages. Green bond principles exist to prevent greenwashing.

Finally, the lecture addresses benchmarking and disclosure. Reliable data and measurement are essential to credibility. Tools include EPA’s Portfolio Manager for utility data, third-party carbon audits, and GRESB (Global Real Estate Sustainability Benchmark), a portfolio-level ESG rating system. GRESB scores are used by REITs and private equity funds; research shows higher GRESB scores correlate with better fund performance and lower loan costs. However, the proliferation of ESG ratings has led to inconsistency and confusion, as different raters’ scores often correlate poorly, prompting research into deriving reliable ESG measures from noisy data.

The NVIDIA Ampere GA10x GPU architecture, fabricated on Samsung's 8nm 8N process, includes the GA102 and GA104 GPUs. GA102 contains up to 10752 CUDA Cores, 84 second-generation RT Cores, and 336 third-generation Tensor Cores. The Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) doubles FP32 processing throughput compared to Turing by enabling FP32 operations on both datapaths. The second-generation RT Core doubles ray/triangle intersection testing rate, adds hardware acceleration for ray-traced motion blur via an Interpolate Triangle Position unit, and supports concurrent RT and graphics/compute workloads. Third-generation Tensor Cores introduce fine-grained structured sparsity, allowing up to 2x throughput on sparse matrices, and support new data types including TF32 and BF16. GA10x GPUs feature GDDR6X memory with PAM4 signaling, achieving up to 19.5 Gbps data rates and 936 GB/sec peak bandwidth on GeForce RTX 3090. PCIe Gen 4 provides double the bandwidth of PCIe 3.0. Third-generation NVLink offers 112.5 GB/sec total bandwidth between two GPUs. RTX IO enables GPU-based lossless decompression and fast SSD-to-GPU loading, working with Microsoft DirectStorage. Display support includes HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC, enabling 8K60 HDR. The fifth-generation NVDEC adds AV1 hardware decode; the seventh-generation NVENC provides hardware video encoding. Error Detection and Replay (EDR) on GDDR6X detects transmission errors and replays transactions to aid overclocking. Products include GeForce RTX 3090 (24GB GDDR6X, 10496 CUDA Cores), GeForce RTX 3080 (up to 2x RTX 2080 performance), GeForce RTX 3070 (GA104, performance rivaling RTX 2080 Ti), NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48GB GDDR6, 10752 CUDA Cores), and NVIDIA A40 data center GPU (48GB GDDR6, same core counts as A6000, optimized for virtual workstations and server workloads).

Spacetime is defined as a manifold of events endowed with a metric. A manifold is a set of points with well-understood connectedness properties. An event is when and where something happens, existing independently of coordinate labels. The metric provides a notion of distance between events. An inertial reference frame is a lattice of clocks and measuring rods that moves freely (no forces, no rotation), with orthogonal rods, uniformly spaced tick marks, uniformly ticking clocks, and clocks synchronized via the Einstein synchronization procedure, which relies on the constancy of the speed of light. A spacetime vector is a quartet of numbers whose components transform between inertial frames via Lorentz transformations; it must obey linearity, and not any set of four numbers qualifies. The geometric object exists independently of its coordinate representation.

The passage describes three procedures. The first, a stackless assembler routine, initializes a pre-memory stack region before main memory is available. It divides the stack among cores, maps to global address space, and sets MTRRs. In protected mode, SS is not modified; ESP is set to a 32-bit offset. In real mode, SS:ESP is a 16-bit segment:offset with upper ESP zeroed. It creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF instance. AARCH64 with PSP does not use this stack; PSP initializes DRAM. Registers destroyed: EAX, ECX, EDX, EDI, ESI (plus DS, ES in 16-bit). Status: SUCCESS, WARNING (re-entry), FATAL (unknown family). The second procedure removes the pre-memory stack when main memory is available, disabling CAR mode, flushing caches, and preserving EBX. It must be invoked only by BSP, requires Big Real mode for 16-bit code. Registers destroyed: EAX, ECX, EDX, ESI, ESP, EDI. Status: SUCCESS. The third, AmdCreateStruct, creates and pre-initializes a parameter structure. Allocation methods: PreMemHeap (uses Cache-as-RAM heap before memory), PostMemDram (uses AgesaAllocateBuffer after memory), and ByHost (host pre-allocates; procedure only initializes; host must ensure sufficient size; StdHeader overlays params; error if insufficient).
