The David Swensen Portfolio (Yale Model) is a diversified investment strategy developed by David Swensen, who served as Yale University’s Chief Investment Officer from the mid-1980s until his death in May 2021. Swensen, along with Dean Takahashi, invented the Yale Model. The portfolio aims to maximize returns while minimizing risk by diversifying across asset classes, with a focus on alternative investments such as private equity, real estate, and hedge funds. It also emphasizes low-cost index funds and passive investment strategies.

Swensen transformed Yale’s endowment from a small, poorly performing 60/40 stock-bond portfolio into one of the world’s largest and most successful endowments. His approach relied on identifying undervalued assets, making unconventional investments, and strong risk management through diversification. The portfolio’s asset allocation includes stocks diversified across sectors, geographies, and market capitalizations, bonds across government, corporate, and high-yield types, and a significant allocation to alternative investments. The allocation is not fixed and can be adjusted for an investor’s needs, goals, and risk tolerance.

Implementation can be done using ETFs. Suggested ETFs include VTI, VNQ, VEA, EEM, IEI, and TIP. No ETF for alternative investments is listed due to short histories, but KMLM is mentioned as an example. The Yale Model portfolio overseen by Swensen from 1985 to 2020 generated an annualized return of 12.5%, outperforming the S&P 500’s 9.7%. Long-term performance is attributed to alternative investments’ low correlation with traditional assets and the diversified allocation. However, past performance is not a guarantee of future results.

A backtest using the suggested ETFs showed annual returns of 6.23%, underperforming the S&P 500, with the underperformance linked to the bond component and emerging markets. Drawdowns were lower than the S&P 500. The article notes that the Yale Model is not a one-size-fits-all solution and advises considering personal investment goals, risk tolerance, and consulting a financial advisor.

The device uses SmartReflex modules with external variable-voltage supplies to minimize power consumption on Core Logic Voltage Domains, advising the host processor to adjust voltage based on process, temperature, and performance. Communication to external regulators can use GPIOs, I2C, SPI, etc. Two techniques are Dynamic Voltage Frequency Scaling (DVFS) and Adaptive Voltage Scaling (AVS), though AVS is noted as not supported. Each Core Logic Voltage Domain operates at one of several Operating Performance Points (OPPs), defined by maximum module frequencies and a supply voltage range; lower OPPs save power. DVFS allows real-time OPP changes without reset. Not all OPP combinations are supported, and the maximum voltage difference between CVDD and other CVDD_x domains must be <150 mV. SRAM blocks can be switched to SHUTDOWN mode to reduce leakage, with automatic shutdown in switchable power domains. Some I/Os support dual 1.8 V/3.3 V voltages, and DDR I/O voltage is selectable between 1.5 V and 1.8 V. Low-Power Standby Mode turns off all switchable power domains, runs the ARM Cortex-A8 in an idle loop at its lowest frequency, and clock gates unused blocks. Power supplies are organized into four sequencing groups (CVDD, DVDD_DDR[x], 1.8 V, 3.3 V) with required power-up and power-down sequences. Decoupling uses 0.1 µF capacitors in small packages (no larger than 0402), one per two power pins, plus bulk capacitors.

The device has multiple reset types: Power-on Reset (POR) resets the entire chip including test/emulation logic and EMAC switch; external warm reset (RESET) resets most logic except test/emulation and optionally EMAC; watchdog reset always asserts RSTOUT_WD_OUT; software cold/warm resets are similar but with exceptions like not re-latching BTMODE. Reset isolation is supported for PCIe and EMAC switch. During reset, most I/Os go Hi-Z except emulation pins and possibly EMAC pins if isolated. Clocking uses DEV and AUX clock inputs from crystals or 1.8 V LVCMOS sources. DEV clock is typically 20 MHz; AUX clock is optional for audio/video PLLs. A differential SERDES clock is required for PCIe. The device contains 12 top-level PLLs and 4 embedded PLLs with bypass mode and frequency limits. SYSCLKs and module clocks have maximum frequencies per OPP. Interrupts: ARM Cortex-A8 AINTC handles up to 128 requests (no FIQ on general-purpose devices); C674x DSP interrupt controller combines 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts with multiplexing. Peripherals include DCAN (CAN 2.0A/B), EDMA (64 channels with default and muxed sync events), AET (hardware breakpoints, watchpoints, counters, state sequencing), Trace (Cortex-A8 and system level via ETB or 5-pin interface), JTAG (TRST pin, internal pulldown, ID 0x0B8F 202F), EMAC switch (3-port gigabit, MII/GMII/RMII/RGMII, MDIO, 3.3 V I/O, CRC inversion on underflow), GPIO (up to 128 pins with interrupt capability), GPMC (glueless interface to NOR/NAND flash, SRAM, with synchronous/asynchronous modes, and ELM for BCH error correction), and HDMI 1.3a transmitter (TMDS differential pairs requiring 100 Ω differential and 60 Ω single-ended impedance, DDC, CEC, supporting up to 1080p with various color depths).

Wireless communication differs from wired channels, where only white Gaussian noise is present, due to fading. In free space, the far electric field decays as 1/r, with antenna patterns and a propagation delay of r/c. Fixed antennas in free space yield a time-invariant channel similar to wired systems. When the receiver moves, a Doppler shift occurs, scaling with v/c times the carrier frequency. A single Doppler shift is not problematic because frequency recovery can track it. The difficulty arises from multiple paths with different Doppler shifts, causing multipath or fast fading. An example with a vehicle moving toward a reflecting wall produces two paths with opposite Doppler shifts, resulting in a beat pattern that periodically fades at the Doppler frequency, disrupting communication. Another example involving a base station and a reflecting road shows that the path-length difference decreases as 1/r, causing received power to fall as 1/r⁴ instead of 1/r². Detailed electromagnetic analysis is impractical; instead, ray tracing models the channel as a sum of paths, each with an attenuation and propagation delay. The channel is linear but time-varying, not time-invariant, so the familiar Fourier transform relationship for convolution does not hold. The output is described by a time-varying convolution. For ray tracing, the impulse response consists of impulses at the propagation delays, making the output a sum of delayed and attenuated copies of the input. When moved to baseband, the carrier frequency introduces Doppler shift terms. Frequency recovery locks onto an average Doppler shift, so the effective time variation depends on how far each path’s Doppler shift deviates from that average. The critical parameter is the Doppler spread—the difference between the largest and smallest Doppler shifts—which determines the time interval over which the channel appears approximately time-invariant. Measurements must be updated roughly every 1/(2 × Doppler spread), a key factor in making wireless systems work.

The lecture continues the theme of folding polygons into convex polyhedra by gluing the polygon's boundary to itself, represented via gluing trees. A combinatorial type of gluing is defined by an abstract gluing tree (ignoring metric lengths) and a specification of which polygon vertices and edges appear at junctions (leaves, branching nodes, and degree-2 nodes with at least one vertex). This makes the number of types finite.

For general polygons, the number of combinatorial gluing types is at most exponential: leaves are at most n+4 (at most four fold points, the rest vertices), giving O(n) nodes, leading to 2^O(n) trees; vertex/edge colorings and vertex labeling add another 2^O(n) factor, yielding an overall 2^O(n) upper bound. A lower bound of 2^Ω(n) is shown via a star polygon with many spikes, where many edge-to-edge gluings exist by squeezing reflex vertices.

Bounded sharpness polygons (every reflex angle ≤ 360 minus a constant) have only a constant number of leaves (curvature per leaf ≥ constant, total curvature 720), leading to a polynomial bound on combinatorial types, specifically n^O(L) where L is the number of leaves.

Algorithms: For edge-to-edge gluings, a dynamic programming algorithm solves subproblems of gluing a chain from vertex i to vertex j. Enumerating all solutions takes exponential time (optimal given exponential output). A polynomial-time decision algorithm (O(n³)) stores only the solution minimizing the angle glued at the endpoints, checking Alexandroff condition. For general (non-edge-to-edge) gluings, subproblems include vertex-to-edge cases. Solutions are represented by combinatorial type, total angle glued, and an interval along the edge where the vertex can glue. The algorithm handles "zip" and "tug" cases, enumerating all solutions in exponential time. No polynomial decision algorithm is known for the general case. For bounded sharpness polygons, the enumeration algorithm runs in polynomial time because the number of gluings considered at each stage is polynomial.

Examples: The Latin cross has 85 gluings (23 distinct convex polyhedra) when non-edge-to-edge gluings are allowed; edge-to-edge yields 5. The equilateral triangle and square have rolling belts, yielding infinite families of gluings; their topologies are illustrated. For a square, the maximum volume convex polyhedron is an octahedron.

The passage describes interrupt handling conventions when #HV is delivered without interrupt shadows. Guests must execute HLT with interrupts disabled; if the host intercepts HLT while interrupts or non-maskable events are pending, it re-enters the guest. Upon resume, the guest examines interrupt state as if receiving #HV. Doorbell page configuration uses VMGEXIT requests: a guest may query the hypervisor-preferred address, must use SET to establish the page when Restricted Injection is enabled, and may QUERY whether a page is set. The host may clear RMP assignment via RMPUPDATE; a well-behaved guest first executes PVALIDATE. The page must be accessed with C=0; remapping does not reassign the old address.

Host behavior: the host emulates APIC faithfully. It presents the highest-priority ready interrupt by writing the vector to PendingEvent.Vector when the vCPU is not running. If Vector and NoFurtherSignal were zero, it schedules #HV and sets NoFurtherSignal. If Vector was non-zero, it overwrites with a higher-priority vector without sending #HV. It records the last presented vector. When no other interrupts are ready, it sets NoEoiRequired; when multiple are ready, it clears NoEoiRequired. For non-maskable events, it sets the appropriate bit and NoFurtherSignal, delivering #HV if NoFurtherSignal was zero. The host observes Vector becoming zero as acknowledgment, marking the interrupt in-service. It observes NoEoiRequired becoming zero as an EOI cycle, performing EOI after checking Vector. After any EOI, it sets NoEoiRequired again if interrupts remain in-service and none are pending. Examination occurs when the guest is not running or APIC state is evaluated. Non-cooperative guest modifications may lose #HV but do not affect host integrity.

Guest behavior: on #HV, the guest prepares for an interrupt. It acknowledges by atomically exchanging PendingEvent to zero, acting only on the exchanged vector. It processes or defers the interrupt, assuming standard APIC acknowledgment. For EOI, it atomically exchanges zero with NoEoiRequired; if the previous value was non-zero, no further action is needed; if zero, it performs an APIC register write via VMGEXIT. With EFLAGS.IF=0, it may dispatch non-maskable events by atomically clearing event flags and NoFurtherSignal while leaving Vector unchanged. The guest must validate vectors against expected interrupts. A non-cooperative host may cause denial of service; #HV received when NoFurtherSignal is non-zero is grounds for panic.

The passage describes defensive strategies against the Triangle Offense. Basic NBA Show & Recover emphasizes packing the paint to deny inside shots and force perimeter attempts. It involves phases: on a corner cut, defenders deny passes and cuts, push the ball to help, and congest the lane. On a post feed, they show and recover against splits, collapse weakside help, and physically pressure the post. Against corner screen and roll, they show and recover, fight over screens, and pack the weakside. In weakside two-man game, they show on screens and congest the area. The SOS Disruption approach aggressively disrupts the offense's initial flow, potentially extending full court. It includes wing pass denial, fronting the post, sagging and switching on post splits, and contact switches on screens. All Out SOS Disruption traps the wing on the first pass to force free-lance play. It details trap rotations: on a skip pass, defenders close out and rotate into I positions; on a corner pass out of trap, they close out and reposition; optional continued trapping on the corner pass with Triangle I rotations.

The passage describes shared tasks organized by the German consortium NFDI4DS, which focuses on FAIR research data infrastructure for Data Science and AI. The paper presents twelve tasks: seven completed, one ongoing, and four under development.

Completed tasks:
- SOMD 2025 (GESIS): Software mention detection in scholarly articles, hosted at SDP 2025. Two phases; best team achieved F1 0.89 (Phase I) and 0.63 (Phase II).
- SciVQA (DFKI): Scientific visual question answering using images of figures, captions, and metadata, part of SDP 2025. Dataset of 3000 images, 21000 QA pairs. Top team achieved ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L 0.80, BertScore 0.98.
- ClimateCheck (DFKI): Fact-checking climate change claims on social media by linking to scholarly articles, at SDP 2025. Subtask I (retrieval) top Recall@10 0.66, Bpref 0.49; Subtask II (relation classification) F1 0.73.
- FoRC2025 (DFKI): Field of research classification of ACL Anthology papers using 170 topics, at NSLP 2025. One team submitted, achieving micro-F1 0.68, macro-F1 0.66, weighted-F1 0.69.
- LLMs4Subjects (TIB): Automated subject tagging for TIBKAT catalog records in English and German, SemEval-2025 Task 5. 14 teams participated; approaches included LLM augmentation, few-shot ensembles, and retrieval-augmented generation.
- LLMs4OL-2024 (TIB): Ontology learning tasks (term typing, taxonomy induction, relation extraction) using LLMs, at ISWC 2024. 14 teams; winning approaches combined traditional ML with LLM prompt-tuning or retrieval.
- Scholarly QALD (Leuphana University): QA over scholarly knowledge graphs, at ISWC 2023 and 2024. 2023: DBLP-QUAD and SciQA tasks, 7 teams. 2024: Hybrid-QA task, 3 teams, evaluated with Exact Match, F-Score, METEOR.

Ongoing task:
- CheckThat!Lab Task 4 (GESIS): Scientific Web Discourse, part of CLEF 2025. Subtask 4.1: classify tweets for scientific claims/references (macro-F1). Subtask 4.2: retrieve source paper for implicit scientific references (MRR@5).

Tasks under development:
- Dataset and ML Model Mention Detection (GESIS): Using GSAP-NER corpora to detect ML models and datasets in scholarly articles.
- ReadMe2KG (FIZ Karlsruhe): Extract entities from GitHub README files and link to NFDI4DS-KG. Subtask I: NER with ~15 classes; Subtask II: entity linking.
- CURED (ICCAS): Clinical uncertainty and evidence-based decision-making, evaluating prognostic models with calibrated uncertainty estimates on electronic health records. Planned for 2026.
- Algorithm2Domain (University Hospital Cologne): Meta-benchmarking platform for algorithm generalisability and domain adaptation, building on ADATIME suite, with shared tasks for benchmarking.

The tasks aim to advance methodological progress and contribute to FAIR, transparent, and reproducible research data infrastructure.

The A100 Tensor Core GPU accelerates HPC with IEEE-compliant FP64 Tensor Cores delivering up to 2.5x the FP64 performance of V100. It introduces mixed-precision Tensor Cores for HPC, with TF32 providing robust convergence and up to 2x geomean speedup over FP64 solvers in iterative refinement. A100 features Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity (2:4 pattern) that doubles Tensor Core compute throughput for inference with negligible accuracy loss. The SM includes a combined 192 KB L1 data cache/shared memory, simultaneous FP32 and INT32 execution, and third-generation Tensor Cores with improved data sharing and asynchronous copy instructions. Memory includes 40 GB HBM2 with 1555 GB/s bandwidth, 40 MB L2 cache (6.7x larger than V100) with residency controls, and compute data compression. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions the GPU into up to seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated memory and compute resources. Third-generation NVLink provides 600 GB/s total bandwidth, and PCIe Gen 4 doubles bandwidth. Additional features include hardware JPEG decode, optical flow accelerator, improved atomics, and five NVDEC units. CUDA 11 advances include task graph acceleration, asynchronous copy and barriers, L2 cache residency control, and cooperative groups enhancements. DGX A100 integrates eight A100 GPUs with NVSwitch, delivering up to 5 PFLOPS for AI workloads.

Wall Street Journal reporter Ben Fritz notes that while tent-pole films are highest-grossing, oversaturation leads to more flops as they compete for the same dollars. 2017 movie ticket sales were at a 25-year low, and competition from Netflix is intensifying. Box office dollars have concentrated on a few films; “Black Panther” accounted for 23 percent of first-quarter ticket sales. Studios are touting diverse slates: Universal is releasing “Skyscraper” and Focus Features films like “Tully” and documentaries; Warner Bros. has no major DC film, instead offering female-driven “Ocean’s 8,” comedies, and “Crazy Rich Asians.” Other offerings include gender-flipped reboots, female-led comedies, action films, unconventional fare like “Uncle Drew” and “Hereditary,” Sundance breakouts, and original films such as “Hotel Artemis.” Director Drew Pearce says audiences want movies with real personality and less cookie-cutter content.

This study examines the global rankings of the top five higher education institutions (HEIs) in ten Asian countries (Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Pakistan, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Russian Federation) from 2015 to 2025 using Times Higher Education World University Rankings (THE WUR) data. It employs a multiple case study design and document analysis to identify ranking trends and propose policy recommendations.

The results show that Chinese and Japanese HEIs were the most successful, with Chinese universities consistently improving and many entering the top 50–100 globally, and Japanese institutions recovering positive momentum in recent years. Russian HEIs maintained stable, relatively high rankings. Indian HEIs displayed a generally positive trend, though only one appeared consistently. In contrast, HEIs in Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Vietnam exhibited neutral or declining ranking patterns with frequent fluctuations. Bangladeshi HEIs were recent entrants with neutral trends. Overall, most Asian HEIs lagged behind international competitors and lacked stable ranking profiles.

The study concludes that Asian countries, except China, Japan, and Russia, need enhanced higher education policies. Recommendations include diversifying global networks, improving international marketing, expanding funding, and establishing overseas offices to boost global visibility and competitiveness. Limitations include the focus on only the top five HEIs in ten populous Asian countries and the exclusive use of THE WUR data.

The lecture discusses renormalization and Sudakov logarithms in SCET, continuing from a b → s gamma example. One-loop diagrams yield IR QCD pieces, UV divergences canceled by counterterms, and leftover terms for matching. The counterterm contains 1/ε² and log terms. The label ω equals m_b due to external kinematics, and the delta function in the operator does not involve loop momenta, so it is external and fixed. In general, if an operator has one building block per collinear direction, ω’s are fixed; otherwise, convolutions appear in the renormalization group equation.

The anomalous dimension derived from μ d/dμ of the bare coefficient includes a regular piece and a cusp piece with log(μ/ω). The cusp term drives leading logarithms, producing Sudakov double logarithms (α log²). In QED with fixed coupling, the Wilson coefficient becomes a Sudakov exponential; in QCD, running coupling yields series α^k log^{k+1} (LL), α^k log^k (NLL), etc. Log counting is performed on log C. Required inputs for LL are tree-level matching and one-loop cusp anomalous dimension; NLL needs two-loop cusp and one-loop non-cusp; NNLL needs one-loop matching, two-loop regular anomalous dimension, and three-loop cusp. The cusp originates from Wilson lines meeting at an angle, such as a heavy-quark Wilson line and a light-like Wilson line, producing the log in the anomalous dimension.

The lecture then addresses deep inelastic scattering (DIS) in the Breit frame, focusing on the region where P_X² ~ Q². The incoming proton is collinear, and the final state is hard. Integrating out hard modes leaves collinear operators. The lowest-dimension (λ²) operators are quark and gluon bilinears with Wilson lines, corresponding to parton distribution functions (PDFs). The forward matrix element of the quark bilinear yields the PDF, with a delta function equating the two ω labels. The unconstrained sum ω+ relates to the momentum fraction ξ, with positive ω+ for quarks and negative for antiquarks. This operator acts as a number operator for partons. The next step will combine this with the Wilson coefficient to obtain a factorization theorem for DIS.

The passage discusses patterns for distributed systems, highlighting the rise of open source software and its role in fostering community-driven development. Patterns are defined as general blueprints for organizing distributed systems without mandating specific technologies, offering value through learning from others’ mistakes, providing a shared vocabulary, and enabling reusable components.

Single-node patterns involve groups of containers co-located on a single machine, motivated by resource isolation, team ownership, and separation of concerns. The sidecar pattern augments an application container with a sidecar container that adds functionality, often without the application’s knowledge. Examples include adding HTTPS to a legacy service via an nginx sidecar, synchronizing configuration from a cloud API, providing a topz process monitoring interface, and building a simple PaaS with a Git-sync sidecar. Designing reusable sidecars requires parameterizing containers (e.g., via environment variables), defining a clear API surface, and documenting usage through Dockerfile directives like EXPOSE, ENV, and LABEL.

The ambassador pattern brokers interactions between the application container and the external world. It is used for client-side sharding, where an ambassador proxy (e.g., twemproxy) routes requests to the appropriate shard of a sharded service like Redis or memcached, allowing the application to connect to localhost. Other uses include service brokering to adapt to different environments (e.g., discovering a MySQL service) and request splitting for experimentation (e.g., sending 10% of traffic to a new service version using nginx with IP hashing). Implementation details involve Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Services, and pods.

The adapter pattern modifies the application container’s interface to conform to a standardized interface expected by the system. Examples include adapting monitoring: a Prometheus exporter sidecar is added to a Redis container to expose metrics in the Prometheus format. For logging, a fluentd adapter normalizes heterogeneous log formats (e.g., capturing Redis slowlog or Storm logs) into a consistent output. For health checks, an adapter container runs a custom query against a MySQL database and exposes an HTTP health endpoint, avoiding modification of the original database image. This pattern promotes modularity and reuse.

Multi-node patterns address distributed systems across machines. The replicated load-balanced service pattern uses identical, stateless replicas behind a load balancer, with readiness probes to indicate when each replica is ready to serve. Session tracking can be added via consistent hashing to map a user’s requests to the same replica. Application-layer replicated services introduce a caching layer (e.g., Varnish) to improve performance and reduce backend load, and an SSL termination layer (e.g., nginx) to handle HTTPS. These layers form a multi-tier architecture, with the caching layer also capable of rate limiting and denial-of-service defense. Deployment examples use Kubernetes Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps.

Sharded services are used for stateful services where data size exceeds a single machine’s capacity. Each shard handles a subset of requests, directed by a root or ambassador. A sharded cache example illustrates how sharding increases the effective cache size and hit rate compared to a replicated cache. The cache’s criticality to system performance and latency is discussed, noting that shard failures can degrade performance. Replicated sharded caches combine replication within each shard to provide resilience and allow independent scaling of hot shards. Deployment examples include a sharded memcached service using a StatefulSet and a twemproxy ambassador, with an alternative of a shared shard routing service that introduces an extra network hop but reduces per-pod complexity.

Wall Street stocks gave up early gains Thursday as bond yields rose and tech stocks retreated. The S&P 500 is on track for its first weekly decline in five as robust earnings are offset by rising yields. The Fed held rates steady amid inflation concerns, and yields rose on data showing tight labor, high factory prices, and rising labor costs. The Dow rose 0.14%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell; financials gained 1%. eBay surged 13.8% after earnings, while PayPal and UPS declined. A method configures hardware for implementing a Deep Neural Network (DNN) that includes an activation module with a programmable lookup table. Calibration data is provided to a representation of the hardware, and inputs to the activation module are monitored to determine a range of input values. Lookup data representing the activation function over that determined range is generated and loaded into the lookup table, configuring the activation module to perform the activation function over that range. The DNN may use the activation module for multiple activation functions, and the providing, monitoring, generating, and loading steps can be repeated for each. The lookup table may store two sets of lookup data, allowing loading of a next activation function concurrently with performing a current one. If an input value falls outside the determined range, the output may be clamped to the value at the closest extreme, or extrapolation from the closest curve may be used. Monitoring may include determining an offset that, when subtracted from each input, centers the range about a predefined value; the activation function then subtracts this offset before lookup. The activation function may interpolate between adjacent data points in the lookup table, using a predefined number of most significant bits as the lookup address and the remaining bits for interpolation. The lookup table may comprise separate data stores for even and odd entries to enable simultaneous lookup of adjacent points. Generating lookup data may involve calculating a set of curves or data points approximating the activation function over the determined range. The range may be determined by identifying maximum and minimum input values or by forming a histogram and selecting bounds that cover a predefined proportion of the input distribution. The determined range may be less than the full possible range given the input bit length, and the number of lookup entries may equal the number of entries in the lookup table. The method may be performed after optimization of the DNN. A data processing system and hardware configured to perform the method are also described.

75% of global honey samples contain neonicotinoids, per a Science study. 45% had two or more compounds, 10% four or five. North America: 86%, Asia: 80%, Europe: 79%. Researchers confirm worldwide bee exposure; coexistence with other pesticides may increase harm.

This study examined whether increasing physical education (PE) hours with cognitively engaging activities improves attention in middle school students. Seventy-five participants from two classes were assigned to an experimental group (Class 6, 4 hours PE/week) or a control group (Class 7, 2 hours PE/week). The PE curriculum included agility drills, coordination circuits, and strategic team games. Attention was assessed using the Bells Test, measuring processing speed (30 seconds) and sustained attention (120 seconds), before and after the intervention. Results showed significant improvements in processing speed for both experimental classes (p < 0.001), while control groups showed no change. Sustained attention improved significantly only in Class 6 (p = 0.012). The study concludes that increased PE hours with strategically designed activities can enhance short-term attention, though benefits for sustained attention were limited. Further research is needed on long-term effects and specific activity contributions.

This review examines multiple studies on new models in higher education. Research on online teaching during COVID-19 assessed service quality dimensions like technological infrastructure and instructor competence. Another study explored leadership spirituality's influence on educational quality in Indonesia. Resistance to change was analyzed as an obstacle to quality in higher education institutions. Factors affecting e-learning quality from students' perspectives were investigated, including technological and pedagogical elements. A gender comparison study examined differential impacts of COVID-19 on male and female students' e-learning experiences. Higher education leaders' perspectives on opportunities and required changes during the pandemic were gathered. A reference model for e-learning interoperability was presented. Studies also covered perceived service quality's influence on student loyalty, e-learning acceptance combining flow theory and technology acceptance models, and merging quality expectations between stakeholders. The relationship between university rankings and academic quality was investigated, along with the pros and cons of rankings, their importance, and their use in combating diploma mills. Other topics included the rise of online learning, equity and inclusion as performance indicators, technology's positive impact, and quality assurance concepts and frameworks. Additional works addressed the UN Sustainable Development Goals in rankings, ISO 21001 for quality assurance, universities shaping the future, career development best practices, virtual universities, ICT-based governance, AI in education, promoting entrepreneurship, the evolution of quality assurance systems, rankings in accreditation, future university orientations, big data in management, recognition of non-formal learning, academic freedom challenges, critiques of rankings, faculty development, Curriculum 4.0, internationalization trends, co-creation in teaching, demonstration for educational quality, and institutional support for online teaching within quality frameworks.

The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has designated Google Search with Strategic Market Status (SMS) under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act, following a 10-month investigation. This first use of the powers allows the regulator to impose measures such as offering users a choice of rival search engines, fair ranking principles, increased data portability, and requiring Google to seek permission for using publishers' content in AI Overviews. The CMA states Google accounts for over 90% of UK search queries and £10 billion in search advertising in 2024. Google responded that interventions could inhibit innovation and force price rises. The regulation affects Google Search's News tab, Top Stories carousel, and Discover, but not Google News or Gemini. The CMA's flexibility is noted as a benefit compared to fixed EU rules.

China will shut down its domestic ivory market by end of 2017. Elephant populations have more than halved in 25 years due to poaching. A 1989 ban failed because legal trade in pre-ban ivory enabled laundering. As the largest ivory market, China's closure is seen as a game changer that could save elephants. China plans to employ carvers on museum pieces and educate the public. The U.S. already restricted ivory trade; the move may influence Vietnam, the UK, and Japan.

The passage describes platinum futures and trading strategies. Platinum futures are standardized, exchange-traded contracts on the CME Globex platform, each representing 50 troy ounces of platinum, settled by physical delivery. A platinum futures strategy uses technical and fundamental analysis to generate entry and exit signals, aiming for speculation, portfolio diversification, or hedging.

Two backtested strategies are provided. The first is a monthly strategy trading both long and short with opposite signals. Combined, it produced 473 trades, an average gain of 0.57%, a win rate of 64%, and a profit factor of 1.7, with returns uncorrelated to the stock market. The second is a seasonal strategy with a volume requirement, trading on a specific day at the open. It yielded 60 trades, a 75% win rate, an average gain of 0.66%, and a profit factor of 2.3. Seasonality observations indicate platinum futures tend to perform better in winter and spring than in summer and fall.

Factors affecting platinum prices include supply and demand, political and economic conditions, production costs, and South Africa’s dominance (about 80% of global supply). Automotive and jewelry demand, as well as the availability of alternatives like palladium, also influence prices. The all-time high for platinum futures was $2308.8 in March 2008, and the all-time low was $267.1 in July 1985.

Contract specifications: tick size is $5.00 per contract, minimum fluctuation is $0.10 per troy ounce, and trading hours are Sunday to Friday 5:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. Central Time with a one-hour halt daily. Trading can be done via a futures broker or a CFD broker. Leverage amplifies risk; for example, with 20x leverage a 5% adverse move can wipe out an account. The passage notes that commodities like platinum are difficult to trade due to macro factors and erratic news, lacking a “natural” edge. It recommends backtesting and diversification, and states that gold is a better long-term investment than platinum. The article concludes that platinum futures can be used for speculation, diversification, or hedging, and the backtests demonstrate that profitable strategies can be found.

In Rockwood School District in Missouri, instead of grouping students across grade levels by reading ability, they keep students in their classroom cohorts for whole-class grade-level instruction. All students, including English multilingual learners and those below benchmarks, participate in daily phonics and comprehension lessons. After whole-group lessons, students move into flexible, needs-based small groups within their grade for reteaching or enrichment, with fluid differentiation based on real-time data. They also use movement as a learning tool, challenge advanced readers with complex texts, and provide scaffolded support for emerging readers. Reading specialists offer targeted interventions. The passage cites a study of nearly 12,000 students showing that low kindergarten reading groups rarely catch up, and notes the "Matthew effect" where lower-track students get less complex instruction. At the end of the 2024-25 school year, Rockwood's kindergarteners outperformed national proficiency averages by up to 17 percentage points, and first and second graders outpaced national averages across nearly every domain. They argue that strong Tier I instruction for all, not ability grouping, prevents gaps.

The President returns without approval a bill to amend immigration laws by adding a literacy test. The bill would exclude immigrants over 16 physically capable but unable to read and write English or another language, with exceptions for certain relatives over 50 or wives/minor children of qualified immigrants. The message calls this a radical departure from the traditional policy of welcoming all immigrants except those posing moral or physical threats, a policy credited with a century of growth through assimilation. It argues that claims of undesirable immigration quality, urban congestion, and labor competition do not justify reversal; unemployment is attributed to business depression, not immigration. The literacy test is criticized as a misleading measure of fitness: illiterate laborers seeking work are safer than educated agitators who incite disorder. The family exception provisions are deemed indefinite and inadequate—they omit siblings, create unclear procedures, and could allow abandonment. The bill also makes it unlawful for male aliens without a declaration of intent to become citizens to work on public works or to come regularly or habitually for manual labor while returning to a foreign country, and penalizes their employment. These sections are called illiberal, narrow, and un-American, especially regarding the northern frontier, risking retaliation and harming citizens. The language “regularly or habitually” and “returning from time to time” is found impossibly vague for a criminal statute. The President concludes the bill is unnecessarily harsh, oppressive, and would cause vexation and harm.

This study introduces GeoSQL-Eval, the first end-to-end automated evaluation framework for assessing large language models (LLMs) on PostGIS query generation tasks. It also constructs GeoSQL-Bench, a benchmark dataset of 14,178 tasks across three categories: 2,380 multiple-choice and true/false questions, 3,744 syntax-level SQL generation questions, and 2,155 table schema retrieval questions. The framework is based on Norman L. Webb’s Depth of Knowledge model and evaluates across four cognitive dimensions and five capability levels. The study evaluates 24 models from six categories. Results show general non-reasoning and reasoning-enhanced models perform best, with reasoning-enhanced models excelling in complex tasks. Key bottlenecks include function call and parameter matching accuracy, and table schema retrieval remains a primary challenge. Primary error types are PostGIS function errors and SQL syntax errors. The study also notes that underspecified prompts significantly degrade model performance.

The national conversation on tutoring has focused on pandemic learning loss, but tutoring done right also cultivates belonging, confidence, and sparks the next generation of teachers. Teach For America’s Ignite Fellowship has reached over 40 communities, trained more than 5,500 virtual tutors, and in the past school year had over 2,000 fellows deliver nearly 200,000 hours of customized learning. Academic results include middle school math test scores growing up to 2.5 times the expected rate and elementary readers growing up to three times faster than average.

Three lessons emerged. First, training and support must be non-negotiable; Ignite provides curriculum-aligned onboarding and ongoing coaching, leading to better student understanding and confidence. Second, technology should expand relationships, not replace them; virtual platforms connect fellows across 43 communities, including rural areas, and human relationships drove a 77-point state assessment score jump in one example. Third, tutoring is a teacher pipeline strategy. Research found working as an Ignite tutor nearly triples the likelihood of applying to TFA’s teacher program, with largest effects among men, people of color, and non-education majors. Since launch, 550 fellows joined TFA’s teaching corps, 280 this year. Tutoring offers direct experience, mentorship, and proof of belonging. Treating tutoring only as an emergency response misses its long-term potential to accelerate learning and leadership, advance student growth, and jump-start educator careers.

Kyle Busch, after winning three consecutive NASCAR Cup races, hopes he isn't peaking too early in the regular season. A win secures a playoff berth, with eliminations leading to four championship contenders. Busch said his momentum is unprecedented, but the season is long. He credits his short-track edge to running his own lower-tier team. He expects a fourth straight win to be difficult at Talladega due to restrictor-plate randomness.

Biosecurity screening software monitors DNA manufacturing orders for harmful proteins. AI can design toxins that evade these filters. A study simulated tests, generating roughly 76,000 blueprints for 72 harmful proteins, including toxins and viral proteins. While original proteins were flagged, many AI-tweaked versions bypassed screening. Software patches improved detection, missing only about 3% of variants, even after genes were fragmented. The work was entirely computational; no physical proteins were created, and it is unknown if the AI-generated variants retained function. Eric Horvitz stressed responsibility with AI advances. James Diggans said malicious protein orders are extremely rare, and screening systems serve as an important bulwark.

In New Orleans' Lower Ninth Ward, Otis Tucker describes the lasting impact of Hurricane Katrina (2005), which killed over 18,000 and destroyed 800,000 homes. Many residents, unable to afford returning, left a neighborhood marked by empty lots, abandoned homes, and gentrification. Since Katrina, the city has adapted to extreme weather: disaster preparation is now routine, with evacuation centers, raised homes, solar panels, and community-taught rain gardens and above-ground planting due to soil contamination. On a larger scale, the Greater New Orleans Urban Water Plan, led by architects Waggonner and Ball, addresses flooding and subsidence by learning from Amsterdam to "live with water," incorporating projects like the Mirabeau Water Garden and green infrastructure. Louisiana's 2017 Coastal Master Plan outlines $50 billion in priority projects, including rebuilding barrier islands and wetlands, sediment diversions, levees, flood gates, and home buyouts, funded partly by local sales taxes. Offshore, oil and gas extraction contributes to land subsidence, while sea level rise—projected at 1 cm per year by 2050—poses a major threat to coastal infrastructure and globally. Tucker, acknowledging unequal resilience, insists that all residents, regardless of means, face the threat together.

At Dumbarton Oaks on October 7, 1944, the U.S., UK, and China informally discussed League of Nations dissolution and transition to the UN, agreeing to exchange papers. The U.S. awaited initiative. In December 1944, the League Supervisory Committee created a Conciliation Committee to confer with a UN Conference group on dissolution and transfer of functions. The Mexican Ambassador requested U.S. expert appointment; no commitment was made pending a UN Conference date. The Supervisory Committee planned a January 19, 1945 meeting on liquidation. The U.S. was to take no initiative, leaving the matter for the UN Conference unless the UK or China acted. On January 31, 1945, at an informal meeting with American republics, the Acting Secretary emphasized the Dumbarton Oaks Proposals' importance and hoped for progress before the Mexico City Conference. Dr. Pasvolsky commented. The Chilean Ambassador corrected the December 29 minutes regarding the phrase "assuring respect for international treaties," stating it was essential but placement undecided. Mr. Rockefeller suggested drafting a statement; Señor Mora preferred recording his words in the current minutes.

The induced graph removal lemma states that for every graph H and ε>0, there exists δ>0 such that if an n-vertex graph has fewer than δ n^{v(H)} induced copies of H, it can be made induced H-free by adding or removing fewer than ε n² edges. The standard regularity proof for the triangle removal lemma fails here because irregular pairs cannot simply be removed; adding edges is also required, which breaks the counting lemma. To address this, a strong regularity lemma is introduced. It produces a pair of partitions P and Q (Q refines P) such that P is ε₀-regular, Q is ε_{|P|}-regular (extremely regular), and the energy difference between P and Q is small. The proof iterates Szemerédi’s regularity lemma using energy increments, yielding tower-type bounds. A corollary gives an equitable partition with subsets W_i inside V_i where all pairs W_i W_j (including i=j) are regular, and edge densities between V_i and V_j approximate those between W_i and W_j for most pairs. Using this corollary, the induced removal lemma is proved: partition the graph, clean by adding/removing edges between V_i,V_j based on densities between W_i,W_j (total changes < ε n²), then if an induced H remains, the counting lemma applied to the W_i’s yields many induced copies of H in the original graph, a contradiction. The lecture also notes a colorful version with r-edge-colorings, the infinite removal lemma (handling infinitely many forbidden induced subgraphs with a finite bound H₀), and a connection to property testing: the triangle removal lemma implies a constant-query randomized tester for triangle-freeness, and the infinite removal lemma implies every hereditary graph property is testable with one-sided error using an oblivious tester.

The passage describes two investment strategies: dollar-cost averaging, which invests fixed amounts at regular intervals to smooth volatility, and lump sum investing, which invests a large amount all at once to capitalize on long-term market growth. It then outlines a backtest of a lump sum buy & hold strategy using a diversified portfolio of five equally weighted asset classes (U.S. stocks, foreign stocks, U.S. bonds, U.S. REITs, world commodities) via liquid ETFs with long histories. Backtesting conditions and performance metrics are listed but not populated. The conclusion states that historically, lump sum investing offers a higher probability of success over long-term horizons, and starting earlier yields greater profits, with the impact of financial crises becoming insignificant over time.

Higher-order Feynman diagrams, such as a self-energy correction loop, lead to an integral that diverges logarithmically, resulting in infinity. This is problematic because physical quantities like cross-sections and lifetimes should not be infinite. Introducing a cutoff scale still leaves an infinite contribution from the cutoff to infinity. However, by redefining, re-scaling, or re-normalizing physical objects, one can express physical values as a bare mass or coupling plus a correction. Although corrections at infinite scale are infinite, experiments are performed at a specific scale, so this issue is not a real problem when comparing theory to experiment. Couplings run as a function of energy scale, shown as a logarithm of energy for electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions. They all depend on scale and do not converge at very high mass scales. Introducing new particles would alter the running behavior, leading to the idea that new physics could unify all couplings at a specific scale into a unified theory. Physical masses and couplings are evaluated at a specific scale and run with scale.

The passage comprises a collection of news headlines and articles dated June 5, 2001. Topics include the California energy crisis, with a PBS "Frontline" documentary, federal price mitigation plans, and a state Senate committee issuing subpoenas to power generators including Enron. Enron's Dabhol power project in India is the subject of a lenders' meeting to salvage the project amid a payment dispute with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board. Enron withdrew from a Saudi Arabian natural gas venture, and Marathon took its 20% stake. Other items mention Enron in connection with a Connecticut fuel cell project, newsprint market activity, and a Bush aide's delayed stock sale involving Enron shares.

NeoWorld is a deep learning framework that constructs an infinitely expandable, interactive virtual world from a single image. It uses a hybrid object-centric scene representation: background regions are rendered as lightweight 2D Gaussian layers, while foreground objects are progressively reconstructed into full 3D models based on user exploration or prompts. An object-centric codebook binds instance-level semantics to Gaussians, and an image-to-3D module with coarse-to-fine alignment integrates 3D objects. A large language model interprets natural language commands to enable object manipulation and physics-based animation. Experiments show NeoWorld outperforms prior 2D, 2.5D, and 3D world generation methods in 3D consistency, scene quality, and user interaction, while maintaining computational efficiency. Limitations include cascading errors from upstream modules such as segmentation, alignment, or LLM misinterpretation.

The cup and handle pattern is a bullish continuation chart formation resembling a cup with a handle. It consists of a U-shaped cup that forms after a price rally, with a rounded bottom, and a handle that develops as a slight downward drift on the right side. The pattern completes when price breaks out from the handle's trading range, signaling continuation of the prior uptrend. William O'Neil first described the pattern in his 1988 book "How to Make Money in Stocks" and incorporated it into his CANSLIM method. Qualifying criteria include: occurring in an existing trend, a U-shaped cup with a 30-50% retracement depth, a handle, and a breakout above the handle's resistance. An inverted cup and handle pattern forms in a downtrend, with an inverted cup (dome-shaped) and a handle drifting upward, signaling continuation of the downtrend.

Backtest results are mixed. A backtest by Ali Akhtari on S&P 500 stocks from 2016-2018 showed the strategy underperformed the S&P 500 but had good metrics due to low market exposure. Thomas Bulkowski's manual backtest of 500 stocks over five years found a 26% failure rate (above his 20% acceptable threshold) and an average gain of 38% (below his 40% preference). Waiting for an upside breakout reduced the failure rate to 10%. Bulkowski considered the pattern inferior to many others. The passage notes difficulty in creating a fully quantified strategy and takes Bulkowski's findings with caution.

Traders identify the pattern by its distinct shape: a rounded bottom cup representing consolidation, a rise to the prior peak (rim), then a handle as a minor pullback with lower volume, not dipping below the cup's midpoint. Breakout above the rim with increased volume confirms the pattern. It can appear across timeframes and markets (stocks, forex, commodities), and traders may use additional indicators like moving averages, RSI, or MACD for confirmation. Duration varies from months to over a year for the cup, and weeks to months for the handle. Volume typically declines during the cup's formation, increases on the right side recovery, declines again during the handle, and spikes on breakout. Stop-loss orders are often placed just below the handle's lowest point or the cup's bottom, after the handle completes and breakout occurs. Common mistakes include entering before full pattern confirmation, ignoring volume, setting inaccurate profit targets/stop-losses, neglecting broader market context, and relying solely on the pattern without other indicators. The pattern fits into a broader strategy as a bullish signal, best used in bullish markets, combined with other technical and fundamental analysis. It may offer insights into long-term trends, reflecting consolidation and investor sentiment, but its effectiveness varies with market conditions, timeframe, and volume. Market volatility affects formation: high volatility makes the pattern erratic and less reliable, while low to moderate volatility yields clearer, more reliable formations. Psychologically, the pattern reflects a cycle from pessimism (price drop) to optimism (recovery), with the handle representing a final test of conviction, driven by fear and greed.

The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2MSPS data acquisition system. Each analog input channel includes an internal clamp protection circuit allowing swings up to ±18V; beyond that, the clamp turns on while operating from a single 5V supply. Input current must not exceed ±10mA, and a series resistor can limit current while also forming an antialiasing low-pass filter with a capacitor. Matching external source impedance on the AINxP and AINxM pins cancels additional offset error.

Every channel has a programmable gain amplifier (PGA) supporting single-ended and differential inputs with bipolar signal swing. The analog input range is independently configurable via RANGE_CHx register fields. An antialiasing low-pass filter follows the PGA, with programmable corner frequencies selectable through the ANA_BW bits. A wide-common-mode voltage rejection circuit supports common-mode voltages up to ±12V, with the range configurable for differential and single-ended inputs. On power-up or reset, the common-mode range defaults to ±12V (CM_CTRL_EN = 0b). The common-mode voltage for differential inputs is defined as the average of the voltages on AINP and AINM.

The ADC outputs 20-bit conversion data in straight-binary or two’s-complement format, selected via the DATA_FORMAT register bits. The LSB size depends on the selected analog input range. The device operates with a differential or single-ended free-running continuous sampling clock. After a sampling clock is applied, the ADC generates valid output data, data clock (DCLKOUT), and frame clock (FCLKOUT) after a specified time. Stopping the sampling clock invalidates these outputs. A positive pulse on the SMPL_SYNC pin, centered around the falling edge of SMPL_CLK, synchronizes multiple ADS9803 devices, aligning the internal channel selection logic and FCLKOUT to the data frame. Synchronization is required once after power-up, after restarting the sampling clock, or after a device reset.

The device contains a precision, low-drift internal voltage reference. A 10µF ceramic bypass capacitor on the REFIO pin filters reference noise. An external reference can be connected to REFIO; the internal reference is disabled either by writing PD_REF = 1b via SPI or by setting the SDI/EXTREF pin to logic 0 when SPI is disabled.

The data interface supports 2-lane and 4-lane modes with single-data-rate (SDR) and double-data-rate (DDR) options. The ADC provides source-synchronous data, DCLKOUT, and FCLKOUT. The 20-bit conversion result is output MSB first in a 24-bit packet with the last six bits as zeroes. Data clock frequency depends on sampling speed, data rate, and number of lanes; frame clock frequency equals sampling clock frequency divided by four.

A data output randomizer can be enabled, performing a bit-wise XOR of the conversion result with either the LSB of the result or a PRBS bit, reducing ground bounce correlation with the analog input. Two data averaging modes are available: simple averaging reduces output data rate by a factor of two, while moving average does not affect the data rate. Test patterns (fixed, digital ramp, alternating) can replace output data for interface debugging, configurable per channel groups CH[4:1] and CH[8:5].

The device is powered down via the RESET pin or register, and a power-down mode is entered with the PWDN pin or PD_CH register field. After power-up or reset, an initialization sequence of register writes is required, with a free-running sampling clock present. User-defined configuration changes include analog input range, bandwidth, common-mode voltage range, and data interface settings.

A speed-boost mode allows up to 8MSPS sampling rate for a user-selected analog input channel pair, while the other six channels are idle. The sampling rate equals the sampling clock frequency, and the selected pair is converted on every clock.

Configuration is done through a SPI interface with three register banks. Register writes involve selecting the bank via address 0x03, then writing to the desired register. Register reads require enabling read mode and using two 24-bit frames. Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology, with daisy-chain length configured in the DAISY_CHAIN_LEN register. Daisy-chain writes require N × 24 SCLKs, and reads involve specific sequences to retrieve register data.

The ADS9803 is suited for ATE applications, offering high precision with total unadjusted error (TUE) of 0.0015% at 25°C ±5°C post-calibration. It supports external switches or multiplexers, with wide-bandwidth mode settling to 99.95% of full-scale in 7.5µs. Power supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) have no required sequence; decoupling capacitors are recommended. Layout guidance includes avoiding digital/analog signal crossing, placing bypass capacitors close to pins, and connecting GND and REFM to a ground plane with short connections.

A whole-body physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed to simulate the distribution of four first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) at extrapulmonary sites, particularly pleura and lymph nodes. The model extended a previous PBPK model by adding a consolidated lymph node compartment and a pleural space sub-compartment. Tissue:plasma partition coefficients were calculated using the Rodgers and Rowland method. Pharmacokinetic parameters (absorption rate, systemic clearance, lung tissue/blood partition coefficient) were estimated by fitting model outputs to reported plasma and lung concentration data. The model was validated using separate plasma concentration data and limited lung tissue data, showing reasonable agreement. Simulations predicted time-dependent drug concentrations in various tissues. Rifampicin and isoniazid generally exceeded their critical concentrations in most compartments, though the model over-predicted rifampicin pleural concentrations. Ethambutol did not reach its critical concentration in brain, kidney, bone, and skin. Pyrazinamide failed to achieve its critical concentration in any simulated organ, even when considering a lower MIC at acidic pH. Isoniazid concentrations varied with acetylator status; slow acetylators maintained higher levels. The model is a first step in incorporating lymph nodes into PBPK models for TB and may help evaluate EPTB treatment regimens. Limitations include assumptions of no drug-drug interactions, no rifampicin autoinduction, and a simplified single lymph node compartment.

Researchers from South Korea and Taiwan harmonized data from the CRCS-K and TREAT-AIS registries to form the K-T collaborative EVT registry, comprising 9,941 EVT-treated acute ischemic stroke patients (7,835 from Korea, 2,106 from Taiwan). Taiwanese patients were older, had higher prevalence of vascular risk factors, more severe strokes, lower pre-stroke functional independence, longer treatment times, and lower rates of IV thrombolysis. Successful recanalization rates were similar (84.0% vs. 80.0%), but 90-day functional independence was lower in Taiwan (34.7% vs. 41.1%) and 90-day mortality higher in Korea (14.2% vs. 6.2%). Age strongly influenced outcomes: patients ≥80 years had lower functional recovery (18.1% vs. 46.9%), higher mortality (19.7% vs. 10.5%), and lower recanalization success (78.6% vs. 81.9%), while symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage rates did not differ significantly by age. The relationship between age and functional recovery/mortality was nonlinear, most pronounced between 75–85 years. Pre-stroke functional independence and bridging IV thrombolysis were key predictors of improved outcomes in elderly patients. The registry highlights real-world EVT practice differences in East Asia and suggests that carefully selected elderly patients can still benefit from EVT.

The lecture introduces probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs), which convert an NP witness into a polynomially larger proof that can be verified by querying only a few random bits. The verifier is a nonadaptive probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine using r random bits and q queries. The goal is a PCP for all NP with polylog(n) query and randomness complexity, completeness 1, and soundness 1/2. The construction uses the GKR protocol: for a 3SAT instance, the prover computes low-degree extensions of all circuit layers and, for every layer i and point z, provides all possible sumcheck transcripts for every possible verifier randomness, forming a tree of size polynomial in the circuit size because the field F and dimension m are chosen so that F^{3m} is polynomial. The verifier runs GKR using the oracle as the prover’s fixed strategy, and at the end checks the input layer via the provided low-degree extension of the witness. Soundness follows from sumcheck soundness and a union bound over the 2d sumchecks, requiring F to be polylog(s). A low-degree test is needed for the input layer since the verifier does not hold the witness. The construction relies on sumcheck protocols and parameter engineering to keep the PCP polynomial size.

Image registration is a non-linear inverse problem that aligns images by finding a coordinate transform. The objective minimizes a cost function plus a regularizer. Modern pipelines use affine and deformable transforms, resulting in a composite transform with a displacement field. Common cost functions include mean squared error, localized normalized cross correlation (LNCC), and mutual information (MI). Registration is fundamental for multimodal data fusion, morphometric analysis, and atlas construction, but current methods struggle with high-resolution images due to memory and computational limits.

The paper identifies three memory bottlenecks in image registration: deformable interpolation/warp composition, cross-correlation loss, and mutual information loss. To address these on a single GPU, it proposes fused CUDA kernels: a composite implicit grid sampler that avoids materializing additional grids in HBM, reducing memory overhead from O(n) to O(1); an implicit Parzen windowing for MI that uses shared memory to compute histograms without materializing large Parzen blocks, achieving O(1) additional HBM usage; and an efficient fused LNCC kernel that reduces intermediate variable storage and computes gradients in-place, yielding up to 76.5% memory reduction.

For multi-GPU scaling, the paper introduces a distributed framework with Grid Parallel (GP), which shards tensors across hosts and provides boundary synchronization for convolution operations, and a distributed ring sampler that decomposes bilinear/trilinear interpolation into partial sums over image shards communicated in a ring topology, avoiding an allgather of the moving image. Distributed loss functions (MSE, LNCC, MI) are adapted to compute correct aggregates across shards.

Experiments show that the fused kernels accelerate existing registration workflows: training TransMorph with LNCC is 6.1× faster and uses 16.5% less memory; MI memory usage is reduced by 24.7%. For optimization-based FireANTs, MI memory savings reach 95.2% with 2.6× speedup, and LNCC achieves up to 7.5× speedup over FastLNCC with 44–59% lower memory. The framework registers a 250µm in-vivo MRI to a 100µm ex-vivo FLASH volume (over 11.8B parameters) in about one minute on 8 GPUs. On a simulated 250µm dataset, the method outperforms patch-based and downsampling baselines, improving Dice by 18.1 points and reducing Hausdorff distance by 62.1% at native resolution, while being Pareto-efficient in accuracy vs. compute cost. Ablations confirm O(1) HBM overhead for grid sampler and MI kernels, significant speedups for LNCC, and that Grid Parallel boundary synchronization is necessary to avoid artifacts. Weak scaling shows peak memory independent of GPU count when using the ring sampler.

The paper investigates the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Big Data (BD), and Advanced Analytics (AA) in digital business platforms, aiming to develop a multidimensional data-driven AI innovation taxonomy framework. It addresses a gap in managerial perspectives on AI innovation. The methodology uses an iterative combination of conceptual-to-empirical and empirical-to-conceptual approaches, with qualitative data from literature review and semi-structured expert interviews with members of the Russian National Technology Initiative. A micro-level AI/BD/AA value chain is created, modeling high-level activities: AI Awareness/Big Data Acquisition, Measurement of AI/Big Data Curation, AI Reporting and Interpretation/Big Data Storage, and AI Decision making/Big Data Usage. A multidimensional framework is developed, adopting a five-level AI maturity model (Human Led/Initial Analytics through Machine Controlled/Advanced Analytics IV) that describes organizational characteristics and human-machine interaction. Each maturity level corresponds to parts of the value chain. The framework evaluates data-driven human-machine relationships and applies AI at different automation scopes. The paper also notes that data and analytics infuse seven overlapping digital platform areas. The framework can be used to identify use cases for AI-based automation and communicate the value of AI capabilities, while highlighting the importance of ethical considerations.

This passage is an excerpt from the AMD Geode™ CS5535 Companion Device Silicon Revision A3 Specification Update, dated March 2006. It documents multiple errata (items 100 through 116, plus an initial SSMI issue) affecting the CS5535 chip. Issues include: SSMI events not being synchronous if an IRQ occurs simultaneously; UDMA transfers failing if the IDE bus master is enabled before sending a PIO command packet; most wake event inputs not functioning from the ACPI S3 state; RTC CMOS RAM returning incorrect data after specific access sequences; block and demand mode legacy DMA blocking I/O to LPC devices; USB controller clock gating causing register read failures; ATAPI packet commands failing after bus master enable; the AuxOutputfull bit in the keyboard emulation logic being incorrectly cleared; tACK bits not affecting UDMA timing as expected; ATAC hangs if PRD addresses are not DWORD aligned; LPC aborts on certain sync patterns; the SMB controller's NEGACK bit behaving incorrectly; the retry counter counting all PCI retries instead of only its own; GPIO High Bank Feature Bit Registers failing after suspend; SMBus hold time being too short; missing LOWBAT_FLAG after abnormal standby; and Sleep_X not deasserting if delay counters exceed the PM_SED delay. For most issues, resolutions or workarounds are provided, such as using specific programming sequences, disabling features, or employing external circuitry.

This study investigated the impact of mydriasis on image gradability and AI performance for diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening using the Phelcom Eyer portable fundus camera. It included 327 patients who underwent retinal imaging before and after dilation with tropicamide 0.5% eyedrops. In the mydriatic group, 82.1% of images were gradable, compared to 55.6% in the non-mydriatic group (P<0.001). In non-mydriatic images, systemic hypertension, older age, longer diabetes duration, and male gender were significantly associated with lower gradability; Indigenous race also showed a significant association with lower image quality.

A ResNet-200d model trained on the mydriatic mBRSET dataset was evaluated on 597 paired gradable images. For DR detection, the mydriatic group achieved 82.91% accuracy, F1 score 0.83, and AUC 0.94, while the non-mydriatic group had 79.23% accuracy, F1 0.79, and AUC 0.93. The mydriatic group had fewer false positives (13.9% vs. 17.8%) but slightly more false negatives (3.2% vs. 3.0%). A Chi-square test showed no statistically significant difference between groups (P=0.3279). The study notes a 44.4% ungradable rate for non-mydriatic portable images, higher than reported tabletop camera rates. Limitations include a learning curve for handheld use, selection bias from analyzing only paired images, and limited generalizability due to a single dataset and camera model.

Ulysses S. Gandy appealed his second manslaughter conviction, which resulted in a ten-year sentence. The case arose from a 1976 two-car collision on Highway 25. Gandy drove south, Daniel Palmer north; Palmer and his two passengers died. Only Gandy witnessed the collision. Testimony conflicted on the cars' post-impact positions: one witness placed the Toyota in the northbound lane and the Pontiac in the southbound lane with a wheel on the center line; others said both vehicles were in the northbound lane with debris concentrated there. Evidence on Gandy's intoxication also conflicted. Some witnesses smelled no alcohol and a doctor and nurse noted alertness; nine witnesses testified to strong alcohol odors, slurred speech, and beer cans/whiskey bottle in Gandy's car, with several concluding he was intoxicated. Gandy had consumed beer earlier that day.

The court addressed four assignments of error. First, it held the evidence sufficient to support the verdict, as the jury resolves conflicts and could reasonably find Gandy was intoxicated and in the wrong lane, establishing culpable negligence under Miss. Code § 97-3-47. Second, refusal of jury instruction D-13 on intoxication factors was not reversible error because other instructions adequately covered the issue. Third, admission of sketches (Exhibits 1, 5, 7) illustrating witnesses' personal observations of the scene was not an abuse of discretion, unlike the prior trial where sketches reconstructed impact. Fourth, the court found no merit in the claim that the jury should have been given a food recess during its 2-hour-50-minute deliberation, as jurors could have requested one and no authority was cited. The conviction was affirmed.

The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2MSPS data acquisition system. It provides simple and moving data averaging to improve SNR; simple averaging halves the output data rate, while moving averaging does not affect it. Test patterns (fixed, digital ramp, and alternating) can replace ADC output for debugging, configured via registers in bank 1 for channel groups CH[4:1] and CH[8:5]. The device can be powered down using the RESET or PWDN pins or register writes, with registers returning to defaults. After power-up or reset, an initialization sequence of register writes is required, using a free-running sampling clock. User settings can adjust analog input range, bandwidth, common-mode voltage, and data interface lanes. A speed-boost mode enables up to 8MSPS sampling on a selected channel pair while other channels are idle. The SPI configuration interface uses 16-bit registers across three banks, with bank selection via register 0x03. Write and read procedures are defined, including a daisy-chain topology for multiple devices, where the daisy-chain length is set in a register. Registers control test patterns, data format, averaging, XOR operations, gain error correction, power-down, bandwidth, reference, and speed-boost. In ATE applications, the device achieves a post-calibration total unadjusted error of 0.0015% and fast settling to 99.95% full-scale in 7.5µs in wide-bandwidth mode. Power supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) have no sequencing requirement, and layout guidelines recommend decoupling capacitors and separation of analog and digital signals.

A Vanderbilt-led team reported in Nature Materials a tenfold improvement in hyperlensing resolution using isotopically purified hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). Hyperlenses resolve objects smaller than light's wavelength. Previous hBN resolution was about 36 times below the infrared wavelength (smallest bacteria size). The new purified crystal could image objects as small as 30 nanometers. Natural boron's two isotopes degrade infrared optical properties; using 99% isotopically pure boron reduced optical losses, tripled surface phonon polariton lifetime and travel distance, significantly enhancing resolution. Hyperlenses aim to image living cells in natural environments with harmless low-energy light, unlike electron/atomic-force microscopes, and provide spectroscopic fingerprinting. Theoretical analysis suggests another tenfold improvement is possible. Researchers are testing small flakes and expect larger crystals to yield further gains.

The passage explains how to beat the offside trap in soccer. Defenders executing the trap move up to place attackers offside. To beat it, attackers must first recognize the trap (via scouting or frequent offside calls), then adjust to avoid offside and exploit space behind defenders. Patience is required: avoid running offside, don't interfere if offside, and use specific tactics. Tactics include: Dribble Through (fake a pass to bait the trap, then dribble); Through Pass (receiver stays onside, pass made before offside); Horizontal/Lateral Run (stay ahead of the next-to-last defender, then break toward goal at a 90-degree angle); Checking Run (run back toward the ball carrier); Pass Short (set up near the ball carrier to enable a give-and-go or long ball); Deep-Lying Run (midfielder sprints past defenders, pass timed before offside); Bending Run (start run toward halfway line to stay onside); Back-Pass (buys time for runs); Delay for Time (square passes/possession negate the trap); Delayed Run (wait to make runs, causing defenders to forget); Designated “Non-Runner” (especially on free kicks, fake a run and receive a short pass). Coaching tips: use fakes before free kicks to reveal the trap; if a defender fails to move up, the trap fails and attackers should exploit it. Success leads to a one-on-one with the goalkeeper; beating the trap once often discourages its further use.

A study in Pediatrics found that from 1990 to 2015, nearly 17,000 children under 6 were treated in ERs for window blind injuries. Grief is an emotional reaction to the loss of someone or something you care about. It is a highly personal experience, unique to each individual. Grief can be triggered not only by death but also by significant life changes, such as becoming a carer, a decline in health, retirement, or moving out of a family home. Anticipatory grief may occur before an impending loss, like a terminal diagnosis, allowing time to say goodbye and prepare. The terminally ill person also grieves. Moving home can cause grief, especially if it holds precious memories; if forced after a partner's death, the person faces two sources of grief. It is advised to defer major moving decisions for several months after bereavement, as memories may later become comforting. Moving to a new area may increase loneliness if it cuts off local support networks. The grieving process after a death is complex and variable, not a set sequence of stages. Emotions depend on factors like life experience, circumstances of death, and personality. Common reactions include feeling numb, denial, acceptance and relief, yearning and searching, repeating the event, restlessness and disturbed sleep, loss of confidence, guilt, anger, and profound sadness or depression. Support may wane over time, and sadness can lead to crying, lethargy, and neglect of tasks. It is normal to feel this way; ask for help from friends, family, or a GP if needed. There is no set duration for grief; time alone does not heal, but eventually good days outnumber bad days. The intense period does not last forever. Information on coping and bereavement support is available.

This study investigated neural noise in Tourette syndrome (TS) by measuring trial-by-trial variability in EEG responses to median nerve stimulation (MNS). Participants were 19 adults with TS and 19 matched healthy controls. Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) were recorded at electrode CP3. Early and mid-latency SEP component amplitudes, timing, and topographies did not differ between groups, except for a 1 ms delay in P1 and a significantly increased P2 (P100) component in the TS group. Trial-by-trial variability (standard deviation) was substantially higher in the TS group throughout the epoch, but the coefficient of variation decreased similarly in both groups following stimulation. Power spectral density analysis showed flatter 1/f slopes in the TS group at high-beta and gamma frequencies, indicating increased neural noise. Inter-trial phase coherence increased after stimulation for both groups, but the TS group exhibited a shallower early rise in alpha, beta, and gamma coherence, and sustained alpha coherence was shorter; beta coherence was increased in the TS group around the P100 timing. Clinical correlations: P2 amplitude was positively associated with tic impairment; change in alpha coherence was associated with motor tic severity; change in gamma coherence and change in coefficient of variation were associated with premonitory urge scores; mean variability and high-frequency PSD were associated with IQ. The findings suggest that trial-by-trial recruitment of sensorimotor neuronal populations is less stable at rest in TS but normalizes in response to stimulation, and that increased P100 may reflect altered central processing linked to tactile hypersensitivity.

The article describes Enron's rise and fall. Less than a year prior, the Houston energy company had money, power, and a CEO aiming to be the world's most important company.
