Enron's headquarters projected modernity and ambition, with a young, diverse workforce and a goal to become "The World's Leading Company." The company transformed from a troubled pipeline firm in 1985 into a trading colossus by 2000, with a stock price increase of 1,700% and revenues from $40 billion to $100 billion. This was largely driven by Skilling, a consultant hired by then-CEO Ken Lay. Skilling created the "Gas Bank," guaranteeing gas supply and price, making Enron a market-maker. Despite initial skepticism, it succeeded, and Enron expanded into trading electricity and other commodities.

Skilling built a culture around intellectual capital, hiring aggressive top-school graduates through rigorous "Super Saturdays." Employees received perks like concierge services, gyms, and massages, with uncapped merit-based bonuses. The Performance Review Committee enforced forced ranking, replacing 15% of the workforce annually ("rank and yank"). The culture prioritized immediate profits, used aggressive accounting (mark-to-market on its own terms, booking multi-year profits upfront), and referred to customers as "counterparties." Success bred internal competition and a mercenary atmosphere. Enron entered broadband and online trading, and announced a video-on-demand deal with Blockbuster.

Problems mounted: the California energy crisis portrayed Enron as a villain, and Skilling made insensitive jokes. The India power plant project was troubled. The telecom division imploded with the tech bubble. Analysts questioned accounting, and the stock fell from $80 to around $35. After a personal epiphany about life's brevity, Skilling abruptly resigned in August 2001 after six months as CEO, citing missed personal life. Ken Lay returned, promising a refocused, gentler Enron. Skilling, still holding most of his net worth in Enron stock, looked to new ventures, believing in a "second wave" of technology.

This paper surveys ontologies and ontology design patterns (ODPs) for process modeling in Materials Science and Engineering (MSE). It defines three domain-specific requirements: Process Structure (organization of steps, sub-processes, execution order), Data and Resources (inputs, outputs, parameters like temperature and pressure), and Project Goals and Participant Roles (collaborations, milestones, agent responsibilities). Based on these, process-related ODPs are manually extracted from relevant ontologies: P-PLAN supports Process and Resource ODPs; Metadata4Ing supports Resource and Project ODPs; OPMW supports Process and Resource ODPs; WILD supports only Process ODP; General Process Ontology (GPO) supports Process and Resource ODPs; PMDcore supports all three ODP categories. A baseline method for automatic ODP extraction is introduced, using sentence transformer embeddings to compute semantic similarity between requirement sentences and ontology concept descriptions, then applying a threshold to retrieve relevant IRIs. ROBOT-based modular extraction (STAR method with no intermediates) generates compact ontology modules. Evaluation against manually curated ground truth shows P-PLAN achieved the highest F1-scores for Process (0.59) and Resource (0.53) ODPs, while PMDcore supported all three ODPs with F1-scores of 0.36 (Process), 0.21 (Resource), and 0.25 (Project). Limitations include bias from annotation quality and requirement phrasing, and the independent processing of each ontology hinders identification of cross-ontology patterns. Future work aims to expand to additional MSE subdomains, integrate ontology mappings, mitigate biases, and develop a platform for publishing extracted patterns.

In July 2021, Public Health Wales received notification of two salmonella gastroenteritis cases who had attended an Eid al-Adha celebration barbecue in a Cardiff park. An outbreak investigation was initiated after further cases were identified. Cases were defined as individuals with diarrhoea and/or vomiting with onset on the day of the barbecue and an epidemiological link to the event. A cohort study of 36 people attending the barbecue and an associated lunchtime event was undertaken, along with a nested case-control study using Firth logistic regression.

Consumption of a traditional raw liver dish, ‘marrara’, at the barbecue was the most likely vehicle for infection (Firth logistic regression, aOR: 49.99, 95%CI 1.71-1461.54, p=0.02). Meat came from two local butchers with the same supplier, and food samples yielded whole genome sequences identical to those from cases. In total, 22 cases were identified, all symptomatic, with an attack rate of 51% among the social network. The epidemic curve suggested a point source, with most symptom onset the day after the barbecue, and five later cases suggestive of person-to-person transmission. Over half of cases sought emergency hospital care, and six were admitted. Univariate analysis showed an association between raw liver consumption at the barbecue and being a case (RR=2.5, 95%CI 1.46–4.28). Firth regression confirmed raw liver as the significant risk factor, while lamb and spicy sauce were not significant after stratification. Microbiological results confirmed Salmonella Typhimurium; five sequenced cases were genetically indistinguishable (0 SNP). Food samples of raw lamb and environmental samples from butchers and the abattoir yielded sequences identical to human isolates.

A communication campaign sensitive to cultural practices was developed in collaboration with the community, community liaison staff, and the Public Health Wales communications team. This included educational sessions and food safety infographics shared in multiple languages. The outbreak highlights the need for appropriate food hygiene advice in communities preparing traditional dishes. It identified a new vehicle of interest, a traditional raw offal dish. Future outbreak investigations, particularly where cultural events are associated with particular foods, should consider dishes beyond those on routine questionnaires to those relevant to the community.

A blitz is a defensive play sending five or more defenders directly into the offensive backfield to attack the ball carrier and disrupt the offense, compared to the typical four-player rush. Blitzes can involve five to eight players rushing the quarterback at the snap, creating risk by leaving fewer defenders to cover receivers. Mobile quarterbacks can evade blitzes, but a well-timed blitz can be catastrophic for the offense. Defensive coordinators call blitzes to outsmart the offense and get the defense off the field quickly. Types include: conventional blitz (five-plus rushers with man coverage), zone blitz (linebacker blitzes while a lineman drops into coverage to confuse blocking), safety blitz (safety rushes, risking a deep gap), cornerback blitz (cornerback rushes, gambling on quick pressure), zero blitz (no deep safety, used when anticipating a run), and run blitz (disrupting the run game by sending defenders to the point of attack). Offenses beat the blitz with quick passes, often targeting the running back on short routes; mobile quarterbacks dodging rushers; and max protection schemes where extra blockers stay in, leaving man coverage downfield. Quarterbacks must identify the blitz and locate the open receiver quickly.

Non-formal training includes library visits, conferences, and mentorship programmes. Although the Law of Libraries mandates allocating 5% of personnel expenses to training, few libraries comply; only 10% of 2016 post-graduation students received institutional financial support.

The Occupational Standard “Librarian (higher education),” developed by the National Library of Romania and acknowledged by the National Authority for Qualifications, details required competences (communication, IT, learning, social, civic, entrepreneurial, cultural, organisational, health/safety, environmental, document management) and professional activities (collection development, recording, cataloguing, storage, communication, automation, valorisation, scientific research, methodology, management, promotion). The standard serves as a national assessment tool for employment and promotion. Conclusions recommend adding competences in internationalisation, information literacy, reading promotion, and psycho-pedagogical skills. Negative stereotyping of the profession hinders lifelong learning’s benefits, so LIS programmes and methodological libraries must develop strategies to better represent new competences.

The passage describes several container and distributed system patterns. The adapter pattern uses an adapter container to modify an application container's interface to conform to a predefined common interface, such as for monitoring, logging, or health checks. This enables heterogeneous applications to present consistent interfaces. Examples include using Prometheus exporters for monitoring, Fluentd for log normalization, and health-check adapters for databases.

Replicated load-balanced services consist of identical stateless servers behind a load balancer, providing redundancy and horizontal scaling. Readiness probes inform the load balancer when an instance is ready. Session-tracked services route all requests from a user to the same replica, often via consistent hashing. Application-layer replicated services can add caching layers (e.g., Varnish) and SSL termination (e.g., nginx) as separate replicated tiers.

Sharded services partition data so each shard handles a subset of requests, used for stateful services where data exceeds single-machine capacity. A sharding function (often hash-based) maps requests to shards; consistent hashing minimizes remapping when shards change. Sharded caches improve memory utilization. Replicated sharded caches combine replication within each shard for fault tolerance and scaling. Hot sharding dynamically redistributes shards to handle uneven load.

The scatter/gather pattern parallelizes request processing by distributing work to all leaf nodes, each returning partial results that the root combines. It can be used with sharding when data is too large for a single leaf. The pattern faces straggler problems and overhead, so the 99th percentile latency is critical. Replicated sharded scatter/gather adds reliability.

Functions and event-driven processing (FaaS) enable request- or event-driven execution. Benefits include simplified deployment and automatic scaling, but challenges include debugging complexity, unsuitability for long-running background tasks or large in-memory data, and cost at high request volumes. Patterns include the decorator pattern for request/response transformation (e.g., adding defaults), event handling (e.g., two-factor authentication), and event-based pipelines.

This paper proposes a formal model that integrates framing effects into information design, combining classic Bayesian persuasion with the ability to influence a receiver's prior belief through natural language framing. The sender can choose a framing c from a space C, which induces a belief µc via a belief oracle ℓ, and may also commit to a recommendation scheme. Three optimization variants are defined: recommendation-only (fixed framing), framing-only (fixed recommendation), and joint framing and recommendation. Theoretical analysis, assuming access to a noisy LLM-based belief oracle, shows that framing-only optimization is problematic: the sender's utility is discontinuous in the induced belief, and the problem is NP-hard even to approximate. In contrast, joint optimization yields a continuous utility function and admits a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS), making it more tractable. Empirically, the authors implement a hill-climbing method using LLMs (GPT-4o-mini) to both optimize framing and serve as the belief oracle, combined with analytical recommendation optimization. Two case studies—a realtor pitching to buyers and a clothing brand's advertising campaign—demonstrate the approach's effectiveness when evaluated by the LLM's reactions. A human subject study confirms that the predictions are directionally correct and approximate the effect magnitude, though with more variance. The work concludes that joint optimization of framing and recommendation holds major promise for systematic, algorithmically driven persuasive communication, while framing-only remains computationally challenging.

The lecture covers numerical methods for the second-order wave equation. It presents the equation as a second-order PDE and as a first-order system with a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues are c and -c, representing left- and right-going waves. The continuous solution is a sum of functions of x-ct and x+ct. The semidiscrete method (method of lines) discretizes only space, leading to a dispersion relation where the continuous factor k is replaced by a sinc function, introducing frequency-dependent phase errors. The fully discrete leapfrog scheme is analyzed by substituting an exponential ansatz, resulting in a quadratic equation for the growth factor g. Stability requires the Courant number r = cΔt/Δx to be less than 1; if r > 1, the method is unstable. The lecture ends by noting that a staggered grid method for the first-order system will be discussed next.

Monolayer MoS2 grown by CVD was irradiated with a 1 MeV electron beam at a fixed flux for 30 s, 60 s, and 120 s to controllably introduce defects. Raman spectroscopy showed shifts of the E¹₂g and A₁g modes and increased intensity of the LO(M) mode, indicating sulfur vacancy formation. XPS revealed the emergence of Mo⁵⁺ and Mo⁶⁺ oxidation states and increased Mo–O bonding with longer exposure, while KPFM measured an increase in work function from 4.8 eV to 5.24 eV, signifying p-type doping from oxygen incorporation at sulfur vacancies. Photoluminescence at 85 K showed a broad defect-related peak (D) 200–300 meV below the A exciton, which intensified and split into deeper (D1, ~1.64 eV) and shallower (D2, ~1.73 eV) defect-bound emissions with irradiation time, while the A exciton spectral weight decreased. Temperature-dependent PL indicated strong electron-phonon coupling for defect-bound excitons and blueshift of the A exciton energy at 0 K with irradiation. Power-dependent PL showed a sublinear power-law exponent for defect emission post-irradiation and a reduced A/D intensity ratio, confirming increased optically active defect states. Circular polarization-resolved PL revealed that valley polarization of the A exciton dropped from 62% to 38% with irradiation, attributed to defect-mediated intervalley scattering. First-principles calculations on a 4×4×1 supercell demonstrated that oxygen interactions at sulfur vacancies introduce acceptor-like states near the valence band, causing p-type doping and transitions between the conduction band and these acceptor levels responsible for the defect emission. The study establishes high-energy electron beam irradiation as a controllable defect engineering method for monolayer MoS₂, with insights into structural, chemical, electronic, and excitonic modifications.

The device enters the ACQ state to acquire the analog input signal on power-up, after an asynchronous reset, or after a conversion. A rising edge on CONVST/CS moves the device to the CONV state for conversion, during which further CONVST/CS transitions are ignored. After conversion, the device returns to the ACQ state.

A data transfer frame begins at the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends at the subsequent rising edge. During the frame, data is shifted in on SDI and out on SDO-x pins with SCLK. A frame with exactly 32 SCLK cycles is an optimal frame; a short frame has fewer than 32, making write operations invalid; a long frame has more than 32, with the last 32 bits used as the command.

The device supports various input commands for register operations, including read and write commands for bytes or half-words. The output data word in a subsequent frame is determined by the prior frame's command and configuration, and can contain conversion results, register data, or fixed patterns, with optional appended data flags.

Data transfer protocols include legacy SPI-compatible modes for configuration and reading, with options for single or dual SDO-x lines. A source-synchronous (SRC) protocol is also available, where the device provides an output clock synchronous with data.

The device has nine configuration registers controlling functions like device ID, reset/power-down, interface protocols, data output formatting, input voltage ranges, and alarm thresholds with hysteresis. Low-power NAP and power-down modes are available to reduce consumption. An application example describes an analog input module using the ADC with an external multiplexer for industrial voltage and current sensing.

The Wing-T offense uses misdirection, unusual formations, and a diverse run game to exploit aggressive, undisciplined defenders by making different plays look similar, forcing defenses to react rather than attack. It was developed at the University of Delaware by Coach Harold “Tubby” Raymond during his tenure from 1966 to 2001, hence the traditional name Delaware Wing-T.

Personnel requirements include at least two solid running backs besides the quarterback, with one ideally a fullback who can run inside and catch passes. The quarterback needs good footwork and occasional mobility, not necessarily a strong arm. Smaller, quicker offensive linemen skilled at pulling and trapping are often effective.

Strengths: slows down physically superior defenses via misdirection, play action, motions, and formations; experienced coaches have adjustments for any defensive look; its rarity today makes it harder to prepare for. Weaknesses: lacks a traditional dropback passing game, though passing is possible; teams may incorporate shotgun spread formations for variety. The offense is versatile and can be molded to player strengths.

Common formations include the Wing Formation (100/900) with two backs and a wingback outside the tight end; Wing-Slot Formation (“Red” or “Doubles 100”) presenting a passing threat with backs near the line; and Unbalanced Formation with the X receiver on the strong side to add a deep threat while enabling runs to either side.

Frequent running plays: Buck Sweep, featuring two pulling guards, a fake to the fullback, and a handoff to the tailback with the quarterback booting away; Down (Belly G) play, where the quarterback reverses out to allow blocking development for the fullback; and Trap, exploiting aggressive linemen up the middle.

Pass plays: Waggle (Buck Sweep Boot) mimics Buck Sweep, with the fullback releasing to the flat and options to the tight end or deep; Single Receiver Option Route isolates a receiver one-on-one, allowing him to adjust based on coverage; Play Action Vertical Pass uses motion and a fake to the fullback to quickly hit the tight end or slot.

The traditional Wing-T is nearly extinct in major college football but thrives in high schools due to its run diversity and formation flexibility. Some coaches, like Gus Malzahn, have blended Wing-T principles with spread offenses at Auburn and UCF.

A novel, scalable fabrication method for visible-wavelength microcavities uses buckled dielectric membrane mirrors on silicon wafers. The process involves wet thermal smoothing to achieve sub-50 pm surface roughness, ion beam sputtering of a SiO₂/Ta₂O₅ dielectric coating, and backside etching to release freestanding mirrors that buckle due to compressive strain. Mirror diameters from 600 µm yield radii of curvature from 0.9 mm to 21 mm, with high rotational symmetry. Cavities formed by two such mirrors achieve a maximum finesse of 0.89×10⁶ and quality factor up to 2.3×10⁹ at 780 nm. Finesse decreases with cavity length due to diffractive loss, while Q initially increases then plateaus. Scattering loss analysis bounds surface roughness at ≤90 pm. Compact cavity assemblies are demonstrated by gluing mirror chips with or without a spacer, yielding a 45 µm cavity with finesse 0.616×10⁶ and Q 7.45×10⁷, and a 1 mm cavity with finesse 0.263×10⁶ and Q 6.74×10⁸. The method is robust, uses standard cleanroom tools, and enables integration for quantum networking, sensing, and compact laser stabilization.

The article presents a trading strategy for the Global X Robotics & Artificial Intelligence ETF (BOTZ), which was founded in 2016 and now has sufficient price data. The strategy combines Donchian Channels with an Exponential Moving Average (EMA). Donchian Channels are normally a trend-following indicator, but short-term settings are used to adapt to BOTZ’s price fluctuations, making it closer to a momentum indicator. The EMA is used to filter false signals. The strategy is long-only.

Optimization tests different input values to assess robustness, not to find a perfect value. The model has two variables: Donchian Channels lookback period and EMA length. Backtesting on a daily timeframe from September 13, 2016, shows that nearly all Donchian Channels length settings yield a Profit Factor of 1.25 or above, indicating reasonable robustness. A Donchian Channels length of 3 is chosen, providing 157 trades before the EMA filter. Adding an EMA filter improves results across almost any length setting. EMA200 is selected as a common setting, though not the optimal one, to increase realism. The resulting equity curve beats buy and hold with less volatility.

The strategy has a low total of 87 trades due to BOTZ’s limited history, making the equity curve less statistically reliable and increasing the risk of curve fitting. The article emphasizes that it is not investment advice and serves only as an example. It strongly encourages out-of-sample backtesting and an incubation period. The strategy also shows good results on a 2-hour timeframe, but short-term trading is difficult, and further validation is required before considering it viable.

A security appliance incorporates a touch screen or similar local input/output interface, enabling command and control over network functions and configuration without requiring network-based login. During denial of service attacks, commands from this local interface receive priority access to processing resources and memory, allowing mitigating actions such as shutting down ports, blacklisting packet sources, or modifying filter rules, thereby avoiding manual reboots or disconnections.

Packet filtering may employ geoprocessing-based analysis, where filter parameters define minimum bounding rectangles and spatial algorithms with R-tree indexes are used to match packets, significantly accelerating searches compared to B-tree methods. Multiple parameters can form multidimensional filter regions.

Rules are categorized as mandatory (for known active threats) or potential (for inactive threats with estimated likelihoods). A management server distributes rule sets to appliances: mandatory rules are sent to all devices, while potential rules are randomly distributed to a subset in proportion to their likelihood scores. This limits rule set size, reduces memory and CPU usage, and provides early attack warnings. When a potential rule detects an attack, its likelihood is increased to 100% for universal distribution. Rule sets may be periodically refreshed, with delta updates to conserve bandwidth.

The security device includes a processor, network interfaces, memory, and a filter analyzer that queries a rules database using R-tree indexes. The local user interface displays statuses and allows configuration. Upon receiving a packet, if it matches an attack pattern, the packet is blocked, a notification is sent, and resources are reserved for the local interface. Administration requests require valid authentication. For packets from unrecognized devices, the packet is buffered and a notification displayed; the user must authorize the device via the local interface within a time limit, or the packet is discarded. This physical interaction requirement prevents unauthorized network-based configuration changes.

Standardized testing options are narrow, constraining school choice benefits by influencing curriculum and teaching. Studies show high-stakes tests cause educators to narrow instruction and teach to the test. Some states impose these tests on private schools in choice programs: Wisconsin requires the state’s Common Core-based exam, and Texas nearly mandated state assessments for private schools. College admissions exams are also used for state accountability and scholarships, forcing schools to prioritize ACT or College Board standards. These tests are becoming biased and degraded; the SAT has shortened reading passages and lowered rigor, AP Literature top scores spiked while reading scores declined, and a study found a 71-point drop in SAT math rigor. Universities that tried test-optional admissions reversed course, affirming standardized tests’ value. Testing choice would allow schools to select assessments matching their pedagogy. The Classic Learning Test (CLT) offers an alternative grounded in classic works, with a high score correlation to the SAT. States should provide a menu of assessments for school choice programs and ensure all admissions tests are usable for public college admissions and scholarships. Arkansas and Florida already permit multiple tests, and Florida requires public universities to accept the CLT alongside the ACT and SAT.

The passage discloses techniques for enhanced trick-play modes during streaming video. A media guidance application receives metadata with frame address information specifying locations of specific video frames within a stream. It maintains a normal buffer window of continuous video content for normal playback. Using the frame address information, it also maintains a trick-play window that buffers only a subset of selected video frames (e.g., key frames) from portions outside the normal buffer window, without buffering intervening frames. During a trick-play operation, playback uses only the buffered subset. Selected frames may be spaced at approximately equal time intervals. A proxy server may generate indexes and metadata if the streaming server lacks support. A performance monitor provides metrics used to determine from which stream to request frames, how many frames to select, and the interval between them. The trick-play optimizer can create multiple trick-play windows for different playback rates, and may expand the normal buffer window by re-using trick-play frames and requesting missing intervening frames. Trick-play windows may be created in response to input, predicted jump points, or when the playback position will move outside the normal buffer window. The streaming client can request individual frames via byte-range requests without downloading entire segments.

Plaintiff sought damages for automobile damage from a street-crossing collision, alleging negligence including failure to sound a horn. The charge was not erroneous for omitting specific horn instruction because it recited the allegations and stated plaintiff's contention of negligence in the described particulars. Omission of right-of-way and speed-reduction instructions was not error because those issues were not pleaded and no special request was made. Charging both parties were lawfully entitled to use the highways was not error, especially with a subsequent ordinary-care instruction. A specific charge on violating state law and a city ordinance did not preclude other negligence allegations due to the detailed charge. Charging on comparative negligence was not error despite no pleading, as evidence authorized finding both parties negligent. Any error in the damage-measure charge was harmless because the verdict was for defendants. Conflicting evidence authorized the verdict for defendants; no error of law appears. Judgment affirmed.

Breast cancer is the UK's most common cancer, with about 56,000 new cases yearly, affecting 1 in 7 women. Early detection is crucial: it may need less treatment, be more effective, and survival rates have nearly doubled in 40 years; over 3 in 4 diagnosed women survive 10 years.

A lump may feel pea-like or larger, hard, irregular, and can be anywhere in the breast or armpit. Regular self-examination helps spot changes. Know your breasts' normal look and feel. Check for swelling, dimpling (pulled skin), shape/size differences, unexplained dryness/redness/rashes, nipple discharge/rash/inward-turned nipples. Examine with arms raised.

Self-examine lying down: use a flat hand with slight pressure, spiral from collarbone to nipple, including underneath. Note unfamiliar lumps. Repeat sitting up for breasts and armpits. Check every two weeks to monthly, same day each month, a week after your period. Moist skin (shower/bath) eases detection. Look for differences from prior exams.

See a doctor for nipple changes (location, inversion, discharge, eczema-like skin) or skin puckering/dimpling. The doctor will ask about medical/family history, medications, smoking, alcohol, and lump discovery, and may examine and refer.

Most breast cancers start in milk ducts; fewer affect lobules. DCIS is the earliest, non-invasive form. Risk factors: combined HRT over five years, contraceptive pill (slightly raises breast cancer risk, lowers ovarian/womb cancer risk), BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, periods before 12, late menopause, no childbirth, or first child after 30. Longer breastfeeding reduces risk, possibly via less ovulation and hormone exposure.

Men can get breast cancer, though rare, usually behind nipples, mainly ages 60-70. Symptoms: a lump and nipple changes. Men should check and seek advice for anything unusual.

A 167-million-year-old fossil lizard named Breugnathair elgolensis, discovered on Scotland’s Isle of Skye, combines snake-like jaws and hooked teeth with a short body and fully-formed limbs. The study does not conclusively determine whether it is a snake ancestor or a stem-squamate that independently evolved snake-like characteristics.

Researchers equipped greater noctule bats with biologgers containing accelerometers, magnetometers, altimeters, and microphones to study their hunting. Pin and Pull is a perimeter run play that uses down blocks for favorable angles and pulls blockers into space as lead blockers. Its strength is getting extra lead blockers to the point of attack on outside runs. It is versatile: linemen exploit pre-snap alignments, and any lineman can down block or pull based on the defensive front. The tailback can run from the C-gap to the sideline following the guards' blocks. The main weakness is personnel: it needs at least two guards who can pull and run, and a speed back who can stretch the defense horizontally and cut vertically; power backs are less effective. Unlike Buck Sweep, which traditionally includes a simultaneous inside run threat (e.g., fullback dive) to force defensive choices, Pin and Pull is a pure perimeter run. The passage provides blocking assignments against 3-4 Odd and 4-3 Even fronts for each position. Two variations are described: Pin and Pull Toss, where a receiver motions, the right guard kicks out the cornerback, and the quarterback tosses to the tailback; and TE-Wing Pin and Pull Toss, adding a tight end and wing for a four-man surface and advantageous angles, with the right guard kicking out the cornerback.

A multi-camera imaging system is described for imaging faint objects using arrays of cameras that are individually incapable of such imaging. The system includes a computing system to process images. The computing system co-registers and combines the captured images to generate a combined image with a greater signal-to-noise ratio than any individual image. Another configuration is a Hybrid Field Array comprising multiple camera arrays, each with its own common field of view region that partially overlaps with another array's region. Natural single crystal zircon was shock-compressed to 13.6 and 51.3 GPa in recovery experiments. At 13.6 GPa, the sample remained zircon, strongly fractured but largely retaining original orientation; no phase transformation was detected. At 51.3 GPa, the material transformed almost completely to textured reidite with (112) planes parallel to the sample surface, consistent with known orientation relations. Relict zircon was present, mainly near fractures. Temperature estimates indicated residual heating of 21°C and 182°C for the two pressures, with higher local heating near pores.

Scanning electron microscopy showed extensive fracturing; back-scattered electron contrast revealed density differences between reidite and zircon. Raman and infrared spectroscopy confirmed reidite, with peak broadening and shifts indicating lattice stresses. Cathodoluminescence (CL) of the starting zircon was greenish with Dy³⁺ peaks. After 13.6 GPa, CL was similar but with reddish patches of lower intensity and weaker Dy³⁺ lines, suggesting defect-rich regions possibly from a metastable intermediate phase. The 51.3 GPa reidite exhibited blue CL with a maximum near 430 nm, about six times weaker, and narrow REE³⁺ lines, notably Dy³⁺ doublets indicating multiple local symmetries. Bright yellow speckles 2–10 μm in size, often aligned along crystallographic planes, were observed in CL images; these are attributed to segregation of REE³⁺ on planar defects.

The rapid segregation of trace elements occurred without prolonged post-shock annealing, suggesting a vacancy or grain-boundary diffusion mechanism. The reconstructive zircon–reidite transition may cause local charge imbalance, expelling some substituting trivalent ions into interstitial positions, where they diffuse quickly to extended defects. This process can concentrate trace elements on low-angle boundaries and interphase boundaries. The findings imply that shock metamorphism can redistribute trace elements in zircon on short timescales, potentially affecting element release during fluid interaction, while isotopic and trace element ratios in the bulk lattices may remain largely unchanged.

This patent application describes a ladar transmitter system incorporating a field splitter/inverter positioned optically downstream from two scanning mirrors. The field inverter splits and inverts the scan area, causing the scan speed to be slower in the center and faster at the edges, thereby increasing gaze time on central regions. The inverter may be a W-shaped reflector or a triangular prism with internal reflective surfaces, and can be configured for overlapping inversion to further increase dwell on a centerline. The system can employ Lissajous scan patterns where both mirrors scan sinusoidally at resonant frequencies. To reduce scan gaps in desired regions, an induced periodic phase drift is introduced by slowly varying the phase of the mirror drive signals, with drift frequencies chosen as rational sub-harmonics of the scan frequencies. A total least squares method optimizes phase drift parameters to minimize gaps in a selected gaze region. Additionally, an ellipsoidal conjugate reflector reimaging system is disclosed for a compact beam scanner. Two scan mirrors are placed at the foci of an ellipsoidal reflector, with a focusing lens upstream of the first mirror. This reimages the first mirror onto the second, allowing both mirrors to be equally sized and closely spaced while maintaining collimation. The ellipsoidal reflector is a section of a prolate spheroid, and the angle of incidence at the first mirror is chosen so that the reflected ray fan lies in a plane containing the center of the second mirror, yielding a scan pattern with linear rows and minimal pincushion distortion. These techniques aim to improve ladar performance for applications such as autonomous vehicles, surveillance, and mapping.

Trees capture and degrade soil pollutants. Probiotic bacteria boost this process, protecting trees and breaking down toxins from contaminated groundwater. UW researchers and small companies conducted the first large-scale field trial on a Superfund site using poplar trees inoculated with microbe to clean up TCE-contaminated groundwater. The successful trial could be a game changer for cleaning TCE-laden sites. Traditional cleanup is expensive, leaving many sites untreated; this method is more effective and cheaper. The researchers isolated over a hundred microbes from poplar wood at a TCE-contaminated Midwest site, selecting one that eliminated nearly all TCE in a flask. TCE is a common industrial pollutant and carcinogen, present at over 1,000 priority cleanup sites. At NASA Ames, they planted poplar trees—some inoculated, some not—above a TCE-contaminated groundwater plume. After one year, inoculated trees were bigger and healthier; after three years, they were more robust with greatly reduced TCE in trunks. Normally, phytoremediation harms tree health, but the microbe enabled TCE destruction with improved growth, survival. Groundwater downstream showed lower toxin levels; increased chloride, a harmless byproduct, was found near roots. Organizations have expressed interest, and landowners are adopting the technology.

The passage describes methods for Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) transmissions and small data transmission in new radio (NR). A network apparatus may configure contention-based radio resources for a physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) to define a configured grant PUSCH, and broadcast this information to user equipment (UE) via a remaining system information block. The broadcast information may include NOMA parameters such as demodulation reference signal (DMRS) port, multiple access (MA) signature, or interleaver. A UE may receive the broadcast and transmit small data via the configured grant PUSCH while remaining in an RRC-IDLE or RRC-INACTIVE state. For idle state transmissions, the UE may use Non-Access Stratum (NAS) security context without Access Stratum (AS) security establishment or RRC reconfiguration. For inactive state, the UE may transmit small data without transitioning to RRC connected state, using stored AS security context. The configured grant PUSCH may support asynchronous transmission with extended cyclic prefix and guard bands. Multiple configured grant resources with different periodicities may be configured. After transmission, the UE monitors a response window for a DCI format with CRC scrambled by a CFG-RNTI.

Another described NOMA transmission scheme mitigates sequence collision by exploiting user-specific reference bits. An apparatus generates reference bits based on a UE-specific identity and an MA identity, encodes them jointly with information bits using a systematic low-density parity coder (LDPC), and uses the encoded reference bits to generate a preamble or DMRS. The reference bits may be constructed via low-correlation binary sequences (e.g., M-sequence, Gold-sequence) or sparse sequences. The encoded bits are processed with a UE-specific interleaver and rate matching, then modulated and optionally spread. The preamble or DMRS derived from reference bits is front-loaded in time-frequency resources for transmission, enabling UE activity detection and channel estimation. The passage also describes a NOMA scheme for PUSCH in a random access procedure (msg3) to reduce collision probability, where a UE selects an MA signature from a cell-specific pool. Additionally, a NOMA transmission scheme robust to inter-carrier interference uses sparse subcarrier activation patterns, where only a subset of subcarriers in a set are activated for symbol mapping, providing MA signatures.

The Tax Court granted summary judgment for the IRS, sustaining a determination to collect by levy unpaid 1994 and 1996 income taxes self-reported by petitioner Poindexter. Poindexter challenged the assessments’ accuracy, claiming they did not reflect his true liabilities due to a royalty dispute with record companies, and he sought IRS assistance to subpoena information. The court rejected the IRS’s first ground—that a taxpayer cannot challenge self-reported liabilities under section 6330(c)(2)(B)—citing Montgomery v. Commissioner. However, it granted summary judgment on the second and third grounds: Poindexter failed to aver specific facts showing error in the assessments. His petition alleged false and fraudulent information, procedural errors, and incorrect advice, but did not identify which income, deduction, or credit items were incorrect, nor provide evidence of proper royalty amounts or copyright claims. He also failed to present facts supporting other claimed errors; no levies had occurred, and the Appeals officer verified legal requirements and balanced collection efficiency with intrusiveness. Therefore, no justiciable issue existed.

In this appeal, the court considered whether the plaintiff insured failed to substantially comply with a burglary insurance policy clause requiring records from which the insurer could accurately determine the loss. The plaintiff kept a check-cashing fund in a safe, nightly totaling the cash and checks on an adding machine and writing only the aggregate on a scratch-pad. On February 5 and 9, 1954, the total was $2,922, with no separate record of cash versus checks. After a burglary, the scratch-pad note was lost. The plaintiff recovered $180–$182 by remembering details of two checks, and the jury subtracted that from $2,922 to find a $2,740 loss. The court stated that substantial compliance with the record-keeping clause is sufficient, but the records must allow the insurer to determine liability with reasonable accuracy without relying on the memory of an interested party. While meager records might suffice for cash alone, the fund here included checks. The minimum required record for checks should list each check’s amount and identifying information (drawer’s name, payee, or check number) to enable subrogation. The plaintiff’s scratch-pad total was inadequate. The fact that he could recoup on two checks from memory highlighted the insufficiency. The court held that the plaintiff failed to keep records enabling accurate determination of the loss, breaching the policy condition, and therefore reversed the judgment and remanded with directions to dismiss the complaint.

This work investigates the application of steady-state global variance reduction techniques (VRTs) to time-dependent Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations and their interactions with population control techniques (PCTs). Two codes are used: Shift, with limited time-dependent features and weight-based combing, and MC/DC, a fully time-dependent code supporting both uniform and weight-based combing and time-dependent weight windows. Test problems include a pulsed slab, the supercritical AZURV1 benchmark, and a 1D moving-slab SCRAM problem.

Results show that combining weight windows with weight-based combing leads to memory exhaustion due to weight resetting causing excessive splitting. Implicit capture paired with uniform combing consistently underperforms, yielding lower figures of merit than analog simulations. In contrast, Cooper-Larsen weight windows combined with uniform combing achieve significant efficiency gains, with time-dependent weight windows outperforming static ones. The pulsed slab problem demonstrates modest improvements from FW-CADIS, with benefits increasing at later time steps as the flux becomes more spatially heterogeneous. The study concludes that selecting compatible VRTs and PCTs is critical for efficient time-dependent simulations, and that adapting steady-state VRTs with time dependence can further improve performance.

This study investigated the association between resting heart rate (RHR) and all-cause mortality (ACM) in patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in the intensive care unit (ICU). Using the MIMIC-IV database, 1,918 adult ICH patients were included and grouped into four RHR quartiles (Q1: 40.4–70.2 bpm; Q2: 70.2–78.5; Q3: 78.5–88.2; Q4: 88.2–147.9). Primary endpoints were ACM at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year. Kaplan-Meier curves showed higher ACM incidence in Q3 and Q4 versus Q1 and Q2. Multivariate Cox regression indicated that when RHR exceeded 78.5 bpm, each quartile increase was associated with 50–100% higher ACM risk. Restricted cubic splines revealed a nonlinear relationship with an inflection point at 90.3 bpm; RHR below 90.3 bpm may be an independent protective factor, while RHR above 90.3 bpm was independently associated with increased ACM risk. Subgroup analyses showed an interaction between RHR and age, with higher hazard ratios in patients over 60 years. Mediation analysis found a direct positive correlation between RHR and ACM, and a negative indirect effect through age, though the interaction was not statistically significant. The study concluded that RHR below 90.3 bpm may serve as an independent protective factor against ACM in ICH patients in the ICU, while RHR above 90.3 bpm is associated with elevated risk, suggesting heart rate control could aid management.

The lecture focuses on quantitatively measuring the benefits of green buildings and cities using hedonic pricing models. It explains that hedonic models decompose a property's total price into components representing various attributes (e.g., number of rooms, location, green certification) to estimate willingness to pay for nonmarket goods. The method relies on revealed preference through real estate transaction data rather than stated preference surveys. A regression is used to derive unit prices (coefficients) for each attribute, with the coefficient for a green label indicating the premium.

The lecture highlights challenges in causal inference, particularly the need for apples-to-apples comparisons to avoid bias from omitted variables, reverse causality, and selection bias. These endogeneity issues arise when unobserved factors (like building "fanciness") correlate with the green attribute. Techniques to address this include randomized controlled trials, geographic matching (comparing nearby green and non-green buildings), and other quasi-experimental methods. Examples include studies finding a roughly 6% rent premium for green buildings and a 7.6% price premium. The lecture also discusses applications such as the Winthrop Center's design decisions, Bryant Park's restoration through private-public partnership, High Line Park's impact on property values and gentrification, and using hedonic analysis to inform subway investment and land value capture.

President Trump pardoned former Bush aide Scooter Libby, convicted in 2007 of perjury and obstruction of justice, shortly after the FBI raided his personal lawyer Michael Cohen’s home and office. The White House said the pardon corrected an injustice by an overzealous special prosecutor, while critics alleged it was meant to signal loyalty to those implicated in the Mueller investigation. The special counsel’s probe into alleged Trump-Russia collusion has expanded to tax and business matters, frustrating the president. Legal experts debate the scope of the pardon power: some argue a corrupt purpose invalidates a pardon, others say it remains valid even if corrupt. Scholars also disagree on whether a president can self-pardon, with no precedent. Historical examples include George H.W. Bush’s pardons in the Iran-Contra affair, which ended that investigation, and Gerald Ford’s pardon of Richard Nixon. Professor Brian Kalt believes the Constitution does not authorize self-pardons, while Professor Saikrishna Prakash contends the text permits it. Prakash also notes a pardon need not serve the public interest, citing Bill Clinton’s pardon of Marc Rich. The White House denied sending any message with the Libby pardon and refused to rule out a future pardon for Cohen. Reports indicated a Trump lawyer discussed possible pardons with lawyers for Michael Flynn and Paul Manafort; the lawyer denied this and resigned. Flynn later pleaded guilty and cooperated, while Manafort pleaded not guilty. Democrats introduced legislation to require disclosure of evidence in pardons involving the president or family, and New York’s attorney general sought to close a double jeopardy loophole to enable state prosecutions. Legal analysts note a pardon removes Fifth Amendment protection, compelling truthful testimony that could advance an investigation.

This paper investigates the social tendencies of Large Language Models (LLMs) in a multi-agent social dilemma using a Schelling-variant urban migration model. The simulation involves 225 agents distributed across 9 blocks, with a utility function that creates a conflict between individual and collective interests. Agents can migrate and interact via a public message board. The study varies guidance on strategic deliberation (GSD) levels and the presence or absence of the message board. Evaluation combines quantitative metrics (Price of Anarchy, Residential Gini Index, and a behavioral archetype matrix classifying actions by their impact on individual and system utility) with qualitative analysis using an LLM-as-judge inspired by Grounded Theory.

Results reveal a bifurcation into two archetypes. "Adaptive Egoists" (o1-mini, o3-mini, Qwen2.5-7B) default to egoistic behavior, settling into sub-optimal equilibria with low collective welfare and high inequality. Their reasoning is dominated by personal utility maximization. The introduction of the message board acts as a catalyst, significantly increasing their altruistic actions and improving system outcomes through emergent social norms. In contrast, "Altruistic Optimizers" (Gemini-2.5-pro, Deepseek-R1, Deepseek-V3.1) consistently achieve the system-optimal state regardless of the message board, exhibiting inherently high rates of altruistic actions and minimal egoistic actions. Their reasoning reflects a collective-centric motivation, prioritizing group welfare even at personal cost.

The authors argue that choosing an LLM for social simulation constitutes a choice of theoretical foundation: Adaptive Egoists are more suitable for modeling complex, bounded-rationality human dynamics, while Altruistic Optimizers fit idealized pro-social scenarios. Limitations include the simplified model and homogeneous agents. Future directions include human-in-the-loop validation and large-scale simulations with real-world profiles.

This study investigated dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) using natural dyes extracted from mangosteen peel (MP) and grass jelly leaves (GJL). MP dye contained anthocyanins, while GJL dye contained chlorophyll. Dye solutions were mixed at volume ratios of MP:GJL of 3:1, 2:1, 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3, along with pure MP (3:0) and pure GJL (0:3). UV-Vis absorption spectra showed that blending combined the absorption features of both dyes, broadening light harvesting across the visible spectrum. Optical microscopy and FESEM revealed that balanced and GJL-rich ratios (1:1, 1:2, 1:3) produced more uniform, crack-free dye films on TiO₂, while MP-rich ratios exhibited cracking. Photovoltaic characterization under a halogen lamp showed the highest power conversion efficiency of 3.50% at the 1:3 MP:GJL ratio, compared to 2.75% for pure MP and 2.12% for pure GJL. Efficiency variations were attributed to changes in short-circuit current and fill factor. Stability testing over ten cycles indicated that GJL-rich compositions (1:3, 1:2) retained higher efficiencies longer, while the 1:1 mixture degraded rapidly. The study concludes that optimizing the MP:GJL ratio enhances DSSC performance through synergistic light absorption and improved dye morphology.

The lecture first reviews the LSZ theorem, which relates scattering amplitudes to time-ordered correlation functions. To obtain a scattering amplitude from an initial state α to a final state β, one takes the momentum-space correlation function for n external momenta, goes to the on-shell limit, and strips off the product of external propagators. Initial-state momenta are distinguished by taking the negative energy root, while final-state momenta take the positive root. Only connected diagrams are considered, and external propagators are truncated, meaning diagrams that only modify external legs (captured by a constant Z) can be ignored. The sign convention arises from whether field operators act on the initial or final state in the Fourier transform.

The lecture then transitions to fermions. After the Klein-Gordon equation was found to have difficulties (no positive-definite probability, negative energy states), Dirac sought a first-order relativistic wave equation. He proposed an equation of the form i ∂_t ψ = (−i α·∇ + β m) ψ, where α and β are constant matrices and ψ is a multi-component vector. To ensure plane-wave solutions with the relativistic dispersion relation p² = −m², squaring the equation must yield the Klein-Gordon equation. This imposes anticommutation relations on α_i and β: α_i α_j + α_j α_i = 2δ_{ij}, β² = 1, and α_i β + β α_i = 0, with α_i and β Hermitian. These require at least 4×4 matrices, so ψ is a four-component spinor. Two explicit representations are given.

Introducing gamma matrices as γ⁰ = iβ, γⁱ = iβ αⁱ, the Dirac equation becomes (γ^μ ∂_μ − m)ψ = 0. The gamma matrices satisfy the Clifford algebra {γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2η^{μν}. Different sets of gamma matrices related by a similarity transformation correspond to a change of basis in the spinor space and are physically equivalent. For massless particles (m=0), the equation can be satisfied by 2×2 matrices (Pauli matrices), so a massless spinor has only two components. The lecture ends by noting that the Lorentz covariance of the Dirac equation remains to be shown, analogous to the scalar field case where φ'(x') = φ(Λ^{-1}x).

The Turtle Trading Strategy is a trend-following approach developed by Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt, originating from a 1983 experiment to determine whether trading skills could be taught. Dennis recruited and trained novice traders, called Turtles, funded their accounts, and many became successful, proving trading can be learned.

The original Turtle trading rules focused on three key elements: volatility-based position sizing using the average true range (ATR) to vary position size according to market volatility; pyramiding, which involved adding to winning positions systematically; and the use of stop-loss orders with predetermined exit points. The strategy identified trends using breakouts, such as a 20-day high for entering long positions and a 20-day low for exits or short entries, with subsequent breakouts like the 55-day high used for pyramiding.

Not all Turtles succeeded; some were dismissed for failing to follow rules, particularly the exit strategy. Richard Dennis later suffered large losses and stopped trading. William Eckhardt admitted the experiment proved him wrong about innate trading talent and later founded a commodity trading advisor that produced a compound annual return of 17.35 percent over 20 years.

Books about the experiment include “The Complete TurtleTrader” by Michael W. Covel and “Way of the Turtle” by Curtis Faith. Faith backtested six strategies from 1996 to 2006, reporting annual returns ranging from 7.2% to 57.2% with maximum drawdowns between 35.2% and 42.2%.

The passage presents backtests from 2007 onward on a basket of continuous futures contracts, using monthly bars, no leverage, no position sizing, no stop losses, no profit targets, and only long signals. Four strategies were tested:
- Close higher than 6 months ago: total profit 1.5%, max drawdown -33.5%, Sharpe ratio 0.01.
- Dual moving average: total profit 1.5%, max drawdown -33.5%, Sharpe ratio 0.01.
- ATR Channel breakout: total profit 1.5%, max drawdown -33.5%, Sharpe ratio 0.01.
- Bollinger Band breakout: total profit 1.5%, max drawdown -33.5%, Sharpe ratio 0.01.

The performance from 2007 was lower than in prior periods, possibly due to market changes, different contract baskets, or backtest conditions. The Turtle Trading Strategy still works today in markets with clear trends, though traders often modify it with technical indicators. It may not be as profitable as in the 1980s, but the Barclay CTA Index and hedge funds like Swedish Lynx indicate it can still earn good returns. The strategy exhibits low correlation to stocks. Trend-following systems typically have many whipsaws, a low win rate, and long drawdown periods, and potential returns occur in relatively short periods.

Lab experiments show that microbubbles of air and methane in water can generate tiny electrical sparks, or microlightning. Researchers used a 3-D printed nozzle to create small, closely packed bubbles, and a high-speed camera captured flashes when differently charged bubbles jostled. This microlightning might ignite methane seeping from swamps, potentially explaining will-o’-the-wisps. However, some chemists remain unconvinced, noting the experiments occurred underwater while will-o’-the-wisps are aerial flames, and historical lanterns could have provided ignition. The findings are considered a promising step in triboelectricity, with possible applications in triggering chemical reactions and breaking down pollutants.

In a daisy-chain topology, all devices share CONVST/CS and SCLK. The host controller connects to the first device's SDI, and each device's SDO-0 links to the next device's SDI, with the last device's SDO-0 returning to the host. All devices are programmed with identical configuration register values and use a single SDO-0 output; SDO_CTL_REG bits 7-0 must be 00h. Sampling occurs on the rising edge of CONVST/CS, and the data transfer frame begins on the falling edge. On each SCLK launch edge, devices shift out the MSB; on each capture edge, they shift in the LSB of the unified shift register. The host receives data from device N first, in MSB-first order. An optimal frame has 32×N SCLK capture edges; shorter frames cause errors, while longer frames require alignment before CONVST/CS goes high.

The document describes multiple AGESA procedures. A stackless routine initializes the processor and cache to create a pre-memory stack region, dividing it among cores, mapping to global address space, and setting MTRRs; it must run on all cores, checks protected mode (SS must point to a GDT descriptor with base 0 if enabled), and creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF instance. AARCH64 APUs with PSP do not use this stack. Registers destroyed: EAX, ECX, EDX, EDI, ESI (plus DS, ES in 16-bit). Status codes include AGESA_SUCCESS, AGESA_WARNING (re-entry), and AGESA_FATAL (unknown family). Another stackless procedure removes the pre-memory stack, preserving EBX for a return address, disabling CAR mode, flushing all cache lines, and must run on all cores; only the BSP invokes it. Registers destroyed: EAX, ECX, EDX, ESI, ESP, EDI. AmdCreateStruct creates and pre-initializes a parameter block using allocation methods PreMemHeap (Cache-as-RAM), PostMemDram, or ByHost (host pre-allocates, StdHeader overlays params). It requires a stack and returns AGESA_SUCCESS, AGESA_ERROR, or AGESA_FATAL. A procedure returns a 31×32-bit data eye bitmap for a specified DIMM, normalized to trained center, requiring operational HyperTransport links and stack. Another obtains the APIC address for a socket/core (x86-64 only). AmdGetExeSize returns available execution cache bytes on the current core during pre-memory time. A procedure obtains the base PCI address (segment, bus, device) for a processor die. A core identification procedure returns socket, die, and core numbers. A memory address identification procedure returns the FRU DIMM (SocketId, MemChannelId, DimmId matching AgesaReadSpd) and error location (chip select, bank, row, column), with DimmId adjustment for quad rank DIMMs.

The document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP, enabling a guest OS to selectively share register state with the hypervisor during Non-Automatic Exits (NAEs). The GHCB is a 4 KB decrypted page whose format mirrors the SEV-ES VMCB save state area. Version 2 of the protocol introduces hypervisor feature advertisement via a FEATURES bitmap (limited to 52 bits for MSR protocol return) and adds support for SEV-SNP, XSS MSR, restricted APIC emulation, and other enhancements. The GHCB MSR protocol uses the lower 12 bits of MSR 0xc001_0130 for request/response actions, including: SEV information request (providing protocol version range and encryption bit position), CPUID request, AP reset hold, GHCB GPA registration (get preferred, register, unregister), page state change, run VMPL, hypervisor feature support request, and termination request. GHCB GPA registration is mandatory for SEV-SNP guests before first use.

NAE events trigger a #VC exception; the guest sets required state in the GHCB, sets valid bits, and executes VMGEXIT. The hypervisor processes the exit and returns results. Standard error handling uses SW_EXITINFO1 (non-zero indicates error, with codes for exception injection, malformed input, etc.). Supported NAE events include: IOIO_PROT, MSR_PROT, VMMCALL, #NPF/MMIO access (using reserved bits to trigger #VC), page state change (using a Page State Change structure in the GHCB shared buffer, with operations like private/shared/PSMASH/UNSMASH and incremental processing), SNP Guest Request and Extended Guest Request (for firmware communication, returning certificates with GUIDs), AP Creation (create/add/destroy VMSA pages for APs at specified VMPL levels), #HV doorbell page (get preferred/set/query/clear), #HV Send IPI, #HV Timer (set/get APIC timer values), APIC ID List (returns list of APIC IDs), SNP Run VMPL, Secure AVIC backing page register/unregister, and Termination Request.

For AP booting under SEV-ES, the AP reset hold NAE event or MSR protocol is used; the hypervisor treats the vCPU as halted until a SIPI, then resumes the guest without modifying registers. An AP jump table (4 KB encrypted page) is communicated from UEFI to OS via the SEV-SNP Secrets Page or AP Jump Table set/get NAE events. Under SEV-SNP with the AP Creation feature, VMSA pages are assigned via RMPADJUST and VMGEXIT, allowing immediate or INIT-triggered use and supporting vCPU hotplug. Restricted Injection uses a doorbell page with PendingEvent (vector, NMI, #MC, NoFurtherSignal) and NoEoiRequired fields. The host writes the highest-priority interrupt vector and sets NoFurtherSignal; #HV is delivered when needed. The guest acknowledges by zeroing the vector, and EOI is performed by atomically clearing NoEoiRequired or via explicit WRMSR. HLT with interrupts disabled is used for halting; the host re-enters if events are pending. NMI handling requires the hypervisor to intercept #DB and not IRET; the guest sends an "NMI Complete" message via VMGEXIT. Debug register virtualization is supported via DebugVirtualization in SEV_FEATURES; otherwise, DR7 intercepts are used with a cached value. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

COPD, a leading cause of death in the U.S., is caused almost exclusively by smoking. Symptoms include chronic coughing and shortness of breath. Testing involves assessing smoking history and a pulmonary function test. Treatments like inhalers, oxygen, or pulmonary rehabilitation can help, but there is no cure. The University of Michigan Consumer Confidence Index measures optimism about the economy. Backtests using OECD US consumer confidence data from 1993 show that when the index is above its 12-month moving average (bullish), the S&P 500 performs better. A strategy investing only during such periods turned $10,000 into $99,000 over 28 years (CAGR 8.4%) with a 23% max drawdown, compared to buy-and-hold's $159,000 (10.4% CAGR, 55% drawdown) and was invested 55% of the time. The opposite strategy, investing when confidence is below the 12-month average, yielded only $15,000 (1.58% annually). Consumer confidence, measured by the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index (CCI), reflects consumer optimism and impacts spending. The CCI is based on a monthly survey of 5,000 households with five questions. Index changes over 5% indicate economic momentum shifts. Weak confidence leads to reduced spending, inventories, lending, and tax revenues; improved confidence boosts production, hiring, and bullish sentiment. The CCI depends on present situation and expectations indices. The University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index is a monthly telephone survey devised in the 1940s, asking about personal finances and economic outlook. Backtests indicate it is an important factor for predicting stock returns: when above its 12-month moving average, it is wise to be invested; when below, stocks perform poorly.

We studied the tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) effect in a Mn3Sn(01¯10)/MgO(110)/Mn3Sn magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) using first-principles calculations. Mn3Sn is a noncollinear antiferromagnet with an inverse triangular magnetic structure that breaks time-reversal symmetry, producing momentum-dependent spin splitting. The chosen geometry is suitable for electrical switching via spin-orbit torque. Tunneling transport was ensured with a thick MgO barrier. The calculated TMR ratio reached more than 1000% for 12 MgO monolayers. Analysis of the momentum-resolved transmission, the spin polarization on the Fermi surface of bulk Mn3Sn, and the complex band structure of MgO showed that the TMR effect arises from the x-component spin polarization (along the easy axis of the cluster octupole moment) and the filtering of tunneling electrons by the MgO barrier. The study provides a realistic reference for Mn3Sn-based MTJ devices with practical barrier thicknesses.

A study in the Journal of Neuroscience found that barn owls can group moving elements by direction, a visual processing ability previously studied only in primates. Researchers showed owls screens of moving dots and measured how quickly they turned toward a target dot moving differently. Owls detected the target, especially when the contrasting direction was uniform. Brain recordings from the ocular tectum indicated this region, involved in basic visual processing, underlies the task. The findings suggest such perceptual grouping is more fundamental than thought, possibly evolved for detecting prey amid moving backgrounds.
Strong US jobs data and wage growth heightened interest rate hike expectations, boosting the dollar and bond yields while stocks fell. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 2.84 percent.

Jeff Bezos proposed building data centres in space to address Earth's digital demands, easing land, energy, and cooling constraints while providing resilience. The concept responds to growing cloud and AI computing needs, as terrestrial data centres consume significant electricity and water. Challenges include radiation shielding, power storage, vacuum cooling, low-latency communication, and high launch and maintenance costs, making near-term viability uncertain. Other aerospace and tech companies are also exploring orbital and lunar infrastructure, driven by falling launch costs and miniaturized hardware. Proponents believe early investment could become commercially feasible as data demand rises exponentially. If realized, orbital data centres would represent a major shift in digital infrastructure, highlighting the pressures and promise of future cloud and AI development.

The President addresses Congress on conservation of national resources. The public domain has shrunk from over one billion acres in 1860 to about 731 million acres, largely in mountains and arid plains, plus Alaska lands. Early land laws led to rapid, often fraudulent disposition, with large areas passing to private hands without regard for national welfare. Recent public concern demands conservation and proper use. Reforms initiated by his predecessor included prosecuting land frauds, preserving remaining public domain, maintaining forests, and amending obsolete statutes to retain governmental control over coal, oil, phosphate deposits, and water-power sites. Under his administration, investigations and prosecutions continue, and temporary withdrawals of power sites have expanded significantly, covering 229 percent more streams than before.

Current statutes are inadequate for modern disposition of public lands. The Secretary of the Interior’s power to withdraw lands from existing laws is unclear. Congress should validate past withdrawals and authorize temporary withdrawals pending legislative recommendations. A pressing need is official classification of lands by the Interior Department through the Geological Survey to reduce confusion and fraud.

It is proposed to separate surface rights from mineral rights: agricultural lands would be disposed under agricultural statutes, while coal, oil, asphaltum, natural gas, and phosphate would be leased on a royalty basis with development requirements and anti-monopoly provisions, applicable to Alaska as well. Experimental laws may be needed to find the best method. Phosphate’s future value and potential for monopolization are noted.

For water-power sites on public lands, the government can control use by owning adjacent land. Electrical transmission makes water power a likely substitute for natural fuels. To prevent monopoly, government-owned sites should be disposed with limits: use rights not exceeding fifty years, reasonable graduated rental, and renewal terms, ensuring competition and reasonable prices.

Soil conservation is paramount. The government should foster all means to conserve soils: conserve new soils, improve old ones, drain wet and swamp soils, levee river overflow soils, grow trees on thin soils, pasture hillsides, rotate crops, develop dry-land cropping methods, find suitable grasses and legumes, and feed grains on farms to enrich soil. The Department of Agriculture is working on this, but state action, such as swamp drainage, is also essential.

The enlargement of homesteads in semiarid areas to 320 acres has benefited dry farming. Millions of arid acres could be made productive through irrigation. The reclamation act uses public land proceeds to fund reservoirs and irrigation works, with the Secretary of the Interior selecting projects. Over 30 projects have been undertaken; a few may fail, but most work is well done. However, too many projects were started given available funds, leaving settlers in distress. The President recommends issuing up to $30,000,000 in bonds, to be retired by reclamation fund returns, to complete projects. He also urges amendments to the reclamation act for settler relief.

Small timbered areas on the public domain not in national forests should be handled by repealing the 1878 acts and selling timber at public sale, then opening lands to agricultural or mineral entry.

The Secretary of the Interior’s recommendations for public domain conservation are embodied in bills; the President urges their enactment, validation of withdrawals, and clear authority for temporary withdrawals.

Forest reserves, some 190 million acres, are under the Department of Agriculture. Forest maintenance is crucial; scientific treatment can yield timber without reducing supply. Over 400 million acres of private forest land exist, but only 3 percent is scientifically managed. The benefit of forests for watersheds is recognized. Regulation of private forests is a state matter. A proposal to spend a moderate amount annually from forestry receipts for reforestation at navigable stream sources, selected by the Geological Survey, would benefit forestry development.

Regarding inland waterways, the West and Mississippi Valley demand improvements. The Mississippi, Missouri, and Ohio rivers offer natural transportation. Projects should only proceed when costs and benefits are assured. A specific project is damming the Ohio River from Pittsburgh to Cairo to maintain a 9-foot depth via slack water; seven dams are built, six under construction, fifty-four needed, remaining cost $63 million. The President recommends starting with this project and completing it in about twelve years. Similarly, the upper Mississippi to a 6-foot depth and the Missouri to 6 feet (Kansas City to St. Louis) and 8 feet (St. Louis to Cairo) are practical and should be funded with continuing contracts. As traffic develops, the lower Mississippi’s 9-foot depth could be increased. European experience shows waterways need adapted traffic; depths rarely exceed 6 to 10 feet, but they carry enormous merchandise and regulate railroad rates better than government regulation. The President hopes this Congress will inaugurate the new inland waterways system.

Congress has ordered an investigation into the Interior Department and Forest Service, but the results are not needed for the recommended legislation. He urges prompt action on these measures without waiting for the investigation.

This study evaluates distance education in sports higher education during the COVID-19 pandemic, based on interviews with 14 lecturers from Turkish universities selected via criterion sampling. A qualitative case study with descriptive analysis was used, and data were analyzed with MAXQDA 20, yielding an inter-coder reliability of 82%. Four themes were identified. Positive aspects included independence from time and space, access to resources (lesson repetition, source diversity), use of information technologies, and socioeconomic impact (reducing pandemic spread, economic savings). Negative aspects encompassed social influences (communication and participation issues, inequality of opportunity), psychological influences (motivation problems, student/educator apathy), technology and access issues (lack of equipment, access problems), and educational issues (ineffective training, exam abuse, inability to conduct applied sports lessons). Challenges encountered were infrastructure issues (connection problems, insufficient infrastructure, platform issues), difficulties with lessons (lesson process, intensity, assessment and evaluation), and ineffective communication. Regarding distance education management, participants criticized process management (poor crisis management, lack of coordinated decision-making, insufficient in-service training, excessive administrative oversight) and education management (synchronous training preferences, platform inadequacies). The discussion aligns findings with existing literature. Conclusions stress that distance education is a necessary alternative but requires field-specific design for applied courses, attention to data security, and further research to enhance effectiveness.

The passage describes a location sharing system that provides a map GUI for a social media application. The system receives location information from a user's client device, determines a current trajectory, accesses historical location information including habitual places and trajectory patterns, and predicts a presumed destination by correlating the current trajectory with historical data. It displays an icon for the presumed destination on friends' maps. The system may extract trajectory patterns from historical trajectories by clustering and averaging, compute correlation scores between current trajectory and patterns, and select an arrival point as the presumed destination. When communication is lost, it predicts updated location based on trajectory patterns. It can compute and display estimated time of arrival, update based on average speed, and show user interfaces with avatars, destination icons, and trajectory illustrations.

The CPU sub system implements an ARM Cortex-M0+ CPU with a pre-fetch/cache, system timer, memory protection unit, and interrupt management. MSPM0G MCUs provide five operating modes: RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, and SHUTDOWN. Two power domains, PD1 and PD0, are implemented. The power management unit generates core supplies and provides supply supervision with brown-out reset. The clock module provides oscillators including LFOSC, SYSOSC, LFXT, HFXT, and SYSPLL, and distributes clocks such as MCLK, CPUCLK, ULPCLK, and HSCLK. The DMA controller allows data movement without CPU intervention and supports various transfer modes and triggers. The event manager transfers digital events between entities through an event fabric. Flash memory features hardware ECC protection and bank address swap. SRAM is split into two banks, with Bank 0 offering ECC protection and Bank 1 being selectively enabled. GPIO supports up to 93 pins with set/clear/toggle functionality and wake-up features. The IOMUX enables IO pad configuration and digital pin muxing. The 12-bit ADC modules support simultaneous sampling and have internal channels for temperature sensing and supply monitoring. The temperature sensor provides a voltage output connected to an ADC channel, with a factory calibration value. VREF contains a configurable voltage reference buffer. The comparator compares voltage levels on two inputs. The DAC converts digital input to analog voltage. Security features include an AES-128/256 accelerator, firewalls, secure key storage, and a CRC module. The TRNG generates 32-bit random numbers. The AESADV accelerator performs encryption and decryption. The Keystore controller manages AES keys. The MATHACL provides hardware-accelerated math functions. UART, I2C, SPI, and CAN-FD communication peripherals are present. The Low-Frequency Sub-System contains a real-time clock (RTC_B) and an independent watchdog timer (IWDT_B). A windowed watchdog timer is also available. Timer peripherals include general-purpose (TIMGx) and advanced (TIMAx) types. A serial wire debug interface and a boot strap loader are provided. Device factory constants are stored in a memory-mapped region.

MIT publicly rejected the Trump administration’s proposed “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which would mandate campus changes in exchange for preferential federal funding. MIT President Sally Kornbluth stated that while MIT meets many of the compact’s standards, the agreement would restrict freedom of expression and institutional independence, and funding should be merit-based. MIT is the first of nine invited universities to reject the compact; others are reviewing it, with Dartmouth expressing commitment to independence but not rejecting, and the UT system showing enthusiasm. Some state officials threatened funding cuts if universities sign. MIT’s decision drew praise from academic groups and some lawmakers, while a former Trump education official hinted at retaliation.

A thousand additional officers are needed, Annapolis classes should be enlarged, and retirement of impaired officers facilitated. Nationally-aided irrigation for arid regions has begun, increasing need for forest protection. Game protection legislation is needed, and elk slaughter for antlers/tusks must stop.

Scientists discovered that blocking the protein Ant2 in T cells rewires their energy metabolism, making them more effective against cancer. Led by Omri Yosef and Michael Berger, the study shows that disabling Ant2 forces T cells to adapt their energy production, increasing their stamina, replication, and tumor-targeting ability. This metabolic reprogramming, focused on mitochondria, can be achieved through genetic modifications or drugs, offering potential clinical applications. The findings highlight the link between metabolism and immunity, suggesting new immunotherapies that enhance the body's own defenses.
