GDDR6X is a new high-speed graphics memory using PAM4 signaling, achieving up to 19.5 Gbps and 936 GB/sec peak bandwidth on GA10x GPUs. The GeForce RTX 3080 uses a 320-bit interface with GDDR6X, delivering 1.5x the memory bandwidth of the RTX 2080 Super. NVIDIA RTX A6000 and A40 GPUs use 48 GB of GDDR6 memory, scalable to 96 GB via NVLink. Third-generation NVLink provides four x4 links, each 14.0625 GB/sec per direction, totaling 112.5 GB/sec between two GPUs. GA10x GPUs support PCIe Gen 4 with up to 64 GB/sec peak bandwidth.

The full GA102 GPU contains seven GPCs, 42 TPCs, and 84 SMs. Each GPC includes a Raster Engine and two ROP partitions (16 ROPs per GPC, 112 total), improving raster operations. Each SM contains 128 CUDA Cores, four third-generation Tensor Cores, one second-generation RT Core, 128 KB L1/Shared Memory, and a 256 KB register file. The SM partitions can execute 32 FP32 operations per clock, doubling FP32 throughput over Turing. The L1 data cache is 128 KB per SM, with double the shared memory bandwidth. The second-generation RT Core doubles ray/triangle intersection testing rate and adds an Interpolate Triangle Position unit for hardware-accelerated ray-traced motion blur, up to 8x faster than Turing. RT Core and graphics/compute workloads can run concurrently.

Third-generation Tensor Cores support TF32, BF16, and fine-grained structured sparsity, providing up to 2x throughput for sparse matrices. DLSS leverages Tensor Cores for super resolution, enabling 8K gaming. RTX IO uses GPU-based lossless decompression with DirectStorage to accelerate storage I/O, offloading CPU work. GA10x GPUs support HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC, 8K60 display. NVDEC adds AV1 hardware decode; NVENC provides seventh-generation encoding. The NVIDIA A40 is a data center GPU with 48 GB memory, PCIe Gen4, and vGPU support. The RTX A6000 offers 48 GB GDDR6, second-gen RT Cores, and NVLink scalability. EDR technology on GDDR6X detects and replays memory transmission errors during overclocking.

Duncan Keith focuses on his own game, doesn't notice changes in another's, but says that player works hard. He believes players mature with age, learning to keep a level head. He acknowledged Tuukka Rask's strong play but noted the team has scored against good goalies before. He praised a coach for not overdoing meetings, being fair, and maintaining an even keel that rubs off on the team. He described a close off-ice friendship with a teammate, having lived together early in their careers, which helps on-ice chemistry. Conversations shifted from nightlife to family as they aged. He defended a misunderstood teammate as always a good guy, and noted he and Toews have matured, now staying in on Friday nights. The team has grown together after consecutive first-round losses.

Ambassador Penfield forwarded a confidential letter from Count Tisza stating that enemy peace terms would mutilate Germany, dismember Austria-Hungary and Turkey, contradicting Wilson’s views and forcing a fight for existence. Tisza argued the dual monarchy best approximates free national development in mixed-population regions like southeast Europe, urging informing U.S. statesmen and public. Separately, German Ambassador Bernstorff relayed thanks, full confidence, and acceptance of Wilson’s peace conference services, but refusal to publish terms while enemies proclaimed destructive aims. It would confidentially share terms it would have offered if its December 12 offer had been accepted, agreed to a post-war conference on Wilson’s Senate message, and could not postpone submarine blockade, believing it would quickly end the war. It would safeguard American interests and end the blockade when peace acceptable to Germany. The blockade was motivated by the Entente’s refusal of peace, its goals to dismember Germany, destroy Austria-Hungary, annihilate Turkey, and its violation of neutral trade, forcing Germany to fully use submarines, reclaiming freedom of action reserved in May 1916.

A girl from Bihar was diagnosed with TB in 2012. Normal drugs failed, and she developed drug-resistant TB. By May 2014, she was at a Delhi TB hospital, but the new drug Bedaquiline was not given. By October 2016, she weighed only 25kg and was brought to Dr Zarir Udvadia in Mumbai. He recommended Bedaquiline, having published a study on it in 2012, but could not administer it due to government restrictions under the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme: the drug was only available in select cities, and she was not from Delhi. Dr Udvadia and the girl’s father petitioned the Delhi High Court. The judge ordered Bedaquiline’s administration. The father expressed gratitude. Dr Udvadia stated that thousands need the drug, he has 30 patients on it with a 70% success rate, but access remains difficult. The passage notes concerns about bureaucratic rigidity, TB resurgence, and the absence of a preventive vaccine for drug-resistant TB.
GBP/USD trades in a narrow range after hawkish Yellen remarks caused a dollar rally. Upcoming UK jobs data and US releases may influence. Resistance at 1.2483-1.2550, support at 1.2379-1.2417.

Merck halted a late-stage trial of its Alzheimer’s drug verubecestat after an independent study found it had virtually no chance of working. This follows Eli Lilly’s discontinuation of solanezumab three months ago due to lack of improvement over placebo. Merck will continue studying verubecestat in less advanced disease. Experts called the failure a substantial setback. No treatment has been proven to slow Alzheimer’s, which affects millions. Verubecestat is a BACE inhibitor targeting amyloid plaques; its failure raises doubts about the beta amyloid theory. Other companies are still trialling BACE inhibitors. Biogen’s aducanumab has shown encouraging signs. Merck’s early-stage trial results are expected in February 2019, and its shares fell nearly 2%.

The speaker discussed the team's first two playoff games. Game one was passive, not their skating/hitting style. Game two they moved, initiated, played physically, winning to tie the series 1-1. They stressed maintaining that intensity and chippy style. Avoiding a 0-2 deficit was key; game two felt like a Stanley Cup Final. They noted a lead with few shots, penalty kills, and expected low-scoring games. The home crowd has been large and supportive; they anticipate a full, loud house. They emphasized aggressive play at home, not sitting back, and denying time and space. Corkum and Stevenson scored; they hope for more offense but strong goaltending limits goals. Game three is crucial; they must stay level, fight for every inch, and draw on recent home performances like a game seven win against Toronto and closing out Pittsburgh.

The Oklahoma Supreme Court reversed a district court's modification of Edward C. Turner's six-month driver's license revocation to three months. Turner had refused a chemical test after a DUI arrest, and the Commissioner of Public Safety revoked his license for six months under the Implied Consent Law. The district court found the revocation justified but the length excessive based on Turner's driving record. The Supreme Court held that under State ex rel. Oklahoma Department of Public Safety v. Kopczynski, the district court lacked authority to modify the six-month suspension. It noted that a 1975 amendment to § 755 created a limited hardship exception but did not reflect the original legislative intent. The suspension was affirmed and the modification reversed. A dissenting opinion argued that Kopczynski was distinguishable because it involved hardship, not excessive length, and that § 6-211(e) permitted modification when the suspension period was excessive. The dissent would have affirmed the trial court's order.

Fellow-citizens: The death of President William Henry Harrison has devolved the presidency upon me, the Vice President, for the first time under the Constitution. I rely on the intelligence and patriotism of the people. Not having had an inaugural address, I present my principles. Foreign policy: justice to all, submitting to injustice from none, cultivating peace while maintaining the honor of the country, with efficient Army and Navy. To prevent concentration of power, a complete separation between sword and purse is essential; the President's power over public money agents must be changed. Patronage is increasing and could lead to an army of officeholders and election interference. I will ask Congress for measures to arrest these evils. I will remove no faithful officer except for active partisanship or secret party use of official influence, applying the same rule to my own appointees. Freedom of opinion and suffrage will be maintained, but official corps must not go further. Public expenditures require rigid economy, avoiding public debt in peace; sinecures abolished; appropriations direct and explicit; strict responsibility with expulsion for peculation. Any war between government and currency must cease; existing financial laws enforced until repealed, though I regard them as unwise and oppressive. I will sanction constitutional measures restoring a sound circulating medium, guided by the fathers of the republican school. Our institutions secure rights; government derives powers from consent of the governed. Administrators must not enlarge powers except by appeal to the people, preserving the federal-state balance designed by the framers. Opposite course would generate factions, sectional jealousies, and lead to disunion or a central system ending in a bloody scepter and iron crown. I will carry these principles into practice, preserving free institutions and transmitting them unimpaired.

Vermont City Electric (VCE) is a municipal utility formed in 1905 to lower electricity costs, serving about 16,000 residential, 2,845 small commercial, and 784 large commercial customers in 2008. VCE has focused on demand-side management (DSM) since 2000 to reduce energy use and shift demand from peak times. In late 2008, an economic downturn forced cuts to DSM spending, and VCE must now optimize its nine DSM programs under a new $800,000 budget limit for 2009.

Daniela Shazar, an MBA graduate working at a wind turbine start-up, joined VCE’s Citizen’s Oversight Board to help evaluate the DSM programs independently. The nine programs, with total direct costs of $1,035,027, include initiatives for business new construction and existing facilities, residential new construction and existing homes, retail products, commercial smartlight, heating/AC, outdoor lighting, and LED streetlights. Each program yields specific megawatt savings across five load blocks, and savings are assumed to last six years.

VCE’s power supply includes the wood-fired McNeil plant (26.5 MW, $50.90/MWh), hydro contracts (14.9 MW, $60/MWh), the oil-fired VCE GT (18 MW, $150/MWh), and wholesale market purchases (up to 50 MW, with prices ranging from $15 to $300/MWh depending on the load block). Carbon emissions vary by source. Wind capacity (5.2 MW, $76.80/MWh) is expected in 2012. Demand is projected to grow due to population and per capita use increases, and load is modeled in five blocks representing different hours of the year.

Daniela aims to build a mixed-integer optimization model to determine which DSM programs to retain under the budget constraint, while minimizing the net present value of electricity supply costs from 2009 to 2014 and accounting for carbon impacts.

The passage is from a Texas Instruments technical reference manual for the TMS320DM814x DaVinci Digital Media Processors. It describes the System MMU, which remaps C674x MDMA accesses to protect ARM Cortex-A8 memory and allows direct buffer allocation; EDMA TC0 and TC1 can optionally be routed through the MMU. The Media Controller manages HDVPSS and ISS modules. The HDVICP2 is a video encoder/decoder hardware accelerator supporting MPEG1/2/4, H.264, VC-1, RV9/10, AVS-1.0, and ON2 VP6.2/VP7. A Face Detection module performs face detection and tracking on QVGA images, providing size, position, angle, and confidence level. The Spinlock module implements 128 hardware semaphores for synchronization. The Mailbox module facilitates inter-processor communication with four-message FIFOs and interrupts. The device has multiple on-chip memories with a unified memory map; the C674x DSP has limited access to certain peripherals. A DDR DMM TILER provides an extended 4-GByte addressing range for rotated and mirrored frame buffer views, accessible mainly to HDVPSS and ISS. The document details pin assignments and terminal functions for interfaces including boot configuration, camera, DCAN, DDR2/DDR3 memory controllers, EMAC (MII/GMII/RMII/RGMII), GPIO, GPMC, HDMI, I2C, McASP, PCIe, reset and JTAG, SD, SPI, timers, UART, USB, video input/output, and analog TV output, along with supply voltage and ground pins. Boot modes are determined by sampling BTMODE[15:0] pins at reset, supporting XIP (NOR), NAND, I2C, MMC/SD, SPI, EMAC, PCIe, and UART. Pin multiplexing is controlled on a per-pin basis by MUXMODE bits in PINCNTL1–PINCNTL270 registers.

The speaker discusses detente, meaning relaxation of tensions with potential enemies, stressing it requires mutual positive actions. One-sided relaxation while the other side builds up military forces does not advance peace. Arms control negotiations are essential but must not be one-sided; the U.S. must maintain defenses. The speaker is willing to negotiate verifiable nuclear reductions to eliminate mutual threat but rejects treaties like SALT II that legitimize one-sided buildup. The successful Austrian State Treaty negotiation is cited as an example of proper negotiation. The American people must understand the security challenge and that promoting welfare and providing defense are inseparable. Soviet objectives include dividing NATO, expanding influence in the Arabian Gulf and South Asia, encircling China, and fomenting Caribbean subversion (targeting Jamaica, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala; leftist takeovers in Nicaragua and Grenada). The Soviets seek military superiority to force submission or conflict; submission would mean peace like Czechoslovakia or Afghanistan. Restoring the margin of safety can achieve real peace and possibly lead to true arms limitation. The U.S. is not belligerent; its arms are for defense. The speaker wishes freedom for the Russian people and criticizes Lenin-Marxist philosophy as primitive, akin to feudalism.

The lecture introduces Effective Field Theory (EFT). The course is videotaped and may appear on EdX/MITx and OpenCourseWare. Prerequisites include quantum field theory 2, with some QFT 3 background; lecture notes are provided. Grading consists of five problem sets and a final presentation; there are no exams. Presentation topics cover a broad range of EFT applications, and students will teach a topic to broaden coverage. The first half of the course covers general EFT ideas and ingredients; the second half focuses on soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) and its LHC jet physics applications. No single textbook covers the material; chapters will be posted.

EFT allows focusing on interesting physics at a specific scale, in contrast to the bottom-up way physics is typically taught. By taking a general theory like quantum field theory and expanding it, one obtains a simpler effective theory that captures essential physics while retaining the ability to correct to arbitrary precision through higher-order terms. The steps to develop an EFT are: identify relevant degrees of freedom, determine symmetries (which may emerge in the expansion), establish the expansion parameter and power counting, and find the leading-order Lagrangian. Power counting is as fundamental as symmetries for the theory's consistency.

A key principle is insensitivity to physics at higher energy scales. This applies not only to mass-scale expansions but also to expansions in dimensionless parameters like velocity. The hydrogen atom illustrates multiple expansions: neglecting quark substructure of the proton, treating the proton as static, using non-relativistic quantum mechanics, and ignoring heavy particles like the bottom quark. The bottom quark's effect is suppressed by (electron mass/bottom mass)^2, but there is a subtlety: if the electromagnetic coupling is defined at a high scale, the low-energy value depends on the bottom quark; if defined at low energy, the bottom quark is not needed. Integrating out particles can change the meaning of couplings. Ultraviolet divergences do not invalidate the EFT approach.

EFTs are used in two ways: top-down and bottom-up. In top-down, the high-energy theory is known; one integrates out heavy degrees of freedom, matches onto the low-energy theory, and computes operators and constants. Examples include heavy quark effective theory, non-relativistic QED/QCD, and SCET. In bottom-up, the high-energy theory is unknown or matching is too difficult; one constructs the low-energy theory using symmetries, power counting, and identified degrees of freedom, writing the most general operators. Couplings are then fit to experiment. Examples include chiral perturbation theory, the Standard Model itself, and quantum gravity.

The Standard Model as an EFT is treated from the bottom up. Its degrees of freedom are gauge bosons for SU(3) color, SU(2) weak, and U(1) hypercharge; fermions (quarks and leptons with a wide range of masses); and the Higgs. The power counting expansion parameter is the ratio of Standard Model mass scales to the scale of new physics left out. Corrections beyond the Standard Model are described by higher-dimension operators built from Standard Model fields.

Renormalizability in the traditional sense means all UV divergences can be absorbed into a finite number of parameters. The EFT definition generalizes this: a theory must be renormalizable order by order in its expansion parameter, allowing an infinite number of parameters but only a finite number at any fixed order. The Standard Model's leading-order Lagrangian is traditionally renormalizable, so the high scale is not directly visible from it. In other EFTs like chiral perturbation theory, higher-dimension operators are needed even for renormalizability at lowest order.

This patent application is a continuation of earlier applications. It describes methods, apparatuses, and systems for multi-user (MU) transmission in wireless local area networks. A wireless transmit/receive unit (WTRU) receives a frame, decodes it, and determines whether it is a null data packet (NDP) MU media access control (MAC) physical layer convergence protocol (PLCP) protocol data unit (PPDU) based on an NDP condition. The NDP MU MAC PPDU corresponds to an MU transmission and includes a PLCP header with an NDP signal (SIG) field containing MU control information. If the NDP condition is met, the WTRU processes the NDP SIG field, generates a response based on the MU control information, and transmits the response. In another example, the WTRU receives an NDP MU MAC PPDU, determines an NDP MAC frame type from the NDP SIG field, and generates a response based on that frame type and the MU control information.

The background discusses limitations of IEEE 802.11ac group ID mechanisms for downlink MU-MIMO, which cannot support large numbers of clusters, combinations of OFDMA and MU-MIMO, or flexible per-transmission scheduling. The detailed description presents MU clustering and scheduling mechanisms, including clustering management frames with membership and position bit-fields, updating position bit-fields per transmission, and using NDP MAC frames for cluster ID assignment. It also describes signaling MU clustering directly in MU data transmissions or preceding MU control frames. Two high-efficiency (HE) NDP MAC PPDU designs are provided: one with a single HE-NDP-SIG field, and another with HE-NDP-SIG-A and HE-NDP-SIG-B fields. Various NDP MU control frames are defined, including MU-RTS (request-to-send), MU-CTS (clear-to-send), and MU-Poll frames, along with corresponding procedures for WTRUs to decode these frames, determine if they are intended receivers, and prepare responses.

Monolayer CrI2 adopts a stripe-type antiferromagnetic (AFx) ground state, with ferromagnetic and other antiferromagnetic orders higher in energy, and is a narrow-gap semiconductor (Eg ~1.12 eV). For bilayers, direct (AA, AB, BA) and indirect (AA′, AB′, BA′) stacking families are investigated. The global ground state is the indirect BA′ stacking with intralayer AFx and interlayer antiparallel alignment (↑↓/↓↑); direct stackings are less stable. Interlayer separation varies with registry, and band gaps in bilayers are slightly reduced (0.99–1.07 eV) due to interlayer hybridization, with non-monotonic dependence on distance. Non-centrosymmetric stackings exhibit spin splittings from broken PT symmetry, with magnitudes sensitive to interlayer magnetic alignment. Controlled sliding maps reveal energy corrugations with barriers of ~25–50 meV/f.u., enabling stacking switching.

Exchange parameters show that in-plane nearest-neighbor A-B antiferromagnetic coupling and A-A/B-B ferromagnetic coupling dominate. Bilayer formation strengthens both by 6–10% relative to the monolayer. Symmetric exchange anisotropy ΔJxy is nearly registry-independent (~1.48 meV for A-B, ~1.03 meV for A-A/B-B). Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions emerge only in inversion-breaking stackings (0.01–0.02 meV in-plane, 0.02–0.08 meV interlayer). Interlayer exchange is weak (|Jiso| ~0.03–0.07 meV) and its sign depends on registry and magnetic texture. The electronic origin is a spin-selective superexchange pathway where Cr-d↑ and I-p states hybridize effectively. Indirect stackings break inversion symmetry, enabling in-plane polarization Px up to ~10 µC/cm², coupled to DMI and anisotropic exchange; spin-orbit coupling reduces this polarization. The findings establish bilayer CrI2 as a platform for stacking-controlled magnetism with potential for reconfigurable spintronic devices.

Pseudospin models are developed for two organic crystals of the 5-phenyl-1H-tetrazole family, APHTZ and MPHTZ, which exhibit ferroelectric and antiferroelectric order due to proton tautomerism. APHTZ is a canted ferroelectric with ferroelectric ordering along the a-axis and antiferroelectric ordering along the b-axis; MPHTZ is a uniaxial antiferroelectric with ferroelectric chains and antiferroelectric interchain ordering. Using mean-field approximations, the models reproduce essential structural features and available experimental data, though fitting is limited by scarce measurements. For APHTZ, the ground state is FE-I, with a second-order phase transition near 425 K, and a transverse electric field along b induces a first-order switching to an FE-II phase, rotating net polarization by 90°; a tricritical point occurs at 409 K. MPHTZ is described by a two-sublattice antiferroelectric Ising model with a Néel temperature of 421 K; a longitudinal field switches it to a ferroelectric phase via double hysteresis loops, with a tricritical point at 413 K. Switching fields are derived and shown to be proportional to the spontaneous order parameter. The models predict critical behavior typical of mean-field Ising systems, but further experimental data on polarization, permittivity, and transition temperatures are needed to validate and refine the parameters.

The study investigated whether genetic variants in vitamin B12 metabolism genes are associated with Parkinson’s disease risk, age-at-onset, or progression. Analyses of common variants from a large PD GWAS found no genome-wide significant associations. Pathway-specific polygenic risk scores for key B12 metabolism genes were not significant (OR=1.025, p=0.061), while a score including all B12-associated genes showed nominal significance (OR=1.061, p=0.038) that did not survive correction for multiple testing. Rare variant analysis identified a significant association for high CADD variants in CUBN in the AMP-PD cohort (P=6.07E-05, FDR=0.005), but this was not replicated in the meta-analysis after correction (P=0.011, FDR=0.292) and likely occurred by chance. Mendelian randomization found no causal link between B12 levels and PD risk, age-at-onset, or progression, and no genetic correlation was observed. The authors conclude there is no robust genetic evidence linking B12 metabolism to PD, and suggest that lower B12 levels in PD patients may stem from non-genetic factors such as gastrointestinal dysfunction and microbiota alterations. Addressing B12 deficiency remains clinically important. Limitations include the European-ancestry restriction and limited power for progression analyses.

The lecture covers energy absorption in foams, including the construction and use of energy absorption diagrams, modeling, and application examples, followed by a discussion of woodpecker impact tolerance.

Energy absorption diagrams are created from compressive stress-strain curves of foams at constant strain rate and temperature. The energy absorbed and peak stress are normalized by the solid modulus and plotted on log-log scales. Each density yields a curve with a linear elastic portion, a vertical plateau region where energy increases without much peak stress increase, and a densification region where stress rises sharply with little energy increase. The shoulder point just before densification represents the most efficient energy absorption. Connecting shoulder points for different densities gives an optimum line. Repeating for different strain rates produces a family of lines, and temperature can be treated similarly.

For elastomeric foams, because both Young's modulus and plateau stress depend on the solid modulus, a single normalized diagram represents all elastomeric foams. For foams with a yield point, the diagram is valid only for a specific ratio of solid yield strength to solid modulus.

Models can also generate these diagrams. The stress-strain curve is divided into linear elastic, plateau, and densification regimes. Equations for energy absorbed in each regime are derived using foam models (e.g., modulus proportional to relative density squared, plateau stress for open-cell elastomeric foams as 0.05 times relative density squared, densification strain as 1 minus 1.4 times relative density). Solving for relative density and substituting yields an equation for the line connecting shoulder points. The fully dense solid curve serves as an upper bound.

The diagrams are used to select foams for impact protection. Given the object's mass, contact area, drop height, and maximum tolerable acceleration, one calculates the required energy absorption and allowable peak stress. In one example, with a flexible polyurethane foam, an iterative process guessing thickness, calculating strain rate, reading normalized energy from the diagram, and updating thickness converges quickly to determine foam thickness and density. In another example, with fixed thickness, one guesses the solid modulus, plots a point on the diagram, moves along a slope-1 line to match the known strain rate, and reads off the required solid modulus and density. A bicycle helmet case study uses a material selection chart plotting compressive stress at 25% strain versus densification strain, with lines of constant energy per unit volume, to identify expanded polystyrene at 5% relative density as suitable.

The woodpecker segment explains that woodpeckers withstand decelerations up to 1500g without special cushioning material. High-speed video from the late 1970s, triggered by a typewriter to induce pecking, measured impact speeds around 15 mph and stopping times of 0.5–1 ms. The high tolerance is attributed to three factors: small brain size (radius about 1/8 of human, giving a factor of 8 in scaling), brain orientation (a factor of 2 due to projected contact area), and short impact duration (an additional factor of 4 based on human tolerance curves). These combine to explain the measured decelerations. Woodpeckers also have stiff tail feathers and zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two back) to brace against trees during pecking.

This edition publishes documents mainly from State Department and American Commission to Negotiate Peace files, plus selected papers from Wilson, Lansing, Bliss, White, Long, Miller, and House. Andrew Lo presents Lehman Brothers' 2007 financials: $19B net revenues, $4B net income, $145B long-term capital, $282B assets under management, and 28,500 employees. He highlights the net leverage ratio as key to the firm's collapse nine months later. Using a home purchase example, he explains leverage: with 20% down on a $500,000 home, leverage is 5:1; a 10% price drop causes a 50% loss of the homeowner's equity. With 5% down, leverage is 20:1, and a 10% drop wipes out all capital and more. Lehman's 16:1 leverage meant small asset declines could quickly erase its $145B capital. Such leverage seemed safe when housing prices rose smoothly with low volatility, but recent volatility increased risk.

He discusses adjustable-rate mortgages, teaser rates, and homeowners walking away when payments rise, leading to defaults. The Fed is expected to cut rates to ease pressure, though low rates risk inflation. The Fed's refusal to backstop Lehman led to its bankruptcy. He addresses job market effects: short-term disruption, but entry-level hiring may be less affected, and opportunities will emerge after a few months.

Lo then covers inflation: real wealth equals nominal wealth divided by an inflation index; real return approximately equals nominal return minus inflation. He advises discounting nominal cash flows with nominal rates and real cash flows with real rates.

He introduces fixed income securities, noting the US bond market's size (e.g., $6.4T in mortgage-related securities) and participants: issuers, intermediaries, and investors. Valuation uses present value of cash flows. He gives an example of a three-year 5% coupon bond with $1,000 face value, paying $50 annually; its price depends on the interest rate. Risks include inflation, credit, timing, liquidity, and currency. He focuses initially on riskless debt like US government bonds. Pure discount bonds are priced by discounting the face value at the appropriate interest rate. STRIPS are created by separating coupon and principal payments. He notes that bond prices imply market forecasts, stating with 99.5% confidence that the Fed will cut rates tomorrow based on current market prices.

The ADS9803 requires an initialization sequence of register writes after power-up or reset, with a free-running sampling clock connected. After initialization, registers hold default values. User-defined configuration changes can alter analog input range, bandwidth, common-mode voltage range, and data interface (number of output lanes, single or double data rate). The device supports a speed-boost mode allowing up to 8MSPS sampling rate for a user-selected analog input channel pair; only that pair is converted while other channels are idle.

Register write access is enabled by setting SPI_RD_EN = 0b. Configuration registers are grouped in three banks, selectable via REG_BANK_SEL bits; bank 0 is always accessible. To write, first select the bank by writing to register 0x03, then write to the desired register. For reads, enable SPI_RD_EN = 1b and SPI_MODE = 1b, select the bank, send a 24-bit frame with the register address, and the ADC returns the 16-bit data in the next frame; then disable read mode.

Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology: CS and SCLK are shared, SDI of the first ADC connects to the controller, SDO of each ADC connects to SDI of the next, and the last SDO goes to the controller. Daisy-chain length is set in the DAISY_CHAIN_LEN register. Writing to registers in daisy-chain requires N × 24 SCLKs per frame. Reading involves enabling reads, sending N × 24-bit frames with the register address, then reading out data with N × 24-bit frames.

The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2MSPS data acquisition system suitable for ATE applications. It achieves total unadjusted error (TUE) of 0.0015% at 25°C ±5°C after calibration. It has two bandwidth modes: low-noise (up to 22.7kHz) and wide-bandwidth (up to 700kHz). In wide-bandwidth mode, it settles to 99.95% of full-scale in 7.5µs when used with multiplexed PMU signals. The device uses three power supplies: AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, and IOVDD, with no required power-up sequence. Decoupling capacitors (0.1µF ceramic) should be placed close to power-supply pins, and the reference decoupling capacitor close to REFIO and REFM pins. Layout should avoid crossing digital lines with analog signal paths and keep analog and reference signals away from noise sources.

Light-field imaging captures a complete 3D scene in a single snapshot by recording the 4D light field—spatial and angular information—eliminating the sequential scanning required in confocal, multiphoton, and light-sheet microscopy. This avoids the inherent trade-off between imaging speed and signal-to-noise ratio, and reduces photodamage. The plenoptic function, originally a 7D description, is reduced to a 4D representation L(x,y,θ,ϕ) or a two-plane parameterization L(u,v,s,t). Geometric optics implementations use microlens arrays to encode ray directions, with configurations including unfocused (Plenoptic 1.0), focused (Plenoptic 2.0), defocused, wavefront-coded, and Fourier. Wave optics models account for diffraction and interference, providing more accurate point spread functions essential for high-numerical-aperture systems. Light-field rendering enables digital refocusing, focal stack generation, synthetic aperture imaging, multi-view outputs, and volumetric reconstruction.

In biomedical sciences, light-field microscopy (LFM) acquires volumetric fluorescence data in a single exposure, greatly increasing speed and minimizing photobleaching. It has been applied to functional brain imaging in C. elegans, zebrafish, and mice, capturing neuronal activity at cellular resolution. Fourier light-field microscopy (FLFM/XLFM) samples spatial frequencies rather than the spatial domain, reducing reconstruction artifacts and improving uniformity. Light-field mesoscopy bridges microscopic and macroscopic scales, imaging millimeter-to-centimeter specimens with cellular resolution. Examples include the mesoscale light-field (MesoLF) system for mouse cortex activity, the computational miniature mesoscope (CM2) for freely moving animals, and the RUSH3D mesoscope with digital adaptive optics for uniform resolution over large volumes. Light-field endoscopy integrates light-field modules into endoscopes for real-time 3D imaging, aiding depth perception in minimally invasive procedures. Approaches include placing a microlens array downstream of conventional optics, designing custom front-end optics, or using GRIN lens arrays. Flexible endoscopy with fiber bundles has been demonstrated by transmitting perspective images or by exploiting intracore modal patterns to extract depth, though resolution and depth range are limited.

Key challenges and advances include: speed limits due to camera readout rates and data volume, addressed by compressive sensing (e.g., event-based cameras capturing only intensity changes, squeezed light-field microscopy compressing spatial redundancy). The field of view, depth of field, and resolution are inherently traded off because the space-bandwidth product is fixed; light-field imaging redistributes it into three dimensions. Solutions include scanning light-field microscopy and virtual-scanning LFM (VsLFM) using deep learning to restore diffraction-limited resolution without physical scanning. Meta-optics employs metalens arrays to control light with subwavelength structures, enabling resolution enhancement via virtual-moving metalens arrays, synthetic aperture multiplexing, and extended depth of field, though optical aberrations remain a challenge. AI-powered reconstruction uses deep learning to convert raw light-field data into high-resolution 3D volumes. Fully deep learning methods (e.g., LFMNet) directly map inputs to outputs, while hybrid methods combine physics-based inversion with neural networks (e.g., DFCAN, DFGAN). View-Channel-Depth (VCD) networks reorganize light-field data to leverage angular information. These approaches improve speed and quality but face issues of generalizability, reliance on training data, and interpretability.

The OpenChart-SE project collected artificial Swedish emergency department electronic health records (EHRs) via citizen science to address the lack of publicly available Swedish clinical text for natural language processing (NLP) research. Swedish physicians and medical students submitted 50 artificial EHRs during a pilot phase using a mock EHR form that mimicked real Swedish emergency care records. All passed quality control by an experienced physician for realistic writing style and content. The resulting OpenChart-SE corpus (version 1) is openly available on Zenodo. The artificial EHRs cover varied adult patient scenarios: text length ranged 954–2738 characters, 12% described priority one patients, 58% female, ages 18–94 (mean 52). Common main diagnoses included abdominal pain, ureter calculus, and dyspnea. The dataset lacks pediatric cases, reflecting separate pediatric emergency departments. The project has moved to its main phase, inviting further submissions for periodic corpus updates. The artificial EHRs are suitable for training and validating clinical NLP tools for Swedish.

More than 200 schools across North Wales are closed today due to snow and ice. Temperatures dropped to -8C overnight, with snow and black ice making travel hazardous. In Flintshire, 78 schools are closed; in Wrexham, 48; in Denbighshire, 47; in Conwy, 11; and in Gwynedd, a number of schools are shut. Anglesey has no weather-related closures. In Denbighshire, Ysgol Plas Cefndy is only open to pupils living north of the A55, except for one class. In Gwynedd, Ysgol Ardudwy is open only to Year 10 and 11 pupils due to a staff shortage.

Tom Lee, BitMine chair, says the bubble in digital asset treasury companies (DATs) has burst. DATs accumulate crypto and offer share exposure. This paper examines the need to optimize teacher education for 21st-century classrooms. Key areas include integrating technology using the TPACK framework, fostering critical thinking through constructivist methods, preparing teachers for diverse learners via inclusive practices and differentiation, promoting collaboration and lifelong learning through professional learning communities and ongoing development, and addressing global challenges like climate change and social justice. The paper is grounded in TPACK and constructivism. Literature emphasizes content knowledge, pedagogical skills, equity, technology integration, differentiated instruction, collaboration, professional development, cultural competence, and global education. Optimizing teacher education requires a holistic approach prioritizing technology, inclusivity, critical thinking, and global awareness, ensuring teachers are responsive to evolving needs.

The passage describes various peripherals and features of MSPM0G series microcontrollers. The Keystore controller securely manages AES keys (128/256-bit, up to 4 keys). CRC-P supports 16-bit CRC-CCITT and 32-bit CRC-ISO3309. MATHACL provides hardware-accelerated 32-bit math functions. UART peripherals offer standard asynchronous communication, LIN mode, FIFOs, and loopback. I2C supports 7/10-bit addressing, speeds up to 1 Mbit/s, SMBus 3.0, FIFOs, and wakeup on address match. SPI supports up to 32 Mbit/s, configurable controller/peripheral modes, 4–16 bit frames, FIFOs, and multiple formats. CAN-FD is ISO 11898-1:2015 compliant, up to 5 Mbit/s, with configurable transmit/receive buffers and FIFOs. The Low-Frequency Sub-System (LFSS) includes RTC_B (real-time clock with calendar, alarms, periodic interrupts, calibration) and IWDT_B (independent watchdog with programmable periods). WWDT is a windowed watchdog with selectable periods and interval timer mode. Timers include general-purpose (TIMGx) and advanced (TIMAx) types with features like PWM, dead band insertion, QEI, and cross-triggering. Device analog connections, I/O diagrams, and serial wire debug (SWD) interface are described. The boot strap loader (BSL) uses UART or I2C, protected by a password, and can be invoked via pin, blank device, or software. Factory constants provide read-only device data. Application recommendations include decoupling capacitors, NRST pullup, external resistor for SYSOSC FCL, and VCORE tank capacitor. Documentation support, device nomenclature, revision history (November 2024 to April 2025 with numerous specification updates), and mechanical packaging information are also provided.

Sana Bhat, a 24-year-old Kashmiri, was diagnosed with leukemia in April 2015. Her family sold land to fund treatment, but she relapsed and died in February 2017. A Facebook appeal for her had raised $40,000 in a month. Inspired by her story, a group of Srinagar businessmen launched the #TwentyRupeesMiracle crowdfunding campaign in February, asking for monthly contributions of 20 rupees to the Lalla Ded Charity, named after a 14th-century poet. Within days, over 50,000 donors worldwide signed up; founders aim for 100,000 donors to generate about $30,000 monthly. Cancer cases are slowly rising in Kashmir. The government-run SKIMS hospital treats 95% of patients, with costs from $600 to $6,000, while per capita income was $970 in 2015. Public healthcare is underfunded. The charity sends collected money through Help Poor Voluntary Service and Cancer Society of Kashmir. One recipient, 18-year-old Towseef Ahmad Bhat, diagnosed with a neurological disorder, received $1,000 for medicines and is recovering. Sana’s sister hopes the charity’s work serves as a tribute to her.

The Italian stock market index, IT 40, comprises the 40 largest companies on the Borsa Italiana, including Monclear, Pirelli, Tenaris, Ferrari, and Campari. It has traded at the same level as in 1998, with poor buy-and-hold returns. Backtests using the ETF EWI (dividends adjusted) reveal seasonal patterns: Tuesdays and Wednesdays are the best-performing days, Thursdays are slightly positive, Fridays are flat, and Mondays are the worst. An end-of-the-month trading strategy yielded a CAGR of 6.17% versus 4.71% for buy and hold, while invested only one-third of the time. March and June are the best months, and May is the worst. The findings suggest the Italian stock market is seasonal, with Tuesdays and Wednesdays strongest and the end-of-the-month effect potentially effective.

The GST Council set a 0.1% tax on goods procured for export, refundable to merchant exporters. To ease cash blockage, it extended AA/EPCG/EOU schemes to domestic and foreign inputs, exempting IGST and cess on imports, and treating domestic supplies as deemed exports with refunds. Specified banks and PSUs can import gold without IGST for exporters. FIEO welcomed the move, citing thin margins. An e-wallet facility for liquidity will be attempted from April 1, with DGFT preparing norms.

In 1902, a directive stated that officers preferring charges against another officer must communicate them confidentially to the Department of State for discretionary disposition. On May 20, the U.S. military occupation of Cuba ceased, and an independent republic under President Tomás Estrada Palma was inaugurated. On May 24, the U.S. instructed its representative to request Argentina's permission for U.S. consular officers to represent Cuban interests until Cuban consuls were appointed. On October 22, a circular informed diplomatic and consular officers that, following a June 14 act, passports could be issued to loyal residents of U.S. insular possessions (Porto Rico, Philippine Islands, Guam) owing allegiance to the U.S. Applications required an affidavit from two witnesses, and the passport would describe the holder as a citizen of the possession owing allegiance to the U.S. The same fee as for citizens applied.

The City of Bisbee petitioned for a writ of mandamus against Cochise County, its treasurer Daniel S. Kitchel, and its board of supervisors, seeking to recover penalties and fees collected by the county treasurer on delinquent city taxes from 1918 to 1931, which the treasurer had deposited into the county general fund. The trial court sustained demurrers and dismissed the complaint. On appeal, the Arizona Supreme Court held that mandamus was a proper remedy against the treasurer, because the money was held in trust for the city, but not against the county or supervisors, as the funds were never legally part of county funds. Interpreting statutes, the court found that under the 1917 law, the county treasurer was required to remit to the city not only taxes and interest but also costs, which included the fees collected under the earlier statute. Therefore, the penalties and fees collected from 1918 to June 13, 1931, belonged to the city. The court further held that the statute of limitations did not bar the action because the treasurer held the money in an express trust, and the limitations period did not begin to run until the treasurer repudiated the trust in 1931. However, a 1931 statute changed the rule, providing that interest, penalties, charges, and fees collected on delinquent taxes after June 12, 1931, shall be credited to the county general fund, so the city had no claim to amounts collected thereafter. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded with instructions to overrule the demurrer as to the treasurer and for further proceedings.

"SOS" Disruptions offer three scenarios. For screens above the free throw line, an aggressive contact switch denies jump shots and middle penetration, followed by snuggle pass denial and a smother on the ballhandler. For screens below the free throw line, a baseline trap is set before the screen, with a Triangle I formation and closeouts on passes. A metagenomic next-generation sequencing protocol using Oxford Nanopore Technology was evaluated for detecting SARS-CoV-2 in clinical oropharyngeal swabs. Pretreatments were compared on pooled positive samples: DNase I treatment, filtration (0.22 µM), DNase I followed by filtration, and no pretreatment. The combination of DNase I and filtration increased the proportion of BLAST hits assigned to SARS-CoV-2 to 99.9% and achieved 99.3% reference genome coverage after 20 hours, compared to 31.8% hits and 7.5% coverage with no treatment. This pretreatment also enabled over 50% genome coverage within 10 minutes of sequencing. On individual samples with CT-values from 18 to >38, all samples with CT ≤30 reached 85.8–100% coverage and could be typed to Delta clade and various Pangolin lineages. Samples with CT ≥33 achieved 40.0–60.5% coverage and clade identification but failed lineage typing. Single pretreatments (DNase alone or filtration alone) produced false-positive Orthohepevirus A hits that were disregarded upon inspection of mapped reads. The protocol incorporates isothermal amplification, a rapid barcoding library preparation without purification steps, and avoids large equipment, aiming for field-deployable virus detection.

Specific heat shows no magnetic ordering transition and exhibits sub-linear behavior between 0.1 K and 5 K; integrated entropy between 0.1 K and 10 K is ~85% R ln(2). This paper proposes a class of bivariate zero-inflated Poisson (BZIP) models for multivariate count data with excess zeros. The model uses a common Bernoulli inflation factor \(W\) (with zero-inflation probability \(\phi\)) and latent Poisson counts \(T=(T_1,T_2)\) with rates \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\). Dependence is introduced by letting \(T\) follow either the comonotonic shock (BP\(^+\)) or counter-monotonic shock (BP\(^-\)) bivariate Poisson model of Genest et al. (2018), governed by a parameter \(\theta\). This yields BZIP\(^+\) for positive dependence and BZIP\(^-\) for negative dependence. Joint probability mass functions, distribution functions, and generating functions are derived. The dependence structure shows covariance and correlation as functions of \(\phi\) and \(\theta\); the BZIP\(^+\) model attains the upper Fréchet-Hoeffding bound when \(\theta=1\), while BZIP\(^-\) does not reach the lower bound unless \(\phi=0\). Estimation methods include method of moments (MoM) using marginal moments and covariance, maximum likelihood (MLE) with one-step and two-step approaches, and an EM algorithm. Simulations across various sample sizes and parameter values indicate that MLE outperforms MoM, with increased variability for high zero-inflation. A data illustration using Australian monthly disaster counts (flood/storm for positive dependence, flood/bushfire for negative dependence) shows significant zero-inflation and dependence, supporting the model over simpler alternatives. Multivariate extension to \(d\) dimensions using the comonotonic shock model is briefly discussed.

The lecture discusses policy evaluation using temporal difference (TD) learning and extends it to continuous state spaces via function approximation. It begins by reviewing TD(λ), which encompasses one-step bootstrapping (TD(0)) and Monte Carlo evaluation (TD(1)), and notes that these algorithms converge for discrete Markov chains but scale poorly due to discretization.

A crash course on least squares function approximation is presented. The goal is to estimate an unknown function from input-output data by minimizing squared error over a parameter vector α. Linear function approximators, where the output is a linear combination of possibly nonlinear basis functions φ(x), are emphasized because they allow an explicit least-squares solution for α without gradient descent. Examples of basis functions include radial basis functions (Gaussians), barycentric interpolators (tent functions), Fourier decompositions, and polynomials. A demonstration shows that a linear combination of Gaussians can accurately reconstruct a nonlinear function from sparse, noisy data in one shot.

The lecture then applies linear function approximation to nonlinear system identification. For many robot manipulators, the dynamics equations are linear in the parameters (though not in the state), allowing parameters like inertia and damping to be estimated via least squares using basis functions derived from the equations of motion. A pendulum example illustrates accurate parameter recovery from simulation data.

To perform TD learning with function approximation, the eligibility trace concept is adapted. Instead of tracing state visits, an eligibility trace is maintained on the parameter vector α, updated using the gradient of the value estimate (which for linear approximators is simply φ(x)). The same TD update rule is applied using this parameter eligibility trace. This algorithm is proven to converge for linear function approximators with λ between 0 and 1.

Finally, least squares temporal difference learning (LSTD) is introduced as a batch method that accumulates sufficient statistics (matrices A and b) from trajectories and solves α = A⁻¹b directly. LSTD is more data-efficient, avoids choosing a learning rate, and does not depend on initial α. Incremental LSTD variants exist for online updates. The lecture concludes by noting that function approximation is crucial for scaling reinforcement learning, with linear approximators being the primary case with strong convergence guarantees.

In this insurance declaratory relief action, the United States District Court for the District of Nevada granted Plaintiff AAA Nevada Insurance Company's Motion for Summary Judgment. Defendant Vinh Chau, insured by AAA, was in a fatal car accident with Benjamin Buenaventura. The policy had bodily injury liability limits of $100,000 per person. The Buenaventuras' counsel sent a two-week policy limits demand, but did not identify all heirs or provide a release. AAA attempted to contact counsel to clarify these issues, including visiting the office and writing a check, but was unable to reach them. The demand expired. The Buenaventuras later filed a wrongful death suit seeking $999,997. AAA sought a declaration that the policy limit is $100,000 and that it did not act in bad faith. The court held that the policy limits recovery to $100,000. On the bad faith claim, the court found that AAA had a reasonable basis for not settling within the two-week deadline because it could not verify the claimants and counsel refused to respond to inquiries. The court rejected Interveners' arguments that there were genuine disputes of material fact, finding the demand letter itself unreasonable and an attempt to set up a bad faith claim. The court also denied Interveners' request for a Rule 56(f) continuance, concluding further discovery would not change the outcome. The court noted that Interveners' counsel had used identical demand letters in other cases. Accordingly, the court ordered that AAA's liability under the policy is fixed at $100,000 and its failure to settle within the time limit did not constitute bad faith under Nevada law.

The passage introduces the Rank-Preserving Structural Equation Model (RAPSEM), a novel framework for mediation analysis with latent variables. It notes that standard structural equation modeling (SEM) for mediation relies on the assumption of no unmeasured confounding (sequential ignorability), which is often unrealistic in psychological research. RAPSEM integrates rank-preserving models (RPMs) with factor score regression and interaction corrections, relaxing this assumption to a no-effect-modifier assumption that allows omitted confounders between mediator and outcome, provided they do not interact with treatment or mediator. The model estimates controlled direct and mediation effects within a potential outcomes framework, using latent factors for mediator, covariates, and outcome, each measured by multiple indicators. The passage defines the controlled direct effect (CDE) as the treatment effect holding the mediator fixed, and the controlled mediation effect (CME) as the mediator effect holding treatment fixed. It then outlines the measurement model, where observed indicators are linked to latent variables. The goal is to enable robust mediation analysis in the presence of measurement error and unobserved confounding.

This work studies profit maximization for a broker in repeated bilateral trade between a seller and a buyer with private valuations, under dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality. Unlike prior work focusing on gains-from-trade, the goal is to minimize regret relative to the best mechanism in hindsight via online learning. Two input models are considered: stochastic i.i.d. (valuations drawn from a fixed, possibly correlated, unknown distribution) and adversarial (oblivious adversary). In the stochastic setting, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves a nearly tight regret bound of Õ(√T), with a matching Ω(√T) lower bound, implying that approximately 1/ε² samples are necessary and sufficient to learn an ε-optimal mechanism. In the adversarial setting, no algorithm can achieve sublinear regret with respect to a 2/3+ε fraction of optimal profit, revealing a separation between the two models. A correspondence with non-excludable mechanism design yields an improved Õ(√T) regret bound for the joint ads problem. Key challenges include the non-parametric action space and non-regular profit function, which make standard fixed discretization insufficient.

This study investigates whether transformers can learn to infer transitive relations, equivalently graph connectivity, from training examples where node pairs and their connectivity are provided individually, rather than as in-context examples. It defines grid graphs, whose nodes can be embedded in a low-dimensional space such that connectivity is easily inferred from embedding differences, and contrasts them with disconnected chain graphs, which lack such an embedding. Experiments show transformers more successfully learn connectivity on grid graphs than on disconnected chain graphs. Scaling model size improves test loss and accuracy for grid graphs, but not for disconnected chain graphs. Scaling graph size (number of nodes) yields consistent performance on grid graphs, while for disconnected chain graphs with a fixed number of chains, larger graphs improve accuracy. Higher grid dimensionality degrades performance; increasing graph size helps more than increasing model size for higher-dimensional grids. For disconnected chain graphs with fixed total nodes, a smaller number of chains yields better performance; scaling graph size improves accuracy for graphs with many chains more than scaling model size does. Overall, data scaling benefits transformers more than model scaling for learning connectivity on higher-dimensional grid graphs and disconnected chain graphs with many chains.

A cross-sectional study in Denan district, south-eastern Ethiopia, determined sero-prevalence, knowledge, attitudes, practices, associated factors, and sand fly vectors of visceral leishmaniasis (VL). Among 187 participants, the overall sero-prevalence by DAT was 9.63% (18/187). Multivariate analysis identified significant risk factors: age 19–36 (P=0.034), damp floor (P=0.022), outdoor sleeping (P=0.001), and sleeping near animal shelter (P=0.031). Only 53.48% had heard of VL; 42% knew sand fly bite transmits it. Most (89%) knew at least one symptom, with 41% citing abdominal swelling. While 78% considered VL treatable, only 36% believed it preventable, and 44% knew it could be fatal if untreated. Prevention practices included bed net use (42%), insecticide spraying (32%), smoking tree branches (14%), and environmental cleaning (8%). Entomological sampling collected 823 sand flies, identifying 12 species. Phlebotomus orientalis was the dominant Phlebotomus species (43.9% of Phlebotomus, 11.42% of total), captured mainly in termite mounds and forest, with none indoors. Sergentomyia clydei was most abundant overall (50.18%). The study concludes that VL sero-prevalence is relatively high in this new focus, adults 19–36 are at elevated risk, and poor housing, outdoor sleeping, and proximity to animals are key risk factors. Knowledge and attitudes were poor. P. orientalis likely contributes to transmission, warranting further epidemiological and vector studies.

The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment to Reisdorf Brothers on the Georges' Clean Water Act and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act claims, the dismissal of state law claims without prejudice, and the denial of attorney's fees to Reisdorf. The court found the Georges failed to raise a triable issue of material fact on their CWA claim because their evidence showed only a single past spill, speculative assertions about fertilizer and pesticide discharge without proof of pollutants in the creek, and insufficient evidence of ongoing or intermittent molasses discharge. The RCRA claim failed because the Georges did not allege or provide evidence of a violation of the relevant federal open dumping regulations. The district court did not abuse its discretion in declining supplemental jurisdiction over the state law adverse possession claim after dismissing the federal claims. The denial of attorney's fees to Reisdorf under 42 U.S.C. § 6972(e) was not an abuse of discretion because the Georges' claims were not frivolous or groundless. The court also declined to consider a newly raised storm water discharge claim, found no error in the district court's handling of consent orders, and assumed without deciding that the defendant waived its objection to the plaintiffs' expert report. Certain other arguments were waived.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Barrett's case, which involves double jeopardy principles applied to federal firearm offenses. Barrett was convicted under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and (j) for armed robberies where a victim was shot. Section 924(c) prohibits using a firearm to advance a crime of violence or drug trafficking; Section 924(j) applies when a § 924(c) violation causes a death. The question is whether § 924(j) creates a separate crime with separate punishment from § 924(c). The double jeopardy test from a century-old case requires comparing elements: if each offense requires proof of a fact the other does not, separate punishments are presumed; if one is a subset, multiple punishments are presumed not intended unless Congress clearly indicated otherwise. Section 924(c) mandates consecutive sentences, overcoming the presumption in some respects. The issue is whether Congress intended separate convictions and sentences under both provisions. A prior decision left this question open. The government and Barrett agree separate sentences are not permitted, but the Second Circuit upheld separate convictions. The Court appointed an amicus to defend that judgment. Barrett argues neither statute authorizes cumulative punishment; the amicus points to § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) requiring consecutive sentences. The case will resolve the double jeopardy question.

This study used multi-state modeling on PREVEND cohort data to estimate age- and sex-specific transition rates between KDIGO risk stages (low, intermediate, high/very high, based on eGFR and UAE) and their association with new-onset heart failure (HF). The model accounted for misclassification and interval-censored observations. Among 8569 participants, forward transition rates increased with age; the intermediate to high/very high transition was lower in women. Backward transition from intermediate to low risk was higher in younger subjects and women. Transitions to HF increased exponentially with age and were lower in women. Predicted progression showed intermediate risk stage prevalence tripled between ages 60–70, and high/very high risk increased between 70–80. Relative risks of HF for intermediate and high/very high stages versus low risk were higher at younger ages (e.g., intermediate vs low: RR 3.4 at 60 years, 1.6 at 80 years), while absolute rate differences were greater at older ages. Misclassification probabilities were notable: intermediate stage misclassified as low 18.4%, high/very high misclassified as intermediate 15.6%. Sensitivity analysis with cystatin C-based eGFR showed lower misclassification and some differing transition patterns. The study concludes that kidney disease progresses rapidly in middle age and advanced KDIGO stages are associated with increased HF risk, suggesting that slowing progression may reduce HF incidence.

This study aimed to develop a valid and reliable scale measuring prospective teachers’ attitudes towards values education through distance education. Following DeVellis’s (2017) scale development steps, an initial 43-item pool was created based on literature review and compositions from 20 prospective teachers. After expert review and a pilot study with 30 participants, 40 items were retained. The main study involved 341 prospective teachers from Gazi University (77.3% female). Exploratory factor analysis using principal components and varimax rotation yielded a two-factor structure: “Necessity and Usefulness” (21 items) and “Feasibility” (15 items), explaining 63.286% of total variance. Factor loadings ranged from .63 to .82 for the first factor and .64 to .83 for the second. The scale lacks additivity, so subfactors must be evaluated separately. Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficients were .969 and .961, respectively, and split-half reliabilities were .934 and .930. Item-total correlations and 27% subgroup comparisons confirmed item distinctiveness. The scale provides valid and reliable measurements of prospective teachers’ attitudes, with higher scores indicating more positive attitudes. Limitations include a predominantly female sample, single-university context, and absence of comparable scales for external validity. Researchers are recommended to conduct confirmatory factor analysis and further validity studies.

Children born to obese women have double the obesity risk by age two. Childhood obesity is linked to both maternal and paternal obesity. Eggs and sperm carry molecules like non-coding RNAs that respond to parental nutrition, influencing offspring obesity risk. Maternal BMI at conception is key; paternal BMI affects birthweight and daughters' body fat. Risk doubles with two obese parents. Sperm non-coding RNAs from obese males can make offspring fatter. Obese females' eggs have more fat and defective mitochondria, which are maternally inherited and alter offspring metabolism, increasing obesity susceptibility. However, embryos are plastic. In mice, exercise and anti-diabetes drugs improve egg and sperm quality, restoring non-coding RNAs and stopping obesity transmission. Human studies show gastric banding before conception reduces child obesity. Pre-conception interventions for both parents, including diet and exercise, are recommended. Preventing obesity in young adults can shape community obesity rates.

This paper analyzes data from 147 student surveys at a Hungarian university to understand how engineering and technical management students evaluate their university education within the framework of Education 4.0 and their acquired skills for the changing job market. The study found that both groups prioritized problem-solving as the most important skill during university. However, significant differences emerged: engineering students favored knowledge related to specialization and technical/mathematical knowledge, while technical management students prioritized learning decision-making techniques and analytical thinking. Regarding international studies, both groups valued improving language skills, but engineering students placed more importance on a new approach to structuring learning material. Students' opinions on higher education's contribution significantly differed concerning knowledge for future jobs, analyzing quantitative problems, teamwork, and self-understanding. A decision tree analysis confirmed that attitudes toward knowledge for future jobs, decision-making techniques, and new approaches to learning material were key factors differentiating the two student groups.

The passage argues that slavery is an undertheorized starting point in pedagogical discourse, particularly as digital surveillance becomes ubiquitous. It uses Michel Foucault's theory of panopticism to examine the relationship between slavery and pedagogy, connected by surveillance as a form of extraction and a tool of power. The text notes that pedagogues in Ancient Greece were typically enslaved people, a fact often omitted in contemporary definitions of pedagogy. It introduces Givens's concept of "fugitive pedagogy," which describes subversive educational practices developed by African Americans to combat racial surveillance and violence. The author advances the concept of "surveillance pedagogy" to describe how modern observation, monitoring, and data extraction in teaching and learning mirror the textualization and control processes that sustained racial chattel slavery. The study highlights how surveillance capitalism, driven by digital platforms, extracts and monetizes personal data to condition behavior, rearticulating historical master/slave dynamics and concentrating control over learning in the hands of a few.

A cross-sectional study was conducted among 302 heroin users on methadone therapy at a MAT clinic in Dar-es-salaam, Tanzania. The mean age was 42.78 years, 95.7% were male, and 20.9% were underweight. Lung function decline (FEV1 <70%) was present in 28.5% of participants. The pattern of decline was obstructive in 11%, restrictive in 13.2%, and mixed in 4.3%. The mean age at onset of decline was 44 years. Underweight (aOR 4.73, 95% CI 2.61-8.59), HIV infection (aOR 2.61, 95% CI 1.20-5.66), and history of pulmonary tuberculosis (aOR 2.48, 95% CI 1.48-4.17) were independently associated with lung function decline. The study concludes that over a quarter of clients had lung function decline and recommends routine screening for lung diseases in this population.

This study examined the association between long-term visit-to-visit blood pressure (BP) variability and cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) burden and its features in 1284 participants from the Kailuan cohort. BP variability (systolic, diastolic, pulse pressure) was calculated from 2006–2022 surveys, and cSVD markers (white matter hyperintensities, lacunae, cerebral microbleeds, perivascular spaces) were assessed via MRI. High systolic BP variability was associated with moderate cSVD burden (OR=1.89) and perivascular spaces (OR=1.62). High diastolic BP variability was associated with lacunae (OR=1.74). High pulse pressure variability showed risk effects on moderate/severe cSVD burden (OR=1.99 and 2.49), lacunae (OR=1.75), and perivascular spaces (OR=1.77). Associations were modified by age and hypertension status. In participants under 60, only high pulse pressure variability was associated with severe cSVD burden (OR=3.33), lacunae (OR=3.02), and perivascular spaces (OR=1.86). The risk effect of systolic and pulse pressure variability on cSVD burden was significant only in hypertensive participants. The study concludes that high long-term BP variability is an independent risk factor for total cSVD burden, lacunae, and perivascular spaces, especially with hypertension, and pulse pressure variability is important in young adults.

The passage describes an experiment where ChatGPT was asked to create a Bollinger Bands trading strategy. It produced a squeeze strategy: a squeeze occurs when Bollinger Bands (20-period SMA, ±2 standard deviations) are inside Keltner Channels (using 2× average true range). Trading rules: buy and hold when the lower Bollinger Band is above the Keltner lower band and the upper Bollinger Band is below the Keltner upper band; sell if either condition fails. A backtest on SPY from 1993 (data not adjusted for dividends/splits) showed low compounded returns, erratic performance, and high drawdown. Adjusting for time in market slightly improved returns and reduced drawdown, but the strategy remained unprofitable. ChatGPT correctly executed the backtest, but the strategy was not suitable for live trading. The article also defines Bollinger Bands and mentions a mean reversion strategy.

NVIDIA Corporation's annual report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2020, describes the company as a pioneer in accelerated computing, initially focused on PC graphics and later expanding into artificial intelligence (AI). The company's platform strategy combines hardware, system software, algorithms, libraries, systems, and services. Its two reportable segments are GPU and Tegra Processor, both based on a single underlying architecture. GPU product brands include GeForce for gamers, Quadro for designers, Tesla and DGX for AI and high-performance computing (HPC), and GRID for cloud-based visual computing. Tegra integrates a computer onto a single chip, powering platforms like DRIVE AGX for self-driving vehicles, Clara AGX for medical instruments, Jetson AGX for robotics, and SHIELD for home entertainment and gaming.

NVIDIA targets four large markets: Gaming, Professional Visualization, Data Center, and Automotive. In Gaming, it offers GeForce GPUs, SHIELD devices, and GeForce NOW cloud gaming. Professional Visualization serves designers with Quadro GPUs and RTX technology for real-time ray tracing. The Data Center market uses NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform for AI and HPC, with products like Tesla GPUs, DGX systems, and the NVIDIA GPU Cloud (NGC). The Automotive market provides the DRIVE platform for autonomous vehicles, including DRIVE AGX hardware and DRIVE AV/IX software, and announced the next-generation Orin SoC.

Key strategies include advancing the GPU computing platform, extending technology leadership in AI and visual computing, advancing the autonomous vehicle platform, and leveraging intellectual property. The company uses a fabless manufacturing strategy, relying on suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited and Samsung for wafer fabrication, and subcontractors for assembly, testing, and packaging. Sales are primarily through a partner network, with Dell accounting for 11% of total revenue in fiscal year 2020. Revenue from outside the United States was 92% of total revenue, with billings to China (including Hong Kong) at 25%. As of January 26, 2020, NVIDIA had 13,775 employees, with 9,823 in research and development.

The report details numerous risk factors, including failure to meet evolving market needs, intense competition from companies like AMD, Intel, and Xilinx, dependence on third-party manufacturing, potential product defects, business disruptions, international operational risks, customer concentration, intellectual property protection challenges, and privacy regulations such as GDPR. It also notes the announced agreement to acquire Mellanox for approximately $6.9 billion and the potential impact of the novel coronavirus on financial results.

On December 7, 1891, Deputy Collector M. Webber certified that the crew list of the bark Cape Horn Pigeon (master Thomas Scullan) was a true copy. On September 1, 1900, Secretary of State John Hay certified that annexed documents were true copies from the Department of State. The whalemen’s shipping paper for the bark Cape Horn Pigeon, bound from San Francisco on a whaling, walrusing, and trading voyage to the North Pacific and Arctic oceans, term not exceeding 12 months, sets forth agreements between owner, master, and crew. Seamen are hired for shares and must obey officers, endeavor to obtain oil, preserve vessel and cargo, and not leave without permission. The log book must record daily breaches of regulations, including drunkenness, absence after sunset or overnight, introduction of women for licentious purposes, and disability with its cause. The officer in charge of the watch must maintain the regulation on women; if any come aboard unperceived, they must be expelled or reported. Failure by an officer to do so forfeits 20 days’ pay per offense. Abetting a breach, refusing to aid, or criminal intercourse with such women forfeits 5 days’ pay. Drunkenness forfeits 2 days’ pay. Sickness or disability from intemperance or licentiousness incurs similar forfeiture. Forfeitures are estimated according to shares and voyage length and go to the owners.

The passage argues that Ontario’s K-12 education system excludes disabled and marginalized students despite claims of inclusion. It opens with a quote from disability advocate Carella (2024): “Inclusion is not just inviting someone to sit at your table. It is believing they belong there,” framing special education as a model that invites students in without ensuring belonging or meeting their needs. Slee (2018) adds that “inclusive education isn’t dead, it just smells funny.” The paper outlines the history of special education in Ontario, from 1860s residential schools using derogatory labels, through the introduction of special classes in the 1880s, to the 1960s civil rights push for integration. Racialized students are noted to be overrepresented in special education, particularly in behavioral, intellectual, and language disability categories, and less likely to be diagnosed with giftedness or autism.

The paper discusses the Individual Education Plan (IEP) process, where disability identification for educational placement relies on a deficit-model approach. Placement options range from regular class with indirect support to full-time special education class. A key issue is the lack of planning for diverse learners, causing disabled and marginalized students to be framed as “unexpected.” The Policy on Accessible Education for Students with Disabilities (2018) guarantees equal treatment and requires accommodations up to undue hardship, defined only by cost, outside funding, and health/safety. However, the policy is critiqued for not holding itself accountable and for failing to address systemic barriers. Teacher preparation is inadequate, with little to no disability training in Ontario teacher education programs, and educators face challenges such as limited resources, large class sizes, and reduced funding. The “empty vessel” concept is rejected, emphasizing that knowledge emerges through interaction, not transmission.

Recommendations include developing policies that involve disabled students and educators, improving teacher training with non-ableist and universal design approaches, and creating inclusive spaces for educators with disabilities. The conclusion reiterates that the education system was not designed for disabled students and continues to segregate them under the guise of special education.

In Meola v. Ziman, the New Jersey Superior Court considered whether an employee's sick time, personal days, and family illness wages are collateral sources under N.J.S.A. 2A:15-97, entitling a defendant to a credit against lost wages. Plaintiff, injured in an auto accident, sought lost wages from defendant tortfeasor; her husband's vehicle lacked income continuation coverage. Defendant argued these wage replacements were collateral sources to be disclosed and deducted. The court examined the statute's purpose to prevent duplicate recovery. Noting no New Jersey precedent, it followed Bruwelheide v. Garvey, where sick leave that could be cashed out was not a collateral source because the employee earned it and using it diminished future benefits. The court agreed with American Jurisprudence that such benefits are earned compensation, and using them due to a tortfeasor's negligence forces surrender of those benefits. Here, plaintiff exhausted her accumulated sick leave and personal/family illness days, losing their future use or cash-out value. Thus, recovery from defendant would not be duplicative. The court held that sick pay and compensation for personal and family illness days are not collateral source benefits and cannot offset a lost wages award.
