The study investigates how online informal education, particularly synchronous workshops and courses, contributes to personalized learning in design education. It distinguishes formal, non-formal, informal, and random learning, and outlines how digitalization has transformed education by enabling virtual, multimedia, collaborative, and personalized learning environments. The research focuses on computational design training offered outside formal curricula. Two synchronous online examples are analyzed: a five-day workshop, “Introduction to Computational Design,” and a 21-day course, “Sustainability through Computational Design.” Both programs involve lectures, demonstrations, assignments, and discussions, using Rhino and Grasshopper software. The workshop provides intensive foundational knowledge with hands-on practice, while the course integrates environmental data and certification standards (LEED, GRIHA) into algorithmic design.

Findings indicate that online informal education offers advantages such as short-term, applied learning, multi-disciplinary interaction, discussion-based environments, open access, and virtual accessibility. Limitations include reliance on individual materials, triggering a competitive medium, varied education approaches, unequal certificates, lack of integration into formal transcripts, and unequal resource accessibility. The programs foster personalized learning by allowing individuals to design their own learning environments, but they may also lead to isolation. The study concludes that digitalization and online informal education personalize design learning, enhance collaboration and rapid skill acquisition, yet create contradictions regarding universal education access and competitiveness. It suggests that integrating informal programs into formal education could make personalized learning more prevalent, though structural differences currently prevent this.

This passage discusses a study on integrating environmental education into expanded opportunity schools in Thailand. It notes that education is key for human and national development, and Thailand's National Education Act aims to provide educational opportunities, leading to the creation of expanded opportunity schools for students in remote areas. This focus aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) for inclusive and equitable quality education.

The study's objective is to develop ways to integrate environmental education into teaching and learning at these schools. The research involved three phases: studying the environmental education situation and community pollution issues via questionnaires and interviews with students, teachers, and directors; conducting a SWOT analysis; and developing and evaluating an integrated environmental education model based on the theory of multiple intelligences.

Findings showed the community faced pollution from agricultural chemicals, wastewater, and garbage. Students had the lowest learning levels in environmental awareness, participation, and skills. The developed integration model had an efficiency (E1/E2) of 81.51/82.11, exceeding the 80/80 criteria. Post-study achievement scores were significantly higher than pre-study scores, and students reported a high level of satisfaction with the model.

The work presents a correct-by-construction approach for formal modeling, verification, and synthesis of a fault-tolerant voter unit (input selection unit) for a synchronous N-modular redundant measurement system used in avionics control. The voter unit selects a prime unit each cycle from N redundant inputs, discarding transient errors and isolating permanently faulty units, while providing a reliable output to the controller along with validity status and output age. A consistent set of 16 functional requirements (R1–R16) is formulated, covering fault identification, isolation of permanently faulty units, and output generation. Fault identification uses mutual deviation checks with a noise threshold δ; soundness and completeness definitions are given, and theoretical limits are derived. Requirements R4 and R5 specify conditions for classifying units as miscomparing or not_miscomparing based on miscomparison counts and remaining fault limits. Under a minimum surviving units assumption, completeness is achieved. The voter unit is designed as a state transition system with five states (S0–S4): S0 (initial valid, no isolated units), S1 (transient fault on prime unit, output retained), S2 (isolated units present but healthy unit available, output updated), S3 (un_id validity when prime unit isolated and no healthy unit identified, output retained), and S4 (not_valid when maximum permanent fault assumption fails). The design ensures bounded output age (≤ persistence_lmt−1 when valid, ≤ 2*(persistence_lmt−1) when un_id). Implementation uses the Rocq interactive theorem prover with higher-order logic and dependent types; voter state and transition functions carry embedded proof terms of invariants. The system is parameterized by number of units, error threshold, maximum simultaneous faults, and persistence limit. Verified code is extracted to OCaml (362 lines, ~3 ms per transition). Consistency of requirements is machine-verified. Future directions include multi-level hierarchical redundancy management and asynchronous fault handling.

Solar energy is now the cheapest power source globally, driving a shift to renewables. The bull market signal is defined as 18 consecutive closes above the 200-day simple moving average (SMA) during a bear market. The strategy sells the S&P 500 when it drops 20% from its all-time high and buys when the index closes above its 200-day SMA for 18 consecutive days. Backtested from 1927 to the present on the S&P 500 (without dividend or split adjustments), it generated 12 signals corresponding to 12 bear markets. The strategy’s metrics include a CAGR of 7.24%, standard deviation of 15.26, Sharpe ratio of 0.24, maximum drawdown of 60% (25% excluding the 1929 crash), time in market of 87.38%, and risk-adjusted return of 8.28%. After a buy signal, the S&P 500 averaged gains of 9.54% after six months and 21.84% after one year. Compared to the golden cross strategy (50-day/200-day SMA crosses), the bull signal performed better but not on a risk-adjusted basis, spent 30% more time invested, and produced fewer signals (12 vs. 49). The signal was last triggered on February 15, 2023.

An augmented reality system for image-guided surgery includes a first head-mounted device worn by a first healthcare professional, comprising a head-mounted display and a first tracking device (e.g., a camera) that tracks a patient marker and a tool marker. The patient marker is configured to allow determination of the head-mounted device's location and orientation relative to the patient using only that single tracking device, without triangulation. A computer processor generates an augmented reality image on the display, showing a virtual image of the tool and patient anatomy overlaid on the patient's body. When both the patient marker and tool are within the first tracking device's line of sight, the image is based solely on data from that device. If line of sight to either marker is blocked, the processor uses data from an additional tracking device, which may be on a second head-mounted device worn by another healthcare professional or a stationary tracking device. In such cases, the display may show the second professional's view, fill the display with the virtual image, or present the virtual tool and anatomy without alignment to the actual patient anatomy. The system can also combine data from multiple tracking devices to determine tool position, and may use an inertial measurement unit on the head-mounted device to track movements when the patient marker is obscured.

The SNP Run VMPL NAE event lets a guest request a VMPL level change, requiring a VMSA for that level. The SEV-TIO extension enables trusted device binding; the SNP TIO Guest Request supplies unencrypted data (Guest PCI ID, MMIO range, TDISP status) and uses data pages for an optional nonce and returning measurements, certificates, and a TDISP attestation report. Secure AVIC uses a guest-owned backing page, registered or unregistered via NAE events. Termination requests provide reason codes and a feature mask. Unsupported NAEs trigger an Unsupported Event exit. Guest identification uses CPUID with SEV support bits. SMP booting relies on initial register values or an AP jump table; the AP Creation NAE event allows VMSA-based AP state setup. NMI handling uses an NMI Complete message after a #DB intercept. Debug registers can be virtualized via DebugVirtualization or DR7 intercept caching. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported. For Restricted Injection, the #HV doorbell page defines PendingEvent (vector, non-maskable events, NoFurtherSignal) and NoEoiRequired for EOI assist. Interrupt shadows are managed by executing HLT with interrupts disabled. Configuration uses VMGEXIT actions (GET_PREFERRED, SET, QUERY). The host presents interrupts by writing the vector, sets NoEoiRequired when no other interrupts are ready, and handles EOI via clearing NoEoiRequired or an explicit MSR write. A study in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that birds and mammals adapt to temperature changes 2-3 times faster than reptiles and amphibians over geological timescales. Researchers analyzed about 300,000 million data points covering nearly 11,500 species and 270 million years of fossil and living records. Traits like regulating their own body temperature and using body heat to control offspring temperature likely aided faster adaptation, allowing them to inhabit more northern and southern regions. However, it is unclear if these traits will help with current rapid climate change. Other pressures such as pollution, hunting, habitat loss, and invasive species are driving extinction, with species disappearing up to 10,000 times faster than normal. Lead author Jonathan Rolland hopes future research will connect macroevolution and microevolution to better understand adaptation to ongoing environmental changes.

Fewer than one in five market corrections (drops of 10-20%) escalate into bear markets (drops over 20%); 80% of corrections do not become bear markets. Panic selling during a correction risks missing a rebound. On average, a correction has occurred every year since 1900, making them routine. A 50-year-old can expect about 35 more corrections. Historically, the average correction decline was 13.5% and lasted 54 days. Emotional reactions are common, but most corrections are “seasonal storms.” Bear markets are more severe: the S&P 500 has averaged a 33% drop, with over a third plunging more than 40%. Even Jack Bogle admits feeling miserable during 50% declines, but he rereads books on staying the course. Bear markets don’t last; over 70 years, 14 bear markets lasted between 45 days and nearly 2 years, averaging about a year. From 1980 to 2015, the S&P 500 had an average intra-year decline of 14.2%, yet achieved positive returns in 27 of those 36 years (75%). The market generally rises long-term despite events like wars and financial crises. Warren Buffett notes that America’s economic magic remains, with population growth and productivity driving future wealth. Ultimately, the stock market transfers money from the impatient to the patient; individuals determine their own outcomes by their decisions.

The TPS7H500x-SP series controllers feature primary switching outputs (OUTA, and OUTB on select devices) with approximately 150 mA peak current, necessitating external gate drivers. OUTA serves buck and single-ended topologies; OUTA and OUTB are used for push-pull and full-bridge. OUTB is active only when the duty cycle limit is set to 50% by connecting DCL to AVSS, applicable to TPS7H5001-SP and TPS7H5004-SP. Synchronous rectifier outputs (SRA, SRB) are available on some devices, also with ~150 mA peak current and external gate drive recommended. TPS7H5001-SP includes SRB, active only with the 50% duty cycle limit. SR outputs remain off during soft-start and begin switching when SS exceeds 1 V.

Dead time between primary and SR outputs is programmable on TPS7H5001-SP and TPS7H5002-SP via resistors from PS and SP to AVSS, setting TDPS and TDSP. TPS7H5003-SP has a fixed 50 ns dead time. Floating PS/SP yields a minimum 8 ns; resistor values range from 10 kΩ to 300 kΩ. Leading edge blank time is fixed at 50 ns on TPS7H5003-SP and programmable on other devices via a resistor from LEB to AVSS (10 kΩ to 300 kΩ, pin cannot float). Pulse skipping mode prevents minimum on-time issues at high frequency, occurring when COMP <0.3 V at the clock rising edge and the previous duty cycle <25%. With a 50% duty cycle limit and both outputs active, skipped pulses are equal to maintain volt-second balance.

Duty cycle is configurable via the DCL pin: TPS7H5001/2/3-SP support 100% (DCL=VLDO), 75% (floating), or 50% (DCL=AVSS). TPS7H5004-SP only supports 50% (DCL must be AVSS). The 50% limit enables OUTB/SRB.

Current sensing and PWM generation use the CS_ILIM pin, which senses primary-side current. The COMP voltage divided by 2 is compared to the sensed current with a 150 mV offset. A resistor from CS_ILIM to AVSS sets the current limit threshold (1.05 V nominal). When exceeded, hiccup mode activates: cycle-by-cycle limiting occurs while a capacitor on HICC is charged by 80 µA pulses. When HICC reaches 0.6 V, SS is discharged, switching stops, HICC is pulled to 1 V then discharged by 1 µA. Restart occurs when HICC falls to 0.3 V. Minimum CHICC is 3.3 nF.

External fault protection via the FAULT pin: rising threshold 0.6 V, falling 0.5 V, minimum pulse width 0.4–1.4 µs. A fault triggers shutdown, SS discharge, and outputs low. After the fault clears, a delay of approximately 15 switching cycles plus logic delay precedes soft-start restart.

Slope compensation is set by a resistor from RSC to AVSS, with the recommended value equal to the falling slope of the inductor current. Frequency compensation uses a transconductance error amplifier (OTA) with Type 2A or 2B networks. Component selection (RCOMP, CCOMP, CHF) is based on crossover frequency and power stage transconductance. Thermal shutdown occurs at 175°C junction temperature, restart at 160°C.

The controllers use fixed-frequency peak current mode control. They are radiation-hardened for space-grade DC-DC converters, supporting topologies like buck, flyback, forward, active-clamp forward, push-pull, and full-bridge, with switching frequencies up to 2 MHz.

A design example for a synchronous push-pull converter using GaN FETs at 500 kHz is provided. Key component selections include: RT resistor for frequency, output voltage divider, dead time resistors (~25 ns target), leading edge blank time resistor (~50 ns), soft-start capacitor (33 nF), transformer turns ratio (2.5) and primary inductance (40 µH), primary and SR FETs, RCD clamp, output inductor (0.47 µH), output capacitance (~2.3 mF), current sense resistor (7.5 Ω), hiccup capacitor (3.3 nF), frequency compensation components (RCOMP=40.2 kΩ, CCOMP=15 nF, CHF=47 pF), and slope compensation resistor (102 kΩ).

Power supply input range is 4 V to 14 V, requiring a minimum 0.1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor (X5R or better) close to the controller. Layout guidelines emphasize separating analog and power grounds, minimizing switch node area, routing feedback away from noise, using short wide high-current traces, placing bypass capacitors close, and filtering sensed current if needed. For the CFP package, connect backside metallization to the AVSS plane with multiple vias. Mechanical, packaging, and orderable information includes CFP and TSSOP package options with tape and reel dimensions.

The case involved an action of trespass to try title and for partition of an undivided half interest in a league of land. The plaintiff claimed through a sheriff’s deed from a judgment against William F. Henderson, who held under an 1839 instrument from Mastin Latham. The court construed that instrument as an absolute, unconditional conveyance, not an executory contract. The recital of consideration referred to past services, and the provision requiring equal division with Latham taking choice of halves did not create a condition subsequent that could defeat the estate. The defense of stale demand was inapplicable because the deed was executed, not executory. The statute of limitations defenses failed: ten years’ adverse possession was not completed due to constitutional tolling from 1861 to 1870; no evidence of tax payments supported the five-year limitation; the three-year limitation failed because the occupants were tenants of Latham and the possession was not under the title or color of title offered; and the ten-year limitation also failed for lack of privity between the defendant and prior possessors. The judgment was reversed and the cause remanded.

Android 8.0 Oreo, released in August, includes under-the-hood refinements and features like Picture-in-Picture (PiP) mode, Notification Dots, Smart Text Selection, Notification Snoozing, and Autofill Framework. PiP mode enhances multitasking beyond Nougat’s split-screen by allowing videos to play in a floating window at the OS level. Not all apps support PiP; supported apps include Google Chrome, Duo, Play Movies & TV, Play Services, Maps, WhatsApp, YouTube, and VLC. YouTube PiP requires a YouTube Red subscription, which is unavailable in some countries. To use PiP with YouTube in Chrome, open Chrome, load YouTube in Desktop mode, play a video, enter full-screen, then swipe up and tap the home button to create a movable floating window. The window can be paused, closed via an X icon, returned to full-screen, or dismissed by dragging to the bottom. If PiP does not work, enable it in Settings > Apps & notifications > Advanced > Special app access > Picture-in-picture. The feature allows power users to watch video or get navigation directions while using other apps.

The speaker advocates moderate reform with plain men, rejecting reactionaries and extremists who push for government ownership. The government should supervise business, not conduct it, to ensure equality of opportunity and burden. Prohibiting all combinations is noxious; combination of capital and labor is necessary. Rigorous control and supervision are needed to prevent public injury, and a combination controlling a necessity is presumed adverse. Current laws forbid all combinations instead of discriminating between good and evil. Rebates often stem from big shippers' pressure. Railroads should be allowed to combine to prevent such advantages if agreements are sanctioned by the Interstate Commerce Commission and published. An unenforceable law that would destroy business is a public evil, making decent men lawbreakers and eroding respect for law. The Interstate Commerce Commission noted that Supreme Court decisions against joint traffic associations had no practical effect and that railways cannot operate without concerted action. The speaker recommends amending the law. On taxation, the federal system poses difficulties. Some taxes are best levied locally, but many require the General Government to prevent driving entities away. The National Government relies on tariffs and excise taxes. A graduated inheritance tax and, if possible, a graduated income tax should be imposed. The wealthy have a special obligation and should pay their full share, but such taxation must be just and moderate, recognizing the danger when voters pay little. The aim is equitable distribution of the burden, treating rich and poor with absolute equality and avoiding injustice to either.

Joseph McGreal, a police officer, was fired on June 28, 2010. He sued the Village of Orland Park and three police officials, claiming First Amendment retaliation for speech at a November 2, 2009 village board meeting, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The district court granted summary judgment for the defendants. The Seventh Circuit affirmed. McGreal provided no admissible evidence that the defendants knew of his protected speech, so he failed to show his speech was a motivating factor in his firing. Even if he had, the defendants offered legitimate non-retaliatory reasons—lying under oath, insubordination, and reckless conduct—and McGreal offered no admissible evidence that these reasons were pretextual; suspicious timing alone was insufficient. For emotional distress, McGreal presented no evidence of extreme and outrageous conduct or severe emotional distress, and he admitted his distress was “garden variety,” which is legally insufficient. The district court’s decision was affirmed.

HoopTactics' baseline and sideline out of bounds plays create high-percentage shots with multiple options, flowing into continuity if no shot. Proven full court plays can win championships. End of game: advance and take timeout if possible; otherwise, inbound safely with baseline out of bounds play and best free throw shooters.

The President reports that efforts to have belligerent nations revoke edicts against neutral commerce failed. He used authority to suspend embargo laws and instructed ministers in London and Paris. Indian peace is maintained; tribes deliver up accused murderers, attachment grows, husbandry advances, and one Cherokee division considers citizenship. Defensive works at seaports are nearly finished except New York and New Orleans. Only 103 gun-boats were built this year, sufficient. Additional military force recruiting is satisfactory. Treasury receipts near $18 million, with prior balance, paid $2.3 million principal, left near $14 million; $5.35 million due January 1 to complete 8% stock reimbursement; total principal extinguished $33.58 million, freeing $2 million interest annually. The passage describes example embodiments for implementing enhanced features in 5G systems, specifically for network slicing and AMF selection for isolated network slices. In Joy v. Helbing, the plaintiff, as assignee of a creditor, sought to set aside a deed of gift from Louis Helbing to his wife Louise. The deed was executed in 1893 when Helbing was solvent, but remained unrecorded until December 1895. Between September and December 1895, Helbing obtained credit from the creditor by representing himself as owner of the property. The trial court found the deed was not made with intent to defraud creditors, and judgment was for defendants. On appeal, the court held that the grantor's intent is a question for the trial court based on all facts and circumstances. The burden was on the plaintiff to prove fraudulent intent. The unrecorded deed was a suspicious circumstance but not alone sufficient to prove fraud. The court also held that the exclusion of testimony about concealment of goods and the wife's claim of ownership nearly four years after the deed was not reversible error. The judgment was affirmed.

The Court of Appeals considered defendant Lawrence B. Schaub’s appeal from a circuit court order that reversed a district court’s dismissal of a child abandonment charge. The charge arose from allegations that defendant transferred his ten-month-old daughter to an undercover police officer for $60,000. At the preliminary examination, the district court dismissed the charge, finding the prosecution failed to show the child was placed without care. The circuit court reversed, concluding sufficient evidence supported bindover on both elements of child abandonment. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the Court of Appeals for consideration as on leave granted.

The Court of Appeals majority held that the child abandonment statute, MCL 750.135, requires proof of two elements: exposing the child and intent to wholly abandon. It found sufficient evidence of intent to wholly abandon because defendant sold the child for money, agreed to relinquish parental rights, and did not intend to participate in the child’s life. However, the majority concluded the evidence did not establish exposure. Relying on Shannon v People (1858), it stated that exposure must subject the child to hazard of personal injury, and leaving a child where it would be certain to be cared for does not constitute exposure. The testimony showed defendant handed the child directly to a person to care for her, so there was no basis to find the child was left without care or at risk of injury from abandonment. The majority reversed the circuit court’s order and remanded, noting the reversal was without prejudice to possible common-law felony charges. It also observed that the Legislature subsequently enacted MCL 750.136c, prohibiting the sale or purchase of people, but ex post facto principles barred its application to defendant.

Judge O’Connell dissented, stating that delivering a ten-month-old infant to a total stranger does expose the child to injury. The dissent argued that the element of exposure is established if the prosecution shows the defendant put the child at risk, and that whether selling a child to a stranger meets the definition of exposure is a question of fact for a jury. The dissent contended that, considering modern circumstances, defendant could not be certain the child would be cared for, and therefore the circuit court’s order should be affirmed.

This retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed factors causing discharge delays from a 23-bed subacute Complex Discharge Unit (CDU) at St James's Hospital, Dublin, during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic (March 2020–February 2021). Data from 390 adult patients with hospital length of stay (LOS) >15 days were extracted from electronic patient records. The median age was 79 years, 59.7% were female, and 48.2% had >4 comorbidities. Median CDU LOS was 19.4 days; the most common primary diagnosis was infection/sepsis (23.33%).

Five factors were examined: complications from primary diagnoses/multimorbidity (MM), healthcare-associated infections (HCAI), frailty/falls requiring rehabilitation, patient-centred needs, and community services. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that age 65–75 years, female gender, and >4 MM were associated with prolonged LOS. Complications from comorbidities, HCAI, frailty/falls/rehabilitation, and community services were not significant contributors, while patient-centred needs significantly prolonged LOS. Stratified Cox regression identified complications from primary diagnoses and patient-centred needs as statistically significant factors across age, gender, and MM strata. For age groups 65–75 and 75–85, patient-centred needs prolonged LOS; both genders and all MM levels showed significant effects from complications of primary diagnoses and patient-centred needs.

Overall, 37.94% of delays were due to complications from primary diagnoses/MM, 25.38% to frailty/falls/rehabilitation, 14.35% to community services, 13.07% to patient-centred needs, and 10.52% to HCAI. Complications arising directly from comorbidities were non-contributory. Patients with ≤4 and >4 MM experienced the same delaying factors. The study was limited by its single-centre design, focus on delaying factors rather than readmission, sample size, and lack of detailed mortality/readmission analysis. The most common factors delaying discharge were complexities from primary diagnoses and patient-centred needs (cognition, psychosocial needs, carer needs). The findings may inform medical decisions and future pandemic contingency planning.

This study assessed the prevalence and factors associated with non-adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) among HIV patients at Kibungo Referral Hospital, Rwanda. A cross-sectional design with a structured questionnaire was used, and 424 participants were surveyed. The overall non-adherence rate was 13% (87% adherence). Multivariate analysis identified significant factors: age below 31 years (Adjusted Odds Ratio [AoR] 15.462), lack of tertiary education (AoR 8.232), stigma interfering with adherence (AoR 2.148), perception that ART is ineffective (AoR 9.333), and not integrating ART into daily activities (AoR 11.180). Setting an alarm as a reminder was not significantly associated. The study concludes that non-adherence is slightly high and driven by younger age, lower education, stigma, perceived ineffectiveness of ART, and failure to incorporate treatment into routines.

The Warren Buffett ETF Portfolio (90/10) is an investment strategy based on a 2013 letter from Warren Buffett, instructing that 90% of his wife’s inheritance be placed in a low-fee stock index fund and 10% in short-term government bonds. The strategy allocates 90% of funds to low-cost, passively managed S&P 500 index ETFs and 10% to government bonds. It aims to provide long-term growth with reduced risk and lower fees compared to actively managed portfolios. The S&P 500 index tracks 500 large U.S. companies, offering diversification and historically strong returns. The 10% bond allocation cushions against market volatility, as government bonds are considered less volatile and safer due to government backing. The approach emphasizes passive investing, avoiding market timing and high fees.

Backtests using SPY (S&P 500 ETF) with different bond ETFs show that the portfolio’s performance closely follows the S&P 500. With SHY (short-term Treasury), it performed slightly worse than SPY. With IEI (intermediate-term), it also underperformed SPY but slightly better than with SHY. With TLT (long-term Treasury), the portfolio performed better than the other two and was almost at par with SPY, demonstrating compensation for taking extra maturity risk. However, the portfolio underperformed in 2022 due to a poor bond market. Past performance is not indicative of future results; performance can be affected by market conditions, economic changes, and geopolitical events.

The ideal asset allocation depends on individual goals, risk tolerance, and time horizon, but the 90/10 split is a common starting point. Investors can build the portfolio via a lump sum or dollar-cost averaging. Benefits include simplicity, low costs, diversification, and reduced risk. Risks include market risk, interest rate risk, and inflation risk. Tax implications arise from capital gains and dividends, varying by individual circumstances. Consulting a financial advisor is recommended.

The paper addresses e-learning governance within digital business ecosystems. E-learning is crucial for business competitiveness, requiring a flexible process model and governance to provide strategic direction, achieve objectives, manage risks, and allocate resources appropriately. It reviews e-learning ecosystems, defined as learning communities united by a learning management system, and notes their benefits such as integrated HR systems and return on investment. Governance is described as decision-making processes and relationships. E-learning governance is framed using structures, processes, and communications/relational mechanisms, with a fourth element of pedagogies and instructional designs added. The framework is enhanced by adopting six characteristics and dimensions from Darking: constitution and balance of interests, culture of communication, credibility/attunement/trust, organisation and synchronisation, licensing and regulation, and technological dimension. Information security governance is emphasized, involving policies, countermeasures, risk management, and trust in services, business, and knowledge. The paper concludes that e-learning governance is a strategic necessity and calls for further exploratory research.

In this 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action, inmate Richard A. Milan alleged that prison officials violated his due process and Eighth Amendment rights by denying him a visit with Judy Ballard on July 10, 1988, without written notice. The defendants moved for summary judgment. Applying Celotex and Anderson standards, the court found no genuine issue of material fact. Under Hewitt v. Helms and Kentucky Department of Corrections v. Thompson, inmates have no general liberty interest in visitation; state regulations must use mandatory language and specific substantive predicates to create one. The relevant administrative procedure allowed denial of visitation without specific criteria and thus did not create a protectable liberty interest. Although the procedure required written denial, the admitted failure to provide it did not amount to a constitutional violation, as procedural guidelines alone do not establish a liberty interest. Plaintiff did not dispute the discretionary denial following his escape attempt. The court denied plaintiff's summary judgment motion and granted summary judgment for defendants, concluding plaintiff failed to establish a substantive constitutional right.

A cloud-integrated storage appliance caches snapshots from data sources before eviction to cloud storage. It arranges snapshot metadata into key-value stores per defined data collection, using locally generated, deterministic snapshot identifiers as key prefixes. Metadata records include inode records, directory records, and data map records; snapshot data is stored in snapshot data files. The appliance can restore a snapshot by merging valid records from the specified snapshot back to the baseline snapshot, using the metadata layout to identify valid data ranges. File restore and snapshot reclamation (deletion) are also supported, with reclamation implicitly transferring ownership of valid records to a succeeding valid snapshot. To prevent eviction of stable data blocks in a forever incremental backup strategy, the appliance creates synthetic baseline snapshots by manipulating snapshot metadata (e.g., expanding data ownership to a recent snapshot or maintaining a reverse incremental synthetic baseline) and refreshes eviction state data (such as time indicators) for valid cached data blocks, thereby reducing the risk of violating recovery time objectives.

The Golden Cross Trading Strategy uses two moving averages: a short-term (50-day) and a long-term (200-day). A Golden Cross occurs when the 50-day moving average crosses above the 200-day moving average. The strategy aims to exploit the stock market's long-term uptrend while reducing losses in bear markets. Trading rules: buy when the 50-day crosses above the 200-day, sell when it crosses below. An example trade on the S&P 500 from July 2020 to March 2022 yielded a 32.4% gain. A backtest on the S&P 500 since 1960 resulted in 33 trades, each lasting about 350 days. 79% of trades were winners, with an average gain of 15.8% and an annual return of 6.8%. The strategy was invested 70% of the time, giving a risk-adjusted return of 9.6%. Its maximum drawdown was 33%, compared to buy-and-hold's 56%. While the annual return did not beat buy-and-hold's 7.2%, the strategy had lower drawdowns. It is prone to whipsaw signals, but a few big winners can compensate.

The study estimated the burden of disease (BoD) of COVID-19 in the Republic of Ireland from March 1, 2020 to February 28, 2021, using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). Data were sourced from publicly available national datasets. Years of Life Lost (YLL) were calculated as deaths multiplied by remaining life expectancy from GBD 2019 life tables, using mortality data stratified by sex and age. Years Lived with Disability (YLD) were calculated for five health states (asymptomatic, moderate, severe, critical, post-acute consequences) using incident cases, disability weights, and durations. Asymptomatic cases were estimated via a 3:1 ratio from seroprevalence studies. DALYs were the sum of YLL and YLD. Ethical approval was obtained from University College Cork.

This passage studies time-delayed feedback in multi-agent learning for normal-form games. Optimistic algorithms like OFTRL normally achieve O(1) regret and convergence to Nash equilibrium, but time delay hinders observation of previous rewards. The authors show that in Matching Pennies with an unconstrained setting and Euclidean regularizer, any time delay m≥1 causes OFTRL to suffer Ω(√T) regret (Theorem 6) and diverge from equilibrium (Theorem 7). The exponential rate of radius change is α = m - n + 1/2, where n is the optimistic weight; for OFTRL n=1, so α>0 for m≥1. To address this, they propose Weighted OFTRL (WOFTRL), which adds optimism n times via mt_i = n u^{t-m}_i. Taylor expansion reveals that time delay m and optimistic weight n cancel out. When n = m+1, WOFTRL satisfies the RVU property with parameters α = h_max/η, β = λ²η, γ = 1/(8η) where λ = (m+1)(m+2)/2 (Theorem 10). With learning rate η = 1/(√8λL), it achieves O(1) total regret (Corollary 11). In poly-matrix zero-sum games, it achieves best-iterate convergence to Nash equilibrium (Corollary 13). Experiments on Matching Pennies, Sato's game, and Rock-Paper-Scissors confirm O(1) regret when n > m, O(√T) regret when n ≤ m, and last-iterate convergence when n > m. Time delay m increases regret and requires a smaller learning rate.

The speaker, addressing the Notre Dame community, commends Father Hesburgh's human rights advocacy and honors Bishop Lamont, Cardinal Arns, and Cardinal Kim for their courage. He then presents a vision for a new American foreign policy. He expresses confidence in democracy and rejects the adoption of adversaries' tactics, citing Vietnam as a failure. He notes that the world has changed dramatically, with decolonization and rising aspirations, and that foreign policy must now integrate justice, equity, and human rights with traditional peace and war concerns. The policy rests on five principles: first, reaffirming commitment to human rights as a fundamental tenet, while acknowledging the limits of moral suasion but emphasizing the power of words and the importance of keeping the human rights discussion alive. Second, reinforcing bonds among democracies through economic cooperation, free trade, monetary strengthening, non-proliferation efforts, and joint defense modernization; all NATO members are now democracies. Third, engaging the Soviet Union to halt the strategic arms race, seeking a freeze on modernization and production, substantial reductions, a comprehensive test ban, chemical warfare prohibition, no space satellite attack capability, and Indian Ocean arms limits, with the ultimate goal of eliminating nuclear weapons. He supports détente as progress toward peace and urges the Soviet Union not to impose its system on others and to join in aiding the developing world. Fourth, improving chances for Middle East peace through consultations with Israel, Syria, Jordan, and Egypt, suggesting a flexible framework for discussing comprehensive peace, security and borders, and the Palestinian homeland. The U.S.-Israel friendship is based on shared respect for freedom and peace, and policy will not be affected by leadership changes; parties should remain bound by UN Resolutions 242 and 338. Fifth, reducing nuclear proliferation and conventional arms spread, including international efforts on peaceful nuclear energy, a review of arms transfer policy, and a national policy to reduce arms sales volume, restrict advanced weapons transfers, and reduce coproduction arrangements, while encouraging other nations to join. The speaker calls for a wider framework of international cooperation, closer ties with Latin America, Africa, and Asia, and addressing global poverty. He advocates normalized relations with China as central to global policy, and a peaceful resolution in southern Africa based on majority rule with minority rights protection, working with European allies and African states. The policy is rooted in moral values, material wealth, military power, and designed to serve mankind.

The passage discusses the distinction between investing and speculation according to Benjamin Graham. The author recounts buying Ask Jeeves stock based on a Peter Lynch strategy, making a 25% gain, but argues it was not an investment because he did not consider safety of principal. Graham defines an investment as selecting securities that protect capital and promise an adequate return; otherwise it is speculation. Most people focus only on upside, ignoring downside protection. Eliminating permanent losses would significantly improve portfolio returns, and Warren Buffett advises avoiding big mistakes. To protect capital, one should buy stocks at large discounts to intrinsic value—the larger the discount, the greater the margin of safety against business deterioration and valuation errors. Financially solid companies have clean balance sheets, low debt relative to equity, high current ratios, and ideally improving ratios, with no debt or steadily paying it off and ample liquid assets. Protecting downside can yield profits even without a bright future, as no one can predict the future and businesses tend to experience average results. Negative sentiment creates a margin of safety; buying unloved firms at steep discounts can be profitable as the price-value gap closes. Temporary problems may cause huge discounts, and if the business remains intact with a solid balance sheet, it can recover and the stock price will rise to intrinsic value. Net net stocks, written off due to significant problems, trade well below reasonable business value, offer protection, and have conservative balance sheets; as long as the balance sheet isn't rapidly deteriorating, they are sound investments. Ultimately, being an investor depends on the selection process, not the asset type. Following Graham's definition—selecting stocks that protect downside and promise a decent profit—leads to good long-run returns. The author discloses no positions or business relationships.

Player roles are defined: point guard directs the offense, shooting guard is the best three-point shooter, small forward is a baseline/corner shooter and offensive rebounder, power forward operates from high and low post, and post is the best inside rebounder. The offense progresses through phases: Basic Overload Reads, Pass & Cut Action, High Post Roll, Ball Reversal, and Continuity. Optional entries include Flop, Exchange, and Triple Stack alignments. Crunch Time specials include "Vegas" (double screen away), "Back" (weakside lob), and "Cat" (attacking double teams with a 2-1-2 alignment). Rules include post rolling to the basket on baseline corner passes and baseline corners back cutting on middle entries.

This document provides a user-level description of the AGESA™ software procedures and abilities for host environment wrapper implementers. It defines procedure call interfaces, recommends a wrapper implementation, and describes configurable options. Related AMD documents include BIOS and Kernel Developer’s Guides, Revision Guides, and industry standards. Terminology defines components such as Link, MCT, Node, Socket, Processor, Die, Core, Wrapper, MP, BSP, and AP.

The software uses a three-level version numbering (X.Y.Z), with the interface specification tracking the first two levels. The release package contains binary compilations, build control files, example user-generated files, and specialized tools. Code complies with UEFI C Coding Standards, uses descriptive file names, and includes comment headers. Public procedures use “Amd” prefix for call-in entry points and “Agesa” prefix for call-out routines.

The interface aims to remain constant across processor generations, with call entry points based on boot time line rather than specific technical functions. Configuration parameters are automatically determined where possible; required parameters must be supplied by the host environment, while optional ones may be modified. Call mechanics use an “initializer” function: allocate a structure pre-filled with defaults, allow host modification, call the main function, check status, and release the structure. Error reporting uses return codes (SUCCESS, UNSUPPORTED, BOUNDS_CHK, ALERT, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, FATAL) and an event log buffer holding the 16 most recent events, retrievable via AmdReadEventLog.

Build design relies on a <Plat>Options.c file to conditionally compile defaults tables, which initializers use. Main technology code is compiled separately as a library. A binary image build style isolates AGESA from the host environment; the binary header contains a signature, entry point, and module headers. The host must locate the image and establish 32-bit flat address mode. The standard header (AMD_CONFIG_PARAMS) includes function identifier, image base pointers, PCIe base, callout pointer, and heap information. Integrated Debug Services macros are compile-time controlled.

The boot time line includes reset, integrity check, recovery or main boot, resume from S3, OS boot, and restoration. AGESA entry points correspond to these: AmdInitReset (minimal processor init, execution cache regions, FCH settings), AmdInitEarly (full init, platform configuration including VRM, PCIe, power management), and AmdInitPost (memory initialization with extensive memory configuration options). Host environment must not call unpublished functions or enable code caching before memory init except via provided functions.

For binary module porting, 16-bit real mode is deprecated; execution occurs in 32-bit protected mode. A Bridge calls the Dispatcher (AmdAgesaDispatcher) in the binary image, and a Router handles call-outs to host procedures. The host must provide a stack. In UEFI environments, four execution stages (SEC, PEI, DXE, RTP) are supported. SEC phase uses AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK to establish a C environment. PEI phase employs two PEIMs (processor init and memory init) that publish PPIs. DXE driver calls AmdInitLate and publishes AgesaDxeProtocol. An AmdGpuVgaControlDxe driver manages iGPU VGA decoding. Reference files reside in the \Addendum directory. UEFI build uses .inf control files and environment variables AGESA_ROOT, AGESA_OptsDir, and AGESA_PLATFORM. Integration steps include copying options files, setting variables, enabling CAR before AmdInitReset with ‘ByHost’ allocation, and not modifying SS/ESP or cache controls during CAR.

Stack procedures include AMD_RESET_ENABLEMENT for very early control, AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK to establish stack, and AMD_DISABLE_UEFI_STACK to tear it down. Service procedures include AmdCreateStruct (allocates parameter blocks via PreMemHeap, PostMemDram, or ByHost methods), AmdReleaseStruct, AmdGetDataEye, AmdGetApicAddress, AmdGetExeCacheSize, AmdGetPciAddress, AmdIdentifyCore, AmdIdentifyDimm, AmdMergeMmioRange, and AmdReadEventLog. Entry point details specify parameters, actions, dependencies, and status codes for each boot time call.

This study compared a hybridization capture-based metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) workflow (Illumina Respiratory Pathogen ID/AMR panel) with a multiplex PCR panel (FTD Respiratory Pathogens 33) using nasopharyngeal samples from 29 individuals with suspected acute upper respiratory infection. The mNGS panel detected 44 microorganisms (27 bacteria, 2 fungi, 15 viruses), while PCR detected 15 (4 bacteria, 11 viruses). Concordance for shared targets was 98.33% positive percent agreement and 100% negative percent agreement. mNGS identified additional pathogens not targeted by PCR, including SARS-CoV-2, Coxsackievirus A, and human rhinovirus C, and revealed frequent co-infections. Detected microorganisms were phenotypically classified into three groups: group 1 (normal flora/colonizers), group 2 (frequently associated with respiratory disease), and group 3 (generally pathogenic). The hybridization capture-based mNGS approach provided broader pathogen detection, species-level differentiation, and potential clinical utility for assessing trafficking risk to the lower respiratory tract. The study suggests this targeted workflow may supplement syndromic testing, offering advantages in cost, throughput, and adaptability for decentralized laboratories, though further clinical validation is needed.

Offensive set pieces off free kicks restart play after a foul. Design must follow Law 13 and consider distance/angle to goal. The referee spots the ball; opponents must be 10 yards away. The ball is in play when touched and moves; the kicker cannot touch it twice. Free kicks are direct (can score directly) or indirect (must touch another player first). The referee signals indirect kicks, ensures the ball is stationary, and indicates readiness.

Basic strategy: defensive-half free kicks are short passes to retain possession. In the offensive third, they become set pieces—planned plays with higher scoring chances. The defense builds a wall. The offensive design aims to defeat the wall, be minimally complex, and produce a shot on goal. Coaches design plays, assign positions, and drill execution based on proximity, direct/indirect status, and player skill.

Proximity locations: five near (outside left/right, near left/right, near center) with varying wall sizes and typical actions (cross, direct shot, pass). Three far locations (far left/right, far center) farther out. Direct/indirect status determines if a touch is needed before scoring. A shortcut: major player-contact fouls and handling are direct; everything else indirect.

Design approaches: up to sixteen set pieces for eight locations and two kick types. Features include: direct shot (bending around/through wall), simple touch (indirect kick with immediate shot), cross, stepover run (misdirection, may include touch for indirect), misdirection (fake runs), screening (obstructing view), committee (group gathering), single pass (lateral for better angle or leading ball), two passes (quick lateral passes to break wall), chip over wall, deception/decoy, ghosting in, crashing (rushing attackers), and rebounds/follow-up. Coaches should study examples.

Player performance: set plays need dedicated, smart players who understand situations. Kickers wait for referee readiness; the ball may be slightly repositioned but must be stationary. A dead-ball specialist with bending ability may be designated, possibly one right-footed and one left-footed. Players must know direct/indirect status and roles. One player in charge may request 10 yards if defenders encroach; play waits for referee signal. At higher levels, vanishing spray marks ball and wall; the ball should not be re-set. Defenses may use offside traps. Coaches adapt set pieces to personnel.

Other considerations: Ceremonial Free Kick (CFK) involves a delay; Quick Free Kick (QFK) is taken immediately to exploit lapses. QFK is rare, usually direct, requires referee readiness, and can be used when the goalkeeper is out of position. The odd case: an indirect free kick awarded within 10 yards of goal (e.g., impeding, dangerous play, goalkeeper back-pass). Defenders must stand on the goal-line between the posts until the ball is touched. Teams rarely prepare; a quick simple touch or direct shot hoping for a deflection may be used.

Practice: run plays from all locations without defenders, then with mannequins, stationary defenders, active defenders. In scrimmages, simulate fouls, enforce rules, correct problems, rotate players. Demonstrate wasted kicks and wall rules. Drill but preserve creativity; ask for player input. Coaching tips: prepare contingencies for missing key players, scout opponents for gaps, incorporate the touch in indirect designs, keep set pieces simple, and understand referee signals (overt or subtle).

This paper proposes an architecture for digitally structured exchange of technical information in industrial business networks, focusing on the lifecycle domain of process industry plants. Existing standards do not cover all technical information types or provide a scalable digital communication medium. The architecture introduces an open consortium to agree on common business practices and information formats, and a network of mediators that route information between enterprises, forming multi-sided platforms. Each business party connects via a single adapter that maps proprietary back-end systems to the common format, enabling scalable system-to-system communication. A prototype was implemented using a web application platform with configurable import/export applications. Experiments involved two equipment suppliers and two plant operators, successfully delivering equipment information (product and device data, attachments) for maintenance and renewal project cases. The prototype demonstrated time and effort savings, though an open consortium and full adapter implementations are still needed. The architecture has potential to increase information management efficiency and indirectly improve production performance. Future work includes forming the consortium, extending the prototype to a mediator network, and covering other domains like financing and logistics.

In Asa B. Meech v. The City of Buffalo, the plaintiffs sought to restrain collection of a second assessment for a sewer in Mariner Street. The city charter empowered the common council to construct sewers, determine the amount to be assessed, and direct assessment on benefited property. It also provided that if an assessment proved insufficient to defray expenses, the council could direct a further assessment for the deficiency.

The common council determined the expense at $1,058.63, directed that sum assessed, and contracted with Robert J. Randolph to construct the sewer for that amount, with security. During work, Randolph encountered a large body of quicksand directly in the sewer line, unknown to both parties and not anticipated. This made it impossible to complete the sewer for the contract price or twice that amount. Randolph stopped work and, with some plaintiffs, petitioned the council to increase the contract price. The council agreed to pay an additional $588.13, which was no more than reasonable compensation and still insufficient to cover actual expenses. Randolph would have abandoned the work otherwise. To raise this sum, the council directed a second assessment on the benefited property, which was confirmed.

At special term, the judge found these facts and held the second assessment illegal, restraining collection. The general term reversed and ordered a new trial. Plaintiffs appealed, stipulating that if the order were affirmed, judgment absolute would be entered against them.

The Court of Appeals affirmed. It held that a municipal corporation with power to make a public improvement and contract for the work may voluntarily increase the contract price where circumstances equitably justify it, unless prohibited by charter. The charter contained no such prohibition. The city could cancel or modify the contract, and the agreement to pay additional compensation was supported by consideration and was not a gratuity. Even if the contract were unenforceable, plaintiffs lacked standing to raise that objection. The court further held that the charter's provision for a further assessment applied: the first assessment proved insufficient to defray the actual expense of the improvement, and the second assessment was a “further assessment” within the meaning of the charter. The duty to assess all expenses on the benefited property implied power to make additional assessments when the first proved insufficient. Judgment affirmed.

This research investigated the experiences of Physical Education Teacher Education (PETE) students in a movement education course that used peer mentoring to develop 21st-century skills. The study was designed as a single case holistic case study with 3 peer mentors and 25 first-year peer learners. Three themes were generated from the results. In the first theme, peer learners excluded group members who did not make an effort, while peer mentors divided responsibilities to complete tasks despite disagreements. In the second theme, both peer mentors and peer learners produced storytelling course content, which increased their awareness of being a teacher and made learning more permanent. In the final theme, using narrative content connected to real life enabled teacher candidates to establish connections between what they learned and their daily lives, making learning more enduring. The conclusion states that providing natural environments through peer mentoring allows prospective teachers to gain experience with 21st-century skills, and that storytelling is effective for permanent learning.

In Hunter v. Bales, Bales (assignee of Thompson) sued Matthew R. Hunter, Moses Hunter, and Moore for specific performance of a land sale contract. The trial court found for plaintiff and decreed specific performance; defendants appealed.

The appellate court stated that when two conflicting theories are supported by evidence, it adopts the theory sustaining the lower court’s finding. The lower court could find that Moore owned the land, promised Thompson the refusal, appointed Phippens agent, and Thompson made a verbal purchase agreement with the agent, who then refused to put it in writing. On December 1, 1856, Moore verbally agreed to sell to Matthew R. Hunter, contingent on the agent not having sold. On December 6, Moore executed a title bond to Thompson. On December 12, Moore deeded the land to Matthew R. Hunter, who knew of the prior written agreement. Thompson tendered the purchase money when due and demanded a deed, which was refused. Matthew R. Hunter later conveyed the land to Moses Hunter.

The court held Thompson had the prior equity and could enforce specific performance, rejecting the argument that his agreement was merely a negotiation. On the statute of frauds, the court ruled that a vendor elects to treat a prior verbal contract as void by making a valid sale, shielding the intermediate purchaser. In equity, a valid contract makes the vendee owner and vendor trustee with a lien; equity only considers as done what ought to be done and only for those entitled to specific performance. The Kentucky cases cited were based on a false premise of moral obligation; the vendor has a legal right to elect to treat the verbal agreement as void.

On tender, the purchase money need not be brought into court; an offer in the complaint to bring it in upon liquidation and decree suffices. After the obligee tenders purchase money and accrued interest and demands a conveyance, he is not chargeable with further interest unless he used the money, and the vendor must prove such use. Judgment affirmed with costs.

The specification defines the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) protocol for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP guests. Version 2 introduces a FEATURES bitmap (limited to 52 bits) that the hypervisor advertises via the GHCB MSR protocol to indicate optional feature support. The GHCB MSR (0xc001_0130) uses its lower 12 bits for request/response actions; the GHCB address must be 4K-aligned. Before the GHCB is established, the hypervisor sets the MSR to provide the supported protocol version range and the SEV page table encryption bit number. The guest can use MSR protocol requests for SEV information, CPUID register values, AP reset hold, GHCB GPA registration/unregistration, page state change, running a vCPU at a different VMPL, hypervisor feature support, and termination.

GHCB GPA registration is mandatory for SEV-SNP guests before first use; a guest may request the hypervisor’s preferred GPA or register its own. The hypervisor must terminate the guest if a supplied GPA does not match the registered one. Multi-VMPL support allows each VMPL to register a GHCB GPA.

Topic modeling (LDA) within each cluster provided interpretable themes. The three clusters are: LLM as Social Minds (theory of mind, moral reasoning, bias, deception), LLM Societies (multi-agent interactions, cooperation, institutions, collective epistemics), and LLM–Human Interactions (trust, reliance, productivity, learning, risks). Study 2 compared the machine-induced taxonomy to expert-coded categories, showing strong alignment (Macro-F1 = 0.954, NMI = 0.811, ARI = 0.867). The taxonomy organizes the literature into levels of analysis, clarifies evidentiary standards, and identifies boundary zones. The discussion emphasizes treating LLMs as social artifacts and calls for institutional design rather than anthropomorphic interpretation.

The document describes optional extensions to SEV and SNP for page migration using AMD's Tiered Memory Page Migration (TMPM) engine. TMPM copies page content and updates virtual-to-physical mappings, supporting tiered memory systems where software moves pages between performance tiers. It off-loads migration and addresses two challenges: pausing DMA traffic during page copy and IOMMU table updates, and acting as a trusted agent to migrate SNP-protected guest pages.

TMPM availability is checked via the ENGINE_READY bit in the PM_Status register; IOMMU enablement is required. Commands include PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO (migrates pages with concurrent DMA, requiring the IOMMU host page table entry location; also migrates Hypervisor state pages in SNP) and PM_PAGE_MOVE_GUEST (migrates guest pages in SNP, with source pages in Guest-Valid/Invalid state and destination pages in a new Pre-Migration state). After migration, source pages become Pre-Migration, and destination pages take the original source state. The Pre-Migration state uses a platform-specific ASID and cannot be validated by a guest; RMPUpdate converts it back to Hypervisor state.

Multi-page commands support up to 128 pages per list, with no adjacency or order-dependence requirements. Per-page status is provided; PM_PARTIAL_SUCCESS requires checking individual entries, while PM_SUCCESS indicates all pages migrated. A status of PM_RMP_NOTEXCLUSIVE signals a retryable conflict.

Performance guidelines recommend commands with 16 or more pages, with maximum bandwidth at 128 pages. The ring buffer should be kept ahead of the engine, and interrupts should be used sparingly, such as on sequence completion or low-water mark. Certain data structures (IOMMU memory structures, vIOMMU page tables, pinned backing storage, ring buffer and argument pages) cannot be migrated. For PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO, source pages must be DMA-mapped via a single IOMMU host page table, and a host page table virtual address space (HPTVA) is defined. TMPM may modify hPTEs non-atomically; host software must avoid concurrent modifications.

Firmware reload requires pausing operations, tearing down the ring buffer, disabling PAGEMIGRATION_EN bits, and using a BIOS-to-PSP mailbox protocol. The ring buffer must not be initialized, and the new firmware version must be the same or greater. EPYC family is distinguished via PM_GET_CAPABILITIES FW_VER_Major (71 decimal for Family 19h). Reload for Family 19h involves placing the firmware image and header in memory and sending a command via ASP registers. For development, single commands can be sent by keeping the tail pointer one entry ahead of the head. TMPM only moves data between 4k-aligned pages; all system physical addresses must be 4k-aligned.

Amid rising hostility towards transgender communities, a knowledge exchange project explored how educators in England create rights-respecting classrooms for trans equality. The project involved the Institute of Education’s Citizenship PGCE course and Diversity Role Models, an LGBTQ+ anti-bullying charity. Over a year (October 2023–June 2024), student teachers participated in workshops on embedding trans-inclusive practices, applied learning during school placements, and presented on integrating rights and identities. The project reflected on opportunities offered by Citizenship education to create safe, empowering environments for transgender youth.

The political context included intense media focus on transgender young people and draft Department for Education guidance (December 2023) on supporting “gender questioning children,” which faced criticism for potentially denying trans pupils’ existence and risking forced outing. A May 2024 draft statutory guidance on Relationships, Sex and Health Education proposed banning discussion of gender identity, raising concerns about teaching human rights under the Equality Act 2010, which protects “gender reassignment.” Existing statutory guidance still requires teaching facts and law on gender identity.

Student teachers learned to “actualise” LGBTQ+ identities—making subjects concrete for real-life context. Examples included teaching about Lesbians and Gays Support the Miner and HIV/AIDS, but actualization focused mostly on sexual orientation, with minimal reference to transgender identities. Teachers attributed this to fear from media debates and proposed guidance, noting lower confidence in discussing trans identities compared to sexual orientation. Citizenship education equips teachers to use legislation (Equality Act 2010, Human Rights Act 1998) and trauma-informed deliberative practices to counter prejudice.

Storytelling was highlighted as a pedagogical tool, with personal narratives from LGBTQ+ role models building empathy and reducing transphobic bullying. Using human rights and equality legislation, particularly the Equality Act 2010, framed lessons to encourage trans allyship by viewing LGBTQ+ young people as rights holders. International frameworks like the UNCRC, Yogyakarta Principles+10, and UNESCO guidance support comprehensive sexuality education and teacher training for trans inclusion.

Beyond curriculum, whole-school approaches such as visibility (displays, Pride clubs), effective behaviour management with clear anti-bullying policies, and bystander training promoting “upstanders” were identified as key. The project underscored the need for specialist Citizenship teachers and training for all educators to actualize transgender experiences, and the value of partnerships with civil society organisations to build inclusive education for all children, including those of diverse gender identities.

This study investigated sex differences in the correlation between the self-reported PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the clinician-administered Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5). The study included 100 adult participants (56 males, 44 females) who completed both assessments. CAPS-5 scores did not differ significantly between males and females, or between those with military versus civilian trauma.

The overall correlation between PCL-5 and CAPS-5 scores was significant (Rho = 0.815, p < 0.0001). However, female participants exhibited a stronger correlation (Rho = 0.907, p < 0.0001) than male participants (Rho = 0.655, p < 0.0001). The odds ratio for PCL-5 predicting CAPS-5 was higher for females (144.6, p = 0.0010) than for males (11.8, p = 0.0031).

When comparing observed scores to an ideal regression line based on diagnostic thresholds (PCL-5 ≥34, CAPS-5 ≥23), male participants showed a significant deviation (mean difference 12.5, p = 0.001), while female participants did not (mean difference 1.068, p = 0.5077). A significant sex difference in deviation from the ideal line was observed (Z(Observed) = -3.5, p = 0.0005).

Using PCL-5 scores alone, 26.8% of males were misclassified relative to CAPS-5 diagnosis: 23.2% were PTSD-positive on PCL-5 but not on CAPS-5, and 3.6% were PTSD-negative on PCL-5 but positive on CAPS-5. Among females, 11.4% were misclassified: 9.1% false positives and 2.8% false negatives.

The correlation between PCL-5 and CAPS-5 was stronger for participants with civilian trauma (Rho = 0.885, p < 0.0001, n = 62) than military trauma (Rho = 0.523, p = 0.0015, n = 38). This pattern held within each sex: males with civilian trauma had Rho = 0.801, military trauma Rho = 0.470; females with civilian trauma Rho = 0.903, military trauma Rho = 0.600 (though the female military group had only 4 participants).

The study concludes that females show stronger alignment between self-reported and clinician-assessed PTSD severity, while males, particularly those with military trauma, have greater discrepancies and higher misclassification rates when using PCL-5. The authors note limitations including a modest sample size and restricted geographical region, and recommend caution when interpreting PCL-5 scores in male and military populations.

Cover 3 is a zone defense with four underneath players and three deep players. It is common at all levels of football and used by coaches such as Nick Saban and Pete Carroll. The scheme features three deep defenders—a free safety in the deep middle and two cornerbacks responsible for deep outside thirds—to eliminate deep passes. Cornerbacks bail or backpedal rather than press. The four underneath defenders are three linebackers and the strong safety, covering Hook, Curl, and Flat zones. Hash marks serve as landmarks to divide deep coverage into thirds. Underneath responsibilities follow “Hook-to-Curl” and “Curl-to-Flat” progressions, aiming to force checkdowns.

Cover 3 adds a third defensive back deep compared to Cover 2, allowing a safety to move closer to the line of scrimmage to help stop the run, effectively putting an eighth man in the box. Its strengths include balanced coverage against deep and intermediate routes and effectiveness against balanced run/pass offenses, making it popular in high school and college where the run game is more dominant. Weaknesses include vulnerability in the flats, where short passes of 5–8 yards can be completed, and challenges against four verticals and seam routes that attack the hash-mark areas and create personnel mismatches. Against the run, the perimeter is weak because the corner bails deep and the safety comes down to the flat, creating edge vulnerabilities that require athletic outside linebackers.

Standard assignments: cornerbacks take deep outside thirds, free safety takes deep middle third, strong safety takes curl flat, Sam and Mike linebackers take hook/curl, and Will linebacker takes curl flat. Variations include flipping safety roles, Cover 3 Fire Zone (sending four or more rushers and dropping defensive linemen into zones to confuse quarterbacks), Cover 3 Buzz (safety plays hook to curl in the middle, outside linebackers/nickel play curl flat), and pattern reading coverages like Rip/Liz that blend zone and man principles to handle vertical and crossing routes.

The lecture continues the discussion of continuity, defined intuitively as: if x is sufficiently close to c, then f(x) is very close to f(c). A theorem is proved connecting continuity to limits and sequences. For f: S → R with c ∈ S, if c is not a cluster point of S, f is automatically continuous at c (a degenerate case). If c is a cluster point, f is continuous at c if and only if the limit as x→c of f(x) equals f(c). Additionally, f is continuous at c if and only if for every sequence (x_n) in S converging to c, f(x_n) converges to f(c). The proof of the sequential equivalence is given: one direction uses epsilon-delta and sequence convergence; the converse uses contradiction by constructing a sequence with x_n within 1/n of c but f(x_n) at least ε₀ away from f(c).

Using elementary properties of sine and cosine (unit circle definitions, bounds, angle sum and difference-to-product formulas), sine is shown directly continuous: choose δ=ε, then |sin x - sin c| ≤ |x-c| < ε. Then, using the sequential characterization and cos x = sin(x+π/2), cosine is proved continuous.

A function discontinuous at every real number is given: f(x)=1 if x is rational, 0 if irrational. For rational c, pick irrational x_n → c, so f(x_n)=0 does not converge to f(c)=1. For irrational c, pick rational x_n → c, so f(x_n)=1 does not converge to f(c)=0.

The sequential characterization yields algebraic properties: if f and g are continuous at c, then f+g, f·g, and f/g (g(x)≠0) are continuous at c. Composition of continuous functions is also continuous: if g is continuous at c and f is continuous at g(c), then f∘g is continuous at c. Proofs use sequences.

Consequences: x^n is continuous for all natural n (induction via product of continuous functions). Polynomials are continuous. The function 1/(3+sin⁴x) is continuous because sin x is continuous, so sin⁴x is continuous (composition), 3+sin⁴x is continuous and never zero, so its reciprocal is continuous.

The lecture previews the min-max theorem (continuous functions on closed bounded intervals attain maximum and minimum) and the intermediate value theorem (a continuous function on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b)).

The President transmits to the House, in response to its resolutions, a report from the Secretary of State with all documents and correspondence relating to the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the Senate’s amendments. He had previously withheld the commissioners’ instructions but now furnishes them as indispensable for understanding the other documents, though he still holds that publishing such instructions soon after negotiations is generally prejudicial.

The commissioners’ instructions of March 18, 1848, confined them to obtaining Mexico’s ratification of the treaty as amended by the Senate; they were not to negotiate any new treaty or modify any provision. They were to explain the Senate’s amendments through personal conferences, avoiding diplomatic notes. The Secretary of State’s letter of the same date, explaining the amendments, was the only explanation before the Mexican Congress. Mexico’s President submitted the amended treaty to its Congress on May 8, 1848, and on May 25 that Congress approved it without modification, before the U.S. commissioners were officially received or held any conference. Ratifications were exchanged on May 30.

The protocol, a memorandum of conversations held after the Mexican Congress had acted, was not regarded as part of the treaty or as modifying it. The President explains its three points: (1) The suppression of the original ninth article and substitution of the Louisiana treaty’s third article did not diminish the inhabitants’ privileges; the amended article secures their liberty, property, and free exercise of religion without restriction, and even without any article, the Constitution and laws would protect these rights. (2) The suppression of the tenth article did not annul legitimate Mexican land grants; valid titles retain their legal value and may be acknowledged before U.S. tribunals. The article was rejected because it unjustly attempted to revive expired grants, and the U.S. had firmly refused to accept it. (3) The suppression of the concluding paragraph of article 12, which would have created transferable certificates for the $12 million payment, did not deprive Mexico of the faculty to assign the obligation; it only prevented the issuance of a government stock, leaving the obligation assignable but without improving the assignee’s condition.

The President deemed the protocol consistent with the treaty and immaterial; since it did not vary the treaty, he took no action on it, treating it as he would verbal explanations reported in a dispatch.

An involuntary bankruptcy petition was filed against John Jacob Beechwood. He denied insolvency and acts of bankruptcy, claiming immunity as a farmer under the Bankruptcy Act. A jury found him insolvent and that he committed the alleged acts of bankruptcy, including a September 20, 1940 conveyance of his farm to his wife with intent to defraud creditors. The court then addressed whether he qualified as a farmer on that date.

The Act defines a farmer as an individual personally engaged in farming or tillage of the soil, deriving the principal part of his income from such operations, with status determined at the time of the act of bankruptcy. Beechwood was a New York attorney employed full-time by a casualty company at a $7,200 salary, with additional private legal income. He resigned on September 23, 1940, retroactive to September 16, after confessing to misappropriating over $100,000. He lived on a farm operated by a hired farmer, and he participated in farm work during leisure time. He argued he reverted to farmer status on September 16.

The court found that on September 20, 1940, Beechwood was a lawyer and businessman dealing with the fallout of his misconduct, not someone personally deriving the principal part of his income from farming. His principal income came from his employment. The cases he cited were distinguishable; the Beach case required that farming be an engrossing occupation consuming the major portion of one’s time, which Beechwood did not meet. The court concluded that extending farmer immunity to him would encourage others to use rural residences to evade creditors. His farmer defense failed, and an order adjudicating him a bankrupt was to be entered.

Without a large margin of safety, unfavorable sequence of returns, high withdrawal rates, or poor diversification can lead to ruin.

FIRE stands for Financial Independent Retire Early. An example illustrates the danger: a couple retires in January 2000 with $1 million invested in a US Large Cap fund, withdrawing $50,000 annually (5% rate). Due to poor early returns and the 2008 financial crisis, they exhaust their capital by 2017, even with the subsequent bull market. Their mistakes included inadequate margin of safety, bad sequence of returns, and lack of diversification.

Sequence risk refers to the order of annual returns. Early negative returns can severely harm compounding. A Monte Carlo simulation by Mark Spitznagel, using S&P 500 annual returns from 1901–2020 and 10,000 random 25-year sequences, found a median CAGR of 9.5% but a 10% chance of a CAGR below 3%. To mitigate sequence risk, the article advises living moderately and spending less.

Withdrawal rate is critical. The 4% rule, introduced by William Bengen, suggests that retirees can withdraw 4% annually without depleting funds, but it was based on traditional retirement lengths. For FIREs with longer horizons, even 4% may be too high. In the example, a 4% withdrawal rate ($40,000) still likely leads to ruin; only a 3% rate ($30,000) allowed the portfolio to recover after 2009. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund has lowered its withdrawal rate to 3%.

Diversification can help. A backtest adding REITs, emerging markets, gold, and long-term Treasuries to the portfolio improved outcomes even with a 5% withdrawal rate, though the article cautions that correlations change and backtests involve survivorship bias.

Edward Thorp’s simulations for perpetual endowments indicate that to preserve capital indefinitely, annual spending should be limited to an inflation-adjusted 2% of the original amount, because a severe early market decline can wipe out a fund with higher withdrawals.

Overall, retirees and FIREs are fragile. A large margin of safety, a conservative withdrawal rate, diversification, and frugality are necessary to avoid running out of money. The likelihood of going broke depends on planning, margin of safety, and frugality.

A study published in the Journal of Hematology & Thromboembolic Diseases investigated the potential leukemogenic properties of Bt toxin biopesticides in GMO crops. They found that Bt toxins target mammalian erythroid cells, causing red blood cell changes indicative of anemia, and suppressed bone marrow proliferation with abnormal lymphocyte patterns consistent with some leukemias. The study showed Cry toxins can exert adverse effects in distilled water without alkaline activation. A dose of Cry1Ab as low as 27 mg/kg induced hypochromic anemia in mice; this toxin has been detected in human blood.
