The ADS9803 supports a speed-boost mode achieving up to 8 MSPS sampling rate for a user-selected analog input channel pair, while the remaining six channels are idle. The sampling rate equals the sampling clock frequency, and the data output interface specifications remain unchanged.

Register access uses 16-bit configuration registers grouped into three banks, addressable with an 8-bit address. Bank 0 registers are always accessible; banks 1 and 2 are selected via the REG_BANK_SEL bits. A register write requires first writing to address 0x03 in bank 0 to select the bank, then writing to the target register. A register read involves selecting the bank (write to 0x03), enabling read mode (set SPI_RD_EN=1b, SPI_MODE=1b in register 0x00), reading the desired register with a 24-bit frame, then disabling read mode.

Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology. All ADCs share CS and SCLK; the SDI of the first ADC connects to the controller, and SDO of each ADC feeds the next SDI. The daisy-chain length (number of ADCs excluding the first) is set in the DAISY_CHAIN_LEN register. Register writes require N×24 SCLKs per frame. Reads involve writing to select the bank and enable reads, then sending frames with 0xFE and 0xFF patterns to retrieve register data.

Key registers include: 37h to enable speed-boost mode and select the channel pair; 0Dh for data format and averaging; 12h for XOR operations; 13h and 18h for test patterns on channel groups; 44h–4Bh for gain error correction; C0h for bandwidth and power-down; C1h for reference and output lane mode; C4h–C5h for common-mode range and wide common-mode enable; and others for initialization and averaging configuration.

In ATE applications, the ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2 MSPS DAQ system. Post-calibration TUE is 0.0015% at 25°C ±5°C. It offers low-noise (up to 22.7 kHz) and wide-bandwidth (up to 700 kHz) modes; wide-bandwidth mode settles to 99.95% FS in 7.5 µs. The device uses three power supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) with no power-up sequence requirement. Layout recommendations include 0.1 µF bypass capacitors near supply pins, avoiding vias between pins and capacitors, and separating analog and digital paths.

This study examined primary school teachers' perspectives on the participation of students with disabilities in inclusive education during virtual learning amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a phenomenology design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 general education primary school teachers who had at least one student with an officially diagnosed disability. Data were analyzed through content analysis.

Findings revealed that students with disabilities who received parental support, had independent connection skills, and sufficient equipment showed high virtual class participation. However, some students could only attend basic courses per doctors' recommendations, and others could not attend at all due to parents' illiteracy or technological barriers. Problems encountered included students' reluctance to watch EBA TV, low interaction, lack of engaging content, absence of teacher or peers on screen, and behavioral issues during lessons. Some students, however, had no difficulties following activities and assignments.

Teachers reported challenges in including students and monitoring their education, such as inability to know the student well, socialization problems, homework tracking issues, students keeping cameras off, and excessive reliance on family support. Causes cited were large class sizes limiting individual attention, lack of parent communication, limited contact with special education teachers in rehabilitation centers, and inability to assess students informally as in person. Parents' failure to provide suitable study environments, low motivation, and prioritizing rehabilitation center education over virtual classes also contributed. Conversely, teachers who experienced no problems attributed this to good family economic status, daily parent communication, and use of EBA's tracking features.

Regarding teacher-parent cooperation, teachers guided parents on student characteristics and development, used EBA support points, and maintained immediate contact when issues arose. Problems in cooperation included crowded classrooms preventing adequate parent attention, families not expressing needs, and underuse of EBA support points.

Solutions applied by teachers included hybrid models allowing home participation when ill, scheduling support sessions at convenient times, requesting video recordings of home study to guide families, and providing psychological support calls. Suggested solutions encompassed ensuring home discipline, providing device and internet support for financially disadvantaged students, conducting activities for social development, keeping schools open continuously for students with disabilities, using EBA support points for emotional motivation, and coordinating with rehabilitation centers.

The discussion highlighted that parental support was key to participation, aligning with literature emphasizing parents' roles as both parents and teachers. Challenges such as difficulty tracking student learning and forcing attendance were consistent with other studies. The study's unique contribution lies in its post-pandemic reflection, as teachers evaluated the entire virtual process after returning to in-person education. Suggestions for practitioners included informing stakeholders about virtual education requirements, delivering materials, improving technological infrastructure, and preparing content that parents can support. For researchers, future studies could investigate experiences of students with disabilities at different levels, compare typically developing and disabled students' experiences, and quantitatively examine factors affecting virtual education effectiveness.

The Nigerian National Youth Policy defines youth as ages 15–29; the UN definition of 15–24 is adopted in this paper for cross-country comparisons. Skills development refers to both hard (technical) and soft skills. Experiential learning, or work-integrated learning, has no standard definition; May (2018) describes it as learning from experiences in educational and practice settings. Co-op is a form of experiential learning fully integrated into the curriculum.

Youth unemployment in Nigeria was historically lower than most regions but increased, and by 2021 was higher than most regions except South Asia and the Middle East/North Africa. SSA’s low unemployment rates understate actual unemployment by excluding discouraged, informal, and underemployed workers. Youth unemployment rates are higher than total unemployment; in Nigeria, the youth rate is at least double the total rate. Factors include job shopping, ease of dismissal, and a disproportionate share of youth as new job seekers. The employment-to-population ratio for youth is about 20 percentage points lower than the total, indicating lower utilization of youth labor. Other characteristics include predominance of the informal sector, a NEET rate of 28% in Nigeria (13% in OECD), stark gender disparity, higher unemployment among the educated, and higher rates in urban areas and among females.

Co-op history traces to industrialized countries, motivated by the need for better-prepared engineers. In SSA, South Africa and Namibia offer co-op. Core dimensions are integrated curriculum, learning from work experience, and logistical coordination. Models include alternating semesters, parallel, and sandwich models. Benefits are identified for students, employers, institutions, and society. Estimated cost per student is about AUD 3,144 per year, likely lower in Nigeria, with costs shared among stakeholders.

Literature shows mixed program effectiveness; almost 70% of school-to-work programs do not raise employment/income, but comprehensive programs combining multiple interventions are more effective. Survey evidence from the UK and Canada indicates co-op graduates have higher employment rates, lower unemployment, better field-of-study matches, higher earnings, and lower overqualification. Prospective students are attracted by skills acquisition, practical experience, and institutional reputation.

Practically, co-op is offered across many undergraduate and some graduate programs. Students must be in good academic standing and typically complete at least one year before eligibility. An alternating sequence example yields five work terms. Students pay a co-op fee during work terms, maintaining full-time status, and must receive compensation. Universities have dedicated co-op units. Quality assurance involves accreditation and membership in bodies like WACE, CEWIL (Canada), and SASCE (Southern Africa).

Nigerian government responses include SIWES (a six-month skills training during breaks), SURE-P’s Graduate Internship Scheme (one-year internship), and N-SIP’s N-Power (two-year paid volunteer program for graduates and training for non-graduates). Reviews note positive impacts but also challenges like poor placement, inadequate funding, and complex governance.

The case for co-op argues that more is needed to improve post-secondary students’ employability. SIWES is not integrated into the academic calendar and lacks close employer-institution collaboration. Co-op aligns with Nigeria’s Medium-Term National Development Plan 2021–2025 to partner with industry on skills gaps. It could be integrated with existing programs like SIWES or N-Power, leveraging infrastructure. The alternating model is recommended. Federal and state governments could provide tax credits, grants, and act as role-model employers. The conclusion calls for multipronged interventions and further research on management structures, models, and applicability to non-tertiary education.

The TLV321/2x comparators consume 40µA per channel with 40ns propagation delay. The TLV321x has a push-pull output; the TLV322x has an open-drain output that can be pulled up to 5.5V independent of supply voltage. Input voltage range extends from 200mV below V– to 200mV above V+, with no phase inversion. Inputs must not exceed supply voltages by more than 200mV; limit current to 10mA and add series resistance. Unused inputs must not be tied together; instead, apply a minimum 50mV differential voltage within the specified input range. Internal hysteresis is 1.8mV. Push-pull outputs must never connect to another output; shorting to the opposite rail can cause thermal runaway, so use a current-limiting resistor. Unused push-pull outputs must be left floating. Open-drain outputs allow wired-OR and level translation; set pull-up resistor current between 100µA and 1mA. Lower pull-up values increase rise-time but raise VOL and power dissipation; large pull-up resistors (>1MΩ) create an exponential rising edge. Shorting an open-drain output to a voltage source can cause thermal runaway; use a series current-limiting resistor. Unused open-drain outputs can be left floating or tied to V–. ESD protection circuits limit input voltages to 0.2V beyond the rails; add a current-limiting resistor for low-impedance sources, limiting current to 10mA. The TLV321x has a power-on reset circuit that holds the output low for up to 32µs after VPOR of 1.65V is crossed, then the output reflects the input state. In basic comparator operation, output is low when VIN < VREF and high when VIN > VREF. Propagation delay is measured as tpLH and tpHL. Overdrive voltage influences propagation delay; smaller overdrive increases delay, especially below 100mV. External hysteresis can be added via positive feedback to prevent chatter. An inverting comparator with hysteresis uses a three-resistor network; a non-inverting configuration uses a two-resistor network and VREF. For low-side current sensing, an amplifier amplifies the shunt voltage and the comparator alerts when the amplifier output exceeds 1.1V. Bypass the supply with a low-ESR 0.1µF ceramic capacitor directly between V+ and ground. Minimize coupling between outputs and inputs; place series input resistors close to the device. A low-value resistor (<100Ω) may be added in series with the output to dampen ringing on long traces.

The GA10x SM contains 128 CUDA Cores, four third-generation Tensor Cores, a 256 KB Register File, four Texture Units, one second-generation Ray Tracing Core, and 128 KB of L1/Shared Memory configurable for different capacities. The GA102 GPU has twelve 32-bit memory controllers (384-bit total) and 6144 KB of L2 cache. ROPs are now part of the GPC, giving the full GA102 112 ROPs.

The SM is partitioned into four processing blocks, each with a 64 KB register file, L0 instruction cache, warp scheduler, dispatch unit, and math units. The four partitions share a combined 128 KB L1 data cache/shared memory subsystem. Each partition has one third-generation Tensor Core, and each Tensor Core is twice as powerful as Turing's. The combined L1 data cache and shared memory capacity is 33% larger than Turing, with doubled cache partition capacity for graphics workloads. Both datapaths in each partition can process FP32 operations, doubling peak FP32 rate; each SM can execute 128 FP32 operations per clock. L1 data cache capacity is 128 KB per SM, and shared memory bandwidth is doubled to 128 bytes/clock per SM.

The second-generation RT Core doubles ray/triangle intersection testing rate over Turing and adds an Interpolate Triangle Position unit to accelerate ray-traced motion blur. It supports concurrent RT Core and graphics or compute workloads. Third-generation Tensor Cores add support for TF32, BF16, and Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity, which doubles throughput for sparse matrices by skipping zeros using a 2:4 pattern. DLSS leverages Tensor Cores and a new 9x Super Resolution factor for 8K gaming.

GA10x uses GDDR6X memory with PAM4 signaling, achieving up to 19.5 Gbps data rates and up to 936 GB/sec peak bandwidth. MTA encoding limits signal transitions to improve SNR. NVIDIA RTX IO enables GPU-based loading and lossless decompression of assets, working with Microsoft DirectStorage to offload CPU work and improve I/O performance. The display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC 1.2a for 8K60, and HDMI 2.1 with DSC 1.2a for 8K60 and 4K120. The fifth-generation NVDEC supports hardware decoding of MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, with AV1 hardware decode being a first. The seventh-generation NVENC provides hardware-accelerated video encoding. The NVIDIA A40 data center GPU offers up to 2X FP32 and ray-tracing throughput, up to 5X (10X with sparsity) AI throughput, 48 GB memory scalable to 96 GB via NVLink, and supports vGPU. The RTX A6000 workstation GPU includes 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 second-gen RT Cores, 48 GB GDDR6, and hardware-accelerated motion blur.

A phylodynamic analysis of 48,615 Omicron BA.1 genomes from England (approximately 1% of cases) and global genomes identified at least 6,455 independent introductions, with the earliest estimated between 5–18 November 2021. Importations increased exponentially until early January 2022 despite travel restrictions on southern African countries; importation intensity from the US was about four times that from South Africa during the restriction period. Most introductions were singletons, but eight large transmission lineages (each >700 genomes) accounted for over 60% of English genomes, and six of these were imported before travel restrictions. Early importations (before 15 December 2021) comprised ~6% of introductions yet caused ~80% of BA.1 infections in England through January 2022. Travel restrictions were largely ineffective due to a shift in importation sources to the US.

Spatial spread initially concentrated in Greater London, which acted as the predominant source of long-distance viral movements to other regions in early December. Local transmission in other cities was not immediately established. A second phase around the New Year saw increased mid-to-long range movements and more outward spread from other regions, while Greater London’s contribution diminished. A generalized linear model showed that during the expansion phase, viral lineage movements were associated with a gravity model (population size and distance) and directional outflow from Greater London; in the post-expansion phase, aggregated mobility patterns became more supported and movements were directed toward areas with later epidemic peaks.

Human mobility declined 20–50% from mid-December to early January, attributed to Plan B restrictions, holiday mixing changes, and behavioural responses to case numbers. A statistical model estimated that for every unit increase in weekly COVID-19 cases per 100 people in a hub city, trips between home and hub decreased by 11.97%, with longer-distance trips less affected. The findings highlight that a small number of early introductions seeded most local infections and that travel restrictions applied after local transmission detection, to few countries, and without local measures were ineffective. Limitations include potential underestimation of introductions and sampling biases.

The Investors Intelligence Sentiment Index, also known as Advisor Sentiment, is a contrarian indicator created in 1963 by AW Cohen. It surveys over a hundred independent market newsletters weekly, categorizing each author’s stance as bullish, bearish, or correction, and publishes the percentages. Initially expected to show the best time to be long when bullishness was high, it was found that advisors were often wrong at turning points, so it is now used contrarily, especially at extremes. Bullish readings above 55% signal excessive optimism and are negative for the market; readings below 35% indicate excessive pessimism and are positive. Weekly figures also track stocks above their 10-week and 30-week moving averages to gauge short-to-intermediate and major market turns, respectively. The index is published by Chartcraft and available via subscription. Investor sentiment generally refers to market mood, and this index focuses on professional advisors, unlike the AAII Sentiment Survey, which since 1987 polls individual investors on their six-month market outlook.

The passage argues that the "out-of-school children" (OOSC) indicator, which measures only formal school enrollment, is inadequate for capturing the complexity of educational exclusion globally. Using Afghanistan as a case study, it highlights how the OOSC indicator overlooks non-formal, informal, and alternative pathways such as community-based education, madrasas, and online learning. The Taliban's ban on girls' secondary education and systemic barriers—geographic disparities, nomadic lifestyles, child labor, and disabilities—further expose the indicator's limitations. The passage advocates replacing OOSC with an "out-of-education children" (OOEC) indicator that defines education as an activity occurring across multiple pathways within an interconnected ecosystem. This shift is presented as broadening the understanding of educational access, catalyzing system transformation, and reimagining education to include diverse learning opportunities. Implementation challenges include developing data systems to capture all pathways, evolving credentialing systems, fostering collaboration among education actors, and reallocating resources equitably. The OOEC indicator is framed as a first step toward achieving inclusive, equitable quality education aligned with SDG 4.

Archaeologists in Mexico will excavate a secret tunnel sealed by the Maya centuries ago to reach a hidden cenote beneath the El Castillo pyramid at Chichen Itza. Cenotes, water-filled sinkholes, were the only freshwater source and central to Mayan spirituality, seen as entrances to the underworld. The Maya made offerings, including human sacrifices, to appease deities like the rain god Chac. El Castillo, a temple to Kukulcan, has 365 steps and faces cardinal directions. A hidden cenote was detected under it two years ago. Last November, divers explored passageways from the Ossuary pyramid but found them intentionally blocked. The team now aims to clear these tunnels over three months. De Anda believes the cenote may represent the axis mundi, the world's center. He also notes that analysis of child sacrifice victims from the Sacred Cenote showed 80% were aged 3-11, often in poor health, and may have been dead before deposition.

This study investigated the views of 82 kindergarten teachers in the Epirus region of Greece on distance education during the COVID-19 pandemic. A web-based questionnaire collected data on demographics, familiarity with distance education, tools used, and opinions on future integration. Most participants were women with many years of service, and about half held basic ICT certification. Before the pandemic, over 75% were little or not at all familiar with distance education, and over 90% had not incorporated it. During remote teaching, synchronous tools (mainly Webex) were preferred, and email was commonly used asynchronously. Teachers expressed largely negative views: they believed distance education was less effective than conventional teaching for developing social skills, limited psychomotor activities, required adult supervision, and faced significant infrastructure and access problems. They saw it as appropriate only when physical presence is impossible. A statistically significant relationship was found between holding a higher-level ICT certificate and greater pre-pandemic familiarity with distance education, but no relationship between years of service and ICT literacy. The study concludes that teachers lacked readiness, highlighted equipment and training needs, and recommended cautious integration, emphasizing improved infrastructure, professional development, and family support.

A Take a Knee Chart helps football coaches determine when to use a kneel-down play to run time off the clock at the end of a game when leading. The offense lines up in a victory formation to minimize mistakes; the quarterback kneels after the snap, counting as a run play so the clock continues. If the opponent has no timeouts, the clock runs out. The chart shows player positions and movement order. Clock management is crucial, especially for head coaches. High school and college football lack a two-minute warning, and with a 40-second play clock, offenses can consume more time. Incomplete passes stop the clock, risking giving the opponent a chance to score.

The European Commission president announced a €545 million ($636 million) investment package for renewable energy and electrification in Africa, targeting the nearly 600 million Africans without electricity. Projects include a transmission line in Côte d’Ivoire, rural electrification in Cameroon, wind/hydro in Lesotho, and mini-grids in Madagascar. The EU estimates 38 million green jobs by 2030. This is part of the Global Gateway initiative, which prioritizes Africa to rival China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). The BRI has invested over $1.3 trillion globally, providing China political influence. Africa has critical minerals like cobalt, lithium, copper, and manganese, where China is active. The Global Gateway, with €300 billion through 2027, is seen as a David-versus-Goliath undertaking compared to the BRI. Africa is a superpower battleground for resources, and its decarbonization is essential for net zero.

The paper introduces ML²B, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on generating complete machine learning pipelines from natural language descriptions in 13 languages. It extends 30 Kaggle competitions (24 public, 6 private) into 390 evaluation instances, covering tabular, text, and image modalities across 12 domains. The benchmark provides structured metadata, human-reviewed task descriptions, and standardized data cards to prevent information leakage. Evaluation of five LLMs using two execution frameworks (AIDE with 3 agents, ML Master with 2 hybrids) reveals a 15–45% performance degradation on non-English tasks compared to English. The benchmark includes a code grader that executes submission code in isolated Docker environments, supporting two submission formats (MONO PREDICT and MODULAR PREDICT) to reduce preprocessing leakage. Translation was performed with GPT-4o and validated by native speakers. Results show English consistently yields lower (better) percentile ranks, while low-resource languages like Kazakh, Belarusian, and Romanian exhibit higher failure rates and degraded performance. Hybrid model stacks partially mitigate gaps in harder domains but do not eliminate cross-lingual disparities. Static leakage analysis of modular submissions found potential data leakage in 5.9% of cases. The benchmark highlights systematic weaknesses in multilingual ML code generation and the need for task-specific model selection.

SFS (Seamless Firmware Servicing) is an AMD firmware feature enabling runtime application of patches without system reboot. Patches are distributed as SFS update packages. Applying a package changes three version numbers: SFSPL (SFS Patch Level, monotonically increasing, identifies the applied package), individual firmware component versions and SPL (Security Patch Level), and SYSPL (System Patch Level, monotonically increasing, tracks run-once code execution). This version information ensures updates apply only to correct firmware levels and is accessible to the host OS. AMD cryptographically signs each package. Customers may optionally co-sign packages by providing a public key to the AMD Security Processor (ASP) during early boot; the ASP then requires both AMD and customer signatures. The ASP acts as root of trust for detection, verifying AMD's signature before applying updates. OEM/ODM owns the root of trust for update; co-signing allows them to maintain that role. SFS does not persist across reboots; patches must be reapplied after reset. In multi-socket systems, the first socket's ASP receives the patch and ensures correct application across sockets. BIOS enables SFS via APCB_TOKEN_UID_PSP_SFS_ENABLE and co-signing via APCB_TOKEN_UID_PSP_SFS_COSIGN_REQUIRED, both off by default. Co-signing uses an RSA key pair (2048 or 4096-bit) with RSA-PSS signature scheme. Each patch checks existing system patch level and firmware versions for applicability. Packages can patch registers, replace firmware images, or update firmware portions. SEV updates are automatically committed and prevent rollback; reverting requires a reboot. With SNP enabled, update pages must be HV-FIXED. For attestation, SFS provides measurements; some attestation schemes may prevent modification of certain firmware. Resiliency: packages verify proper firmware versions before applying; if any part fails, the entire update is aborted to avoid forcing a reset. Updates are non-persistent, applied via OS boot or runtime. Commands require memory alignment: TEE_EXT_CMD_BUFFER on a 2MB-aligned page, with output or package data at specific offsets. The ASP process: protect DRAM from x86 access, verify customer (if enabled) and AMD signatures, load and run the patch, update patch levels, return status. A GET_SFS_VERSION_INFO command retrieves firmware versions, SFSPL, SYSPL, and SPL values. Packages are named fam_<family>-<AGESA-Release>-SFS-<n>.pkg. Updates run in parallel with x86/DMA traffic, aiming for minimal performance impact; some SEV/ES VMs may need to stop/restart, while SEV/SNP VMs can continue operation.

A class action lawsuit was filed in California Superior Court against Reliant Energy, Southern Company, NRG Energy, Dynegy, AES Corporation, Williams Energy, and Duke Energy. The 9 EMA trading strategy uses the 9-period exponential moving average to generate buy and sell signals. A buy signal occurs when price moves above the 9 EMA, and a sell signal when price moves below it. The strategy aims to identify short-term market swings and can be applied to securities like stocks, forex, and commodities. Benefits include ease of implementation. Key components involve the 9 EMA line and price crossovers. Implementation requires monitoring price relative to the 9 EMA. Risk management strategies include setting stop-loss orders, adjusting position sizes, and diversification. Advantages are simplicity and short-term trend identification; disadvantages include potential whipsaws. Common mistakes to avoid are not using confirmation and poor risk management. To optimize, traders can use indicators like RSI or Bollinger Bands, and volume data for confirmation. The strategy can be combined with other strategies, using the 9 EMA as a filter for entries and exits. Backtesting on Bitcoin showed 284 trades with an average gain of 2.65% per trade, avoiding large drawdowns. On the S&P 500, the strategy produced an untradable equity curve. The strategy works well in trending assets like Bitcoin but fails in mean-reverting markets like stocks. Adding a 200-day moving average trend filter reduced Bitcoin trades to 153 with a 4% average gain, and slightly improved the S&P 500 result but remained untradable. The strategy is suitable for trending assets and short-term momentum, excluding most mean-reverting assets.

The passage argues that the real efficiency of law often depends on acts that attract little public excitement but face opposition from interested parties. The government has begun using criminal law in trust and interstate commerce cases, and while there have been some failures, successes have had a deterrent effect through fines or imprisonment. Judge Holt's opinion describes a flagrant rebate case where evidence was clear, the illegal contract involved large sums, and the discrimination could have driven competitors out of business. The crime was deliberate, committed by educated men of standing on behalf of a railroad corporation. Such crimes are secretive and difficult to prove; despite long-standing complaints and legislation, very few prosecutions have occurred. The court concluded that a penalty commensurate with the offense's gravity should be imposed, primarily on the corporation, as the traffic manager acted without personal advantage.

The passage presents the Atlas of Human-AI Interaction, a framework for mapping empirical findings in human-AI interaction research. It addresses the challenge of synthesizing a rapidly expanding, fragmented research landscape. The methodology uses large language models to analyze over 1,000 paper abstracts from major HCI venues, extracting findings as structured triplets in the form [cause, relationship, effect] to construct a knowledge graph. The system offers three visualization modes: a 3D Graph View for exploring the research landscape, a Cause-Effect View for tracing directional relationships, and a Paper View for examining individual studies.

Analysis of the knowledge graph identified topic clusters across human, AI, and concept types, revealing dominant research themes such as AI in educational contexts, explanation and trust, design relationships, and decision support. Network analysis using structural hole detection identified concepts like Large Language Models, generative AI, and trust as key opportunities for cross-community research integration. A user study with 20 expert researchers found the Atlas effective for landscape visualization, relationship discovery, and identifying research gaps, though participants noted limitations in information depth and applicability to highly technical domains. The work demonstrates how AI can transform literature synthesis, offering a scalable framework for evidence-based design.

Small group differentiation is a pedagogical strategy aimed at tailoring teaching methods, content, and assessment to diverse student needs in elementary and higher education. It benefits all students, not only those struggling, and addresses increasing diversity in U.S. classrooms. Data show shifts in racial/ethnic enrollment, a rise in students speaking languages other than English at home, and a notable percentage of English language learners. Differentiation counters the insufficient one-size-fits-all approach by matching curriculum to learning styles, interests, and abilities.

The study’s systematic literature search covered 2000–2023 and was guided by constructivist theory (learners construct knowledge from experiences) and sociocultural theory (learning through social interaction and scaffolding). Differentiation can modify content, process, products, and learning environment. Teachers must consider student profiles—linguistic needs, skills, cultural backgrounds—when forming small groups. Elementary settings involve less independent students and foundational content, while higher education features greater specialization, student independence, and changing group compositions. Both settings require differentiation to accommodate backgrounds and abilities.

Five principles of differentiated learning are: flexibility in goals/content/process/product; ongoing assessment and adjustment; respectful, challenging experiences for all; collaboration; and student autonomy. Effective small group instruction uses instructional-level materials, verbal scaffolding, and regular assessment to guide instruction. It increases student engagement, accountability, and opportunities for modeling, discussion, and relationship-building. In higher education, inclusive, culturally responsive environments and reflection exercises can improve outcomes.

Challenges include significant planning time, large class sizes, insufficient administrative support, and the need for deep teacher understanding of each student. Student diversity encompasses varying abilities, disabilities, and linguistic backgrounds. Data show 7.3 million students received special education services under IDEA in 2021–22, with specific learning disabilities being the most common category. Disability prevalence varies by state.

The study’s limitations include a lack of comparative data on pedagogy across settings, difficulty assessing the relationship between small group instruction and learning outcomes, and a shortage of studies linking small group instruction to test scores. Recommendations for future research include longitudinal studies tracking students exposed to differentiation from elementary through higher education and studies evaluating outcomes based on learning styles.

The 4-3 defense consists of four defensive linemen, three linebackers, and four defensive backs, using smaller, more athletic players in the front seven. In a traditional Under front, it employs two 5-technique defensive ends, a 1-technique nose guard, and a 3-technique defensive tackle, the latter being arguably the most important position. Defensive ends are responsible for one gap and contain the quarterback. The 1-technique is the biggest lineman, taking on double teams in the strong A gap. The 3-technique is more athletic and slightly smaller. Linebackers range from the big Sam (strong side) to the athletic Will (weak side), with the Mike linebacker needing to stop the run and cover the pass. Defensive backs include a bigger strong safety and a free safety.

Strengths include being strong against the run with seven defenders in the box, gap-sound assignments where each defender has a gap, and the ability to play multiple coverages. The 1-technique occupies double teams, freeing the 3-technique to rush the passer. Weaknesses involve struggles against modern spread offenses, which pull linebackers out of the box and leave only five defenders, and personnel specificity, as bigger linebackers have coverage difficulties, often leading to nickel personnel.

Offenses attack by spreading the field to displace the Sam linebacker and force nickel packages, and by running to the edge with extra blockers like fullbacks or H-backs, outflanking the defense. Common blitzes include the Will Edge Blitz, sending the Will off the weak edge, and a Zone Blitz where a defensive end drops into coverage while the Sam and Mike rush. Coverages include Tampa 2, where the Mike drops deep to the middle, and Cover 3, which uses three deep defenders with the strong safety rotating down. Notable users are the early 2000s Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the 2006 Chicago Bears under Lovie Smith, and Montini Catholic High School under Mike Bukovsky, who won multiple state championships.

Ray Dalio’s All Weather Portfolio, created by Bridgewater Associates, is a diversified investment strategy designed to perform across inflation, deflation, and stagflation. It includes stocks, bonds, and commodities, with a heavy allocation to bonds and a smaller allocation to stocks. The portfolio uses a risk parity approach, balancing risk exposures through diversification and low correlation among asset classes. Backtests from July 2007 show a CAGR of 4.5% (excluding dividends) versus 6.7% for the S&P 500. Maximum drawdowns were substantially smaller: 17% during the 2008/09 financial crisis (versus 55% for stocks), about 6% during the Covid-19 selloff in 2020 (versus 33%), and approximately 12% in 2022 when both stocks and bonds fell but commodities rose. Leveraging 1.5 times increased CAGR to 6.5% with a 25% max drawdown, matching S&P 500 returns with lower volatility. The strategy is defensive, suited for risk-averse investors, retirees, and FIRE seekers, prioritizing capital preservation and smoother equity curves. Rebalancing is recommended at least annually, preferably in a tax-deferred account. It underperforms in strong bull markets and may not suit young investors. The portfolio can be constructed using five ETFs, and Amibroker code is available for backtesting. Past performance does not guarantee future results, as shown by the 2022 bond selloff.

Under Section 4075 (amended June 14, 1902), passport rules: Passports expire in two years. Naturalized citizens may substitute the old passport for a naturalization certificate if the original application contained sufficient information. One passport may cover the applicant, wife, minor children, and servant; a woman's passport may include her minor children and servant. Professional titles are not inserted. A $1 fee (currency or postal money order to the disbursing clerk) must accompany applications; no drafts/checks. The Department does not procure visés. Blank forms furnished to applicants, not agents except as samples. Address Passport Bureau with return address. Secretary may reject applications for unlawful purposes or noncompliance. In insular possessions, apply to chief executive; abroad, to diplomatic/consular officers. Passports only for those owing U.S. allegiance, not mere declarants. Applications must be sworn affidavits, attested under seal or authenticated; two witnesses if signed by mark. Applicants state birth date/place, occupation, permanent residence, declare temporary sojourn, intent to return and reside in U.S. or insular possessions.

Mother appealed a dissolution judgment awarding $31 monthly child support per child for two children. She argued the support was too low and that abating support during father's visitation was error. Father, a law partner, earned $16,930 in 1985 with expected increases. Mother, a school librarian, had disputed income due to a $6,000 settlement. The visitation schedule gave father care about half the time, resembling joint custody. The trial court abated support based on father's visitation expenses. The appellate court agreed with factoring those expenses but found $31 per child insufficient. Due to difficulty estimating father's future income, standard formulas were not applied. The court modified support to $65 per child per month, effective from the decision date. Affirmed as modified; no costs.
Order affirmed with costs; Thomas, J., dissented: ex parte order denied statutory reply right.

"Please, Continue (Hamlet)" is a participatory theatre piece by Yan Duyvendak and Roger Bernat, performed at the Melbourne Festival. It stages a trial of Hamlet for the murder of Polonius, using real lawyers, a real judge, and a real courtroom, with a jury of 12 selected from the audience. The show adapts to the local legal system of each country where it is performed, only in those with jury systems. The creators were inspired by their shock at Guantanamo trial transcripts and subsequent research into criminal trials. They incorporated a real-life case of a young man accused of killing his girlfriend's father, using its social context of poverty. Duyvendak and Bernat had opposing views on the real defendant's guilt, which led them to create a format that highlights the complexity of justice. Audience members often change their opinions during the trial, and jury participants report a perspective shift, finding sentences heavier after serving. The show aims to demonstrate the justice system's complexity, attracting participation from legal professionals.

The GHCB VALID_BITMAP field must have bits set for fields provided by the guest and hypervisor during NAE events. The guest sets bits for SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, SW_EXITINFO2; the hypervisor sets bits for SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2. Both must reset the bitmap before each event. Bit positions are calculated from field offsets.

NAE events are generally handled via a standard method, with exceptions documented. The guest may use a #VC handler or para-virtualize instructions to invoke VMGEXIT. Software must disable interrupts and preemption around GHCB updates and VMGEXIT. For NMIs, a separate GHCB or save/restore is recommended. Hypervisor errors are communicated via SW_EXITINFO1[31:0] non-zero, with SW_EXITINFO2 providing details like exception injection or malformed input.

Specific NAE events include: IOIO_PROT (guest supplies decrypted buffer in GHCB shared area, SW_SCRATCH points to it); MSR_PROT (guest parses RDMSR/WRMSR or para-virtualizes); VMMCALL (hypervisor-specific hypercalls); #NPF/MMIO access (guest uses reserved bit in NPT to trigger #VC, supplies decrypted buffer for MMIO read/write, SW_EXITINFO1/2 and SW_SCRATCH used); Page State Change (guest requests page state changes via a structure in GHCB Shared Buffer, with operations like private/shared/PSMASH/UNSMASH, progress tracked via cur_entry/cur_page, errors reported in SW_EXITINFO2); SNP Guest Request and Extended Guest Request (guest makes firmware requests using shared request/response pages, hypervisor translates GPAs, manages RMP, returns certificates in data pages for extended requests); AP Creation (SEV-SNP guest creates/destroys/updates AP vCPU state using VMSA pages, with forms for immediate use or pending INIT-SIPI); #HV Doorbell Page (guest registers a doorbell page for hypervisor injection, with actions GET_PREFERRED, SET, QUERY, CLEAR); #HV Send IPI (guest sends IPI via SW_EXITINFO1 formatted as x2APIC ICR); #HV Timer (guest sets/gets virtual APIC timer values); APIC ID List (guest requests list of APIC IDs using shared pages); SNP Run VMPL (guest requests running at a different VMPL level); SNP TIO Guest Request (for trusted devices, similar to SNP Guest Request with additional unencrypted data); Secure AVIC (guest registers/unregisters backing page for APIC state); Termination Request (guest requests termination with reason code and info).

AP booting under SEV-ES uses a method where the hypervisor does not update initial register values; the AP uses a memory location or predetermined CS/IP, and after first boot, the AP issues an AP Reset Hold request (via GHCB or MSR protocol) to park. The hypervisor completes the hold on SIPI, and the AP transitions to real mode at the supplied reset vector. An AP jump table is used for UEFI-to-OS handoff. Under SEV-SNP with AP Creation, the guest uses RMPADJUST to mark VMSA pages and VMGEXIT to create/update AP state, supporting vCPU hotplug.

NMI handling requires the hypervisor to intercept #DB, not IRET; the guest sends an "NMI Complete" message via VMGEXIT when ready. Debug register virtualization is supported if hardware DebugVirtualization is enabled; otherwise, DR7 accesses are intercepted and cached. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

For Restricted Injection, the #HV doorbell page contains PendingEvent (vector, NMI, #MC, NoFurtherSignal) and NoEoiRequired. The host presents interrupts by writing the vector and may set NoEoiRequired to avoid explicit EOI. The guest acknowledges by atomically exchanging PendingEvent with zero, and performs EOI by atomically clearing NoEoiRequired or via explicit APIC register write. Non-maskable events are handled by clearing relevant bits and NoFurtherSignal. The host must emulate APIC behavior faithfully, and both host and guest must validate data to avoid denial-of-service from non-cooperative parties.

This study conducts a systematic review and bibliometric analysis of metaverse in education research using 270 articles from the Scopus database (2015–July 2024), following PRISMA guidelines and employing VOSviewer. The research questions address annual publication trends and productive countries, influential journals and articles, and prominent topics and future exploration areas.

Results show no publications before 2020; numbers rose from 4 articles each in 2020 and 2021 to 36 in 2022, peaked at 131 in 2023, with 91 already in 2024, indicating growing interest. The most productive countries by document count are South Korea (40), China (35), and the United States (31); by citations, South Korea leads, followed by the United Kingdom and China. The most influential journals include IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies (21 articles, 237 citations) and Sustainability (Switzerland) (18 articles, 447 citations). The most cited article is Dwivedi et al. (2022) with 890 citations, followed by Hwang & Chien (2022) and Akour et al. (2022). Co-occurrence analysis of author keywords identified 22 frequent keywords in 6 clusters, with top terms being "metaverse," "virtual reality," "education," "augmented reality," and "artificial intelligence." Keyword timeline shows terms like "virtual worlds" and "avatar" appearing in 2021, "augmented reality" and "gamification" in 2022, and "education" and "learning" in 2023. Prominent topics revolve around virtual reality, augmented reality, and artificial intelligence, with future areas including extended reality, blockchain, sustainability, and gamification. The research categorizes into two main themes: using the metaverse to create virtual educational environments (integrating VR/AR/AI for immersive learning, simulations, and gamified experiences) and investigating perceptions and attitudes of students and teachers, which are mainly positive, influenced by perceived usefulness, ease of use, innovativeness, and enjoyment. The study notes gaps such as a lack of longitudinal studies and concentration of research in East Asia and the US, suggesting future research on long-term impacts, scalability, and cross-cultural comparisons.

Good transition defense begins with good offense: taking care of the ball, good shot selection, strong offensive rebounding, and maintaining defensive balance. The passage outlines twelve musts of transition defense, including sprinting back ahead of the ball, never running with backs to the ball, forcing at least two passes, and knowing how to defend outnumbered situations. Defenders must seek the level of the ball, play up the lane, and avoid uncontested passes over 15 feet. Outnumbered situations require sprinting back, pressuring the ball, delaying advancement, forcing extra passes, preventing easy shots, and boxing out. Specific techniques cover break aways, 2-on-1, and 3-on-2 scenarios. On missed field goals or free throws, the closest defender jams the rebounder while the point defender denies the outlet pass to the primary ballhandler; other defenders sprint back. Five methods to disrupt outlet passes are detailed. After a made basket, the defense can set up full or half court pressure. Turnover recovery emphasizes containing the ball, sprinting back, and erasing bad plays. Block shot recovery mirrors missed shot principles. Game strategies stress ball security, offensive rebounding, scouting, denying outlet passes, and substituting players who fail to sprint back. Teaching transition defense uses the whole-part-whole method, with objectives like developing awareness, offensive decision-making, rebounding attitude, defensive balance, sprinting habits, and outnumbered defense. Drills such as "Wolf" and three-on-two continuous are recommended.

The Court of Civil Appeals of Texas reversed a judgment awarding $30,890 to the surviving wife, children, and mother of J.W. Summers, who died in an automobile collision with an employee of Columbian Fuel Corporation. The court found reversible error in the trial court's jury instructions. The charge on the wife's damages improperly assumed a 34½-year life expectancy for the deceased, removing that fact question from the jury. The charge on the mother's damages similarly assumed a 20-year life expectancy. The instruction for the minor son erroneously allowed consideration of loss of love and fatherly advice, which are not recoverable pecuniary benefits. The charge for the minor daughter suggested college education expenses without sufficient evidentiary basis and was on the weight of the evidence. The court also failed to instruct the jury to exclude sorrow and grief as elements of recovery. Additionally, the appellees' counsel made improper argument criticizing the appellants for introducing admissible divorce suit records, and the trial court erred by not instructing the jury to disregard it. The court held there was no error in refusing to submit requested issues on sole proximate cause or new and independent cause. The cause was remanded for a new trial.

This study uses hydrodynamical simulations, time-dependent chemistry, and radiative transfer to create synthetic line observations of a collapsing prestellar core. It evaluates the Myers et al. (1996) method for estimating infall velocities from self-absorbed molecular line profiles. The results show that measured infall velocities consistently underestimate the true mass-weighted infall velocity, often by a significant margin (up to an order of magnitude). This discrepancy arises because self-absorption features primarily originate in outer core regions where velocities are low, rather than at the peak infall velocity. The non-thermal velocity dispersion from optically thin lines is found to be within a factor of two of the true mass-weighted infall velocity, suggesting it may be a better indicator. The authors conclude that prestellar mass accretion rates derived from such line-profile methods are likely underestimated by potentially an order of magnitude.

A light emitting diode device includes a thin film transistor substrate with light emitting areas, first and second diode electrodes on the substrate, a first passivation pattern between the electrodes, micro light emitting diodes on the first passivation pattern, a first bridge pattern electrically connecting the first diode electrode to the micro light emitting diodes, and a second bridge pattern connecting the second diode electrode to the micro light emitting diodes. Each sidewall of the micro light emitting diodes and each sidewall of the first passivation pattern form the same plane. The micro light emitting diodes have a cylindrical shape with a light emitting material comprising sequentially arranged p-type, intermediate, and n-type semiconductor layers, and a protective layer surrounding the light emitting material. The first sidewall exposes the p-type layer and contacts the first bridge pattern; the second sidewall exposes the n-type layer and contacts the second bridge pattern. The diode electrodes include fine electrode lines alternately arranged in parallel. A manufacturing method forms the first passivation pattern, micro light emitting diode, and a second passivation pattern using a single mask process with two etching steps: a first, more anisotropic etching for a longer time, and a second, more isotropic etching for a shorter time using an additive gas including oxygen, so that the sidewalls form the same plane. The micro light emitting diode is aligned by applying a voltage difference between the electrodes.

The study analyzed pre-treatment biopsies from 67 sarcoma patients enrolled in three immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) trials. RNA-seq deconvolution identified two immune clusters: immune-hot and immune-cold. Immune-hot tumors showed higher immune cell infiltrates, a significantly greater overall response rate (30% vs. 8.1%), and longer progression-free survival (median 3.65 vs. 1.7 months). Lasso logistic regression revealed that expression of specific transposable elements (TEs) and the epigenetic regulator IKZF1 predicted immune-hot classification. TE score and IKZF1 expression positively correlated with innate immune pathways (cGAS-STING, type I interferon) and antigen presentation, and high expression of both was associated with prolonged progression-free survival. Validation in 190 TCGA sarcoma samples confirmed that immune-hot tumors had better overall survival, and high TE score and IKZF1 expression correlated with immune pathway activation and improved survival. The findings suggest TE de-repression and IKZF1 as potential predictive biomarkers for ICI response in sarcomas.

This study explores physics teachers' perspectives on science education research, focusing on potential scepticism. The research gap is noted due to the theory-practice gap and the assumed practical value of evidence-based teaching. Science scepticism towards science education research (SSSE) is defined as scepticism regarding any potential positive impact of science education research on teaching practice.

A two-step mixed-methods approach was used. First, an interview study with 13 German physics teachers identified seven main attitudes, both sceptical and non-sceptical, towards physics education research. Second, a survey of 174 physics teachers from Germany and Austria used items developed from the interviews. An exploratory factor analysis of the survey data identified four factors contributing to SSSE: relevance for the individual teacher, feasibility of findings, relevance for general teaching practice, and cooperation between research and school practice.

Latent profile analysis identified four teacher profiles: The Sceptical Ones, The Uncertain Ones, The Undersupplied Ones, and The Research Advocates. A multinomial logistic regression found that among professional variables, only the frequency of reading instructional journals significantly predicted profile membership, increasing the likelihood of belonging to The Uncertain Ones or The Research Advocates profiles compared to The Sceptical Ones. All profiles exhibited sceptical attitudes towards the cooperation between research and practice.

The lecture reviews the propagator G_+(x,x') = ⟨0|φ(x)φ(x')|0⟩, interpreted heuristically as a transition amplitude from x' to x and as a correlation function. G_- has the opposite order. The Feynman propagator G_F is the time-ordered combination. In momentum space, these functions have singularities at ω = ±ω_k on the real axis. Different contour prescriptions (retarded goes above both poles, advanced below, Feynman one above one below) yield the different Green's functions. An epsilon prescription shifts the singularities infinitesimally off the axis to keep the integration contour fixed.

For free field theory, vacuum n-point correlation functions factorize into sums of products of two-point functions. Composite operators like φ^2 are often singular and require renormalization.

To introduce interactions, a φ^4 term is added to the Lagrangian. The resulting nonlinear equation of motion cannot be solved exactly. If the coupling λ is small, one can expand perturbatively. Scattering experiments are the primary way to probe interactions. The S-matrix is defined as the transition amplitude between initial free-particle states at t = -∞ and final free-particle states at t = +∞, where particles are infinitely far apart and interactions are negligible. The S-matrix is written as S = 1 + iT, with T containing the interaction. Extracting overall momentum conservation gives the scattering amplitude M. The S-matrix is unitary and respects symmetries of the Hamiltonian. The LSZ theorem states that the scattering amplitude can be obtained from time-ordered correlation functions of the full interacting vacuum. The lecture ends by noting that the path integral approach will be introduced next.

This application provides a sidelink positioning method and apparatus. A first terminal device receives a first sidelink positioning configuration from a network device and sends a first sidelink positioning reference signal to a second terminal device. The second terminal device measures the first sidelink positioning reference signal to obtain a first measurement value, which may include an Rx−Tx time difference and/or an angle of arrival measurement. The position of the first terminal device is determined based on the first measurement value and a position of the second terminal device. In some implementations, the second terminal device also sends a second sidelink positioning reference signal, and the first terminal device measures it to obtain a second measurement value. The first terminal device or the network device may determine the position of the first terminal device using the measurement values and the second terminal device's position. The positioning process is hosted by the network device without requiring core network control, reducing positioning latency. The method supports scenarios where the first terminal device does not support sidelink reference signal measurement, with the second terminal device performing the measurement. Configurations include time-frequency resources, sequence information, and reporting methods via Uu or PC5 interfaces.

AI technology has advanced to potentially augment human cognitive abilities, boost learning, expand creativity, and develop new skills, but its impact depends on design, deployment, and usage choices. Two risks are over-reliance on AI systems, which may undermine learning and critical thinking, and limited internalization of learned capabilities, risking independent knowledge retention. Mitigations include avoiding over-reliance, delegating non-essential tasks, encouraging critical mindsets, and developing AI as enhancers rather than replacements through personalized learning and coordinated efforts.

LLMs may challenge the social division of labor by addressing knowledge scarcity and blurring job boundaries, potentially shrinking the traditional middle class. This could lead to a gig economy with flexible but insecure work, requiring policies like flexible contracts and social welfare. AI also reshapes collaboration toward dynamic, individual-to-organization partnerships, fostering innovation. Addressing these changes requires studying labor market impacts, creating regulations, and evolving social welfare and education systems.

In social sciences, LLMs offer low-cost data synthesis by simulating demographic behaviors, but concerns exist about accuracy and bias. They can automate data analysis with zero-shot capabilities and in-context learning, though ethical challenges like misinformation require alignment and watermarking. LLMs may also help explore novel social theories, but human-AI collaboration is needed to ensure originality and validity.

AI governance faces challenges from rapid technological development, including misinformation, deepfakes, and bias. Existing regulations in the EU, US, and China, along with industry principles, aim to mitigate risks, but gaps remain between industry and government, and across countries. Micro-level challenges include emergent risks like jailbreaking. Solutions include fostering partnerships among industry, academia, and policymakers, forward-looking regulations, and a dual top-down and bottom-up governance approach where developers and users report issues transparently.

Unused comparator inputs must not be tied together; instead, apply a voltage within the input range with at least 50mV differential (e.g., one input grounded, the other to V+). The TLV32xx family has 1.8mV internal hysteresis. TLV321x push-pull outputs can sink and source current; unused push-pull outputs must float, and shorting to a supply can cause thermal runaway. TLV322x open-drain outputs sink current only, allow pull-up to 0–5.5V, recommended pull-up current 100µA–1mA; unused open-drain outputs may float or connect to V-. ESD protection diodes limit input voltages to 0.2V beyond the rails; for low-impedance sources, add a current-limiting resistor (≤10mA). A power-on reset holds the output low for up to 32µs after V+ crosses 1.65V, then the output reflects the input. Basic comparator: output low when VIN < VREF, high when VIN > VREF; propagation delay increases with smaller overdrive, especially <100mV. External hysteresis can be added via positive feedback to prevent chatter; inverting and non-inverting configurations are described. A low-side current sensing application example requires 0.1µF ceramic bypass capacitors at supply pins, stable power, and high-speed layout practices to avoid ringing and oscillations.

President Johnson transmitted to the House of Representatives a copy of his February 10, 1868 letter to General Grant, along with accompanying papers, in compliance with a House resolution requesting further correspondence regarding Grant’s vacation of the War Office. Johnson’s letter responds to Grant’s letter of February 3, stating that the controversy has reached a point where further assertion between the parties should cease, and instead presents statements from five Cabinet members who were present at the January 14 Cabinet meeting. Johnson asserts that Grant admitted in that meeting that he had previously agreed either to remain as Secretary of War ad interim to allow a judicial test or to return the office to the President before Senate action, and that Grant’s subsequent actions violated that understanding. Johnson accuses Grant of having accepted the office with the intent to defeat the President’s purpose and of insubordination for refusing to obey a direct order to disregard War Department orders unless known to be authorized by the President. The Cabinet members’ letters (from Welles, McCulloch, Randall, Browning, and Seward) generally support Johnson’s account of the conversation, with some variations in detail. On February 11, Johnson transmitted a letter from Grant received after the initial communication. Grant acknowledges receipt of the Cabinet statements, declines to admit differences, and addresses the insubordination charge. He explains that his January 30 letter did not refuse to obey a legal order but gave his interpretation of what would constitute satisfactory evidence of the President’s sanction. He notes that he was the only subordinate instructed to disregard Stanton’s authority, and encloses correspondence showing that the Treasury and Post Office departments recognized Stanton as Secretary of War, requiring Grant to act on orders from Stanton. Grant disclaims any intention of disobeying a distinct legal order from the President.

This study investigated medical students' perceptions of a curriculum-based resilience skills building course at Mohammed Bin Rashid University of Medicine and Health Sciences in Dubai, UAE. The course, integrated into Year 4 of the MBBS program, comprised 6 hours of instruction on stress, burnout, resilience, cognitive behavioural therapy, emotional intelligence, mindfulness, and coping strategies. It was designed using constructivism experiential learning theory to foster self-directed learning through reflection, journaling, and active experimentation. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, researchers analyzed reflective essays from 37 consenting students (29 female, 9 male). Inductive thematic analysis generated a conceptual framework of three interlinked themes: Awareness, Application, and Appraisal. Awareness included personal interpretations of resilience, perceived associations with mindfulness and social support, relevance to personal and professional life, and the need for conscious practice. Application covered the concept of resilience, specific exercises (e.g., meditation, breathing, reframing, physical activities), and challenges such as scepticism, time constraints, and effort. Appraisal encompassed students' evaluations of building resilience, the course, and the exercises. Students reported increased awareness, application of skills, and positive appraisal, citing benefits for well-being, academic performance, and future professional sustainability. The study concludes that integrating such a course into medical curricula is likely to be positively received, raising awareness and proactive application of resilience skills, particularly when anchored in experiential learning and self-directed learning. Limitations include a single-institution focus, potential social desirability bias, and absence of pre-post quantitative measures.

The passage describes an undergraduate course, "All Means All: Inclusive Teaching for Students with Disabilities," designed to integrate advocacy as a central theme rather than a standalone lesson. The five-credit, ten-week course meets weekly for three hours and satisfies general education and advanced writing requirements. Learning goals include demonstrating dignity toward disabled individuals, critiquing special education through critical disability studies, analyzing sources, applying critical reflection, communicating effectively, synthesizing research and lived experience to argue for an ideal inclusive environment, and exploring one's role in educational equity.

Advocacy skills are built through scaffolded assignments. Students watch recommended TED Talks weekly to understand persuasive structure. They complete five low-stakes reflection assignments, two requiring argument development. A jigsaw activity has groups research landmark special education court cases (P.A.R.C. v. Pennsylvania, Mills v. Board of Education, Board of Education v. Rowley, Oberti v. Board of Education, Smith v. Los Angeles Unified School District) and share findings. An in-class debate on full inclusion randomly assigns students to affirmative or negative teams, using a graphic organizer for evidence and rebuttals, followed by debriefing. Week nine focuses on policy and advocacy, with pre-work on the ADA's passage and legislative advocacy videos; in class, students write a diary entry from the perspective of a disability advocate, congressperson, or lobbyist. The final project is a TED Talk-style presentation arguing a position on inclusive education and a corresponding paper, graded with rubrics, with peer feedback collected.

The passage emphasizes that advocacy is a professional responsibility rooted in special education's history and the Council for Exceptional Children's ethical principles. It argues teacher preparation must explicitly teach advocacy through practice-based opportunities. The course models interactive strategies that pre-service teachers can later use. Implications include that without such training, novice teachers face unmanageable workloads and systemic barriers; integrating advocacy equips them to navigate these challenges. The conclusion states advocacy should be seamlessly woven into every special education preparation course. Ten steps for legislative advocacy from Fisher and Miller (2021) are referenced.

The lecture, a substitute session, addresses regulating tech giants, focusing on challenges of too little cooperation in two-sided platforms. A platform connects consumers and merchants/apps, with concerns about behavioral manipulation, contestability, and fair access/compensation. The Chicago School argument that platforms won't discriminate because they can charge consumers fails for three reasons: a zero lower bound on consumer prices (optimal price is negative but arbitrage prevents it, so price is zero and cannot be raised); contestability issues where favoring in-house apps may cause third-party exit, protecting the core segment from future entry; and a second zero lower bound on apps, leading to supranormal profits.

Regulating platforms like public utilities is difficult because they are global and fast-changing, complicating rate-of-return regulation. The Digital Markets Act designates platforms, imposes fairness obligations, and relies on self-execution. Contestability measures include promoting multihoming, portability, and interoperability. Traditional one-sided access pricing gave the ECPR ceiling. In a two-sided model with zero lower bounds, if the access charge a is below the ancillary benefit b, the app zero lower bound binds, the in-house app price is zero, the rival earns excess profits, and the platform wants to foreclose. If a is high, a core zero lower bound may bind, squeezing apps. The platform’s preferred access charge is high to squeeze the rival; the optimal regulated access charge is b. Eliciting b could involve asking the third-party app its willingness to pay under threat of foreclosure. Simple, operational rules are needed for regulators.

The speaker contrasts climate change (high probability, gradual) with nuclear war (low daily probability but catastrophic, potentially causing nuclear winter). He focuses on pathways to nuclear war, proliferation, the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abolition, and Obama's record. Debates on nuclear weapons include claims they saved lives in WWII and prevented WWIII, while counterarguments say their use was unnecessary, especially the second bomb on Nagasaki, and started the Cold War. No nuclear wars have occurred since 1945; explanations include deterrence, a nuclear taboo, or luck. The Ukraine case is a special one, as it never had operational control of Soviet weapons. Present stability is questioned; many suspect luck is involved. US-Russia relations are at a low point, making arms control bleak. Abolition is remote but should be considered long-range.

The Franck Report recommended demonstrating the bomb and sharing its existence to avoid an arms race, but the Baruch plan was rejected. Scientists in 1946 imagined a worst-case of 100 weapons each, yet the buildup reached tens of thousands driven by fear, leading to Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD). One US submarine can carry 96 warheads with explosive power three times WWII. Current global inventory: US and Russia have about 1,500 strategic warheads under New START; other states have a few hundred. Numbers are estimates. China is coy and keeps missiles off alert.

Fear is the main factor in nuclear escalation. Two primary pathways: accidental launch between US and Russia from early warning system malfunction, and escalation from conventional war between India and Pakistan. North Korea is less likely, seeking deterrence and regime survival. Pakistan's aggressive deployment posture stems from conventional inferiority and historic enmity with India. Obama's India visit disappointed the speaker by selling nuclear reactors and not addressing Pakistan tension. India focuses on China; China aids Pakistan. Resolution requires diplomacy, not force.

Accidental war could arise from early warning errors. The US and Russia keep roughly 900-1000 missiles on hair-trigger alert, with decision times of minutes. The system allows only retaliation. Cyber attack on early warning is a new nightmare. Obama promised to address this but abandoned the effort.

The NPT is the cornerstone against proliferation. It is enforced for nonproliferation but not for disarmament under Article VI, creating tension. Non-nuclear states demand a timetable. The upcoming five-year review in May is expected to be stormy. Four states remain outside the NPT: Israel, India, Pakistan, North Korea. The AQ Khan network sold obsolete centrifuge technology, ironically setting back Iran. Fewer countries have nuclear weapons than predicted in the 1960s; the political norm now favors renunciation and disarmament.

Iran's enrichment capabilities exceed power needs, suiting weapons production. Ongoing negotiations involve an interim agreement with deadlines in March and June. Hardliners in the West demand zero centrifuges, while Iran wants many. The speaker argues the best feasible solution is continuing the interim agreement: Iran claims no weapons intent, has a fatwa, remains in the NPT, and endures rigorous IAEA inspections. Breakout would require expelling inspectors. Hidden sites might be discovered, as when Soviet physicist Flyorov deduced the Manhattan Project from the halt of fission publications. One weapon is insufficient; breakout time calculations assume one weapon. The Menendez-Kirk bill is temporarily stalled.

Past NPT reviews: 2005 was disastrous under Bush; 2010 was productive under Obama with 22 disarmament steps, including a timetable for zero and a Middle East nuclear-free zone conference. Follow-through has been nonexistent, fueling predicted stormy weather.

Obama's 2009 Prague speech raised hopes for a nuclear-free world but was hedged. Arguments against abolition include loss of deterrence and unlikelihood of achievement. Deterrence has flaws: it has not coerced others, enables brinkmanship and instabilities (e.g., Pakistan's delegated command and rogue commander risk), requires rationality, and fails against terrorists. Deterrence needs only a small number of weapons (under 100). Abolition involves minimizing risk, not eliminating it, and is vital for NPT health.

Obama's record is mixed: New START and improved nuclear security, but engagement with Russia failed. The nuclear posture review left many weapons on hair-trigger alert. His North Korea policy of "strategic patience" is criticized as inaction; North Korea seeks engagement but is ignored. Modernization of nuclear weapons continues, drawing criticism, while maintenance is necessary; the two are conflated and classified.

Reasons for optimism include the CTBO monitoring system, which detected a half-kiloton North Korean test via seismic signals and radioactivity. Public opinion and arms control organizations matter. The present situation is stable only with luck. More can be done, such as accelerating reductions to New START levels; Russia is already below limits. Inspections under New START are more critical than warhead numbers, as 100 weapons is overkill. Below 1,000, multilateral negotiations become necessary. Conventional Global Strike capabilities could replace nuclear deterrence but remain frightening, potentially merging conventional and nuclear arms control. Pakistan has 100-200 weapons and is building more; India is more restrained but not pursuing political solutions like Kashmir. US policy is not evenhanded, spurring Pakistan's buildup due to commercial interests in power plant sales and military hardware.

This lecture introduces the course 18.100A Real Analysis, which has two purposes: gaining experience with reading and writing proofs, and proving statements about real numbers, functions, and limits. The initial material reviews sets. A set is defined as a collection of objects called elements. Notation is introduced for element of, not element of, for all, there exists, implies, and if and only if. Subset, equality, and proper subset are defined. Examples of sets include natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real numbers; a first goal of the course is to properly define the real numbers. Set operations are defined: union, intersection, set difference, complement, and disjoint sets. DeMorgan's Laws are stated, and a detailed proof of the first law (complement of union equals intersection of complements) is given. The lecture then covers induction. The well-ordering property of natural numbers is taken as an axiom. The theorem of induction is stated: if a statement P(n) satisfies P(1) true and P(m) implies P(m+1), then P(n) is true for all natural numbers. A proof by contradiction using the well-ordering property is provided. Two examples of induction are demonstrated: proving the formula for a finite geometric series, and proving Bernoulli's inequality (1+c)^n ≥ 1+nc for c ≥ -1.

President Ford's EO 11905 replaced the 40 Committee with the Operations Advisory Group (OAG), composed of the Assistant for National Security Affairs, Secretaries of State and Defense, Joint Chiefs Chairman, and DCI. It banned political assassinations and domestic intelligence activities. President Carter retained the NSC and replaced the OAG with the Special Coordination Committee (SCC), later called SCC-Intelligence (SCC–I), with the same membership plus the Attorney General and OMB Director as observers. EO 11985 formalized this, and EO 12036 reaffirmed it, making the Attorney General and OMB Director full members. The SCC–I established the Special Activities Working Group (SAWG), chaired by Deputy Assistant David Aaron, which later fell out of use and was succeeded by an interagency group known by various names. The Carter administration used a category of worldwide/general covert operations, continuing a Ford-era practice. These lower-risk operations were guided by "Perspectives" documents drafted by the CIA and cleared by State, detailing themes for policy goals. Riskier operations required separate presidential findings or Memoranda of Notification. Initially, Perspectives did not need further coordination. From 1978, worldwide actions were authorized as line-item additions to an existing worldwide finding, with Perspectives still providing details.

Funders can extend philanthropy to this area. CBOs are uniquely positioned to complement school-based efforts, building a more cohesive support network.

The study developed and externally validated machine learning (ML) models—logistic regression, random forest, and boosted tree—to predict restriction from spirometric, demographic, and anthropometric data, aiming to improve upon current ERS/ATS guidelines that use a normal forced vital capacity (FVC) lower limit of normal (LLN) to exclude restriction. Development used 42,462 pulmonary function tests (PFTs) from one academic health system; external validation used 24,524 PFTs from a second. Restriction was defined as total lung capacity (TLC) below the LLN, with race-neutral reference equations. The random forest model performed best, achieving a negative predictive value (NPV) of 88.3% in validation versus 72.7% for the FVC LLN, though it excluded the need for static lung volume measurement in fewer tests (56.7% vs 78.4%). Sensitivity was 83.3% (vs 46.0%) and specificity 82.9% (vs 94.4%). The model showed improved equity: NPV for non-Hispanic Black patients was 74.6% (vs 49.5% for FVC LLN) and for non-Hispanic White patients 90.9% (vs 79.6%), with a higher ratio of NPVs between groups. Decision curve analysis favored the random forest model across most threshold probabilities. The authors concluded that ML models enhance both accuracy and equity in excluding restriction from spirometry, though significant racial disparities in performance remained and calibration was poor in external validation.
