In a certiorari proceeding, plaintiff Cox challenged Judge Burnham's jurisdiction to grant a liquor permit to pharmacist P. E. Bell at a term subsequent to the one in which the application was filed. The application was filed March 2, 1901, for the April 1901 term; a remonstrance was filed, but the matter was not heard and was continued to the September 1901 term, where, after a hearing, the permit was ordered. Plaintiff contended the court lost jurisdiction because the hearing occurred after the first term.

The court construed Code sections 2387–2389 and 2431. It held that the statutory provisions requiring applications to be tried at the first term if business allows are not mandatory but involve discretion. An adjournment of the term does not automatically dismiss the application or deprive the court of jurisdiction; the matter stands continued to the next term under the general continuance statute. The court presumed, absent a showing to the contrary, that cause existed for continuing the hearing. The September 1901 hearing was held after consultation with the applicant’s attorney and the county attorney, who represented the public and assumed to represent the remonstrants. The proceedings were regular and not evasive. Because the remonstrants did not appear separately or demand a hearing, they could not complain. The writ was dismissed.

This meta-analysis examined the effectiveness of AI-related technologies in education by synthesizing 13 studies from eight countries, following PRISMA guidelines. The overall effect size was 0.86 (95% CI [0.45, 1.27], p < 0.0001), indicating a large positive effect. Sub-analyses showed chatbots and generative AI had an effect size of 1.02 (p < 0.0001), online learning and virtual reality 0.79 (p < 0.07), and learning management systems/AI platforms 0.62 (p < 0.05). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² ranging from 54.03% to 93.23%), and publication bias was detected. Novel algorithmic approaches were applied: a Naive Bayes-based algorithm yielded a positive overall effect; re-weighting Hedges’ g using TF-IDF and BERT-based methods produced overall effect sizes of 0.86 and 0.84, respectively; a weighted hybrid model combining random and fixed effects gave an effect size of 0.88 (p < 0.0001). Tesla, Inc. filed an Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2018. The company designs, develops, manufactures, and sells high-performance fully electric vehicles and energy generation and storage systems, operating as a vertically integrated sustainable energy company. Its electric vehicles include the Model S sedan (deliveries began June 2012), Model X SUV (September 2015), and Model 3 sedan (July 2017), a lower-priced mass-market vehicle. Future planned vehicles include Model Y, Tesla Semi, a pickup truck, and a new Roadster. Vehicles offer long range, proprietary Supercharger fast charging, advanced Autopilot driver assist, over-the-air software updates, and lower cost of ownership versus internal combustion vehicles.

Energy storage products consist of Powerwall 2 (14 kWh home battery) and Powerpack 2 (scalable commercial/utility system). The company sells and leases solar energy systems, including Solar Roof (glass tiles integrating solar generation), and sells solar electricity. Solar panel manufacturing occurs at Gigafactory 2 in Buffalo, New York, in collaboration with Panasonic.

Core competencies include powertrain engineering, vehicle engineering, and energy storage. The powertrain comprises battery pack, power electronics, motor, gearbox, and control software. Battery packs are designed for high energy density, safety, and low cost. Power electronics include drive inverters and chargers. Dual motor all-wheel drive is offered. Vehicle control and infotainment software is internally developed. Autopilot provides auto-steering, traffic-aware cruise control, automated lane changing, and parking. Since October 2016, all vehicles include hardware for full self-driving (cameras, ultrasonic sensors, radar, onboard computer) with over-the-air updates and field data learning.

Energy storage products leverage vehicle technologies. Powerwall 2 provides backup power and solar self-consumption. Powerpack 2 systems scale to MWh/GWh for peak shaving, load shifting, grid services, and microgrids. Solar energy systems include panels, inverters, racking, and monitoring; most components are purchased from multiple vendors.

Vehicles are marketed and sold directly through company-owned stores, galleries, and Service Plus locations. Used cars are sold from trade-ins and lease returns. Charging options include Superchargers (strategically placed fast chargers), Destination Chargers, and home charging. Orders are taken online or in stores. Media coverage and word of mouth drive sales without traditional advertising. Solar and energy storage products are sold via stores, channel partners, and an international sales organization.

Vehicle service is provided at company-owned service centers, Service Plus locations, and by Mobile Service technicians. Vehicles support remote diagnostics via wireless data upload. New vehicles have a 4-year/50,000-mile limited warranty. Model S/X battery and drive unit warranty is 8 years/infinite miles; Model 3 is 8 years/100,000 or 120,000 miles with minimum 70% battery capacity retention. Maintenance plans and extended service plans are offered. Energy storage products have 10-year (Powerwall 2) or 15-year (Powerpack 2) warranties covering defects and energy retention, with optional extended warranties. Solar energy systems have workmanship warranties up to 20 years; Solar Roof has lifetime tile, 30-year installation and weatherization, and power output warranties.

Financial services include vehicle financing through financial institutions, direct leasing of Model S/X in the U.S. and Canada, and resale value guarantees in some non-North American markets. Solar loans, leases, and PPAs are offered; customer payments are monetized through investor funds. Energy storage loans/leases are available when purchased with solar systems.

Manufacturing facilities: Fremont, California (Tesla Factory); Lathrop, California; Tilburg, Netherlands; Gigafactory 1 in Nevada (battery cell, module, pack, and drive unit production with Panasonic, expanding beyond 500,000 vehicle capacity, likely to produce Model Y); Gigafactory Shanghai in China (construction began January 2019, targeting Model 3 production for local market by end of 2019, subject to uncertainties, with lower targeted capital expenditures per unit and local debt financing).

Raw materials include aluminum, steel, cobalt, lithium, nickel, copper. Energy storage products share supply chain and components with vehicles. Solar panels/inverters are purchased from multiple manufacturers; a long-term agreement with Panasonic covers PV cells/modules at Gigafactory 2.

Governmental incentives: California sales tax exclusions on manufacturing equipment; Nevada tax abatements and transferable tax credits (maximum $195.0 million earned); tradable regulatory credits (ZEV, greenhouse gas, fuel economy, clean fuels, SRECs). Competition: automotive market highly competitive; Model S/X compete with premium sedans/SUVs, Model 3 with small/medium sedans; many manufacturers offer electric/hybrid vehicles. The present invention provides compositions and methods for enhancing the efficacy of immune effector cells engineered to express a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) by reducing or eliminating the expression and/or function of methylcytosine dioxygenase genes Tet1, Tet2, and/or Tet3. Disruption of a single allele of a Tet gene decreases total 5-hydroxymethylcytosine levels, leading to enhanced proliferation, effector cytokine production, and degranulation, thereby increasing CAR T cell proliferation and function. The CAR comprises an antigen-binding domain (which may target tumor antigens such as CD19, among others), a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular signaling domain containing a primary signaling domain and optionally a costimulatory signaling domain. Inhibitors of Tet genes include gene editing systems (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9, zinc finger nucleases, TALENs, meganucleases) targeted to the Tet gene or its regulatory elements, siRNA or shRNA, small molecules, and dominant negative proteins. Methods of increasing therapeutic efficacy involve contacting CAR-expressing cells with a Tet inhibitor ex vivo or in vivo. Also provided are methods of treating a subject by administering the engineered cells, optionally with a Tet inhibitor, for diseases associated with tumor antigen expression, including hematologic cancers and solid tumors. Vectors encoding both a CAR and a Tet inhibitor, gene editing systems specific for Tet genes, and compositions for ex vivo manufacture are described. Data from a patient and in vitro experiments demonstrate that Tet2 disruption reduces 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, promotes expansion of Tscm cells, and enhances antigen-driven proliferation and cytokine production.

This Mendelian randomization (MR) study investigated the causal relationship between genetically determined pericardial adipose tissue (PAT) and multiple cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), and the mediating role of hypertension. Using 11 single-nucleotide polymorphisms as instrumental variables from a genome-wide association study of PAT in 28,161 white British individuals, the study assessed outcomes including CVD, heart failure, hypertension, coronary heart disease, ischemic heart disease, ischemic stroke, venous thromboembolism, and others. The primary inverse-variance weighting analysis, supported by sensitivity analyses, found that genetically predicted PAT was significantly associated with higher risks of CVD (OR 1.15), heart failure (OR 2.62), hypertension (OR 1.11), coronary heart disease (OR 3.53), ischemic heart disease (OR 2.31), ischemic stroke (OR 3.18), and venous thromboembolism (OR 1.02). No significant associations were observed for cardiac arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, aortic aneurysm, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, cardioembolic stroke, small vessel stroke, large artery stroke, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. A two-step mediation MR analysis showed that hypertension mediated the effects of PAT on heart failure (13.23%), coronary heart disease (13.51%), ischemic heart disease (19.18%), and ischemic stroke (14.51%). The study concluded that PAT promotes CVD progression and hypertension plays an intermediary role, suggesting PAT as a potential therapeutic target and supporting conjunctive use of antihypertensive drugs, especially in people with obesity. Limitations include the European-only sample, potential sample overlap, and small case numbers for some outcomes.

"Russian math" after-school programs, notably the Russian School of Mathematics (RSM), are a growing trend in the U.S. RSM, co-founded by Inessa Rifkin in Newton, Massachusetts in 1997, now has 22,000 students across 40 branches nationwide. Students attend once a week, paying about $2,000 a year. The curriculum, based on Russian teaching traditions, emphasizes reasoning, deep understanding, and early introduction of algebra and geometry, rather than memorization and drills. Parents choose Russian math for various reasons: dissatisfaction with school math, a child's love of math, or a belief that strong math skills will open future doors. Some parents worry their children will be at a disadvantage without it, leading to what Harvard professor Jon Star calls an "arms race" of after-school instruction. The roots lie in the Soviet Union's elite math schools and the emigration of Russian Jews, many of whom settled in the Boston area. Rifkin started RSM after discovering her eighth-grade son lacked expected math knowledge. The Studio of Engaging Math, another program run by Larisa Itina, uses small groups, manipulatives, and engaging problems to develop critical thinking. However, the rise of Russian math poses challenges for schools: some students have already covered topics, potentially causing overconfidence, and it may widen performance gaps between those who can afford it and those who cannot. RSM's Rifkin claims the number of honors classes grows in towns with RSM, but no data confirms a direct link. Russian math teaching methods remain largely unstudied by American researchers. Teachers report that students become more willing to think through difficult problems.

The passage presents a metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) workflow using HostEL and AmpRE kits to address limitations of conventional mNGS. HostEL depletes human background via magnetic bead-immobilized nucleases after selective lysis, enriching pathogen DNA and RNA. AmpRE is a single-tube additive library preparation for both DNA and RNA with minimal clean-up steps, reducing processing time. Analytical validation used human plasma spiked with ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard (8 bacteria, 2 fungi) at concentrations from 1.4 million to 70,000 cells/mL. With HostEL treatment and low-depth sequencing on iSeq 100 (median ~56,500 paired-end reads per sample), all 10 species were detected at all dilutions, while untreated samples lost signal at lower concentrations. HostEL achieved ~2-4 fold enrichment of non-human reads. Sensitivity was 96% and specificity 96% with HostEL, versus 82% and 97% in controls. At the lowest concentration (70,000 cells/mL), sensitivity was 88% with HostEL vs 63% without. Clinical validation on 42 banked patient plasma samples (34 positive, 8 negative for pathogens) showed 93% agreement with clinical molecular diagnosis after excluding 13 samples with Ct≥33 or undetectable by qPCR. The workflow detected DNA viruses (Hepatitis B, CMV, EBV), RNA viruses (Hepatitis C, Dengue, HIV), and bacteria. Sequencing reads correlated linearly with qPCR Ct values, with detection confidence up to Ct~30. The workflow was tested on iSeq 100 (2x150, 19h run, 27h total turnaround), a simulated shorter iSeq run (2x100, 13h), and MiniSeq (single-end 100nt, 5h run, 13h total). All three protocols showed comparable sensitivity and specificity. The method preserves relative species composition and enables rapid, cost-effective unbiased mNGS as a potential first-line diagnostic, though it is not applicable to parasites. The study concludes that the HostEL and AmpRE workflow reduces time, cost, and effort while maintaining high sensitivity and specificity.

Backtests indicate NIFTY 50 has a robust positive end-of-month effect, comparable to the US turn-of-the-month effect. Using Yahoo Finance data from 2007, optimization found the optimal exit at the close of the second trading day of the new month, and entry on the fifth last trading day gave the best profit factor. The strategy goes long at the close of the fifth last trading day and sells at the close of the second trading day of the new month. A backtest with 100,000 compounded shows a CAGR of 10.5%, outperforming buy and hold with only 30% market exposure and a 26% maximum drawdown. The backtest is somewhat curve-fitted but remains reasonably robust when entry and exit are varied by a few days. The positive end-of-month effect can be used as a turn-of-the-month trading strategy.

Researchers developed and externally validated deep learning models to identify extra-prostatic extension (EPE) and seminal vesicle invasion (SVI) on prostate MRI using 820 patients from Yale, with internal and external test sets. The EPE model achieved an AUC of 0.719 on the Yale test set and validated externally (AUCs 0.743 and 0.611). The SVI model achieved an AUC of 0.724 on the Yale test set and validated externally (AUCs 0.678 and 0.775). Both biomarkers were significantly associated with biochemical recurrence (BCR). Combining the biomarkers improved prognostic value; patients with both positive biomarkers had lower 5-year BCR-free survival. Integrating the imaging biomarkers into NCCN risk groups reclassified 26.4% of patients and improved the C-index for predicting BCR (from 0.592 to 0.617). Grad-CAM heatmaps showed the models localized to the prostatic capsule and seminal vesicles. Limitations included not evaluating overall survival or prostate cancer-specific mortality, lack of comparison to tissue-based classifiers, and underrepresentation of African American patients.

An autonomous vehicle includes multiple independent control systems for redundancy in safety-critical situations. One or more auxiliary bypass control units operate independently, using dedicated sensors to detect specific predefined conditions or events (e.g., imminent collision, system malfunction) and generate a vehicle response output. This output can be communicated directly to vehicle interfaces to implement a predetermined bypass action that overrides the primary system, or sent to the primary system for trajectory verification. The auxiliary units are optimized for reliability, may use hardware/firmware architectures, and can provide responses such as braking, steering, or stopping. The vehicle can operate with the primary system while auxiliary units continuously monitor, and their responses can be sustained until the triggering condition clears or a safe state is achieved.

The "Power" offense is a set used by almost every NBA team to free up shooters through baseline and down screens, attacking both sides of the defense simultaneously. The basic action begins with wings crossing under the basket (touching right hands, faking optional), then curling off down screens set by O4 and O5. Point guard O1 looks to pass to the shooters or to the screeners rolling to the basket. Players must know defensive reads and counters: if the defender chases, curl for a jump shot; if chases late, basket curl; if cheats over, fade to baseline; if cheats over early, back cut; if defenders switch, screen and roll with post or wing isolation; if show and recover, slip the screen. Offensive rebounding is integral, requiring anticipation and hustle; the offense always positions two rebounders on the weakside. Automatic counters against defensive overplays include fake cross, misdirection, back cut, direct post entry, and dribble drive entry. When initial screens fail, continuity options are Motion (pass and screen away, with base cross), Side Screen (on-ball screen for the wing), Drive & Kick (dribble hand-off and penetration), and Triangle Post (sideline triangle and two-man action). A Single/Double variation uses a double screen for a great shooter, allowing options to go either way. Teaching requires whole-part-whole method, drills, and individual skill work. Game strategies emphasize scouting, varying alignments, attacking weak defenders, and using side screens as the clock winds down. Even if not using the offense, one should know how to defend it.

The message informs Congress that the British reply to the US representation regarding the Great Britain-Venezuela boundary dispute has been received. The reply, in two communications from the British prime minister, argues that the Monroe doctrine is being extended in a new and strange way, is inapplicable to present conditions and this controversy, and is not a principle of international law based on general consent. The message maintains that the Monroe doctrine is vital to US peace, safety, and free institutions, applies at every stage of national life, and that any European extension of territory on this continent is dangerous. It asserts that the doctrine has a place in international law if justly claimed, and the US is confident of its rights. The British prime minister acknowledged sympathy with Monroe's policy but denied its inscription in international law, while concurring that territorial disturbance would be inexpedient. The US proposed arbitration to determine whether Britain sought to extend her possessions without right or merely territory within her lines, and to clarify the US standing. The British Government declined this proposition on grounds deemed unsatisfactory. The message expresses disappointment. Since arbitration was refused, and assuming Venezuela's attitude unchanged, the US must determine the true boundary line. It recommends Congress appropriate funds for a commission to investigate and report. Upon acceptance of the report, the US will resist by every means any British appropriation of territory determined to belong to Venezuela. The message acknowledges the responsibility and consequences, but affirms that submission to wrong and injustice would cause loss of national self-respect and honor, which protect a people's safety and greatness.

This study investigated the perspectives of 16 early childhood teachers (8 bilingual, 8 monolingual) in Ankara, Türkiye, on bilingualism and bilingual education. Five themes were identified: benefits of bilingual education, bilingual children in monolingual schools, bilingual education programs, issues in bilingual education, and the impact on children’s development. Both groups agreed bilingualism offers advantages such as enhanced self-confidence, communication skills, and career prospects. Bilingual teachers more frequently viewed attending monolingual schools as a disadvantage due to potential loss of the second language, while some monolingual teachers considered it not disadvantageous, emphasizing the need for Turkish proficiency. Teachers showed limited knowledge of bilingual program models; both groups stressed that school staff should be proficient in both languages. Challenges included ineffective use of both languages by teachers, insufficient financial and human resources, children’s native language deficiencies, and lack of parental familiarity with the second language. All teachers supported expanding bilingual schools in Türkiye and recognized the importance of parental support. The study underscores the need for professional development and improved teacher competencies in bilingual education.

This review examined lung cancer screening methods using biomarkers. A PubMed search identified 32 articles meeting criteria: US-based research within 10 years, clinical setting, and primary lung cancer. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for various biomarkers. Volatile organic compounds showed 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) had 80% sensitivity and 96% specificity. miRNA molecules (miR-146-5p, miR-324-5p, miR-223-3p, miR-223-5p) had sensitivities of 93–96% but specificities of 23–33%. Methylation beads for genes SOX17, TAC1, HOXA7, CDO1, HOXA9, ZFP42 in sputum and serum showed sensitivities ranging from 34% to 93% and specificities from 8% to 92%. Ga-Alfatide II scans had 86% sensitivity and 85% specificity. Combined score had 78% sensitivity and 50% specificity. WT-IDH had 63% sensitivity and 93% specificity. The review highlighted ctDNA and Ga-Alfatide II CT/PET scans as promising screening methods due to their higher sensitivity and specificity. Limitations included the restriction to US articles and a 10-year timeframe. The study suggests these biomarkers could improve early detection and reduce lung cancer mortality.

The study compared three surveys on physician EHR use and interoperability: the 2021 National Electronic Health Records Survey (NEHRS), the 2022 Continuous Certification Questionnaire (CCQ) from the American Board of Family Medicine, and the 2022 UCSF Physician Health IT Survey. NEHRS is a voluntary survey with an 18.2% response rate; CCQ is required for recertification (100% response rate); the UCSF survey is voluntary (3.6% response rate). Analysis focused on primary care physicians using EHRs. Respondent demographics differed: CCQ respondents were younger and more often in health systems, NEHRS had more private practice physicians, and UCSF had more academic center physicians. Epic was the most common EHR platform. Satisfaction with EHRs varied: 29.1% of NEHRS, 26.7% of CCQ, and 19.4% of UCSF respondents were very satisfied. On identically worded interoperability questions, CCQ and NEHRS showed similar results (45.8% and 45.4% reported EHR integrates outside information; 22.8% and 21.9% often had access to outside clinical information), while UCSF responses were lower (37.6% and 14.6%). Differences persisted in stratified analyses by age, EHR platform, and practice type. All surveys indicated low EHR satisfaction, substantial after-hours documentation, and significant interoperability challenges. The authors suggest response bias and differing survey compositions contribute to observed differences, and that mandatory recertification surveys like CCQ may provide more representative data, though limited to one specialty. They conclude that augmenting NEHRS with data from certifying boards could improve reliability for policy decisions.

A dementia-specific exercise and functional activity rehabilitation programme (PrAISED) was evaluated in a randomised controlled trial involving 365 participants with mild dementia or mild cognitive impairment. The 12-month intervention, delivered by therapists in participants’ homes, included progressive strength, balance, and dual-task training, functional activities, and carer involvement. The programme was well received but had no effect on the primary outcome, activities of daily living (Disability Assessment for Dementia score adjusted mean difference -1.3, 95% CI -5.2 to +2.6), or on physical activity, quality of life, falls, cognition, or other health status outcomes. Small statistically significant differences favoured the control group in dual-task mobility and self-reported quality of life. Falls outcomes showed no significant difference, with an incidence rate ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.3) for months 4–15. Underpowered cognitive analyses suggested possible benefits in executive function and working memory. The trial was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, but sensitivity analyses did not alter results. The authors conclude that exercise and functional rehabilitation did not improve functional ability in early dementia, and that new approaches to defining wellbeing and supporting people with dementia are needed.

Stenabolic (SR9009) is a synthetic Rev-ErbA ligand, not a SARM, developed by Scripps Research Institute under Professor Thomas Burris. Taken orally, it binds and activates the Rev-Erb protein, influencing circadian rhythms, lipid and glucose metabolism, fat-storing cells, and macrophages. This increases mitochondria in muscles, enhancing endurance and strength; mice ran 50% longer. It raises resting energy expenditure by 5%, reduces fat storage and liver cholesterol production, and burns more fat and glucose. Studies showed reductions in plasma triglycerides (12%), total cholesterol (47%), non-esterified fatty acids (23%), glucose (19%), insulin (35%), and IL-6 cytokine (72%).

The Department of Homeland Security proposed a rule to replace the duration of status policy with a four-year cap on international students' stay, requiring extensions and barring major changes or transfers. DHS aims to reduce visa overstays. The comment period closed with over 15,700 comments. Many higher education institutions, hospitals, and private sector leaders opposed the rule. Commenters argued that international students are already closely monitored, and the Student Exchange and Visitor Information System alerts ICE to overstays. NAFSA noted DHS overestimates overstay rates. Opponents highlighted that many students need more than four years for undergraduate or Ph.D. programs due to emergencies, internships, or program requirements (e.g., five-year B.Arch., over 30 UI programs requiring >120 credits). Extensions are costly, time-consuming, and uncertain, with a 6.5-month processing time; the University of Illinois system estimated needing 13 new employees and over $2 million in the first year. Commenters warned the rule could deter international students, harming U.S. research and competitiveness. International graduate students contribute to fundamental research and fill critical roles. J-1 physicians (about 17,000) fill residency slots in high-need specialties and underserved areas, sustaining healthcare access. Industry leaders stressed that long-term research, such as clinical trials, would be disrupted. A small number of comments supported the rule, claiming international students take jobs and college spots. The Council for Christian Colleges and Universities suggested limiting the rule to colleges with admission rates under 30 percent to address displacement concerns.

The debtors, Jeffery Wayne Smith and Paulette Monee Smith, filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition on October 7, 1997, and proposed a pre-confirmation amended plan. The Standing Chapter 13 Trustee objected, arguing the plan unfairly discriminated against NBD Bank by proposing to pay Chrysler Financial Corporation’s claim in full while treating NBD Bank less favorably, lacked good faith, and failed to apply all projected disposable income as required by 11 U.S.C. § 1325(b)(1)(B). Chrysler responded in support of the debtors.

At trial, the debtors testified they purchased a 1997 Dodge Stratus financed by Chrysler in May 1997, made no payments before filing, and the vehicle was repossessed the day of filing but returned. They proposed to pay Chrysler’s $20,800 claim in full with 8% interest, while paying NBD Bank the replacement value of its collateral. Mrs. Smith participated in an ERISA-qualified Profit Sharing Plan with an anti-alienation clause; she elected to defer a 1998 distribution to a 401(k) plan rather than take cash. The debtors’ schedules showed monthly income of $4,338.90, expenses of $2,422.00, and a plan payment of $1,733.33, leaving a cushion for emergencies and maintenance.

The court addressed three issues. First, under § 1322, it found the disparate treatment of Chrysler’s claim did not unfairly discriminate. The debtors had a reasonable basis, acted in good faith, and the plan likely could not be carried out without full payment to Chrysler given the circumstances. However, the court reduced the interest rate on Chrysler’s claim from 8% to the contract rate of 3.9%.

Second, the court found the plan was proposed in good faith under § 1325(a)(3). The debtors’ failure to initially disclose life insurance cash value was inadvertent, and Mrs. Smith’s deferral of profit sharing benefits was not bad faith given the tax penalties of taking cash.

Third, regarding disposable income, the court required modifications: (a) debtors must submit pay stubs every six months and increase plan payments by any net overtime income exceeding the projected amount; (b) the monthly emergency cushion was excessive, so the plan payment was increased by $75 to $1,808.33; (c) ERISA-protected profit sharing benefits are not disposable income until actually received in cash, so Mrs. Smith’s deferral did not violate § 1325(b)(1)(B), but any future cash distribution must be paid to creditors; (d) any voluntary contributions from the debtors’ income to a retirement or 401(k) plan must cease and be devoted to plan payments.

The court granted in part and denied in part the Trustee’s objection and confirmed the amended plan as modified.

Plaintiff Steven C. Gittens, Sr., proceeding pro se, filed a complaint alleging disability discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act against his employer, Garlocks Sealing Technologies. Defendant moved for summary judgment, serving the motion with supporting affidavits, a Local Rule 56 Statement of Material Facts, and a memorandum of law. The court ordered plaintiff to respond by April 22, 1998, and after he failed to do so, sua sponte extended the deadline to August 24, 1998, warning that failure to respond could result in dismissal. Plaintiff did not file any response, request an extension, or oppose the motion. The court granted the motion and dismissed the complaint with prejudice on three alternative grounds: (1) failure to prosecute under Fed. R. Civ. P. 41(b), finding plaintiff’s total failure to comply with court orders was willful and in bad faith, he had received warnings, and lesser sanctions would be ineffective; (2) failure to obey scheduling orders under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(f), incorporating Rule 37 sanctions; and (3) summary judgment under Rule 56, because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a genuine issue of material fact. On the ADA claim, the court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. Plaintiff alleged a lower spine injury resulting in a 25–30 pound lifting restriction. The court held that this impairment did not constitute a disability under the ADA because it did not substantially limit a major life activity; the inability to perform a single job does not substantially limit the major life activity of working, and plaintiff remained employed in other positions. Even if a prima facie case had been established, defendant articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for reassigning plaintiff, and there was no evidence of pretext or discriminatory animus. The complaint was dismissed with prejudice.

This study investigated Greek primary teachers’ views on STEM education and the conditions for its implementation. A sample of 114 primary teachers (23 male, 91 female) from public schools in Attica, Greece, completed a questionnaire with 26 Likert-scale and 4 open-ended questions; 27 also participated in structured interviews.

Teachers considered the development of students’ scientific thinking very important (63%) or extremely important (20%). The main justifications were that it helps students solve everyday life problems (38%), engages them in inquiry and fosters critical thinking (26%), improves social skills (15%), offers a new experiential/interdisciplinary way of learning (12%), and contributes to knowledge acquisition (7%). Some teachers also highlighted its role in reducing inequalities by enhancing participation of all students.

Regarding fundamental STEM practices, 70–75% of teachers rated problem-solving, group work, making testable predictions, making observations and measurements, using data-collection tools, constructing logical explanations, and presenting results as very important. However, only 7–19% reported that students often have opportunities to develop these practices in the classroom or lab, revealing a gap between perceived importance and actual implementation.

Self-reported teaching efficacy was low: only 20–30% felt effective in teaching science, and 30–40% in teaching mathematics. Teachers expressed insecurity, fear of failure, and a need for equipment and guidance.

Teachers identified several advantages of STEM education: it is a new, attractive, experiential and interdisciplinary way of learning (46%), connects school to everyday life through problem-solving (38%), introduces scientific methodology and technology (32%), cultivates cooperation and teamwork (29%), engages students in inquiry and creativity (29%), and increases interest, active participation, and critical thinking (25%).

Perceived weaknesses included lack of teacher training and limited educational materials (58%), lack of infrastructure and equipment in schools and high costs (42%), insufficient time and unclear curricular placement (31%), and a minor concern about over-attachment to techno-centrism (3%).

To successfully implement STEM education, teachers requested more training (71%), appropriate infrastructure and equipment (31%), more training materials (21%), constant support and guidance (16%), sample teachings and best practices (13%), and more time in timetables along with curriculum reshaping (11%). Interviews emphasized the need for practical, experiential training, manuals, co-teaching, and peer collaboration.

Teachers viewed STEM education positively but felt its introduction in Greece was hasty and disorganized, lacking necessary prerequisites. They saw it as a tool to reduce educational inequalities by offering all students, including those with learning difficulties or disadvantaged backgrounds, opportunities for active participation, socialization, and skill development. The study concludes that successful STEM implementation requires teacher training, infrastructure provision, and dedicated curricular time.

This statistical analysis plan (SAP) describes the analysis methods for a multicenter study comparing dasiglucagon 0.6 mg, placebo, and GlucaGen®. Concomitant medications and current diabetes treatments will be coded using WHODrug Global (ATC level 4) and summarized by ATC class (level 2) and preferred name, with prior medications flagged. The primary efficacy endpoint is time to plasma glucose recovery (≥20 mg/dL increase from baseline within 45 minutes without rescue IV glucose), analyzed in the full analysis set (FAS) using Kaplan-Meier methods and a stratified log-rank test (age group, injection site). Patients receiving rescue IV glucose are censored at 45 minutes. Sensitivity analyses include no censoring for rescue, censoring at rescue time, and a linear interpolation of recovery times. A hierarchical testing procedure controls multiplicity for dasiglucagon versus placebo comparisons across primary and secondary endpoints; GlucaGen® comparisons are not part of the hierarchy. Secondary endpoints include plasma glucose recovery within 10, 15, 20, and 30 minutes (analyzed via Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test) and plasma glucose changes from baseline at those times (analyzed via ANOVA). Pharmacokinetic (PK) analyses of dasiglucagon and GlucaGen® will derive non-compartmental metrics, with specific rules for handling concentrations below the lower limit of quantification. Pharmacodynamic (PD) analysis includes area under the effect curve (AUE0-30min) for plasma glucose. Safety analyses (based on the safety set) cover extent of exposure, local tolerability, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) coded with MedDRA, laboratory evaluations, vital signs, ECG (including QTcF categorical summaries), and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies). The SAP notes changes from the protocol, including reworded primary analysis and added sensitivity analyses. Appendices specify data presentation standards, programming QC requirements, and a list of planned tables, figures, and listings.

The Single/Double offense effectively attacks the Triangle & Two defense by using screens to free shooters from chasers skilled in pass denial. Communication between shooters is essential: when the left shooter initiates the screen action, the right shooter forms the double screen, and vice versa. Options include the double screen option (faking off the single screen and reversing off the double screen), single screen right (secondary shooter uses the single screen), single screen option (reversing off the single screen if the double screen is overplayed), and pop out left (secondary shooter pops out when the primary uses the single screen). If a post defender helps, the screener seals off the chaser and rolls to the basket. Base screen action flows from a point-to-wing pass, with post O4 screening and opposite post flashing; point O1 screens opposite, and if defender X5 follows O5, a lob pass to O1 opens. Side screen action begins when a post steps out after a point-to-wing pass, leading to screener roll, drop pass, or kick out pass counters. Success requires execution, coordination, defensive recognition, non-verbal communication, timing, and experience. Game strategies include scouting opponents, educating players on defensive reads and counters, varying alignments, and attacking the weakest defenders. The Triangle & Two defense uses three players in a triangle zone and two chasers in aggressive pass denial.

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Japanese universities lagged in ICT use for education due to perceptions favoring in-person learning and structural factors. The pandemic forced an immediate shift to full-time online classes. This study examines the developing situation through the roles of MEXT, academic staff, students, and lifelong learning.

MEXT had planned for digitalization, but the pandemic prompted emergency measures, including allowing more remote credits. Subsequent policies emphasized a return to face-to-face classes while sustaining rules for remote learning. A 2022 report did not eliminate the credit limit for remote learning but proposed exceptions for universities with quality assurance. MEXT also launched subsidy projects for digitalization. The Cabinet pushed for more aggressive digitalization, including using "My Number" at universities, which raised personal information protection concerns.

Before the pandemic, faculty use of LMS was low due to preferences for paper-based education and technological anxiety. The pandemic forced a rapid increase in distance learning, but challenges included ineffective communication, practical skill instruction, and faculty computer literacy. Sharing good practices online emerged as a useful asset.

The "substantiation of the credit system" was a pre-existing issue, with students spending little time studying outside class due to high course loads and job-hunting. Online classes led to increased out-of-class learning time via assignments, offering a potential solution, but the burden of assignments was a noted drawback. Experts propose combining ICT tools with reduced course credits.

Lifelong learning in Japanese HE has low institutionalization. In degree programs, university distance learning serves adult learners, and its digitalization began before the pandemic but remained marginal and separate from commuter courses. In non-degree programs, traditional public lectures (Kokaikoza) saw little digitalization, while newer vocational programs were relatively more digitalized due to policy and pandemic impacts.

The pandemic dramatically changed university education, visualizing content and managing learning via ICT. Challenges remain, including addressing educational culture and the credit system issue. Digitalization in lifelong learning is still developing. Essential issues for reform, like non-existing support structures, became apparent. The digitalization is part of a government-wide societal transformation, but sharing digitized student records with external entities entails risks requiring careful discussion on protecting personal information.

The SUSHI study aimed to develop an online version of the Social Inclusion Questionnaire User Experience (SInQUE) for mental health supported accommodation services and examine its acceptability and perceived usefulness. The study comprised a lab-testing stage with six staff and a field-testing stage with twelve staff and twelve service users in one inner London borough. The online SInQUE was generally perceived as acceptable and potentially useful. Both staff and service users found the tool user-friendly and relevant, suggesting it could promote more targeted care planning and improve their relationship. Some staff expressed concern that certain questions could be perceived as intrusive, a sentiment not echoed by service users. An implementation strategy was developed to encourage use. In the borough with the strategy, 27 staff registered and 30 assessments were completed with 28 service users, representing just over 10% of the estimated total. In two areas without an implementation strategy, no assessments were completed, suggesting implementation support is essential. Uptake was highest in supported housing. A logic model was developed summarising the intervention, context, actors, mechanisms, and potential outcomes. The study concluded the SInQUE can be recommended as a potentially useful and acceptable tool, particularly for supported housing services, and that active leadership endorsement is essential for its widespread use.

The NVIDIA A100 GPU, built on the Ampere architecture, features third-generation Tensor Cores that share data across all 32 threads in a warp (up from 8 on Volta), reducing register file bandwidth and redundant data loads. A100 Tensor Core instructions increase the k-dimension of matrix multiplies per instruction by up to 4x, resulting in 8x fewer instructions and 2.9x fewer register file accesses for matrix multiply operations. A new asynchronous copy instruction loads data directly from global memory into shared memory, bypassing L1 cache and the register file, saving bandwidth and eliminating register file storage for in-flight data. Asynchronous barriers work with this instruction to enable efficient data fetch pipelines, and maximum shared memory allocation per SM is increased 1.7x to 164 KB.

The A100 GPU provides a 40 MB L2 cache (nearly 7x larger than V100) with improved cache management controls to minimize writebacks and keep reused data in L2. DRAM bandwidth reaches 1555 GB/sec via a 5-site HBM2 subsystem, over 1.7x faster than V100, and L2 cache read bandwidth is 2.3x higher. Compute Data Compression saves up to 4x DRAM and L2 read/write bandwidth.

Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions the A100 into up to seven GPU Instances, each with dedicated SMs, isolated paths through the memory system (crossbar, L2 cache slices, memory controllers, DRAM), ensuring predictable throughput and latency with fault isolation. GPU Instances are built from GPU slices, each containing a GPC, L2 slice group, and memory. Compute Instances within a GPU Instance allow multiple contexts to run simultaneously, with separate context switching. MIG supports multi-tenant, single-tenant multi-user, and single-user scenarios, and enables vGPU migration between instances.

Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links per GPU (up from 6), each delivering 25 GB/s per direction, for 600 GB/s total bandwidth. All writes are non-posted, and error detection/recovery features are enhanced. PCIe Gen 4 support doubles bandwidth to 31.5 GB/s per direction, and SR-IOV allows sharing of a PCIe-connected GPU among multiple VMs. Error and fault detection, isolation, and containment are improved, especially for MIG and NVLink-connected GPUs.

Additional features include a 5-core hardware JPEG decode engine (NVJPG), an Optical Flow Accelerator for optical flow and stereo disparity estimation, improved throughput for FP16 and FP32 atomic operations (11x and 2.7x over V100), and five NVDEC units for video decode.

CUDA 11 introduces task graph acceleration with reduced launch overhead and improved dependency tracking, an asynchronous copy API that bypasses the register file, hardware-accelerated asynchronous barriers allowing any subset of threads to synchronize, L2 cache residency controls to set aside portions of the 40 MB L2 for persistent data, and Cooperative Groups enhancements including warp reduce operations and asynchronous memory copy collectives.

The DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs connected via six NVSwitches with 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional bandwidth, delivering up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance. It includes Mellanox ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand adapters and a software stack with NGC containers for deep learning, data analytics, and HPC.

The document also describes fine-grained structured sparsity, where a 2:4 pattern maintains accuracy while enabling compute and memory bandwidth savings.

The lecture continues the proof of Freiman's theorem. It recaps Ruzsa's modeling lemma: if a set A has small doubling, a subset of A of at least 1/8 proportion is Freiman 8-isomorphic to a subset of a small cyclic group. The focus then shifts to extracting additive structure from a constant-proportion subset of a group.

In the finite field model F₂ᵐ, a set A of density α does not guarantee that A+A contains a large subspace. A counterexample is a Hamming ball of appropriate radius, which has constant density but whose sumset lacks bounded-codimensional subspaces. However, Bogolyubov's lemma states that 2A−2A (equivalent to 4A in F₂) contains a subspace of codimension less than 1/α². The proof uses convolutions and Fourier analysis: define f as the convolution of indicators of A, A, −A, −A, so its support is 2A−2A. The Fourier transform of f is |1̂_A|⁴. Using Fourier inversion and Parseval's identity, one identifies the set R of characters where |1̂_A| ≥ α^(3/2). The size of R is less than 1/α². For x in the orthogonal complement of R, f(x) is expressed as a sum of a main term α⁴, non-negative contributions from large Fourier coefficients, and an error term strictly smaller in magnitude, so f(x) > 0. Thus the orthogonal complement of R is contained in 2A−2A, proving the lemma. The underlying philosophy is that adding is smoothing, and convolution is smoothing.

To work in the integers, the natural analog of subspaces in Z mod n is Bohr sets. Given R ⊂ Z mod n and ε > 0, the Bohr set Bohr(R, ε) consists of x such that ‖rx/n‖_{ℝ/ℤ} ≤ ε for all r ∈ R. The size of R is the dimension, and ε is the width. Bogolyubov's lemma for Z mod n states: if A ⊂ Z mod n has density α, then 2A−2A contains a Bohr set Bohr(R, 1/4) with |R| < 1/α². The proof is essentially the same as in the finite field case, with the Fourier transform defined using a primitive n-th root of unity. The width 1/4 ensures that for x in the Bohr set, the cosine terms are non-negative, preserving the positivity argument.

The next goal is to show that a large Bohr set contains a large generalized arithmetic progression (GAP). This requires tools from the geometry of numbers. A lattice in ℝᵈ is the integer span of d linearly independent vectors. Its determinant is the volume of a fundamental parallelepiped. For a centrally symmetric convex body K and a lattice Λ, the i-th successive minimum λᵢ is the infimum of λ ≥ 0 such that λK ∩ Λ spans a subspace of dimension at least i. One can select directional basis vectors bᵢ corresponding to these minima. Minkowski's second theorem states that λ₁⋯λ_d · vol(K) ≤ 2ᵈ det(Λ).

To apply this, given a Bohr set Bohr(R, ε) with R = {r₁,…,r_d}, define a lattice Λ in ℝᵈ consisting of points congruent mod 1 to integer multiples of (r₁/n,…,r_d/n). Its determinant is 1/n. Take K as the box of width 2ε. Let λ₁,…,λ_d be the successive minima of K with respect to Λ, and bⱼ the directional basis vectors. Then ‖bⱼ‖_∞ ≤ λⱼ ε. Define Lⱼ = ⌈1/(λⱼ d)⌉. For integers lⱼ < Lⱼ, the vector ∑ lⱼ bⱼ has ℓ∞-norm at most ε. Each bⱼ is congruent mod 1 to xⱼ·(r₁/n,…,r_d/n) for some integer xⱼ. The ℓ∞-bound translates to ‖(∑ lⱼ xⱼ) rᵢ / n‖_{ℝ/ℤ} ≤ ε for each i, so the GAP {∑ lⱼ xⱼ : 0 ≤ lⱼ < Lⱼ} is contained in the Bohr set. By Minkowski's second theorem, the size of this GAP is at least (ε/d)ᵈ n. Properness is verified by showing that if two such combinations are congruent mod n, their difference yields an integer vector with ℓ∞-norm < 1, hence zero, forcing equality of coefficients. Thus every Bohr set of dimension d and width ε contains a proper GAP of dimension at most d and size at least (ε/d)ᵈ fraction of Z mod n.

These ingredients—modeling lemma, Bogolyubov's lemma, and the extraction of a large GAP from a Bohr set—will be combined with a covering argument to complete the proof of Freiman's theorem. The lecture concludes by mentioning the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture as an important open problem.

The document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) to enable guest OS interoperability with hypervisors supporting SEV-ES and SEV-SNP. The GHCB is a 4,096-byte decrypted page, mirroring the SEV-ES VMCB save state area. Version 2 of the protocol introduces SEV-SNP support, hypervisor feature advertisement via a bitmap, and additions such as XSS MSR handling and restricted APIC emulation. Subsequent revisions add support for VMPL levels, APIC ID list retrieval, page state change notifications, SEV-TIO, Secure AVIC, and updated error handling.

The GHCB MSR protocol uses the lower 12 bits of MSR 0xc001_0130 for requests and responses, including GHCB GPA registration (required for SEV-SNP), CPUID requests, AP reset hold, page state change, and termination. Hypervisor feature support is communicated through a FEATURES bitmap.

Non-Automatic Exit (NAE) events are defined for VMGEXIT handling, with required guest state and valid bitmaps. Standard NAE events cover I/O, MSR, VMMCALL, MMIO, page state change, SNP guest requests (including extended and TIO variants), AP creation, #HV doorbell, timer, APIC ID list, and Secure AVIC backing page management. AP booting under SEV-ES uses AP reset hold and jump tables; SEV-SNP allows AP creation via VMSA pages. NMI handling uses a “NMI Complete” message. Restricted Injection defines a doorbell page with PendingEvent and NoEoiRequired fields for interrupt delivery and EOI optimization. The specification also covers debug register virtualization, SMM and nested virtualization limitations, and the SEV-SNP Secrets Page format.

A compilation of news articles from November 17–18, 2001, reports on Enron Corp.'s financial collapse and its repercussions. Enron's stock, which had traded at $82 earlier in the year, fell to single digits, losing about 90% year-to-date. The company overstated profits by $586 million over four years and reduced shareholder equity by $1.2 billion due to dealings with affiliated partnerships that hid debt. Enron agreed to be acquired by Dynegy Inc. for roughly $9 billion in stock, with Dynegy assuming about $13 billion in debt. Dynegy can withdraw from the deal under certain conditions. ChevronTexaco provided a $1.5 billion cash infusion to Enron through Dynegy, gaining rights to the Northern Natural Gas pipeline. Enron also closed a $550 million loan from J.P. Morgan and Salomon Smith Barney, secured by Transwestern Pipeline assets, with another $450 million loan expected.

Enron executives sold significant amounts of stock before the collapse: Jeffrey Skilling sold over $5 million, Andrew Fastow $14 million, and Kenneth Lay at least $20 million. Lay declined a $60.6 million severance package. Employees of Portland General Electric, an Enron subsidiary, saw retirement savings decline and were unable to change 401(k) allocations during a fund manager transition. Some large pension funds, including those in New York, are considering legal action. Investors awaited Enron’s 10-Q filing for more details on liabilities, job cuts, and the SEC investigation.

Enron’s UK water utility, Wessex Water, is up for sale, with WestLB and other parties expressing interest; Dynegy intends to divest non-core assets. UtiliCorp United sought to increase its stake in Quanta Services and expressed interest in buying Enron’s share of a UK power station. Broader market coverage noted a stock rally and bond decline, long-term bullishness on energy stocks, and commentary on the importance of diversification, citing Enron as a cautionary example.

The speaker addresses Cabinet, White House staff, and friends, noting the event is arranged but spontaneous. He says goodbye with "au revoir" and asks them to serve the next President with devotion. He reflects that the White House is not the biggest or finest, but the best because of its heart from those who serve, who always lifted his spirits. He expresses pride in the Cabinet, sub-Cabinet, and White House Staff. He acknowledges mistakes over 5 1/2 years but emphasizes that no man or woman ever profited at public expense or left with more worldly goods. He wishes he could recompense their sacrifices. He states government service offers a cause bigger than oneself: making the nation the world leader to ensure peace and plenty, requiring strength in hearts, souls, belief, and willingness to sacrifice. He urges them to tell young people that not everyone in government feathers their nest; in this Administration, no one did. He shares that his father worked as a streetcar motorman, farmer, lemon rancher, and grocer, and was great because he did his job. He calls his mother a saint who nursed others while losing two sons to tuberculosis. He quotes Theodore Roosevelt's diary about his wife's death, writing that the light went from his life forever, but notes TR went on to become President and serve. He uses this to illustrate that setbacks—failing an exam, losing an election, suffering defeat—are not the end but a beginning. Greatness comes from being tested by knocks, disappointments, and sadness; only by being in the deepest valley can one know the magnificence of the highest mountain. He says they leave proud of those who served, wants them to continue serving if they wish, always giving their best, never discouraged or petty, and remembering that hating others destroys oneself. He concludes with high hopes, good spirit, deep humility, and gratefulness, saying they will always be remembered, kept in hearts and prayers, though they come from many faiths and pray to different gods but the same God.

The standard Shakura-Sunyaev disc model fails to explain AGN variability, including stochastic changes on months-years timescales and complex SEDs with X-ray tails, UV downturns, and soft excesses. The soft excess may arise from a warm corona or X-ray reflection. Monitoring campaigns show optical/UV variability poorly correlates with X-rays, and time lags exceed reverberation predictions. Fairall 9, a clean Seyfert 1 AGN, was monitored for ~1000 days by Swift, NICER, and LCO. Its UV-X-ray lags vary and sometimes switch sign; the soft excess may lead both X-ray and UV variability. This paper uses Fourier-resolved timing of Swift data, employing Gaussian Process regression to obtain evenly sampled light-curves. Time-averaged SEDs from three segments show an increased disc component, likely from a higher mass-accretion rate, while integrated X-ray power remains constant but softens. Power spectra reveal a steep UV drop at high frequencies and a flat X-ray spectrum. Phase-lag and coherence analysis shows: in segments without a sharp rise, X-rays lead the UV with moderate low-frequency coherence; in the segment including the rise, the UV leads with high coherence; in the final segment, coherence drops and no clear lag is detected. An analytic model indicates that the latter two segments are consistent with UV-X-ray linkage via disc reverberation and seed photons, with low coherence from intrinsic coronal variability interference. The segment with the rise requires an additional slow inward-moving component, possibly from an increasing mass-accretion rate. The authors conclude that the inner accretion structure evolves on observable timescales, complicating ensemble averaging for timing studies, and that SED changes should be considered alongside timing analyses.

The paper applies Bacchi’s “What’s the Problem Represented to be?” (WPR) framework to South Australia’s “World Class” public education policy, initiated in 2018. The policy, inspired by McKinsey & Company, aimed to make the state’s system “world class” by 2028, measured via a Universal Scale combining NAPLAN and international assessments. The WPR analysis draws on publicly available and FOI-accessed policy documents.

The problem represented: The Department saw the problem as too many competing educator voices and agendas hindering accelerated change. The solution was centralising information and driving change through McKinsey’s roadmap, using NAPLAN as a high-stakes proxy. Schools were differentiated (ranked 1–5) based on NAPLAN performance, with low performers subjected to greater central control.

Underpinning assumptions: The Department presumed excellence could be bought and that the McKinsey Universal Scale was a true measure of quality. Trust was placed in a “single source of truth” (a centrally produced School Improvement Dashboard) and scripted curriculum materials, eroding professional trust in teachers and principals. Complexity reduction was achieved through simplified, repeated messaging and a 50% increase in Education Directors, who functioned as surveillance mechanisms to enforce compliance.

Effects: The policy marginalised social and democratic purposes of schooling, reduced complex disadvantage to a single number, and forced principals to focus on narrow test scores. After four years, SA saw PIRLS scores decline, PISA equity gaps widen, increased absenteeism, disengagement, and lower retention. The World Class agenda intensified New Public Management quality control, stifling dissent and alternatives.

The authors propose a “Beyond World Class” framework emphasising equity, inclusion, democratic policy-making, professional trust, and alignment with the Alice Springs (Mparntwe) Declaration. They advocate for an iterative, inquiry-based system that values educator knowledge and treats social justice as fundamental to good education.

This study investigates domain boundaries in the distortive polar metal (DPM) Mn₅Al₈. Polar metals combine a polar crystal structure with metallic conductivity; DPMs undergo a centrosymmetry-lifting structural transition. Mn₅Al₈ exhibits a cubic γ-brass (I4̄3m) to rhombohedral γ₂ (R3m) transition at ~880°C, confirmed by XRD, resistivity, and DFT. The transformation produces a herringbone microstructure of rank-2 laminate twins with four orientation variants. EBSD and HAADF-STEM reveal {100} and {110} pseudo-cubic twin boundaries. 4D-STEM DPC and divergence mapping identify head-to-head (H-H) and tail-to-tail (T-T) domain boundaries forming an ‘interlocking Y pattern’. Low-voltage SEM, EFM, and preferential copper deposition show enhanced surface reactivity at H-H boundaries and depletion at T-T boundaries, attributed to variations in local electronic work function and density of states. Surface oxidation also follows this pattern. A chemical sorting of polar compounds in the ICSD identifies 134 metallic polar metals, of which ~20% are DPMs; notable examples are tabulated. The findings suggest that geometric polarization discontinuities influence free carrier concentration at domain boundaries in a metallic DPM, a phenomenon unexpected for a simple metal and distinct from insulating ferroelectrics.

Jane Goodall, pioneering primatologist, died at 91 in California of natural causes. She discovered chimpanzees use tools, wage war, and have personalities. The passage describes stock trading strategies as methods for buying and selling stocks, including ETFs, with defined rules to guide decisions. It distinguishes these short-term approaches (ranging from seconds to weeks) from long-term investing, which focuses on holding assets for years. Numerous strategies are outlined: day trading (intraday), swing trading (days to weeks), momentum trading (following trends), scalping (frequent small gains), trend following (riding trends without prediction), arbitrage (exploiting price differences), high-frequency trading (algorithmic, fast), event-driven (trading on news), sector rotation (shifting between sectors), pair trading (correlated stocks), market-neutral (spread trading), statistical arbitrage (statistical models), technical analysis (using past price/volume data), seasonality (cyclical patterns), long-short equity, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 trading, overnight trading, mean reversion, and oscillator trading. The passage emphasizes that quantified, backtested strategies are preferable, and that automation via algorithms is possible. It highlights the importance of discipline, managing emotions (fear and greed), diversification to reduce risk, accounting for trading costs and fees, and adapting to volatility. Research and backtesting are crucial. Single-stock trading is presented as highly risky for retail traders due to potential company insolvency and black swan events; diversification across many stocks and strategies is recommended. The 3 5 7 rule posits a pattern of three initial pushes, five counter-moves, and seven moves reaffirming the original trend. The best strategy depends on individual requirements, mindset, and goals.

The Dark Cloud Cover is a bearish reversal candlestick pattern occurring after an uptrend or upswing. It consists of a bullish candle followed by a bearish candle that opens above the previous close but closes below its midpoint, signaling a potential shift to bearish sentiment. The pattern is used as a signal for short selling or closing long positions, especially in a rally within a down-trending market. Confirmation can come from subsequent price action or technical indicators like Moving Averages, MACD, or RSI. It is not a guarantee of reversal but a warning sign; traders should consider market news, fundamental analysis, and risk management. Backtesting is recommended, with results varying by market, timeframe, and parameters; past performance does not guarantee future results. Benefits include early warning, easy identification, insights into market sentiment, and aiding risk management, but it should not be relied upon exclusively. To trade, identify a preceding upswing, look for the two-candle formation with the second candle closing below the first's midpoint, and confirm with resistance levels or indicators. Tips: combine with other indicators, wait for confirmation, set stop-loss orders, consider market context, and avoid trading against the trend. Risk management involves placing a stop-loss above the bearish candle's high, proper position sizing, evaluating risk-reward, and not risking more than one can afford. Pros: clear entry/stop-loss, compatibility with other analysis, works across asset markets. Cons: false signals, need for confirmation, limited in bullish markets, subjective interpretation. Compared to other strategies, it is a short-selling approach based on a candlestick pattern that can be combined with other methods, unlike strategies relying solely on indicators. Timeframe choice varies: shorter timeframes (15-minute, 1-hour) yield more signals but more false ones; longer timeframes (daily, weekly) capture larger trends but may miss opportunities; multiple timeframes can diversify risk. The strategy suits bearish markets, trading reversals of rallies in a downtrend, applicable to stocks, Forex, commodities, cryptocurrencies. It is limited in bullish conditions. Incorporating it can improve performance by enabling short-selling profits in bearish markets, providing clear risk management, and fostering discipline. Common mistakes: trading against the trend, not waiting for confirmation, ignoring risk management, overtrading, and not adapting to market conditions.

This randomized controlled trial compared Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) combined with group psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy (PAP) to MBSR alone in frontline physicians and nurses with depression and burnout related to COVID-19. Twenty-five participants (mean age 40.4 in MBSR-only, 47.4 in MBSR+PAP; 72% women; 96% white) with DSM-5 depressive disorder and burnout symptoms were randomized 1:1. Both arms received an 8-week MBSR course; the MBSR+PAP arm additionally received 25 mg psilocybin in a group format after four weeks of MBSR, including preparatory, dosing, and integration sessions, while the MBSR-only arm attended a silent meditation retreat on the dosing day. The primary outcome was change in Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptoms (QIDS-SR-16) at 2 weeks post-intervention.

No serious adverse events, emergent suicidality, or self-injurious behaviors occurred. Attendance was high. At 2 weeks, MBSR+PAP showed significantly greater reduction in QIDS-SR-16 scores (between-group effect 4.6, 95% CI 1.51–7.70, p=0.004, d=1.04), with mean score 4.75 (indicating no depression) versus 2.66-point reduction in MBSR-only. Significant between-group differences favoring MBSR+PAP were also observed for depersonalization at 2 weeks, emotional exhaustion at 6 months, demoralization at 2 weeks, and general connectedness (including connectedness to self and others) at 2 weeks. Expectancy was higher in the PAP arm but was not associated with improvement in that arm; it was significantly associated with improvement in the MBSR-only arm. Mystical experience scores correlated with improved outcomes across both arms.

The study demonstrates safety and preliminary efficacy of group PAP combined with MBSR for depression and burnout in healthcare providers, with large antidepressant effects consistent with prior psilocybin research. Limitations include small sample size, demographic homogeneity, lack of blinding, non-equivalent control experience, and inclusion of participants with prior psychedelic use. The authors recommend larger, double-blind, factorial design studies.

Stripe launched Open Issuance, a product enabling businesses to create and manage their own stablecoins and earn yield on reserves, following its $1.1 billion acquisition of Bridge and new U.S. legislation establishing a regulatory framework for stablecoins. The 3-2 zone defense is a variation of the 1-2-2 zone. The point defender drops to the free throw line, enabling wing defenders to play wide and deny wing entry passes, disrupting zone offenses. It also protects the high post. The point guard may get open shots, but if a good shooter, adjust to 1-2-2 or 1-3-1. The point and a taller wing can interchange, making high post passes harder and allowing the weakside baseline defender to stay for rebounding. The 3-2 zone is effective for fast breaks due to lane alignment. Basic shifts are described for ball positions: middle, wings, and corners. A point-wing interchange option exists for tall, athletic wings.

A storage system comprises a grid formed by perpendicular rails, uprights defining a framework, and stacks of containers beneath the grid. Load handling devices move on the rails and lift containers. The framework includes service means routed via the uprights and grid underside, carrying power, data communications, lighting, sensing, and fluids (e.g., water, gas). Services can be supplied to containers through connectors or non-contacting methods such as induction. Sensors on the framework monitor structural condition, fire, smoke, heat, or gas. Containers may have transparent sides or no sides, and may incorporate heating, cooling, or lighting means. Partitioning can isolate sections of the system.

The ADS9803 is a 20-bit, eight-channel simultaneous-sampling data acquisition system. Each analog input channel can be configured as single-ended or differential, and includes an input clamp protection circuit and a programmable gain amplifier (PGA) with user-selectable bandwidth options. The input clamp tolerates voltages up to ±18V; beyond that, the clamp circuit turns on while operating from a single 5V supply, and input current must not exceed ±10mA. The PGA supports bipolar signals and multiple input ranges, with an antialiasing low-pass filter at its output. A wide-common-mode voltage rejection circuit supports common-mode voltages up to ±12V, configurable for differential or single-ended inputs.

The device uses eight 20-bit successive approximation register (SAR) ADCs, achieving a maximum throughput of 2MSPS per channel. It has a 4.096V internal reference, which can be disabled to use an external reference. The data interface outputs 20-bit conversion data in straight-binary or two’s complement format, MSB first in 24-bit packets with trailing zeros. It supports 2-lane and 4-lane modes with single-data-rate or double-data-rate, and provides a source-synchronous data clock (DCLKOUT) and frame clock (FCLKOUT). A data output randomizer can XOR the conversion result with a PRBS bit or the LSB to reduce ground-bounce interference. Data averaging (simple or moving average) can improve noise performance; simple averaging halves the output data rate.

Test patterns (fixed, digital ramp, alternating) can replace output data for interface debugging, configurable for channel groups. A speed-boost mode allows up to 8MSPS sampling on a user-selected analog input channel pair, while other channels are idle.

The device operates from 5V and 1.8V analog supplies, and a separate IOVDD for digital interfaces. It offers a constant 1MΩ resistive input impedance. Power-down and reset are controlled via pins or register writes. An initialization sequence of register writes is required after power-up or reset, with a free-running sampling clock. Configuration is done through a 16-bit SPI interface with three register banks; daisy-chain topology is supported for multiple devices. An application example for automatic test equipment (ATE) highlights total unadjusted error <0.01% after calibration, fast settling, and use of wide-bandwidth mode for multiplexed signals.

The article examines the options expiration week effect, defined as the week containing the third Friday of each month when US-listed stock options expire. It backtests a strategy of buying the S&P 500 (via SPY) at the open of options expiration week and selling at the close of expiration day (usually Friday). The backtest shows a CAGR of 2% and an average gain of 0.2% per week, higher than a random week, with the effect present only from 1990 onward. Entering at the close before expiration week increases the average gain to 0.3%. Results vary by month: April is the best, while July and January show negative returns. The effect is not considered tradeable alone and may require additional parameters.

The article also backtests performance on the expiration day itself (from prior close to expiration close), finding negative average returns for SPY, with a win rate around 50% and an average loss. Adding a 50-day moving average filter does not make it profitable. The week after options expiration week shows lower-than-average returns overall, with a CAGR of 1.5%. Monthly performance varies: August is the best (0.55% average weekly gain), while September is the worst (−0.94% average loss). The day before expiration day shows poor S&P 500 returns (0.03% average gain), while bonds (TLT) perform better. The day after expiration day also shows negative average returns for SPY. A strategy buying at the close on the Friday of expiration week and selling the next Friday yields an average gain of 0.09%, better than a random day.

Quadruple witching days occur four times a year (March, June, September, December) when stock options, index options, index futures, and single-stock futures expire simultaneously. Calendar-based trading strategies exploit recurring date-based patterns.

The lecture focuses on understanding corporate carbon footprints, using a case study of WidgetCo, a chair manufacturer. It covers the mechanics of calculating emissions, including defining organizational boundaries (equity share or control approach) and categorizing emissions into Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (indirect from electricity), and Scope 3 (other indirect). Data gathering challenges such as aggregation issues, missing values, and unit conversions are discussed. WidgetCo’s footprint varies significantly based on boundary choices, ranging from around 200,000 to 580,000 tons of CO2. The competitor FerretCo reports a much lower footprint (55,000 tons) largely because it uses contract manufacturers, excluding manufacturing emissions from its Scope 1 and 2. This illustrates how different boundaries can make direct comparisons misleading. The lecture notes that most large companies disclose emissions via the Carbon Disclosure Project, often driven by investor pressure, but Scope 3 emissions—especially product use and end-of-life—are frequently underreported despite being substantial. The session concludes by introducing product-level life cycle assessment as a more detailed methodology for end-to-end product comparisons.

This retrospective study analyzed medical records of 1,383 noma patients managed at the Noma Children’s Hospital in Sokoto, Nigeria, from 1999 to 2024 to estimate incidence and describe clinical presentation in northern Nigeria. Patients ranged from 8 months to 80 years old (median 6 years), 54.2% were male, and most resided in Sokoto state (51.3%). Acute noma (WHO stages 1–3) accounted for 67.3% of cases, with gangrene (stage 3) being the most common presentation (59.7%). Arrested noma (stages 4–5) comprised 32.7%. The right cheek was the most frequently affected site (55.5%).

Using the WHO Delphi method, the overall noma incidence was estimated at 114.5 cases per 100,000 population (120.7 for males, 108.1 for females). Annual incidence ranged from 0.2 to 21.3 per 100,000, with an average of 4.4 and median of 2.2 per 100,000. Incidence was highest in Sokoto state (921.9 per 100,000) and lowest in Adamawa (6.3 per 100,000). Children under 10 years had the highest incidence, and a notable increase occurred between 2020 and 2024. The incidence of gangrene (101.5 per 100,000) far exceeded that of oedema (12.4) or acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (0.6). The study underscores the burden of noma in northern Nigeria and the need for awareness and early detection programs.

This study investigated barriers to distance education perceived by 13 faculty members teaching university mathematics education courses in Turkey after the 2023 earthquake forced a shift to online learning. Using Q methodology, participants sorted 50 statements derived from e-learning barrier literature. Factor analysis revealed three factors: Factor 1 (student-related barriers) highlighted low student engagement, reluctance to take responsibility, and distraction; Factor 2 (technology-related barriers) emphasized insufficient access to digital libraries and ethical barriers like camera avoidance; Factor 4 (pedagogical barriers) focused on unreliable online assessment and the incompatibility of distance education with mathematics teaching. No teacher-related barrier factor emerged. Overall, curriculum-pedagogy barriers had the highest average Z-score, followed by teacher, technology, and student barriers. Participants agreed that distance education alone is not suitable for mathematics education and favored blended models.

This patent filing is a continuation of earlier applications, claiming priority from a provisional application. It addresses secure sharing of encrypted data, particularly personal health information, where existing systems burden healthcare providers and have poor patient enrollment. The disclosed system uses client-side encryption keys withheld from servers and cloud providers to achieve zero-knowledge storage. A key hierarchy structure (KHS) includes derived keys (password-based PDK and question-based QDK) that encrypt a master encryption key (MEK), which in turn encrypts data encryption keys (DEKs) and a private key. User data is encrypted with DEKs. For sharing with multiple users, a shared data KHS (SD-KHS) is created with a shared DEK (SDEK) encrypted with each recipient's public key; recipients decrypt using their private key. Edits to shared data require owner approval. A printer driver can also initiate secure transmission of content to another user via encrypted sharing. The system allows password or security question recovery without exposing plaintext keys in non-volatile memory.
