This study examines whether high-impact medical journals disseminate more interdisciplinary research (IDR) than less impactful journals. Using PubMed articles, correlation networks of second-level MeSH terms under the Disease branch were constructed for 1999, 2010, and 2022. Journals were classified as impactful (I) if in the top 10% of the SCImago Journal Rank in medicine; others were non-impactful (NI). To address sample size effects, a subset of NI articles from June (NI-June) was used for comparison. Networks were analyzed using mean node strength, average shortest path length, modularity, global clustering coefficient, and node strength assortativity. Positive and negative difference networks (I minus NI-June) were also constructed.

Results showed that NI-June networks had higher average node strength and density, indicating greater interdisciplinarity than I networks. I networks exhibited higher modularity, suggesting more compartmentalized knowledge. Both network types had similar global clustering coefficients and negative node strength assortativity. Core analysis revealed stable inner cores across time and journal types, centered on topics such as sexually transmitted diseases, communicable diseases, and immunologic deficiency syndromes. Neoplasms by Site ranked highest in node strength and betweenness centrality. At a higher MeSH level, Infections led in intra-community connections, while Nervous System Diseases and Neoplasms were prominent in inter-community bridging.

Difference networks showed a weak tendency for strong differences to co-locate and clustered into topic areas that varied over time. Stronger links in I networks tended to correspond to stronger differences, following a power-law relationship. The inner cores of difference networks changed across years, contrasting with the stable cores of the original networks.

The authors concluded that high-impact medical journals produce less interdisciplinary work than less impactful journals, with cancer-related research as a key driver of interdisciplinarity. Relative prominence of IDR in impactful versus non-impactful journals shifts over time, while a universal core knowledge structure remains stable. Potential explanations include peer-review bias and an evidence-to-guideline pipeline favoring disciplinary studies. The paper suggests accommodating IDR within existing reporting frameworks to improve integration of interdisciplinary findings.

The lecture covers simplified equilibria used in plasma spectroscopy to model ionization and excitation states without solving all atomic processes. Thermodynamic equilibrium (TE) requires a single temperature for electrons, ions, and radiation, with all processes balancing their exact opposites; it is optically thick and rare. Local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumes an optically thin plasma where collisional processes dominate and balance opposite processes, leading to the Saha equilibrium that relates electron density, ionization state densities, temperature, ionization potential, and degeneracy. Corona equilibrium (collisional radiative equilibrium) applies to low-density, optically thin plasmas: excitation occurs via collisions, but de-excitation occurs only by spontaneous radiative decay because collisions are too infrequent. Non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (nLTE) is the general case requiring solving all relevant processes, though the set may be reduced depending on the plasma (e.g., neglecting collisions in a photo-ionized plasma).

The modeling workflow for spectroscopy starts with a plasma blob of given mass density and temperature, determines the appropriate equilibrium, calculates ionization state densities, then excited state populations for each ion, line strengths for all transitions, and predicts the spectrum. If the plasma is not optically thin, radiation transport and reflections must be considered, along with detector response, before comparing to experimental data and iterating. A simpler line ratio technique uses strong, isolated, identified lines to infer the ratio of ions in different ionization states and then applies an equilibrium like Saha to estimate temperature.

X-ray spectroscopy focuses on characteristic lines from transitions between low principal quantum number levels. K-shell transitions are to n=1, with Kα (n=2→1) being the strongest, followed by Kβ (n=3→1). L-shell transitions are to n=2. Highly ionized atoms with few electrons are referred to as helium-like or lithium-like. These lines serve as signatures of impurities and plasma conditions. X-ray filters are thin foils whose absorption edges (K, L edges) arise from photoionization of inner shells, allowing selection of specific energy bands.

X-ray imaging lacks transmissive lenses because the refractive index is near unity. Pinhole imaging uses a small aperture; geometric blurring scales with pinhole diameter and magnification, while diffraction blurring depends on wavelength and aperture size, creating a trade-off. Bent crystals can provide monochromatic imaging by diffracting specific wavelengths and acting as focusing elements. Detectors discussed include film (time-integrated, high resolution, well-characterized), image plates (store energy in metastable states, read out by laser-stimulated fluorescence, reusable), time-gated cameras, and streak cameras (which record a 1D spatial profile versus time using a swept electron beam, offering high speed but non-linear intensity response).

Reverse osmosis is widely used at dairies to concentrate milk, but moving this process to farms could reduce water transport. Researchers from Aarhus University and Arla studied on-farm concentration's impact on milk quality. They note limited documentation exists on how reverse osmosis affects quality parameters like protein breakdown, free fatty acids, and bacterial count, which influence final product taste, smell, and appearance. On-farm concentration leaves milk unpasteurized, making it more delicate. Experiments with reverse osmosis showed no negative effects on bacterial count, FFA levels, or protein breakdown. Concentrated milk was suitable for cheese and milk powder. Milk powder quality and durability matched that from ordinary milk. In cheesemaking, coagulation was delayed about ten minutes, possibly because thicker milk hinders enzyme action. On-farm concentration is practiced in places like Texas. Implementation models include farmer purchase, dairy provision, or leasing. Profitability depends on herd size and distance to dairy; small installations use more power. A play action pass is a play designed to look like a run but is actually a pass, aiming to deceive the defense. The quarterback fakes a handoff to the running back, bootlegs, and looks for an open receiver downfield. The entire offense must sell the run, with the offensive line initially blocking for a run before switching to pass protection. Play action is most effective when a team has established its run game, causing defenders to press toward the line of scrimmage and leave space behind. It is often called in short-yardage, goal-line, or red-zone situations where a run is expected. Some professional offenses use play action on 30–40% of pass plays. Common concepts include the Double Post, where two receivers run deep post routes after the fake, challenging man coverage or a single high safety; and the Bubble Y Over, a spread formation play with a running back swing route and a slot bubble route as short options, while three receivers run deeper routes (go, post, crossing) to exploit vacated space. Play action differs from a run-pass option (RPO): a play action pass is always a pass with all options being pass routes, whereas an RPO gives the quarterback the choice to hand off or throw a quick pass based on the defense's reaction.

The United States appealed a Court of Federal Claims judgment that the estate of Christine H. Roberts was entitled to Public Safety Officers’ Benefits Act (PSOBA) death benefits. Sheriff Harold Ray Presley died in the line of duty in 2001, survived by three adult children (ineligible under PSOBA) and his mother, Christine Roberts. Roberts filed a claim but died months later. The Bureau of Justice Assistance denied benefits, concluding she had not filed a claim and that her death precluded payment. The trial court reversed, holding eligibility is determined at the time of the officer’s death, not at payment, and awarded $250,000.

The Federal Circuit affirmed. The majority (Judge Moore, joined by Judge Newman) held that the PSOBA, 42 U.S.C. § 3796(a), unambiguously requires beneficiaries to survive the officer’s death, not the administrative processing and payment. The statute repeatedly uses “surviving” to modify spouse and child, and the agency’s regulation adds “surviving” before parent, which is a permissible construction to fill a gap. Both parties agreed “surviving” means living beyond the officer’s death. The prefatory language “shall pay a benefit” does not impose an additional temporal requirement. The court rejected the government’s argument that the statute is ambiguous because it does not explicitly state payment can be made to an estate; the statute clearly vests entitlement upon surviving the officer’s death. The agency’s interpretation would make eligibility dependent on administrative delays, which Congress did not intend. Because Congress spoke directly to the timeframe, the agency’s interpretation and its 2006 regulation requiring a living payee are not entitled to deference and conflict with the statute. The court also declined to consider legislative history, as the statutory language is plain.

Judge Prost dissented. The dissent argued the precise question is whether estates are eligible recipients, an issue on which the PSOBA is silent or ambiguous. The dissent would defer to the agency’s permissible interpretation that payment shall only be made to a living payee, as stated in 28 C.F.R. § 32.6(b)(1). This interpretation ensures benefits go to living eligible beneficiaries rather than estates, preventing ineligible individuals from receiving benefits. The dissent noted that under the majority’s view, if a higher-priority beneficiary died before payment, the benefit would go to their estate rather than to living lower-priority beneficiaries, contrary to the statute’s purpose of providing economic support to survivors. The dissent would reverse.

The AEGEAN study assessed apixaban compliance and adherence in atrial fibrillation patients. Mean compliance exceeded 95% at Weeks 4, 12, and 24, and was >94% at Week 48 across all groups, with no significant differences between the Primary SOC and Additional Educational Program groups. Mean adherence at 24 weeks was 91.64% (Primary SOC) and 91.88% (Additional Educational Program), with no significant difference. Adherence declined significantly over time in both groups. At 48 weeks, mean adherence from first dose was 89.52% and 90.93%, respectively, without significant differences. Persistence at 24 weeks was 91.7% and 91.3%, and at 48 weeks ranged from 85.2% to 87.8% across groups, with no significant differences. Fully adherent subjects at 24 weeks were 28.1% and 26.5%, and at 48 weeks approximately 14.5–14.9%, with no significant group differences. Predictive factors for non-adherence in the Primary SOC group included alcohol consumption, technical occupations, and permanent atrial fibrillation (increased risk), while higher MMSE score decreased risk; no significant predictors were found in the Additional Educational Program group at 24 weeks. At 48 weeks, non-adherence decreased with MMSE score in the Primary SOC group, and increased with age and in VKA-naïve subjects in the Additional Educational Program group. Subgroup analyses showed no significant interactions for adherence at 24 and 48 weeks, but significant interactions by atrial fibrillation type and sex for adherence from Week 24 to 48. Safety endpoints were similar between groups. Before Week 24, any AE occurred in 51.2–52.0% of subjects, serious AEs in 12.4–14.7%, and bleeding in 6.5–9.0%; one fatal bleed occurred in the Additional Educational Program group. Between Weeks 24 and 48, any AE occurred in 33.8–40.8%, serious AEs in 11.8–14.0%, and bleeding in 3.2–4.1%; two fatal bleeds occurred (one in Primary SOC, one in Secondary SOC). Overall, 24 deaths were reported. No pregnancies or hepatic/renal safety signals were observed. The educational program did not improve adherence or persistence.

Industry 4.0 is an era where all company businesses depend on information technology, which increases productivity and connects customers easily. In Indonesia, digital startup companies have grown rapidly but often lack good management and business models, leading to losses or bankruptcy. A business model describes how a company organizes itself to get benefits, meet customer needs, and distribute value. The lean canvas business model is advantageous for digital startups to map and implement efficient business strategies. This research used a descriptive qualitative method, applying the Canvas Business Model to digital startups with 120 respondents (founders, project managers, coworkers, customers). Data was collected through semi-structured interviews (primary data) and observations (secondary data), using purposive sampling and triangulation of data sources. The lean canvas business model consists of nine components: customer segment (analyzing specific market segments), value propositions (including newness, customization, accessibility, convenience), channels (e.g., websites, applications), customer relationships (dedicated personal assistance, community), revenue streams (usage fees), key resources (strengths to maximize opportunities), key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure (fixed and variable costs). An easy way to use it starts with determining target customers, formulating problems, finding solutions, defining unique value proposition, determining channels, revenue streams, cost structure, key metrics (KPIs), and unfair advantage. The study implemented the lean canvas for a digital startup called 'Beautiful Memories.' Its problems include limited photo/video/decoration/souvenir packages and difficulty finding providers quickly. Solutions include not offering packages, connecting customers with photographers, video editors, decoration services, and souvenir companies, and cooperating with the best souvenir companies. Unique value propositions are features to find photographers, video editors, decoration services, and souvenirs, plus certifications. Customer segments are couples marrying, families, birthdays, graduations, and official/non-official events. Key metrics include certifications and 10% of each order. Channels are social media.

CoSn2 single crystals exhibit a resistivity slope change below 25 K without corresponding anomalies in specific heat or magnetic susceptibility. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 22 K reveals weak superlattice reflections at commensurate positions, indicating a symmetry lowering from tetragonal I4/mcm to acentric monoclinic C2 with a 2a×b×2c supercell. Angle-dependent magnetoresistance shows a transition from four-fold to two-fold symmetry in the ab plane below 20 K. Phonon calculations confirm dynamical stability of the high-temperature structure, while electronic susceptibility calculations suggest an electronically driven instability that can break rotational symmetry. Polarization-dependent ARPES measurements show a four-fold symmetric Fermi surface under linear horizontal polarization but a two-fold anisotropy under linear vertical polarization, pointing to an orbital-selective anisotropy. ARPES also reveals a nodal loop in the electronic structure. The findings position CoSn2 as an itinerant, nonmagnetic nodal line semimetal hosting an electronic nematic state.

This paper presents a causal Bayesian Network (BN) model for improved diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD). AD is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles, with late-onset (≥65) and early-onset forms, and stages including preclinical, mild cognitive impairment (AD MCI), and dementia. Clinical diagnosis faces shortcomings: many primary care physicians are uncomfortable diagnosing AD MCI, and misdiagnosis rates are estimated at 12–23%. The objective is to develop an interpretable BN that combines knowledge and data to provide probabilities of both suspected AD (having the disease) and diagnosed AD (formal diagnosis), distinguishing between the two.

The BN is structured using medical idioms, classifying variables as conditions, manifestations (signs/symptoms, medical tests), risk factors, treatments, comorbidities, and complications. Key nodes include C: Suspected AD, C: Diagnosed AD, C: Other dementia, C: Reversible condition, and Formal Testing. Signs/symptoms cover memory, language, visuospatial, executive function, orientation, attention, behaviour change, gradual onset, and level of independence. Medical tests include cognitive assessments (MMSE, CDR, MoCA) and biomarker tests (CSF Aβ42, PET amyloid, tau, FDG-PET, MRI atrophy). Risk factors are age, family history, known causative mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2), and history of traumatic brain injury. Comorbidities include depression; complications include delusions, hallucinations, appetite/eating problems, and incontinence, linked to dementia severity via CDR. Treatment nodes cover FDA-approved AD medication, antidepressants, and antipsychotics.

Parameters were specified using a combination of data from the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set (NACC UDS), literature extraction, and knowledge-based judgement. Prior probabilities for risk factors came from census and published studies. The NPT for Suspected AD was manually set and calibrated to a prevalence of 3.336%. Other dementia prevalence was estimated at 2.379%, reversible conditions at 8%, and formal testing at 95%. Remaining NPTs were learned from NACC data, with adjustments for dataset biases (e.g., underrepresentation of cognitively normal individuals under 65) and manual entries where needed.

Internal validation confirmed the prior marginal of Suspected AD matches the target prevalence. External validation through clinical scenarios demonstrated the model’s behaviour: observing symptoms increases AD probability; entering evidence for other dementia reduces AD probability via explaining away; positive biomarkers raise AD certainty; age and genetic mutation combinations yield appropriate probabilities; and backwards reasoning updates risk factor probabilities given symptoms. The model also predicts treatment likelihood and complication probabilities.

Limitations include simplistic aggregation of non-AD conditions into two broad categories, which reduces accuracy and may cause statistical paradoxes. The model relies on data from diagnosed individuals, not accounting for undiagnosed or misdiagnosed cases. Other weaknesses are the lack of certain causal relationships (e.g., age and family history), manual parameter setting based on judgement, and uneven sample sizes in NPT cells. Future work aims to model individual causes of cognitive impairment comprehensively, incorporate autopsy data for definitive diagnosis, expand the model for AD management and non-drug interventions, and develop a research-oriented BN including preclinical AD and genetic risk factors.

The plaintiff, Susan Ann Vansickle, was arrested for obstructing a public highway at the instance of the defendant, a road overseer. She waived a preliminary examination, was indicted, and after a nolle prosequi was entered, sued for malicious prosecution. The trial court excluded evidence of the arresting officer’s uncivil conduct (absent proof the defendant instigated it), a judgment in a later trespass suit by her husband against the defendant, and later county court proceedings that did not vacate the road. The court admitted verbal directions from the county court to the defendant to show his good faith and lack of malice, and allowed him to testify to his good faith and absence of ill feelings. The court refused a plaintiff’s instruction that the only inquiry was whether there was probable cause, and gave instructions requiring proof of both malice and want of probable cause, stating that voluntary waiver of examination and recognizance constituted prima facie evidence of probable cause, and that if the defendant acted without malice under the order and verbal directions he should be found not liable. On appeal, the Missouri Supreme Court affirmed, holding that probable cause is a belief of guilt based on reasonable grounds, overruling Hickman v. Griffin; that waiver of examination is evidence of probable cause; that verbal directions were admissible to show good faith; and that malice is not an inference of law from want of probable cause.

This document describes optional extensions to SEV and SNP for page migration using the Tiered Memory Page Migration (TMPM) engine. TMPM offloads page migration, pausing DMA traffic during copy and enabling migration of SNP-protected guest pages. It supports multi-page commands (up to 128 pages) via a ring buffer. A new Pre-Migration Reverse Map Table state facilitates SNP guest page migration. IOMMU enablement is required; certain data structures (IOMMU tables, ring buffer, etc.) are non-migratable. The PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO command migrates pages with concurrent DMA by updating IOMMU host PTEs, while PM_PAGE_MOVE_GUEST migrates SNP guest pages. Performance guidelines recommend commands with 16 or more pages. TMPM firmware can be reloaded, with family-specific procedures (e.g., EPYC Family 19h). The ring buffer is managed through mailbox registers, with interrupts for completion, errors, and queue thresholds. Status codes indicate success, partial success, or errors such as PM_RMP_NOTEXCLUSIVE. Error handling reports errors in command status and via Machine Check Architecture for hardware errors.

This passage describes a planned randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate Thai cannabis oil in metastatic breast cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. The study will enroll 90 women aged 18–70 at a Bangkok hospital, starting January 2023. Participants will be randomized 1:1:1 to receive Ganja Oil (THC 2 mg/ml, CBD 0.02 mg/ml), Metta Osot (THC 81 mg/ml), or placebo oil once daily before bedtime for 90 days. The primary aim is to assess symptom relief using the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System and quality of life. Secondary objectives include evaluating adverse effects, changes in microbiome profiles (blood, saliva, stool, skin), cytokines, bacterial metabolites, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacogenetics. Soccer position numbering began in 1920s England with a 2-3-5 formation, assigning numbers 1–11 back-to-front, right-to-left. The 1950s W-M formation moved inside forwards back, creating the "Number 9" central striker and "Number 10" playmaker concepts, and shifted the center halfback to defense. From the 1960s, experimentation and Total Football broke the jersey-position link. In 2012, U.S. Soccer standardized numbers for a 4-3-3: 1 goalkeeper, 2/3 outside backs, 4/5 center backs, 6/8/10 midfielders, 7/11 wingers, 9 center forward. Terms "False 9" (dropping center forward) and "Double-9s" (paired strikers) emerged.

The MOVE Index measures U.S. interest rate volatility through implied volatility of 1-month OTC options, referred to as the “VIX of the bond market.” It was created by Merrill Lynch in 1998 and later acquired by ICE. In 2022, it spiked due to rapid Fed rate hikes and banking concerns, reaching 199 in March, with an all-time high of 264 in October 2008. Its average since 2000 is around 85. Unlike the VIX, high MOVE readings do not signal a good time to buy bonds. A trading strategy was backtested from 2002: hold TLT when the MOVE index is below its historical mean (around 86) and sell when above. The equity curve showed linear growth, but the strategy was not super profitable. It avoided high volatility periods, which was slightly harmful in 2008 but helpful in 2022, reducing maximum drawdown by half compared to buy-and-hold. The conclusion is that the MOVE index is a good volatility indicator but not a good trading indicator for bonds; avoiding high volatility is not recommended, though other uses may exist.

The DAWN-plasma study was a randomized, open-label, phase 2 proof-of-concept multicenter trial comparing standard of care (SOC) plus convalescent plasma versus SOC alone in hospitalized adult COVID-19 patients. The primary objective was to evaluate clinical efficacy and safety, with the primary endpoint being the percentage of patients alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15. Randomization was 2:1 (plasma:SOC). Between May 2, 2020 and January 26, 2021, 499 patients were assessed, and 489 were randomized (326 to plasma, 163 to control). The Full Analysis Set (FAS) excluded patients with no confirmed SARS-CoV-2 or who withdrew consent immediately after randomization with no post-baseline data. Baseline characteristics and concomitant COVID-19 therapy were well matched between groups. In the plasma group, median time to first transfusion was 5 hours (IQR 4-7), median volume administered was 884 ml (IQR 807-906), and 80.7% of plasma units had neutralizing antibody titers ≥1/320. Six plasma-group patients never received plasma; 91.9% received all 4 units and were included in the Per Protocol Set. Protocol violations leading to exclusion from the Per Protocol Set included receiving less than 4 plasma units (26 patients) and SOC patients receiving plasma before Day 30 (3 patients). The study was conducted per Declaration of Helsinki and ICH GCP, with IEC approval and informed consent. The trial statistician remained blinded until database lock.

Diversification involves including investments whose returns do not move in tandem to cushion losses. Effective diversification requires considering how assets respond to risk factors and align with financial goals and investment horizon. Common mistakes that reduce its efficacy include: not counting all investments, such as ignoring provident fund balances or stock options, which can skew asset allocation decisions; having too many investments, which dilutes benefits, increases risk from poorer-quality holdings, raises costs, and makes tracking difficult; buying what you don’t understand, which can lead to losses, though limiting oneself to only understood products may create a concentrated portfolio—using financial advisers or mutual funds can help, but investors should still learn about different assets; losing sight of goals, where asset allocation mismatches goals, such as a retiree holding equal equity and gold instead of income-generating assets, or creating an illiquid portfolio that forces loans or penalty redemptions; and letting allocation drift by treating diversification as a one-time exercise, as varying returns skew allocation away from what is suitable, requiring periodic rebalancing on a fixed schedule. Additionally, within-asset-class diversification, like mixing market capitalizations and sectors in equity or credit profiles and tenors in debt, can improve risk and returns.

A new cloud-based distance education platform called UZEP was developed to meet emergency online learning needs of higher education institutions during the Covid-19 pandemic. UZEP uses an Education as a Service (EaaS) model, eliminating the need for universities to own infrastructure, and can be rapidly deployed. It integrates a learning management system, virtual classroom (BigBlueButton), online exam, homework-project, digital material sharing, announcement, survey, and reporting modules. The system was tested by 12 Turkish universities in the Fall 2020 semester, serving over 78,000 users and 11,000 virtual classrooms.

Expert evaluation compared UZEP to Moodle, edX, and Google Suite. UZEP scored highest overall in LMS and assessment features, but lacked social networking and collaboration tools present in Google Suite. Experts highlighted its ease of use, simple interface, fast readiness, and integration with university information systems. Suggested improvements included adding communication/social modules, learning analytics, enhanced reporting, and more exam question types.

Administrator surveys (22 participants) rated UZEP above midpoint on most items, with highest scores for ease of learning/use, openness to development, and team consultation availability. Lower scores concerned attractive features and positive user attitudes. Lecturer evaluations (29 respondents) gave highest scores to the virtual classroom module, followed by assessment and LMS. Student evaluations (111 respondents) showed satisfaction above midpoint but indicated a need for social tools to communicate with peers and easier access to instructors.

Overall, UZEP was found suitable for rapid transition to distance education in emergencies, with an integrated and scalable structure, though it requires enhancements in social communication, exam security, and reporting.

The present disclosure provides apparatus and methods for measuring tissue viability around wounds, such as burns, by assessing sub-epidermal moisture (SEM). Tissue damage is characterized by zones: a necrotic core with low SEM, a surrounding zone of stasis with reduced SEM and edema, and an outer zone of hyperaemia with elevated but viable SEM. Capacitance measurements from electrodes are converted to SEM values to map these zones.

One apparatus includes a substrate with a plurality of electrodes that form virtual capacitive sensors, and visual indicators (e.g., LEDs) to display boundaries between viable and non-viable tissue. A drive circuit, processor, and instructions receive capacitance data, determine boundaries, and activate indicators accordingly. The substrate may have perforations for marking tissue. Electrodes can be configured as virtual center and ring electrodes.

Another apparatus uses a projector and a sensor with a fiducial. A camera tracks sensor position, and as measurements are taken, the projector displays visual indicators (e.g., dots) on the tissue to indicate boundaries between tissue types. A printer may produce images with overlaid markings.

A method for mapping damage involves obtaining capacitance measurements over an area using electrodes, converting each to an SEM value, and marking a first boundary encompassing regions with SEM values below a first threshold. A second boundary may be marked around the zone of stasis based on peak SEM values and a second threshold.

An apparatus for determining burn depth uses a pair of electrodes forming a capacitive sensor. Measured capacitance is compared to a data array of capacitance-depth pairs to determine depth. Alternatively, capacitance is converted to an SEM value and compared to an SEM-depth array.

The disclosure also describes monitoring healing by periodic SEM measurements, comparing to reference values from healthy tissue, and adjusting therapies based on trends.

Systems, methods, and instrumentalities are disclosed for low latency medium access control (MAC) protocol data unit (PDU) assembly in wireless systems, such as 5G flexible radio access technology (5gFLEX). Latency may be reduced by a wireless transmit/receive unit (WTRU) determining network transmission parameters and signaling prior to a transmission grant. A WTRU may receive a modulation and coding scheme (MCS) and resource range prior to a grant for use in future grants. Data blocks may be incrementally created and encoded prior to a grant. Data units may be segmented, assembled, and multiplexed based on data block sizes that allow MAC and radio link control (RLC) processing prior to a grant. Flexible grant sizes and a minimum guaranteed transport block size (TBS) may be provided for early generation of transport blocks.

A WTRU may monitor for downlink control information (DCI), decode a first DCI containing scheduling information for a data transmission, determine at least one decoding parameter used to decode the first DCI, and determine one or more transmission or reception parameters for the data transmission based on that decoding parameter. The decoding parameter may include a cycle redundancy check length, an aggregation level, or a subset of resources such as control channel elements (CCEs). The determined transmission or reception parameters may include a quality of service (QoS) level, a spectrum operating mode (SOM), or a hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) feedback parameter. The WTRU may receive a configuration from a network entity indicating a mapping between the decoding parameters and the transmission or reception parameters.

The device features programmable high and low alarms on the analog input with independent thresholds and a common hysteresis setting. The input high alarm triggers when the digital output exceeds the high alarm upper limit and resets when it falls below the high alarm lower limit. The input low alarm triggers when the digital output falls below the low alarm lower limit and resets when it rises above the low alarm higher limit. An AVDD alarm has fixed trip points: high alarm if AVDD exceeds 5.3V typical, low alarm if AVDD drops below 4.7V typical.

The device has three functional states: RESET, ACQ, and CONV. The RST pin can issue an application reset or power-on reset. In ACQ state, the device acquires the input signal. A rising edge on CONVST/CS starts conversion (CONV state), which uses an internal clock. After conversion, the device returns to ACQ state. The RVS pin indicates conversion status.

The multiSPI digital interface supports various data transfer protocols. A data transfer frame begins with a falling CONVST/CS edge, during which data is shifted in/out via SCLK. The frame ends with a rising CONVST/CS edge. The device uses a 32-bit input-output shift register. Input commands include register writes, reads, and bit set/clear operations. Output data can include conversion results, register data, or fixed patterns, with optional appended flags (device address, range, alarms, parity).

Protocols for configuring the device are SPI-00-S, SPI-01-S, SPI-10-S, or SPI-11-S. For reading, legacy SPI-compatible protocols with single or dual SDO-x are available, as well as source-synchronous (SRC) protocols where the RVS pin provides an output clock synchronous with data. Dual SDO mode uses two data lines to halve the required SCLK cycles. Daisy-chain topology connects multiple devices, with all sharing CONVST/CS and SCLK, and data shifted through the chain.

The device has nine configuration registers, including DEVICE_ID_REG, RST_PWRCTL_REG, SDI_CTL_REG, SDO_CTL_REG, DATAOUT_CTL_REG, RANGE_SEL_REG, ALARM_REG, ALARM_H_TH_REG, and ALARM_L_TH_REG. These control reset behavior, power modes, interface protocols, data output formatting, input range, and alarm thresholds/hysteresis.

An application example uses the input alarm with hysteresis for temperature sensing via an NTC thermistor, preventing false triggers. Power supply recommendations include decoupling AVDD and DVDD with capacitors. Low-power NAP and power-down (PD) modes reduce consumption at lower throughputs. PCB layout guidance emphasizes separating analog and digital sections, proper bypassing, and short connections for reference and supply pins.

This study investigated the capacity of diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps to predict pTERT mutation status in glioblastoma (GBM) using a ResNet deep learning model, compared to conventional structural MRI. A total of 266 GBM patients were retrospectively included, with DWI available for 147. ResNet models were trained on different MRI modalities (T1WI, T2WI, CE-T1, DWI, ADC) and combinations, using various regions of interest (entire tumor, tumor core, enhanced tumor). Clinical characteristics (age, necrosis volume, tumor location) were also analyzed.

Conventional structural MRI models achieved low predictive accuracy (around 50–52%, AUC 0.527–0.571). DWI alone yielded 54.58% accuracy (AUC 0.626), while ADC map reached 78.63% (AUC 0.865). The combination of DWI and ADC (DWI*) achieved the best slice-based accuracy of 85.20% (AUC 0.934) and patient-based accuracy of 86.6%. Using the entire tumor as ROI performed best (accuracy 85.20%, AUC 0.934), outperforming tumor core and enhanced tumor ROIs. Clinical characteristics alone had a prediction accuracy of 70.91% (AUC 0.735), and adding them to the DWI* model did not improve performance. The study concluded that DWI techniques, particularly DWI combined with ADC maps, provide significant value for non-invasive prediction of pTERT mutation in GBM, and the whole tumor ROI offers the best predictive capacity.

In this automobile accident case, the Colorado Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for Shelter Mutual Insurance Company, declaring it had no obligation to make uninsured motorist payments beyond $100,000. Breit was injured by a third party, received $100,000 from that party's insurer, and sought an additional $100,000 from Shelter under two policies each providing $100,000 underinsurance coverage. Damages exceeded $200,000. Shelter refused, relying on anti-stacking provisions. The court held that the policy's "Limits of Liabilities" and "Other Insurance in the Company" provisions unambiguously prohibit stacking of uninsured motorist benefits when multiple policies are issued by the same insurer, following Thompson v. Shelter Mutual Insurance Co. Breit argued that an "Other Insurance" provision created ambiguity, but the court distinguished Compton v. State Farm Mutual Insurance Co., noting that case involved separate carriers and conflicting language, whereas here the "Other Insurance" provision is unambiguous and does not conflict with the anti-stacking clause. The "Other Insurance" provision limits total recoverable damages to the highest applicable limit and provides a pro rata formula for different insurers, while the anti-stacking clause addresses multiple policies from the same company. The doctrine of reasonable expectations was inapplicable because the policy language was not ambiguous, conflicting, or contrary to legislative policy. The appeal was not frivolous, so no attorney fees were awarded.

A Phase I pilot trial in Kisumu, Kenya, assessed acceptability of self-administered intravaginal 5-Fluorouracil (5FU) cream among 12 women living with HIV who had prior treatment for high-grade cervical precancer. Participants self-administered 2g of 5FU every other week for eight doses. Quantitative questionnaires and in-depth interviews were used. All 12 participants completed the questionnaire; initially some reported anxiety or fear, but all ultimately strongly agreed the cream was safe, were confident in correct use, and would prefer 5FU over their previous ablation or excision procedures. All would recommend it. Partner support was high among those with partners. Most had no discomfort with the applicator; all were comfortable using tampons, though some found tampons made use harder. Qualitative findings, mapped to acceptability dimensions, showed participants valued 5FU for less pain, less fear, and ability to continue daily activities compared to LEEP. Education from study staff increased confidence. Challenges included measuring the correct dose, limited anatomical knowledge, and initial difficulty with tampons. Side effects (itching, burning, discharge) were manageable and expected. Home administration was preferred for convenience and privacy, though some faced privacy constraints in one-room homes. Condom use for dual contraception caused partner disagreements. Participants expressed hope and faith in the treatment’s efficacy. The study concludes high acceptability supports further research on topical therapies for cervical precancer in low- and middle-income countries, where access to provider-administered treatments is limited.

This passage describes a protocol for a scoping review on antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome (MS) in community-dwelling adults. Antipsychotics, effective for severe mental illness, cause MS in 40–80% of users, characterized by weight gain, glucose dysregulation, and dyslipidaemia, increasing risks of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Non-modifiable determinants include gender, ethnicity, age, and family history; modifiable determinants include diet and physical activity. Non-pharmacological interventions targeting these behaviours have limited clinical efficacy, and the optimal delivery context is unclear. The review aims to map evidence on modifiable and non-modifiable determinants, describe non-pharmacological interventions, and identify preferred contexts for delivery. Using the PICOTS framework, it will include quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies. The methodology follows JBI scoping review guidance and the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Searches will cover multiple electronic databases and grey literature from inception. Two reviewers will independently screen titles/abstracts; one reviewer will screen full texts with a 10% check. Data will be extracted using a standardized form and synthesized narratively, with results presented in diagrams. A formal quality assessment will not be performed; instead, JBI levels of evidence will be assigned. The review incorporates patient and public involvement, and a stakeholder consultation will be conducted. Findings will be disseminated via peer-reviewed journals and conferences to identify knowledge gaps and inform future research.

Options trading in EEM allows investors to profit from both rising and falling markets and use leverage, but it carries a high level of risk. Risks include potential significant losses from adverse market movements, time decay (decrease in option value as expiration approaches), liquidity risk (difficulty finding buyers/sellers at desired prices), and volatility risk (changes in underlying asset volatility affecting option prices).

Potential profits and losses are determined by the difference between the option's buy/sell price and its exercise price, plus any fees or commissions. The Black-Scholes option pricing model, which considers the underlying asset's market price, time to expiration, strike price, and implied volatility, can also be used to calculate potential rewards and risks.

Common option trading strategies include long call, long put, covered call, covered put, straddle, strangle, collar, and butterfly spread. Long call/put strategies involve buying options expecting the underlying asset to move in the option's direction. Covered call/put strategies involve buying the underlying asset and selling options simultaneously. Straddle and strangle strategies involve buying both a call and a put with the same strike price and expiration date. Collar strategies involve buying a call and selling a put with the same strike and expiration. Butterfly spreads involve buying and selling multiple options with different strike prices and expiration dates.

Leverage, the use of borrowed funds to increase potential returns, can magnify profits and losses and should be used with caution. It can increase position size and thus potential reward and risk. The passage advises against using leverage when starting out and recommends maintaining a margin of safety.

The cost of option trading depends on the broker, underlying asset, option type, position size, and exchange. Some brokers charge commissions or other fees. Option trading is described as complex and more difficult than stocks. The minimum deposit requirement generally ranges from $500 to $2,000, and margin requirements typically range from 10% to 50%, varying by broker and contract type.

Option delta measures how much an option's price changes for a one-point move in the underlying asset. It can be used to calculate potential reward/risk and to adjust existing positions, such as buying or selling options with different deltas to manage risk or increase reward.

The best way to analyze option pricing is the Black-Scholes model, which calculates theoretical value. Technical analysis tools like trendlines, support/resistance levels, and chart patterns can also be used. Backtesting trading ideas is recommended to determine if a statistical edge exists.

Advantages of trading options include profiting from both market directions, using leverage, carrying less risk than other trading forms if understood and played safe, managing risk through hedging, and cost-effectiveness since options contracts typically cost less than buying the underlying asset.

Expiration dates are generally the third Friday of the contract month. Hedging involves taking offsetting positions in the same or different markets to reduce potential loss, such as buying a call and simultaneously selling a put with the same strike and expiration.

Risk management involves setting appropriate stop loss levels and position sizing, using hedging strategies, and analyzing potential risk/reward with the Black-Scholes model and technical analysis before entering a trade. However, stops may work better in theory than in practice.

Tax implications depend on the trader's country; profits or losses are generally reported as capital gains or losses, and other taxes like stamp duty or local taxes may apply.

To select the right option contract, use the Black-Scholes model and technical analysis tools to analyze the option chain. Setting up an options trading account requires selecting a reputable broker with competitive fees, good customer service, a user-friendly interface, and checking margin requirements, minimum deposit, and liquidity/bid-ask spreads.

Liquidity and bid-ask spreads are tighter for actively traded contracts and wider for less active ones. The options chain displays current market prices, bid/ask prices, implied volatilities, and option deltas, and can be used to analyze pricing and select contracts.

Best practices include using the Black-Scholes model and technical analysis, setting stop losses and position sizing, hedging, managing risk, selecting a reputable broker, and being aware of the risks. Traders should not trade options unless they absolutely understand how options are priced, and they should backtest ideas before committing money.

This study evaluated six machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network, Decision Tree, SuperLearner) on a synthetic dataset for pancreatic cancer diagnosis. All models achieved similar accuracy (76.05%–76.35%), but sensitivity was very low. Random Forest and Decision Tree had 0% sensitivity. SVM had the highest sensitivity (1.90%), while SuperLearner had the highest precision (66.67%) but sensitivity of 0.42%. Logistic Regression and Neural Networks both had sensitivity 1.47% and precision 58.33%. The results underscore challenges with class imbalance. The manuscript also includes figures of gene expression profiles in metastasized cancer and normal colon tissues, showing distinct clustering that could inform feature engineering. The authors conclude that improving sensitivity requires addressing class imbalance through resampling, cost-sensitive learning, threshold tuning, and enhanced interpretability.

The Indiana Supreme Court reversed a trial court's grant of partial summary judgment that had barred recovery of survivor damages in a wrongful death action. Preflop hand equities are categorized: bigger pair vs smaller pair is roughly 80/20; a pair against no overcards (e.g., AA vs AK) is about 93%; a pair against one overcard is about 70/30; dominating hands (e.g., AK vs AQ) are about 70/30; two overcards against a pair is close to 50/50 (AKs vs 22 is about 50%); when all four cards differ, the highest card gives roughly a 60/40 edge. Suitedness adds more equity when behind than when ahead.

The all-in rule: with effective stacks below 12 big blinds (with antes) or 10 (without), go all-in if playing the hand. From the small blind, all-in ranges can be wider than from the button because postflop position does not matter. An example shows that if the big blind calls only 25% of hands, the small blind can profitably shove any two cards. The Nash equilibrium for 15 big blinds with antes is small blind shoving about 66.8% of hands and big blind calling about 38.5%. Nash ranges vary by position and stack size; position matters more than the number of big blinds. Suited connectors depend more on stack depth, while Ace-x offsuit depends more on having fewer players left to act.

When facing all-ins, calling with short stacks is often correct because preflop equity rarely falls below 30%, and folding can be a larger mistake. Re-raising preflop should avoid minimum raises; a size of about 2.5 times the original raise is reasonable. If a re-raise would commit more than a quarter of the stack, going all-in is preferable. Calling a raise instead of re-raising can be correct to deny the original raiser the option to re-raise all-in, especially when deep-stacked.

When there are limpers, increase the raise size by one big blind per limper to maintain similar odds. Giving opponents free options (e.g., not going all-in when short, or betting very small) can be a “sucker bet” if they will make mistakes, but generally it is better to avoid giving free options. Examples illustrate going all-in with small pairs, Ace-x, and suited connectors when short; not slow playing with AK when short; re-raising all-in with small pairs against late-position steals; and with strong hands and 20 big blinds, going all-in rather than making a small re-raise.

The device has an active-high alarm output on a multifunction pin. Two alarm types: input alarm monitors ADC input against user-programmable thresholds; AVDD alarm monitors AVDD supply (low 4.7V, high 5.3V). Both enabled by default, disabled via IN_AL_DIS and VDD_AL_DIS bits. Each alarm has active and tripped flags in ALARM_REG. Active flag clears at conversion end if condition clears; tripped flag clears only after ALARM_REG read. Flags update at conversion end, read during CONVST/CS low data frame. Readable via ALARM pin (high indicates over/undervoltage, interrupt host), ALARM_REG, or appended to output.

The lecture covers the supply side of static demand models, empirical results from BLP, Nevo’s cereal market study, and the common ownership hypothesis. On the supply side, a multi-product firm’s first-order conditions can be inverted using an ownership matrix and demand derivatives to recover marginal costs. With flexible marginal costs, any conduct assumption rationalizes the data, making the model untestable without further restrictions. Imposing a functional form on marginal costs allows joint estimation of demand and supply, adding moment conditions that can improve precision of demand estimates, especially random coefficients, and enable testing of conduct models via overidentifying restrictions.

BLP’s random coefficients model for the U.S. auto market (1971–1990) shows that accounting for heterogeneous tastes yields more realistic substitution patterns. Compared to a simple logit, BLP estimates reveal that lower-end car buyers are more likely to switch to the outside option when prices rise, while high-end buyers substitute to other expensive cars. The model finds significant standard deviations on attributes, indicating heterogeneous preferences, and supply-side restrictions help produce precise estimates.

Nevo’s paper on the ready-to-eat cereal market asks whether high observed margins stem from collusion or from multi-product firms catering to heterogeneous tastes. Using a BLP-style model with demographic interactions, he estimates demand and recovers markups under different conduct assumptions. Comparing model-implied markups to accounting data, he rejects the full collusion model but cannot reject own-profit maximization (with or without multi-product internalization). The logit model would not reject collusion, highlighting the importance of flexible substitution patterns.

The common ownership hypothesis posits that large diversified institutional investors holding shares in competing firms create incentives to soften competition. The Ichimoku trading strategy is a technical analysis indicator developed by Goichi Hosoda, a Tokyo-based newspaper writer, in the late 1930s or 1968. Its full name, Ichimoku Kinko Hyo, means "one look equilibrium chart." It defines support and resistance levels, trend direction, and momentum by plotting multiple averages that form a "cloud" forecasting future support/resistance. The indicator has five components: Tenkan-Sen (average of highest high and lowest low over 9 periods), Kijun-Sen (same over 26 periods), Senkou Span A (average of Tenkan-Sen and Kijun-Sen shifted forward 26 periods), Senkou Span B (average of highest high and lowest low over 52 periods shifted forward 26 periods), and Chikou Span (closing price shifted back 26 periods). Price above the cloud indicates an uptrend, below a downtrend; cloud thickness reflects volatility. The Tenkan/Kijun crossover generates signals, and the Chikou Span crossing price confirms trend. Senkou Span lines serve as support/resistance. Traders can create quantified strategies using these components, such as combining a crossover with a cloud breakout filter. Backtesting on various assets with default parameters showed that the strategy reduces time in the market and drawdowns (e.g., MDY max drawdown less than half of buy-and-hold), but risk-adjusted returns generally underperform buy-and-hold. For QQQ, the strategy was invested 63% of the time, yielding an adjusted CAGR of 12.13%. The passage stresses the importance of backtesting and forward-testing, notes that the Ichimoku strategy is not among the best based on backtests, and warns that signals may be inaccurate. Benefits include identifying trend, support/resistance, and momentum. The conclusion states that following the rules avoids much drawdown but often underperforms risk-adjusted buy-and-hold returns, representing a trade-off.

The 60/40 portfolio strategy allocates 60% of capital to equities and 40% to bonds, creating a diversified portfolio. Its diversification relies on the typical non-correlation of stocks and bonds: when stocks decline, bonds often appreciate, cushioning returns. The passage notes this is not unprecedented—there have been nine instances since 1980 of intra-year declines over 10%, and in eight of those nine, the following year had positive returns. Historical annual return since 1926 is 8.8%, and despite average intra-year drawdowns of -7.7%, annual returns were positive in 35 of 42 years. The maximum drawdown since January 2010 was 21.85% in March 2020, recovering in 79 sessions. The article argues the 60/40 portfolio is not dead, as it is based on diversification principles; the problem is unrealistic return expectations. BlackRock’s key lesson is that bonds may be a reliable diversifier when growth slows but not necessarily when inflation rises. Valuations became cheaper (blended earnings yield and yield-to-worst rose from 3.5% to 5.3% by Q2 2022), implying a potential average annualized return of 6.1% over the next decade. Alternatives to the 60/40 portfolio include the 80/20 portfolio (80% equities, 20% bonds), the All-Weather Portfolio, trend-following (CTA) strategies, adding gold, crypto (suggested 1–2% allocation), international equity markets, tail risk strategies, and Thomas Carlson’s “Defense First” strategy. A backtest adding a trend-following ETF (KMLM) to a 60/40 mix, creating a 60/20/20 allocation, showed that the trend-following component recouped losses in 2022, outperforming the standard 60/40 and S&P 500 over the period.

The lecture covers entanglement entropy (EE) in quantum systems and its holographic dual. EE is defined for a pure state partitioned into A and B by tracing out B to obtain the reduced density matrix ρ_A, then computing its von Neumann entropy. For pure states, S(A)=S(B); for mixed states, they differ and include classical correlations. Key properties include subadditivity and strong subadditivity.

In many-body systems with local Hamiltonians, the ground state EE typically obeys an area law: the leading term is proportional to the area of the boundary of A divided by a short-distance cutoff, reflecting short-range entanglement near the boundary. Subleading terms can reveal long-range entanglement, such as a topological constant in 2+1D gapped systems or the central charge c in 1+1D CFTs, where S(A) = (c/3) log(L/ε).

The Ryu-Takayanagi proposal states that for a CFT with a gravity dual, the EE of a region A equals the area of a minimal surface γ_A in the bulk that ends on the boundary of A, divided by 4G_N. This formula satisfies strong subadditivity through a simple geometric argument. In AdS₃, the minimal surface is a semicircle, reproducing the 1+1D CFT result with c = 3R/(2G_N). At finite temperature, when A is the entire space, the minimal surface wraps the black hole horizon, recovering the black hole entropy. The proposal suggests a deep link between spacetime geometry and quantum entanglement.

This study compared group-based and individualized brain parcellations in early psychosis patients and healthy controls using resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project - Early Psychosis. The individualized parcellation algorithm (GPIP) reallocated on average 42.56% of vertices to different regions, preserving the same regions across individuals while adjusting borders, shapes, and sizes. Individualized parcellations yielded higher functional homogeneity than group-based ones, with a small but significant improvement. Both parcellation methods revealed widespread functional connectivity (FC) decreases in patients, but the group-based approach produced larger case-control differences, as indicated by a right-shifted t-statistic distribution and a significant difference in means. The shift function showed that parcellation type had a greater effect on edges with larger group differences. Network Based Statistic (NBS) analysis identified a single significant component of dysconnectivity for both methods, but the group-based component was approximately 9% larger (2,712 vs 2,461 edges). The specific edges and regions identified as dysconnected differed, with 643 edges unique to one method, and regional differences noted in insula and medial prefrontal cortex. However, network-level inferences were highly consistent across parcellation types, with the control network most affected. Parcel size changes did not differ significantly between groups, but larger group FC differences were moderately correlated with greater size differences. The findings indicate that group-based parcellations inflate case-control FC differences, while individualized parcellations provide more conservative and refined estimates of dysconnectivity, though network-level conclusions remain robust.

This study investigates software engineering challenges in integrating large language models (LLMs) into financial report analysis workflows through a case study at Getinge AB. Two research questions guide the work: (1) primary software engineering challenges, and (2) comparison of open-source and commercial LLMs regarding complexity, performance, and maintainability. Using Design Science Research, the study includes domain exploration, development of a local multi-agent open-source LLM system (Cycle 1) and a cloud-based GPT-4o system (Cycle 2), expert evaluation, and refinement via prompt-chaining. Key challenges identified are high task specificity demanding precise output formats, data preparation from heterogeneous sources, and data sensitivity constraints. The local LLM solution exhibited instruction-following difficulties, hallucinations, and error propagation in multi-agent chains, though it offered data control. GPT-4o produced more concise, professional summaries but sometimes mixed trends, omitted key drivers, or rigidly imitated examples. Both approaches required manual review and were not fully reliable for formal reporting. The study highlights trade-offs between local deployment (control, privacy) and cloud-based models (ease, performance) and underscores the need for improved engineering practices, verification mechanisms, and architectural support for LLM integration in precision-critical domains.

The DAWN-plasma trial was a randomized, open-label, phase 2 proof-of-concept multicenter study comparing standard of care (SOC) plus convalescent plasma versus SOC alone in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Between May 2020 and January 2021, 483 patients were randomized 2:1 (320 plasma, 163 control) after exclusions. The intervention consisted of 4 units of convalescent plasma (total 800–1000 mL) with high neutralizing antibody titers (≥1/160, 80.7% of units ≥1/320), administered early (median time to first transfusion 5 hours). The primary endpoint—proportion of patients alive and free of mechanical ventilation at Day 15—was not different between groups (plasma: 83.7% vs control: 84.1%; odds ratio 0.99, p=0.976). No statistically significant differences were found in any secondary endpoints (clinical status, time to improvement, mortality, etc.). Adverse event rates were similar (28.13% plasma vs 30.06% control), with fatal AEs in 10.31% vs 9.82% and SAEs in 20.63% vs 20.86%. Transfusion-related side effects occurred in 6.0% of the plasma group. The trial concluded that early administration of high-titer convalescent plasma did not alter the natural course of COVID-19 in hospitalized patients.

A proof-of-principle study investigated whether deep-sequencing of DNA from saliva and plasma liquid biopsies could detect cancer gene mutations in Fanconi anemia (FA) patients before clinical diagnosis of oral potentially malignant lesions (OPMLs) or oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Sixteen FA patients without prior solid or blood malignancies were enrolled in a prospective longitudinal study. Saliva and plasma samples were collected repeatedly, and DNA was analyzed using the Oncomine Pan-Cancer Cell-Free Assay targeting 52 genes. Non-synonymous small variants were found in 15 samples from 9 patients, with TP53 being the most frequently mutated gene. Among 14 patients with clinical follow-up, 6 of 7 who developed lesions or carcinomas had at least one liquid biopsy sample with a mutation detected before clinical diagnosis (lead times 23–630 days). No mutations were found in samples from 5 of 7 patients who remained lesion/tumor-free. The presence of a mutation was significantly associated with higher risk of developing oral lesions or carcinomas, with a diagnostic accuracy of 92% (sensitivity 86%, specificity 100%). The study suggests that mutation analysis of saliva and plasma can stratify FA patients into risk groups for OPMLs and OSCC.

The study lasted up to 26 months for participants, with the entire study taking about 33 months and ending in February 2023. BNT162b2 was 95% effective in preventing COVID-19 from 7 days after Dose 2 to the end of the monitoring period (03 December 2020), regardless of past infection. Immune response assessments showed that a booster dose of BNT162b2 produced immune responses against the original COVID-19 strain similar to those after Dose 2, and a booster of BNT162b2SA produced responses against the Beta variant comparable to responses against the original strain after Dose 2. In participants without prior BNT162b2, two doses of BNT162b2SA induced immune responses against the Beta variant as good as those against the original strain after two doses of BNT162b2.

In Phase 1, a few participants had a temporary drop in lymphocytes 1–3 days after Dose 1, which resolved by 6–8 days. Injection site reactions (redness, swelling, pain) were common, mostly mild or moderate, with pain being the most frequent. Systemic events (fever, tiredness, headache, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle/joint pain) were also common, mostly mild or moderate, with tiredness and headache most frequent. These reactions were well tolerated and short-lived.

Within 1 month after Dose 2 or booster doses, BNT162b2 30 µg was well tolerated. Few participants left the blinded part of Phase 2/3 due to medical problems (less than 1% in both BNT162b2 and placebo groups). Commonly reported medical problems included injection site reactions and systemic events. No single medical problem occurred in more than 1% of participants aged 12–15 years. In those aged 16 years and older, nausea occurred in 1% of BNT162b2 recipients.

Serious medical problems were infrequent. In Phase 1, two participants had serious problems (inflamed appendix, inflamed nerves), not considered vaccine-related. In Phase 2/3, few participants had serious problems; some were considered possibly related to BNT162b2, including numbness/tingling of arms/legs, portal vein clot, and mini stroke. No single serious problem occurred in at least 1% of any group. In booster groups, serious problems were rare and not considered vaccine-related.

Deaths occurred in 85 of 23,141 participants who received BNT162b2 at the start, 62 of 21,371 who received placebo then BNT162b2, and 23 of 23,141 who received placebo only before unblinding. Researchers did not attribute any deaths to BNT162b2. No deaths occurred among those who received BNT162b2SA without prior BNT162b2.

The passage compares value and growth investing strategies. Value investing involves buying undervalued stocks with strong fundamentals, aiming for long-term appreciation and income, and is generally considered less risky with lower returns. Growth investing focuses on stocks with high future growth potential regardless of current valuation, targeting short-term gains but carrying higher risk and volatility. Backtesting applies strategies to historical data to assess performance and identify an optimal mix. Backtests of specific ETFs from 2000/2001 showed growth outperforming value, but longer-term data since 1926 indicates value significantly outperformed growth (1,344,600% vs. 626,600%), with recent growth outperformance described as an anomaly. Risk, measured as volatility, is highest for small-cap high-volatility stocks. A rotation strategy that switches between value and growth based on momentum (using a ratio and two moving averages) was backtested from 2000 and produced higher returns with lower volatility and drawdown than either factor alone. The conclusion states that historically value outperforms growth, but the rotation strategy is superior.

The SM doubles FP32 throughput by enabling FP32 on both datapaths, achieving up to 30 TFLOPS in RTX 3080. Second-generation RT Cores double ray/triangle intersection rate (58 RT TFLOPS) and add an Interpolate Triangle Position unit for hardware-accelerated ray-traced motion blur, up to 8x faster than Turing. Concurrent RT and graphics/compute workloads are supported. Third-generation Tensor Cores deliver up to 238 sparse Tensor TFLOPS in RTX 3080, support TF32 and BF16, and introduce fine-grained structured sparsity (2:4 pattern) that doubles throughput for sparse matrices. Products include GeForce RTX 3090 (GA102, 10496 CUDA Cores, 24GB GDDR6X, 8K gaming), RTX 3080 (GA102, 8704 CUDA Cores, 10GB GDDR6X, 2x RTX 2080 performance), RTX 3070 (GA104, 5888 CUDA Cores, 8GB GDDR6, faster than RTX 2080 Ti). Professional GPUs: NVIDIA RTX A6000 (GA102, 10752 CUDA Cores, 48GB GDDR6, NVLink scalable to 96GB) and NVIDIA A40 data center GPU (same core counts, passive cooling, virtual GPU support). Pollen gathered by honeybees contains antimicrobial-producing bacteria, specifically Streptomyces, that protect hives against disease. DNA analysis showed the same or closely related species occurred in both sources, with 72% belonging to Streptomyces. Competition assays demonstrated these bacteria inhibited the mold causing stonebrood and two bacterial honeybee pathogens. Genomic evidence confirmed the bacteria are endophytes that colonize plant tissue. The findings suggest these natural antibiotics could lead to ecofriendly treatments by introducing beneficial bacteria into hives, and that plant diversity supports a greater variety of protective endophytes for bees.

The court addressed three issues on summary judgment in a dispute between the Kays (guarantors) and CIT (lender/factor) over CIT's liquidation of the Kays' collateral after their corporations, Top Form and Top Blush, filed for bankruptcy in 1988 and the cases were dismissed without discharge in 1991. First, CIT was entitled to charge postpetition interest on Top Form's debt. Interest continued to accrue during the bankruptcy, and because the petitions were dismissed without discharge, the debt and accrued interest remained obligations of the corporations and thus of the Kays under their unconditional guarantees. Second, CIT's settlement with the EDA for less than the full 90% guarantee of a term loan did not reduce Mr. Kay's liability. The guarantee expressly permitted CIT to release security without affecting the guarantor's obligations, and CIT reserved its rights against other guarantors. Third, the Kays' amended complaint, which added claims based on CIT's reduction of Top Blush's advance rate in 1988, did not relate back to the original complaint and was time-barred. The new claims arose from different transactions and timeframes, requiring different discovery, and were dismissed with prejudice. The court granted CIT's motion in part, holding CIT acted within its rights in liquidating the collateral, but could not determine the exact balance of debt or credit on the record.

The paper proposes an AI-based Computer Science Laboratory management system to address issues of student disengagement, cheating, and insufficient practical skill development in computer science education. The system generates unique programming lab questions for each student based on faculty-provided topic keywords and difficulty levels, using a CodeLlama model fine-tuned on a synthetic dataset of 10,000 ML/AI questions. It includes an AI viva assistant that conducts oral assessments on the assigned question to evaluate conceptual understanding and reasoning. The system offers faculty and student dashboards, supports proctored and non-proctored modes, and structures assessment through gamified quizzes, coding tasks, and interactive viva. A server-side evaluation engine uses a fine-tuned XGBoost regressor on SBERT embeddings to automatically grade submissions and provide feedback. The synthetic dataset, constructed with Python scripts and ChatGPT, covers classical ML and deep learning topics, with each record containing an ID, question, answer, difficulty label, AI score, and faculty score. Dataset validation showed high question-answer semantic similarity and diversity, with faculty rating question appropriateness at 4.7/5. Experiments demonstrated strong alignment between AI and faculty grading: Pearson correlation of 0.914, Spearman correlation of 0.892, and Cohen’s κ of 0.69. The fine-tuned evaluator achieved an RMSE of 3.37 and R² of 0.861, with prediction errors centered near zero and most deviations within ±5 marks. Larger errors occurred in sequence-heavy tasks like LSTMs and Transformers. The system also provides progress profiling and analytics for both students and faculty, and allows faculty to override AI scores. The goal is to reduce plagiarism, personalize learning, and produce graduates with stronger practical skills.

The passage defines various offensive line blocks in football. A Trap block leaves a defensive lineman unblocked at the snap, then kicks him out with another lineman aiming for the upfield shoulder to maintain inside leverage. Base blocks are 1-on-1 blocks requiring inside leverage, used in run and pass. Reach blocks establish outside leverage on a frontside defender by targeting the far shoulder with a 45-degree drop step, used on perimeter runs. Down blocks are angle blocks on an inside defender on the frontside, using favorable pre-snap leverage and a 45-degree step to the near shoulder. Log blocks occur when a pulling lineman seals a defender inside to the frontside, either as a reaction to a failed kick out or pre-determined, with the ball going outside. A Pull is when a blocker moves from one position around another to gain a numbers or leverage advantage. Veer blocks involve a drop step and rip through to climb to the second level, used in triple option with wide splits. Combo blocks involve two players blocking a first-level defender to a second-level defender, with eyes on the second level. Drive blocks are one-on-one run blocks driving a defender off the line with inside leverage. Double Team blocks are the first part of a combo, with a post player and trail player working together to overpower a defender. Scoop blocks are backside combo blocks aiming for far-point leverage on both levels, using post-trail principles. Cut blocks involve diving at a defender's legs to get them down or hands down, often for quick passes. Crack blocks are when a perimeter player comes back to block an interior defender, used on perimeter runs or screens. Kick Out blocks are similar to trap but wider, traveling across a gap to an edge defender to create a C-gap lane; if wrong-armed, it becomes a log block.

The passage presents a DFT+DMFT study incorporating non-local self-energy corrections for itinerant magnets. The formalism uses a multi-orbital Hubbard model and an expression for the non-local self-energy that includes charge and spin fluctuation contributions. Numerical results are reported for α-iron, CrO₂, CrTe₂, and CrSb. For iron and CrO₂, near the Curie temperature, DMFT spectral density resembles the non-magnetic DFT band structure, while adding non-local corrections induces band splitting that qualitatively matches the ferromagnetic DFT bands, driven by non-local spin fluctuations. For CrTe₂ and CrSb, with d-state filling closer to half-filling, strong band splitting already occurs in DFT+DMFT due to large local susceptibility; non-local corrections produce only minor changes. The resulting split bands are dispersive, carry partial spectral weight, and lack definite spin polarization. They are expected to affect transport properties and be highly sensitive to magnetic fields, potentially allowing spin-polarization control with weak fields. The density-density approximation overestimates magnetic transition temperatures, and extending the approach to SU(2) symmetric Hund interaction is suggested for future work.

The Triangle Game is an inside-oriented offense featuring wing shooters and heavy screening. Options include a back screen for a lob pass after a base screen or skip pass, skip passes to the opposite wing, and back door cuts against overplay (with a flash to the free throw line or a weakside lob). Proper execution of baseline screens is stressed, with both screener and receiver setting up the screen.

Reads and counters address post defense: if the defender plays low, the post goes over the screen; if high, the post goes under. On a switch, mismatches are exploited inside (post-up against smaller defender) or outside (clear-out for one-on-one). Against "show & recover," the screener slips to the basket. When fronted, the post seals and receives a lob, or a ball reversal is used. Post isolation reads include: high side denial leads to a power lay-up; baseline side denial to a baby hook; defender behind to a face-up triple threat; fronting to a lob; double teams to a release to the elbow or short corner. Crunch time specials include Stagger Pop, Double Base Cross Screen, Point One-On-One Isolation, Single Double Screen, and Side Screen actions. Tex Winter's "line of deployment" concept aids in reading defensive post positioning.

AMD provides performance guidelines for the TMPM engine: commands with 16 or more pages yield higher bandwidth, with maximum performance at 128 pages per command. The ring buffer should be kept ahead of engine processing, and interrupts should be requested at the end of command sequences rather than per command. Certain data structures do not support migration, including IOMMU memory data structures accessed via SPA, IOMMU page tables for vIOMMU Private Address Space, vIOMMU pinned backing storage buffers, and the Ring Buffer and argument pages. The HV/OS must not issue page migration commands for these. For PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO, source pages must be DMA-mapped using IOMMU host page tables, with only one IOMMU host page table per system physical page; a host page table virtual address (HPTVA) is constructed to map the memory containing those IOMMU host page tables. The TMPM engine may modify IOMMU host page table entries non-atomically and may set Access and Dirty bits; host software must avoid concurrent modifications.

TMPM firmware reload cannot occur during in-flight operations. The HV/OS must pause operations, tear down the ring buffer, disable PAGEMIGRATION_EN bits, and issue a reload command via the BIOS to PSP mailbox protocol. The ring buffer must be uninitialized, or an error is returned. The reload firmware version must be the same or greater. Reload capability is determined by executing PM_GET_CAPABILITIES and checking FW_VER_Major; for EPYC Family 19h, this value is 71 decimal. The reload process involves placing the firmware image and a reload firmware header in system memory, then following a register-based algorithm.

The ring buffer uses DEFAULT or HV_FIXED pages and can hold 256 commands per page. Each command contains a parameter page with 1–128 migration entries. SPAs must be 4k aligned, except host page table entry addresses which are 8-byte aligned. Initialization requires checking ENGINE_READY, setting the ring buffer SPA (4k-aligned, 1–255 contiguous pages), configuring NUM_PAGES and QThreshold, setting WritePtr to zero, hooking interrupts, and setting DRIVER_INITIALIZED. Completion is indicated by DRIVER_INIT_COMPLETE. Shutdown involves waiting for queue empty or paused state, clearing DRIVER_INITIALIZED, and cleanup. The ring buffer can be paused/resumed via the PAUSE bit. Interrupts share one x86 signal and include RBWritePtr_Err (tail pointer out of range), RBMem_Err (command read error), queue empty, queue threshold, interrupt on error, and interrupt on completion. Precise halting requires the target command to be the last in the queue.

Commands include PM_GET_CAPABILITIES (returns capabilities and version), PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO (moves hypervisor-owned pages, updates IOMMU host PTEs, requires CPU TLB shootdown and handling of ATS devices if present), PM_PAGE_MOVE_GUEST (moves SNP guest pages between specific states, requires exclusive RMP access and matching page sizes), and PM_NOP (marks end of command sequences). Errors are reported in command status, migration list entries, PM_STATUS register, or via MCA. Hardware errors during batch processing may render pages unrecoverable, and the system may eventually cease to function.
