A system and method for real-time determination of material strength and depth control during tissue penetration are described. The system includes an instrument with a working tool, a sensor generating real-time torque signals, a controller processing those signals into torque, energy, or power, and a display providing the processed signals. The controller can determine regional material strength based on energy. A motor sub-assembly includes a rotational drive motor, drive shaft, sensor, and motor mount, suspended between a front bearing and the rear motor mount so the sensor does not directly contact the body. An axial drive motor and a guide harp with rods and a distal guide element provide real-time depth control and measurement; withdrawal of the guide harp extends the working tool. Axial force sensors measure forces on the guide harp and working tool. The method involves penetrating tissue, generating torque signals, processing them into energy or power, and displaying accumulated energy as a function of position or time to indicate material strength, or displaying power to prevent inadvertent plunge by stopping upon a power drop. Drilling energy correlates with pullout strength and regional bone density. The instrument can communicate wirelessly with an external computing device for graphical display and user input.

Gap-opening papers, which create topological holes in concept networks, are found to have superior generative capacity compared to other forms of conceptual recombination. Analyzing 34,363,623 articles (1900–2020) from Microsoft Academic Graph, the study models knowledge as evolving networks of level-3 fields, with edges formed when concepts first co-occur. Persistent homology identifies gaps as cycles of unconnected concepts sharing neighbors. Papers are classified as gap openers (0.84% of articles), non-gap openers with novel pairs (new combinations without gaps), or non-gap openers without novel pairs. Gap openers bridge newer, less popular concepts, use more creation-oriented language, exhibit higher novelty, and cite fewer references. Regression models controlling for team size, references, year, and discipline show gap openers are significantly more likely to be top 1% cited, have higher disruption percentiles, and show a positive but non-significant association with Nobel Prize wins. Non-gap openers with novel pairs show no advantage for top 1% citations and are less likely to appear in top 5–20% cited papers. Gap openers receive fewer citations in the first five years but 31% more over 20 years, with higher Sleeping Beauty Index scores, indicating delayed recognition that turns positive after eight years. Gap-opening papers emerge from smaller, younger, fresher, and more geographically proximate teams. The findings suggest that topological gap creation, not novelty alone, drives generative impact, and that short-term evaluation metrics may undervalue such work.

A recent study published in Thorax examined the association between cured meat consumption and asthma symptoms using data from 971 adults in the French EGEA study. Participants were categorized by weekly cured meat intake: low (≤1 serving), medium (1–4), high (>4). Overall, asthma worsened in 20% of participants. Worsening symptoms occurred in 14% of low, 20% of medium, and 22% of high consumers. After controlling for smoking, physical activity, age, sex, and education, high consumers were 76% more likely to experience worsening asthma than low consumers. Body mass index accounted for only 14% of symptom worsening, suggesting an independent effect of cured meats. The study is observational, so causation cannot be inferred; results relied on self-reported data and could be confounded by smoking or COPD. Cured meats may damage lungs via nitrite-induced stress and C-reactive protein-driven inflammation. Previous research also links processed meats to lung cancer, reduced lung function, and COPD.

The authors report an electrically driven polariton laser based on a solution-grown CsPbBr₃ perovskite microplate integrated within an optical microcavity. Single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) thin-film electrodes are used. A two-stage cooling protocol (first to 280 K, then to 8 K under a constant 0.5 µA current) redistributes mobile ions to transform the metal-semiconductor-metal Schottky diode into a rectifying p-i-n structure, enabling efficient carrier injection. Under continuous electrical injection at 8 K, polariton lasing is achieved with a threshold current of 60 µA (current density ~2.8 kA cm⁻²). The emission exhibits strong coupling with upper, middle, and lower polariton branches, linewidth narrowing, and an energy blueshift. The carrier density remains below the Mott density. This demonstrates a solution-processed perovskite polariton laser diode operating under continuous electrical pumping.

The passage discusses the potential and challenges of large language models (LLMs) in social science and AI governance. LLMs can synthesize research data by simulating demographic preferences and behaviors, but concerns exist about bias, underrepresentation, and oversimplified stereotypes; memory mechanisms and in-depth interviews may improve personalization. LLMs demonstrate zero-shot capabilities in stance detection, sentiment analysis, and coding, aiding computational social science, while in-context learning enables task customization with few examples. Ethical challenges include misinformation generation; model alignment and watermarking are proposed mitigations, but responsible use requires multidisciplinary engagement. LLMs might also contribute to novel social theory generation, though originality and validity are debated, emphasizing human-AI collaboration.

The passage then addresses regulatory frameworks for AI. Rapid generative AI advances bring transformative changes alongside legal and ethical risks such as misinformation, deepfakes, bias, and discrimination. Balancing innovation and regulation is difficult, especially given national power dynamics. Timely policies should align with ethical values like rights, inclusiveness, security, transparency, and accountability. Existing efforts include laws in the EU, US, and China, and voluntary industry principles. Challenges remain: a communication gap between industry and government, lack of international consensus, and micro-level risks like jailbreaking that evade pre-deployment detection. The passage calls for partnerships among industry, academia, and policymakers; forward-looking regulations; a governance framework combining top-down and bottom-up approaches; transparent issue reporting; and using social computing to monitor regulatory needs.

The passage describes several container and distributed system patterns. The ambassador pattern uses a proxy container to route requests to sharded backends, broker services across environments, or split requests for experimentation. The adapter pattern modifies an application container’s interface to standardize monitoring, logging, or health checks. Replicated load-balanced services use identical replicas behind a load balancer for redundancy and scaling, optionally adding caching layers, rate limiting, and SSL termination. Sharded services partition data across replicas, with sharding functions (including consistent hashing) to map requests; they can be combined with replication for hot shards. The scatter/gather pattern parallelizes requests across leaves to reduce latency, with sharding for data scale, but faces straggler issues. Event-driven function-as-a-service (FaaS) enables request-driven, stateless processing with decorator patterns for request/response transformation, but has limitations for background processing, memory-heavy tasks, and sustained high load.

Biological sex and gender identity are distinct. Biological sex is determined by sexual differentiation pathways guided by genes on sex chromosomes, notably SRY on the Y chromosome, which is largely responsible for testis formation. A single amino acid change in SRY can cause XY embryos to develop as female, and inserting SRY into female mice embryos transforms them to male anatomically and behaviorally. Gender identity is poorly understood, but cases like David Reimer and XY individuals raised female who later transitioned to male suggest it is more biological than social. While genetic studies exist, specific genes are not fully understood; genes likely play a major role in transgender identity, and some may reside on sex chromosomes. The author believes seeking biological arbiters of gender identity is not a good idea.

The lecture presents a proof of a cell probe lower bound of Ω(log n) per operation for dynamic connectivity, even when connected components are restricted to paths. The graph is an √n by √n grid with perfect matchings between consecutive columns, each defining a permutation. Bulk updates set an entire permutation, and queries check whether the composition of permutations up to a given index equals a specified permutation (verify sum). The bad access sequence uses bit reversal order, interleaving updates and queries. A balanced binary tree is built over time, and for each node, the argument counts cell probes in the right subtree that read cells last written in the left subtree. A warm-up lower bound is proved for a sum operation that outputs the composition. For verify sum, where the query argument is unknown, the decoding algorithm simulates all possible query arguments, using an encoded separator family to distinguish reads from the left subtree that were not in the actual access pattern. The encoding size is bounded using perfect hash functions, leading to two cases: either the total reads and writes in the subtree are large, or the intersection of reads and writes is large. Summing over tree nodes yields the Ω(log n) bound, implying optimality of link/cut trees.

The Simons Observatory (SO) is a cosmic microwave background project in the Atacama Desert with three small-aperture telescopes and one large-aperture telescope. This work summarizes laboratory characterization of 25 production-design ultra-high-frequency (UHF) detector modules for the 220/280 GHz bands. Each module contains 1720 antenna-coupled transition-edge sensor (TES) bolometers plus dark calibration devices, read out via microwave SQUID multiplexing with SLAC Microresonator RF electronics. Testing involved I-V curve measurements while varying bath temperature and cold load temperature to derive critical temperature, normal resistance, saturation power, optical efficiency, time constants, and noise-equivalent power.

Across all modules, average resonator identification yield was 98%, decreasing to 86% after cuts for frequency spacing and SQUID response. Median resonator internal quality factor shifted down by 9% after coupling to detectors, with negligible noise impact. Readout noise peaked at 35 pA/√Hz; 87% of channels were below the 65 pA/√Hz baseline target. Average operable TES yield was 83% (minimum 71%), with all modules meeting the 70% baseline yield target. Median critical temperature was 163 mK, close to the 160 mK target, though batch-to-batch variation existed. Median saturation powers were 24 pW (220 GHz) and 26 pW (280 GHz), with 91% of detectors above the lower target edge. One module was rejected for low saturation power and one for excessively high saturation power. High saturation power and fast time constants limited stable operating range, but instability is expected to disappear on-sky. Median dark noise-equivalent power was 39 aW/√Hz (220 GHz) and 42 aW/√Hz (280 GHz), with 89% of detectors meeting requirements; photon noise is expected to dominate. Median optical efficiencies were 0.62 and 0.63, with most detectors exceeding the ~0.5 adequacy threshold. One module with re-annealed wafer showed low efficiency tails and will not be deployed. Overall, 23 modules met performance requirements, surpassing the 19 needed. Thirteen UHF modules have been deployed in one SAT and the LAT, with six more to be installed in an upcoming LAT upgrade.

This paper introduces the concept of popular dimension to address the frequent nonexistence of popular matchings in matching markets. It studies three classical problems: house allocation, marriage, and roommates. A popular matching is one that is not strictly preferred by a plurality of agents over any other matching. A popular winning set is a collection of matchings such that no single matching is strictly preferred by a plurality of agents over the set; the popular dimension is the minimum cardinality of such a set.

Results are summarized in a table. For the house allocation problem, the popular dimension is exactly 2 for all cases (unweighted/weighted agents, strict/weak preferences). For the marriage problem with unweighted agents and strict preferences, the dimension is 1; for weighted agents or ties, it is at least 2 and at most 3. For the roommates problem with unweighted agents and strict preferences, the dimension is exactly 2; for the other cases, it is between 2 and 3. Algorithms are provided to construct popular winning sets of the stated sizes in polynomial time.

Climate change and natural disasters cause approximately 21 million internal displacements annually, disproportionately affecting lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with limited adaptive capacity. Displaced children risk losing educational access, yet education is often neglected in climate discussions. This study investigates how climate change affects K-12 internally displaced learners in LMICs, examining disruptions before and after displacement.

The conceptual framework combines the Human Rights-Based Approach (HRBA) to education, emphasizing access, quality, and respectful environments, with Education in Emergencies (EiE) research, which addresses both acute and chronic crises. This integrated framework captures direct and indirect impacts, long-term consequences, and systemic challenges.

The methodology is a literature review of 73 English-language sources, including academic and grey literature, selected for relevance to displacement, education, and climate change in LMICs. Analysis identified recurring themes and synthesized findings.

Findings show climate change restricts educational access and quality through physical barriers (destroyed infrastructure), socioeconomic pressures (loss of income, inability to pay fees, child labor), and environmental conditions (heat impairing learning, malnutrition affecting cognition). In new destinations, displaced learners face additional financial constraints, administrative hurdles like registration systems, discrimination, and limited effectiveness of distance learning due to technology gaps. Schools and governments often lack preparedness and data systems. Learners’ well-being suffers from psychological trauma, health issues, and developmental impacts; early-life climate shocks correlate with lower cognitive scores. Girls face heightened barriers due to increased household responsibilities, prioritization of boys’ education, and risks of early marriage, exacerbated by displacement.

The discussion highlights persistent financial barriers, the need for streamlined administrative processes and support systems, and gender-sensitive policies. Research gaps include limited focus on climate displacement in EiE, lack of long-term outcome studies, and reactive policy responses. The study frames climate displacement as an educational emergency requiring proactive, climate-specific policies integrated with adaptation strategies. The conclusion advocates for comprehensive, systemic solutions to ensure educational continuity as a right and component of climate resilience.

The study recorded local field potentials (LFPs) from the thalamus (including VIM and VOP) and accelerometer-based tremor in 34 patients with essential tremor, multiple sclerosis, or Parkinson’s disease undergoing DBS surgery. It found a moderate correlation between tremor and low-frequency LFP spectral power (alpha/theta bands) but a strong correlation with peak coherence between LFPs and acceleration. Postural tremor was decoded from LFPs with an AUC of ~0.7. High-frequency DBS (~130 Hz) reduced low-frequency spectral power, and tremor could be decoded from LFPs during DBS. Computational modeling showed that simulated LFP low-frequency power varied with electrode location, spatial distribution of tremor cells, and the proportion of tremor cells, which may explain inter-participant variability and the only moderate correlation with tremor.

In Mock v. Watson, the Iowa Supreme Court held that a widow’s statutory share of her deceased husband’s real estate is not subject to the debts of the estate and must be set apart free from them. The Code abolished dower but created a new estate entitling the widow to one-third in value of all legal or equitable real property possessed by the husband during marriage, not sold on execution or relinquished. Her interest attaches upon the concurrence of the husband’s seizin and the wife’s coverture, and is not subject to the husband’s control or to charges against the estate, unlike the heirs’ interest. Code sections permitting sale of real estate to pay debts refer only to the estate’s interest, not the widow’s share. The provision forbidding arrangements that prejudice creditors merely prevents the widow from receiving more than one-third. The lower court’s order setting apart the widow’s share was affirmed.

The authors present two all-optical thermometry methods using microdiamonds containing silicon-vacancy (SiV) centers. The methods, multi-feature regression (MFR) and two-stage multi-feature regression (2SMFR), predict temperature from temperature-dependent photoluminescence (SiV zero-phonon line and phonon sideband) and Raman signals. MFR uses linear regression with exhaustive feature selection, achieving generalized accuracy of 1.7 K and resolution of 1.2 K·Hz⁻¹/² with only 3–4 training diamonds and temperature set points, a ~26% improvement over the best single-feature model. 2SMFR employs partial least squares, Lasso regression, and spline correction, achieving 0.7 K accuracy and 0.6 K·Hz⁻¹/² resolution with seven training diamonds and set points, ~70% better than single-feature models and ~59% better than MFR. Both methods evaluate performance on independent test sets to avoid optimistic bias, require minimal calibration data, and automatically select optimal feature subsets. The approach is flexible, data-efficient, and adaptable to different instruments, suitable for practical nanoscale thermometry.

A penalty kick taker is a player who takes a penalty kick, a restart where a shot is taken from the penalty mark (12 yards out) with only the opposing goalkeeper defending. It is awarded for a direct-free-kick foul by a defender inside their own penalty area. Success requires technique, mental fortitude, and practice to accurately place the ball beyond the goalkeeper’s reach.

Law 14 requires the ball stationary on the mark, the goalkeeper on the goal line facing the kicker until the kick, and all other players outside the penalty area and arc, behind the mark. The ball must be kicked forward; the goalkeeper must have part of one foot on or behind the line. The ball is in play when kicked and clearly moves. The kicker cannot play a rebound off the goal frame until another player touches it, but may play a rebound from the goalkeeper.

Coaches must identify kickers before a game, along with an alternate. The fouled player should not take the kick if injured or upset. A designated kicker uncomfortable taking a kick should tell the coach. Developing a consistent routine is critical, covering ball placement, relaxation, run-up, and kick. Kickers should experiment with inside-of-the-foot, instep drive, or instep-face kicks, prioritizing accuracy over power. Preferred targets are the lower corners; upper corners are harder to stop but risk missing high. Other locations include side netting, under the crossbar, or straight down the middle, depending on goalkeeper movement.

Mental preparation involves blocking distractions, using techniques like clear focus, measured breathing, visualization, and self-confidence. After the whistle, the kicker must wait for the referee’s signal. The run-up can vary in length, speed, and angle. Feinting during the run-up is permitted, but feinting after completing the run-up is not. The plant foot should point at the target, body over the ball. Follow-through is essential. After the kick, players must be ready for rebounds.

Practice should be regular, using cones and disks as targets, gradually removed. Kickers should practice with a goalkeeper, receive feedback, and also practice as a goalkeeper. Repetition builds muscle memory. Coaches should simulate game conditions, including fatigue and distractions. Visualization is recommended. Selection is based on success rate in scrimmages or kick-offs.

Advanced techniques include scouting opposing goalkeepers’ tendencies and keeping a written record. Kickers should develop at least two different kicks to counter goalkeeper habits. Changing kickers by having a teammate initially hold the ball can deceive the goalkeeper. The “tap” penalty kick involves a short pass to an onrushing teammate. Coaches should simulate disturbances and ensure teammates know their roles. The kicker is not responsible for teammates’ positioning.

The quarterback is widely seen as the most important position in sports and the leader of the offense. Along with the center, the quarterback touches the football every play. Responsibilities include calling plays, communicating formations, calling audibles, and extensive study of playbooks and opponent film. The main job is taking the snap, throwing to open receivers, and occasionally running. The term originated from the quarterback being a “quarter back” from the running back. Other names include Signal Caller, Field General, Gunslinger, and QB. Body types have evolved from big, strong, tall quarterbacks to a mix including smaller, more athletic ones. Key skills are Football IQ (understanding the game, complex communication, field awareness), Decision Making (anticipating throws), Accuracy (throwing to the correct area for receivers to maintain momentum and avoid hits), Leadership (setting an example, being a coach on the field), Footwork (crucial for passing against great defenses), Athleticism (creates extra problems for defenses), and Arm Strength (important, but not everything; a prerequisite for the NFL). Notable quarterbacks include Otto Graham, who led the Browns to 10 consecutive championship games; Peyton Manning, who called his own plays and won two Super Bowls; Dan Marino, the first to reach 50,000 yards and 400 touchdowns but never won a Super Bowl; Joe Montana, who won four Super Bowls; and Tom Brady, a former sixth-round pick considered the best ever with the most Super Bowl championships. The quarterback is important because he touches the ball every play, and if he struggles, the offense likely struggles as a whole.

Carol Christ, 73, is the new chancellor of UC Berkeley, the first woman to hold the position and the oldest in its history. She previously taught at Berkeley, rising to vice chancellor and provost, and later served as president of Smith College before retiring in 2013. She says she did not need the job but felt she could do good. UC Berkeley faces challenges including sexual assault scandals, a $110 million budget deficit that must be halved this year, a student housing shortage, a fractured community, free speech debates, and low black student enrollment (around 3 percent). A state audit revealed $175 million in undisclosed funds, and Governor Jerry Brown withheld $50 million pending improved financial transparency. Christ plans to prioritize increasing black student enrollment, address sexual assault through cross-group conversations, designate the 2017-18 school year as a "free speech year" with point-counterpoint debates, partner with Berkeley and Oakland on housing and homelessness before considering building at People's Park, and increase private philanthropy and make administrative cuts to tackle the deficit. She aims to improve the campus's relationship with Sacramento and restore community. Christ, a Victorian literature scholar and self-described "child of the women's liberation movement," previously served as Title IX compliance coordinator. She will earn nearly $532,000 annually, will not live in the official chancellor's house, and plans to spend time walking campus and attending student events.

John F. Kennedy accepts the Democratic nomination for President, expressing gratitude to Adlai Stevenson, running mate Lyndon Johnson, and other supporters. He calls for lighting a candle rather than cursing the darkness, emphasizing the need to focus on the future.

He describes a changing world: shifting power balances, new weapons, new nations, Communist advances, and the threat of nuclear extinction. At home, he points to revolutions in farm technology, urban population, human rights, medicine, and automation that have created unresolved problems, along with a decline in intellectual and moral strength. He calls for a new generation of leadership to address new problems and opportunities.

The findings, published by Doctors Without Borders, have led some facilities to adopt the rapid test, enabling same-day treatment. Mathabire previously worked with Doctors Without Borders diagnosing malnourished children, teaching HIV-positive pregnant women, and treating war wounds in South Sudan. She recently moved to Sweden to marry an infectious disease specialist and is sewing her own wedding dress.

The passage defines options expiry as the time an options contract becomes void. In the US, the expiration date is the third Saturday of the expiration month, with the last trading day usually the preceding Friday (or Thursday if Friday is a holiday). The expiration time is 11:59 a.m. EST on that Saturday, but holders must indicate exercise intent by 5:30 p.m. ET on the last trading day. The expiration week is the third week of the month, during which large-cap stocks with actively traded options tend to have higher average weekly returns (the Options Expiration Week Effect). When stock options, stock index futures, and stock index options all expire on the same day, it is called quad witching, occurring four times a year (March, June, September, December).

The article presents backtests of expiry trading strategies focused on stocks, not options, due to complexity and data limitations. One backtest shows the S&P 500 (SPY) during options expiration week had an average gain of 0.3% per week, significantly higher than random weeks, with only January and July negative. Another backtest on the healthcare ETF XLV yielded an average gain of about 0.7% per trade. A third strategy on SPY, an overnight trading strategy, averaged 0.46% gain. A fourth backtest, a short day trading strategy on SPY that enters and exits on expiry day, had 306 trades with an average gain of 0.18% per trade. The passage also notes that expiry days, especially quad expiration days, have slightly higher volatility than normal trading days. Developing trading strategies involves researching models, backtesting over at least 15 years or different market cycles, and forward-testing. The article suggests seasonality strategies are robust.

The passage discusses the Santa Claus rally, a stock market phenomenon where stocks tend to perform well in the last days of December and the first days of January. Christmas Day is a U.S. federal holiday and not a trading day; the days before and after may be trading days depending on the weekday, and the bond market closes early on the preceding trading day. If Christmas falls on a weekend, the holiday is observed on the adjacent Friday or Monday.

Backtests of the S&P 500 from 1960 show a Santa Claus rally exists. One strategy produced 0.7% per trade, a 66% win ratio, and a profit factor of 2, though recent years had losses. A longer holding period yielded 1.6% per trade, a 72% win ratio, and a profit factor of 4. Another variation entering after December 20 and selling on the first new year trading day gave 1% average gain, 67% win ratio, and profit factor 4.5. Possible reasons include fund rebalancing, low macro news, and holiday sentiment.

Backtests on German stocks (via EWG ETF) showed an average gain of 2.1% per trade, 81% win ratio, and profit factor of 13, though returns declined recently. Euro Stoxx 50 (via FEZ ETF) had 1.5% average gain, 81% win ratio, and profit factor 9, with weaker returns in the last six years. Performance during the Christmas period was significantly better than random periods.

In emerging markets (using FEMKX fund data from 1990), the average gain was 2.7% per trade, win ratio 73%, profit factor 6, but the effect has waned recently. For India’s NIFTY 50 (data from 2007), the average gain was 1.2% per trade, win ratio 71%, profit factor 6. The Santa Claus rally typically starts on the third Friday of December. Most holiday periods show positive performance, but the end-of-year effect is the strongest.

This study uses density functional theory (DFT) to predict three novel out-of-plane ordered MAX phases, Mo₂A₂AlC₃ (A = Zr, Nb, Ta), and investigates their structural, electronic, mechanical, thermodynamic, and optical properties. The compounds crystallize in a hexagonal P6₃/mmc structure. Stability is confirmed by negative formation energies, phonon dispersion without imaginary frequencies, and satisfaction of mechanical stability criteria. Electronic band structures and density of states reveal metallic behavior with dominant Mo-4d contributions and mixed ionic-covalent-metallic bonding. Elastic constants and moduli indicate brittleness (Pugh’s ratio >0.571, Poisson’s ratio <0.26, negative Cauchy pressure) and mechanical anisotropy. Vickers hardness values range from 6.02 to 6.28 GPa. Debye temperatures are 634 K (Zr), 632 K (Nb), and 525 K (Ta); melting temperatures are 2064 K, 2237 K, and 2131 K, respectively. Minimum thermal conductivities are low (0.74–0.90 W/m·K), and thermal expansion coefficients (9.90–11.47×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) align with typical thermal barrier coating requirements. Optical spectra show high reflectivity (>44%) across infrared, visible, and ultraviolet regions. The results suggest these phases are promising candidates for thermal barrier coatings and solar heat-shielding applications.

The arrival of generative AI is fundamentally different from prior educational technologies, presenting both dangers and possibilities. This paper addresses how to employ AI in future educational contexts in a humanizing and ethical manner. It draws on Anders, who argues technologies modify what it means to be human and create a "Promethean discrepancy" between what can be produced and what humans can grasp. Foucault's concept of "regimes of truth" is used to analyze AI as a system of power that can manipulate epistemologies. Freire's concepts of humanization and conscientization are applied, arguing technological adoption is not inherently harmful if it promotes humanizing ends. The paper explores how AI fits within Bloom's taxonomy, noting AI performs better at lower cognitive tiers, and supplements this with Arendt's hierarchy of labor, work, and action to prioritize learning that improves the human condition. The central finding is a framework for assessing AI use in education on a spectrum from consumptive labor to humanizing action, serving as an ethical guidepost for educators. Applied examples, including community-based political action and Socratic dialogue for research, are provided to operationalize the framework. The paper concludes that educators must use such guideposts to help students realize their full humanity and agency to act in the world.

A method and apparatus handle reduced available processing time in systems using configurable or short transmission time intervals (TTIs). A wireless transmit/receive unit (WTRU) may determine processing capabilities, send a processing capability indication to an eNodeB, receive a processing capability configuration, determine a maximum timing advance or maximum Rx-Tx time difference based on the configuration or determined capabilities, and limit an applied timing advance or Rx-Tx time difference to the maximum for a specific TTI length. The WTRU may also measure a processing value, determine headroom as the difference between the processing value and processing capability, and report the headroom based on a condition. In examples, the WTRU may receive a TTI configuration, determine a processing capability based on the TTI configuration and processing criteria, and transmit a report of the determined capability. The WTRU may receive downlink control information including an uplink grant, determine available processing time based on the end of a time unit at the end of the downlink control information and the start of a time unit at the start of a scheduled transmission, and transmit the scheduled transmission if the available processing time is at or above a threshold based on a processing capability of the WTRU. The WTRU may receive downlink control information including a downlink grant and a scheduled downlink transmission, determine a start time for an uplink transmission including hybrid automatic repeat request-acknowledgment information, determine an available processing time, and transmit the uplink transmission if the determined start time is later than an uplink symbol time that is at least the determined available processing time after the end of a time unit at the end of the downlink transmission.

A device includes a processor and a matrix multiplication accelerator (MMA) with buffers for multiplier (1×32) and multiplicand (two 32×32) matrices, and result buffers (two 32×32). The MMA executes a single Load, Store, and Execute (LSE) instruction per cycle, performing matrix multiplication between a row in the multiplier buffer and a multiplicand buffer, with optional load/store of background buffers and operations like += or −= on results. Configurable format components handle data types, a row offset component enables diagonal loading, and a nonlinearity (ReLU) can be applied to outputs. The processor includes streaming engines that transfer data from a level 2 cache according to programmable multi-dimensional nested loops. To execute a fundamental computational primitive, control software configures the streaming engines to stream data in a required order and configures the MMA’s format, row offset, and nonlinearity components. The device then executes the primitive by issuing LSE instructions. Examples of implemented primitives include batch small matrix multiplication (loading multiple matrices diagonally), large matrix multiplication (tiling), matrix point wise multiplication (loading rows diagonally), matrix addition (using identity matrix), small vector matrix multiplication, vector summation, affine transformation, two-dimensional convolution for CNNs (tiling feature maps and filters), matrix row/column permutation, fast Fourier transforms, discrete cosine transforms, convolution/filtering, correlation, matrix assignment, and matrix transpose.

The article argues that scalping trading is a waste of time. Scalping is defined as a trading style aiming to profit from small price changes over very short time frames (seconds to minutes). The article states that almost no scalpers are profitable because they compete against better-equipped traders and institutions, including high-frequency traders with superior software, lower latency, and greater capital. Scalping involves significant stress due to the short time horizon and the need to watch price changes constantly. Automation is necessary for scalping, but it introduces risks like errors and requires self-developed software. Transaction costs, including commissions and especially slippage (the hidden cost of order execution), accumulate and erode profits, making it a major hurdle. Backtesting scalping strategies is unreliable because short-term data contains too much noise and randomness, and backtests rarely reflect real-world execution. The article recommends finding trading edges and strategies on longer time frames, which offer larger profit potential per trade and more robust backtests. It suggests that stocks and indices may be easier to trade than forex. Long-term investing in mutual funds is presented as a simpler alternative with better odds of reasonable success. The FAQs reiterate that scalping is challenging due to competition, market randomness, and difficulty in finding profitable opportunities; finding an edge requires understanding market ecology and mental skills, but high-frequency traders pose significant challenges; automation is required for efficient execution but comes with potential errors and the need for a safety cushion.

LLMs are increasingly used as synthetic agents to simulate human populations and predict social behaviors, with studies showing they can replicate survey results and anticipate treatment effects. However, treating LLM outputs as random draws from a population distribution is misleading because LLMs are not Bayesian inference engines; they do not maintain or update posterior beliefs but instead pattern-match based on training data. A critical limitation is the violation of the martingale property, meaning predictions can depend on the arbitrary order of generated agents, leading to “introspective hallucination” and undermining credibility for exchangeable data. While predictive success stems from massive-scale pattern matching and emergent abilities, fine-tuning and alignment may improve task-specific performance but can degrade statistical coherence, creating specialized mimics rather than generalizable models. The passage argues against a universal “homo silicus” and advocates for domain-specific approaches. Practical guidelines include treating LLMs as high-capacity predictors under explicit conditioning, measuring algorithmic fidelity and subgroup calibration, flagging hyper-accuracy distortion and unnaturally low variance, and using confidence sets that account for mismatch with human data. Constructing agents from individual-level human data improves calibration but still shows heterogeneity. Sampling protocols must ensure independence and avoid order sensitivity. Stress-testing is essential, as agents often fail on novel stimuli, interaction effects, and identity-sensitive interventions. Full disclosure of pipeline details, reproducibility checks, and reporting of failure modes are necessary. While LLMs offer promise for ethically fraught or impractical research, their limitations as non-Bayesian black boxes must be acknowledged, and they should be used as analytic tools for near-term interpolation rather than as universal models of human behavior.

NIST revised its password guidelines, now recommending simple, long, and memorable passwords using phrases, lowercase letters, and typical English words. This study assessed early childhood education (ECE) quality in 71 Anganwadi centers (AWCs) across 25 villages in Nuh Block, Mewat district, Haryana, using checklists and interviews with Anganwadi workers (AWWs). Infrastructure safety was lacking: only 23 centers had safe building structures, 14 had leveled floors. No center had desks, chairs, or mats; only three had lights/fans. Health and hygiene were poor, with only three centers having functional toilets, clean drinking water, and safe kitchens. Learning resources such as books, blocks, puzzles, and play equipment were largely absent. Many AWWs were underqualified: 31 had passed only 8th grade, five had passed 5th grade. They demonstrated limited knowledge of school readiness, curriculum content, and developmental domains. Pedagogically, 63% relied on repetition and memorization. Parental involvement was minimal, and no center maintained child progress records. The findings highlight infrastructure, resource, and training gaps that undermine ECE quality and equity in rural preschool education.

This document excerpt from the AMD Geode™ CS5535 Companion Device Silicon Revision A3 Specification Update lists multiple hardware issues (errata) with descriptions, implications, and resolutions. Issues include: PIT deviation from industry standard operation (read-back command cancellation failure), debug port hangs, incorrect PIT count mode 3 value load, PIC IRR bit clearing delay causing double interrupts with AEOI, DMA rotating mode not rotating correctly, thermal alarm recovery failure due to domain mismatch, PMC Sleep_Clock control disable side effect, GLIU debug pattern detection failure, GLIU error MSR unexpected address flag failure, UART registers inaccessible during DMA cycles, 8237 software DMA memory write from LPC fails, I/O cycles at 10000h or higher hang system, USB over-voltage protection non-compliance, LBARs allowing I/O base at 10000h or higher, PIC fails if processed interrupt still high when clock goes off, ATAC and ACC PRD alignment prefetch hazards, UDMA write CRC corruption after device termination, and ATAC SSMI during DMA not blocking I/O. Workarounds include avoiding certain command sequences, not using debug port, enabling sleep clock at PMC register, not using automatic clock gating, aligning PRD tables, and using UDMA I/O blocking feature.

This email is the final "Friday Burrito" newsletter of 2000 from Gary Ackerman. It reviews recent events in California's electricity crisis: FERC orders, emergency filings, rate stabilization filings, data subpoenas, credit crunch, and high price spikes. He recounts a journalist's advice to write as if explaining to one's mother, then shares a conversation with his own mother, a fixed-income retiree, who voiced concern about rising electric bills rather than underlying causes. He concludes the public is primarily worried about bill increases and suggests the industry focus on adding generation, expanding consumer choice, and ensuring a provider of last resort.

The newsletter covers California political developments. Senator Steve Peace wrote to FERC Commissioner Hoecker, citing a report about Kaiser Aluminum shutting a smelter and reselling electricity for $52 million; a WPTF board member called it an example of demand response. Peace's letter also criticized Commissioner Hebert as a "fellow traveler." Ackerman describes a satirical "Peace Train" with gift items. Southern California Edison CEO John Bryson issued a press release calling for re-regulation, including utility responsibility for power planning and cost-based rates. Ackerman discusses credit problems causing Pacific Northwest producers to limit sales to California due to delayed ISO payments, and notes SCE and PG&E hold leverage as major buyers. He mentions WPTF's past calls to break up utility default customer bases. The CPUC reversed its suspension of PG&E and Edison rate stabilization plans, putting them back on the docket. Ackerman announces an upcoming radio debate with CPUC President Lynch and quotes Lynch's claims that California has 41,000 MW available, plant outages are artificial, and the PX market design pays all bidders the highest price.

On federal matters, Energy Secretary Richardson invoked a rarely used authority to compel out-of-state generators to sell into California and ordered BPA and WAPA to ship power. BPA drafted hydro reserves and PowerEx delivered additional power, risking BPA's own supply and possibly affecting salmon. Ackerman sent recipes for "smashed salmon" and recalls a previous satirical letter about Christmas lights causing grid strain. The mailbag includes responses: Julie Blunden notes the changing demographics of the power industry; Rich Counihan announces the retail energy alliance renamed to CREC and hired a PR firm; Tom Allen emphasizes consumer messaging on competition's value and investment climate; Marcie Edwards says farewell as she leaves LADWP. Micro E-mini Nasdaq 100 futures are electronically traded contracts one-tenth the size of E-mini Nasdaq 100 futures, with the Nasdaq 100 Index (largest 100 non-financial Nasdaq companies) as the underlying asset. The minimum price fluctuation is 0.25 index points ($0.50 per contract) for outright trades and 0.05 index points for calendar spreads; tick sizes are $0.50 and $0.10, respectively. Trading hours run from Sunday 6:00 p.m. ET to Friday 5:00 p.m. ET with a daily maintenance break; CME ClearPort hours are also specified. The all-time high is 16,676.50 (November 2021) and the all-time low is 6,628.75 (March 2020). As of December 18, 2022, the contract traded at $11,344.75. Settlement is financial, using cash to the special opening quotes on the third Friday of the contract month. There is no block trade eligibility. Risks stem from leverage: losses are calculated on the index value, not just margin, and can exceed deposited funds. Factors affecting prices include movements of highly weighted component stocks, macroeconomic reports, interest rate policies, economic conditions, and sociopolitical events. Seasonality indicates better performance in spring and fall than in winter and summer. A trading strategy involves technical indicators, fundamental analysis, and risk management. A backtested strategy (behind a paywall) uses three buy variables and one sell variable, was first published around 2017, and was offered as a monthly trading edge in August 2021. The backtest used daily bars from contract inception, with no risk management parameters. ETFs that track the market exist. Unlike futures, CFDs for Micro E-mini Nasdaq 100 trade continuously without contract expiry. To begin trading, open an account with a futures broker and fund it above the required margin; some brokers offer CFDs. The trading symbol is MNQ.

In these two cases, Toll sought to reopen a probate proceeding and enjoin foreclosure of a trust deed on his home. The property, 820 Detroit Street, Denver, was originally conveyed by Owens to McKenzie by unrecorded deed. McKenzie borrowed from Casey, secured by a recorded trust deed. McKenzie died, leaving a widow and two minor daughters; his will gave all to the widow. Casey found the unrecorded deed and will, and to avoid probate, arranged a new backdated deed from Owens to Mrs. McKenzie, destroying the old deed, and replaced his trust deed with one from Mrs. McKenzie, eliminating the minors’ half interest. Mrs. McKenzie then sold the property to Toll, who paid the purchase price above the encumbrance and made improvements. Toll later learned from Casey that the minors owned half. Unable to restore the status quo, Mrs. McKenzie and Casey entered contract “A” with Toll, agreeing to probate the will, institute guardianship, disclose all facts, sell the minors’ interest to Toll in guardianship, provide funds, and pay all costs to perfect Toll’s title. They probated the will, obtained a sale order, reported sale to Toll, and conducted guardianship proceedings; all appeared regular and were approved. Toll later filed a disclaimer in probate to set aside the sale; a demurrer to his reply was sustained. He also sued to enjoin foreclosure, alleging fraud and contract violations. The court found constructive fraud but no intent to injure minors; the dispute was settled in good faith by “A.” The probate court had all material facts and its discretion was properly exercised; the sale gave Toll good title. Casey, having instigated the fraud, could not foreclose until the wrong was undone. The court ordered: In No. 12,391, Toll pays his own costs, other costs paid by Mrs. McKenzie individually, judgment affirmed as modified. In No. 12,392, Toll pays his own costs, Casey pays other costs; Toll must pay Casey the balance due on the encumbrance with 6% interest by June 1, 1931, less Casey’s obligations under “A”; Casey must release the trust deed; judgment affirmed as modified. On rehearing, case No. 12,392 remanded to effectuate the judgment with up to 30 days extension; rehearing denied.

A leveraged ETF uses derivatives and debt to amplify daily returns of an underlying index, aiming for 2:1 or 3:1 ratios, or inverse. They are short-term instruments due to high risk and costs, unsuitable for long-term holding because of volatility decay and daily rebalancing. The most effective strategy is day trading or swing trading to capitalize on short-term momentum. Risks include magnified losses; a 3:1 ETF can lose over 6% if the index falls 2%. Risk management includes stop-loss orders and diversification across directional and inverse ETFs. Tax implications: short-term gains taxed as ordinary income, long-term gains at lower rates, but holding long-term is discouraged. Performance can be measured using Sharpe ratio, Jensen's alpha, appraisal ratio. Backtests of a strategy on QQQ (unleveraged) and QLD (2x leveraged) show higher average gain per trade (2.25% vs 1.25%) and annual returns (13.6% vs 7.6%), but max drawdown for QLD exceeded 35% in 2008/09 and over 55% in a less robust RSI strategy, which is psychologically difficult to withstand. The passage warns that leverage can be lethal, forcing traders to quit at the worst time, and max drawdown above 25% often causes traders to fold.

Injection site reactions (redness, swelling, pain) and systemic events (fever, tiredness, headache, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle or joint pain) were common after vaccination with BNT162b1 or BNT162b2. These reactions were mostly mild or moderate in severity and resolved quickly. Pain at the injection site was the most common injection site reaction; tiredness and headache were the most common systemic events.

In Phase 1, all tested doses of BNT162b1 and BNT162b2 were well tolerated except BNT162b1 100 µg, which was stopped after dose 1 due to reactions. BNT162b2 30 µg was selected for Phase 2/3. No participants left Phase 1 due to medical problems.

In Phase 2/3, BNT162b2 30 µg was well tolerated. Few participants (less than 1% in both vaccine and placebo groups) left the blinded part of the study due to medical problems. Most medical problems were mild or moderate and involved injection site reactions or systemic events. Among participants aged 12–15 years, no single medical problem occurred in more than 1% of either vaccine group. In those aged 16 years and older, nausea occurred in 1% of BNT162b2 recipients.

Serious medical problems were uncommon. In Phase 1, two participants had serious problems (inflamed appendix, inflamed nerves) not attributed to the vaccine. In Phase 2/3, few participants had serious medical problems; researchers considered three events possibly related to BNT162b2: numbness/tingling of arms or legs, portal vein clot, and a mini stroke. No single serious medical problem occurred in at least 1% of any group.

Deaths occurred in Phase 2/3: 85 of 23,141 who received BNT162b2 initially, 62 of 21,371 who received placebo then BNT162b2, and 23 of 23,141 who received placebo only. Deaths were from various causes and not attributed to BNT162b2. No deaths occurred in Phase 1 or among those receiving BNT162b2SA in Phase 3.

The TLV322x has an open-drain output that can be pulled up to 0V–5.5V independent of supply, enabling wired-OR and level translation. Pull-up resistor current should be 100µA–1mA; lower values improve rise-time but increase VOL and power dissipation. Rise-time depends on the RC time constant; resistors >1MΩ cause exponential edges and longer rise-time. Shorting the output to a voltage source may cause thermal runaway; use a series current-limiting resistor if shorts are possible. Unused outputs can float or connect to V-.

ESD protection diodes clamp inputs to V+ and V-; input voltage must not exceed 0.2V beyond the rails. For low-impedance sources, add a series resistor to limit current to ≤10mA.

A POR circuit holds the output low for up to 32µs after V+ crosses 1.65V, then the output follows the differential input once the supply is valid.

A basic comparator outputs low when VIN < VREF and high when VIN > VREF; swapping inputs inverts logic. Propagation delay is measured from input midpoint. Overdrive voltage is the excess beyond VREF; smaller overdrive (<100mV) increases delay. For fastest speed, maximize overdrive. Rise/fall times are 20%–80% output levels.

External hysteresis prevents chatter near the offset voltage. The TLV321x has 1.8mV internal hysteresis. An inverting hysteresis circuit uses three resistors to VCC; a non-inverting circuit uses two resistors and a reference. Equations define trip voltages and hysteresis.

In low-side current sensing, an amplifier and comparator detect over-current; the comparator alerts when the amplifier output exceeds 1.1V. Bypass V+ with a 0.1µF ceramic capacitor close to the pin. The device works with split or single supplies. Keep inputs within the specified range. Treat outputs as high-speed logic; minimize input-output coupling, place input series resistors close to the device, and optionally add <100Ω at the output to dampen ringing. For long traces, use controlled impedance and back-termination.

Technology Education Corporation (TEC) appealed a judgment holding it liable for breach of contract as a successor corporation to Educational Leadership Corporation (ELC). Plaintiffs had contracted with Paraprofessional Institutes of Ohio (PIO), which sold assets to ELC, which later sold to TEC. The trial court found TEC liable under exceptions to the general rule of successor nonliability, concluding TEC expressly and impliedly assumed liabilities and was a mere continuation of ELC.

The Court of Appeals reversed. The asset purchase agreement, incorporated into the assignment from ELC to TEC, explicitly provided that the buyer assumed no liabilities arising before the purchase except those listed in a schedule that did not include student contract claims. Thus, TEC did not expressly assume liability. Implied assumption based on constructive knowledge of pending litigation was unsupported, as the agreement unambiguously allocated such liabilities to the seller. The continuation theory failed because there was no evidence of common identity of stockholders, directors, or stock; mere continuation of the business operation is insufficient. Additionally, the case sounded in contract, not products liability, and plaintiffs had not proven the merits of their breach of contract claim. The trial court’s judgment was reversed and the case remanded.

The passage discloses techniques for preventing ransomware from encrypting files on a target machine. An endpoint agent monitors file system activities and uses honeypot files and folders. Honeypot files are implemented as virtual files via a mini filter driver: when a process queries a protected directory, the driver adds falsified entries at the beginning and end of the results, describing files that do not physically exist on disk. When a process attempts to open such a spoofed entry, the request is redirected to a real file in a specific folder maintained by the agent. The agent detects unauthorized activity on honeypot files, including creating a file handle for deletion, deleting, renaming, or writing to the file. Honeypot directories are similarly spoofed and redirected to real directories containing files of interest. Upon detecting unauthorized activity, the agent performs an action based on a policy, such as terminating the process. The virtual approach reduces storage footprint, avoids residue files on mounted disks, and allows honeypot files to be hidden from end users by checking for shell-related DLLs in the call stack to exclude legitimate GUI processes. Protected directories and exceptions lists can be configured. The techniques can be applied on various operating system platforms.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, a Bitcoin critic, said “blockchain is real” and that stablecoins and his bank’s deposit token have real-world uses. The Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO) is a technical indicator created by Tushar Chande and introduced in his 1994 book *The New Technical Trader*. It measures momentum by calculating the difference between the sum of higher closes and the sum of lower closes over a chosen period, divided by the sum of all price movements, then multiplied by 100. The oscillator ranges from -100 to +100. Positive values indicate strength, negative values weakness. Overbought conditions are signaled above +50, oversold below -50, but reliability depends on trend direction. The CMO can be combined with trend indicators like moving averages to spot the end of pullbacks and trade in the trend direction. A backtest on SPY using a 9-day period and a 5-day maximum holding period showed high risk-adjusted returns and lower drawdown than buy-and-hold. The indicator does not perform well in non-trending volatile markets and cannot identify the main trend alone. Common mistakes include using it without trend confirmation. The best period setting and timeframe depend on backtesting for the specific asset and strategy. False signals include overbought/oversold readings in strong trends. The CMO differs from RSI by using the ratio of the difference to total price movement rather than the ratio of higher to lower closes. In sideways markets, it can be used for mean-reversion at range boundaries. To set up on platforms, check for built-in or install a custom indicator. The CMO improves trading by signaling when momentum fades in pullbacks.

This bibliometric study analyzed 2,295 peer-reviewed journal articles on primary science education from the Web of Science Core Collection, using VOSviewer for bibliographic coupling and co-word analysis. Bibliographic coupling revealed five thematic clusters: (1) augmented reality, virtual reality, and ICT integration; (2) equity, engagement, and teacher competence in science achievement; (3) cognitive and metacognitive supports for conceptual understanding; (4) dialogic teaching, integration, and teacher beliefs in science literacy; and (5) artificial intelligence, computer science, and computational thinking in early and primary education. Co-word analysis identified four clusters: (1) dialogic argumentation, discourse, and scientific literacy; (2) teacher beliefs, pedagogical knowledge, and professional development; (3) achievement, engagement, and conceptual change; and (4) computational thinking and technology integration in STEM education. The findings indicate a shift toward student-centered, digitally mediated pedagogies, while highlighting gaps in culturally responsive computational thinking and teacher identity in reform efforts. The study proposes the DIG-EDU-QUEST framework to integrate dialogic, inclusive, and generative approaches for quality, equity, science, and technology. It underscores the need for inclusive digital integration, culturally responsive teaching, and interdisciplinary frameworks, and suggests future research expand database coverage for a more global perspective.

Multi-organ research integrating AI into imaging genetics offers promise for precision medicine by introducing endophenotypes. Three catalysts advanced genetics: large-scale multi-omics datasets (UK Biobank, FinnGen), open science sharing GWAS summary statistics (FinnGen, PGC, public platforms), and advanced computational methods using these statistics (LDSC, Mendelian randomization). The genetic basis of AI endophenotypes in multi-organ disease endpoints remains largely unexplored. The authors previously derived 2024 multi-organ AI endophenotypes (MAE) including brain network patterns, neuroimaging endophenotypes, and biological age gaps, and publicly released UKBB GWAS summary statistics. FinnGen and PGC also made extensive GWAS data available. This study harnesses these public resources to characterize the genetic architecture of the 2024 MAEs and 525 disease endpoints, expanding on prior work by systematically including FinnGen and PGC data and benchmarking statistical methods, aiming to compute SNP-based heritability.

Center for Diagnostic Imaging Miami provides diagnostic medical imaging services using technologically advanced techniques and a team of board-certified physicians, radiologists, and technicians. Microbiota, the diverse microbial communities in and on the human body, were once considered freeloaders but are now recognized as essential to health, participating in digestion, metabolism, immune responses, and inflammation. Disruption may contribute to asthma, obesity, colitis, and colon cancer. Recent research shows the microbiota exhibits circadian rhythmicity, potentially explaining adverse effects from late-night eating or electric light exposure. The microbiome varies between morning and evening, indicating it is not static. A mouse study demonstrated that gut microbiota releases molecules (amino acids, lipids, vitamins) into the blood, and their daily fluctuations alter liver gene expression for metabolic enzymes—the first clear evidence of the microbiota changing an organ's circadian activity. Antibiotics or altered feeding times changed liver physiology. The liver's response to acetaminophen overdose varied by time of day (less toxic at dawn, more toxic at dusk), showing the microbiota regulates detoxification rhythms. This may apply to drug metabolism generally, suggesting medication timing could affect effectiveness and side effects. Advances in DNA sequencing and the recognition that the microbiome functions as a whole community enabled these findings. Implications for humans include risks for those on long-term antibiotics or shift workers eating at inappropriate times, potentially leading to higher obesity and metabolic syndrome rates, as seen in night workers. The gut microbiota's well-being may be a root cause.

The passage details specifications from the SD Physical Layer Simplified Specification Version 6.00. UHS-II card contacts use pins 7 and 8 for RCLK; first row contacts in non-UHS-II mode match Table 3-1. Unused lines (CLK, CMD, DAT[3:2]) must not float; host keeps them at defined high or low. ROM Card is read-only memory with register settings per Table 3-4, treats CMD24,25,27,28,29,30,32,33,38 as illegal, optionally supports CMD42 and security commands, and has no WP switch.

UHS-I provides up to 104MB/s on 4-bit bus with modes DS (25MHz 3.3V), HS (50MHz 3.3V), SDR104 (208MHz 1.8V), DDR50 (50MHz 1.8V). UHS-I applies to SDHC/SDXC, not SDSC. DDR50 is mandatory for microSD, optional for standard SD. Initialization: after power-up, card is in 3.3V signaling. Host uses ACMD41 with S18R=1 to request 1.8V signaling; if card responds S18A=1, host issues CMD11 to invoke voltage switch sequence. After switch, card enters SDR12 default. Host selects UHS-I mode via CMD6 Function Group 1, driver strength via Group 3, and power limit via Group 4. CMD19 sends tuning block for sampling point tuning in SDR50/SDR104.

UHS-II card operation modes include SD bus interface modes (DS, HS, SDR104, DDR50) and UHS-II interface modes: FD156 (156MB/s), HD312 (312MB/s, optional), FD312 (312MB/s), FD624 (624MB/s). UHS-II card types are UHS156 and UHS624. Initialization: after power-up, both SD bus I/F and UHS-II I/F are enabled. Host provides RCLK and STB.L to D0 lane, waits for D1 lane to change EIDL to STB.L. If detected within 200us, host starts UHS-II initialization (PHY init, device init, enumeration, configuration, SD-TRAN init). Otherwise, host initializes card in SD Bus I/F mode. UHS-II card disables UHS-II I/F before ACMD41 completion if initialized via SD bus. CMD0 restarts SD-TRAN initialization.

Card identification mode uses CMD0 to reset, CMD8 to verify interface condition, ACMD41 to set voltage window and HCS, CMD2 to get CID, CMD3 to publish RCA. Data transfer mode uses CMD7 to select card. Read commands (CMD17,18) can be aborted by CMD12; write commands (CMD24,25,27,42,56) also aborted by CMD12. Erase sequence uses CMD32,33,38; DISCARD (CMD38 arg 00000001h) and FULE (CMD38 arg 00000002h) are supported for SDHC/SDXC. Lock/unlock uses CMD42 with password; COP feature adds FEP, COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]), and FEP Force Erase. Locked cards accept only basic class commands, ACMD41, CMD16, and lock card class. CMD6 switches functions: access mode, command system, driver strength, power limit.

Food scientist Paul Dawson tested double-dipping. Double-dipped chips in water transferred a thousand more bacteria per milliliter. In dips, single-dipped samples had no bacteria; double-dipped salsa contained 1,000 bacteria/ml, five times more than chocolate and cheese dips (150-200/ml). Dawson attributed salsa's higher count to its lower viscosity. After two hours, salsa's bacteria dropped to match the others, likely due to acidity. This research is a content analysis of 273 studies on modern physics education conducted in Turkey between 2000 and 2023, accessed from various databases. Studies were examined using the "Modern Physics Education Publication Classification Form" and analyzed via content analysis. Findings indicate that most studies were published between 2010 and 2020, predominantly as Turkish-language articles. Study objectives varied, with quantitative research designs, especially quasi-experimental and descriptive surveys, preferred. Purposive sampling was common, and samples mostly consisted of high school and undergraduate students, with sizes typically between 31 and 100 individuals. Intervention durations often ranged from 0 to 8 weeks. Data collection relied heavily on interviews, tests, questionnaires, and scales; quantitative analyses frequently used frequency/percentage and t-tests, while qualitative analyses used content analysis. Validity and reliability methods were employed but often insufficiently reported. Results showed both positive developments (e.g., increased academic achievement, concretization of knowledge) and negative situations (e.g., persistent conceptual misconceptions, negative emotions) in modern physics education. Discussions were generally supported by literature but lacked sufficient explanation. Recommendations included using different analytical methods, increasing sample sizes, enriching methods and intervention examples, incorporating modern physics philosophy, and updating curricula and textbooks.

The passage describes systems and methods for automated recognition of objects in video and image content. A video stream is received, and frames are selected according to a frame selection rate. Selected frames are partitioned into image blocks. A machine-learning algorithm with learned parameters recognizes regions of image blocks that may contain an object. A likelihood metric, determined based on at least the frame selection rate, is used to decide if a region corresponds to an object. Recognized objects are identified and displayed, and may be added to a digital shopping cart. Product and merchant databases provide information such as price and availability. The system can generate title profiles of recognized products and personalize shopping carts based on viewer data.

The money flow index (MFI) is a momentum indicator that combines price and volume data to measure money flow into and out of a security over a specified period. It oscillates between 0 and 100, indicating overbought (above 80) and oversold (at or below 20) conditions, and is used to predict potential price reversals. The MFI is similar to the Relative Strength Index but incorporates volume, making it a volume-weighted RSI. It generates overbought/oversold signals and bullish/bearish divergence signals: a bullish divergence occurs when price makes lower lows while MFI makes higher lows; a bearish divergence occurs when price makes higher lows while MFI makes lower lows. Traders use these signals to anticipate reversals, looking for momentum cool-offs at overbought/oversold levels or divergences. The default lookback period is 14 days; shorter periods produce more signals (many false), longer periods fewer but potentially more reliable. The best setting depends on the market and should be determined by backtesting. The Chaikin money flow (CMF) oscillator differs by using only price data and exponential moving averages, whereas MFI includes volume. A trading strategy was presented combining MFI overbought/oversold conditions with bullish engulfing patterns for long trades and bearish engulfing patterns for short trades. Backtesting on Pepsi (PEP) from 2000 showed 581 trades, average gain 0.42%, win rate 71%, profit factor 1.8, annual return 10.4% (vs. 9.8% buy-and-hold), invested 39% of the time, risk-adjusted return 26%. On SPY, CAGR was 10.6% (vs. 9.7% buy-and-hold) with 35% invested time. A combined PEP and SPY portfolio yielded 15% CAGR, invested 48% of the time, performing best in the 1990s and recent five years. The strategy performed poorly on gold (GLD), as mean reversion does not work well on commodities. The article also notes that the trading rules are available for purchase as part of a compilation.

This study used CiteSpace visual analysis to examine research hotspots and trends regarding the relationship between open education and vocational education in China and other countries. Chinese literature data came from CNKI (515 valid documents, 2012–2023), and foreign literature from Web of Science (319 documents, 2012–2023, using keywords like “adult education and vocational education”).

Keyword visual analysis for China identified open education, vocational education, integrated development, and others as research hotspots, with integrated development showing significantly higher frequency. For other countries, high-frequency keywords included vocational education, adult education, online learning, and vocational training, but there was no clear hotspot directly addressing the open-vocational education relationship; focus was on adult education and online learning.

Timeline analysis of Chinese research showed a shift before 2016 from separate development models to investigating interrelationships, and post-2016 deeper exploration of integrated development, teaching models, and curriculum systems. The timeline for other countries indicated increasing focus on adult vocational education and skills since 2013, and after 2018 growing research on online learning for vocational education participants.

Analysis of keywords with the strongest citation bursts in China revealed that since 2018, keywords like integration and development, integrated development, and coordinated development had high burst strengths, indicating growing interest in closer integration. In other countries, from 2020 to 2023, online learning and vocational education and training showed strong bursts, along with blended learning, technology, and personality, highlighting online learning and technology as hot topics.

The study concluded that integrated development has been the primary research hotspot in China, while international research focused on improving adult vocational skills and online learning. China’s research intensified post-2016, whereas other countries shifted from adult skills enhancement to online learning since 2018. The findings suggest future research could use quantitative methodologies, big data analytics, and statistical models to further quantify interactions and guide policy and practice.

The passage describes a system and method for multiple-factor verification of vision-based interactions, using at least two monitoring systems to generate independent evaluations. A verification system compares these evaluations to determine monitoring alignment and trigger actions. The monitoring systems are preferably orthogonal, with different attack vectors. A primary application is retail automatic checkout (checkout-free shopping), where a virtual cart of selected items is generated. Monitoring systems may include a computer vision (CV) monitoring system with distributed cameras, RFID-based monitoring, smart infrastructure (e.g., smart shelves), user applications, smart carts, point-of-sale (POS) systems, or profile prediction systems. The method involves executing a first monitoring system to produce a first evaluation, executing a second monitoring system to produce a second evaluation, determining monitoring alignment by comparing the evaluations, and triggering an action based on the alignment. Actions include enabling or disabling a checkout process, directing worker handling (e.g., generating worker instructions for spot checks), scoring a customer profile, providing operational instructions (e.g., item stocking placement), or updating at least one monitoring system. Exemplary implementations include CV with RFID for spot-checking, CV with a security tag barrier for theft detection, smart cart with CV for redundant checkout lists, user application with CV for verification, and CV with profile prediction for confidence adjustment. The system and method aim to enhance reliability, mitigate errors and adversarial attacks, and improve performance over time.

Using group theory and density functional theory, the study investigates higher-order atomic magnetic multipoles in collinear altermagnets MnF₂, CrSb, and KMnF₃. Altermagnetism breaks time-reversal symmetry but preserves its combination with certain crystallographic symmetries, yielding compensated net dipole moment and spin-splitting without spin-orbit coupling. Projecting spin density onto tesseral harmonics quantifies multipole magnitudes and identifies in-phase (IP) versus out-of-phase (OP) components. In MnF₂ (d-wave), IP collinear multipoles include the dxymz octupole and gxyz2mz 32-pole; in CrSb (g-wave), the lowest IP collinear multipole is the 32-pole gyz(y2−3x2)mz. Noncollinear spin density (NSD) components, though smaller, exhibit higher-order multipolar patterns. Without SOC, NSD vanishes; with SOC, noncollinear multipoles appear linearly in SOC strength, while collinear multipoles change quadratically. In MnF₂, IP noncollinear multipoles include dyzmx+dxzmy; in CrSb, IP noncollinear octupoles emerge. In KMnF₃, octahedral rotations drive an antiferromagnetic-to-altermagnetic transition, with the IP 32-pole gxy(x2−y2)mz linearly proportional to rotation angle. Multipoles connect to response tensors like piezomagnetism and magnetoelectric effects. The work highlights the importance of NSD, higher-order multipoles, and SOC in altermagnets.

This cross-sectional study assessed cardiovascular disease risk by evaluating lipid profiles in HIV/AIDS patients receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) at the University Teaching Hospital of Butare (CHUB). It included 150 HIV-positive participants on ART (108 first-line, 39 second-line, 3 third-line) and 49 HIV-negative controls. Lipid parameters measured were total cholesterol (TC), LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C), HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C), and triglycerides (TG). Among ART recipients, 32% had hypertriglyceridemia, 19.3% had low HDL-C (hypercholesterolemia), 8% had high LDL-C, and 15.3% had high TC. Compared to controls, the ART group showed significantly higher TG, LDL-C, and TC, and lower HDL-C (p<0.05). The study concludes that ART is associated with dyslipidemia, increasing cardiovascular disease risk, and recommends routine lipid profile monitoring in HIV patients on ART.

The application provides a screen display method for an electronic device. When displaying interfaces of at least two applications, including a first interface in full-screen mode and a second interface as a floating window over the first interface, the method includes receiving a first operation performed on the first interface and, in response, automatically displaying the second interface in a minimized state within the first interface. The minimized state may be a floating ball, an icon of the second application, a contact avatar, or a video pop-up window.

In one implementation, the first interface contains an edit box, and the first operation is performed on that edit box. This generates a focus obtaining event in the edit box, which triggers the automatic minimization of the second interface. A subsequent focus loss event in the edit box can automatically restore the second interface to its floating window state. The minimized second interface may be placed at a location whose distance from a cursor in the edit box exceeds a threshold.

The method also covers receiving an operation on the second interface while it is a floating window, which can cause the second interface to be displayed in full-screen mode while the first interface is minimized and shown in a minimized state within the second interface. If the second interface includes an edit box, a focus obtaining event in that edit box can trigger this full-screen display and minimization of the first interface.

When three or more application interfaces are displayed (e.g., a third interface as an additional floating window), an operation on one floating window can automatically minimize at least the third interface, or display that floating window full-screen while minimizing the first and third interfaces. An operation on the full-screen first interface can automatically minimize all floating windows.

In another aspect, the method displays a first interface and a second interface side by side with no overlapping area. Upon receiving a first operation on the first interface, the first interface is displayed in full-screen mode, the second interface is minimized, and the minimized second interface (floating ball, icon, avatar, or video pop-up) is shown within the full-screen first interface. If the first interface includes an edit box, a focus obtaining event in that edit box triggers this behavior. A focus loss event restores the side-by-side display. The minimized second interface may be placed away from the cursor. A maximization function option on the first interface can also trigger the full-screen and minimization. An operation on the minimized second interface can restore the side-by-side arrangement.

The 1-3-1 zone defense is versatile, overplaying passing lanes to force cross-court passes and interceptions. Its main weakness is corner shots, but it often invites corner passes to trap. Rebounding can be weak, with a wing as the primary weakside rebounder. It requires active defenders moving as a unit, reading the passer's eyes. Placement: strong rebounder on left wing, quick agile player on baseline, tall player at top against small guards. Shifts adjust to ball position: point, wings, baseline, and middle defenders move to cover ballside, deny passes, and protect the basket. Baseline and point defenders work in unison; wing defenders work opposite and rebound weakside; the middle defender stays between ball and basket. Adjustments include weakside skip pass close-outs and an exchange option for baseline and middle defenders. Dribble penetration is stopped by the post, leading to traps. The "Three in a Line" variation keeps a big defender near the basket, with wings covering corners. Trapping is a key feature, using corners as primary trap zones with out-of-bounds lines. Traps can be hard or soft, alternated. Defenders trace the ball with both hands, elbows together, forcing lob or bounce passes. Off-ball defenders anticipate passes out of traps. Trap actions cover top and corner traps, with a variation where the middle defender traps with the wing and baseline protects the basket. A skip pass adjustment exchanges middle and baseline roles. The 1-3-1 can be extended to quarter-court, half-court, or full-court pressure.
