This study evaluated the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) in patients with urinary tract infections (UTIs) and its association with kidney damage. It was an open-blinded, cross-sectional study conducted at a single center in Bangalore, India. From an initial 80 adults (20–65 years) with symptomatic, drug-naïve UTIs and positive urine protein strip tests, 34 were excluded due to low creatinine or absent proteinuria, leaving 46 participants (67% female, mean age 38.11 years). Urinary protein and creatinine were measured, and the P/C ratio was calculated. Based on KDIGO guidelines, participants were classified into three proteinuria stages: Stage I (<15 mg/mM creatinine, n=12, 26%), Stage II (15–50 mg/mM, n=16, 35%), and Stage III (>50 mg/mM, n=18, 39%). Urinary creatinine excretion was significantly reduced across all stages compared to the reference interval (p<0.001), with mean values of 33.9, 31.2, and 29.0 mg/dL for Stages I, II, and III, respectively. Urinary protein excretion was significantly elevated in Stage III (48.6 ± 46 mg/dL) compared to the normal reference (9.0 ± 2.6 mg/dL, p<0.001). The P/C ratio increased across stages, with Stage III showing the highest mean (180.6 ± 142.9 mg/mM creatinine). The study concluded that proteinuria is significantly associated with UTIs, urinary creatinine is reduced across disease severity, and the P/C ratio is a reliable diagnostic marker for assessing renal impairment in UTI patients.

The passage describes patterns for integrating sharded services with frontend or middleware code. One approach builds all sharding logic into the sharded service itself, using a stateless load balancer that directs traffic to the appropriate shard, effectively a distributed ambassador as a service. This eliminates the need for a client-side ambassador but complicates the sharded service deployment. The alternative integrates a single-node ambassador on the client side to route traffic to the appropriate shard, simplifying the sharded service deployment but adding complexity to the client. The choice depends on application specifics, team lines, and whether code is written or off-the-shelf software is deployed. The single-node ambassador pattern for client-side sharding introduces an ambassador container that contains all routing logic, so the application connects to what appears to be a single storage backend on localhost, while the ambassador proxy handles sharding. This separates concerns between the application container and the sharding ambassador, enabling reuse.

The ambassador pattern is also applied to service brokering, where a service broker ambassador introspects the environment and brokers connections, allowing the application to always connect to a service on localhost. This supports portability across environments. Another application is request splitting or experimentation, where an ambassador redirects a fraction of requests to a different implementation, such as a beta version, or tees traffic to both production and a new version, returning only production responses. This separates concerns and allows reuse of the request-splitting ambassador.

The adapter pattern modifies the interface of an application container to conform to a predefined interface. It addresses heterogeneity in logging, monitoring, and other conventions by using an adapter container that transforms the application’s interface into a consistent one. For monitoring, an adapter can convert an application’s monitoring interface to the expected interface of a general-purpose monitoring system, decoupling the application from the monitoring tool and allowing reuse. For logging, an adapter can redirect log files to stdout or transform varied log formats into a single structured representation. For health checks, an adapter container can contain rich health-check scripts that run diagnostic queries, avoiding modification of the base application container. This modularity enables sharing and reuse.

The passage then introduces multi-node distributed patterns, contrasting microservices with monolithic systems. Microservices break applications into small, independent services communicating over defined APIs, offering benefits in reliability, agility, independent scaling, and decoupled team workflows. Challenges include debugging complexity and design difficulty, motivating the use of distributed patterns.

The replicated load-balanced service pattern consists of a scalable number of identical servers behind a load balancer. Stateless services require at least two replicas for high availability, and horizontal scaling adds more replicas. A readiness probe is essential to inform the load balancer when an application is ready to serve requests, distinct from health probes. Session-tracked services ensure all requests from a particular user map to the same replica, often using consistent hashing to minimize remapping when scaling. Application-layer replicated services leverage HTTP-specific features. A caching layer, such as Varnish, can be deployed as a separate replicated tier to improve performance, but care must be taken to avoid breaking session tracking; cookie or header-based affinity is recommended. The caching layer can also provide rate limiting and denial-of-service defense, returning 429 errors and headers like X-RateLimit-Remaining. SSL termination is added via a replicated nginx layer, which handles HTTPS and forwards to the cache.

Sharded services are used for stateful services where data size exceeds a single machine. Each shard serves a subset of requests, with a root distributing requests. A sharded cache increases the fraction of the total data set that can be stored compared to a replicated cache. The cache’s hit rate affects system capacity and latency; failures or rollouts of a shard can degrade performance. Replicated, sharded caches replace each shard with a replicated service, providing resilience and enabling scaling of hot shards. Sharding functions map requests to shards, typically using a hash function and modulo operator. Determinism and uniformity are critical. The choice of shard key must group identical requests while distinguishing those that produce different responses; for example, using request path or country and path. Consistent hashing functions minimize key remapping when the number of shards changes. Hot sharding systems dynamically scale individual shards in response to uneven load.

The scatter/gather pattern achieves parallelism by distributing a request to multiple leaf nodes, each performing part of the processing, and the root combining partial results. It is suited for embarrassingly parallel problems. In a sharded scatter/gather system, each leaf holds a shard of the data, and the root unions the results. The number of leaves must be chosen carefully: overhead and the straggler problem (the slowest leaf determines overall latency) limit gains from increased parallelism. The 99th percentile latency becomes more critical because each user request spawns many internal requests. For reliability and scale, each leaf shard can be replicated as a replicated service, allowing load balancing across healthy replicas and safe upgrades.

Finally, the passage covers functions and event-driven processing (FaaS). Benefits include simplified deployment, automatic scaling, and granular modularity. Challenges include difficulty in obtaining a comprehensive view of the system, detecting problems like infinite loops, and the need for rigorous monitoring. FaaS is poorly suited for background processing due to time-bounded execution, for applications requiring large in-memory data sets due to loading latency, and for sustained high request loads where per-request pricing may become less cost-effective than long-running services.

The President returns a bill making appropriations for certain public works, offering a detailed constitutional objection. The central question is the General Government's power over internal improvements, a phrase absent from the Constitution and lacking precise meaning. If Congress could construct railroads and canals, the power would logically extend to turnpikes, bridges, levees, irrigation, and even public education and hospitals, dangerously expanding federal functions and patronage.

The federal government possesses only enumerated powers; the preamble and the “general welfare” clause do not grant additional authority. No specific constitutional provision authorizes a general system of internal improvements. Advocates point to powers like establishing post-roads, regulating commerce, and maintaining armed forces, but any improvement must be necessary to execute those enumerated powers, not a pretext for a broad system. The magnitude of such a system is illustrated by existing state and private railroads and canals, costing hundreds of millions and employing hundreds of thousands; federal involvement would have paralyzed state and private efforts, corrupted legislation, and burdened the nation with debt. The clause granting exclusive legislation over federal districts and purchased places does not confer a general power to purchase for internal improvements; purchases are limited to objects within enumerated powers.

Regarding navigation aids, early Congresses from 1789 appropriated only for lighthouses, beacons, buoys, and piers, requiring cession of jurisdiction. For over thirty years, no appropriations removed natural obstacles. The first harbor improvements appeared in 1824. While a belief in the power to erect lighthouses and beacons for safe navigation exists, extending this to river and harbor improvements raises the same constitutional issues as land improvements. The definition of federal navigable waters, established by the Judiciary Act of 1789 and later acts, includes waters navigable from the sea and certain lakes and connecting waters for interstate commerce, a standard upheld by the Supreme Court but inherently variable.

The President recommends that permanent harbor works require cession of soil and jurisdiction to the United States, that each work receive a separate legislative bill, and that federal appropriations be confined to works necessary for undoubted powers, leaving other improvements to the states or private enterprise.

The present disclosure relates to autonomous vehicles that include a machine-learned yield model. The model receives feature data descriptive of perceived objects (e.g., other vehicles, traffic signals) and outputs yield decisions describing a yield behavior (yield or do not yield). Feature data can include object state, required deceleration or acceleration, traffic signal transition timing, stop line locations, and gap data for temporal gaps between vehicles. The yield model may be part of a yield controller within a motion planning system. The motion planning system uses the yield decision to generate a motion plan, for example via an optimization planner that evaluates cost functions. The machine-learned yield model can be trained using supervised learning on log data annotated with yield labels, which may be derived from scoring functions that compare outcomes of yielding versus not yielding. The model can also provide yield decisions to prevent gridlock at intersections.

Options trading in TSLA involves buying or selling derivatives granting the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell TSLA shares at a specific price by a certain date. It offers profit generation and risk management through leverage, but carries substantial loss risk and complexity, especially for novices.

Pros: leverage (controlling more shares with less capital, loss limited to premium paid when buying), hedging against volatility, speculation. Cons: potential large or complete losses if price moves against you, complexity, market forces.

Strategies: long calls (expect price rise), long puts (expect price fall), covered calls (buy call, sell underlying stock), spreads (simultaneously buy/sell options to reduce risk, maximize returns). Strategy choice depends on risk tolerance, investment goals, market outlook; conservative investors may use covered calls/spreads, aggressive ones long calls/puts. No one-size-fits-all approach.

Potential return: difference between strike price and underlying price at expiration. Higher underlying price yields profit; lower yields loss. Options are more complex than stocks.

Risks: large losses from small price moves (leverage), complete investment loss, market forces. Best practices: understand strategies and their risks/returns, use quantified analysis (analyzing past price patterns for trends, entry/exit, support/resistance), employ risk management (stop losses, take profits when analysis indicates). Backtesting and quantified analysis strongly recommended; avoid options trading if unable.

Developing a strategy requires understanding strategies, potential returns/risks, market sentiment, quantified analysis, and risk management. Order types: limit (specify price), market (current price), stop (trigger at a certain underlying price). Best entry time depends on market sentiment, quantified analysis, risk tolerance.

Options types: calls, puts, spreads. Common mistakes: overtrading, entering trades without understanding risks/returns, neglecting risk management. Backtesting is paramount to find a statistical edge; most retail traders fail from lack of a trading plan and edge.

Tax implications vary by trade and country; consult a tax professional. Capital gains taxes generally sourced to owner's residence. Fees: commissions, platform, regulatory, margin fees, varying by broker and option type. Profits cannot be protected; markets fluctuate, overnight risk exists. Rely on quantified backtests and follow the plan. Liquidity: higher for shorter expirations and higher volume, lower for higher premiums and lower volume. Monitoring unnecessary with a clear plan; automation avoids behavioral mistakes. Market sentiment useful but must be backtested, no discretionary judgments.

Options trading in TSLA requires understanding risks/rewards, using quantified analysis, and backtesting before committing money.

This paper investigates how early-stage startups develop Internet-of-Things (IoT) systems, using a multiple-case study of eight startups. The study employs the SEMAT Essence framework to analyze team, system, work, and way of working. Teams typically combine internal software engineering competence with external partners, as startups often lack all needed skills. Systems are developed starting from either the application layer or the perception layer of the three-layer IoT architecture. Work is represented by Minimum Viable Products (MVPs), categorized into three types: type 1 (looks-like, simulating user experience with manual functionality), type 2 (functional works-like, demonstrable features with acceptable quality), and type 3 (quality works-like, focusing on non-functional attributes and integration). Common ways of working include outsourced implementation and manufacturing, rapid prototyping (e.g., 3D printing, CAD), reuse-oriented development (using ready-made components like Arduino and Raspberry Pi), and Agile development with iterative releases, though hardware iterations are longer than software sprints. The development prioritizes speed, employing opportunistic and work-around solutions similar to software startups, but faces extra dependencies due to hardware-related complexities and external reliance. The study contributes empirical insights into IoT development processes in startups and highlights methodological adjustments needed compared to pure software development.

The lecture presents link-cut trees, a data structure for maintaining a dynamic forest of rooted, unordered trees. It supports operations: make-tree (create a vertex), link (add an edge from a root v to a node w in a different tree), cut (remove the edge from a node v to its parent), find-root (return the root of v's tree), and path aggregation (compute min, max, sum, etc. on the root-to-v path). All operations are achieved in O(log n) amortized time.

The structure uses a preferred path decomposition. A node's preferred child is the child whose subtree contains the last access within v's subtree, unless the last access was v itself (then no preferred child). Following preferred child pointers partitions the represented tree into preferred paths. Each preferred path is stored in an auxiliary splay tree keyed by depth. The root of each auxiliary tree stores a path-parent pointer to the parent of the path's top node in the represented tree. The collection of auxiliary trees and path-parent pointers forms the tree of auxiliary trees.

The core operation is access(v). It splays v within its auxiliary tree, removes v's right child (making it a separate tree with a path-parent to v), then repeatedly follows path-parent pointers upward: for each w = v.path-parent, splay w, replace w's right child with v (clipping off the old right child and giving it a path-parent to w), and splay v again. This makes the root-to-v path preferred and v the root of the tree of auxiliary trees.

Other operations reduce to access. find-root(v): access(v), then walk left to find the root r, and splay r. path aggregate: access(v), then return the augmented value from v's auxiliary subtree. cut(v): access(v), then set v.left.parent = none and v.left = none, splitting the tree. link(v,w): access(v) and access(w), then set v.left = w and w.parent = v (or equivalent), joining the trees.

Analysis uses heavy-light decomposition on the represented tree. An edge is heavy if the child's subtree size is more than half the parent's size; otherwise light. Any root-to-node path has at most log n light edges. The total number of preferred child changes over m operations is bounded by counting light preferred edge creations and heavy preferred edge destructions. Access creates at most log n light preferred edges and destroys at most log n heavy preferred edges. Link/cut operations also affect at most log n such edges. This yields O(m log n) preferred child changes.

Applying the splay tree access lemma with a potential based on the size of a node's subtree in the tree of auxiliary trees (including sizes of trees hanging off via path-parents), the amortized cost of an access telescopes to O(log n + number of preferred child changes). Combined with the bound on preferred child changes, the overall amortized cost per operation is O(log n).

Recent studies indicate that spending time outdoors, rather than reducing near-work activities, protects children against developing myopia (nearsightedness). Myopia occurs when the eye grows too long, causing blurry distance vision, and typically begins in early elementary school. It is a lifelong condition requiring glasses or contact lenses, and can lead to blinding eye diseases later in life. While near-work like reading and screen use was long suspected as a cause, a 20-year study of 4,979 children (CLEERE) found it is not an important factor. Instead, outdoor time has a significant protective effect. For children with two myopic parents, low outdoor time results in a 60% chance of needing glasses, but about 14 hours per week outdoors can reduce that risk to 20%, matching the risk of children without myopic parents. However, outdoor time does not slow progression in already nearsighted children. The dominant theory is that brighter outdoor light stimulates dopamine release in the retina, promoting normal eye growth. Parents should still ensure children use sunscreen and sunglasses to avoid UV damage.

The Commodity Channel Index (CCI) is a momentum oscillator that measures a security’s current price relative to its average price over a given period. It identifies extreme conditions, with relatively high readings when prices are far above their average and low readings when far below. Originally developed for commodities, it is now used on stocks and ETFs. The indicator oscillates above and below a zero point. Generally, readings above +100 are considered overbought and below -100 oversold, but these levels are unbound and vary by security; traders should examine historical reversal points for each asset.

The CCI was invented by Donald R. Lambert in 1980 and published in Commodities magazine. Its formula calculates the typical price (mean of high, low, close), a simple moving average of that typical price, the mean deviation, and then the CCI using a constant of 0.015. The calculation is automated in trading software.

The CCI can show bullish or bearish divergence with price, which may warn of weakening trends, though divergence is not always an accurate reversal signal. The indicator is useful for spotting overbought and oversold conditions. Its advantages are that it is based on a specific formula and allows quantification. Disadvantages are that it is a lagging indicator, works only on stocks and bonds, and is not particularly useful for detecting trends. It is not a precise timing tool, and markets can remain at extreme levels for prolonged periods.

The best setup uses the CCI as an overbought/oversold indicator with a relatively short lookback period on daily bars. For stocks, a lookback period between 5 and 9 works well. The best assets are stocks and bonds, as they tend to mean revert. Similar technical indicators include the Relative Strength Index (RSI), Rate of Change (ROC), Stochastics, and MACD.

A backtest on SPY (S&P 500 ETF) using a 9-day lookback period and a buy threshold of -90, selling when the close exceeds the previous day’s high, produced a profit factor of about 1.8, an average gain per trade of 0.55%, and a maximum drawdown of 23%. The best CCI trading strategy uses oversold levels with relatively short lookback periods applied in the stock market. The passage notes that while the CCI is good, there are better indicators, such as the RSI.

This systematic review synthesized existing evidence on bibliotherapy practices in educational settings. Following PRISMA-P guidelines, 35 articles (quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods) published between 2006 and 2021 were included. Five themes emerged.

Theme 1, Perceptions and Practices, showed varied awareness of bibliotherapy among practitioners (14.29% to 80%) and a lack of formal training. Practitioners identified benefits but also challenges such as time constraints, resource shortages, reader reluctance, and boredom. Social stories and self-help books were commonly used.

Theme 2, Socio-Emotional Outcomes, indicated bibliotherapy reduced aggressive behaviors and social anxiety, and improved socially appropriate behaviors, emotional awareness, and social skills, including for children with autism or emotional/behavioral disorders. Affective bibliotherapy was more effective than cognitive bibliotherapy for social problems.

Theme 3, Academic Outcomes, reported improvements in reading comprehension, vocabulary, writing, articulation, and English language and mathematics performance.

Theme 4, Self-esteem, Resilience, and Hope Outcomes, found significant improvements in general self-esteem, hope, and resilience, particularly among vulnerable populations like orphans.

Theme 5, Stress, Trauma, Anxiety, and Depression Outcomes, showed bibliotherapy reduced anxiety and depression, with mixed results for stress. It allowed discussion of past trauma but did not treat its effects.

The review noted limitations including small sample sizes, limited institutional scope, insufficient methodological detail, and geographical variation. Overall, bibliotherapy demonstrated potential benefits across multiple domains in education, though improved practice and training are needed.

Inflation is defined as a gradual decrease in consumers’ purchasing power over time due to a broad increase in the prices of goods and services, calculated as the average price increase of a selected basket of goods and services. Major causes include a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output (currency oversupply), demand-pull inflation from excess demand, cost-push inflation from increased production costs, and built-in inflation from expectations of future price increases.

High inflation makes stock prices more volatile. The overall market suffers because consumers spend less money. Value stocks may outperform, while growth stocks with high P/E ratios are typically avoided. A sudden increase in inflation is considered the most painful type, as it takes time for businesses to pass on higher input costs, reducing corporate profits and leaving consumers with less savings. Inflation also leaves investors with less money to invest, potentially causing a stock market decline. The central bank may raise interest rates to combat inflation, increasing borrowing costs for businesses; excessive rate hikes can lead to recession and a stock market crash. The interest rate is a key factor for stock market returns, and inflation determines the interest rate. Value stocks tend to perform better when inflation rises, while growth stocks have an inverse relationship. Dividend-paying stocks may drop in price if dividends fail to keep up with inflation.

A backtest of the S&P 500 assuming high inflation leads to higher rates showed poor trading metrics and an abysmal historical performance, with less money after 60 years than at the start, indicating stocks perform poorly when inflation is high, at least in the short term. In the long run, companies should be able to pass on increased prices to consumers, and stocks have produced positive real returns. Investments suggested during inflation include diversified index funds, stocks, bonds, commodities, gold, real estate, and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), whose prices reflect inflation changes. The paper proposes VN-HGCN, a heterogeneous graph convolutional network that introduces hierarchical virtual nodes to capture long-range dependencies without predefined meta-paths. Type-level virtual nodes are randomly connected to each node type, and a central virtual node connects all type-level virtual nodes, shortening the distance between any node pair to at most 4 hops. This design enables message passing over long distances using only 4 layers, mitigating over-smoothing and avoiding the computational cost of stacking many layers. The model performs transformation to project node types into a shared space, node-level aggregation via normalized adjacency matrices, and type-level aggregation using an attention mechanism to update embeddings. VN-HGCN can serve as a universal framework applicable to other heterogeneous graph models. Experiments on node classification using ACM, DBLP, and IMDB datasets show that VN-HGCN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across most training ratios, particularly with smaller training data. Parameter sensitivity analysis demonstrates robustness to hidden layer dimension, number of layers, and number of virtual nodes. The time complexity is linear in the number of nodes and edges.

Postoperative hyperglycemia after cardiac surgery is common and linked to worse outcomes. Current protocolized insulin management often fails to account for individual patient variability, resulting in poor glucose control. The study developed GLUCOSE, a distributional offline reinforcement learning model using conservative Q-learning with Implicit Quantile Networks, to personalize hourly regular insulin dosing during the first postoperative day. Trained on MIMIC-IV (6,148 patients) and externally validated on eICU-CRD (649 patients), GLUCOSE achieved significantly higher estimated performance returns than clinicians’ actual dosing. Time in range (70–180 mg/dL) was highest when administered doses matched model recommendations. In multi-phased human evaluations, GLUCOSE’s dosing aligned more closely with endocrinologist recommendations than clinicians’ actual dosing, and its safety, effectiveness, and acceptability ratings were comparable to or exceeded those of senior intensivists. Feature importance analysis highlighted clinically relevant factors like current glucose and mechanical ventilation. Limitations include retrospective design, restriction to the first postoperative day, lack of dietary data, and exclusion of patients with ambiguous medication records. The authors conclude GLUCOSE shows promise for improving glucose management and warrants prospective trials.

SimulRAG is a simulator-based retrieval-augmented generation framework for long-form scientific question answering. To improve efficiency, uncertainty estimation scores and simulator boundary assessment (UE+SBA) selectively identify uncertain and verifiable claims for verification. A benchmark covering climate modeling and epidemiology was constructed, with ground truth verified by simulators and human annotators. Experiments show SimulRAG outperforms traditional RAG baselines by 30.4% in informativeness and 16.3% in factuality, while UE+SBA improves claim-level generation efficiency and quality.

It portrays the Taliban as a product of two decades of war, funded by billions in arms from the U.S. and Soviet Union, and notes their brutality toward women. The piece warns that bombing will kill civilians, worsen famine, and that air-dropped food packets are a cynical public-relations exercise unlikely to reach the needy. It argues that war will create more terrorists, questions the definition of terrorism, and points to U.S. support for various insurgent groups. The article suggests that oil and gas interests in the Caspian region, including a proposed Unocal pipeline through Afghanistan, may be a motive, and highlights connections between the Carlyle Group, former U.S. officials, and the defense industry. It calls for an immediate halt to the war, asserting that continued violence will escalate global anger.

The lecture discusses TaintDroid, a system to prevent data exfiltration by Android apps. Traditional Android permissions cannot restrict specific data types. TaintDroid tracks sensitive information from sources (e.g., GPS, contacts) to sinks (the network) using 32-bit taint bitvectors. Taint propagates through Dalvik VM instructions: move operations copy taint, binary operations union taint. Arrays, IPC messages, and files each receive a single conservative taint tag (union of components). Native methods require manual taint policy analysis. Taint flags are stored adjacent to variables for cache efficiency. Performance overhead is 3–5% memory and 3–29% CPU. TaintDroid cannot handle implicit flows (e.g., branches influenced by tainted data). Alternative approaches include low-level x86 taint tracking (expensive, risks taint explosion), static information flow systems with programmer-defined labels and compile-time checking, and TightLip, which uses doppelganger processes reading scrubbed data to detect leaks in unmodified legacy applications by comparing system calls.

Annetta Gibson sued Max Gibson for specific performance of their property settlement agreement. The trial court ordered Max to remove a trust provision allowing him to use cash value of insurance policies, and awarded Annetta attorney fees. Max appealed. The appellate court affirmed.

The agreement required Max to pay maintenance and secure it with an insurance trust. Originally term insurance was specified, but later whole life policies were substituted. Max's trust retained his right to borrow, pledge, or use cash value. Annetta sought removal of that provision, which the trial court ordered.

On appeal, Max argued the court created a new agreement. The court disagreed, finding the provision could defeat the trust's purpose by impairing the security, and enforced the original agreement. Max's contention that Annetta pleaded a different agreement failed because the petition and enforcement were consistent. Max challenged venue, but the agreement provided for jurisdiction in Platte County, where the dissolution was granted; the parties waived venue privilege, which was not unfair or unreasonable. Max claimed an adequate remedy at law existed via a claim against his estate, but the court held that remedy was not as plain, adequate, complete, and efficient as specific performance. Max contested attorney fees, but the agreement indemnified the successful party for litigation expenses caused by the other's failure to perform. Annetta was the successful litigant, so fees were proper. Affirmed.

The 52-week high is the highest daily closing price of a stock over a one-year period. It is used as a technical analysis tool to assess current price, calculate the percentage off the 52-week high, and gauge bullish sentiment. The 52-week range spans from the 52-week high (resistance) to the 52-week low (support), based on closing prices; intraday breaches that do not close beyond these levels are not recognized. The 52-week high trading strategy involves buying stocks trading near their 52-week highs, contrary to the “buy low, sell high” approach, because such stocks have been shown to outperform those far from their highs. Academic studies identify a “52-week high effect” where stocks near highs have better subsequent returns. A backtest by The Chartist of a momentum strategy using 52-week highs reportedly beat the S&P 500 over two decades. The passage then backtests two 52-week high strategies on the S&P 500 using SPY. The first uses moving average crossover rules opposite the Death Cross; its equity curve shows it is not a tradable strategy, and flipping the rules does not improve it. The second simple strategy also produces an untradable equity curve. The author concludes that while academic research on individual stocks supports the effect, backtests on the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 did not replicate a good 52-week high strategy, possibly due to the index’s tilt toward large stocks.

The Box & One defense uses four zone defenders and a chaser who denies the star player. To counter this overplay, an effective attack isolates the star in the post, exploiting the chaser's poor post defense and the difficulty of guarding against four outside feeders. The "Chase" Box & One offense begins with a Shuffle Cut entry: the high post sets a back screen for the star as the ballhandler penetrates and a post steps out. If the star is not fed, options include a screen-and-roll with O3 rolling to the basket, a base screen for O5, or a reversal pass to the star for weakside two-game action. A "Give & Go" entry involves a pass to O4, a basket cut by O1, and a high post screen for the star. If a reversal pass is unavailable, the star back cuts off a double screen from O3 and O5, flowing into Single/Double continuity. Success requires executing screens and post ups, defensive recognition, non-verbal communication, timing, and experience. Scouting is advised to anticipate defensive reads; otherwise, scout during the game, vary alignments, and attack weak defenders.

The Patient Charter, part of the NHS Constitution, sets out patients' legal rights, NHS pledges, and patient responsibilities. Rights include care free at the point of use (with some exceptions), treatment that meets needs and preferences, equal access regardless of personal characteristics, and waiting time standards with explanations if not met. The NHS must also consider community health needs. Quality and safety rights guarantee treatment by qualified staff in safe settings, clean facilities, nutritious food, and continuous improvement monitored by bodies like the CQC. Patients have a right to NICE-recommended treatments if clinically suitable, with fair local decisions and explanations for non-funding. Respect and consent rights allow refusal or acceptance of treatment, clear information on risks, and privacy of health information. Choice and involvement rights include choosing a GP, accessing comparative service information, involvement in treatment decisions, and the duty of candour if something goes wrong. Complaints rights ensure quick acknowledgment, investigation, escalation to the Ombudsman, judicial review, and compensation for negligence. Patient responsibilities include looking after one's health, treating staff and others with respect, following treatment plans, and participating in vaccination and screening. The Charter balances expectations with contributions, emphasizing partnership and shared responsibility.

Soccer coaches must prepare players for varying field conditions, as ideal conditions are rare. Pre-match inspections identify hazards or unplayable fields. Field surface factors include artificial turf (faster ball, heat risks), natural grass (type, cut length affecting speed and fatigue), crowns, crumb rubber, ground hardness, wet grounds (ball skips, body blocking needed), standing water (often unplayable), and slope. Anomalies like hard/soft dirt, clumps, uneven surfaces, weather effects (puddles, mud, ice), rocks, repairs, sprinkler heads, worn artificial surfaces, and baseball elements pose dangers. Field size variations require tactical adjustments: longer fields need fitness and weighted through balls; shorter fields need earlier, lighter passes; wide fields need more weight on crosses; narrow fields favor short passing. Weather demands vigilance: severe weather and lightning require evacuation (30-minute rule); cold requires proper clothing; dew mimics wet grounds; heat and humidity risk hyperthermia; rain increases wetness; snow accumulation makes fields unplayable (packed snow playable with contrasting lines); wind affects ball flight, advantage often with wind at back in second half. Referees are part of conditions: failure to appear requires contingency plans; rebounds off officials are live; players must adapt to varying calls and play to the whistle on offside. Perimeter factors include ad boards (landing awareness), drainage ditches (cover openings), running tracks (walk in cleats), people (avoid collisions, report thrown objects), crowd noise (use non-verbal communication), and overhanging branches (local rules). Lighting: sunlight into defenders’ eyes (use caps, eye black, keep attacks low), shadows, floodlights (prepare for outages), glare (shade eyes), darkness (abandon if goals not visible). Equipment: combination goals (local rules for hitting football posts), unanchored/unstable goals make field unplayable, missing corner flags replaced with cones, no nets are a nuisance (caution about referee errors), goal shape affects rebounds. The ball: extra balls are dangerous; multiple game balls must be identical; defective, wrong size, or waterlogged balls must be replaced; light/heavy/sticky balls require adaptation. Field markings: lack of lines supplemented with cones/saucers; multiple lines require recognizing soccer markings; non-parallel/wavy lines may be corrected or played as is. Coaching tips include using practice conditions to teach, establishing pre-game routines, knowing local rules, and applying safety measures to practices.

Most SARS-CoV-2 infections resolve within weeks, but some develop long COVID (symptoms ≥4 weeks post-infection), affecting an estimated 200 million people globally (43% prevalence). By the third pandemic year, 68.3% of the world had ≥1 vaccine dose; vaccines were highly effective against infection and severe outcomes. Despite this, susceptibility to infection and long COVID persists, and long COVID has caused >3,500 deaths. Long COVID can follow mild or severe disease. Risk factors in non-hospitalized adults include female sex, socioeconomic deprivation, obesity, and comorbidities. Healthcare workers (HCWs) are more vulnerable due to occupational exposure. Most vaccinated individuals report symptom improvement; a cohort study linked more vaccine doses to lower long COVID prevalence. Additional studies on vaccine effectiveness against long COVID in HCWs are needed. This case-control study at Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein (Brazil) included HCWs ≥18 years with RT-PCR-confirmed COVID-19 (symptomatic testing) from March 2020–July 2022. Cases had long COVID (symptoms >4 weeks, no alternative diagnosis); controls recovered within 4 weeks. RT-PCR used nasopharyngeal swabs. This study compared rapid eye movement (REM) sleep microstructure between patients with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), RBD associated with Parkinson’s disease (PD+RBD), and controls. Compared to controls, iRBD patients showed increased phasic REM sleep proportion. PD+RBD patients exhibited reduced sawtooth wave (STW) density and duration. Both patient groups had altered STW spectral characteristics with a shift toward higher frequencies. NREM/REM sleep transition durations increased progressively from controls to iRBD to PD+RBD, with PD+RBD having the longest transitions. These findings indicate that REM sleep anomalies in RBD extend beyond atonia loss and dream enactments, encompassing broader microstructural changes.

The lecture continues modeling honeycomb mechanical behavior. For in-plane brittle crushing, the plateau stress is derived by equating the applied bending moment on a cell wall to the fracture moment, yielding a strength proportional to the modulus of rupture times (t/l)². In-plane compressive properties are summarized: elastic moduli and three plateau stresses corresponding to elastic buckling, plastic yielding, and brittle crushing. In tension, elastic moduli are identical; there is no elastic buckling, and the plastic plateau stress is similar to compression. For brittle honeycombs, fracture toughness is calculated using continuum fracture mechanics, assuming a crack much larger than the cell size. The resulting toughness depends on cell size and is proportional to the modulus of rupture times (t/l)² times √l.

Triangular honeycombs are analyzed as pin-jointed trusses deforming axially; their modulus scales linearly with t/l, making them much stiffer than hexagonal honeycombs (which scale as (t/l)³).

Out-of-plane behavior is then addressed. The Young’s modulus E₃ equals the solid modulus times relative density, scaling linearly with t/l, creating large anisotropy. Poisson’s ratios ν₃₁ and ν₃₂ equal the solid’s Poisson’s ratio; ν₁₃ and ν₂₃ are approximately zero for small t/l. Shear moduli are estimated to scale linearly with t/l. Out-of-plane compressive elastic buckling is approximated using plate buckling with an end constraint factor of 4, giving a strength proportional to (t/l)³. Plastic buckling is approximated by plastic hinge folding; an energy balance gives a strength proportional to (t/l)², while an exact solution yields a (t/l)^(5/3) dependence. Brittle tensile fracture strength and toughness, and brittle crushing strength, are proportional to relative density. The lecture concludes by introducing wood and cork as natural honeycombs for future discussion.

An optimistic view holds that China's economy stabilized, but a 'dollar' perspective sees only a lower-level repeat of 2013-14, a reprieve from erosion rather than revived growth. The author contends China's global growth role is a myth, and the economy follows a globally synchronized trend, making another downturn likely. Past IP accelerations, such as in late 2012, proved insignificant. The 7.6% IP figure would only be positive if it starts a durable, sustainable acceleration, which appears unlikely given other statistics and the possibility of artificial stability.

The Turing GPU architecture introduces a unified L1 data cache and shared memory subsystem, reconfigurable up to 64 KB, and larger L2 caches. RT Cores in each SM accelerate bounding volume hierarchy traversal and ray/triangle intersection for real-time ray tracing, enabling hybrid rendering that combines rasterization and ray tracing. Enhanced Tensor Cores add INT8 and INT4 precision modes for inference, supporting NVIDIA NGX neural services such as DLSS, InPainting, AI Super Rez, and AI Slow-Mo. Turing uses GDDR6 memory with 14 Gbps signaling, improved compression, and delivers up to 50% higher effective bandwidth. New features include Variable Rate Shading, Texture Space Shading, Mesh Shading, Multi-View Rendering, VirtualLink for VR, NVLink for SLI, and an enhanced video engine with 8K encode/decode. The Tesla T4 GPU provides up to 130 TOPS INT8 and 260 TOPS INT4, achieving up to 40X higher inference performance and over 50X energy efficiency compared to CPUs. The RTX-OPS metric weights operations from CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, RT Cores, and integer units to reflect hybrid rendering workloads.

In Maclam v. City of Marquette, the plaintiff sued for injuries from stumbling over poultry crates obstructing a sidewalk. The city’s charter (Act No. 409, Local Acts 1895, subd. 16, §1, chap. 7) authorized compelling occupants to keep sidewalks clear but stated the city would never be liable for damages from neglect to do so. The trial court directed a verdict for the defendant under this provision. On appeal, the plaintiff contended the general state law imposed liability, the charter provision was repealed by Act No. 423, Local Acts 1899, and it was unconstitutional class legislation. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed, holding the charter provision exempted the city from liability, the general law did not repeal it, the later act did not repeal or modify it because both could stand without conflict, and the provision was not invalid class legislation under Michigan precedents. The court noted that many municipalities have similar limitations on sidewalk injury liability and they have been upheld. Judgment affirmed.

Cheryl Tickles appealed the Superior Court's affirmance of the Industrial Accident Board's denial of her workers' compensation claim against PNC Bank. Tickles was driven to work on February 17, 1994, arriving at Building 103 of PNC's Bellevue Complex an hour early to work overtime. She worked in Building 400, but her job had moved from Building 103. She stopped at Building 103 to use the only ATM in the complex, which was exclusively accessible to PNC employees via employee identification card. She withdrew ten dollars for lunch. Returning to the car in the parking lot, she slipped on ice and injured her back and left arm. She reported the accident, went to the hospital, and later underwent shoulder surgery causing twelve weeks of total disability.

The Board denied benefits, finding no nexus between the premises and her presence, primarily because her workday had not begun and she could have used any ATM. The Superior Court assumed she was on the premises but concluded she was on a personal errand unconnected to employment.

The Delaware Supreme Court reversed. It held that Tickles was injured at her place of employment. The "going and coming" rule bars compensation for travel to work, but an exception applies for injuries on the employer's premises, which includes parking lots. The record showed a business relationship between Buildings 103 and 400, and employees often walked between them via that parking lot. Thus, Tickles was on the employer's premises when injured.

The Court further held that the injury occurred in the course of employment. A reasonable interval before work is in the course of employment when the employee is on the premises engaged in preparatory or incidental acts. Using the employer-provided ATM, accessible only to employees, to obtain lunch money within a reasonable time before her shift was a reasonably necessary act of personal convenience incident to employment. Therefore, Tickles was entitled to benefits. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Lake Havasu City is the hottest place in Arizona. On June 29, 1994, it reached 128 degrees, the state's highest recorded temperature, making it the second hottest U.S. location after Death Valley, where Furnace Creek Ranch hit 134 degrees in 1913. Many of Arizona's highest temperatures occur along the Colorado River, including Bullhead City (record 126 degrees) and others. Phoenix's 122-degree record does not rank in the top 10. State Climatologist Nancy Selover attributes the extreme heat to the area's location downhill of California mountains, isolation, abundant rocks, lack of monsoon circulation, dry air, a heat-island effect from rocky terrain, and absence of irrigated agriculture. In a mandamus proceeding, the Michigan Supreme Court reviewed a trial court's denial of a motion to dismiss a law action. The underlying suit began as a chancery case in Livingston County against defendants who resided in Washtenaw County and were served there. Defendants appeared and moved to dismiss for lack of equity jurisdiction. The court transferred the case to the law side under 3 Comp. Laws 1915, § 12351. After plaintiffs filed a declaration, defendants moved to dismiss because they were not served with process in Livingston County as required by § 12430 for transitory law actions. The trial court denied the motion. The Supreme Court held that the transfer statute did not confer personal jurisdiction over defendants not served in the county where the law action was brought. The court further held that defendants' appearance and answer in the chancery suit, and their counsel's remarks during a colloquy about timing for filing a declaration, did not waive their right to object to jurisdiction in the law action. The writ of mandamus was granted.

The lecture introduces an advanced class on the evolution of proofs in computer science, beginning in the mid-1980s. The class focuses on interactive proofs (IP), which add interaction and randomization to classical proofs. NP is the class of languages with classical polynomial-time verifiable proofs. IP allows a polynomial-time verifier to interact with an all-powerful prover, using randomness; without randomness, interaction adds no power. The sum-check protocol is presented as a fundamental interactive proof: given a multivariate polynomial f of degree d in each variable over a finite field F, and a subset H, the prover convinces the verifier that the sum of f over all points in H^m equals a claimed value beta. The protocol has m rounds. In each round, the prover sends a univariate polynomial obtained by summing f over all but one variable, leaving that variable free. The verifier checks that the polynomial has degree at most d and that its sum over H equals the previous claim, then sends a random challenge from F. This reduces the problem by one variable each round. Finally, the verifier checks the last polynomial against an oracle evaluation of f at all random challenges. Completeness is 1. Soundness error is at most m·d/|F|, because distinct low-degree polynomials agree on at most d points. The verifier’s runtime is polynomial in m, d, |H|, and log|F|, assuming oracle access to f. The sum-check protocol is central to many results, including IP=PSPACE. The course will later cover doubly efficient interactive proofs, PCP, MIP, and using cryptography for succinct and non-interactive arguments via the Fiat-Shamir paradigm.

Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) is the non-traumatic, non-drowning death of a person with epilepsy, and a leading cause of lost life years. Risk is highest in patients with uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS), but even benign epilepsy carries risk. New medications have not improved seizure freedom rates. The strongest risk factor is poor GTCS control; peri-ictal respiratory dysfunction leads to apnea within ~3 minutes. Nocturnal GTCS and prone position are major risks: ~70% of SUDEP follows a nocturnal GTCS, and up to 87.6% of patients are found prone, though postictal prone positioning is uncommon (4.2–7.2%). Central apnea and autonomic instability are key mechanisms; prone position blunts arousal and reduces heart rate variability, contributing to both. The relative risk of SUDEP in prone versus non-prone position after GTCS is over 60-fold. SUDEP can be prevented by avoiding the postictal prone position, as shown by SIDS “back to sleep” campaigns reducing risk up to 75%, video-EEG documented SUDEP cases all in prone position, and reduced risk with nocturnal supervision. Intervention must occur within 25–180 seconds postictally; current seizure detection devices cannot deliver timely intervention, making autonomous intervention imperative.

The study aimed to develop an autonomous body repositioning mattress, Korus, for nighttime seizure management. The mattress is a twin XL size with an array of inflatable cells that expand up to 14 inches in 7 seconds (2 inches/sec), with 1000 lb/cell capacity. Cells are arranged in an 8 by 4 matrix with pad, spring, and base sections, using natural rubber and nylon cord, and include safety valves. A sheet sensor with 1,152 pressure-sensing nodes is embedded. Body position detection uses a Random Forest Classifier model trained on pressure maps to recognize prone, supine, left, and right positions. An iOS/Android app displays real-time body position and allows cell control. Ten normative control subjects underwent testing. Repositioning from prone to recovery position via manual control succeeded in 100% of cases, with an average time of 21.75 ± 5.85 seconds. Body position recognition accuracy for prone was 96.8%, with no supine/prone misidentifications; overall accuracy across all positions was 92.4%, with most errors in side positions. During long-term sleep recording, correct position was detected 97.3% of the time, with a false position change rate of 2.3 events/hour, always from supine misidentified as left/right; no incorrect prone detections occurred. One subject was excluded due to poor recognition from leg bending during sleep not captured in training.

The Korus system has first-in-class potential to monitor and autonomously intervene to prevent SUDEP, with an expected risk reduction of >50% comparable to SIDS prone avoidance. Remaining tasks include improving map quality, optimizing computing, and implementing a biomechanical framework. The device may be paired with seizure detection wearables, and future development includes seizure detection algorithms using the mattress sensors.

The PGA848 output-stage difference amplifier uses a 6.67kΩ feedback resistor with external access via DA_IN– and DA_IN+ pins, allowing parallel capacitors for noise filtering/shaping and custom attenuating gains. Internal resistor accuracy is 0.01% (CMRR ≥80dB), but mismatched leakage currents can degrade CMRR. Resistors have ±15% absolute variation; consider this for custom gains/filters. Do not source/sink current through these pins to avoid damage. The device has a single functional mode, operating with input-stage supply >±4.5V (9V) and output-stage supply >±2.25V (4.5V). The PGA848 is a monolithic, high-voltage, high-bandwidth, precision programmable gain instrumentation amplifier with single-ended output, combining a current-feedback input stage, matched gain resistor network, and four-resistor differential output stage. It offers eight binary gains (0.5–100V/V) via A0–A2 pins, for applications such as factory automation, data acquisition, and test and measurement. Linear input range extends within 3V of supplies with excellent CMRR; common-mode range depends on input common-mode, differential voltage, gain, and reference voltage. A typical application driving an ADS8860 16-bit 1MSPS SAR ADC uses ±15V input-stage and 5.3V output-stage supplies to prevent ADC overloading. REF6250 provides a 5V reference; the PGA848 REF pin is set to 2.5V via a precision divider buffered by OPA192. Three filters are employed: an input EMI/RFI filter, a CFB capacitor across feedback resistors (75pF gives 318kHz cutoff, varying with resistor tolerance), and an ADC charge reservoir filter. Overall bandwidth is 318kHz nominal, –0.1dB flatness to 41kHz. The REF buffer uses dual-feedback with RISO=20Ω, RF=2kΩ, CF=2nF for 86° phase margin; noninverting input has a low-pass filter. Modifying REF capacitance requires simulation to ensure >60° phase margin. Power supply recommendations: nominal performance at ±15V, custom voltages allowed within limits; output-stage supplies are clamped to input-stage levels. Supply voltages >40V (±20V) cause permanent damage. Layout guidelines include symmetrical input paths, low-ESR 0.1µF bypass capacitors close to supply pins, keeping input traces away from noisy traces, minimizing leakage/parasitic capacitance on DA_IN± pins, using keep-out areas in ground planes below input pins, minimizing thermal junctions, and managing thermal sources. The passage also covers PSpice for TI and TINA-TI simulation software, related documentation, update notifications, support resources, trademarks, ESD precautions, revision history, and mechanical/packaging/orderable information.

The European Space Agency's Gaia space observatory, deployed in 2013, has cataloged over a billion astronomical objects to create a 3D map of the Milky Way. Using Gaia's initial data release combined with data from the RAdial Velocity Experiment (RAVE), a University of Toronto team led by Jason Hunt calculated the Sun's orbital speed around the galactic center at 240 km/s. They observed a lack of stars with a specific negative relative velocity, corresponding to zero angular momentum, which indicated the Sun's speed. Combining this with proper motion calculations of Sagittarius A*, they triangulated the distance to the galactic center, deriving a refined estimate of 7.6 to 8.2 kiloparsecs (about 24,788 to 26,745 light years). This improved upon earlier work by co-authors Ray Calberg and Kimmo Innanen, who used only 400 stars. Hunt anticipates that future Gaia data releases will further increase measurement precision.

The ADS9803 uses the SMPL_SYNC signal to simultaneously sample all analog input channels of multiple devices sharing the same SMPL_CLK and SMPL_SYNC signals with identical external delays. A positive pulse on SMPL_SYNC centered around the falling edge of SMPL_CLK synchronizes all ADCs; this signal is required once after power-up with a free-running sampling clock, after restarting the sampling clock, or after a device reset. The SYNC signal resets the internal analog channel selection logic and aligns FCLKOUT to the data frame. Without SYNC, channel output data and FCLKOUT are not synchronized.

The device has a precision, low-drift internal voltage reference. For best performance, a 10µF ceramic bypass capacitor is connected to the REFIO pin to filter noise. An external reference can also be connected at REFIO; when used, the internal reference is disabled either by writing PD_REF = 1b via SPI (SPI_EN = 1) or by setting the SDI/EXTREF pin to logic 0 (SPI_EN = 0).

The ADS9803 supports 2-lane and 4-lane modes with single-data-rate (SDR) and double-data-rate (DDR) interfaces, selected via SPI. The ADC generates data (D[3:0]), data clock (DCLKOUT), and frame clock (FCLKOUT) from the SMPL_CLK input. The 20-bit conversion result is output MSB first in a 24-bit packet with the last six bits zero. In 4-lane mode all four lanes are used; in 2-lane mode D3 and D1 are used. FCLKOUT delimits each set of 2-channel data. Data clock frequency depends on sampling clock speed, data rate, and number of lanes; frame clock frequency equals sampling clock frequency divided by 4.

A data output randomizer can be enabled, XORing the conversion result with either the LSB of the result or a PRBS bit appended to the data. This randomization makes ground bounce uncorrelated with the analog input, reducing interference.

Two data averaging modes improve SNR: simple averaging reduces output data rate by a factor of 2, while moving average does not affect the output data rate. Test patterns (fixed, digital ramp, alternating) can replace ADC output data for debugging, configured via registers for channel groups CH[4:1] and CH[8:5].

The device is powered down by a logic 0 on the RESET pin or by writing to the RESET field, or by a logic 0 on the PWDN pin or writing to the PD_CH field. After power-up or reset, an initialization sequence of register writes is required with a free-running sampling clock. A speed-boost mode allows up to 8MSPS sampling rate for a user-selected analog input channel pair, with the other six channels idle; the sampling rate equals the sampling clock frequency.

The SPI interface uses 16-bit registers in three banks. Register write access is enabled with SPI_RD_EN = 0b. Reads require setting SPI_RD_EN = 1b and SPI_MODE = 1b, then using two 24-bit frames. Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology, with daisy-chain length configured in the DAISY_CHAIN_LEN register. Daisy-chain writes require N × 24 SCLKs per frame, and reads involve specific sequences.

Application information describes use in ATE systems, highlighting total unadjusted error (TUE) post-calibration, bandwidth modes (low-noise up to 22.7kHz and wide-bandwidth up to 700kHz), and step-settling performance. Power supply decoupling and layout recommendations are provided, including placement of bypass capacitors and avoiding digital/analog signal crossing.

The present disclosure relates to systems and methods for neuromuscular stimulation with volitional control by decoding neural activity to determine desired movements and delivering electrical signals to a target. Methods include measuring neural activity, removing artifacts, extracting features (e.g., signal amplitude, frequency range amplitude, wavelet scale amplitude, firing rate), and feeding features to decoders. Decoders may be individual single-motion decoders or a discrete multiclass decoder combined with a movement effort decoder. A body state observer, a physics-based dynamic model, uses decoder outputs and sensor inputs to estimate body part position and velocity, enabling dynamic adjustment of stimulation patterns (electrode movement compensation). Stimulation signals can be multiplexed with interleaved patterns to produce compound movements without interference. Training involves presenting visual cues (e.g., a graphical hand) while recording neural data, and using machine learning (e.g., support vector machines) to build decoders. The system can decode both discrete and rhythmic movements; a central pattern generator oscillator model can generate rhythmic patterns. An experiment with a quadriplegic participant demonstrated decoding and stimulation for thumb flexion, extension, and rhythmic wiggle, achieving high accuracy. The system provides a neural bypass for motor impairments due to neural damage.

Lawyers for Venezuelan TPS holders asked the Supreme Court to leave in place a district judge's order temporarily barring the Trump administration from ending their protected status. The TPS program, created in 1990, allows the DHS Secretary to designate countries for protection. Venezuela was designated in 2021, redesignated in 2023, and extended through October 2026. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem terminated the 2023 designation and extension. The National TPS Alliance and Venezuelan holders challenged the termination as violating federal law and the Constitution. District Judge Edward Chen temporarily barred Noem's action on March 31, calling it unprecedented. The Supreme Court stayed that order on May 19, with Justice Jackson dissenting. Chen later issued a final ruling on Sept. 5 that Noem acted unlawfully. The 9th Circuit declined to stay that ruling. The government returned to the Supreme Court, arguing the prior order made denial of a stay indefensible. The challengers countered that the prior stay order did not foreclose final judgment, as Chen's ruling was under a different authority and based on a new claim with a more developed record.

This study aimed to determine the proportion of excess mortality in India attributable to SARS-CoV-2, as opposed to the pandemic overall, and to evaluate verbal autopsies as a method for measuring pandemic burden in lower-income countries. A representative sample of decedents was obtained from the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) for 2018–2021. WHO-compliant electronic verbal autopsies (VA) were administered to next-of-kin, and cause of death was assigned by physicians using ICD-10 codes. SARS-CoV-2-attributable excess deaths were calculated by subtracting average annual rates of potential SARS-CoV-2 deaths (codes U07, U08) in 2018–2019 from those in 2020–2021. Statistical adjustments addressed over-inclusive deaths (pre-2018), under-inclusive reporting delays, and non-response to the VA survey.

The living sample included 892,905 unique individuals; 30,447 deaths were reported to CPHS, with 22,178 VA surveys completed (72.8% response). After excluding pre-2018 deaths, the final VA sample was 20,453. The all-cause annual death rate in 2020–2021 was 81.19% higher than in 2018–2019. SARS-CoV-2 accounted for 17.93% of all deaths during the pandemic and 33.15% of excess deaths. Cardiovascular disease accounted for 27.18% of all deaths and 23.15% of excess deaths. Respiratory deaths declined. SARS-CoV-2 death rates spiked during the lockdown (May–June 2020) and after the second wave (May 2021), but not during the first wave. Death rates increased with age, peaking in those over 80, though the largest number of deaths occurred in the 61–80 age group. SARS-CoV-2 death rates were higher among females, urban residents, and the highest income quartile, but not significantly so. Non-COVID death rates were higher among males and rural residents. State-level excess SARS-CoV-2 death rates were highest in Goa, Meghalaya, and Tripura, and lower in the Gangetic plain.

Limitations include potential misclassification of vaping-related deaths as SARS-CoV-2, imperfect statistical corrections for reporting delays and non-response, and an unvalidated modification of the VA instrument for COVID-19. Cardiovascular deaths may partly reflect undiagnosed SARS-CoV-2, leading to possible underestimation.

This study examines inclusive education for children with visual impairment in Myanmar, focusing on a phased system in Yangon. Inclusive education, promoted by the Salamanca Declaration and CRPD, emphasizes education in regular schools. Myanmar ratified CRPD in 2011 and enacted relevant laws, but inclusive education remains understudied. The study aimed to analyze actual practices.

Literature indicates regular schools foster non-cognitive skills like social and communication skills, while special schools provide specialized skills (Braille, mobility), role models, and safer environments. Debates continue over placement, with many countries using multiple-track systems. In low-income countries, one-track inclusion often proceeds without addressing educational needs.

In Myanmar, after 2011 reforms, 12.8% of the population has disabilities. The 2015 Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities guarantees equal education access. Public special schools, under the Department of Social Welfare (DSW), include two for visual impairment. Enrollment of children with disabilities is low.

The study used case study methods in Yangon, where visually impaired children attend special schools for primary education (Grades 1–5) and then regular schools for lower secondary education (Grades 6–9). Two special schools (A, public; B, Christian-run) and two connected regular schools (C and D) were selected. Data were collected via interviews, focus groups, observations, and document reviews with students, parents, teachers, principals, and officials.

Findings describe this as “limited inclusive education in phase,” close to a dual-track system. Informants valued special schools for Braille education, life skills training, supplementary study time, computer skills, and mental satisfaction, including safety from bullying. Regular schools were valued for developing social and communication skills in visually impaired students and fostering understanding and empathy in non-disabled students, with spontaneous peer support observed.

Limitations included lack of communication and cooperation between special and regular school teachers, partly due to different governing ministries. Regular school teachers depended on special school teachers, leading to insufficient consideration for visually impaired students. Relationships between students with and without disabilities were limited; only one of 12 visually impaired students reported a close non-disabled friend. Interaction outside class was rare, influenced by age differences, pre-existing friendships in special schools, and bullying. Additionally, many parents, especially in rural areas, were unaware of special schools, leading to delayed or forgone schooling.

The discussion concludes that the phased system effectively uses existing resources, meeting diverse needs beyond educational ones, such as life skills and mental well-being. However, challenges like poor inter-school communication and student isolation need addressing through training and inclusive programs. The study underscores that inclusive education must consider wider needs of children with disabilities and that low-income countries should adapt models to their contexts, rather than uncritically adopting one-track systems. The Ministry of Education and DSW must cooperate to develop a dynamic, context-appropriate inclusive education model.

The NVIDIA GA10x Ampere architecture delivers up to 2x performance improvements in programmable shading, ray tracing, and AI compared to Turing. The second-generation RT Core doubles ray/triangle intersection performance, adds hardware acceleration for ray-traced motion blur via a new Interpolate Triangle Position unit, and supports concurrent ray tracing with shading or compute. Third-generation Tensor Cores introduce Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity, doubling effective throughput for sparse matrices, and support new data types (TF32, BF16) alongside existing precisions. DLSS leverages these Tensor Cores and a 9x scaling factor to enable 8K gaming at 60 fps. GDDR6X memory uses PAM4 signaling to achieve up to 19.5 Gbps data rates and 936 GB/sec peak bandwidth. RTX IO, working with Microsoft DirectStorage, offloads asset decompression from the CPU to the GPU for faster loading and reduced CPU utilization. The A40 data center GPU provides up to 2x FP32 and ray-tracing throughput, up to 5x (10x with sparsity) AI throughput, 48 GB memory scalable to 96 GB via NVLink, and supports PCIe Gen4. Display engines support 8K60 with DSC, HDMI 2.1, and HDCP 2.3. The fifth-generation NVDEC adds AV1 hardware decode, and the seventh-generation NVENC provides high-quality, low-latency encoding. GeForce RTX 30-series and RTX A6000 GPUs realize these advances, with the RTX 3090 offering 24 GB GDDR6X and the A6000 featuring 48 GB GDDR6 and hardware-accelerated motion blur.

The passage outlines the contents of a volume of Foreign Relations papers. It begins with editorial notes and a list of papers by topic. The professor discussed quiz results (average 78–79) and outlined the lecture: continuing full factorial design of experiments, ANOVA for linear models, checking model adequacy for higher-order terms, and introducing blocks, confounding, and fractional factorial designs. Reading assignments were noted.

The lecture reviewed 2² factorial designs with two factors at two levels, using corner points to fit a regression model with mean, main effects, and interaction. Contrasts are formed by taking the difference between average outputs at high and low settings for each factor; the interaction column is generated by multiplying factor level columns. Scaling coded variables from −1 to +1 yields regression coefficients as half the effect estimate. The approach extends to 2³ designs with three factors and eight corner points, where contrasts for main effects and interactions (including three-way) are similarly constructed.

Regression can be performed using the design matrix with columns for mean, main effects, and interaction products. With only means at each corner, the model fits exactly; with replicates, pseudo-inverse provides coefficient estimates and residuals. ANOVA tests significance of effects: sum of squares for each effect is computed from contrasts, and F-tests compare mean squares against an error estimate.

An example using a break-forming experiment with factors punch depth (continuous) and material type (discrete) was presented. A 2² design with 10 replicates per corner was analyzed. Residual plots and ANOVA indicated all terms (mean, main effects, interaction) were significant.

To check model adequacy for curvature, center points can be added. For discrete factors, intermediate depth points can be used. A lack-of-fit test compares the deviation due to a quadratic term against replication error. An example showed a non-significant quadratic term, so the linear model was adequate.

Nuisance factors (e.g., temperature, time) can be addressed by holding constant, randomizing, or blocking. Blocking arranges runs so the nuisance factor is confounded with a higher-order interaction (e.g., AB interaction in a 2² design) to avoid confounding main effects. This concept leads to fractional factorial designs, where some interactions are deliberately confounded to reduce experimental runs.

This prospective diagnostic accuracy study in Madang Province, Papua New Guinea, enrolled 342 newborns within 72 hours of birth to assess foot length as a proxy for low birth weight (LBW, <2.50 kg) and preterm birth (PTB, <37 weeks). Birth weight was measured with electronic scales, and gestational age was based on last menstrual period or ultrasound. Foot length was measured using a plastic ruler on a cardboard box, averaging two measurements. The optimal cut-off was <7.7 cm for both LBW (sensitivity 84.7%, specificity 69.6%) and PTB (sensitivity 88.0%, specificity 61.8%). Positive predictive value was 42.7% for LBW and 15.4% for PTB. In 123 paired measurements, the mean difference between researcher and trained volunteers was 0.07 cm (95% limits of agreement -0.55 to +0.70 cm). The study found foot length measurement feasible for identifying LBW and PTB in resource-limited settings, though digit preference and implementation challenges require further research.
