In mid-May 2007, Victor Reinoso had 12 hours to recommend a chancellor for the Washington, DC Public Schools (DCPS) to Mayor Adrian Fenty. Mayoral control of DCPS, a system of 150 schools and 55,000 students, was set to begin in one month. DCPS was considered one of the nation's worst urban school systems, with half its schools failing federal standards, high administrative spending, and rampant patronage. Leadership turnover was high, with six superintendents since 1998.

Reinoso, named deputy mayor for education, had previously served on the DC school board. He became frustrated with the board's decision-by-committee culture and Superintendent Clifford Janey's incremental approach. After Fenty's election, Reinoso built a team, hired the Parthenon Group to collect data on DCPS's performance, and drafted the legislation for mayoral control. The Parthenon report ranked DCPS last in student achievement among reviewed cities and identified six core "Pain Points." The legislation, passed in April 2007, made DCPS a subordinate agency under the mayor, to be managed by a chancellor, and removed non-core responsibilities like facilities management.

Reinoso conducted a search for a chancellor, seeking someone who would rethink public education and not make excuses. Candidates included Rudy Crew, known for aggressive reforms in New York City and Miami-Dade, and Michelle Rhee, founder of The New Teacher Project, who focused on teacher quality. Reinoso also considered retaining Clifford Janey, wondering if the new governance structure would free him from his cautious approach. The search was interrupted when Reinoso took blame for copying portions of an education plan without attribution. With hours until his recommendation was due, Reinoso needed to choose a leader for DCPS.

The 13/48 trading strategy is a technical analysis method that uses the crossover of the 13-period and 48-period exponential moving averages (EMAs) to generate signals. A bullish signal occurs when the 13-period EMA crosses above the 48-period EMA, and a bearish signal when it crosses below. The strategy is momentum-based, performing better in trending markets but risky in sideways or choppy conditions. Backtesting on the S&P 500 from 1960 shows the strategy invested 66% of the time, yielding a 5.1% annual return versus 7.2% for buy and hold, with a risk-adjusted return of 7.8%. The strategy is a lagging indicator prone to whipsaws and is not a guaranteed path to riches.

This paper develops quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) methods for uncertainty quantification in a semi-linear parabolic reaction-diffusion PDE model of tumor growth. The model describes tumor invasion and proliferation with uncertain diffusion and proliferation coefficients modeled as random fields. The goal is to efficiently estimate expectations of clinically relevant quantities of interest by integrating over finitely many random variables from a truncated series expansion. QMC methods are employed to achieve faster convergence than standard Monte Carlo. The work extends QMC theory to nonlinear parabolic equations, providing well-posedness results and rigorous error estimates for uniform random fields, with numerical experiments including log-normal fields on complex domains. A key intermediate result is a bound on solution derivatives with respect to uniform parameters, requiring a novel proof due to the non-monotone nonlinear term. The paper is organized with problem formulation, parametric regularity bounds, QMC error analysis, and numerical experiments.

Mesh is a short to intermediate passing concept from the Air Raid Offense that creates natural picks and confusion. It works against man coverage by keeping playmakers on the move, and against zone by letting receivers find voids. It is a stable call against many coverages. Against man, the QB reads the RB rail route then the slot receiver using a pick. Against base zone (Cover 2, 3, 4), drag routes settle, and the corner route attacks Cover 2 safeties or soft corners. Mesh struggles against zone blitzes or simulated pressure that speed up the QB. Route coaching points: TE runs a deep drag (4-5 yards), FB an arrow route, TB a flare, X a shallow drag (3-4 yards), Z a corner route (vertical to 10 yards then steep cut). Against zone, drag routes sit in voids after passing the tackle alignment. QB progression is flare, shallow drag, deep drag, FB arrow, same against all looks. The mesh rail variation makes the RB the primary option on a rail route, with Z running a sit route over the ball. The sit route (8-10 yards) is a zone answer; against man it sets picks. Bruce Eien uses mesh as a smash concept variation in the single wing offense.

The passage describes technology for sealing high-pressure flow devices, such as plug valves and fluid ends, to address erosion of the device body. In prior plug valves, seals were mounted in recesses on inserts or retaining nuts and sealed against the valve body bore, causing bore erosion. The disclosed technology instead forms recesses in the valve body that intersect the bore, with seals mounted in these recesses and extending to seal against sealing surfaces on the inserts or retaining nut, transferring wear to the less complex and less expensive insert or nut. Similarly, in fluid ends, previous designs mounted seals on components like discharge plugs, suction plugs, and stuffing box sleeves, which sealed against the body bore and eroded it. The technology provides endless grooves or recesses in the fluid end body, intersecting the bore, with seals mounted therein to seal against sealing surfaces on the discharge plug, suction plug, discharge valve seat, suction valve seat, stuffing box sleeve, and suction manifold, shifting wear to those replaceable components. The passage also details a fluid end assembly comprising a housing with an internal chamber, intersecting conduits, and an endless groove formed in a conduit wall to receive a seal, as well as a manufacturing method involving forming such a groove. The approach aims to increase operating life and reduce downtime by making the mating components, not the body, the sacrificial erosion points.

The lecture defines entanglement as the inability to factorize a total wave function into a product of subsystem wave functions. For entanglement to serve as a resource, the subsystems must be physically separable and individually addressable. A single photon after a beam splitter is not an entangled state because the vacuum is not a separate system; similarly, the helium ground-state singlet is not a resource because the electrons cannot be separated. Photons are suitable because they can be separated. Entangled states exhibit non-local correlations and are fragile against decoherence. Weakly entangled states can be purified: by taking many copies, applying a controlled-NOT gate, and measuring target qubits, one can probabilistically obtain maximally entangled Bell states (e.g., 0 1 ± 1 0, 0 0 ± 1 1). The success probability relates to the degree of entanglement. Entanglement is quantified by the von Neumann entropy of the reduced density matrix after tracing out one subsystem; for pure states, this entropy measures entanglement, with Bell states having entropy 1. Creating entangled atoms is more difficult. One proposal is photo-dissociating a molecule to separate a spin singlet, but it is experimentally challenging. A probabilistic method uses light: two atoms emit photons that are mixed at a beam splitter. Hong-Ou-Mandel interference shows that two identical photons incident on a balanced beam splitter always bunch together, never exiting one per output. If both detectors click, the photons were not identical (e.g., different polarizations). By adding quarter-wave plates to scramble polarization, a coincidence detection can project the atoms into an entangled state.

CTPNet is a framework for multivariate long-term time series forecasting that learns three complementary dependencies: inter-channel (I1), intra-subsequence (I2), and inter-subsequence (I3). It addresses limitations of prior methods that neglect inter-subsequence and inter-channel dependencies. For I1, it uses temporal query-based multi-head attention with a learnable query matrix. For I2, it applies a linear-complexity Transformer to downsampled subsequences after linear encoding, capturing trend variations. For I3, it uses the same network on transposed outputs to model periodic dependencies. The architecture includes downsampling, a linear encoder, trend-wise and periodic-wise representation learning, a decoder, and de-downsampling, with a residual connection between I1 and the input. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, with CTPNet achieving the best results in most settings.

Ray Jones, Jr. was convicted of first-degree murder of his two-and-a-half-month-old son and sentenced to life imprisonment without probation, parole, or suspension. On appeal, he raised two assignments of error. First, he argued the trial court improperly admitted three inculpatory statements. The court found the first statement to a psychiatrist was voluntary and unsolicited, not requiring Miranda warnings. The second statement to hospital staff was also unsolicited and not the product of police interrogation. The third statement at the police station, made after defendant invoked his right to counsel, was held not to constitute interrogation under Rhode Island v. Innis because the officer’s remark about God caring for babies was consoling rather than reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response. Even if admission of the third statement was error, it was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt given the two prior consistent statements and other overwhelming evidence. Second, defendant contended the trial judge improperly restricted cross-examination of the psychiatrist. The court found the question about potential bad information irrelevant and no abuse of discretion. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.

The passage explores the integration of generative AI into higher education assessment. It highlights AI's rapid advancement and its disruptive impact on traditional assessment methods, such as essays and multiple-choice questions, which are vulnerable to AI-generated content. ChatGPT can produce high-quality, undetectable text and answer MCQs at or above student levels, raising academic integrity concerns. The paper outlines three strategies: avoiding AI through in-person exams, designing assessments that AI cannot perform well, or embracing AI by incorporating it into assessment design. A case study redesigned a postgraduate immunology coursework essay to integrate ChatGPT. Students received training, used ChatGPT to generate a draft outline, participated in peer evaluation of these outlines, and then wrote the final essay without AI. Surveys of 20 students showed 57.9% had used generative AI, mostly ChatGPT, but only 5% felt very confident. Students used AI for planning, drafting, and summarization, recognizing capabilities like text generation and limitations such as inaccuracy and superficiality. On plagiarism, 26% agreed using AI in assessments is plagiarism, 37% were unsure, and 37% disagreed. Students found AI-generated outlines useful but generic, and valued learning about AI's capabilities and limitations. The discussion stresses the need for AI literacy for students and educators, the potential for AI to provide immediate, personalized feedback, and the shift toward assessing higher-order cognitive skills. It cautions against unreliable AI detection tools and advocates transparent AI use. The conclusion recommends holistic AI integration, updated assessment policies, and training to prepare students for an AI-driven society while maintaining academic integrity.

A mobile agricultural machine includes a pose detection sensor that identifies its geographic position and orientation at various points along a route, generating corresponding position and orientation signals. A point cloud identification system uses these signals to identify a point cloud comprising points estimated to correspond to the ground surface over which the machine travels. An elevation generation system generates an elevation value for each point in the point cloud. A control signal generator produces a control signal to control a controllable subsystem based on the elevation values. The controllable subsystem may include a height control actuator for a movable portion such as a header or boom. A plane identification system may identify a plane through the point cloud to provide predictive elevation values of the ground surface ahead of the machine. Weighting function logic can assign a weight value to each point based on its distance from the pose detection sensor, indicating confidence in the elevation estimate. The point cloud is configurable via resolution, width, length, and offset settings. A geographic map location identifier generates a map structure of cells representing a field, and elevation values from multiple point cloud passes are aggregated with weighting to produce georeferenced map layers storing elevation, confidence, and other data. The method involves detecting pose, generating the point cloud, generating elevation values, and controlling the subsystem accordingly.

This document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP encrypted virtualization guests. It defines a 4KB shared memory area for guest-hypervisor communication during Non-Automatic Exits (NAEs), which occur when the guest must selectively expose register state. The GHCB MSR protocol uses the lower 12 bits of MSR 0xc001_0130 to exchange information before a GHCB page is established, including protocol version negotiation, encryption bit position, CPUID requests, AP reset hold, GHCB GPA registration, page state change, and termination requests.

Version 2 introduces hypervisor feature advertisement via a FEATURES bitmap, supporting optional features like SEV-SNP base support, AP VMSA creation, Restricted Injection, timer, APIC ID list, multi-VMPL, page state change for SEV-ES, SEV-TIO, and GHCB unregistration. The GHCB layout mirrors the VMCB save state area, with valid bits indicated in a bitmap. NAE events include standard VMGEXIT processing for exceptions like IOIO_PROT, MSR_PROT, VMMCALL, and #NPF/MMIO access, as well as specialized events: Page State Change (using a shared buffer structure to request private/shared page transitions or PSMASH/UNSMASH hints), SNP Guest Request and Extended Guest Request (for firmware requests with certificate data returned via GUIDs), AP Creation (to create/destroy APs at specified VMPL levels using VMSA pages), #HV doorbell page (for Restricted Injection event notification), #HV Send IPI, #HV Timer, APIC ID List, SNP Run VMPL, SNP TIO Guest Request (for trusted IO device binding and attestation), Secure AVIC (register/unregister APIC backing pages), and Termination Request.

SMP booting under SEV-ES/SEV-SNP requires methods like AP reset hold via NAE or MSR protocol, or the SNP AP Creation feature which allows VMSA-based AP state management and supports vCPU hotplug. NMI handling uses #DB intercept and an "NMI Complete" message. Debug register support relies on DebugVirtualization or DR7 intercept caching. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported. SNP Restricted Injection defines a doorbell page with PendingEvent (vector, NMI, #MC, NoFurtherSignal) and NoEoiRequired fields, and specifies host/guest behaviors for interrupt delivery, EOI optimization, and HLT interaction.

A qualitative study in Mauritius explored perceptions of micro-credentials among 10 educational leaders (public and private higher education) and four industry leaders (ICT and finance) through semi-structured interviews. Research questions addressed familiarity with micro-credentials, integration into academic credit systems, and perceived value for professional recognition.

Educational leaders defined micro-credentials as short, competence-based courses with assessment, representing less than a full qualification. Industry leaders described them as mini-personalised qualifications or credentials that build competency profiles. Interpretations varied; some did not distinguish certified micro-credentials from attendance-based short courses, though formal assessment was expected for credibility. The concept of badges was less familiar, with mixed views: some saw badges as interconnected with micro-credentials, others considered them equivalent, and some viewed badges as non-award representations while micro-credentials could stack toward larger qualifications. Respondents used “micro-credits” and “micro-credentials” interchangeably.

Regarding integration, most respondents favoured a hybrid model that allows existing credit systems to coexist with micro-credential-based recognition, enabling flexible credit transfer and minimal disruption. Micro-credentials were seen as allowing personalised learning paths and timely response to industry demands, though concerns about skills relevance over longer programmes were noted. The IT sector was suggested as a potential starting point, with enrolment numbers influencing adoption.

On perceived value, respondents viewed micro-credentials as a disruptive innovation requiring incremental implementation, experimentation, and prototyping. Short-term, they were recommended for professional development; long-term, with formalised structures and quality frameworks, they could contribute to degrees. Most education leaders considered micro-credentials and badge systems as the future of education, though some believed they would only complement existing systems. Recognition within the National Qualifications Framework (NQF) was deemed essential, but industry leaders highlighted challenges in balancing quality and flexibility, and the need for an agile NQF that accommodates informal learning. Policies should not hinder innovation.

The discussion confirmed a local willingness to accept micro-credentials, aligning with global trends. Varying definitions reflected the absence of a universal definition. Employers desired verifiable, quality-assured credentials and a shift toward competency-focused approaches. Reliable assessment by recognised awarding bodies was seen as key to employer confidence, while employers needed to transform qualification requirements into competency profiles. Mapping micro-credentials to existing qualification frameworks and credit systems was considered necessary for formal recognition. The NQF must evolve to integrate micro-credentials without necessarily assigning level descriptors, instead allowing micro-credentials to accumulate toward recognised levels via defined pathways. A competency-based approach with reliable assessment, credit mapping, and qualification pathways was identified as important for uptake.

The study concluded that although micro-credentials were not fully understood, there was broad agreement on their importance and the need for integration, especially post-COVID-19. A lack of a national framework was noted, with institutions using their own credit systems. The recommendation was to integrate micro-credentials into a unified framework enabling contribution toward recognised university credits and employer acceptance, formalising diverse learning and enhancing employment and career growth.

A Phase 2 clinical trial found that combining a 16-week initial course of omalizumab with oral immunotherapy (OIT) improved efficacy for children with multiple food allergies. The findings suggest omalizumab may safely facilitate desensitization to multiple food allergens, but larger studies are needed.

The passage details SD card bus speed modes and initialization sequences. After power cycle, cards start in 3.3V signaling. CMD0 selects SD or SPI mode; 1.8V signaling is only available in SD mode and, once entered, cannot revert to SPI or 3.3V without a power cycle. UHS-I uses 1.8V signaling for SDR50, DDR50, and SDR104 modes. Voltage switch is negotiated via ACMD41 (S18R/S18A bits) and executed by CMD11; success is indicated by DAT[3:0] high. UHS-I supports only 4-bit bus mode except for CMD42. Locked cards require CMD42 to unlock before ACMD6 can set 4-bit mode. Host selects driver strength (CMD6 Function Group 3) and bus speed mode (CMD6 Function Group 1). CMD19 provides a tuning block for sampling point adjustment in 1.8V signaling while the card is unlocked; tuning is mandatory for SDR104 hosts and optional for SDR50. Power cycle resets signal voltage to 3.3V.

UHS-II cards support both legacy SD and UHS-II interfaces. After power-up, the host checks for STB.L on the D1 lane within a timeout; if detected, UHS-II initialization proceeds through PHY initialization, device initialization, enumeration (assigning a Device ID), configuration, and SD-TRAN initialization that emulates SD commands. CMD0 restarts from SD-TRAN initialization. During SD bus initialization, the UHS-II interface is disabled before ACMD41 completes. UHS-II modes include FD156, HD312, FD312, and FD624; performance is based on Full Duplex mode. UHS-II hosts should support at least SDR50 for backward compatibility. Application Performance Class, Cache, Self Maintenance, and Command Queue features are defined. Low Voltage Interface enables initialization in 1.8V IO mode. UHS-III (FD624) extends UHS-II with a maximum bus speed of 624MB/s.

Card identification mode uses CMD0 to reset cards to Idle State with default RCA=0x0000. CMD8 verifies interface operating conditions and is mandatory before the first ACMD41 for SDHC/SDXC cards. ACMD41 identifies voltage range and capacity support (HCS, CCS bits); the host repeats ACMD41 until the busy bit indicates initialization is complete. CMD2 retrieves the CID, and CMD3 publishes the RCA. Data transfer mode begins after RCA assignment. CMD7 selects a card; data read/write commands can be aborted with CMD12. Wide bus (4-bit) mode is set by ACMD6 only when the card is unlocked. Erase, Discard, and Full User Area Logical Erase (FULE) operations use CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38 with specific arguments.

Password protection uses CMD42 to lock/unlock the card with a password (PWD) and optional Force Erase Password (FEP) for Card Ownership Protection (COP). COP cards require COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]) after power-on if FEP is set. Force Erase erases all data and PWD; FEP Force Erase requires the FEP. Locked cards accept only a limited set of commands. The switch function command (CMD6) uses Mode 0 to query supported functions and Mode 1 to set them, covering Access Mode, Command System, Driver Strength, and Power Limit. Function switching completes within 8 clocks after the status data.

This preprint reports a Phase 2/3 observer-blind, randomized, controlled study of the SII-NVX-CoV2373 vaccine in 920 Indian children and adolescents aged 2–17 years, randomized 3:1 to receive two doses of vaccine or placebo. Primary objectives were non-inferiority of anti-S IgG and neutralizing antibody responses compared to Indian adults, and safety assessment. At 14 days post-second dose, both the 12–17 and 2–11 year age groups met non-inferiority criteria (lower 95% CI bounds of 1.08 and 1.38 for anti-S IgG, and 1.17 and 1.70 for neutralizing antibodies). Seroconversion rates exceeded 98%. Immune responses against Delta, Omicron BA.1, and BA.5 variants were demonstrated. Solicited adverse events (injection site pain, tenderness, headache, fatigue, fever) were mostly mild and transient. No causally related serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest were reported. The study concludes the vaccine is safe, well tolerated, and highly immunogenic in this pediatric population, with responses non-inferior to adults.

A study examined the experiences of 17 third-year distance B.Ed. students and four lecturers regarding Physical Education (PE) teacher training at North-West University (NWU) in South Africa. The qualitative research used open-ended questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. Five themes emerged. First, interaction: lecturers were highly available via email and WhatsApp, responding promptly, which students appreciated, though some missed physical contact. Second, competence and passion: lecturers’ enthusiasm motivated students, and students reported increased confidence and subject knowledge. Third, obstacles: students often lacked foundational PE knowledge and sport experience; technological illiteracy and limited internet access hindered learning; and administrative delays in assignment processing at the management center caused late feedback. Fourth, practical training: videos were valued for demonstrating skills and allowing repeated viewing, but inadequate videos led to self-doubt. Delayed feedback on practical video assignments prevented immediate correction. Some students acknowledged expecting practical difficulties in distance mode. Fifth, program influence: the interesting content positively changed students’ perceptions of PE’s importance, with some shifting from viewing it as a waste of time. Recommendations included more face-to-face contact, technology training for students, increased use of videos, enhanced student interaction in the learning management system, and improved administrative systems.

The lecture covers hinged dissections, including the lack of general animation software and potential project ideas. It describes a hinged dissection construction for polyominoes using an inductive proof: a spanning tree of the shape is used, leaves are removed, and a base case ensures a hinge is present on every edge. The pieces are right isosceles triangles forming a cyclic chain. Similar methods apply to polyiamonds and polyabolos. Hardware examples include mesoscale salt-triggered folding, DNA origami, and chain-of-balls robots that can fold into any shape by feeding through a non-self-intersecting tube. A historical rectangle-to-rectangle dissection technique (Montucla, 1778) is shown, using superposition of tessellations. For a pseudopolynomial bound on the number of pieces in hinged dissections, the approach uses grid-aligned vertices, triangulation into equal-area triangles, chaining them, and gadgets to move hinges and overlay cuts without deep recursion. Finally, 3D dissections are discussed: volume equality is insufficient; the Dehn invariant (sum over edges of length tensored with dihedral angle modulo rational multiples of π) must also match. Dehn proved necessity (1901), Sydler proved sufficiency in 3D (1965), and the same holds in 4D, but conditions for higher dimensions remain unknown.

A passport requires proof of citizenship, U.S. domicile, and intent to return to reside and perform duties. Expatriated persons cannot receive passports. Expatriation is defined as quitting one's country, abandoning allegiance, and intending permanent residence and citizenship elsewhere. Residence abroad with intent to return and no inconsistent acts does not expatriate. Permanently withdrawing, acquiring a political domicile abroad, and avowing no return creates a presumption of expatriation. Expatriation is determined case by case. Even without expatriation, permanent domicile abroad bars a passport. Settling abroad after majority stamps one with the new domicile's national character; protracted residence presumes intent to remain, requiring explanation. Failure to fulfill a stated return intention raises doubt. Adverse factors: severed U.S. ties, no kindred/property, foreign marriage/home, wholly foreign business, plans excluding U.S. domicile. Favorable factors: maintained U.S. family/property ties, health reasons, financial exigencies, representing American enterprises abroad. For citizens in semibarbarous countries or under U.S. extraterritorial jurisdiction, former subjects face the same residence restrictions; others may reside indefinitely. The Department protects them with passports if pursuits are legitimate and not prejudicial to friendly relations. In Turkey, members of American communities with extraterritorial rights may inherit citizenship; section 1993 does not apply, and descendants are considered within U.S. jurisdiction.

The 200-day moving average (200 DMA) is a technical indicator that calculates the average closing price over the past 200 trading days to smooth short-term fluctuations and identify trends. A simple moving average sums the last 200 closes and divides by 200. It is a trend-following tool: a close above the 200 DMA indicates an uptrend, while a close below indicates a downtrend. Paul Tudor Jones uses the 200 DMA as a key metric, stating it helps avoid losing everything by getting out of positions. The strategy works mainly by exiting before bear markets, as shown by the S&P 500 in 2007–09 and oil in 2020. Without recessions, it underperforms buy-and-hold due to whipsaws. A backtest from 1960 shows the strategy nearly matches S&P 500 returns with substantially lower drawdowns, though it may trigger tax bills. From March 2009 onward, it returned a CAGR of 8.5% versus 12.8% for buy-and-hold, with a max drawdown of 19% versus 34%. Jeremy Siegel tested a variant requiring a 1% close above/below the 200 DMA on the DJIA from 1886 to 2006, finding improved risk-adjusted returns; after transaction costs, risk-adjusted returns remained higher but absolute returns fell short. The S&P 500 has spent 70% of the time above the 200 DMA since 1960 and 85% since 2010. The strategy has a win rate of 28% and a maximum of nine consecutive losers. Volatility tends to be lower when price is above the 200 DMA and higher when below. Daily bars are most frequently used; the simple moving average is preferred for its simplicity. A stock below its 200 DMA is considered in a bear market but may still be tradable. The 200 DMA rule serves as a long-term trend filter.

A memory device uses address obfuscation to map logical addresses to physical addresses within a memory array via a selectable mapping function. This study analyzed 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey data to identify demographic factors associated with insecticide-treated net (ITN) use among children under 5 and pregnant women. In Nigeria, 56% of households owned at least one ITN, with significantly higher ownership in rural areas, the North West and North East geopolitical zones, and lower wealth quintiles. Among children under 5, 41.4% slept under an ITN; usage was significantly associated with younger age, rural residence, North West and North East zones, and lower household wealth. Among pregnant women, 49.6% used an ITN; usage was higher in the North East and North West, among those with no or primary education, and in lower wealth quintiles. The findings show progress but reveal disparities, with coverage remaining below the 80% national target, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address regional and socioeconomic gaps.

The document specifies the GHCB protocol for communication between SEV-ES and SEV-SNP guests and the hypervisor. Non-Automatic Exit (NAE) events trigger a #VC exception; the guest inspects the error code, copies required register state to the GHCB, and invokes VMGEXIT to request hypervisor services. The hypervisor processes the request and resumes the guest after VMRUN. The GHCB uses a VALID_BITMAP to indicate which fields are valid; guest and hypervisor must set appropriate bits and reset the bitmap before each event.

Standard NAE handling involves copying faulting context registers to the GHCB, setting SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, SW_EXITINFO2, and advancing RIP after VMGEXIT. Specific NAE events include: IOIO_PROT (IN/OUT instructions, using a decrypted buffer for string operations), MSR_PROT (RDMSR/WRMSR), VMMCALL (hypercalls), #NPF/MMIO (MMIO access with reserved bit in nested page tables, using decrypted buffer and SW_SCRATCH), Page State Change (using a structure in the GHCB Shared Buffer to request page private/shared or PSMASH/UNSMASH hints; progress tracked via cur_entry and cur_page; error codes in SW_EXITINFO2), SNP Guest Request (requires shared request/response pages; hypervisor uses SNP_GUEST_REQUEST API, manages RMP updates, and may rate-limit; SW_EXITINFO2 returns status), SNP Extended Guest Request (returns certificate data in a GUID-indexed table; hypervisor validates page count), AP Creation (create/add or destroy/remove vCPUs at a VMPL level using VMSA pages; supports immediate or INIT-triggered use; enables vCPU hotplug), #HV Doorbell Page (GET_PREFERRED, SET, QUERY, CLEAR actions to manage a doorbell page for Restricted Injection), #HV Send IPI (uses x2APIC ICR format), #HV Timer (emulates APIC timer via SET/GET actions), APIC ID List (returns list of APIC IDs in shared pages), Run VMPL (switches vCPU to a different VMPL with associated VMSA and GHCB), SEV-TIO (trusted device binding; uses data pages for nonce, measurements, certificates, and TDISP attestation report; hypervisor returns required page count), Secure AVIC (register/unregister a private backing page per vCPU), Termination Request (guest requests termination with reason code and optional info), and Unsupported NAE (guest uses “Unsupported Event” exit code).

Guest identification of SEV-ES support uses CPUID leaves with specific bits for SEV, encryption bit position, and physical address reduction. SMP booting under SEV-ES uses an AP reset hold via VMGEXIT or MSR protocol; the hypervisor parks vCPUs and resumes them on SIPI without modifying registers. An AP jump table (4K, encrypted, page-aligned) is communicated from UEFI to OS via SEV-SNP Secrets Page or software NAE events. Under SEV-SNP with AP Creation, the guest uses RMPADJUST to mark VMSA pages and VMGEXIT to create/update AP state, eliminating the need for AP reset hold. NMI handling requires the hypervisor to intercept #DB but not IRET; the guest sends an “NMI Complete” message via VMGEXIT when ready. Debug register virtualization is supported via DebugVirtualization feature or by intercepting DR7 and caching writes. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

The #HV doorbell page (Restricted Injection) defines a PendingEvent field (vector, NMI, #MC, NoFurtherSignal) and NoEoiRequired byte. The host presents interrupts by writing the vector and setting NoFurtherSignal; it manages EOI via NoEoiRequired or explicit MSR write. The guest acknowledges interrupts by atomically exchanging PendingEvent with zero and performs EOI by atomically clearing NoEoiRequired or issuing an explicit WRMSR. Interrupt shadows are handled by executing HLT with interrupts disabled and re-evaluating pending events upon resume. Configuration uses VMGEXIT SW_EXITCODE 0x8000_0014 with GET_PREFERRED, SET, QUERY, and CLEAR actions.

This systematic review examines the application of artificial intelligence in assessment, grading, and feedback within higher education. It follows a rigorous methodology, searching databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ERIC, and Scopus for peer-reviewed articles published between 2010 and 2023. Twenty studies were included in the final review. The review is guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which emphasizes the integration of technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge.

The reviewed literature indicates that AI technologies, including machine learning and natural language processing, can automate and standardize assessment processes, enhancing efficiency and scalability. AI-driven grading systems demonstrate comparable accuracy to human graders in objective disciplines like STEM, reducing manual grading efforts and providing rapid feedback. AI also facilitates personalized feedback by analyzing individual student performance data in real time, offering tailored guidance that supports self-regulated learning and addresses specific learning needs. Students generally perceive AI-driven feedback positively, appreciating its immediacy and personalized nature.

However, the review identifies persistent challenges. Concerns exist regarding the accuracy and fairness of AI in evaluating complex constructs such as critical thinking and creativity. Algorithmic bias, arising from biased training data or design choices, may perpetuate inequalities based on race, gender, or socioeconomic background. Ethical issues, including data privacy, algorithmic transparency, and the need for informed consent, are highlighted as critical. The acceptance and adoption of AI tools by educators and students are necessary for successful implementation, requiring both technological proficiency and a cultural shift.

The findings suggest that AI should complement, not replace, human judgment. Educators play an indispensable role in interpreting assessment outcomes and providing contextualized feedback. The review calls for transparent policies, diverse training data, and ongoing monitoring to mitigate bias and ensure equitable outcomes. Future research should focus on validating AI-driven assessment methods across diverse contexts, assessing long-term impacts on learning outcomes, and developing ethically sound frameworks through interdisciplinary collaboration. In conclusion, AI holds transformative potential for higher education assessment, offering efficiency and personalization, but its integration must address algorithmic bias, validity concerns, and ethical considerations to foster inclusive and effective learning environments.

The author argues that K-12 education overemphasizes skills like critical thinking, metacognition, and 21st-century skills while devaluing the teaching of actual knowledge. He critiques "portrait of the graduate" lists that focus on metacognitive, behavioral, and ethical goals without emphasizing knowledge acquisition, noting that critical thinking requires something to think about. Two reasons for neglecting knowledge are addressed: the equation of knowing with "memorization" (though experts rely on memorized information) and the belief that one can always "look it up." Using string theory as an example, he shows that understanding complex topics requires deep prior knowledge, not just internet searches. Research indicates that background knowledge is essential for reading comprehension; for instance, understanding a cricket reference requires cultural knowledge. Evidence of knowledge's decline includes grade inflation, reduced state testing requirements, and the fact that only one state with a content-rich curriculum showed NAEP gains through the COVID years. A counter-push involves high-quality instructional materials (HQIM), with fifteen states joining a network to adopt them, but many approved ELA curricula still lack sequential knowledge building. AI misuse threatens to dumb down strong curricula. The author concludes that poorer students' reading gaps have widened, and that knowledge is essential for a fully livable life, as Socrates suggested.

On April 20, 2010, an explosion and fire occurred on the Deepwater Horizon rig, which was drilling the Macondo well for BP in the Gulf of Mexico. The disaster killed 11 workers and resulted in the largest marine oil spill in U.S. waters, releasing nearly five million barrels of oil by the time the well was capped. The passage details three key decisions made in closing the well that involved trade-offs of cost, time, and safety. BP chose a long string casing design with fewer barriers to gas flow over a more expensive liner/tieback option. Despite a Halliburton model recommending 21 centralizers to prevent gas flow issues, BP decided to use only six. BP also chose not to run a cement bond log to evaluate the cement job's integrity, sending Schlumberger workers home. The passage also outlines BP's history, including its organizational restructuring into an "asset federation" model and previous safety incidents at Texas City and Prudhoe Bay. In the aftermath, BP established a $20 billion escrow fund to compensate affected individuals and businesses.

Fossils once thought to be decomposed material may be reclassified as animals. Researchers analyzed 39 fossils from Newfoundland near Mistaken Point, dating to about 560 million years ago. The spongelike creature, named after punk rocker John Lydon for its spiky look, had fingerlike tubes and pores, indicating it was a filter feeder. It was almost 53 cm long, rounded at one end, pointed at the other, with a domed upper body, and likely lived on other organisms. The name also references a spiky fruit called jiggamint by the Beothuk. The creature resembles a sponge and may be an ancestor of modern sponges. Pores confirmed it was an animal, not decomposed gunk. The discovery aids understanding of early life.

The lecture covers limited attention. It first reviews evidence of inattention, including change blindness experiments, the gorilla test, and dichotic listening tasks, which show attention is limited and can be directed but misses unattended information. Factors affecting attention include physical environment, distractions, worries, sleep, and poverty. Even in high-stakes settings like stock markets, inattention occurs: the EntreMed case showed a stock price jump on old news when it became more salient, and confusion between Zoom Technologies and Zoom Video Communications led to mispricing.

To measure inattention, Chetty et al. study tax salience using a model where perceived value depends on a visible component and an opaque component weighted by (1−θ), with θ as the inattention parameter. In a grocery store experiment, making sales tax fully salient via modified price tags reduced demand by 8.8% relative to baseline. A triple-difference estimate, combined with a price elasticity of 1.59, yielded θ≈0.75, meaning consumers react only about a quarter as much to sales tax changes as to other price changes. Non-experimental evidence on beer consumption comparing excise taxes (included in the price) and sales taxes (added at register) found near-complete inattention to sales taxes. The discussion notes that inattention to taxes can be beneficial for revenue generation by minimizing distortion, but for sin goods where behavior change is desired, salient taxes are preferable.

The lecture then addresses whether inattention can have large welfare effects. A model by Schwartzstein posits that current beliefs determine what is attended to, which shapes future beliefs; if people lack the correct theory, they may never attend to important information, leading to persistent biases. An example is seaweed farming in Indonesia: experienced farmers neglected pod size as a relevant factor, could not state optimal pod size, and did not learn from their own experimental trials. When trial data was summarized and presented to them, farming behavior changed significantly, indicating prior inattention due to not considering pod size important. This demonstrates that limited attention can cause arbitrarily large and persistent welfare losses because individuals never encode or learn from available information that contradicts their existing model.

In his first inaugural address, President Franklin D. Roosevelt calls for candor and asserts that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." He describes material difficulties: shrunken values, rising taxes, curtailed government income, frozen exchange, industrial decline, farm surpluses, lost savings, and widespread unemployment. He states that distress stems not from lack of resources but from the failure and abdication of the "money changers," whose practices are indicted. He calls for restoring social values above monetary profit, and for an end to selfish wrongdoing in banking and business. The primary task is to put people to work through direct government recruiting as in wartime, while undertaking projects to use natural resources. He proposes addressing population imbalance by land redistribution, raising agricultural prices, preventing foreclosures, reducing government costs, unifying relief, and national planning for transportation and utilities. He demands strict supervision of banking and credits to end speculation, and an adequate but sound currency. He will urge detailed measures on a special session of Congress. He prioritizes national economic recovery over international trade, though he will work for world trade readjustment. He dedicates the nation to a "good neighbor" policy. He emphasizes interdependence and the need for discipline and sacrifice as in armed strife. He states that if Congress fails to act and the emergency remains critical, he will ask for broad executive power to wage war against the emergency as if invaded. He concludes with a call for national unity, moral values, and God's blessing.

The flexbone offense is a run-heavy system evolved from the wishbone, moving two running backs (A-backs) closer to the line of scrimmage to add a pass threat. It relies on option plays and misdirection. Required personnel: a decisive, running quarterback with adequate passing ability; a powerful, athletic fullback (B-back) for inside running; quick, agile A-backs who can block, run, and catch; wide receivers who are strong blockers and deep threats; and athletic offensive linemen skilled in cut and combo blocks. Strengths include its uniqueness causing defensive preparation challenges, ball control, time of possession, assignment confusion, and physically wearing down opponents. Weaknesses are a limited passing game making comebacks difficult, heavy practice demands for option timing, and struggles in bad weather due to timing and ball security. Common formations: Double Slot (balanced, often with motion), Trips (one A-back split wide), and Receivers Over (outside receiver moves to opposite side, ineligible, to test defensive adjustments). Key run plays: Triple Option (fullback dive, quarterback keep, or pitch to A-back based on reads), Midline Option (attacks middle, reading a defensive tackle with no pitch option), and Rocket Toss (quick pitch to motioning A-back). Pass plays: Play Action Wheel Route (fakes triple option, looks for post, wheel, checkdown), Toss Boot (fakes toss, bootleg with flat and crossing routes), and 4 Verts (four vertical routes with outside receiver options). The offense is used by service academies (Navy, Army, Air Force), was run by Paul Johnson (Georgia Southern, Navy, Georgia Tech, winning the 2009 ACC title), and Harding University (2023 Division II national champion). It remains common at smaller high schools.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU introduces TF32 tensor cores for deep learning training, providing up to 10x throughput over V100 FP32 with no script changes, and FP16/BF16 mixed-precision for up to 20x over V100 FP32. A100 Tensor Cores accelerate HPC with IEEE-compliant FP64 support, delivering 2.5x the FP64 performance of V100 (19.5 TFLOPS peak). Mixed-precision Tensor Cores for HPC, via the TCAIRS solver in cuSOLVER, show TF32 delivers the fastest and most robust convergence, with a geomean speedup of 2.0X over FP64 solver.

A100 introduces Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity using a 2:4 pattern, doubling compute throughput for deep neural networks. Sparse MMA instructions skip zero-value computations, achieving 2x speedup. The combined L1 data cache and shared memory is 192 KB/SM. Simultaneous execution of FP32 and INT32 operations is supported. HBM2 memory provides 40 GB capacity and 1555 GB/sec bandwidth (1.7x V100). The L2 cache is 40 MB (6.7x larger than V100) with 2.3x bandwidth increase, residency controls, and compute data compression.

Third-generation Tensor Cores improve data sharing across threads, reduce register file accesses, and include asynchronous copy instructions and asynchronous barriers for efficient data movement. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions the A100 into up to seven GPU Instances with dedicated compute, memory, and fault isolation. Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links and 600 GB/sec total bandwidth. PCIe Gen 4 with SR-IOV is supported. Error detection, isolation, and containment features enhance resiliency. Additional hardware includes NVJPG decode, optical flow accelerator, improved atomics, and five NVDEC units. CUDA 11 advances include task graph acceleration, async copy, async barriers, L2 cache residency controls, and cooperative groups. The DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs with NVSwitch and Mellanox InfiniBand, delivering 5 PFLOPS. A sparse neural network primer describes fine-grained structured sparsity and its accuracy preservation.

The MACD and RSI strategy is a trading method that uses both the Moving Average Convergence/Divergence (MACD) and Relative Strength Index (RSI) indicators. MACD is a moving average-based momentum oscillator primarily used to analyze trends; it consists of a MACD line (12-period EMA minus 26-period EMA) and a signal line (9-period EMA of the MACD line), oscillating above and below a zero line. RSI is a momentum oscillator that measures the speed and change of price movements, oscillating between 0 and 100, with traditional overbought above 70 and oversold below 30.

One specific strategy incorporates both indicators plus a third mean reversion filter. A buy occurs when all three conditions are met, and a sell when the mean reversion filter reverses. A backtest on SMH from 2001 showed 235 trades, an average gain of 0.88% per trade (including commissions and slippage of 0.03%), and a 73% win rate.

Other combination methods include using MACD to identify the overall trend direction while RSI identifies price swings, or using both as swing-trading oscillators for confirmation. For example, a long signal could be generated when the MACD line rises above the signal line and the RSI rises after falling into the oversold region; a short signal when the MACD line falls below the signal line and the RSI descends after rising to the overbought region.

Opinions differ on combining the two. Some technical analysts argue that both are momentum indicators, making the combination redundant. Others find it beneficial for additional confirmation. The passage states that the combination can be good but requires clear rules and backtesting to determine suitability. It also notes that the strategy does not work for all assets, mentioning XLP as a sector that moves somewhat independently and is favored for uncorrelated trading strategies. The focus should be on creating profitable strategies rather than determining which indicator is more accurate.

This paper examines how an Australian university addressed the gap in primary pre-service teachers’ arts education competencies by developing an Arts Specialism. Using a qualitative methodology grounded in Stephen J. Ball’s education policy sociology theory, the study analyses three contexts of policy-making: influence, policy text production, and policy practice. The context of influence reviews literature on neoliberal policies that reduced arts education curriculum time, leaving pre-service teachers unprepared. The context of policy text production employs critical discourse analysis to examine the Arts Specialism curriculum text and associated documents, revealing how language and negotiations shaped a four-course specialism covering dance, drama, media arts, music, and visual arts, with emphasis on experiential learning and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander arts. The context of policy practice describes implementation, including course structures, staffing, and adaptations during COVID-19, with pre-service teacher feedback indicating transformative experiences and increased confidence. Findings show the specialism provides 600 hours of arts education, countering the lack of training. Discussion notes ongoing challenges of time allocation and resources, but the specialism aligns with government requirements and fosters culturally responsive pedagogies. The conclusion presents the Arts Specialism as a pioneering model, identifies opportunities for expansion and further research, and acknowledges persistent time pressures and the need for ongoing policy-practice dialogue.

The Larry Swedroe Portfolio is a diversified investment portfolio based on evidence-based investing, allocating 30% to stocks and 70% to bonds. It typically includes small-cap value (15%), international small-cap value (7.5%), emerging markets (7.5%), and intermediate bonds (70%). The portfolio aims to provide long-term growth while minimizing risk, volatility, and drawdowns, and is intended as a “set it and forget it” strategy with periodic rebalancing. Larry Swedroe advocates value investing using a bottom-up approach to identify undervalued companies with strong fundamentals, and he favors small-cap value investing for its potential higher returns, less market efficiency, and diversification benefits. Rebalancing should occur at least annually or when an asset class deviates from its target by a set percentage (e.g., 5%), using a systematic, disciplined approach. A backtest from 2012 using VIOV as a proxy for US small-cap value showed an annual return of 3.71%, lower than historical returns, and the large bond allocation is expected to cause the portfolio to trail stocks over the long term, making it potentially suitable for risk-averse investors or pensioners. The passage also cites a presumed 30-year compound annual return of 6.28% with a 5.46% standard deviation. Swedroe’s strategies emphasize low-cost index funds, diversification across asset classes and geographies, a long-term perspective, and avoiding market timing.

Buying an iPhone involves trading off Android's open-ended features for security. Apple's closed platform prioritizes user privacy, though iPhones are not immune to vulnerabilities. iOS 10.3.1 security features include data encryption via password, PIN, or thumbprint, with prompts for two-factor authentication and an option to auto-erase data after ten failed login attempts, plus iCloud backups. iOS has built-in anti-malware, unlike Android's reliance on third-party software, and benefits from constant updates and an exclusive app store. Find My Phone allows remote location, locking, or data erasure via iCloud. Permissions require user confirmation for app data access, with fewer loopholes than Android. Apple's hardware and software exclusivity contrasts with Android's fragmentation, which hinders patching. In 2015, iOS had 375 disclosed vulnerabilities versus Android's 130, but iOS devices receive regular security patches while Android devices rarely do.

Danny Langston appealed a final summary judgment in favor of The Personal Service Insurance Company and George Johnson, Jr. Langston was injured in a Florida car accident while a passenger in a vehicle owned by George Johnson and operated by Fred Johnson. George Johnson had a surety bond issued in Ohio by Personal Service. The trial court granted summary judgment, ruling the bond covered only George Johnson's personal acts. The appellate court reversed. It held that under Florida tort law, George Johnson could be personally liable for Fred Johnson's negligent operation. The bond's coverage is governed by Ohio law. The bond was issued under Ohio's Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act, and Ohio Rev. Code § 4509.60 provides a lien for any final judgment against the principal for damages resulting from ownership, maintenance, or use of a motor vehicle. The court distinguished Kerr v. Personal Service Insurance Co. because the accident here occurred in Florida, making Florida tort law applicable. The court concluded Personal Service would be liable for a judgment if Langston obtains one against George Johnson, Jr., and remanded for further proceedings.

The passage describes SEV-ES guest-hypervisor communication. For NMI injection, the hypervisor must intercept #DB, not IRET, and use the guest’s “NMI Complete” message to allow another NMI. An example guest method sets a per-CPU variable, sets TF before IRET, triggers #VC on #DB intercept, and issues the message via VMGEXIT. Debug register virtualization: if hardware supports DebugVirtualization, the hypervisor clears intercepts; otherwise, it intercepts DR7, with the #VC handler caching writes and returning cached values for reads. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported. For SNP guests with RestrictInjection, the host uses #HV exception. A doorbell page defines PendingEvent (16-bit: NoFurtherSignal, reserved, #MC, NMI, vector) and NoEoiRequired (byte). The page is host-owned, accessed with C=0. NoEoiRequired non-zero means no explicit EOI; the guest atomically clears it for EOI, else performs VMGEXIT WRMSR. Interrupt shadows: guests HLT with interrupts disabled; host re-enters if events pending, guest then checks state as if #HV received. Doorbell page configuration uses VMGEXIT 0x8000_0014 with GET_PREFERRED, SET, QUERY. Host emulates APIC, writes highest-priority vector to PendingEvent, sends #HV if vector was zero and NoFurtherSignal zero, overwrites otherwise, sets NoFurtherSignal when sending #HV. It sets NoEoiRequired when no other interrupts ready, clears when multiple ready. For non-maskable events, it sets the bit and NoFurtherSignal, delivers #HV if NoFurtherSignal was zero. It marks interrupt in-service on guest acknowledgment, performs EOI on NoEoiRequired transition to zero. Guest acknowledges by atomically exchanging PendingEvent with zero, processes vector, and for EOI atomically clears NoEoiRequired or does explicit write. With IF=0, it clears non-maskable flags and NoFurtherSignal atomically. It validates vectors; non-cooperative host may cause denial of service, unexpected #HV with NoFurtherSignal set causes panic.

A single shot can determine winning, losing, and playoff hopes. Last shot situations are not simply about drawing up a play; they vary by court location and time remaining. Teams must maintain poise and confidence through preparation. Get the ball to your best player; never let them inbound. Read the defense and exploit overplay. Defensive strategy depends on the score: soft if ahead, pressure if behind. Non-shooters should crash the offensive boards, as most last-second games are won on putbacks. Keep plays simple to avoid breakdowns. Practice various scenarios with the game clock to develop timing, spacing, execution, and confidence. Physical conditioning is vital; a better-conditioned team can expect to win at least two additional games per season.

Holding for the last shot of a period, when combined with the first possession of the next period, can create a score swing of up to 12 points (14 if fouled). Automatically hold for the last shot with under 30 seconds left when leading or trailing by fewer than 8 points. Timing: at 10 seconds, players must be in position; at 8 seconds, initiate the play; at 3-5 seconds, shoot and go for offensive rebounds; at 0-2 seconds, an opponent rebound leaves insufficient time to advance.

Fundamentals: master long passes (skip pass, baseball/semi-hook pass to the opposite elbow) or last-second plays become worthless. Practice half-court shots and tipping for rebounds. Intentionally missing a free throw must be taught; the ball must hit the rim.

Strategies: save timeouts (minimum two needed). Communicate timeout situations. With 1-3 seconds, take a timeout. With less than 4 seconds, inbound to half court and then call timeout. Use a counter break with 3-4 seconds after an opponent scores. Take shots in line with the basket, dribbling down the middle. Have the bench stand and count down the clock. Remind the timer not to start the clock until the ball is touched inbounds. Practice plays from both sides. Develop passing skills and designate a reliable inbound passer.

Guidelines vary by time and situation: for 1-3 seconds, use inbounds pass only (Fly or predetermined SOB/BOB plays); for 3-6 seconds, use press break or predetermined plays with 2-3 passes max; for 6-12 seconds, push the ball and execute a last shot play. After opponent field goals or free throws, use Fly plays or quick breaks. On own free throws, intentionally miss and crash the boards, or make and then try to take a charge or intercept. On jump balls, anticipate the tap and call timeout. Maximum dribbles: 3 seconds—1 dribble; 5 seconds—3 dribbles; 7 seconds—5 dribbles.

Sixty-six years after the Battle of Kapyong, a Korean War turning point, Canadian veteran John Bishop doubts Canada could again play a pivotal role amid renewed tensions, citing U.S. President Trump's unpredictability. Former ambassador Marius Grinius notes Canada's "controlled engagement" policy under a previous government severed diplomatic ties with North Korea, costing influence. North Korea continues nuclear and missile tests despite UN resolutions. U.S. Vice-President Pence warned that "strategic patience is over," while North Korea accused the U.S. of risking thermonuclear war. Veteran Doug Finney urges action, citing North Korean suffering and the legacy of 27,000 Canadian veterans. A homework correction was announced; typos occur and are corrected to keep assignments manageable. The lecture then addresses reordering in Gaussian elimination using permutation matrices. Permutation matrices are unitary (their transpose is their inverse) and multiply a matrix to swap rows (left multiplication) or columns (right multiplication). Reordering is a form of preconditioning: it minimizes numerical error (pivoting) or fill-in, making large systems solvable.

The Plinko game is used as a diffusion example. A sparse matrix with two off-diagonals of 1/2 spreads probability equally to neighboring cells. Repeated multiplication shows the distribution flattening. A special uniform distribution satisfies A·A·P = P, illustrating an eigenvector: a vector that, when multiplied by a matrix, returns a stretched version of itself. The stretch factor is the eigenvalue.

For an N×N real matrix, eigenvectors and eigenvalues may be complex. Eigenvectors are not unique (any scalar multiple is also an eigenvector), but eigenvalues are unique for a given direction. To find eigenvalues, solve det(A - λI) = 0. This determinant is a polynomial of degree N, the characteristic polynomial, whose roots are the eigenvalues. A real matrix has at most N distinct eigenvalues; complex eigenvalues appear in conjugate pairs. The determinant equals the product of eigenvalues, and the trace equals their sum.

In a chemical reaction network, the rate matrix’s eigenvalues correspond to rate processes: a zero eigenvalue indicates a steady state, while nonzero eigenvalues give transformation rates.

Given an eigenvalue, the corresponding eigenvector lies in the null space of A - λI. Gaussian elimination on this singular matrix reveals the geometric multiplicity—the number of freely specifiable components, i.e., the dimension of the null space. Algebraic multiplicity is the multiplicity of the eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Geometric multiplicity is at least 1 and at most the algebraic multiplicity. When they are equal for all eigenvalues, the matrix has a complete set of eigenvectors and can be diagonalized.

With a complete set, form matrix W whose columns are eigenvectors and diagonal matrix Λ of eigenvalues. Then A = W Λ W^{-1}. This eigendecomposition allows easy solution of linear systems: x = W Λ^{-1} W^{-1} b. It also decouples systems of linear ODEs: ẋ = A x becomes ẏ = Λ y, with each component evolving independently with rate λ. For symmetric matrices, eigenvectors can be normalized so W^{-1} = W^T, making the decomposition simpler.

When geometric multiplicity is less than algebraic multiplicity, the matrix lacks a complete set and cannot be diagonalized. Other transformations exist, such as the Jordan normal form (almost diagonal) or Schur decomposition (upper triangular). The next lecture will cover the singular value decomposition.

Taylor Swift has broken numerous records. In 2006, she became the youngest artist to write and perform a No. 1 on the Hot Country Songs chart with "Our Song" at age 17. In 2009, she was the youngest CMA Entertainer of the Year. At the 2010 Grammys, she was the youngest Album of the Year winner for "Fearless" (later surpassed by Billie Eilish). She became the first woman to win Album of the Year twice with "1989" in 2016, the first woman to win it three times with "Folklore" in 2021, and the first artist to win it four times with "Midnights" in 2024. She holds the most American Music Awards (40), surpassing Michael Jackson and Whitney Houston. She has the most No. 1 hits on Billboard's US Digital Song Sales chart (29). She has the most Grammy Song of the Year nominations (eight, including "Anti-Hero" and "Fortnight"), though she has never won. She broke Shania Twain's record for most weeks at No. 1 on the Top Country Albums chart (99 weeks). "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" is the longest song to reach No. 1. She broke her own record for most VMAs Video of the Year wins with "Fortnight." Her Eras Tour is the highest-grossing tour ever at $2 billion. She became the richest female musician with a net worth of $1.6 billion.

A systematic literature review examined digital business strategy, digital transformation, and business digitalization in 16 selected Information Systems journals from 2000 to 2017. Search terms were applied to titles, abstracts, and keywords. From 292 initial articles, 54 were selected after title/abstract/keyword screening, and 28 after full-text review. Analysis followed Wolifswinkel’s guidelines: open coding, axial coding, and selective coding to identify dimensions. Publication activity increased from 2009, peaking in 2016. Studies concentrated on automotive, banking, telecommunications, healthcare, oil and gas, and manufacturing sectors, primarily in the US and Europe. The review identified 12 dimensions of digital transformation, 6 of digital business strategy, and 10 of organizational capabilities. Overlapping dimensions included external collaboration of ecosystem of digital platform (shared by all three), use of technology and structural changes (digital transformation and digital business strategy), digital leadership, agile and scalable operations, digitally enabled CEX, and digital artefacts (digital transformation and organizational capabilities), and dynamic capabilities (digital business strategy and organizational capabilities). A conceptual framework illustrates inter-relationships, positioning digital transformation as digital business strategy in action, enabled by organizational capabilities. The study offers theoretical contributions and practical guidance for C-suite management and IS researchers.

Editors of the Foreign Relations series have complete access to retired State Department records: central files, lot files, Executive Secretariat files, and overseas post files. Central files (1981–1989) and selected decentralized files will be transferred to the National Archives for declassification and access. Research uses restricted documents at the Reagan Library and other agencies. Printed material is declassified, but some comes from still-classified documents; full availability may be delayed. The Remote Archives Capture project scanned many records for declassification, but not all, causing uncertainty about attachments (noted as “Not found attached”). Editorial methodology: documents are chronological by Washington time; memcons by conversation time. Original text is reproduced exactly, marginalia in footnotes. Spelling and punctuation are retained, obvious typos corrected silently. Bracketed insertions show corrections, additions, omitted unrelated or classified text, with amounts noted. Underlining becomes italics. Abbreviations are preserved. Withheld documents are listed.

The paper addresses the multi-period resource allocation problem under stochastic demands. The static formulation determines all allocations at the beginning, yielding a convex optimization problem solved via bisection on the dual variable, but it uses only marginal distributions and ignores temporal correlations and sequentially revealed information. To overcome this, a sequential adaptive policy based on shrinking horizon optimization is proposed: at each time, an allocation is made for the current period by re-solving the problem for the remaining horizon, conditioning the joint distribution of future demands on observed demands. This heuristic does not guarantee global optimality but is designed to improve upon the static solution. The primary contribution is the formulation and empirical evaluation of this shrinking horizon policy. Simulations use synthetic data with jointly log-normal demands. The sequential method achieves higher revenue than the static solution and a roll-forward baseline, and its performance is close to an oracle upper bound. For independent demands, the sequential policy reduces to the static solution. The approach requires only conditional quantile functions of the demands.

The passage presents backtests of exponential moving average (EMA) strategies on the S&P 500 ETF (SPY). Strategy 1 (mean-reversion) buys when the close crosses below the EMA and sells when it crosses above. The 5-day EMA produced a CAGR of 7.41% and a max drawdown of 30.54%. Strategy 2 (trend-following) buys when the close crosses above the EMA and sells when it crosses below. The 200-day EMA yielded a CAGR of 7.84% and a max drawdown of 25.94%, half that of buy and hold. Strategies 3 and 4 use the same entries but exit after a set number of days. The best result was buying on a cross below the 50-day EMA and selling after 200 days, returning 10.17% per trade. An EMA is a moving average that gives greater weight to recent prices, making it more responsive than a simple moving average (SMA). It is a lagging indicator, not predictive. The formula is EMA = (K x (C – P)) + P, where K = 2/(n+1). EMAs can identify trend direction, act as support/resistance, and be used in crossover strategies. Mean-reversion works best with short-term EMAs, while trend-following suits long-term EMAs. Drawbacks include lag and false signals if the period is too short. The article concludes that EMA strategies are most effective with either a low or high number of days.

Research finds a strong correlation between a company's technological maturity (tech intensity) and business performance, with digital leaders outperforming laggards on revenue and enterprise value growth. Leaders include both digital natives and successfully transformed traditional enterprises, while laggards have legacy infrastructure and practices.

The study identifies four key cultural themes that differentiate companies with strong data cultures:
1. Adopting a growth mindset toward risk and continuous learning, viewing data as critical for evolution.
2. Leveraging data to create shared context, enabling collaboration, transparency, and decision-making.
3. Encouraging and empowering teams to examine data, set realistic goals, and measure performance against metrics.
4. Using common targets and objective measurements to align the organization, granting teams autonomy to pursue goals creatively.

Digital leaders actively embed these cultural elements into daily operations. They encourage risk-taking, experimentation, and long-term development, treating failures as learning opportunities. They invest in employee training on critical thinking skills. Leaders promote data transparency, making data widely available and discouraging hoarding, while maintaining appropriate governance. They embrace measurement to learn, using data-driven metrics and 360-degree reviews to track progress, which provides teams flexibility and autonomy. They align the organization through shared, transparently developed objectives that connect individual efforts to company strategy.

Digital laggards optimize their comfort zone, prioritizing short-term efforts and narrow training. They discourage risk, tightly control data access, and often hoard data as a source of power. Decisions rely on business judgment and a "culture of genius" rather than data. They set aspirational goals ungrounded in data, leading employees to avoid measurement and focus on process adherence instead of outcomes. Their goals often lack clear connection to strategy, causing misalignment.

Case studies illustrate a pharmaceutical company fostering localized experimentation within a regulated environment, and a retail company implementing real-time sales reporting to enable data-driven decisions.

Organizations tend to fall into one of four patterns: data novice, insight ready, tech enabled, and data reliant, each requiring targeted actions to build a strong data culture. Digital leaders emphasize that cultural change is challenging but essential, requiring consistent alignment between beliefs, espoused values, and day-to-day behaviors.
