This study examined pre-service teachers' views on a special education course delivered via distance education. Using a phenomenological qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 45 pre-service teachers at a private university during the 2022–2023 academic year. Findings showed that the majority were satisfied with taking the course through distance education. However, participants reported difficulties due to internet connection problems and concluded that distance education was less effective than face-to-face instruction. They emphasized the importance of class attendance for success, even in distance learning. Most participants recommended the distance education system, noting its importance for working individuals, the opportunity to become familiar with technology, and its economic advantages. A limited number also highlighted that it allowed practice in using technological tools. Conversely, some participants stated that distance education was not efficient for applied courses and should only be used when compulsory. Regarding preferences, 58% of participants wanted to take the special education course through traditional face-to-face education, while others preferred distance education. Reasons for preferring face-to-face included its effectiveness, quality, and understandability, whereas distance education was valued for flexibility in time and place, though technical issues and distractibility were drawbacks. On the obligation to attend, the majority believed attendance should be mandatory to learn and succeed, while some argued it should not be compulsory due to lack of digital tools, the availability of video recordings, or because conscious individuals would attend voluntarily. Participants also identified technical/material deficiencies in distance education, with most stating that the system should be developed, internet infrastructure improved, and technical support services enhanced; some called for free internet access and digital material support. The study concluded that addressing these deficiencies could improve the quality of distance education.

The Turing GPU architecture introduces a new display engine with native HDR processing and tone mapping per ITU-R BT.2100 to avoid color shifts. An enhanced NVENC encoder supports HEVC 8K encode at 30 fps, offering up to 25% bitrate savings for HEVC and 15% for H.264. The NVDEC decoder adds support for HEVC 4:4:4 8/10/12-bit and VP9 10/12-bit HDR. Turing improves encoding quality over Pascal and software encoders, enabling 4K streaming.

Turing GPUs include hardware support for USB Type-C and VirtualLink, an open standard delivering power, display, and data through a single USB-C connector for VR headsets. VirtualLink uses an alternate mode of USB-C with four lanes of HBR3 DisplayPort and SuperSpeed USB 3 simultaneously, unlike standard USB-C which supports either four lanes of DisplayPort or two lanes plus USB 3.

For SLI, TU102 and TU104 use NVLink instead of MIO/PCIe. TU102 has two x8 second-generation NVLink links (50 GB/sec bidirectional each, 100 GB/sec total), TU104 has one x8 link (50 GB/sec bidirectional). Two-way SLI is supported; 3-way and 4-way are not. NVLink enables advanced display topologies.

Ray tracing is computationally intensive, simulating realistic lighting, reflections, refractions, shadows. Turing introduces RT Cores in TU102, TU104, TU106 GPUs, enabling real-time ray tracing with NVIDIA RTX technology. Hybrid rendering combines rasterization and ray tracing: rasterization for primary visibility, ray tracing for secondary rays (reflections, refractions, shadows). RT Cores accelerate BVH traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, offloading the SM. Turing achieves over 10 Giga Rays/sec, about 10x faster than Pascal's software ray tracing. Denoising reduces required rays per pixel. Ray tracing supports physics, audio, AI visibility, and path tracing.

NVIDIA NGX is a deep learning-based technology stack using Tensor Cores for AI-based graphics acceleration. It requires Turing GPUs. NGX features are pre-trained, integrated via API, and managed by GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience. DLSS (Deep Learning Super-Sampling) uses a DNN trained on 64x supersampled images to produce high-quality output from lower input sample counts, improving performance. DLSS 2X mode renders at target resolution and produces output approaching 64xSS quality. DLSS provides better temporal stability than TAA. InPainting uses AI to replace removed image content with synthesized content. AI Slow-Mo interpolates frames for smooth slow-motion video. AI Super Rez increases image/video resolution by 2x, 4x, or 8x, creating new pixels intelligently.

Mesh Shading introduces Task Shaders and Mesh Shaders with cooperative thread models, enabling elimination of CPU draw call bottlenecks and more efficient geometry processing. It supports dynamic LOD selection and culling, and can implement effects like dynamic cutaways.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) allows shading rate to vary per 16x16 pixel region, with options from 1x1 to 4x4. It decouples shading rate from visibility rate. Applications include Content Adaptive Shading (lower rate in low-detail regions), Motion Adaptive Shading (reduce rate on moving objects due to perceived blur), and Foveated Rendering (reduce rate in peripheral vision). VRS can also increase shading rate with MSAA.

Texture Space Shading (TSS) decouples shading from screen space, shading texels in texture space and reusing them. It improves temporal stability and allows independent control of shading rate via MIP levels. TSS can be used for stereo rendering by sharing shaded texels between left and right eye views.

Multi-View Rendering (MVR) expands Pascal's SMP, supporting up to four views per pass (32 at API level). It efficiently processes geometry once for multiple viewpoints, with view-dependent attributes computed per view. Uses include canted HMDs, single-pass shadow maps, and instanced characters.

Turing supports DX12 Resource Binding Tier 3 (bindless constant buffers and UAVs) and resource heap Tier 2.

VR-specific features: VirtualLink single-cable, MVR for canted displays, VRS for foveated rendering, and RT Core-accelerated VRWorks Audio for ray-traced sound.

TU104 GPU: 6 GPCs, 48 SMs, 256-bit memory, 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, one NVLink. Used in GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, Tesla T4. Tesla T4 uses a TU104 with 5 GPCs, 40 SMs, 2560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, 256-bit memory, 320 GB/s bandwidth.

TU106 GPU: 3 GPCs, 36 SMs, 256-bit memory, 2304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, 36 RT Cores, no NVLink. Used in GeForce RTX 2070.

RTX-OPS is a workload-based metric for hybrid rendering. It derates peak operations by usage: Tensor 20%, FP32 80%, RT 40%, INT32 28%. Example: RTX 2080 Ti RTX-OPS = 78.

Ray tracing overview: Rays are cast from camera through pixels into scene. BVH tree structure accelerates ray/triangle intersection. BVH building/refitting handles scene changes. Denoising filters improve noisy images. Ray-traced shadows provide correct contact hardening from area lights, overcoming shadow map limitations. Ray-traced ambient occlusion (RTAO) offers more realistic definition than SSAO. Ray-traced reflections avoid artifacts of screen-space reflections and cubemaps, enabling physically correct glossy reflections. Game examples: Battlefield V and Shadow of the Tomb Raider use RTX for reflections and shadows. Real-time ray tracing is enabled by hybrid rendering, denoising, BVH, and RT Cores.

A "Reversal Day" refers to a stock or market index experiencing a substantial change in direction, either upward or downward, often with high volume. A "Bullish Reversal Day" (Selling Climax) occurs when a market moves upward after an extended downtrend, making a new low lower than the previous day but closing above the previous day's high. A "Bearish Reversal Day" (Blowoff) occurs when a market declines after a prolonged rally, making a new high higher than the previous day but closing below the previous day's low.

Causes of reversals include changes in market sentiment, economic conditions (e.g., interest rates, GDP), company-specific news, and technical analysis patterns. Spotting a Reversal Day involves identifying a change in trend direction, heavy trading volume, and using technical indicators like moving averages, RSI, and Bollinger Bands. Different markets (stocks, currencies, commodities, bonds) are prone to reversals for various reasons.

A backtest of a bullish reversal day strategy in gold (GLD) used rules: RSI(2) below 10 yesterday, today's low below yesterday's low, and today's close above yesterday's high. Exiting after 24 trading days yielded the highest average gain per trade (2.02%), with a good profit factor but few trades. A bearish reversal backtest flipped the rules (RSI(2) above 90 yesterday, today's high above yesterday's high, close below yesterday's low) and produced losses, with average gains significantly lower than the bullish version. The article concludes that the idea of a Reversal Day has merit based on the backtests.

The speaker, a coach, comments on the Stanley Cup Finals after his team was swept. He acknowledges Detroit beat them in every area, citing their finals experience and ability to capitalize on mistakes. He notes the series was closer than some sweeps, with one-goal games. He states he is proud of his team and organization, rejecting any notion they should be embarrassed, as other teams would have wanted to reach the Finals. He and George McPhee laid the foundation and instilled a new attitude. He is disappointed he couldn't make the team believe they could beat Detroit, but sees it as a learning experience, especially for young players who realized the extra effort required. He believes they will rebound and be better next year.

This study investigated burnout prevalence, associated factors, and coping strategies among prison officers at Nsawam Medium Security Prison in Ghana. A cross-sectional design was used, with 243 officers analyzed. Burnout was defined as high emotional exhaustion, high depersonalization, and low personal accomplishment. The overall burnout prevalence was 9%. Perceived causes included irregular shifts (71.6%), heavy workload (49.0%), and lack of training (47.7%). Emotional exhaustion was significantly associated with shift allocation, and depersonalization with junior rank. Female officers had higher odds of burnout; those with a diploma/certificate had lower odds compared to postgraduates. Common coping strategies were talking to colleagues (62.5%), looking forward to off duty (60.1%), and talking to family (54.3%); alcohol use was least reported (29.2%). The study concludes that addressing irregular shifts, workload, and training opportunities is needed, and notes that officers adopted positive coping mechanisms.

Health savings accounts (HSAs) are tax-advantaged personal savings accounts for medical expenses, available only to those with high-deductible health plans. They are a GOP concept gaining renewed interest as a potential replacement for the Affordable Care Act. Only about 20 million of 176 million insured individuals participate, partly because many lack upfront funds and face psychological barriers like stress and denial about future needs. Behavioral economist Mitesh Patel notes people are predictably irrational and hate losing money; a study showed that framing incentives as a loss (paying upfront and docking for missed goals) increased adherence. Making HSAs opt-out like 401(k)s could encourage saving, though it may cost the government. A study found HSA users consume less health care, with lower prescription costs but higher emergency room visits, especially among lower-income families. However, it is unclear if health improves. A financial therapist says people must confront their future decline and save more, but HSAs only help those with surplus cash after daily expenses, and many lack even emergency savings.

Cocoa futures are standardized contracts to buy or sell 10 metric tons of cocoa at a pre-agreed price on a future date. They trade on ICE Futures US (symbol CC, settled by physical delivery) and on CME Globex/NYMEX (symbol CJ, financially settled). Contracts expire in March, May, July, September, and December. The minimum price fluctuation is $1.00 per metric ton, equivalent to $10.00 per contract. The tick size is $10.00 per contract. The block minimum is 100 contracts. As of November 25, 2022, cocoa futures traded at $2,484 per metric ton. Stanford’s Program in Writing and Rhetoric (PWR) is a mandatory undergraduate writing program that the authors describe as widely regarded as a joke and failing to teach academic writing skills. Students are told to write from the heart rather than engage in rigorous source analysis. Grade distributions show over 80% of students receive A-range grades, making PWR an exercise in box-checking rather than skill development, with professors allegedly fearing negative reviews. The program is criticized for political bias, offering courses with liberal buzzwords (e.g., “Rhetoric of Social Justice”) and hosting events with a political agenda, while lacking conservative alternatives. Plans for a PWR minor are deemed ridiculous, as PWR’s mission is to provide foundational writing skills. The authors propose replacing PWR with a standardized, rigorous, source-based class designed by seasoned humanities professors and taught by current PWR faculty, free of overt political content.

Current cytogenetic testing for hematologic malignancies (karyotyping, FISH, microarrays) has limitations in resolution, subjectivity, and the need for multiple assays. Optical genome mapping (OGM) is an alternative that detects balanced structural rearrangements and copy number variants from 5kbp to aneusomies. The International Consortium for Optical Genome Mapping in Hematologic Malignancies provided a framework for clinical OGM implementation. This study extended that framework with a procedure for analysis and reporting of OGM data using Variant Intelligence Applications (VIA) software, focused on myeloid neoplasms. Ten retrospective samples (nine AML, one MDS) were analyzed five to six times each by independent technologist-director teams. Technologists performed timed reviews using custom VIA views and panels, checking sex chromosomes, ploidy, and curating variants against guideline-based panels. Directors then reviewed, classified, and generated reports. All standard-of-care (SOC) variants were identified by OGM via VIA; in five of six positive cases, sentinel Tier 1A variants were unanimously reported and classified. OGM detected additional novel variants not reported by SOC in five positive cases, with classifications ranging from Tier 1B to Tier 3. Technologist review times averaged 25.2 minutes for negative cases, 28.5 minutes for simple cases, and 47.3 minutes for complex cases, representing a roughly 50% time reduction compared to previous Bionano Access alone. The study concludes that OGM analysis with VIA offers a streamlined, efficient approach to interpret and report cytogenomic variants in hematological disorders, with potential to standardize analysis.

Industrial enterprises face geopolitical uncertainties, rising energy prices, raw material shortages, supply chain disruptions, skilled labor shortfalls, and sustainability demands, while digitalization drives fundamental changes in value creation. An IDC White Paper, based on a December 2021 telephone survey of 200 IT and departmental decision makers from discrete and process manufacturing enterprises with more than 500 employees in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, examines goals, challenges, and usage of IT-based simulation, modeling, data analysis, and high-performance computing (HPC).

Key business objectives for simulation, modeling, and analytics include increasing innovation (75% of respondents), improving product and service quality (57%), speeding product development and time to market, reducing costs, and strengthening decision-making. Deployment is highest in product development, production and process planning, and quality management, with expected deployment rising to up to 90% within two years. Challenges include data silos and the absence of a holistic data strategy; a unified “single source of truth” is deemed essential.

Technology usage includes virtual prototyping, simulation-based digital twins, high-performance data analytics (42% already use), and design optimization. Digital twins enable detailed digital mapping, monitoring, and simulation of products and processes, and are expected to drive new business models such as Product as a Service.

Demand for high-performance calculations is projected to rise significantly: currently 8% report high demand, while nearly half expect high demand in two years. 42% say their simulations are already outdated or inaccurate, and half report iterations and calculations take too long. 81% of respondents view HPC as a game changer for product and process innovation. HPC enables complex calculations, increases quality and usage intensity, unlocks new scenarios, and boosts innovation and agility. Currently, 26% of enterprises use professional HPC infrastructures, 39% plan or pilot deployment, and 15% are not engaging with HPC, citing high investment costs and limited awareness.

Among HPC users, 87% prefer external HPC infrastructures (e.g., cloud), 74% use or plan colocation, and only 6% operate on-premises HPC. Key challenges include security concerns (72%), high energy consumption and sustainability (58%), inadequate computing performance, complexity, and lack of internal/external expertise (42%). Cloud-based HPC architectures, especially public and hybrid cloud, are expected to be most important. HPC as a Service (HPCaaS) offers benefits such as cost optimization, flexibility, scalability, access to cutting-edge methods, and outsourcing of infrastructure operation. 81% of HPC users intend to implement HPC-based business models.

The paper concludes that HPC technologies are becoming a prerequisite for modern simulations and modeling, and that cloud and HPCaaS unlock significant potential. Recommendations include setting up virtual product development, devising a holistic data strategy, evaluating HPC operating models, considering scalability, security, and energy efficiency, and leveraging external expertise.

This study examines the influence of digital customer experience through e-commerce and electronic word of mouth on sustainable supply chain performance, mediated by brand image and supply chain image, within Indonesian ICT companies. Data were collected from 315 employees involved in distribution, using a questionnaire distributed to 568 randomly selected respondents from 10 randomly chosen clusters out of 15 in Indonesia. Analysis employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model confirmed reliability and validity: factor loadings exceeded 0.7, composite reliability was above 0.7, average variance extracted exceeded 0.5, and cross loadings supported discriminant validity. The structural model results supported all seven hypotheses. Digital customer experience had a positive effect on brand image (β=0.214, t=3.086), and electronic word of mouth had a positive effect on brand image (β=0.745, t=11.084). Brand image positively affected supply chain image (β=0.752, t=25.167), and supply chain image positively affected sustainable supply chain performance (β=0.907, t=84.298). Mediation effects were significant: brand image mediated the relationships between digital customer experience and supply chain image (β=0.161, t=3.059), between electronic word of mouth and supply chain image (β=0.56, t=10.274), and supply chain image mediated the relationship between brand image and sustainable supply chain performance (β=0.682, t=22.993). The model explained 82.3% of the variance in sustainable supply chain performance, and predictive relevance (Q²) values were above zero. The findings indicate that e-commerce-based digital customer experience and electronic word of mouth enhance brand image, which improves supply chain image and ultimately sustainable supply chain performance.

A gas turbine engine includes a core with compressor and turbine sections, a motor connected to a low-speed shaft, and a controller. Since 1789, each Inauguration day has renewed dedication to the United States. Washington's task was to create the nation, Lincoln's to preserve it from internal disruption, and the present task is to save it from external disruption. A nation's life is measured by its spirit and will to live, not years. Some doubt democracy, believing tyranny is the future, but Americans know otherwise, having acted decisively eight years ago when the Republic seemed frozen. Democracy survived crisis, built new structures, and maintained its principles within the Constitution, with functioning branches, an inviolate Bill of Rights, and free elections. Democracy is not dying; it has revived and cannot die because it is built on individual initiative and the free expression of a majority. It enlists enlightened will, constructs unlimited civilization, and is the most humane and unconquerable society. A nation has a body, a mind, and a spirit—the faith of America, born from centuries of freedom-seekers. This aspiration runs from Magna Charta to the Gettysburg Address. Though the nation must address material needs, the spirit is paramount; if it dies, America perishes. It speaks in daily life and governance. Washington's first inaugural warned that preserving liberty and republican government is staked on the people. Losing it to doubt and fear rejects that destiny. Preserving the spirit and faith justifies sacrifice for defense. Facing perils, the purpose is to protect democracy's integrity, mustering America's spirit and faith to go forward.

Singapore is a densely populated, multiethnic city-state in Southeast Asia with a meritocratic ethos and a globally competitive economy. Its education system, historically focused on economic needs, has seen special education evolve from a welfare-sector responsibility prior to 2004, when a dual system separated special schools from mainstream schools and integration placed the onus on students to cope. The year 2004 marked a watershed, as Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong called for an inclusive society, leading to Enabling Masterplans, ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and a dramatic rise in students with disabilities in mainstream schools (now about 80% of all students with special needs, with 20% in special schools).

Teacher preparation expanded accordingly. The National Institute of Education (NIE) began training Special Needs Officers (now Special Educational Needs Officers, SENOs) in 2005 through a one-year Diploma in Special Education. A Certificate in Special Needs Support was launched to train mainstream teachers (Teachers Trained in Special Needs, TSNs), and a professional development roadmap now requires all mainstream educators to gain foundational special-needs competencies. For special schools, teacher training began with the Certificate in Special Education (1984), later upgraded to the Diploma in Special Education (DISE) for special school teachers and SENOs, followed by an Advanced Diploma and master’s/doctoral pathways.

Contextual influences include top-down policy from the Prime Minister, a tripartite relationship among the Ministry of Education, NIE, and schools, and the uninterrupted rule of the People’s Action Party, enabling continuous, long-term planning. Salient issues remain: special schools are run by social service agencies rather than the Ministry of Education, with teachers recruited and paid differently; a continuum of options lacks special classrooms within mainstream schools for students with moderate-to-severe disabilities; and special educator preparation is shorter and less comprehensive than mainstream teacher training, with no undergraduate degree in special education. Recent shifts toward holistic education and the “Learn for Life” movement signal a growing inclusionary space, anticipating an expanding partnership between special and mainstream education.

The mass of a D-brane is defined as the ground state energy, which is the vacuum energy of all open strings living on it. This vacuum energy is computed by summing over two-dimensional surfaces with boundaries. The simplest surfaces are the disk (Euler number χ=1, weight g_s^{-1}) and the annulus (χ=0, weight g_s^0). In weak coupling, the disk dominates, so the D-brane tension scales as 1/g_s.

An alternative approach considers the gravitational interaction between two separated D-branes. At low energies, this interaction is mediated by massless closed strings, corresponding to a cylinder diagram with boundaries on the two branes. The same cylinder can be viewed as a one-loop open string diagram, where an open string connects the branes and goes around a loop. This channel duality shows that a tree-level closed string exchange is equivalent to a one-loop open string process.

The low-energy effective action for massless modes on a D-brane is the Dirac-Born-Infeld action. For constant field strength and small derivatives, it involves the determinant of the induced metric and the gauge field strength. When the gauge field is zero, it reduces to the relativistic volume element of the brane. The scalar fields describing transverse motion are massless because they are Goldstone bosons for broken translation symmetries.

Open strings interact by joining endpoints. The open string coupling g_o is related to the closed string coupling by g_s proportional to g_o^2.

When multiple D-branes coincide, open strings can end on any brane, giving N^2 types for N branes. Each string excitation becomes an N×N matrix. String interactions naturally produce matrix multiplication. A phase symmetry on endpoints combines with permutation symmetry to yield a U(N) symmetry on the worldsheet. In spacetime, this becomes a gauge symmetry, and the low-energy effective action is Yang-Mills theory with gauge group U(N). The Yang-Mills coupling squared is proportional to g_s times (α')^{(p-3)/2}.

Separating branes by a distance d in a transverse direction modifies the boundary condition for strings stretching between them, giving those strings a mass equal to the string tension times d. This corresponds to giving a scalar field an expectation value, breaking the gauge symmetry via the Higgs mechanism. The potential term vanishes when scalar fields commute, allowing diagonal configurations where branes are placed at distinct locations, breaking the gauge symmetry into a product of unitary groups.

This note traces the history of categorizing work by skill level in the United States. In 1917, Alba Edwards formalized a classification system with six "Social Economic Groups," where "skill" was applied only to work using "muscular force," and "unskilled" referred to occupations requiring no special training, judgment, or manual dexterity. Worker identity also affected classification; occupations with many children, young persons, or women were sometimes classified as semiskilled. In 1930, 14 million people worked in four "unskilled" groups: farm labor, servant occupations, factory labor, and other laborers. African Americans were much more likely to work in these occupations.

In the 21st century, "low-skill" and "unskilled" remained common terms, with skill level defined by education/experience requirements or job content analysis. Low-wage work paralleled 19th-century "unskilled" jobs and was expected to grow. The note details the history of four "unskilled" occupational groups. Farm labor, initially reliant on enslaved Africans and later on exploited sharecroppers, convicts, and low-wage immigrants, remained physically demanding and poorly paid, with a largely foreign-born workforce by the 21st century. Factory labor grew with industrialization, employing children, women, and immigrants for repetitive tasks; employment later declined due to automation and offshoring, with some remaining "unskilled" manufacturing using prison labor. Servant occupations, initially performed by indentured servants and house slaves, later became a dominant job for African American and foreign-born women; these declined but were replaced by service occupations like retail, fast food, and direct-care work, which were characterized by low wages, repetitive tasks, and unstable scheduling. Other labor included dangerous work in construction, coal mining, and warehousing, as well as new forms of digital micro-tasks and independent contracting.

Improvements to pay and conditions involved government, labor advocates, and employers. The Fair Labor Standards Act established a minimum wage and banned child labor, but exempted agricultural and domestic workers. Union activity secured wage increases and better conditions, but union membership declined significantly. Some employers adopted a "Good Jobs Strategy" involving higher wages and better work design. During the Covid-19 pandemic, nearly 70% of essential workers were in "unskilled" jobs, often working without adequate protection. The note concludes that the primary future-of-work challenge is job quality, especially for lower-wage workers, questioning how to think about work, workers, and pay for jobs historically categorized as "unskilled" but deemed essential.

A February collision between a passenger jet and an Army helicopter near Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people.

Reasons for the shortage include costly and time-consuming training, which can take 16 months to several years, and a high washout rate—about a third of trainees do not complete the program. The pandemic paused coaching and prompted older controllers to retire. Controllers must retire by age 56, and the FAA only hires candidates under 31. Less than 10% of applicants meet the criteria, which include U.S. citizenship, a medical exam, security investigation, FAA pre-employment tests, English fluency, and three years of progressively responsible work experience and/or a bachelor’s degree. Training involves months at the FAA Academy and two to three years of on-the-job experience.

Air traffic controllers earn an average of $144,580 per year. The profession is projected to grow 3% from 2023 to 2033, with 2,200 new openings annually. However, the job involves long hours, unaddressed mental health concerns, and unpredictable shifts.

T-Tamer is a framework for managing bi-objective trade-offs (e.g., accuracy–latency) in cascaded inference, where multiple sub-models of varying complexity are invoked adaptively. Existing policies are heuristic-driven, lack generalizability, and offer no efficiency guarantees. T-Tamer formulates routing and termination as a costly exploration problem over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with nodes as sub-models and edges encoding precedence constraints and performance dependencies. It computes a theoretically optimal strategy as a data-driven learner, operating as a plug-in component agnostic to sub-model training.

The work distinguishes no-recall strategies (final prediction from the last consulted model) from with-recall strategies (can return the best inspected model). It proves an information-theoretic impossibility: no-recall strategies cannot achieve any constant-factor approximation to the optimal utility, even in a two-node directed line, revealing fundamental limitations of confidence-based heuristics.

For with-recall settings, a dynamic indexing strategy is developed. In the single-line case, at each step a dynamic index is computed; if the current minimum loss falls below the index, the policy stops and returns the best model seen. This policy is provably optimal and precomputed via dynamic programming in polynomial time. The approach extends to directed trees and the transitive closure of a directed line (allowing skips while preserving order), remaining optimal and computationally efficient.

Experiments on synthetic data and real-world vision (VGG-11/13) and NLP (BERT-base, GPT-2) early-exit classification workloads show the recall-based strategy consistently achieves favorable accuracy–latency trade-offs, significantly reducing latency with limited accuracy degradation. Main contributions are: a general-purpose, model-agnostic T-Tamer framework; a proof that no-recall strategies cannot approximate optimal utility; and a provably optimal, polynomial-time dynamic indexing policy for routing and stopping over common DAG structures.

A training intervention research in Palghar District, Maharashtra, used a Training of Trainer (TOT) model to build a sustainable cadre of competent trainers for maternal and newborn health (MNH) in-service training within the public health system. The project scaled up a pilot from Pune District, adapting content to local MNH issues and targeting multiple health provider cadres.

The approach involved two phases. Phase 1 prepared eight clinically competent “Core” trainers (CTs) from the Pune pilot through refresher learning and virtual sessions with UK experts. Phase 2 developed local master trainers (MTs) in Palghar via six steps: (1) Pre-TOT screening of 48 candidates assessed teaching skills, work profile, and commitment, selecting 32 (25 doctors, 7 General Nurse Midwives). (2) TOT with pre- and post-assessments of clinical knowledge, skills, and teaching skills using adult-learner-centric principles and simulation; 18 achieved >85% composite scores, 14 scored 70–84%. (3) Staggered induction paired intermediate-scoring MTs with highest-scoring ones before independent training. (4) Continuous support from Pune CTs during training batches provided clinical guidance and feedback on pedagogy. (5) Virtual quality assessment by UK experts ensured standardized content delivery and corrected initial challenges in case-based teaching. (6) Virtual refresher sessions using the ECHO platform reinforced essential MNH skills through case-based discussion over 10 months.

Results: The methodical six-step approach optimized resource use, enabled objective assessment, allowed peer learning, and maintained quality. Post-training assessment scores of 463 trainee health providers showed significant improvement in clinical knowledge and skills (abdominal palpation, newborn resuscitation, eclampsia management). Palghar MTs reported increased clinical competency, application of protocols (e.g., DR ABC approach, SBAR referral tool), and avoidance of harmful practices. They gained confidence as trainers, adopting adult-learner-centric methods in other settings, and experienced career growth through recognition and motivation.

The discussion notes that the TOT model addressed skill deficits by upskilling existing human resources. Key elements included careful trainer selection, appropriate participatory pedagogy, longer time frames with supervised practice, and hybrid virtual/in-person delivery. The study recommends systematic investment in trainers, enabling service conditions, and further evaluation of long-term retention and costing.

The passage reviews the ESCAPE Dark Matter Test Science Project (TSP), which operates within the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) to facilitate open and FAIR dark matter research. It outlines the historical evidence for dark matter, the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, and unresolved astrophysical problems such as the core-cusp and missing satellites issues. The TSP integrates particle physics experiments: the ATLAS collider detector (dilepton resonance and semi-visible jet searches), the DarkSide direct detection experiment (WIMP-nucleon scattering), and indirect detection via Fermi LAT (gamma rays from dwarf spheroidal galaxies and brown dwarfs) and KM3NeT/CTA (neutrinos and gamma rays). These experiments produce constraints on dark matter properties like cross-sections, and the TSP provides common tools on the ESCAPE Virtual Research Environment (VRE), including the Baler data compression tool and astronomical software such as Aladin Lite and Gammapy.

The passage then translates these efforts to astrophysical constraints. Gravitational lensing by galaxies and clusters probes dark matter substructure; different models (CDM, warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter) predict varying subhalo abundances and density profiles, which can be constrained by lensed image distortions and flux ratios. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are key targets for indirect dark matter detection via gamma rays, with the expected flux expressed as a product of a particle physics term (annihilation cross-section, mass, spectrum) and an astrophysical J-factor (line-of-sight integral of squared dark matter density). J-factors are subject to uncertainties from halo substructure and stellar velocity measurements.

Several software tools are described: pyHalo simulates dark matter halos with substructure for lensing studies and can incorporate self-interacting dark matter core-collapse fractions; GAMBIT is a global fitting framework that combines particle physics and cosmological data (via DarkBit and CosmoBit modules) to test beyond-Standard-Model theories; AxionLimits and the Dark Matter Limit Plotter generate summary plots comparing experimental constraints. The review concludes by encouraging astronomers to use ESCAPE services to integrate astronomical dark matter searches with particle physics constraints, aiming for a collaborative, multi-messenger approach.

The ADS868xW device uses a standard SPI interface with CONVST/CS, SCLK, SDI, and SDO-0 pins. Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology, where all devices share CONVST/CS and SCLK, and the SDO-0 of one device connects to the SDI of the next. The device has three operational states: RESET, ACQ, and CONV, determined by the RST and CONVST/CS pins. A data transfer frame begins on the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends on the rising edge, which also starts a conversion. The device supports various data transfer protocols for configuration and reading data, including legacy SPI-compatible protocols with single or dual SDO-x, and source-synchronous protocols where the RVS pin provides an output clock. The device features nine configuration registers for settings such as device ID, reset/power control, SPI protocol selection, data output control, input range selection, and alarm thresholds.

By notes dated September 8, 1900, the United States and Russia agreed to arbitrate claims for indemnity of U.S. citizens for losses from the arrest and seizure of American vessels by Russian agents. Knees endure wear and tear, often leading to surgery in those over 50. Active lifestyles and healthy choices reduce joint, cartilage, and ligament damage risk. Maintain a healthy weight and exercise regularly to keep muscles strong and joints mobile. Hila Glick advises strengthening muscles around the knees and entire body, and working on flexibility and length. Danielle Wills recommends targeting hamstrings, quads, glutes, and hip flexors, gradually increasing weight. Keeping muscles long and flexible increases range of motion, protects against tightness, and improves balance. Stretching exercises like yogi squats and child's pose should be done only to a stretch, not pain. Low-impact cardio (cycling, swimming) maintains circulation, delivers oxygen and nutrients to ligaments, keeps cartilage healthy, and may prevent atrophy. Excess weight adds knee stress, increasing joint force and injury risk, including osteoarthritis. Persistent knee pain warrants a physiotherapist assessment for a tailored plan. Recovery involves strength and flexibility exercises to protect against further damage; physiotherapy can restore motion and help avoid surgery. Glick's exercises include quad strengthening with a bolster, glute bridges, wall squats, calf and quad stretches, and knee-to-chest with leg slide, repeated 10+ times and modified per injury. Do not ignore knee pain; stay active to prevent stiffening and compensation damage. Online physiotherapy platforms offer convenience. Knee issues can occur at any age, but most knee replacements are in those over 50, half over 70, due to cumulative wear. Osteoarthritis (cartilage and bone tissue degeneration) is the most common cause. Genetics matter, but healthy habits protect against excessive damage. When physiotherapy alone cannot rehabilitate a knee, surgery can improve quality of life; about 160,000 total knee and hip replacements occur yearly in England and Wales. Surgery carries risks like infection and deep vein thrombosis, and should be a mutual patient-surgeon decision. Modern knee replacements often last 25 years: over 4 in 5 total and 7 in 10 unicondylar replacements. Post-surgery physiotherapy speeds recovery and protects the new knee. Regular low-impact exercise improving flexibility and building joint muscles can protect healthy joints and relieve pain. Varying exercise routines benefits overall health.

The empirical stochastic inverse problem (eSIP) addresses situations where unknown parameters of a system are modeled as random, and observations correspond to a function of those parameters (the quantity of interest, QoI). The goal is to determine a probability distribution on the parameters such that observed data is a random sample from the induced distribution. Because the QoI map is generally not one-to-one, multiple solutions exist. A Bayesian approach is used, conditioning on a prior distribution. The solution is formulated via disintegration of measures, leading to a posterior density: \(\rho_\Lambda(\lambda) = \frac{\rho_D(Q(\lambda))}{\tilde{\rho}_{p,D}(Q(\lambda))} \cdot \rho_p(\lambda)\), where \(\rho_D\) is the output density, \(\rho_p\) is the prior density, and \(\tilde{\rho}_{p,D}\) is a surface integral over the generalized contour. Main results state that under general conditions there is a unique posterior with an explicit density formula, the density is continuous almost everywhere, the solution corresponding to the uniform prior has maximum entropy, and a numerical estimator based on importance sampling is asymptotically unbiased and strongly consistent. The uniform prior is the default choice as it assigns equal probability to points on the same contour. The posterior distribution is used to estimate probabilities of parameter combinations and for prediction.

Telecom, information technology, and energy suffered the most catastrophic losses; utilities had the fewest. Overall, 40% of stocks experienced catastrophic losses. When measuring excess returns relative to the Russell 3000, utilities ranked worst, followed by energy and materials. The median stock produced negative lifetime returns, while a minority achieved spectacular gains, explaining the index's positive performance. The conclusion reaffirms that utilities, information technology, energy, and materials are the worst sectors to invest in based on the JP Morgan data.

The document describes AMD AGESA (AMD Generic Encapsulated Software Architecture) boot procedures, call-out functions, and configuration options. It defines a sequence of entry points for system initialization and resume. AmdInitReset performs minimal processor initialization after reset, configuring execution cache regions and basic FCH parameters. AmdInitEarly completes full processor initialization, including HyperTransport links and power management, and allows additional cache regions. AmdInitPost initializes main memory, transitions from pre-memory to post-memory phase, and outputs memory configuration. AmdInitEnv transfers hand-off blocks from temporary storage to permanent buffers allocated by the host environment. AmdInitMid handles graphics display configuration after PCI enumeration. AmdInitLate generates ACPI and DMI tables (e.g., IVRS, P-State, WHEA, CRAT, CDIT) for the OS. AmdInitRtb saves processor context for S3 suspend and prepares for suspend. For resume, AmdInitResume re-initializes memory and silicon using saved context, AmdS3LateRestore restores registers after PCI re-establishment, and AmdS3FinalRestore performs final restoration before OS handoff.

Required host environment call-outs include AgesaAllocateBuffer and AgesaDeallocateBuffer for post-memory buffer management, AgesaReset for system resets, AgesaLocateBuffer to find allocated buffers, AgesaReadSpd to read DIMM SPD data via SMBus, and AgesaRunFcnOnAp/AgesaRunFcnOnAllAps to execute code on application processors, with AmdLateRunApTask as the AP entry point. Optional call-outs allow customization at specific points, such as AgesaHookBeforeDramInit, AgesaHookBeforeTraining, AgesaHookChangeExtVref, AgesaHookFchCustomize, and others for voltage adjustments, PCIe clock requests, and video BIOS repost.

Build options (BLDOPT_REMOVE_*) enable removal of code for unsupported features like specific DIMM types, memory technologies, interleaving, ACPI tables, and processor families to reduce ROM size. Build configuration elements (BLDCFG_*) specify platform-specific settings including VRM properties (current limits, slew rates, low-power thresholds), CPU frequency limits, PCI MMIO base/size, number of IO APICs, ACPI table customization, C-State and CPB modes, core leveling, and memory interleaving options. Customization mechanisms include build settings, wrapper modifications after AmdCreateStruct, Integrated Debug Services (IDS), and defined call-outs.

The AMD Security Processor (ASP) verifies AMD signatures on all AMD-owned boot firmware and acts as the root of trust for detection. SFS enables runtime firmware updates and extends the ASP's role by requiring signature verification before applying each update package. The system designer (OEM/ODM) owns the firmware root of trust for update. Unless AMD Platform Secure Boot is enabled, the OEM/ODM is also responsible for root of trust for detection of their own firmware.

Early OEM/ODM x86 code has full read/write ROM access, then enables restrictions (e.g., AMD ROM Armor) so only the SMM handler can write to the ROM. After lockdown, untrusted code executes. SFS allows the OEM/ODM to co-sign update packages to maintain their update root of trust. During early boot, the OEM/ODM may present a public signing key; the ASP then requires updates signed by AMD and countersigned by that key. Customer key maintenance is the customer's responsibility; AMD does not countersign customer keys. Subverting early trusted code to replace the co-signing key would already allow overwriting baseline firmware.

SFS patches are non-persistent across reboots and must be applied at runtime. In multi-socket systems, the first socket's ASP receives the patch, and the patch ensures correct application across sockets. Multiple updates are applied sequentially and in numerical order. BIOS developers enable SFS via APCB tokens (both off by default). If co-signing is configured, the SFS package authenticates first against the customer key, then the AMD key. The customer provides a public RSA key (2048-bit or 4096-bit) during early boot before BOOT_DONE, using RSA-PSS signatures. The key cannot be updated later.

Each patch checks existing System Patch Level and firmware versions for applicability. Packages can patch registers, replace firmware images, or update portions. SEV updates are automatically committed and prevent rollback; reverting requires a reboot. With SNP enabled, update pages must be HV-FIXED using RMPUPDATE. SFS provides measurements for attestation; some attestation schemes prevent updates to certain firmware, and AMD will not modify that firmware. Update packages ensure proper firmware versions exist before applying; if any part fails, the entire package is not applied to avoid a reset.

SFS commands require a 2MB-aligned TEE_EXT_CMD_BUFFER. For GET_FW_VERSIONS, the output page follows at +4k. For UPDATE_FW, the update package starts at +4k, with an optional co-signing header at +4k. A deployment agent creates the buffer, appends the co-sign header, the AMD package, and the co-sign signature, then communicates the request via the TEE mailbox. The ASP process: checks DRAM protection, verifies customer signature (if enabled), verifies AMD signature, loads and runs the patch, updates patch level, and returns status. GET_SFS_VERSION_INFO returns API version, current patch levels, and firmware version entries. UPDATE_FW loads, verifies, and executes the package only after full validation. Packages are named fam_<family>-<AGESA-Release>-SFS-<n>.pkg, with <n> starting at 1. Updates must match the specific firmware combination on the system. The update process runs in parallel with minimal performance impact; SEV/ES VMs require stop/restart for SEV firmware updates, while SEV/SNP VMs can continue operation.

This article addresses power consumption in HF-band RFID systems, particularly NFC used in mobile devices like smartphones, where communication increases battery drain. The target system consists of a battery-powered reader and passively powered transponders that receive power via inductive coupling. Typically, the reader provides maximum magnetic field strength, causing oversupply and energy waste. Measurements show a smartphone consumes 50% more power with NFC activated and no transponder, and up to 107% more when reading a transponder.

The article proposes dynamic magnetic field strength scaling to reduce energy consumption. Three investigations are presented: scaling during card detection, during communication (accounting for changing distance and transponder operations), and with multiple transponders. A method called PTF-Determinator is detailed for the card detection phase. It determines the power transfer function (PTF) by gathering electrical parameters from reader and transponder, approximating the physical relation factor (distance) through successive approximation of the magnetic field until the transponder responds, and integrating this into the existing communication flow. A library provides the PTF for power management.

A case study implements the PTF-Determinator for reading digital business cards with a maximum transmission distance restriction. Simulation with modified hardware shows up to 80% transmission energy savings. Measurement on real hardware shows 26% energy reduction for the transmission when the distance is within the maximum, and 75% reduction when the distance exceeds the maximum (by cutting off power). Combined with smartphone power measurements, the method could reduce battery drain by up to 13% in a real environment and 39% when power is cut off beyond the maximum distance.

The 4-2-5 defense combines elements of the 4-3 and 3-3-5 defenses. It features 4 down linemen, 2 linebackers, and 5 defensive backs, keeping 6 in the box to defend the run while using 5 DBs against the pass, making it effective against modern spread offenses. The key personnel is the Sam (or Rover) linebacker, a hybrid player who must cover, take on pulling guards, and rush the passer. Coordinators prefer athletic players, often using bigger defensive backs as linebackers to apply pressure. Strengths include versatility against run and pass, ability to cover 2x2 spread formations while maintaining 6 in the box, and the capacity to play any coverage from base alignment, causing confusion. It is a high-pressure defense with expanded blitz packages thanks to the athletic Sam. Weaknesses: it is not a mirror defense; the Sam creates an overhang on one side, leaving the opposite side without an overhang, allowing offenses to attack the weak side. The weak safety must fill that alley and cover. Additionally, the generally smaller personnel can struggle against big offensive lines and backs. Offenses commonly attack the side away from the Sam, especially on the boundary, using plays like buck sweep or outside zone. Common blitzes include a 6-man Cover 0 blitz with inside linemen slanting and linebackers blitzing, and a 6-man Cover Zero Field Blitz involving a long stick by the end and a blitzing Sam. Both can add a 7th rusher. Common coverages are Cover 4, where corners and safeties take deep quarters and the Sam covers the flat, and Cover 3 Sky, which shows a 2-high shell but rotates a safety down to the flat. Notable coaches: Gary Patterson, whose TCU defenses led the nation multiple times using the 4-2-5 with smaller, speedy players, and Greg Etter, who ran the 4-2-5 at Carthage College and Concordia University, achieving high defensive rankings.

This paper reports on a study of a sleep psychoeducation module within a multitopic mobile app for chronic disease self-management targeting older adults with chronic health conditions and low health literacy. App content was developed from existing resources, qualitative input from potential users, and a multidisciplinary team; modules were created at three reading levels (3rd, 6th, and 8th grade). The study took place in Fort Lauderdale, Florida and Atlanta, Georgia. Participants were recruited via past studies, clinics, and word of mouth. Eligibility required age ≥40, at least one treated chronic condition, education below college graduate, and health literacy ≤8th grade level per the Rapid Estimate of Adult Literacy in Medicine. Assessments occurred at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up using audio computer-assisted self-interviews. Measures included the FLIGHT/VIDAS health literacy scale, a socioeconomic status (SES) index from education and income, a structured health conditions interview, the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). The sleep module covered sleep stages, two-process theory, sleep hygiene, sleep logs, and sleep restriction, with content individually tailored based on ISI responses and feedback on depression and stress.

Of 286 participants completing baseline and the module, 195 had ISI scores ≥8 indicating insomnia and were analyzed. The sample was 53.3% women, 86% Black, Indigenous, or Other People of Color, and 61% reported annual incomes below $10,000. Insomnia severity: 45% subthreshold, 41% moderate, 15% severe. Average health literacy was basic; stress and depression scores were elevated. Mean PSQI and ISI scores indicated substantial sleep disturbance. Average time on the module was 32 minutes.

Chi-square analyses showed sleep disturbance (PSQI >5) significantly associated with hypercholesterolemia, depression, other nervous condition, and bipolar disorder, with trends for COPD and angina. Random intercept mixed effects models for PSQI evaluated covariates sequentially: baseline (age, race, gender), site, SES, health literacy, total health conditions, time, and treatment group. SES, health literacy, and total health conditions were significantly associated with sleep quality. The intervention effect over time was statistically significant, with a small-to-medium effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.40). Model-estimated PSQI scores declined by 0.85 points (95% CI [0.11, 1.60]).

The discussion notes the brief tailored intervention produced a modest but significant improvement in sleep quality. The sample included individuals with comorbidities and medication use often excluded in other studies, potentially increasing representativeness. The intervention’s brevity and online delivery may suit a stepped-care approach. Limitations include the study’s primary focus on chronic disease self-management rather than sleep alone, possible influence of other modules (mood, pain, stress), reliance on a single self-report sleep measure, limited generalizability due to the low-income and minoritized sample, and the small-to-medium effect size. The authors conclude that a brief, personalized sleep information intervention at appropriate reading levels may help improve sleep in this population, and further development is warranted.

The lecture focuses on pleat folding, particularly the hyperbolic paraboloid model made from a square paper with concentric squares and diagonals folded in alternating mountain and valley. When released, it pops into a saddle shape, an example of self-folding origami where physics finds the 3D form. Paper has elastic memory but creasing causes plastic deformation, so creases want to stay bent while uncreased areas want to stay flat; equilibrium produces the shape. Simulations using spring approximations matched real models, and origami skeletons were built from 3D-printed spheres and rods based on virtual models. Hyperbolic paraboloids can be joined algorithmically to form polyhedral sculptures called hyperhedra. Curve crease variations include circular ramps and joined circles, demonstrating that complex 3D structures could be deployed from flat crease patterns, with potential applications at nano or large scales, though reverse engineering remains an open problem. A glassblowing collaboration explored tactile folding inside enclosures.

The hyperbolic paraboloid dates to the Bauhaus in the late 1920s. The central mathematical result is that the traditional concentric-square crease pattern cannot be properly folded into a non-flat 3D form where every crease is bent by a non-zero, non-180° angle. However, adding triangulating diagonals makes folding possible. A construction method works from the inside out by intersecting three spheres to locate vertices, and interval arithmetic proves existence for specific parameters (up to 100 rings, fold angles between 2° and 178°). The resulting shape closely approximates a hyperbolic paraboloid but with a tiny, non-zero error.

Folded paper is assumed piecewise C2 and intrinsically flat (zero Gaussian curvature). At any smooth point, the surface is locally cylindrical (parabolic) or planar, and lies on a rule segment that ends at creases or boundaries. The surface is torsal ruled, with a common tangent plane along each rule line. Two lemmas are proved: a region with a polygonal boundary and no interior creases must be planar; and straight creases remain straight in a proper folding. Consequently, interior faces of a straight-crease pattern must stay rigid. This explains why the hyperbolic paraboloid crease pattern fails: interior trapezoids would need to be rigid, causing a contradiction at the center where both diagonals cannot be partially folded. The same holds for any interior ring not touching the boundary, and for concentric pleated shapes where diagonals meet at a point.

Other topics include the tea bag problem—inflating a doubly-covered square or Mylar balloon to maximum volume, which is open. Volume can be increased by applying "karate chops" to edges, and the limit shape is not polyhedral, likely smooth with ripples. Finally, the lecture discusses ongoing work to recreate and understand David Huffman's curved-crease models, using CAD and robotic scoring to document his design methods and underlying mathematics.

Stochastic Texture Filtering (STF) introduces randomness into texture sampling to reduce aliasing and moiré patterns, useful when traditional filtering is impractical, and can provide higher-order filtering at the cost of a single point sample. It runs fast on Blackwell GPU due to 2x point-sampled texture filtering rate improvements.

Neural Radiance Cache (NRC) uses a neural shader to cache and approximate radiance, taking path-traced rays after one bounce and inferring final lighting values for many bounces. It trains tiny neural networks on live game data in real-time, improving performance by reducing ray tracing and enhancing indirect lighting quality.

RTX Skin applies subsurface scattering, borrowed from film rendering, for real-time path tracing of translucent materials like skin, enabling light penetration and scattering.

RTX Neural Faces uses a real-time generative AI model to infer a more natural face from a simple rasterized face and 3D pose data, trained offline on images under various conditions.

This study used peer-to-peer interviews with 21 medical students who experienced mistreatment to understand factors influencing their decision to report. Four overarching groups of factors emerged: personal, situational, structural, and climate. Personal factors included concern for repercussions, a sense of justice, and lack of personal motivation. Situational factors involved the type and severity of mistreatment, the opinions of confidants, the inaction of bystanders, and the victim’s assessment of the perpetrator. Structural factors related to the reporting apparatus, including beliefs that no action would be taken and logistical barriers like not knowing where to report or what happens with reports. Climate factors were perceptions of the medical hierarchy and culture, where mistreatment was expected and reports were not taken seriously. Only personal and situational factors promoted reporting; students mostly cited reasons not to report. The study concludes that primarily targeting the culture of an institution may improve reporting.

Micro E-mini futures are 1/10th the size of E-mini futures, launched by the CME Group in 2019 and traded on the CME Globex electronic platform. They are mostly financially settled and were created to make futures accessible to retail traders with smaller capital, offering lower margin requirements. Initially covering the four major indexes—S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq 100, and Russell 2000—they now also include bitcoin, copper, crude oil, Treasury yield, and FX futures.

A micro E-mini futures strategy is a method for trading these contracts, often using technical and fundamental analysis for market timing, position sizing, and risk management, and can be used for speculation, portfolio diversification, or hedging. The passage includes a backtest of an overnight strategy on the Nasdaq 100 E-mini (NQ-Mini) because the Micro E-Mini has a shorter history; the strategy’s rules are not disclosed.

Seasonality in micro E-mini futures depends on the specific asset; for example, Treasury note futures tend to perform better in the second half of the year. Factors affecting prices also depend on the underlying asset—Treasury micro contracts may be influenced by interest rate changes, inflation, economic conditions, and sociopolitical events.

Trading hours vary by asset. For micro E-mini S&P 500 futures, trading runs Sunday to Friday from 6:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET with a one-hour break each day; CME ClearPort has a slightly different schedule. Contract specifications differ: the micro E-mini S&P 500 contract unit is $5 times the index value, quoted in USD and cents per index point, with quarterly contracts (Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec) listed for five consecutive quarters. It is financially settled, and trading terminates at 9:30 a.m. ET on the third Friday of the contract month. The minimum fluctuation is 0.25 index points ($1.25) for outright trades and 0.05 index points ($0.25) for calendar spreads; tick sizes are $1.25 and $0.25 respectively.

To start trading, one must register with a futures broker and fund an account, depositing initial margin since futures are leveraged. An alternative is trading CFDs that track micro E-mini futures; CFDs differ from futures in that they have no fixed expiration dates.

All-time highs and lows depend on the underlying asset. For S&P 500 futures, the all-time high was 4808.25 in January 2022 and the all-time low was 665.75 in March 2009, according to TradingView charts. The biggest risk in trading futures is adverse price movement, especially with leverage—e.g., 20x leverage means a 1% adverse move causes a 20% loss, and a 5% move wipes out the account. Settlement is by cash, calculated using special opening quotes on the final settlement day. ETFs track the underlying assets, not contract sizes. Micro E-mini futures provide retail traders with small capital a way into the futures markets.

A research paper in Climate Change argues that the Eldgjá eruption (spring 939–autumn 940 CE) may have spurred Iceland's Christianisation. The eruption, the Common Era's largest lava flood, devastated settlers by blocking sunlight, lowering temperatures, and hindering agriculture. Researchers point to the 10th-century poem Völuspá, which describes eruptive activity and meteorological effects as an allusion to the end of pagan gods, suggesting it used first-hand Eldgjá experiences to intentionally promote Christianisation. The paper concludes the eruption catalyzed conversion, with the poem framing it as a sign pagan ways were doomed. Official conversion was in 999/1000 CE after a parliament at Þingvellir. A 13th-century saga also associates conversion with volcanic events, likely the Eldgjá eruption.

Delta expects premium seat sales to surpass main cabin sales for the first time in 2026, a year earlier than previously forecast. Premium revenue rose 9% to nearly $5.8 billion last quarter, while main cabin sales fell 4% to around $6 billion. Corporate travel rebounded 8%. The shift aligns with U.S. wealth concentration, with the top 10% of households accounting for nearly 50% of consumer spending.

An international team used Bell's test on a superconducting quantum processor with up to 73 qubits to confirm genuine quantum correlations, achieving energy measurements 48 standard deviations below classical limits. They also certified genuine multipartite Bell correlations involving all qubits up to 24 qubits. The study demonstrates that large quantum systems exhibit authentic quantum behavior, enabling more secure communication and stronger quantum algorithms. Additionally, the passage mentions a 6,100 neutral-atom qubit array, qubit-fiberoptics integration, a new superconducting processor design, room-temperature qubits, tantalum for quantum processors, a new quantum correlation test method, a protein that punches holes in the heart, a dark matter detector, Parkinson's trigger observed in the brain, and ancient rock art in Arabia.

This article presents research from D’harawal Country in south-west Sydney, where Indigenous community members were asked what education could look like grounded in Indigenous knowledges. The author, a Gamilaroi woman, uses Indigenous, decolonising, and relational methodologies. The study involved 35 anonymous online survey respondents and over 15 face-to-face yarn participants. To protect anonymity, findings are re-presented through a story, “Our Education, Our Way,” which layers the community vision by amalgamating quotes into fictional characters. The story depicts a community gathering where elders, parents, and children critique the harm and marginalisation caused by current schooling and envision an education system designed by Aboriginal people. Key themes include learning on Country, prioritising identity and belonging, intergenerational knowledge transmission through storytelling, and community control. The paper draws on Indigenous futurities and envisioning as decolonial approaches to imagine education sovereignty outside colonial schooling.

The nation should not alienate its remaining coal lands. The writer temporarily withdrew coal lands from settlement, but legislation should permanently withdraw them from sale, retaining U.S. ownership. Private individuals would mine them under a royalty system, with government supervision to prevent excessive consumer prices and ensure common carriers do not favor competitors. This mirrors forest land withdrawal, treating coal as public property for public benefit. Congress has advanced in regulating interstate corporations via the railway rate bill, pure food bill, and beef-packing control. Further legislation may wait to assess these laws, though packing house inspection should eventually require date labels and charge packers for inspection. The interstate commerce law increased railroad earnings and prompted many voluntary rate reductions. However, more national control over interstate capital is needed, including enlarging the Interstate Commerce Commission's powers. State legislatures cannot effectively regulate multi-state corporations. A national license law or similar measure should provide complete control to prevent overcapitalization and compel disclosure of stockholders, properties, and business, stopping inordinate profits for favored individuals. The aim is to supervise, not prevent, consolidation to avoid public harm. Reactionaries label such control socialism, but they increase socialistic feeling. To avert agitation, remedy the well-founded 20% of evil. Adequate government control of railways will prevent calls for government ownership. Abolishing abuses in wealth use counters agitation against the wealthy. Governmental control does not destroy individual initiative; failing to encourage it would be calamitous. Unregulated competition, like pure socialism, destroys individual character by allowing one corporation to dominate and eliminate competition.

Meb Faber’s 2012 paper presented a simple trend-following strategy for the S&P 500: go long when the price crosses above the 200-day moving average and sell when it crosses below. The strategy focuses solely on price, ignoring news, earnings, and other factors. Paul Tudor Jones endorsed the 200-day moving average as a defensive tool to avoid significant losses. Backtesting from 1960 shows the strategy largely avoided the 2008/09 global financial crisis and limited the COVID-19 drawdown to 19%. Using monthly data with a ten-month moving average, $100,000 invested in 1960 grew to $4.7 million, a 6.3% CAGR versus 7% for buy-and-hold, with a maximum drawdown of 26% in October 1987. The 200-day moving average is a simple, reasonably effective tool that keeps investors on the sidelines during downturns and roughly matches long-term market returns.

The binary image build model routes all interface call-out functions through a single interface portal, requiring the host environment to implement a call-out router that translates function numbers into execution addresses. The UEFI BIOS environment spans SEC, PEI, DXE, and RTP phases across 16-bit, 32-bit, and 64-bit execution modes. AGESA™ core files are organized into libraries, with additional UEFI libraries, to generate build targets for each phase. Specific Microsoft assembler and compiler versions are used for each mode. Configuration options are described in Chapter 181, with no additional UEFI-specific user options at this time. Porting notes include UEFI redefinition of StdHeader content and use of environment-specific library routines.

The SEC phase establishes a C environment using AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK. PEI phase is split into two PEIMs: AmdProcessorInitPeim (calls AmdInitReset, AmdInitEarly, AmdInitPost) publishes AmdCpuEarlyInit PPI, AmdInitEarly PPI, AmdInitPost PPI, and a memory info HOB; AmdMemoryInitPeim (calls AmdInitPost) publishes AmdMemInit PPI. A reset coordination PEIM handles warm reset requests. The DXE driver calls AmdInitLate, generates tables, and publishes AgesaDxeProtocol. An AmdGpuVgaControlDxe driver monitors VGA decoding for the iGPU. Reference files in \Addendum include Cpcar32.asm, <Plat>Options.c, and <Plat>RecoveryOptions.c. UEFI build control files (AgesaPei0Libs.inf, AgesaPei1Libs.inf, AgesaDxe0Libs.inf) and environment variables (AGESA_ROOT, AGESA_OptsDir) are required. Integration steps include copying options files, setting variables, enabling Cache-As-RAM before AmdInitReset, and not modifying MTRRs during CAR.

Stack procedures AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK and AMD_DISABLE_UEFI_STACK are provided as assembly macros to establish and remove a pre-memory stack. Service procedures include AmdCreateStruct (allocates and initializes parameter structures with methods PreMemHeap, PostMemDram, ByHost), AmdReleaseStruct, AmdGetDataEye, AmdGetApicAddress, AmdGetExeCacheSize, AmdGetPciAddress, AmdIdentifyCore, AmdIdentifyDimm, AmdAddMmiRange, AmdReadEventLog.

Entry procedures are listed in time-point order. AmdInitReset performs minimal processor initialization, HyperTransport link init, and execution cache allocation with specific rules. AmdInitEarly performs full processor initialization, power management configuration, and may request a warm reset. AmdInitPost initializes system memory, transitions from pre-memory to post-memory, and outputs memory configuration parameters. AmdInitEnv transfers artifact data (HOBs) from temporary memory to host-allocated buffers. AmdInitMid performs graphics display hardware configuration before video BIOS. AmdInitLate generates ACPI and DMI tables (DMI, PState, WHEA, ALIB, IVRS, CRAT, CDIT) using AgesaAllocateBuffer. AmdInitRtb (AmdS3Save) saves processor context for suspend, providing NvStorage and VolatileStorage pointers. AmdInitResume re-initializes silicon and memory for resume using saved context. AmdS3LateRestore restores registers after PCI control space is re-established. AmdS3FinalRestore performs final restoration before OS handoff.

Required call-out procedures: AgesaAllocateBuffer allocates post-memory buffers, AgesaDeallocateBuffer releases them, and AgesaReset initiates cold or warm system resets. The host environment must implement these.

The passage examines language teacher education across English as a Second Language (ESL), World Languages (WL), and Bilingual Education (BE), applying a historical perspective and Valdés’ framework of language curricularization. It describes a curricular innovation at an urban Illinois institution, developed in three phases to bridge these fields. Phase 1 redesigned an ESL methods course around translanguaging pedagogy to serve diverse candidates, including WL teachers, by emphasizing multilingual repertoires and culturally responsive instruction. Phase 2 created a combined ESL and WL methods course focused on Chinese, integrating bilingual materials, case studies, and field experiences to support future Chinese language teachers across program models. Phase 3, future work, aims to cross from WL to BE by fostering critical consciousness, linguistic ideological clarity, and critical curricular analysis through activities like linguistic autobiographies, drama-based scenarios, and case studies of BE program models. Throughout, the authors advocate a heteroglossic vision, a multilingual turn, and an equity-oriented, historically aware approach to prepare critically conscious language educators for diverse learners.

Congress has not appropriated for antitrust enforcement; a special appropriation under the Attorney-General would enable more. Reducing the tariff to address trust evils is advocated but would be ineffective and ruin weaker competitors. Trust regulation is separate from tariff revision. Stability of economic policy is the prime need. The protective-tariff principle is accepted; violent or radical changes are undesirable. Fixity of principle should combine with a system allowing careful reapplication to shifting needs to avoid paralyzing business. Changes must preserve the principle of putting American business on full equality with foreign interests, with duties sufficient to more than cover labor cost differences. No change should jeopardize wage-workers' standard of comfort or wages. Readjustment can be achieved through reciprocity treaties, widening markets and lowering duties when protection is no longer needed. If treaties cannot be ratified, direct legislation should secure reciprocity. Where reciprocity is not applicable, duties can be lowered outright after full consideration by practical experts. The passage compares dollar-cost averaging (DCA) and lump-sum investing. DCA involves investing a sum via many installments over time, while lump-sum invests all capital at once. A Morningstar study found lump-sum beats DCA most of the time: DCA outperformed only 27.8% over 10-month periods and 10% over 10-year periods. Backtests using S&P 500 from January 2000 to December 2019 with $60,000 show lump-sum grew to $193,157 (CAGR 6.02%), while DCA resulted in $173,949 (CAGR 5.5%). When the sequence of returns was reshuffled (2010-2019 returns placed before 2000-2010), lump-sum CAGR dropped slightly to 5.93%, but DCA end value fell to $87,396 (CAGR 1.9%), demonstrating sequence of returns risk: DCA suffered because the market rose in the first half when cash was high and stagnated later when more was invested. The article concludes lump-sum investing is the best option, as randomness and sequence of returns can significantly impact DCA results. DCA can reduce fear and behavioral biases, but recency bias and market changes make lump-sum preferable when capital is available. DCA and scale-in are similar, both involving gradual investment. DCA mitigates sequence risk by investing at different price levels, smoothing volatility.

The professor notes satisfactory enrollment for the alternate-year course 6.451. The class will be videotaped for OpenCourseWare by cameraman Tom White. Problem sets are weekly, due Wednesdays, graded 0–2, and count for 15% of the grade; they are learning tools and collaboration is allowed.
