The passage describes systems and methods for periodic beam failure measurements. A user equipment (UE) determines a measurement period duration based on the periods of periodic beam failure detection (BFD) reference signals (RSs) in a BFD RS set that have a quasi-co-located (QCL) relationship with demodulation RSs (DMRSs) of physical downlink control channel (PDCCH) receptions monitored by the UE. The UE monitors a subset of these BFD RSs occurring during a measurement period. If measures of all BFD RSs in the subset do not meet a specified threshold, the UE reports a beam failure (BF) instance to a higher layer entity. This approach ensures at least one assessed BFD RS is present in each measurement period, preventing the resetting of a consecutive BF instance counter and missed beam failure detection. The measurement period duration can be determined by the shortest period of the assessed BFD RSs, potentially bounded by a specified value. A beam failure may be declared after a specified number of consecutive BF instances. The passage also addresses scenarios where no BFD RS is transmitted in a measurement period, proposing to either ignore the period in updating the counter or treat it as a BF instance.

The MOTO (multi-objective three-layer optimization) framework is introduced for systematic mapping of local energy landscapes. It comprises: (i) a multi-objective explorer that uses NSGA-II to generate diverse, feasible initial configurations by optimizing masked perturbations with objectives of diversity, feasibility, and minimum-mode separability (spectral gap); (ii) a bilayer minimum-mode kernel where an inner layer uses HVP-based Krylov eigensolvers (Lanczos or LOBPCG) to estimate the lowest-curvature modes, and an outer layer performs minimum-mode-force ascent (using L-BFGS or CG) to locate index-1 saddles; (iii) deterministic two-sided minimum-mode descent to certify connectivity between saddles and minima.

Benchmarks on atomistic spin systems show HVP-based Lanczos/LOBPCG achieve near-unity cosine similarity to explicit Hessian eigenvectors while drastically reducing wall time and peak memory, with Lanczos scaling favorably. The multi-objective explorer increases spectral gap and diversity over generations. Bilayer MMF converges to index-1 saddles with both L-BFGS and CG.

Applied to a DFT-parameterized Pd/Fe/Ir(111) spin model, MOTO maps local transition-state networks around a Néel skyrmion and an antiskyrmion, identifying twelve index-1 saddles and revealing meron/antimeron-mediated mechanisms (duplication, chiral droplet formation, charge transfer) with up to 32 pathways connecting basins. Applied to a Ni(111) heptamer using Cartesian coordinates and an EAM potential, the same workflow recovers canonical low-barrier rearrangement motifs without algorithmic changes, demonstrating generality across differentiable potential energy surfaces.

Limitations include the need for physics-informed masks and sensitivity to hyperparameters. Future directions include automation and coupling with two-end path solvers.

The passage challenges this with neuroscience: brains are plastic, changing with experience; cognitive sex differences exist on a spectrum, not binary; brains are a mosaic of male and female characteristics. Training improves spatial skills, and the gender gap in them is diminishing. Stereotype threat, where anxiety about group stereotypes affects performance and brain activity, can create perceived differences. The study examined ICT and CALL integration in EFL initial teacher education at a Vietnamese university. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, it surveyed 67 final-year EFL pre-service teachers and conducted a focus group with six of them, plus individual interviews with three teacher educators. Survey results showed a high perceived opportunity to learn CALL-related knowledge (M=3.05), particularly for searching and downloading teaching materials, using word processors, and creating lessons with digital content. Lower opportunities were reported for troubleshooting equipment, setting online work, and selecting online exercises. Focus group data revealed both satisfaction and some dissatisfaction with the quality of technology education. Teacher educators reported frequent ICT use but identified barriers. Factors impacting ICT integration included: individual educator obstacles (limited skills, confidence, fear of change, time concerns); inadequate infrastructure (unstable internet, poor-quality equipment, slow technical support); pre-service teacher obstacles (laziness, disengagement); and the absence of official institutional policies requiring or guiding CALL technology use. Educators expressed a desire for clear policies and professional development. The study, framed by Hong’s (2010) model, concluded that opportunity to learn CALL knowledge and supportive policies are pivotal, and highlighted the need for improved infrastructure, educator training, and explicit guidelines.

The article argues that global citizenship education (GCE) does not adequately equip young people to understand current international conflicts, such as the war in Ukraine and rising tensions with China. GCE offers diverse concepts of a globalised world and citizen engagement but provides insufficient guidance on why violent conflict erupts, how to relate to it, and the conditions for peaceful cooperation among nations. The authors propose supplementing GCE with theories of international politics from political science.

GCE literature emphasises tolerance, multiculturalism, global interconnectedness, and advocacy issues like environmentalism, human rights, and development. However, it neglects problems of national security, economic cooperation, and trade, which are central to recent international developments. Cosmopolitan notions of global citizenship provide moral standpoints but do not explain why aggressive conflicts occur or how citizens can promote cooperative state actions. Political cosmopolitanism focuses on supranational governance or civil society activism but does not address why cooperation among states is difficult or how states may promote peace.

To fill these gaps, the article discusses three perspectives from international politics. Realism, exemplified by John Mearsheimer, views international politics as anarchic, with states prioritising security and power. It explains the Ukraine war as Russia reacting to NATO expansion to preserve its security, and it sees such conflicts as normal state behaviour. Citizen participation is limited, but influencing national foreign policy becomes crucial. Regionalism explains how states contain rivalry by developing shared economic interests, making conflict too costly. The EU is a key example, though it has not fostered a strong European citizenship. The war challenged the assumption that economic integration prevents conflict, and both Western and Russian responses involve realigning economic blocs. Institutionalism highlights the role of international organisations and rules, which provide predictability and can develop independent agendas. Institutions like NATO and the EU have been pivotal in responding to the war, while the UN’s limitations show institutional constraints. Global citizenship does not drive institutional development; states remain primary actors.

International cooperation depends on state interests and issue characteristics. Global public goods, such as financial stability or climate change mitigation, require different types of efforts: single best efforts, weakest links, or aggregate efforts. Cooperation can succeed without global citizenship, as seen in smallpox eradication or ozone layer protection. Coordination on technical standards also facilitates cooperation and can reduce emissions. Successful examples include Franco-German integration within the EU and joint fishing quota management between Norway and Russia.

Citizen engagement should expand beyond transnational NGOs and advocacy to include influencing the foreign policy of one’s own country. Foreign policy pursues security, economic welfare, prestige, and values, using tools such as negotiation, propaganda, economic measures, and military means. States address global problems when they align with these objectives, making national foreign policy a key arena for global engagement.

The article concludes that GCE should incorporate insights from international politics to help students understand conflict, cooperation, and realistic avenues for political engagement. Teaching should cover institutional arenas for transnational activism, foreign policy processes, conditions for cooperation, and historical examples of successful problem-solving. The agenda should broaden to include state security and economic positioning, while acknowledging the frightening nature of conflicts and the importance of truthful education. The authors share GCE’s values but argue for a more comprehensive approach that includes power dynamics and state dependencies.

Home hospital programs across the U.S. are shutting down as a Medicare waiver allowing inpatient care at home is set to expire on Sept. 30, coinciding with a potential government shutdown. Other hospitals, including Hackensack Meridian Health, ChristianaCare, and Mass General Brigham, have also halted or reduced admissions. An estimated 1,000 hospital-at-home beds exist nationwide, often in capacity-constrained areas. Hospital leaders express terror and frustration, noting the program eases crowding. This study explored the use of music software (Sibelius) as a contemporary strategy in a general music education course at a Caribbean university. The existing course used traditional lectures, discussions, and instrument playing, with technology limited to the Canvas LMS for materials. The purpose was to introduce technology to deliver specific music content to pre-service teachers in Certificate and Bachelor of Education programs (early childhood and primary). Significance included potential impact on teaching methodology, alignment with UN Sustainable Development Goal 4, and the COVID-19 context requiring digital readiness.

The literature highlighted music's importance in early childhood development, the availability of music notation software, trends in music education technology (e.g., shareability, self-paced learning, emerging VR/AI), and challenges like lack of equipment and staff competence. The study used a mixed-methods phenomenological approach with 24 participants (22 female, 2 male). Data collection involved a questionnaire and an assignment where students composed eight bars of music using Sibelius in 2/4, 3/4, or 4/4 time signatures with specified note values.

Questionnaire results: most rated the course "very good"; the software was rated "fair" by a majority; 11 of 24 said it enhanced understanding, 6 said no, 7 unsure; most preferred traditional approaches; half felt somewhat or very comfortable with the software; motivation was mostly neutral; 67% supported continued technology use; 75% desired further training. Assignment results: 20 of 24 submitted; 12 used 4/4 time; overall accuracy was 90%, though some had minor note placement challenges.

Analysis found the software could be integrated, students comprehended concepts, performance was positively impacted, and motivation was neutral but implied by success. Recommendations included continued use for selected content, progressive training, adding technology criteria to practicum assessments, and incorporating technology into final music assessments. The conclusion stated that music software is relatively easy to integrate and can positively impact student outcomes, with ongoing research and training needed.

The disclosure relates to methods of creating a virtual game environment from a real-world scene. A user selects physical objects with predetermined physical properties, arranges them as a physical model, and scans the model with a capturing device to obtain a digital three-dimensional representation including information on the physical properties. The digital representation is converted into a virtual toy construction model made of virtual toy construction elements that correspond to physical toy construction elements having coupling members. Game-controlling elements are defined in the virtual toy construction model using the physical property information, thereby creating the virtual game environment. Conversion rules translate physical properties into virtual properties; rules may be static or adaptive and may depend on recognized objects or themes.

Another aspect involves recognizing at least one physical object as a known object and creating the virtual game environment responsive to the recognized object. This may include creating a virtual object associated with the recognized physical object and generating a modified scene where the recognized object is removed, optionally placing the virtual object in the environment. A library of known physical objects with associated digital representations and attributes may be used.

A voxelization method receives a digital three-dimensional surface representation comprising surface elements, defines a plurality of points within each surface element, maps each point to a corresponding voxel, and creates a digital three-dimensional representation from the identified voxels. Points may be distributed in a triangular planar grid. Voxel attribute values are determined from surface attribute values. A color identification method finds a target color from a predetermined set by representing colors in a three-dimensional color space, determining a current candidate, and analyzing a subset of colors whose distance from the origin is no larger than the sum of the input color's distance from the origin and the distance between the input color and the current candidate.

An interactive game system includes a capturing device, display, data storage, and processor configured to perform the methods. The game may be played in a cyclic manner: creating a virtual game environment from a physical model, playing game segments, and initiating a new cycle based on the outcome. A physical playable character constructed from toy construction elements may be scanned and represented as a virtual playable character with corresponding tools, skills, or powers.

This article examines the experiences of leaders of education-related undergraduate degree provision in further education (FE) colleges in England, using Hodgson and Spours’ four-level lifelong learning ecology model (macro, exo, meso, micro). The macro layer covers national policy, including the expansion of undergraduate and foundation degrees in FE, widening participation, and the development of education studies programmes distinct from teacher training. The exo layer addresses institutional relationships with local employers, communities, and higher education partners through validation or franchising arrangements. The meso layer positions undergraduate programme leaders as a “keystone species” central to learners’ ecologies, providing high-quality support and nurturing student identities. The micro layer focuses on diverse, often non-traditional learners, with programme leaders motivated by social justice and personalised learning.

The study involved an online questionnaire (70 programme leaders, 14 from FE) and follow-up interviews. Findings show most FE programme leaders assumed the role informally rather than through open application, all held master’s degrees, and few held doctorates or Higher Education Academy fellowships. Teaching qualifications were predominantly post-16 PGCEs. Teams were small, and leaders often combined teaching with line management. Their responsibilities fell into three strands: administrative and organisational demands from colleges and HE partners; providing academic support and fostering a higher education culture; and responding to students’ pastoral needs. Tensions arose from balancing FE regulations with HE requirements, managing small cohorts through combined classes, and limited opportunities for scholarship and continuing professional development.

The conclusion highlights programme leaders as keystone species whose effectiveness is hampered when macro and exo demands obscure meso and micro priorities. The authors argue for improved “sightlines” enabling leaders to engage beyond their institutions through research, scholarly activity, and wider partnerships, to better support students and communities.

In Flinn’s Estate, the testator died in 1924, leaving trusts for his children with income to life tenants. The dispute concerned the date for fixing intact value of stocks to allocate undistributed earnings between life tenants and remaindermen. The court held that, as a general rule, intact value is fixed at the date of death, and the will did not clearly postpone the trust’s effective date; fixing a later date would risk illegal accumulation of income. However, for stock owned by the separate entity Booth & Flinn Company that was later distributed as a dividend to the executors in 1925, intact value should be fixed at the book value when the executors received it, not at death, because the company’s separate identity must be respected. The court also upheld the lower court’s method of averaging yearly earnings on a per diem basis to calculate income accumulated to the date of death, as the appellant did not challenge the evidence or propose a better method. The decree was affirmed as modified.

Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers identified the progenitor of supernova SN2025pht in spiral galaxy NGC 1637, about 40 million light-years away. The source was a massive red supergiant star enveloped in thick dust, making it the reddest and dustiest such progenitor ever observed. The dust, unexpectedly carbon-rich rather than oxygen-rich silicate, dimmed the star's visible light over 100 times. This finding supports the hypothesis that many red supergiants do explode as predicted but are hidden by dense dust clouds, explaining why their progenitors are rarely seen. JWST's mid-infrared vision enabled this first direct detection of a supernova progenitor, bridging a long-standing gap between theory and observation. The team plans future searches using the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

The passage presents the Simplified Egg and Changing Yolk Model to explain ventricular repolarisation and T-wave morphologies on ECGs. The model represents the heart as an egg shape with Wilson’s Central Terminal (WCT) at its centre. Repolarisation expands from the WCT; the asymmetric ‘T-zone’ generates the T-wave. The ST segment is isoelectric until the signal reaches the T-zone. Damage on the positive side of the WCT causes ST depression, while damage on the negative side causes ST elevation. The model reproduces abnormal T-waves (peaked, flattened, inverted, biphasic) by placing damaged areas. It suggests repolarisation begins with the Q-wave, unifying the ST and T-wave as a single process. This challenges the conventional view that ST depression indicates ischaemia and ST elevation indicates infarction, instead focusing on locating myocardial damage. The model highlights limitations of the QTc interval and proposes the QTp interval (Q-wave start to T-wave peak) as more clearly defined and reliable, especially for assessing arrhythmia risk and medication effects. The model may improve ECG interpretation and patient management, with future research planned on U-wave origins and atrial repolarisation.

This protocol describes a register-based cohort study using Danish Hip Arthroplasty Register data from 1995 to 2022. The study aims to describe trends in revision surgery for periprosthetic joint infection after primary total hip arthroplasty, categorizing revisions as debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention, one-stage exchange, or two-stage exchange, and to describe the risk of a second revision following each approach. Participants are adults (≥18 years) who underwent primary total hip arthroplasty for any reason, excluding hemiarthroplasty and simultaneous bilateral arthroplasty. Yearly numbers of revisions overall and for periprosthetic joint infection will be presented, subdivided by time from primary surgery (within 4 weeks, 4–12 weeks, over 12 weeks). Risk of second revision will be analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for calendar time, age, and sex, and presented with Kaplan-Meier plots. The register has high completeness, though some private clinics have lower reporting. Periprosthetic joint infection diagnoses are surgeon-reported, which may cause misclassification, but the study focuses on surgeons’ practice. No external funding was received; costs are covered by the orthopedic department. The protocol’s privacy identifier is p-2023-14990, and it has not yet been uploaded to OSF. The preprint is not peer-reviewed.

This study examined teachers' opinions on culturally responsive education in the Turkish education system using Q methodology with 21 teachers from Denizli, Mardin, Erzurum, and Şanlıurfa. Thirty Q statements were constructed from literature and sorted by participants. Analysis revealed three factors: Unification, Student Support, and Teacher Support. Factor 1 (Unification) most strongly agreed that there are inequalities between different cultures and disagreed with disseminating local culture's values and beliefs. Factor 2 (Student Support) most agreed with emphasizing equality of different cultures in education and disagreed with examining local culture characteristics in the curriculum. Factor 3 (Teacher Support) most agreed that cultural diversity is given importance in visual media and disagreed that teachers are encouraged to use examples of different cultures in the curriculum. Consensus statements included neutral agreement on increasing students' cultural competence skills and positive agreement on presenting life practices for general culture. Disagreement occurred on statements about measures against discrimination, viewing different cultures as a threat, and class as a reflection of society. Participants declined to explain their extreme statement placements, possibly due to the topic's sensitivity. The findings suggest that while the Turkish education system accepts cultural diversity as richness and has taken initial steps, it has not fully achieved a culturally responsive structure, with inequalities still perceived and insufficient teacher and student support.

The Give & Go isolation offense uses 2-1-2 spread, post weakside. O1 passes to O2, cuts; O2 feeds or dribbles out to O1, cuts; repeat. Wing back cuts if denied; drives if soft, or uses move if cut off. Post O5 steps out as release; O1 passes to O5, return pass, continue. If return denied, O1 cuts; post feeds. If post denied, O5 back cuts. O1 passes to O3 for return if O2/post unavailable. O3 can pass to O4 to initiate; post moves weakside. O4 dribbles out if O3 not open, passes to O3 or cross-court to O1. If defenders sag, O3 and O4 exchange or set screens; screens must be stationary.

The dual momentum trading strategy by Gary Antonacci selects assets that have outperformed their peers over a given period and have positive returns. It uses two types of momentum: absolute momentum, which is the percentage rate of change of an asset’s price over a specified period (calculated as [Current Price / Price at a past period] x 100, with values above 100 indicating positive momentum), and relative momentum, which compares the absolute momentum of one asset to that of others. The strategy aims to buy assets with both positive absolute and positive relative momentum, and in markets where shorting is possible, to sell assets with both negative absolute and negative relative momentum.

The origin traces to Jagadeesh and Titman (1993), who showed relative momentum could be profitable, and Antonacci’s 2012 book added absolute momentum to reduce volatility. To apply, one first identifies assets with positive absolute momentum, then compares them to select the one with the highest relative momentum for buying; for negative absolute momentum assets, the one with the lowest relative momentum is chosen for shorting. Examples: comparing the S&P 500 Index (10% gain) and gold (5% gain) over three months, the S&P had higher absolute and relative momentum, signaling a buy. Comparing crude oil (10% decline) and natural gas (5% decline), crude oil had lower absolute momentum (90% vs. 95%) and negative relative momentum, signaling a short.

Backtests of Antonacci’s Global Equities Momentum model from 1950–2018, compared to a global asset allocation benchmark, showed low correlation to the S&P 500 (0.50) and averaged 1.5 trades per year. A separate backtest using SPY, EFA, and AGG with monthly rebalancing yielded a 6.75% annual return and 30% maximum drawdown, underperforming the S&P 500’s 9.2% return but with a much smaller drawdown than its 55%. The strategy is best implemented with ETFs tracking geographically diversified equity indexes. Gary suggested a modular approach: monthly, compare two related sectors, buy the better performer if it has positive absolute momentum, otherwise shift to bonds. Benefits include better results than buy-and-hold and lower volatility. The strategy can also be applied to sector rotation by ranking ETFs by absolute momentum and buying the top performers. It may underperform during strong bull markets or sharp rebounds but has outperformed long-term by weathering bear markets.

The rapid advancement of large language models and generative AI brings transformative changes and challenges, including misinformation, deepfakes, bias, and difficulties fitting these technologies within existing legal frameworks. Balancing innovation promotion with strict risk mitigation complicates regulation, especially given national power implications. Timely, forward-looking AI policies are needed to align technology with ethical values like fundamental rights, inclusiveness, safety, transparency, and accountability. The EU, US, and China have introduced regulations, and companies like Microsoft have published AI principles and responsible AI policies to mitigate harm.

Despite these actions, macro-level challenges persist: a communication gap between the technology industry and government leads to inconsistent understanding of AI benefits and risks, and countries lack regulatory consensus, increasing compliance costs and potentially hindering innovation. At the micro-level, the complexity of large language models means certain risks, such as jailbreaking prompts, may only be identified by users in practice, raising barriers for timely and comprehensive regulation.

To address these challenges, the passage calls for partnerships among industry, academia, and policymakers to enhance mutual understanding and reinforce regulatory frameworks that respect human values while boosting technology. Regulations should be forward-looking to handle foreseeable challenges like unemployment before damage occurs. Governance should combine top-down and bottom-up approaches, making it the responsibility of regulators, developers, users, and the whole community. Developers and users should report issues throughout the AI lifecycle, with transparent handling and prompt updates to regulations. Governments and companies should build effective channels for collecting instances and mechanisms to investigate risks. Social computing techniques can monitor and trace regulatory needs in specific communities for timely and targeted governance.

The advance-decline indicator (also called advance/decline index or AD line) is a market breadth indicator that plots the cumulative difference between advancing and declining stocks daily. It is used to confirm stock index trends and predict reversals via divergence. The indicator is cumulative: each day's net advances are added to or subtracted from the prior value. It reflects market sentiment—rising values suggest momentum, falling values suggest loss of momentum. Advance/decline issues are lists of advancing (price above prior close) and declining (price below prior close) stocks. Advance/decline distribution shows the number and volume of advancing/declining stocks for sentiment analysis. Advance Volume and Decline Volume refer to shares traded of advancing/declining stocks; the Advance/Decline Volume Line cumulates their daily difference to confirm trend strength. The NYSE advance-decline line is the cumulative difference for NYSE stocks. A backtest of the indicator on SPY (S&P 500 ETF) with strict trading rules yielded 229 trades, average gain 0.6%, inconsistent results, and a profit factor of 1.55, below the 1.75 threshold. Multiple strategy versions failed to produce a good trading strategy. The article concludes the advance-decline indicator is likely not useful for profitable trading strategies and suggests other oscillating indicators like RSI, Williams %R, or IBS.

The paper addresses learning Linear Temporal Logic on finite traces (LTLf) from sets of positive and negative traces. It surveys applications in software engineering, cyber-physical systems, and AI, and notes state-of-the-art tools Scarlet and a GPU-accelerated VFB algorithm. The key insight is to separate Boolean operators from temporal operators by using Boolean Set Cover: after enumerating LTLf formulas up to a size limit, the method searches for a Boolean combination of these formulas that separates the traces. The paper proposes a framework combining LTLf learning with Boolean Set Cover, implements it in the tool Bolt, and introduces a consolidated benchmark suite of over 15,000 tasks. Bolt uses the VFB algorithm up to a fixed formula size, then switches to a Boolean Set Cover solver employing beam search with domination-based pruning and divide-and-conquer. Experiments show Bolt significantly outperforms Scarlet in wall-clock time and size of learned formulas, solving more tasks with smaller formulas. An ablation study demonstrates the benefit of incorporating Boolean Set Cover. The paper concludes that Boolean Set Cover is a fundamental problem with potential applications beyond LTLf learning.

New research by Adam Anderson, published in Psychological Science, reveals that eye expressions originated as universal reactions to environmental stimuli and evolved to communicate emotions. The study found narrowed eyes, which enhance visual discrimination, are associated with disgust and suspicion, while open eyes, which expand vision, are linked to fear and awe. Participants accurately discerned six basic emotions from eyes alone. Eye openness was the feature most closely related to reading mental states: narrow eyes reflected states like suspicion and disapproval, open eyes reflected curiosity. Additional studies showed eyes convey emotions more robustly than other facial areas. The work supports Darwin’s theory that expressions evolved for sensory function before communication, and demonstrates how eyes now provide interpersonal insight.

The passage introduces offensive positions in American football for new viewers. The offense aims to advance the ball and score. Receiver types include split end (X, physical, on the line), flanker (Z, off the line, speed), and slot receiver (inside, quick, gets open underneath). The document provides hardware design guidelines for a Texas Instruments device. For power supplies, PLL and analog supplies require filters or ferrite beads with capacitors placed close to device pins; decoupling capacitors should be 0.1 µF in small body sizes (≤0402), with at least one capacitor per two power pins and one bulk capacitor per ~10 power pins. Reset types include Power-on Reset (POR), external warm reset (RESET), emulation warm reset, watchdog reset, software global cold/warm resets, test reset (TRST), and local resets, each with defined sequences, pin behaviors, and priority. Clocking uses DEV and AUX clock inputs (crystal or 1.8-V LVCMOS), SERDES differential clock, optional AUD_CLKIN and 32-kHz clock, and multiple PLLs with specific frequency limits and bypass modes. Interrupts are handled by ARM Cortex-A8 and C674x DSP interrupt controllers with mapped events. Peripheral interfaces include EMAC (MII/GMII/RMII/RGMII) with MDIO, GPIO, GPMC for NOR/NAND flash with synchronous/asynchronous timings, HDMI transmitter with TMDS routing guidelines, HDVPSS video input/output with timing, video DAC with normal and bypass modes, and I2C modules.

A study collected 15 untreated wastewater samples from three zones in Western Uttar Pradesh, India, during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021). From these, 150 Enterobacteriaceae isolates were obtained: 62% E. coli, 24% K. pneumoniae, 8% other Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., Pantoea agglomerans, Alcaligenes faecalis, Shigella), and 6% mixed populations. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 19 antibiotics showed 74% of isolates were resistant to one or more antibiotics; 79.3% of resistant isolates were ESBL producers. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was found in E. coli (57.14%), K. pneumoniae (28.57%), and Pantoea agglomerans (5.71%). Zone 1 had the highest MDR percentage, but zonal differences were not statistically significant (p=0.85). Significant resistance patterns were observed for E. coli in all zones, and K. pneumoniae MDR prevalence was significantly higher than E. coli (p=0.0081). Resistance to carbapenems, cephalosporins, quinolones, and other classes was documented; colistin resistance was detected in some isolates from Zones 1 and 2. The study concludes that increased antibiotic use during the pandemic likely contributed to elevated AMR in wastewater, posing a health risk, and recommends periodic surveillance, molecular characterization of resistance genes, and improved wastewater treatment, especially in non-metropolitan cities.

Anthony Davis and Eric Simmons appealed their convictions for Class A felony conspiracy to deal in cocaine in excess of three grams. Davis also appealed his sentence. The Court of Appeals of Indiana affirmed. Evidence showed that Simmons, Davis, and others transported cocaine from Detroit to Marion, Indiana, where they prepared and packaged it. Davis gave Harris money for cocaine, and Simmons stayed with Davis at a 9th Street apartment. A confidential informant made two controlled buys there, purchasing 1.61 grams and 1.51 grams, totaling 3.12 grams. The State charged both with conspiracy, alleging multiple overt acts including transportation, preparation, and sales. The jury convicted both of conspiracy and acquitted Simmons of a separate dealing charge. On appeal, the appellants argued insufficient evidence because no single transaction exceeded three grams. The court held the conspiracy charge was not limited to a single transaction; evidence of an agreement to deal, including transportation, preparation, and the closely timed sales, supported the conviction. The court distinguished Washington v. State, where no agreement linked multiple buys. Regarding inconsistent verdicts, the court found no inconsistency for Davis because he faced only one charge. For Simmons, the jury could have found him guilty of conspiracy based on overt acts other than the sale, and the verdicts were not irreconcilable. Davis’s sentence of forty years was challenged under Blakely v. Washington. The trial court had found aggravating circumstances: lengthy criminal history, probation status, and need for correctional treatment. The court held that the criminal history alone justified the enhanced sentence beyond a reasonable doubt, making any error harmless. The convictions and sentence were affirmed.

Boredom and alcohol led to self-wounding. An 1876 report noted two insane patients, one placing a hot coal in his pocket. The post library had 1,100 books and periodicals. Abandoned later, a museum opened in 1963, and other parts were restored.

This study examined the relationship between science education and citizenship education in Turkey by analyzing the science curriculum and interviewing eight science teachers. The analysis found that both the curriculum and teachers conceptualized the connection through the themes of environment, society, and scientific literacy. The curriculum contains objectives related to scientific literacy, and teachers viewed it as an essential attribute for contemporary citizens. The "environment" was the most frequently highlighted theme, with teachers drawing a direct correlation between active citizenship and environmental challenges. The connection between science and "society" was established through socio-scientific topics and daily life applications like health and safety. Teachers also linked science lessons to values such as responsibility and patriotism, and skills like observation and critical thinking. However, a notable finding was that teachers felt science education often falls short of its citizenship-related goals in practice due to problems like an exam-oriented system, overcrowded classrooms, and inadequate laboratories.

A study investigated future preschool and primary school teachers' conceptions of robots using a mixed-method approach, specifically the Draw-A-Robot Test (DART), with 121 fourth-year students from the Faculty of Education, University of Belgrade (75 future preschool teachers, 46 future primary school teachers), after excluding 22 drawings showing misconceptions. Participants drew a robot and answered questions about its appearance, function, context of experience, and reason for depiction. Two independent evaluators coded the drawings with high inter-rater reliability (Pearson correlation 0.99). Most respondents had accurate conceptions: 98 had real-life experience with robots, 21 had media-based experience, and 2 had no experience. The most common robot appearance was animal-like (47.1%), particularly Bee Bot, followed by typical (24.8%), mechanical object (24%), and humanoid (4.1%). Regarding emotions, 76 depicted neutral expressions, 44 positive, and 1 negative. The dominant perceived function was educational (52.9%), primarily associated with animal-shaped robots, followed by assistive (31.4%), with game and communicative functions less frequent. Future preschool teachers emphasized the educational function, while future primary school teachers valued both educational and assistive functions equally. Most respondents encountered robots at the faculty (61), where animal robots were most common. Reasons for choosing the depicted robot were classified into cognitive domain (33.9%), affective domain (23.1%), behavioral domain (16.5%), and undetermined (26.4%). The 22 misconceptions involved depicting robots as electrical appliances (68.18%), humanoid stick figures, VR hardware, or avatars. The study concluded that most future teachers hold accurate conceptions with minimal misconceptions, and recommended more frequent, purposeful integration of educational robots in teaching to enhance digital competencies and algorithmic thinking, while ensuring safety and inclusivity.

Out of bounds situations are a major part of the game; teams must be prepared to inbound from baseline, sideline, and full court, and players must know the rules. The primary objective is to inbound successfully and get the ball to the best players for a high percentage shot. Do not expect execution of unpracticed plays; keep out of bounds plays simple, prioritizing the best player, then height, then best shooter. Inbounding requires fundamental skills, vision, communication, execution, timing, and commitment. A turnover on an inbounds pass creates a five-on-four advantage, but taking the five-second count allows the defense to set with over a 60% chance of a stop. Automatic reads are the first option: cut to the basket if the defender’s back is turned; execute a give-and-go if the inbounder is unguarded; throw a lob if the defender faces up with back to the passer. Scout opponents, as they typically use one defensive technique. Rules include: the inbounder cannot be changed after designation; the ball must be released within five seconds; the inbounder cannot touch the ball first; the inbounder may toss the ball off a defender’s back and score after stepping inbounds; a timeout must be requested before the five-second count elapses. After a made shot, the inbounder may run the baseline; otherwise, only one step is allowed. The ball can be inbounded from the frontcourt to the backcourt without an over-and-back violation. An untouched inbounds pass that goes out of bounds returns to the original throw-in spot. A timeout after a made basket preserves baseline movement; a defensive infraction does not remove the right to run the baseline. The inbounder cannot throw over the backboard or directly into the basket. After a made basket, it is legal to pass to a teammate stepping out of bounds along the baseline and receive a return pass. Reaching over the out-of-bounds vertical plane and touching the ball is a technical foul. Coaches should test players’ rule knowledge.

Neutrino sources include supernovae, Big Bang relics (low energy, difficult to observe), cosmic ray showers, the sun, accelerators, and nuclear reactors. Experimental parameters are baseline length, neutrino energy, and sensitivity to mass squared difference (Δm²). Solar neutrinos have a fixed Earth–Sun distance, energies around 1 meV, probing Δm² ~10⁻¹⁰ eV². Early experiments like the Davis chlorine tank detected fewer electron neutrinos than theoretically expected. The SNO experiment used neutral scattering to measure the total neutrino flux, finding agreement with theory and indicating flavor conversion—first evidence for solar neutrino oscillation. Atmospheric neutrinos are produced in cosmic ray interactions, decaying from pions and kaons; the expected muon-to-electron neutrino ratio of about 2 was not observed, and muon neutrinos were seen to disappear as a function of zenith angle, demonstrating oscillation. Accelerator-based experiments (e.g., NuMI at Fermilab, CERN, T2K in Japan) use a near detector to measure total flux and a far detector to study appearance or disappearance; T2K data show clear oscillation compared to unoscillated predictions. Reactor neutrinos come from nuclear fission of heavy isotopes, mainly uranium and polonium. They are used to study anti-electron neutrino disappearance via inverse beta decay (anti-electron neutrino + proton → positron + neutron). Experiments in France, Japan, and China observe survival probability as a function of length over energy, directly showing oscillation. Neutrino physics advanced significantly in the 2000s.

The device includes a programmable gain amplifier (PGA) that converts single-ended or differential inputs to drive the SAR ADC, adjusts common-mode level, and sets gain via RANGE_SEL[3:0] bits (default 0000 for ±3V×VREF). A precisely trimmed resistor network ensures low gain error. A second-order antialiasing low-pass filter at the PGA output has a typical –3dB cutoff of 500kHz. An integrated high-bandwidth, low-noise ADC driver buffers the sample-and-hold capacitors. The reference can be internal (4.096V nominal) or external, selected by the INTREF_DIS bit. With internal reference, the REFIO pin outputs the reference voltage and requires a minimum 4.7µF decoupling capacitor; smaller capacitors increase noise. Soldering heat causes reference shifts; solder the device in the second pass to minimize stress. The internal reference is temperature-compensated. An active-high alarm output is available on the ALARM/SDO-1/GPO pin when configured. Both alarms are enabled by default but can be disabled. Each alarm has an active flag (cleared at conversion end if condition gone) and a tripped flag (cleared only after reading ALARM_REG). Alarm flags can be read via the pin, internal registers, or appended to output data. The input high alarm triggers when digital output exceeds the high threshold and resets when below the threshold minus hysteresis minus one; the low alarm triggers when output falls below the low threshold and resets when above the threshold plus hysteresis plus one.

A data transfer frame begins on the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends on the rising edge. During the frame, SCLK clocks shift data in on SDI and out on SDO-x. A frame with exactly 32 SCLK cycles is optimal; shorter frames invalidate writes but allow reading MSBs, longer frames use the last 32 bits as the command. Commands include NOP, register read/write operations (byte or half-word), and set/clear bit operations. In SRC mode, the RVS pin provides a clock synchronous with output data; the clock source can be external (SCLK) or internal. Dual SDO mode uses two data lines to halve the required SCLK cycles. Daisy-chain topology connects multiple devices by linking SDO-0 of one to SDI of the next, with common CONVST/CS and SCLK; the host receives data from the last device first.

A parameter-free diffusion-controlled growth model was derived from Fick’s first law with an external potential, using the metadynamics free-energy profiles, MD-computed N diffusivity, and calculated N solubility in Ga. The model predicted facet-dependent steady-state growth rates. Predicted rates (0.01–0.04 nm/s) and facet trends agreed with experimental observations, validating the framework. The work establishes that for systems with low solubility of key elements like N in Ga, the interfacial free-energy profile governs growth kinetics. Limitations include neglect of impurities, transferability of the interatomic potential, simplifying model assumptions, and experimental averaging over multiple facets.

Three themes emerge: (1) the rapidly changing AI policy landscape, with expected oscillations between safety-focused and dominance-focused policies, making AI developers with policy familiarity more desirable; (2) the challenge of technical compliance with non-technical specifications, requiring translation of abstract policy goals into concrete controls and recognition of the technical frontier where solutions do not yet exist; (3) cross-border implications, illustrated by the GDPR’s “Brussels Effect,” suggesting the EU AI Act may similarly influence global practices. In soccer, after the first defender sets up to control the opponent with the ball, the second defender arrives to provide individual support. The second defender positions behind and to the inside of the first defender, goalside and far enough back to react if the first defender is beaten, forcing the dribbler toward the sideline. They maintain appropriate distance to avoid overrunning the play and adopt the same stance as the first defender. The second defender announces their arrival with phrases like “support” or “you have help,” and adjusts position as the first defender moves. When ready, they may tell the first defender to tackle by saying “take him” or “tackle.” Practice involves demonstrating stationary positioning, then movement, half-speed, and full-speed with oral communication. Key communication includes: support/help (cover is set), jockey/delay/control/contain (manage the attacker to buy time), and challenge/tackle (attempt to take the ball). If the first defender is beaten, the support defender takes over, possibly performing a defensive switch. The second defender gives these calls because they can see the field while the first defender focuses on the ball.

This study compared air-conduction (AC) and bone-conduction (BC) auditory brainstem response (ABR) and auditory steady-state response (ASSR) thresholds in infants aged 0–6 months with normal hearing (NH) and conductive hearing loss (CHL). CHL was only observed at 500 Hz. AC ABR and ASSR thresholds were significantly higher in the CHL group than in the NH group; BC thresholds did not differ significantly between groups. Air-bone gaps (ABG) were larger for CHL than NH for both measures, but the mean ABR ABG in CHL (36 dB) was larger than the ASSR ABG (21 dB), and ASSR showed greater overlap between NH and CHL groups. Minimum normal ASSR intensities were 40 dB HL for 500 and 2000 Hz AC, and 30 and 40 dB HL for BC. Sensitivity and specificity for detecting CHL were highest for AC ABR thresholds; ASSR thresholds and ABG had lower specificity. The authors conclude that ASSR, with the parameters used, is less effective than ABR in identifying mild low-frequency CHL, and ABR should remain the gold standard for infant hearing assessment in early hearing detection and intervention programs.

Turing GPUs introduce RT Cores that accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, enabling real-time ray tracing. A hybrid rendering model combines rasterization, ray tracing, and AI, with RT Cores offloading the SM so it can handle other shading work. Advanced denoising filtering reduces the number of rays required per pixel. Tensor Cores power NVIDIA NGX deep learning features, including Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS), which uses a neural network trained on 64x supersampled images to produce high-quality output from lower sample counts, improving performance. DLSS 2X mode processes input at final resolution to approach 64x super-sample quality. Other NGX features include InPainting for content removal and replacement, AI Slow-Mo for frame interpolation, and AI Super Rez for resolution upscaling.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) allows shading rate to vary per 16x16 pixel region, supporting content adaptive shading (lower rates in low-detail areas), motion adaptive shading (reduced rates for moving objects), and foveated rendering (lower rates in peripheral vision). Mesh Shading introduces task and mesh shaders with cooperative thread models, enabling efficient processing of large object counts and dynamic level-of-detail selection, reducing CPU draw call bottlenecks. Texture Space Shading (TSS) decouples shading from screen space by caching shading results in texture space, allowing temporal reuse and independent control of shading rate via MIP levels. Multi-View Rendering (MVR) expands single-pass stereo to up to four views per pass, supporting canted VR displays and cascaded shadow maps.

For VR, Turing supports VirtualLink via USB-C, foveated rendering through VRS, and RT Core-accelerated audio ray tracing. The TU104 GPU contains 48 SMs, 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, and a 256-bit memory interface. TU106 has 36 SMs, 2304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, 36 RT Cores, and no NVLink. The RTX-OPS metric combines derated peak operations: Tensor (20% of frame time), FP32 (80%), RT (40%), and INT32 (28%) to reflect hybrid rendering workloads. Ray tracing fundamentals include casting rays from the camera through pixels, using BVH trees to efficiently test intersections. Ray-traced shadows provide correct contact hardening from area lights, ray-traced ambient occlusion improves over screen-space techniques, and ray-traced reflections avoid artifacts of screen-space reflections and cubemaps. Examples from Battlefield V and Shadow of the Tomb Raider demonstrate these effects.

The passage describes a study on inclusive education legal frameworks and educational leaders' awareness in Addis Ababa's inclusive education resource centers. Inclusive education ensures equal opportunities for all children, removing barriers and embracing diversity (UNESCO, 2005; Ainscow & Sandill, 2010). Legal frameworks at global, regional, and national levels are crucial for implementation. Global documents like the UNCRPD emphasize the right to inclusive education; regional frameworks like the African Union’s policy advocate for diverse needs; national policies such as Ethiopia’s Education and Training Policy and National Special Needs Education Strategy provide localized guidelines. Understanding these policies helps leaders create strategies, advocate resources, design curricula, and ensure teacher development (Sharma et al., 2018; Forlin, 2010). Existing studies focused on barriers like infrastructure and teacher preparedness, neglecting legal frameworks and leaders' awareness (Girma, 2017). This study aims to fill that gap.

The literature review notes the historical medical model of disability and the importance of inclusive leadership (Ainscow & Sandill, 2010; Cobb, 2015) and leaders' role in raising awareness (Opoku, 2021). The problem statement defines policy frameworks as rules ensuring equal access (UNESCO, 2009) and stresses that leaders' awareness is key to successful implementation (Sharma et al., 2018; Deng & Zhu, 2013). Research questions ask what global, regional, and national frameworks exist and how aware leaders are.

The methodology used a qualitative case study design with three purposively selected inclusive schools in Addis Ababa. Participants were 15 individuals: itinerant teachers, teachers, school principals, and Ministry of Education experts. Data collection involved semi-structured interviews and document review. Thematic analysis was applied, with ethical measures including consent, pseudonyms, and member checking.

Findings for Research Question 1 identified global policies: UDHR (foundational equality principles), ICERD (non-discrimination), CRC Article 23 (rights of disabled children), Salamanca Statement (inclusive pedagogies), CRPD Article 24 (inclusive education commitment), Marrakesh Treaty (accessible formats), and SDG 4 (inclusive quality education). Regional policies: ACHPR (dignity, non-discrimination), ACRWC Article 13 (equal access for handicapped children), and the African Disability Protocol (accessible education, eliminating harmful practices). National frameworks: Ethiopian Constitution Articles 25 and 41(5) (equality, state support), Proclamation No. 1263/2021 (inclusive policy mandates), ETP 2023 (curricula for special needs), ESDP VI (improving access and equity), Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23-2029/30) (access, capacity, environment, governance), and National Children’s Policy (2017) (inclusive education priority). The study notes a comprehensive framework but highlights the need for leader awareness.

For Research Question 2, Ministry of Education experts showed awareness of global frameworks like EFA, Salamanca, and CRPD, and national documents, though one noted the lack of a specific inclusive education policy. School principals had limited awareness: one had basic training but no detailed knowledge, another was too busy, and a third lacked exposure to international policies. Itinerant teachers, with special needs backgrounds, were knowledgeable about global, regional, and national policies, but observed that principals and district leaders often lack awareness due to non-specialized backgrounds. Teachers believed inclusion is about compassion and were unaware of any legal frameworks.

Conclusions indicate a favorable policy environment but varying awareness: MoE experts and itinerant teachers are more aware than principals and teachers, attributed to training. Increasing awareness is essential. Implications for educational planning include equipping leaders with knowledge through professional development and integrating policies into curricula. Recommendations: regular professional development for school leaders on frameworks; strengthen integration of frameworks into teacher training; and MoE monitoring of policy awareness at school level.

The document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP encrypted virtual machines. The GHCB is a 4KB shared memory page that allows a guest to selectively expose register state to the hypervisor during Non-Automatic Exit (NAE) events. Version 2 introduces hypervisor feature advertisement via a FEATURES bitmap, support for SEV-SNP, and new NAE events. The GHCB MSR protocol enables early communication before the GHCB page is set up, including version negotiation, CPUID requests, AP reset hold, page state change, and GHCB registration. Supported NAE events include IOIO_PROT, MSR_PROT, VMMCALL, #NPF/MMIO access, Page State Change, SNP Guest Request, SNP Extended Guest Request, AP Creation, #HV doorbell page, #HV Send IPI, #HV Timer, APIC ID List, SNP Run VMPL, SNP TIO Guest Request, Secure AVIC, and Termination Request. Each event defines minimum guest state to provide and return. SMP booting under SEV-ES uses AP reset hold and an AP jump table; under SEV-SNP, the AP Creation NAE event allows direct VMSA assignment. NMI handling requires the guest to send an “NMI Complete” message. Debug register virtualization is supported on hardware with DebugVirtualization; otherwise, DR7 accesses are intercepted. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported. SNP Restricted Injection uses a shared doorbell page with PendingEvent and NoEoiRequired fields to deliver interrupts and non-maskable events via #HV, along with IPI and timer NAE events. The specification also defines the SEV-SNP secrets page, an EFI configuration table for the secrets and CPUID pages, and termination request protocols.

This study systematically evaluates fine-tuning (FT) and multi-head fine-tuning (MHFT) strategies for extending universal interatomic potentials (UIPs) to material surface systems. Using the MACE foundation model, three surface systems were examined: unary gold (Au), binary ruthenium(IV) oxide (RuO₂), and ternary bismuth vanadate (BiVO₄). For each, models trained from scratch (TS), zero-shot (ZS) predictions, and FT models were compared. FT consistently achieved lower energy and force prediction errors than TS and ZS, even with limited training data. Diatomic potential energy curves showed that FT models produced physically reasonable interactions, whereas TS models exhibited unphysical features at short and long ranges. In the BiVO₄ case, FT reduced the number of high-force outliers compared to TS and ZS, leveraging the foundation model’s knowledge of high-force environments.

To address catastrophic forgetting, MHFT was tested by simultaneously training on gold surface data and a subset of the original bulk training set. When evaluated on other noble metal surfaces (Ag, Cu, Pt, Ir), MHFT significantly improved surface energy predictions over both ZS and FT, reducing root-mean-square error by nearly half relative to ZS. However, MHFT incurred roughly 100 times longer training time than FT. The study notes that aligning computational conditions between pre-training and fine-tuning datasets is important for MHFT, while conventional FT tolerates moderate discrepancies. Practical guidelines are offered: for limited target data, researchers can fine-tune a foundation model with related data and compare against zero-shot performance to select an optimal starting point. Overall, FT and MHFT effectively enhance predictive accuracy for surface systems, with MHFT better preserving generalizability to out-of-domain materials.

This paper investigates whether the textual content of earnings press releases predicts stock returns on earnings announcement days. Using over 138,000 press releases from 2005–2023, it evaluates natural language processing techniques including Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), BERT, MPNET, and FinBERT. A rolling window approach constructs real-time return forecasts without look-ahead bias. Soft information extracted from press releases is found to be as informative as earnings surprises in explaining announcement-day returns. FinBERT provides the most effective extraction, while LDA-based representations improve interpretability by highlighting key themes. Stock prices fully incorporate this soft information by market open, making it impossible to profit from post-release trading, consistent with market efficiency. However, if information is available before the scheduled release, traders can identify high-return stocks with significantly better-than-random accuracy. Combining hard and soft information improves precision in identifying top-performing stocks. Topic analysis reveals a self-serving bias: positive returns are associated with internal factors like financial performance, while negative returns relate to external factors. The paper contributes an online learning framework, integration of bag-of-words and BERT models for explainability, and evidence that earnings surprise and text are equally important in predicting returns.

SpinGPT is a large language model-based agent for the Spin & Go poker format, built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It uses a two-stage training pipeline: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 320,000 professional decisions from high-stakes games, followed by offline reinforcement learning with the ORPO algorithm on 270,000 solver-generated hands mixed with 50,000 human hands to align with game-theory optimal (GTO) strategy. Game states are encoded as structured text prompts, and the model outputs actions with flexible bet sizes. SpinGPT-SFT achieved 80% exact accuracy and 86% macro F1 on a professional test set. After reinforcement learning, the final SpinGPT model showed 79% exact accuracy on professional data but improved bet-size calibration (MAE 0.30 BB vs. 0.61). On solver test data, it reached 72% exact and 78% tolerant accuracy. Against the Slumbot benchmark, SpinGPT-SFT with a heuristic all-in patch achieved a win rate of 13.4 BB/100. In head-to-head play, SpinGPT beat SpinGPT-SFT by 13.2 BB/100 over 10,000 hands. Limitations include no evaluation of the final model against Slumbot, occasional numerical errors, and a compute cost of 5.2 kgCO2e. Future work may explore stronger models, retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought reasoning, opponent adaptation, and explainability.

Six COVID-19-related intensive care recommendations were selected and encoded in FHIR. The system was deployed across five university hospitals with distinct IT infrastructures, evaluating over 82,000 intensive care episodes from January 2020 to May 2023. A validation study compared system outputs against manual reviews by intensive care physicians and a ground truth established by supervising physicians. The system achieved 97.0% accuracy, significantly outperforming human reviewers (86.6% accuracy). Most discrepancies were due to human error; system errors primarily arose from unstructured free-text data not transferred to the OMOP CDM. Automated processing was substantially faster than manual review. Adherence rates varied by recommendation and hospital, generally ranging from 10–60%, with some increase over time. Factors contributing to low adherence included newly introduced guidelines, incomplete documentation, and imprecise recommendation wording. The study demonstrates the feasibility, accuracy, and scalability of using interoperable standards for automated guideline adherence monitoring in intensive care.

The document is a Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) version 1.0, dated 16AUG2019, for study ZEA-DNK-02170. It describes planned analyses for plasma glucose concentration and pharmacodynamic metrics, including summary statistics by treatment group and time point, mean and individual glucose concentration versus time curves.

Safety analyses will use the safety set. Extent of exposure summaries include insulin administration prior to hypoglycemia induction, the hypoglycemia induction procedure, trial medication administration, and post-treatment rescue glucose infusion. Time to first IV glucose infusion after IMP administration will be described with descriptive statistics, calculated as start of first glucose administration minus time of study medication administration; no censoring is applied if no infusion is given.

Local tolerability at the injection site is assessed at 30, 120, and 300 minutes post-dose. A summary table will display counts and percentages of patients with local symptoms by time point, symptom, and grade, excluding "other types of reactions."

Adverse event (AE) summaries are restricted to treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs), defined as AEs occurring after dosing or pre-existing AEs that worsened. If onset date is partial and cannot determine if treatment-emergent, it is counted as such unless the end date is before dosing. AEs are coded using MedDRA version 21.0 or higher. Causal relationship is assessed as not related, unlikely related, possibly related, or probably related; possible and probable are subsumed as "related." Missing relationship is set to related if not clarified. Severity is graded mild, moderate, severe; missing severity is not imputed.

An overview AE summary table will present number and percentage of patients with at least one event and total events for: AEs during screening, TEAEs, TEAEs of special interest (AESIs), other important TEAEs, injection site reactions (investigator-assessed and a special search category), study drug-related TEAEs, serious TEAEs, serious study drug-related TEAEs, and deaths. Frequency tables by system organ class and preferred term will be prepared for TEAEs, AESIs, other important TEAEs, injection site reactions, study drug-related TEAEs, and TEAEs by causal relationship. Summaries are ordered by descending incidence in the dasiglucagon group. Special search categories include SMQs for Torsade de pointes/QT prolongation (broad) and drug-related hepatic disorders (broad), with external PT files.

Laboratory data will be listed with high/low flags relative to reference ranges. For summaries, the most recent value is used if multiple measurements exist at a visit. Tabulations for each lab parameter by treatment group include: descriptive statistics for continuous variables at each scheduled time point with counts/percentages for below/within/above reference range; categorical results as counts/percentages; and change from baseline (screening visit V1 to follow-up V3) with descriptive statistics. Hematology, biochemistry, and urinalysis follow this presentation; coagulation parameters at screening are tabulated; pregnancy test results are tabulated by visit; alcohol breath test data are listed.

Vital signs are summarized with descriptive statistics at baseline and each postbaseline time point. Categorical analysis of pulse rate uses specified thresholds. Physical examination results are only listed.

ECG data: number of patients with normal/abnormal clinically significant/abnormal not clinically significant assessments are tabulated. Descriptive statistics for each ECG parameter by visit and treatment group are presented. Categorical summary of QTcF values includes counts of patients with >450 ms, >480 ms, >500 ms at each visit, and change from baseline >30 ms and >60 ms at postbaseline time points.

Immunogenicity: ADA occurrence is analyzed descriptively. ADA incidence includes treatment-induced (ADA-negative at baseline, positive after drug) and treatment-boosted (baseline-positive with ≥5-fold titer increase) patients. The denominator is evaluable patients (at least one post-drug sample with reportable result). Baseline-positive patients without post-drug samples are excluded.

Changes from the protocol in the SAP include rewording the primary efficacy parameter statistical analysis and adding sensitivity/supportive analyses, and changing secondary efficacy variable terminology from "within" to "at" specific minutes.

Appendices specify presentation conventions: specialized text styles only if adding value; standard keyboard characters; footnotes left-justified; means/medians to one more decimal place than raw data, standard deviations to two more; percentages to tenths; zero-count categories displayed; P values rounded to three decimal places. Figures include legends, black and white with optional color, and source/program footnotes. Listings are sorted by treatment, center, patient, visit, date/time; dates in SAS date format; times in 24-hour HH:MM:SS. Missing/incomplete AE onset dates are assumed treatment-emergent unless partial date or stop date indicates otherwise. Derived variables formulas are provided for days, months, years, unit conversions, BMI, and change from baseline. SAS programming QC requirements cover program structure, log review, output review, dataset structure validation, data verification (spot-checks, macro validation), and documentation. A list of planned tables, figures, and listings is included, organized by ICH E3 headings, with mock shells and footnotes.

A new study by Nic Lewis and Judith Curry in the Journal of Climate finds that future global warming is likely 30–45% lower than projected by most computer climate simulations. Using observed warming from the mid/late 19th century to 2016 and updated forcing data, the paper estimates a median equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) of 1.66°C (range 1.15–2.7°C) and transient climate response (TCR) of 1.33°C (1.15–1.9°C), compared to CMIP5 model medians of 3.1°C and 1.9°C. The estimates are insensitive to the analysis period. The study addresses criticisms, showing that time-varying climate feedbacks have negligible impact and that potential biases from forcing efficacy, temperature data issues, or sea-surface temperature patterns are minor. The results indicate that high ECS and TCR values from most CMIP5 models are inconsistent with historical warming.

The manuscript aims to illustrate the value of critical approaches to quantitative research and serve as a guide to critical quantitative scholarship in education, advancing epistemological and methodological considerations. Its primary audience includes scholars employing quantitative methods and/or critical perspectives, such as students, faculty, researchers, institutional research staff, and methods instructors. It also seeks to help evaluate scholarship applying critical theories to quantitative methods and encourage researchers to apply critical theories.

The authors assert that quantitative research is not objective; biases and assumptions are inherent. They provide their positionalities: Jay, a white cisgender queer researcher, studies queer and trans collegians using quantitative methods and aims to dismantle white cisheteropatriarchy. Jimmy, a Vietnamese-Chinese American, notes that aggregating Asian identities masks inequalities and emphasizes critical reflection to minimize harm and advance equity.

Quantitative criticalism combines methods and epistemologies. While quantitative research is historically post-positivist, criticalists examine phenomena through positionality and subjectivity, advocate for social justice, and challenge existing policies and measures. They view numbers as not neutral, requiring analyses to account for systemic oppression. Justice-driven scholarship must permeate the entire research process, from research questions to implications. Community and solidarity among quantitative criticalists are important, especially for emerging scholars. Research should connect to transformational change, involve community partners, consider data sovereignty, and ensure transparency in authorship and power dynamics.

Tensions exist. First, white supremacist and cisheteropatriarchal notions are embedded in the founding of statistics (e.g., Galton, Pearson, eugenics), and criticalists must work to dismantle this legacy. Second, the threshold of criticality is unclear; authors' intentions are crucial but difficult to discern, and incremental change may be viewed as a tool of white supremacy. Methodological tensions include challenges in operationalizing complex social identities, essentialist demographic data in surveys, limited analytical power for intersectional approaches, and underrepresentation constraining generalizability. Nonparametric tests are under-taught but useful for small or unbalanced samples. Quantitative research often blames minoritized communities rather than systems; criticalists instead question systems and policies. Generalizability, a post-positivist logic, centers white students and assumes homogeneity among BIPOC communities. Tensions can be generative, revealing methodological fault lines.

The manuscript reviews four examples. In Critical Race Theory, QuantCrit combines CRT with quantitative methods. Sablan (2019) operationalized community cultural wealth into scales, embedding CRT throughout; the study shows that criticality requires lengthy effort and clear intentions, though generalizability is limited. In Queer Theory, Garvey (2017) demonstrated the danger of collapsing LGBQ categories and advocated for a separate queer option, acknowledging the tension between categorization and queer theory's fluidity. In Intersectionality, Szymanski and Lewis (2016) examined African American women's coping with gendered racism using interaction effects, while Wilson and Urick (2022) used latent class analysis to study opportunity gaps. There is no consensus on integrating intersectionality; interaction effects are researcher-defined and may neglect groups, while latent class analysis may not center desired populations.

Implications target scholars and methods instructors. Two principles: claiming expertise is antithetical to critical thought, and positionalities ground the work. The authors offer musings on intentions and the threshold of criticality. Intentions matter but are hard to discern, especially with post-hoc analyses. Criticality is a continuum with no universal threshold, yet incremental change can be a tool of white supremacy. Three reflective questions are posed: What are your intentions for using quantitative criticalism? Can methods rooted in white supremacy be vehicles for justice? What is your threshold of criticality?

The closing states the goal is to advance social justice and equity. The authors have felt marginalized but reclaim quantitative methods through critical frames to dismantle power structures. They hope to build a coalition. Quantitative methods without philosophical grounding cause harm; readers are encouraged to move beyond objectivist approaches and embrace criticality despite tensions, as collective advocacy outweighs complacency.

Mega Geometry is an RTX technology that increases geometric detail in ray-traced applications by addressing cluster-based level-of-detail updates and high object counts. It introduces Cluster-level Acceleration Structures (CLAS) for BVH construction, reducing processing by two orders of magnitude, and Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures (PTLAS) that update only changed partitions. Mega Geometry also enables real-time ray tracing of displaced subdivision surfaces. It is supported on all RTX GPUs from Turing onward, with Blackwell RT Cores featuring cluster engines and up to 2x the ray-triangle intersection rate.

Linear Swept Spheres (LSS) is a hardware-accelerated primitive for ray tracing curves, providing about 2x faster rendering and 5x less VRAM than DOTS for hair. Shader Execution Reordering (SER) 2.0 on Blackwell doubles reorder logic efficiency, improving coherence extraction for path tracing and neural shading. The AI Management Processor (AMP) is a programmable RISC-V context scheduler on the GPU that offloads scheduling from the CPU, reducing latency and improving multitasking, compatible with Windows Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling.

Blackwell adds hardware encode and decode support for 4:2:2 chroma-sampled video. The ninth-generation NVENC encoder improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% BD-BR PSNR, with an AV1 Ultra High Quality mode for an extra 5% improvement. The sixth-generation NVDEC decoder offers 2x faster H.264 decoding and 4:2:2 support. DisplayPort 2.1b UHBR 20 enables 8K at 165Hz and 4K at 480Hz.

Max-Q power efficiency features advanced power gating with separate voltage rails, accelerated frequency switching 1000x faster than prior architectures, and low latency sleep 10x faster than Ada, yielding up to 50% power savings in some inference workloads.

DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation, generating up to three additional frames per rendered frame using a faster AI model and hardware Flip Metering. Transformer-based models replace CNNs for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing, improving image quality, stability, and detail.

Neural shaders, enabled by the Cooperative Vectors API, allow AI models in graphics shaders. RTX Neural Materials compress complex materials, RTX Neural Texture Compression provides up to 7:1 VRAM compression, Neural Radiance Cache infers indirect lighting, RTX Skin enables real-time subsurface scattering, and RTX Neural Faces uses generative AI to improve face rendering.

The Blackwell GPU family includes GB202 (92.2 billion transistors, 24,576 CUDA Cores, 512-bit memory interface), GB203 (45.6 billion transistors, 10,752 CUDA Cores, 256-bit), and GB205 (31 billion transistors, 6,400 CUDA Cores, 192-bit). Arizona has been a leader in school choice, with open enrollment, charter schools, tax credit programs, and the first Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) voucher program in 2011, later expanded to universal eligibility in 2022 despite voters rejecting a capped expansion in 2018. Grand Canyon Institute (GCI) research finds that while a growing share of universal ESA participants come from charter or district schools, nearly three-quarters of enrollees did not or would not have attended public schools. About 90% of new universal entrants in FY2025 had attended a district or charter school. Zip code analysis shows ESA vouchers primarily enroll children from higher-income zip codes, though the income gap has narrowed. GCI presents evidence that a significant number of ESA users are not using funds for private school tuition; no more than 40% of students used allocations for private school tuition in FY2023, with many using them for homeschooling or extracurriculars.
