The Tax Court addressed whether noncharitable gifts made by check were complete for federal gift and estate tax purposes upon delivery in 1980 or upon payment in 1981. The decedent delivered six $3,000 checks on December 24, 1980, but the donees did not present them for payment until January 28, 1981, when additional $3,000 checks were also delivered and cashed. The parties agreed that if the gifts were complete in 1980, they qualified for the annual exclusion and the estate tax assessment was barred by the three-year limitations period; if complete in 1981, they did not qualify and the assessment was not barred.

Petitioner argued that under the relation-back doctrine, payment related back to delivery. The court noted that prior Tax Court decisions applied the doctrine only to charitable contributions, and federal courts in McCarthy and Cullis refused to extend it to noncharitable gifts. The court found that petitioner failed to prove unconditional delivery because of the 35-day delay, lack of explanation, and absence of evidence regarding sufficient funds or donative intent. It did not decide whether the relation-back doctrine could ever apply to noncharitable gifts, holding only that petitioner did not meet its burden.

Applying Oklahoma law, the court determined that under the Uniform Commercial Code a check does not assign funds, and a donee who gives no consideration is not a holder in due course, allowing the donor to stop payment. Therefore, a gift by check is not complete until payment or acceptance by the bank. The court held that the decedent parted with dominion and control over the funds when the checks were paid in 1981, making the gifts complete at that time.

Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) leverages a deep neural network and Tensor Cores to construct high-quality images from multiple frames. The memory subsystem uses GDDR6X, developed with Micron, which employs PAM4 signaling to transfer two bits per clock edge, doubling the I/O data rate. The NVIDIA A40 data center GPU, based on GA10x, delivers up to 2x FP32 throughput, 2x ray-tracing throughput, and up to 5x (10x with sparsity) AI training throughput versus the Quadro RTX 6000. Ampere GPUs support 4K at 120 Hz and 8K at 60 Hz via DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC 1.2a, and are the first discrete GPUs with HDMI 2.1. The fifth-generation NVDEC decoder provides hardware-accelerated decoding for MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, with AV1 hardware decode being a first for GPUs. The seventh-generation NVENC encoder offloads video encoding, delivering quality on par with x264 Medium while reducing CPU usage, and supports up to 8K HEVC encoding.

The GeForce RTX 3090 incorporates the GA102 GPU with 82 SMs, 10496 CUDA Cores, and 24 GB of GDDR6X memory. The GeForce RTX 3070 uses the GA104 GPU with GDDR6 and delivers performance faster than the RTX 2080 Ti. Error Detection and Replay (EDR) technology on GDDR6X detects transmission errors and replays them, allowing overclocking until performance plateaus rather than crashes. The NVIDIA RTX A6000 features a GA102 GPU with 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 second-generation RT Cores, 48 GB of GDDR6, and supports NVLink for up to 96 GB combined memory.

This study investigated genetic variants and plasma cytokines as biomarkers for aggressive cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) phenotypes. In a cohort of 103 patients, genotyping of PTPN2rs72872125, VDRrs7975232, VDRrs731236, VDRrs11568820, and FCGR2Ars1801274 was performed, and plasma levels of 18 cytokines were measured. Symptomatic patients (hemorrhage or seizure) were compared to asymptomatic patients.

The PTPN2rs72872125 CT genotype and VDRrs7975232 CC genotype were independently associated with an asymptomatic phenotype in multivariable analysis. Patients with PTPN2rs72872125 CT had higher plasma IL-10 and lower IL-18 and IFN-γ, while those with VDRrs7975232 C allele had lower IL-27 and IL-23. A diagnostic biomarker combining PTPN2rs72872125 CC genotype and GM-CSF plasma levels distinguished symptomatic from asymptomatic patients (AUC 0.663, sensitivity 41.3%, specificity 85.7%). This formula performed well in familial and infratentorial lesion subgroups.

In a prospective follow-up of 42 patients, the FCGR2Ars1801274 GG genotype predicted symptomatic events (hemorrhage, lesion growth, or new-onset epilepsy) with high accuracy (AUC 0.796; in propensity-matched analysis AUC 0.875). In silico analysis showed the FCGR2Ars1801274 variant causes a His131Arg substitution in a domain conserved among higher primates.

Regarding symptom onset, VDRrs731236 AA genotype was associated with later symptom onset, while VDRrs11568820 CC genotype correlated with earlier symptoms.

The study suggests that these genetic variants and cytokine patterns may serve as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for CCM aggressiveness.

This passage describes a numerical model for methane bubble growth in shallow aquatic muds. Methane bubbles nucleate from microbial decomposition, grow beyond pore scale by deforming sediment, and form disc-shaped cavities. The mechanical behavior of consolidated muds is described by Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics (LEFM), treating bubbles as Mode I tensile cracks. The model couples solute transport of dissolved methane and solid mechanics. Outside the bubble, diffusion of dissolved methane is governed by a conservation equation with uniform boundary concentration, and sediment elasticity is modeled via force equilibrium with overburden load and gravity. The bubble itself is modeled by integrating methane flux over its surface, applying Henry's law for gas–aqueous equilibrium, ideal gas law for internal pressure, and elastic displacement for volume. Fracture propagation uses the displacement extrapolation method to compute stress intensity factor (SIF) along the 3D crack front, with crack growth direction determined by the strain energy density criterion, ensuring pure Mode I propagation. Crack increments are proportional to the square of local SIF, with maximum increment at the bubble head. Fracture occurs when maximum SIF exceeds sediment fracture toughness. The model is implemented in COMSOL Multiphysics using finite elements, with a refined meshing strategy near the bubble front. Validation against analytical solutions for mature bubble shape and size shows good agreement across varying fracture toughness. Limitations include applicability only to individual bubbles and lack of upscaling methods to relate single-bubble characteristics to bulk sediment properties, which is needed for remote sensing and geohazard assessment.

Social media platforms are using artificial intelligence to moderate content like hate speech and fake news. AI can recognize offensive language and images using natural language processing, but accuracy varies. It fails to understand context, as seen when Twitter's algorithm mistakenly blocked LGBT hashtags. AI is biased because it learns from human-tagged data; for example, Google Photos mislabeled dark-skinned people as gorillas. Training data biases spread when shared among developers. AI cannot determine intent, flagging educational or photojournalistic content, such as Facebook removing a swastika image opposing hate or the 'napalm girl' photo. Human moderators remain essential for final decisions, with Facebook doubling its review team to 20,000. AI assists by prioritizing posts for human review, like identifying suicidal content that led to emergency calls. Experts say AI facilitates faster human moderation but is far from fully automated. The rapid growth of technology outpaces ethics, potentially increasing demand for employees with humanities backgrounds.

This study developed and evaluated a teacher education program integrating collaborative inquiry with panoramic cameras to improve teacher education students' (TESs) diagnostic and instructional design capabilities. Effective teaching requires diagnosing student learning problems by observing behaviors that reflect cognitive processing of instructional material. Instructional activities, designed to align with cognitive processes, can be assessed by documenting student responses. Collaborative inquiry provides a framework for identifying and solving student learning issues through lesson preparation, classroom observation, evidence collection, post-teaching discussion, and reflection. However, observers often lack sufficient evidence of student learning problems. Panoramic cameras can capture comprehensive video and audio of student groups, allowing observers to review, verify, and supplement records.

The study implemented a course titled 'Professional Teaching Practicum' with 22 TESs in five groups, each paired with a junior high school class. The course had two stages: a five-week preparation stage covering collaborative inquiry concepts, lesson plan design, observation training using videos, and panoramic camera operation; and a 12-week collaborative inquiry cycle. In the cycle, TESs alternated as teaching educators and observers. Each three-week cycle included collaborative lesson planning, teaching practice with observation and panoramic camera recording, post-lesson review of footage and records, sharing observations, and reflection leading to instructional plan adjustments. This cycle repeated four times.

Data were collected using an Observation Record Form based on student responses to teaching activities, evaluated with a three-rank checklist: rank 2 for concrete evidence linking student performance to learning objectives, rank 1 for insufficient evidence, rank 0 for irrelevant descriptions. A questionnaire on perceived instructional design capabilities covered lesson preparation, linking student learning with teaching during observation, and adjusting plans post-discussion. Pre- and post-tests were analyzed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

Results showed that observation report scores improved across four cycles, from an average of 0.47 to 1.88 out of 2, after guidance emphasizing evidence-based diagnosis. Perceived capabilities significantly increased in all three facets (p<0.05). The study concludes that the program enhanced TESs' diagnostic and instructional design abilities, demonstrating feasibility. The researcher notes that collaborative inquiry and panoramic camera use facilitated evidence-based discussions, though further research is needed on the effectiveness of TESs' proposed strategies. The approach may be applicable to other professional education fields.

This study reports outcomes of COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) transfusion in patients with hematological malignancies and SARS-CoV-2 infection. A cohort of 112 patients (median age 62.5 years) with hematological malignancies received CCP through a French national monitored access program. Most had B-lymphoid neoplasms (74%), and 72% had prior anti-CD20 or anti-CD19 therapy. At transfusion, 87% were seronegative for SARS-CoV-2. CCP was associated with significant decreases in temperature, C-reactive protein, ferritin, and fibrinogen, and an increase in PCR cycle threshold values. The 90-day overall survival was 64.9% for the whole cohort, 77.5% for B-lymphoid neoplasm, 20% for myeloid neoplasm, and 36.8% for plasma-cell neoplasm. In multivariable analysis, age >70 years, high blood pressure, and severe COVID-19 were associated with lower survival, while prior anti-CD20/CD19 therapy was associated with better survival. A nested propensity score analysis compared 81 CCP-treated B-cell neoplasm patients to 120 untreated patients. In the main inverse probability of treatment weighting analysis restricted to anti-CD20 pre-exposed patients alive 16 days after hospitalization, CCP was associated with a 63% reduction in risk of death. Sensitivity analyses showed consistent benefit. The authors conclude that CCP may be beneficial, particularly in B-cell lymphoid malignancy patients pre-treated with anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies who are unable to mount a humoral response. Limitations include the observational design, lack of viral strain data, and the fact that no patients were vaccinated or received anti-spike monoclonal antibodies.

A playback device receives digital data representing audio content, sends at least a portion of that data to an identification system configured to identify the audio content, receives associated information from the identification system, and in response sends the received information to a control device that controls the playback device. The control device may send a command to the playback device to retrieve such information while the playback device is playing the audio content, receive the information from the playback device, and display a representation of the received information or metadata retrieved from a metadata curating device at a network location indicated by the received information. The playback device can extract digital data from different positions of an audio pipeline, perform sample rate conversion, detect discontinuities in the digital data to trigger identification, send portions periodically, and segregate the digital data into frequency-range portions for identification. The system operates within a media playback environment comprising playback devices, control devices, and zone configurations.

A directional illumination apparatus includes an imaging directional backlight with a waveguide for guiding light, and an illuminator array providing light to the waveguide. The waveguide has first and second opposed guide surfaces, an input end where light sources are disposed, and a reflective end. Light extraction features on the second guide surface deflect reflected input light through the first guide surface as output light. The waveguide images the light sources in a lateral direction so that output light is directed into respective optical windows distributed according to input positions.

A display device comprises such a backlight, a transmissive spatial light modulator, an input polariser, an output polariser, at least one additional polariser arranged on the input side of the input polariser or on the output side of the output polariser, and at least one retarder arranged between the additional polariser and the respective polariser. The retarder may include at least one correcting passive retarder and at least one switchable liquid crystal retarder. This arrangement provides a privacy display with reduced off-axis image visibility to a snooper while substantially maintaining on-axis luminance. The additional polariser may be a reflective polariser, and its electric vector transmission direction may be parallel to that of the adjacent polariser.

The retarder may comprise crossed A-plates (with slow axes in the plane of the retarders that are crossed, optionally at 45° to the polariser transmission direction), a C-plate (retarder with slow axis perpendicular to the plane), an O-plate (retarder with a slow axis having components both perpendicular and in-plane), or combinations thereof. The switchable liquid crystal retarder can be switched between an O-plate retarder and an A-plate retarder by an applied voltage, enabling switching between a privacy mode with reduced off-axis luminance and a wide angle mode with no reduction. The switchable liquid crystal retarder may have homeotropic or homogeneous alignment, and may include independently addressable regions for patterned privacy or camouflage. Multiple retarder layers with parallel or orthogonal alignments can further control the polar region of reduced luminance.

The backlight waveguide may have curved light extraction features with positive optical power in the lateral direction, and a reflective end with positive optical power. The light sources may be arranged at the input end opposite the reflective end, or at the sides. A rear reflector with pairs of reflective corner facets may be used to convert polarization of rejected light. A control system controls the light sources and, in some embodiments, the applied voltage across the switchable liquid crystal retarder. The backlight can switch between modes outputting light into viewing windows of differing widths. The control system may synchronize the spatial light modulator and light sources to display primary and secondary images in a temporally multiplexed manner, obscuring the primary image for off-axis viewers. The display may be used in a vehicle, arranged beneath a transparent window or in front of a seat, to reduce reflections.

Mortimer J. Adler, a perennialist philosopher, emphasized eternal values and continuity in education, focusing on self-development and universal truth. He viewed philosophy as opinion and essentialized knowledge, advocating for lecture and memorization methods as enduring. Adler considered docility and obedience as virtuous, involving postponement of judgment and submission to authoritative teachers, not as slavery but as intellectual enlightenment. He linked democracy to education, rejecting the idea that schooling is merely job preparation, and argued that children should be educated according to their full capacity, though the researchers note his lack of differentiation between men and women. The paper examines posthumanism, questioning human deconstruction, anthropocentric supremacy, and the impact of technology, AI, and robotics on human agency and social interaction. It reviews Christian education management studies, including family-based interventions, spirituality in health, multi-country moral education, and character education. The researchers conclude that educational management should go beyond administration to embrace perennialist values, and that justice involves empowering women and not scapegoating children for educational failures.

Intel has included a microcontroller called the Intel Management Engine (ME) in its CPUs for the last decade. It is always on, connected to storage and network interfaces, and can be woken over a network. Parts were included at the NSA's behest. Researchers presented an exploit at BlackHat Europe allowing arbitrary code execution on the ME, but it requires physical access. The ME is part of a collection of hardware and software including Trusted Platform Modules and Active Management Technology. It runs the Minix operating system. Intel kept it closed-source, but now the wall was breached; anyone can execute arbitrary code via USB stick. Mitigation options exist: System76 released a firmware update to disable the ME, and Dell sells a laptop with ME disabled by default. Intel provides a detection tool, but there is no generic way to turn it off; implementation is left to motherboard manufacturers. Some OEMs have provided methods. The Evil Maid exploit only works on ME versions above 11, excluding Macs. A computer without valid ME firmware shuts down after 30 minutes, but the me_cleaner tool tricks the ME by deleting the first page of its ROM, stopping it while allowing the computer to function. The current exploit is a physical access Evil Maid variant, considered overblown in realistic threat models. The ultimate network-based exploit does not yet exist. The passage emphasizes that unauditable code cannot be trusted.
I am unable to summarize this passage.

The document describes the MSPM0C1105 and MSPM0C1106 microcontrollers. The CPU subsystem implements an Arm Cortex-M0+ processor with clock frequencies up to 32 MHz, pre-fetch logic, a 2-line I-cache, a 24-bit SysTick timer, and a nested vectored interrupt controller with 4 priority levels. Five operating modes are provided: RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, and SHUTDOWN, with two power domains (PD1 for CPU/memories/high-performance peripherals, PD0 for low-speed peripherals). PD1 is powered in RUN and SLEEP; PD0 is powered in RUN, SLEEP, STOP, and STANDBY; both are disabled in SHUTDOWN. A power management unit includes brown-out reset with programmable thresholds and a core regulator. The clock module offers internal LFOSC (32 kHz) and SYSOSC (32 MHz), plus support for external crystals or clock inputs, and distributes multiple clocks (MCLK, CPUCLK, ULPCLK, MFCLK, LFCLK, ADCCLK, CLK_OUT, HFCLK, HSCLK). A DMA controller provides 2 full-feature channels and 1 basic channel, supporting various transfer modes and triggers from ADC, UART, SPI, or timers. An event manager routes peripheral events to the CPU, DMA, or other peripherals via static and programmable routes. Memory includes flash with 1 KB sector erase, up to 100,000 program/erase cycles on select sectors, and SRAM with zero wait states, retained down to STANDBY mode, with write protection. GPIO supports up to 45 pins with set/clear/toggle, wake from SHUTDOWN, and FastWake. IOMUX enables pad configuration and digital pin muxing. A 12-bit ADC operates up to 1.6 Msps with 10.6-bit ENOB (external reference), internal channels for temperature, supply, and signal chain, and configurable internal references of 1.4 V or 2.5 V. A temperature sensor provides a linear voltage output connected to an ADC channel, with a factory calibration value. The low-frequency subsystem includes a real-time clock (RTC_B) with calendar, alarms, and calibration, and an independent watchdog timer (IWDT) with a 25-bit counter. A shared voltage reference module supports 1.4 V and 2.5 V internal references or external reference. A comparator supports blanking sources, wake from low-power modes, and an 8-bit reference DAC. Security features include flexible firewalls and a CRC-16 module. Communication peripherals include UART (with LIN, FIFOs), I2C (up to 1 Mbps, SMBus, wake on address match), and SPI (up to 16 Mbps, controller/peripheral, multiple formats). The windowed watchdog timer (WWDT) offers selectable periods and interval timer mode. Timers include general-purpose (TIMG) with QEI and advanced (TIMA) with PWM, dead band, and fault handling. The presidential election cycle theory posits that U.S. stock market performance follows a four-year pattern tied to presidential terms. It asserts that the first two years of a president's term likely outperform the last two, and midterm election years show poor performance until the fourth quarter. Yale Hirsch, founder of the Stock Trader’s Almanac, first quantified this effect. According to the Almanac, the Pre-Election Year is the best and Election Year second best; since 1952, the S&P 500 averaged 12.5% in election years with an incumbent running, 6.7% in all election years, and –1.5% in open-field elections. Midterm years are typically the weakest, but the fourth quarter of those years has the best performance, and volatility tends to increase. Some attribute this to presidents stimulating the economy in the second half to aid re-election. However, the theory is not always predictive; for example, the market performed best in the year after the last three presidential elections. Analysis of S&P 500 data since the 1930s shows stock and bond markets tend to underperform in the year before a presidential election, with equities averaging less than 6% growth versus an overall 8.5% average, and bonds returning about 6.5% compared to a 7.5% average. After midterm elections, the S&P 500 performed better, and the party in power was not a significant factor. Market trends remain consistent barring major shocks. Rob Haworth of US Bank notes uncertainty increases every four years, which markets dislike. Eric Freedman adds that policy-driven economic instability is usually sector-specific, not economy-wide. Healthcare and energy sectors often see heightened pre-election volatility due to potential policy shifts. Hainlin emphasizes that election outcomes significantly impact the economy and commerce, with trade policy dependent on Congress. Post-election, it is important to reassess how new policies affect the global economy. While monitoring affected industries is prudent, there is no need for excessive concern about election volatility, as higher volatility has become a permanent feature of the financial system. The key is to stay invested and rebalance portfolios. Backtests confirm the Presidential Cycle's influence, making it a notable seasonal pattern for market timers and dollar-cost averaging.

An optical waveguide display apparatus includes an optical waveguide with a first diffractive part (input Bragg grating) that receives display light and diffracts it into an angle for guided propagation along the waveguide by total internal reflection (TIR), and a second diffractive part (output Bragg grating) optically coupled to the first that receives and diffracts the light to an angle for output. External surfaces of the waveguide against which guided light reflects internally are coated with a material having a refractive index value substantially equal to or less than 1.0 at optical wavelengths. This material may be a meta-material. The coating reduces the critical angle for TIR, allowing light from outside the original field of view to be retained and guided, thereby expanding the total field of view and/or extending the operable wavelength range.

The meta-material may comprise a spatially periodically repeating planar array of unit cells, each including a magnetic resonator sandwiched between opposed conductive meshes. The magnetic resonator may consist of an alumina layer between two conductive plates. The meshes define grids of crossed conductive lines, with crossing points located adjacent the resonator. The waveguide may be a multi-layered slab structure with separate component slab waveguides for different colours, each having input and output diffractive parts tuned for respective wavelengths, joined by an intermediate layer of the low-index material. Protective outer layers may be placed over outermost meta-material coatings. The diffractive parts may be mutually conjugated to reduce geometric distortions and chromatic dispersion. A method for displaying light using such a waveguide is also described, involving receiving light at the first diffractive part, diffracting it for TIR propagation, and outputting it via the second diffractive part, with the external surfaces coated as above.

The lecture reviews renewal theorems and introduces countable-state Markov chains. The strong law for renewals states that the sample-path limit of arrivals per time equals 1/x-bar with probability 1. The elementary renewal theorem gives the same limit for the expected rate. Blackwell's theorem says that for arithmetic inter-renewal intervals with span λ, the limit of the expected number of renewals in an interval of length λ is λ/x-bar; for non-arithmetic distributions, the limit of (m(t+δ)−m(t))/δ as t→∞ is 1/x-bar, but limits cannot be interchanged.

For an arithmetic renewal process with span 1, the joint probability of age i and duration k at time t is the probability of an arrival at t−i times the pmf of the inter-renewal interval, provided k>i. As t→∞, the arrival probability tends to 1/x-bar, so the joint distribution becomes independent of age. The limiting marginal pmf of duration is k·p_X(k)/x-bar, giving expected duration E[X²]/E[X]. Expected age is E[X²]/(2E[X]), differing by a factor 1/2 from the sample-path average due to integer-time effects.

Countable-state Markov chains are then discussed. A Bernoulli random walk on integers with probabilities p and q has variance growing with n, causing state probabilities to approach zero; no steady-state distribution exists. All states communicate with period 2. For p=1/2, return to 0 occurs with probability 1 but expected return time is infinite. A birth-death chain on nonnegative integers is recurrent if p<1/2, transient if p>1/2, and null recurrent if p=1/2.

Recurrence is defined by f_jj(∞)=1, meaning eventual return to state j with probability 1. Returns then form a renewal process. First-passage probabilities f_ij(n) satisfy f_ij(1)=p_ij and for n>1, f_ij(n)=∑_{k≠j} p_ik f_kj(n−1). The smallest solution to related equations yields the correct probabilities. If state j is recurrent, the number of returns up to time t goes to infinity, and the sum of p_jj(n) diverges. Communicating states share the same recurrence/transience status. Recurrent states are positive recurrent if expected return time is finite, or null recurrent if infinite (steady-state probability zero).

A custom dataset was created from 51 experiment videos with dense annotations for faces and instruments. Experiments compare MSFF-YOLOv8 with and without CAOR against YOLOv8, SAM, and Edge SAM. The lecture discusses auctions, contrasting them with standard price-setting models. It introduces the independent private values model, where bidders have private signals equal to their values, are risk neutral, and values are independent. In a second-price sealed bid auction, bidding true value is a weakly dominant strategy; the seller's expected revenue is the expected second-highest value. An ascending button auction yields the same outcome. In a first-price sealed bid auction, bidders shade bids below true values, balancing profit margin against win probability. The equilibrium bid equals the expected second-highest value conditional on having the highest value, leading to the revenue equivalence theorem: any mechanism that awards the object to the highest-value bidder and gives zero surplus to the lowest type yields the same expected revenue and bidder surplus.

The theorem's limitations are noted: with risk-averse bidders, first-price auctions raise more revenue; with positively correlated values, second-price auctions may raise more. The theorem also ignores reserve prices. Optimal reserve price in a second-price auction is the monopoly price, regardless of the number of bidders, though entry costs and commitment problems can reduce its desirability.

The lecture then covers common value auctions and the winner's curse, where winning reveals that others had lower signals, so rational bidders shade bids accordingly. An empirical study by Hendricks and Porter on U.S. offshore oil lease auctions is presented. Drainage tracts adjacent to existing wells have higher value and lower risk but attract fewer bidders and yield higher profits for incumbents due to asymmetric information and severe winner's curse. The model predicts: incumbents bid more often, win over half the time, earn positive profits, while uninformed bidders earn zero expected profits (negative when incumbent does not bid, positive when incumbent bids). The paper tests multiple predictions using data from 1959–1969, finding support for the asymmetric information explanation. The lecture concludes by noting that allowing joint bidding on drainage tracts might effectively transfer rents to the initial wildcat auction, where competition is symmetric.

In Africa and the Middle East, governments are opening power sectors to foreign investment, mainly through IPPs, and regional transmission links are being developed. The passage proposes a methodology for a trusting agent in a digital business ecosystem to determine the probability of not achieving the full benefit of its invested resources when interacting with a trusted agent. The trusting agent first analyzes possible risk, which combines probability of failure and consequences. The methodology involves determining the FailureLevel, which quantifies the probability of failure on a failure scale. The interaction is divided into pre-interaction and post-interaction start time phases, further split into time slots to account for dynamic risk. In pre-interaction time slots, a crisp FailureLevel is determined from past interactions or recommendations, according to the specific context and criteria of the future interaction. In post-interaction time slots, the trusting agent determines the magnitude of occurrence of each failure level rather than a crisp level, to better capture uncertainty. The resources invested are financial, and the trusting agent calculates an Amount Invested Curve (AIC) for each time slot, showing the probability of a net amount being at stake throughout the slot, considering progressive or lump-sum investment. The AIC is then convolved with the FailureLevel distribution using cumulants to produce a Factual Amount Invested Curve (FAIC), which indicates the increased probability of net amount needed to achieve desired outcomes given the trusted agent's failure likelihood. The Loss of Resource Benefit (LORB) index is the value of the FAIC at the end of the AIC, representing the probability that the trusting agent will not achieve the full benefit of its resources in that time slot. The trusting agent can use the LORB across time slots to inform its decision on which trusted agent to interact with, alongside risk analysis.

Each SM has 128 CUDA Cores, four third-gen Tensor Cores, one second-gen RT Core, 128 KB L1/Shared Memory, and a 256 KB register file. The SM doubles FP32 throughput by adding FP32 capability to both datapaths, supporting 128 FP32 operations per clock. L1 cache capacity is increased to 128 KB per SM, with double the shared memory bandwidth over Turing. Second-gen RT Cores double ray/triangle intersection rate and add hardware-accelerated motion blur via an Interpolate Triangle Position unit. Third-gen Tensor Cores support TF32, BF16, and Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity, providing up to 2x throughput for sparse matrices. GDDR6X memory uses PAM4 signaling, achieving up to 19.5 Gbps and 936 GB/sec peak bandwidth. RTX IO enables GPU-based decompression and fast SSD streaming with Microsoft DirectStorage. Display support includes HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC, enabling 8K60 and 4K120. NVDEC adds AV1 hardware decode; NVENC provides seventh-gen encoding. The NVIDIA A40 data center GPU offers up to 2x FP32 and ray-tracing throughput, 48 GB memory, and vGPU support. GeForce RTX 3090 features 82 SMs, 10496 CUDA Cores, 24 GB GDDR6X. EDR technology detects and replays memory transmission errors during overclocking.

The SD Memory Card has a User Area and a Protected Area, with total capacity as their sum. Three capacity types are defined: Standard Capacity (SDSC) up to 2GB, High Capacity (SDHC) over 2GB up to 32GB, and Extended Capacity (SDXC) over 32GB up to 2TB. Hosts supporting higher capacities must also support lower ones. Five Speed Classes (0, 2, 4, 6, 10) indicate minimum sequential performance in MB/s (1 MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes/s). Communication uses command, response, and data tokens with CRC protection; commands are host-initiated, responses are from cards, and data transfers are block-oriented with single or multiple blocks. Card identification mode uses only the CMD line, while data transfer mode uses addressed commands. Initialization involves reset, voltage validation with CMD8, and ACMD41 to set operating conditions and capacity support; cards publish an RCA for addressing. UHS-I provides up to 104MB/s using 1.8V signaling with modes SDR12, SDR50, DDR50, SDR104. UHS-II adds full-duplex and half-duplex modes up to 624MB/s. ROM cards are read-only with specific command restrictions. Write protection includes a mechanical switch, internal write protect, and password-based card lock/unlock. Card Ownership Protection (COP) adds a Force Erase Password (FEP) to prevent unauthorized force erase and password reset. Erase, Discard, and Full User Area Logical Erase (FULE) operations are defined for clearing data.

The AEGEAN study compared adherence to apixaban in patients with atrial fibrillation receiving either standard of care (SOC) or an additional education program. The primary endpoint was the percentage of days with correct dosing at 24 weeks, measured via electronic monitoring. Among 1162 randomized subjects, mean adherence at 24 weeks was 91.64% in the Primary SOC group and 91.88% in the Additional Educational Program group, with no significant difference (p=0.8117). Adherence declined significantly from the first 12 weeks to weeks 12–24 in both groups. At 48 weeks, adherence from week 24–48 was 87.59% (Primary SOC), 87.51% (Secondary SOC), and 88.41% (Continued Additional Education), again without significant differences. Persistence at 24 weeks was 91.7% and 91.3%, and at 48 weeks ranged from 85.2% to 87.8% across groups, with no significant differences. Safety outcomes, including adverse events and bleeding, were similar between groups. Predictors of non-adherence in the Primary SOC group included alcohol consumption, technical occupations, permanent atrial fibrillation, and lower MMSE score; no significant predictors were found in the Additional Education group. Overall, adherence and persistence were high through 48 weeks, and the educational program did not improve adherence or persistence.

The Shuffle offense, a predecessor of the Princeton, Flex, Hawk, and Reverse Action offenses, originated with Bruce Drake at Oklahoma. It uses constant movement of all five players to create high-percentage shots, eliminate defensive help, and draw tall players away from the basket. The offense is a sequential series of options with players rotating through each position, making it ideal for teams lacking height. Very little dribbling is involved; players must be highly trained in passing, receiving, spacing, screening, rebounding, and valuing ball possession.

The basic continuity begins with O3 making a reversal pass to O1, walking defender X3 into O5's screen. O1 passes to O2, who looks to feed O3 on a rub cut off O5's screen for a layup, while O4 rebounds. If O3 is not open, O2 passes to O5 popping off O1's down screen. The third option is O4 flashing to the middle. If O4 is not open, O4 screens for O2, O5 steps out, and O2 passes to O5 to initiate shuffle cut action on the opposite side, where similar options repeat.

The rub cut is the heart of the offense. Reads and counters include: if the defender chases over the screen, O3 cuts over the top; if the defender plays inside in pass denial, O3 cuts under; if the defense switches, O5 rolls to the basket; if the defender cheats under early, O3 bumps back off a double screen for a shot; if the post defender shows and recovers, O5 pops out for a shot. The best shooter should start in the five spot.

Flash cut options involve the corner player rebounding, flashing to the middle, or setting a screen. A back cut lob counters denial of the flash. Against defensive overplay, the offense uses immediate back cuts: wing back cut, dribble clear, point back door, and post lob, exploiting overplayed passing lanes for easier shots.

This study examined associations between placental biomarkers (sEng, β-hCG, INHA, PAPP-A, PlGF, sFlt-1, and sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) measured in the first (6–14 weeks) and second (16–22 weeks) trimesters and a composite proxy for postpartum hemorrhage—retained placenta and/or hemorrhage requiring blood transfusion (RP/PPH)—in 2,192 nulliparous participants from the NuMoM2b cohort. The sample overrepresented adverse outcomes. RP/PPH occurred in 67 participants (3.1%). Second trimester median levels of sEng, β-hCG, INHA, PAPP-A, and sFlt-1 were significantly higher in the RP/PPH group; first trimester sFlt-1 and sFlt-1/PlGF ratio were also significantly elevated. PlGF did not differ at either time point. Among non-preeclamptic women, second trimester β-hCG, INHA, PAPP-A, and sFlt-1 remained significantly higher in the RP/PPH group; among preeclamptic women, no significant biomarker differences were observed between groups. Non-preeclamptic women with RP/PPH showed a greater increase in sFlt-1 from first to second trimester, while preeclamptic women with RP/PPH had a greater increase in PAPP-A and decrease in sEng. The findings suggest that second trimester angiogenic biomarkers are associated with postpartum hemorrhage proxies, highlighting potential for early risk screening, though limitations include absence of direct blood loss measurement, small RP/PPH sample size, and overrepresentation of adverse outcomes.

Scientists discovered that the Phoenix cluster’s central black hole recycles extremely hot gas into cold star-making fuel. Researchers from MIT and the University of Cambridge observed jets of 10-million-degree gas blowing bubbles, which normally quench star formation, but here also produce cold gas that rains back onto the galaxy, fueling starbursts. The Phoenix cluster, located 5.7 billion light-years away, contains about 1,000 galaxies; its central galaxy produces roughly 1,000 stars annually. Using ALMA, the team mapped cold gas via carbon monoxide and found giant filaments extending 20,000 light-years from the black hole. Chandra X-ray Observatory data showed hot gas bubbles. Superimposing the maps revealed cold gas filaments draped over the bubbles, providing a clear picture of black hole influence on cold gas. The study, published in the Astrophysical Journal, explains the cluster’s extreme star production and offers insight into black hole–galaxy co-evolution.

This study assessed the first year of COVID-19 vaccination in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from April 2021 to March 2022. The DRC launched its vaccination campaign in April 2021, aiming to vaccinate 20% of the population by end of 2021. By March 2022, 16 of 26 provinces had started immunization; 5.7% of the population had received at least one dose and 1.03% were fully vaccinated. Coverage varied widely: Kasai Oriental had the highest fully vaccinated rate (6.91%), while Equateur had the lowest (0.02%). The number of functional vaccination sites increased over time, with Kinshasa having the most. A spike in doses administered occurred in February 2022. More men were vaccinated than women in most provinces. Among high-risk groups, 8,302 healthcare workers and 46,495 elderly individuals completed their primary series. The most administered vaccine was Janssen (48%), followed by Moderna (25%) and Pfizer (17%). Compared to nine other Central African countries, DRC had the lowest percentage of doses administered over doses received (8%) and the lowest proportion of the population with at least one dose (2%). Challenges included vaccine hesitancy linked to safety concerns about AstraZeneca, competing disease outbreaks (Ebola, cholera, etc.), health worker strikes, logistical issues such as expired doses, and the introduction of multiple vaccines targeting an adult population not typically prioritized. An acceleration plan from April to June 2022 resulted in over 2.5 million people vaccinated in three months. The study concludes that progress was slow and underscores the need for health system strengthening and integration with other health interventions.

The government appealed the district court’s denial of a continuance requested shortly before trial. The continuance was sought because a key witness, Spera, had been deported by immigration authorities without notice to the prosecutor, despite an earlier request to be informed of any custody change. The district court denied the continuance, citing the age of the case, Speedy Trial Act concerns, the government’s institutional negligence, and the likely six-to-twelve-month delay to obtain the witness’s testimony abroad. The government also moved to depose Spera abroad, which the court denied as moot.

The government appealed under 18 U.S.C. § 3731, arguing the orders had the practical effect of excluding evidence. The First Circuit examined the second paragraph of § 3731, which authorizes government appeals from pretrial orders suppressing or excluding evidence. The court traced the provision’s history, noting it was designed to allow appeals from rulings that directly deny admissibility to evidence, not from routine case-management decisions. The court held that the orders at issue were denials of a continuance based on trial delay, not evidentiary rulings. While some case-management orders can have the direct effect of excluding evidence and thus be appealable, the record showed the district court was managing its docket and preserving the defendants’ right to a timely trial. Any effect on evidence-gathering was incidental, not the proximate cause of exclusion. The court rejected the government’s reliance on a case where a deposition request was denied on merits-based grounds, distinguishing it because here the denial was delay-based. The court concluded the orders did not fall within § 3731’s jurisdictional reach and dismissed the appeal for want of appellate jurisdiction.

When stock markets are oversold, strong short-term returns can be expected, but long-term returns gravitate toward the average. Oversold refers to a significant decline over a defined period, best measured with objective indicators like the 3-day RSI. Mean reversion is the tendency for extreme deviations to reverse. A backtest on the S&P 500 from 1985 onward, buying when the 3-day RSI is below 20 and selling when the close exceeds yesterday's high, produced 484 trades (or 448 in a later mention), an average gain of 0.64%, a 75% win rate, a CAGR of 7.6–7.7%, a max drawdown of 26%, and a profit factor of 2.4–2.5. The equity curve was smooth, but the strategy did not work well before 1990. Before S&P 500 futures launched in 1982, markets were not prone to mean reversion, so mean reversion may not continue forever. Oversold conditions only forecast short-term rebounds, and backtesting is strongly encouraged.

The concept of social capital originated in a West Virginia education report a century ago, gained academic attention through James Coleman in the late 1980s, and was advanced by Robert Putnam. Putnam, an Italian politics expert, used it to explain northern Italy's stronger performance versus the south, citing historical civic engagement in the north and autocratic Spanish rule leading to mafia dominance in the south. He claimed civic choral group membership in the 1870s explained 90% of regional economic growth differences. His 1990s book *Bowling Alone* documented declining civic group involvement in the U.S., triggering widespread academic and policy interest. Two definitions emerged: civic group membership (Putnam's focus) and generalized trust. A 1996 study by Knack and Keefer found no growth effect from civic membership but positive effects from generalized trust. Another distinction is bridging social capital (cross-group, linked to generalized trust) versus bonding social capital (in-group solidarity). Putnam's research indicated ethnic diversity does not increase social capital, a finding adopted by ethnonationalists. The passage notes Putnam's retirement from Harvard and the author's personal acquaintance with him.

The NVIDIA Turing GPU architecture introduces RT Cores within each SM to accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, offloading the SM and enabling real-time ray tracing. New shading technologies include Mesh Shading, which adds Task Shaders and Mesh Shaders using a cooperative thread model to efficiently process geometry, eliminate CPU draw call bottlenecks, and support dynamic level-of-detail and culling. Variable Rate Shading (VRS) allows developers to vary shading rate per 16x16 pixel region, enabling content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering optimizations. Texture Space Shading (TSS) decouples shading from screen space by computing and storing shading values in texture space, allowing reuse and temporal stability. This work presents a local flow architecture for Boltzmann Generators (BGs) that scales to large crystalline materials, overcoming limitations of previous global approaches. BGs are generative models that learn a direct mapping from a prior distribution to the equilibrium Boltzmann distribution, enabling one-shot generation of independent samples and bypassing slow mixing in molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo. The proposed method uses augmented coupling flows with auxiliary variables and graph neural networks to model coordinate transformations based on local environments, allowing energy-based training without target samples. The architecture is transferable across system sizes: models trained on small systems (e.g., 216–256 particles) can be applied to much larger ones (up to 1728 particles), drastically reducing training costs. Conditioning on thermodynamic states or interaction parameters further amortizes training. Experiments on Lennard-Jones and Stillinger-Weber potentials (including monatomic water, germanium, and silicon) demonstrate that local BGs achieve higher effective sample sizes and faster convergence than global BGs. They accurately reproduce radial distribution functions and energy histograms for large systems without reweighting. The method yields accurate Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies for systems well above 1000 atoms, with significant computational savings over standard MD+MBAR approaches. Volume-conditional training enables Gibbs free energy calculations, correctly capturing the cutoff-radius dependence of the FCC/HCP stability in Lennard-Jones crystals. Conditioning on the three-body interaction strength in the Stillinger-Weber potential allows a single model to generalize across different materials and map phase diagrams. A silicon phase diagram computed with temperature and pressure conditioning accurately predicts the diamond cubic/β-tin coexistence line. The local architecture’s linear scaling with system size and transferability make it a scalable tool for studying complex materials across thermodynamic conditions.

The SOS Disruptions defensive scheme aims to deny middle penetrations, weakside reversals, and limit the offense's operating space. When the ball handler is on the wing below the free throw line extended, the on-ball defender pushes them toward the corner or baseline checkpoint. Three baseline disruption actions are used: Straight (smothering the ball handler when they pick up the dribble before the baseline checkpoint), Base Go I (an automatic trap by the low Helpside I defender if the dribbler penetrates inside the baseline checkpoint, with the other three defenders rotating into a Triangle I), and Base Go Red (a predetermined early sideline trap initiated immediately when the ball is received or dribbled below the free throw line extended, with the closest defender trapping and others rotating into a Triangle I). All rotations occur as the ball leaves the passer's hands.

For side screen/roll situations below the free throw line, an aggressive trap is used near the baseline or corner checkpoints. When the post sets a side screen, the defender traps the ball handler before the screen is set, with rotations to deny the roll and cover outlets. An "All Out SOS Disruption" variant traps the point guard before any screen or pass, forcing the offense into freelance play. Subsequent rotations follow near-player concepts, with defenders assuming Helpside I, snuggle denial, or fronting positions as described.

President Kennedy, speaking at American University's commencement, addresses the topic of world peace. He defines genuine peace not as a Pax Americana enforced by weapons, but as a peace for all people and all time that enables growth and hope. He argues that total war makes no sense in an age of massive nuclear forces, where a single weapon can exceed the explosives of World War II and poisons would spread globally. While acknowledging that arms expenditures are essential to keeping peace, he states that idle stockpiles are not the only or most efficient means.

He calls for a reexamination of attitudes. First, regarding peace itself: the belief that war is inevitable is defeatist. Problems are manmade and can be solved. He advocates a practical, attainable peace based on gradual institutional evolution, concrete actions, and agreements—a dynamic process of solving problems, not requiring love but mutual tolerance and just settlement of disputes.

Second, toward the Soviet Union: he warns against seeing only a distorted view of the other side. While finding communism repugnant, he hails the Russian people's achievements. Both nations share an abhorrence of war, have never fought each other, and the Soviet Union suffered immense losses in World War II. Both would be primary targets in a new war and bear heavy burdens in the cold war, devoting resources to weapons instead of combating ignorance, poverty, and disease. They have a mutual deep interest in a just peace and halting the arms race, and even hostile nations keep treaty obligations in their own interest. He urges attention to common interests and making the world safe for diversity, noting our common link as inhabitants of a small planet.

Third, regarding the cold war: it is not a debate for scoring points. The U.S. must deal with the world as it is, persevere in peace, and avert confrontations that force a choice between humiliating retreat or nuclear war. America's weapons are nonprovocative and designed to deter; its diplomats avoid unnecessary hostility. The U.S. seeks to strengthen the United Nations as a world security system, keep peace inside the non-Communist world, and adjust differences with neighbors. Alliances exist because vital interests overlap; the U.S. will make no deal at the expense of others. The primary cause of tension is the Communist drive to impose its system; peace would be more assured if all nations refrained from interfering in self-determination.

He announces two decisions: high-level discussions will begin in Moscow toward a comprehensive test ban treaty, and the United States will not conduct atmospheric nuclear tests so long as other states do not. He hopes this declaration helps achieve a formal treaty.

Finally, he addresses peace and freedom at home, stating that the quality of American society must support efforts abroad. Peace and freedom walk together; where freedom is incomplete, peace is not secure. All branches of government and all citizens must protect freedom and respect rights. Peace is fundamentally a matter of human rights—the right to live without fear, breathe clean air, and ensure a healthy future. No treaty offers absolute security, but an effective one can offer more security than an uncontrolled arms race. The United States will never start a war; it seeks to build a world where the weak are safe and the strong are just, laboring toward a strategy of peace.

The speech marks a day of democracy prevailing after a violent challenge to the Capitol. It celebrates the peaceful transfer of power and the triumph of the cause of democracy, noting that the will of the people was heard and heeded. The speaker acknowledges the resilience of the Constitution and thanks predecessors from both parties. The American story depends on “We the People.”

The nation faces a once-in-a-century virus that has taken as many lives as World War II, millions of lost jobs, closed businesses, a cry for racial justice, a desperate cry from the planet, and a rise in political extremism, white supremacy, and domestic terrorism. Overcoming these challenges requires unity. The speaker invokes Abraham Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation and pledges his whole soul to bringing America together and uniting the people.

Unity is needed to fight common foes: anger, resentment, hatred, extremism, lawlessness, violence, disease, joblessness, hopelessness. With unity, the nation can right wrongs, create good jobs, teach children in safe schools, overcome the virus, rebuild the middle class, secure health care, deliver racial justice, and be a force for good in the world. The speaker acknowledges that forces dividing the country are deep and real but not new, and that history shows “better angels” have prevailed through struggle.

The path forward is unity: seeing each other as neighbors, treating each other with dignity and respect, stopping the shouting, and lowering the temperature. Without unity, there is no peace, progress, or nation. The speaker calls for rejecting a culture where facts are manipulated and manufactured, and says America must be better. He notes the setting: the Capitol dome completed during the Civil War, the Mall where Dr. King spoke, the site of a past inaugural protest against women’s suffrage, and the swearing-in of the first woman Vice President. He declares that violence will never silence the will of the people.

He pledges to be a President for all Americans, fighting as hard for those who did not support him. He defines common objects of love as opportunity, security, liberty, dignity, respect, honor, and truth. He says there is truth and lies, and leaders must defend truth. He urges ending the uncivil war between red and blue, rural and urban, conservative and liberal, by opening souls, showing tolerance and humility, and standing in each other’s shoes. The nation must face the pandemic as one, and he promises that joy comes in the morning.

To the world, he says America has been tested and come out stronger, will repair alliances, and lead by the power of example. He asks for a moment of silent prayer for the 400,000 pandemic victims. The nation faces cascading crises: an attack on democracy and truth, a raging virus, growing inequity, systemic racism, a climate in crisis, and America’s role in the world. He calls for boldness and says they will be judged by how they resolve these crises. He quotes “American Anthem” and pledges to defend the Constitution, democracy, and America, giving his all for the public good. Together, they will write a story of hope, unity, light, decency, dignity, love, healing, greatness, and goodness, ensuring democracy, hope, truth, and justice thrive.

The ProShares UltraPro QQQ (TQQQ) is an ETF tracking the Nasdaq-100 index, offering access to equity markets and potential higher returns in the technology sector. Option trading in TQQQ can increase profits and reduce risk. Option trading involves buying and selling call and put options, which give the right to buy or sell a security at a certain price. It is more complex than stock trading, requiring awareness of the option's terms, underlying security, volatility, time frame, and risk amount. Stock trading simply involves buying and selling shares.

TQQQ options are available in European style (exercisable only at expiration) and American style (exercisable any time before expiration), with various expiration dates and strike prices. The two types are put options (right to sell, used when expecting price decreases or for hedging) and call options (right to buy, used when expecting price increases).

Common strategies include buying call options, buying put options, writing covered calls, and writing put options, each with advantages and disadvantages. The best strategy depends on investor goals, risk tolerance, and trading style. A risk-managed strategy is crucial: determine maximum risk beforehand and stick to it. Choose options with high liquidity for easy exit. Backtesting trading ideas before committing money is strongly emphasized.

Option trading in TQQQ carries high risk because options are leveraged products, magnifying both potential returns and losses. It is a speculative endeavor not suitable for everyone. Key risks include unexpected moves in the underlying security, changes in option terms, and shifts in market sentiment. Investors should never invest more than they can afford to lose and should use risk management techniques like stop loss orders (though they have flaws). Diversification and cautious use of leverage are also recommended. Leverage should only be used by experienced traders who have backtested strategies.

Benefits include potential for higher returns than traditional investments, ability to use leverage, hedging against losses, reducing risk, and taking advantage of short-term market movements with quick entry and exit.

Regulations exist to protect investors, covering minimum capital requirements, maximum leverage, margin calls, stop loss orders, and hedging rules; consult a qualified broker for jurisdiction-specific rules. Tax implications vary, but profits are generally subject to capital gains tax; consult a tax specialist.

The minimum money required depends on the broker; ensure a margin of safety above the minimum. Entry and exit timing depends on goals and risk tolerance; generally enter when the underlying is expected to move favorably and exit when the target is reached. Backtesting provides clues for timing. When selecting an option, consider the underlying security, volatility, time frame, risk amount, liquidity, and personal goals. Fair value can be estimated using the Black-Scholes model, which considers underlying price, volatility, time, and risk amount, but it is an estimate and should be supplemented with other analysis. Performance analysis should use quantified strategies and backtesting, along with fundamental and technical analysis.

The passage describes techniques for low latency and scalable gate control in time-sensitive networks (TSN), configuring multiple time-sensitive applications (TSAs) to share a physical network link, and time-aware energy efficient communication. It discusses time-aware network (TAN) architecture using Precision Time Protocol (PTP) and generalized PTP (gPTP) for clock synchronization, with PTP instances (end and relay) and grandmaster selection via Best Master Clock Algorithm. Transmission selection uses traffic class queues and algorithms (strict priority, credit-based shaper, ETS). Enhancements for scheduled traffic employ gate control lists (GCL) to open/close per-queue transmission gates according to a cyclical schedule. Existing NIC implementations store the GCL in on-chip memory, causing large silicon area, high power consumption, and complex programming. A new NIC architecture moves the GCL to host memory, using a small prefetch buffer (e.g., 32 bytes) and a dedicated DMA channel to prefetch gate operations. This reduces on-chip memory from 4 KB to 32 bytes, saves power, and enables sub-nanosecond resolution and lower cycle times by direct memory programming. The MAC prefetches GCL entries, parses them to determine queue open times, and fetches data payloads ahead of gate openings. Two GCL banks in host memory allow ping-pong execution while one bank is updated. The passage also addresses configuring complex end stations hosting multiple talker applications. Such an end station is presented to a centralized network manager as a combination of virtual end stations (each with one talker) and a virtual switch, with virtual links providing propagation delay reports. The manager computes a configuration for the virtual switch, which is applied to the physical network interface, enabling multiple talkers to share the same physical link. A gate control engine (GCE) manages gate operations according to the GCL. The computational effort for computing GCLs for all ports grows exponentially with the number of streams and network size.

Schools need comprehensive renewal because society is changing rapidly. Education must adapt while allowing critical reflection. Bloom's taxonomy and a learner-centred strategy are emphasized for the Net generation (Millennials, Gen Z, Gen Alpha), who learn differently. Two key drivers are technological possibilities and fundamentally different learners. The world now consists of physical and cyber realms, and intelligence includes biological and artificial forms. Learning environments evolved from Internet 1.0 to 4.0, and education shifted to blended and non-formal models. This necessitates a shift from digital pedagogy to generative pedagogy, where teachers treat generative AI (GAI) as a colleague rather than a tool. Technological change means AI and cyber-physical systems increasingly perform human psychomotor and cognitive tasks. Six waves of technological-social change are outlined, culminating in the sixth wave of generative AI, marked by OpenAI, transformers, and large language models. The educational response followed the Kübler-Ross grief cycle: shock, denial, anger, depression, and acceptance of GAI. Web 4.0-based GAI is already impacting economies and cultures, and its rapid development poses high stakes for education. AI raises questions about the nature of knowledge and the teacher's value. A new generative pedagogy must emerge. Key unanswered questions concern the teacher's role when GAI knows everything, the value of content creation, and assessment when GAIs act autonomously. The teacher's role will shift from being the sole knowledge carrier to focusing on the affective domain—developing relationships and values—while GAI becomes a partner. The transition will require a quantum leap, and educators will be one voice among many in a symbiotic human-GAI world.

The Mid Screen offense, a common tactic involving a "Big" screening for a "Little," threatens dribble penetration and creates mismatches if the screener can post up or shoot. Defenses must be prepared. Two strategies are detailed: Basic NBA Show & Recover and All Out SOS Disruption.

Show & Recover avoids switching. Phase 1: The on-ball defender pushes the ballhandler to the sideline while the screener's defender shows hard, with other defenders denying passes and helping against the roll. Phase 2: The on-ball defender recovers, the showing defender recovers to the post, and pass denial continues. Phase 3: After a pass, defenders match up with on-ball pressure, post denial, and weakside help.

All Out SOS Disruption preemptively traps the point guard before a screen, forcing freelancing. Phase 1: A double-team traps the ballhandler while others rotate to help. Phase 2: On a pass out, defenders rotate aggressively to deny return passes and close out. Phase 3: Final alignment includes on-ball pressure, helpside positions, and fronting the post, with trap rotations available for baseline drives or post passes.

Cell2Text is a multimodal generative framework that converts single-cell RNA sequencing profiles into natural language descriptions. It uses a frozen Geneformer encoder to extract gene-level embeddings, a trainable adapter module to project these embeddings into a language model’s semantic space, and an instruction-tuned large language model decoder (Meta-Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct or Gemma3-4B-it) to generate structured descriptions covering cell type, tissue, disease, and pathway activity. Training employs full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient LoRA. The dataset comprises 1 million cells from CELLxGENE, enriched with ontology terms, tissue and disease metadata, and MSigDB Hallmark pathway annotations. Generated descriptions achieve high lexical overlap (BLEU-2/4 up to 80.96/77.39, ROUGE-L up to 82.17) and exceptional semantic fidelity (BioBERT F1-score over 93.9). For classification tasks, Cell2Text models outperform Geneformer+Head and LGBM baselines on cell type (accuracy up to 77.83%), tissue (73.04%), and disease (77.84%) prediction. Ontology-aware PageRank similarity evaluation shows that even incorrect cell type predictions remain biologically close (average similarity up to 85.62%). In pathway activity identification, Cell2Text achieves competitive subset accuracy (up to 42.31%) and weighted F1 (up to 66.27) without explicit optimization for this task. The results indicate that training for text generation yields richer cellular representations than traditional classification heads.

ChatGPT is an AI developed by OpenAI, based on the GPT architecture and trained on a large dataset of human-generated answers. In trading, ChatGPT can help create technical indicators, trading strategies, and algos, as well as perform sentiment analysis on unstructured data like financial news and social media, and generate predictions. However, it can be incorrect and overly confident. The passage states that artificial intelligence is still in its infancy and human intuition and experience are better for trading strategies. ChatGPT cannot identify the most profitable strategies; backtesting is essential to validate any generated strategy. The recommended approach is to use ChatGPT to generate or refine trading ideas, then code, debug, and backtest them on platforms such as Amibroker, TradingView, MT4, or MT5. A test example of a mean reversion strategy using the Relative Strength Index for Amibroker produced logical rules but code with many errors, leading to the conclusion that ChatGPT is useful for hints but not for correct results. The passage also defines AI pattern trading as using algorithms to identify patterns in historical market data, offering speed and adaptability but facing challenges like unpredictable market dynamics and algorithmic biases. Additionally, the passage notes that the authors offer pre-made, backtested trading strategies for purchase.

A gap is price levels with little or no trading between the previous close and the next open. Gaps occur in any timeframe but are most frequent on daily charts as overnight gaps, caused by news and imbalances. Most overnight gaps are "common gaps" with little significance. Other types include exhaustion gaps (after extended moves, price reverses), runaway gaps (sharp moves from consolidation), and breakaway gaps (indicating market direction).

Gap trading strategies have been popular for decades, but profitability has diminished as computer power and the number of traders increased. The "low-hanging fruit" has been arbitraged away, and gap trading is not as profitable as before. Strategies are static while markets are dynamic; some work temporarily, others fail permanently. Finding profitable strategies now requires more criteria and filters, increasing curve-fitting risk.

Gaps can be faded (buying a gap down) or followed (selling a gap down). Stocks tend to be better for fading. A gap is filled when price returns to the pre-gap level; small gaps are more likely to fill. A high fill rate does not guarantee profitability if the strategy is negatively skewed. Backtested S&P 500 data (25 years, E-mini futures) shows same-day fill rates: for gaps of 0.1%, bullish gaps fill 59%, bearish 61%; for 0.5%, 43% and 42%; for 1%, 28% and 33%. Bearish gaps fill slightly more due to the market's upward bias.

Simple backtest examples using 5-minute futures data (2011–2021) include a strategy buying large gap downs below -0.7%, which had a negative expectancy of -0.11% per trade. Narrowing criteria to opens between -0.7% and 0.15% improved but remained unprofitable. Adding a condition that the open exceeds the 25-day moving average yielded 0.06% per trade, still not profitable. Short-side variations were worse. Finding gap trading strategies is difficult; the author currently trades very few. A swing trading strategy that holds overnight and exits on a same-day gap fill with a higher close showed an average gain of 0.48 and profit factor of 1.8, attributed to a risk premium. Testing on SPY gave similar results. Competition in stock indices is intense, but opportunities may exist in other markets. Predicting gaps beforehand is nearly impossible. Overall, gap trading is now reasonably difficult in popular indices and asset classes.

This study investigated whether oxytocin (OT) enhances pleasantness and neural responses to social touch primarily via CT-fiber stimulation (gentle stroking touch) or non-CT fiber pressure (medium pressure massage), and whether effects differ between intranasal and oral administration. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled between-subject design, 171 healthy adults received 24 IU OT intranasally, orally, or placebo. Behavioral ratings and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured responses in orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), and somatosensory cortex (S1). Plasma OT concentrations were assayed.

Both intranasal and oral OT significantly increased plasma OT concentrations, with intranasal producing greater increases. Both routes selectively enhanced pleasantness ratings for gentle stroking touch but not medium pressure massage, with no effects on arousal, intensity, or willingness to pay. Neural responses showed that both intranasal and oral OT significantly increased oxyhemoglobin concentration changes in bilateral medial OFC, mediolateral OFC, and pSTS only during gentle stroking touch; no treatment effects were found in lateral OFC or S1, or for medium pressure massage. Time-course analyses revealed OT prolonged neural responses to gentle touch. Classification based on these time courses discriminated OT groups from placebo (64–70% accuracy) but could not distinguish intranasal from oral OT. Post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes positively correlated with pleasantness ratings and mediated the enhancement effects of both intranasal and oral OT on pleasantness. The findings indicate that exogenously administered OT selectively facilitates behavioral and neural responses to CT-fiber-mediated social touch via peripherally mediated routes, with similar effects regardless of administration route.

A smart gateway platform is provided that includes a memory storing model templates associated with respective industrial business objectives, and a processor executing components. A user interface component receives selection of a model template and mapping data that maps the template’s data inputs to data tags of industrial devices. A model configuration component customizes the template based on the mapping data. A device interface component collects data values from the defined data tags. A data modeling component normalizes the data values and adds modeling metadata based on relationships between data inputs defined by the template to yield structured data. An analytics interface component sends the structured data to an artificial intelligence analytics system.

The platform leverages domain expertise encoded in the model templates to identify subsets of industrial data relevant to a desired business objective. Each template defines data inputs and relationships (correlations, causalities) relevant to that objective. Users map the generic data inputs to specific data tags on their industrial devices. The platform collects both smart data (pre-contextualized) and raw data, normalizes and contextualizes it, and adds AI metadata such as mathematical relationships and analytic problem types. The structured data is fed to AI analytics systems at various levels (device, edge, cloud) to derive actionable insights and recommendations. This approach reduces data storage and processing requirements compared to unconstrained big data analysis, and can include local analytics and control outputs to alter device operation. The architecture supports scalable analytics across operational technology and information technology environments.

A study in Nature led by UT Austin finds that hundreds of built and proposed hydroelectric dams in the Amazon basin threaten to trap nutrient-rich sediments and modify climate from Central America to the Gulf of Mexico. The Madeira River (DEVI >80) has seen a 20% sediment decrease after two dams, with 25 more planned. The Tapajós River faces impoundment from 90 proposed dams and deforestation. Amazon sediments nourish mangroves and affect rainfall patterns; cumulative dam impacts could hinder regional climate on an interhemispheric scale.

Robots navigating unstructured, partially observed environments generate world models that inform motion planners. These models are subject to uncertainty from sensor noise, occlusions, and state estimation errors, causing inconsistencies between successive maps. Deterministic planners relying only on the most recent map can produce oscillating trajectories. The authors propose a multi-hypothesis approach that uses multiple temporally sampled environment maps to compute edge costs in a kinodynamic search space (KEASL). Each map is treated as an evolving hypothesis; the most recent is the primary hypothesis where the final solution must be collision-free, while additional hypotheses guide search.

Four methods were explored. Valid in Every Hypothesis (VEH) expands edges only if collision-free in all hypotheses, yielding overly conservative plans. Per-Edge Hypothesis (PEH) allows expansions valid in at least one hypothesis and invokes a sub-search to reroute edges around obstacles in other hypotheses, but is computationally impractical. Goal-Edge Hypothesis (GEH) defers multi-hypothesis consideration until an edge reaches the goal, then reroutes from divergence points and updates the goal-edge cost, but concentrates expansions near the goal. Goal-Edge Graph Revision Hypothesis (GEGRH) improves GEH by adding a graph revision step that identifies the first divergence point, revises the graph, and focuses expansions there.

Experiments used 221 planning problems from field data on a UGV, testing with two and three successive environment maps. ARA* search was used with a 1-second time limit. SH (single-hypothesis), VEH, and GEGRH were compared. GEGRH reduced average planning time by 15.4% (two hypotheses) and 29.27% (three hypotheses) compared to VEH, and reduced path duration by 6.64% and 18.72%, respectively. Performance gaps widened with more hypotheses. Case studies showed GEGRH can generate more direct trajectories by accepting risk of rerouting, but in some obstacle configurations VEH found lower-cost paths due to suboptimal rerouting within the time limit.

The work demonstrates that reasoning about perception uncertainty during deterministic graph search is feasible. Future directions include increasing the number of hypotheses, handling non-binary map information, exploring different cost functions for node cost recalculation, and incorporating hypothesis certainty estimates.

Prosecutors allege Lane’s cybercrime activity dates back to at least 2021, involving at least eight victims including a school athletic association, private companies, and foreign governments. A threat intelligence report from cybersecurity firm Cyble linked Lane to online personas such as “g0re,” “netsaosa,” and “fuckmarykill,” which were active on cybercrime forums and systematically targeted educational institutions, government agencies, and corporate networks. Cyble analysts described the PowerSchool hack as a predictable escalation, not the work of a first-time offender.

Lane was described by neighbors and acquaintances as introverted and soft-spoken, with a low profile in his hometown of Sterling, Massachusetts. Online, he adopted flamboyant personas and boasted about exploits. Prosecutors detailed sophisticated methods, including VPNs, eSIMs, anonymized email addresses, stolen credentials, and foreign servers. The PowerSchool attack cost the company more than $14 million, including the ransom payment and identity theft services. After the breach, some school districts received secondary extortion demands.
