Linguistics expert Martin O'Leary researched etymology and revealed that seemingly unrelated words share roots in Proto-Indo-European (PIE). For instance, 'flamingo', 'phlegm', and 'blue' derive from 'bhel' ('to shine'); 'architect' and 'dachshund' from 'teks' ('to weave'); and 'science' and 'sh*t' from 'sek' ('split/peel'). PIE was spoken between 4,500 and 2,500 BC, likely originating north of the Caspian Sea, and evolved into over 440 modern languages including English, French, Spanish, German, Punjabi, and Persian. No texts survive, complicating reconstruction. Such related words are called cognates. O'Leary shared charts on Twitter, garnering thousands of retweets and comments from users who expressed fascination or noted omitted language branches.

The ADS7828 is a 12-bit A/D converter. In hold mode, the selected analog input voltage is captured on an internal capacitor array. Input current depends on conversion rate; the source charges a 25pF sampling capacitor during the sample period. The device can use an internal 2.5V reference or an external reference. With a 5V supply, an external 5V reference is needed for full 0V–VDD dynamic range; with a 2.7V supply, the internal 2.5V reference provides full range. Reducing the reference voltage decreases the LSB size (Vref/4096), making offset, gain errors, and internal noise appear larger in LSBs. Internal noise is Gaussian and can be reduced by averaging.

The digital interface supports I2C standard (100kHz), fast (400kHz), and high-speed (3.4MHz) modes, with the ADS7828 as a slave. Bus protocol: START is a data HIGH-to-LOW while clock HIGH; STOP is LOW-to-HIGH while clock HIGH; data must be stable during clock HIGH. Transfers are byte-wise with an acknowledge after each byte. Two transfer types exist: master transmitter to slave receiver, and slave transmitter to master receiver. The address byte has five fixed bits (10010), two device select bits (A1, A0), and a R/W bit. Up to four devices can share the bus.

A command byte controls power-down and channel selection. Power-down options include combinations of internal reference and A/D converter on/off. Data is read by read-addressing the device; each 12-bit result is returned in two bytes. In high-speed mode, the clock is stretched after the read address until conversion completes. To remain in high-speed mode, use a repeated START instead of STOP. The internal reference defaults off; turning it on requires setting the PD1 bit in the command byte and issuing a STOP or repeated START. Proper settling time is needed for 12-bit accuracy. For external reference, PD1 must be 0.

Layout considerations: the SAR architecture is sensitive to glitches near comparator latching. Use a 0.1µF bypass capacitor close to the device, plus 1–10µF if supply impedance is high. External reference inputs have no noise rejection; supply noise appears in results. Connect GND to a clean analog ground, away from digital grounds. The document also includes ordering, package, and tape/reel information, and legal disclaimers.

This study reports a 4-year naturalistic follow-up of the ePOD-methylphenidate randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigating long-term effects of stimulant medication (methylphenidate) on brain development in ADHD. The original RCT included 50 boys (aged 10-12) and 49 men (aged 23-30) with ADHD, all stimulant treatment-naive. At follow-up, 33 adolescents and 25 adults returned. Pharmacological MRI was used to assess resting relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF) and rCBF-response to an acute methylphenidate challenge (dopamine-reactivity) at baseline and follow-up. Stimulant medication use (cumulative dose, exposure duration) was calculated from trial and pharmacy prescription data.

The study found no evidence for long-term age-dependent effects of stimulant treatment on development of resting rCBF or rCBF-response over time (no significant age*medication*visit interactions). This contrasts with previous short-term findings from the initial RCT. However, across visits, age-dependent associations were observed: in adults, greater medication use was associated with lower thalamic resting rCBF; in adolescents, greater medication use was associated with lower rCBF-response in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). These associations were present at baseline and were not related to ADHD symptom severity. Whole-brain exploratory analysis revealed that the CBF-response was significantly associated with noradrenaline transporter distribution, but not with dopamine transporter or receptor distributions.

The authors conclude that there is no evidence for long-lasting effects of stimulant treatment on dopamine system development. The age-dependent associations may hold predictive value for the extent of stimulant medication use after ADHD diagnosis. Strengths include the longitudinal design with treatment-naive participants at baseline. Limitations include assumed complete medication adherence, a male-only sample, participant attrition, and use of different MRI scanners at baseline and follow-up. Future large-scale longitudinal studies are encouraged to further explore pharmacological MRI for optimizing ADHD treatment.

Interfacial mobility is a key coarse-grained parameter for microstructural evolution. Connecting atomistic simulations to continuum models remains challenging, particularly for solute-interface interactions with solute-drag effects. Mobility is typically extracted from molecular dynamics via the capillary fluctuation method (equilibrium fluctuations, assumes overdamped Langevin dynamics, limited to high temperatures) or linear response (imposed driving force, useful at low temperatures but may cause non-linear response). Both methods assume Markovian, memory-free motion, but memory effects arise from a hierarchy of relaxation times, causing transient sub-diffusion that complicates mobility extraction, as seen in grain boundaries in Fe–C alloys. Non-Markovian memory makes the conventional Langevin description inadequate; generalized approaches from biochemistry can correct for memory. This work adapts such techniques using a simplified kinetic Monte Carlo model of interface migration with interacting solute. The model is a discrete two-dimensional lattice model with a connected-line interface, periodic boundary conditions along x, and open along z. The study will demonstrate inconsistency with the capillary fluctuation method, present an alternative mobility extraction based on mean boundary motion, and apply a time convolutionless propagator approach.

Using the Netherlands as a case study, this paper develops an agent-based epidemiological framework to analyze the first COVID-19 wave (February 27–June 1, 2020). The framework combines demographic data, mobile phone mobility data, and mixing matrices to create a dynamic proxy contact network at municipality and hourly resolution, coupled with an SEIR transmission model. Calibrated to national hospital admissions, the model reproduces the epidemic’s temporal and spatial spread. Assessment of national non-pharmaceutical interventions shows that mobility reductions contributed most to epidemic control (without them, hospital admissions would have approximately doubled), behavioral changes had a considerable but smaller impact, and school closure had little effect. The study then evaluates subnational interventions triggered when local infection prevalence exceeds a threshold. With thresholds of 0.33% or 1%, cumulative hospital admissions remain close to the national lockdown level, while many municipalities (e.g., 167 at 0.33%) delay or avoid interventions, reducing societal burden. The framework is exportable to other countries with comparable data, though limitations include the absence of household structure, simplified mobility assumptions, and reliance on national-level mobility change data.

The paper investigates whether large reasoning models (LRMs) can be distinguished by their reasoning patterns and what traits differentiate them. Existing studies often use predefined, researcher-defined taxonomies, which may bias analyses and miss unexpected behaviors. To address this, the authors introduce the LLM-proposed Open Taxonomy (LOT), an inductive method that identifies distinguishing reasoning features directly from model outputs. LOT operates in three stages: (1) an LLM compares reasoning traces from two LRMs on the same question and proposes distinguishing traits in natural language; (2) the LLM annotates these features in other traces, converting them into feature vectors; (3) a logistic classifier is trained on these vectors to predict the source model. When classification fails on a new trace, LOT iteratively adds new features observed in the failed sample, yielding an open taxonomy that reliably separates thought processes.

LOT is applied to classify reasoning traces of 12 open-source LRMs across varying parameter scales, base model families, and task specializations, using five datasets (GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500, AIME 24 & 25, CRUXEVAL, LiveCodeBench). It achieves 80–100% accuracy in pairwise classification, outperforming few-shot prompting (by 23.8% on average), the automatic prompt engineer method VML (by 19.6%), and a human-defined reasoning taxonomy (by 11.7%). The natural-language taxonomies provide human-readable explanations of reasoning differences. For example, smaller Qwen3 models more often exhibit circular reasoning, while the largest variant more reliably recalls relevant knowledge and verifies applicability of approaches. A code-specialized model occasionally uses Python functions to solve math problems, indicating domain-specific inertia. Comparisons across base model families show that models sharing a base model exhibit more similar reasoning patterns.

A case study links reasoning differences to performance gaps. By modifying the reasoning of smaller Qwen3 models to align with the largest Qwen3’s style during test time, accuracy on GPQA-Diamond improves by 3.3–5.7%. The intervention pipeline involves summarizing reasoning into steps, editing the summary based on feature correlations, and re-expanding it. Limitations include the inability to establish causal links between meta-attributes and reasoning due to uncontrolled training recipes, potential variability of taxonomies with random seeds, and the test-time nature of the intervention.

This lecture discusses policy with behavioral agents, focusing on paternalism. It begins by reviewing neoclassical reasons for government intervention—externalities, equity, market failures like monopoly, public goods, information problems, macroeconomic policy, and redistribution—before introducing behavioral “internalities,” where individuals fail to fully account for effects on their future selves. Paternalism is defined as an attempt to influence people’s conduct for their own good, not due to externalities.

The lecture examines when paternalism is warranted. Not all behavioral phenomena justify intervention: risk preferences, reference-dependent preferences, and social preferences are not biases to fix. However, self-control problems, time-inconsistent preferences, and non-standard beliefs (limited attention, memory failures, learning failures, overoptimism, overconfidence, projection bias, attribution bias) may warrant intervention. Motivated beliefs are tricky and not an automatic reason. Discrimination warrants intervention. Defaults, frames, and nudges are instruments, not reasons. Poverty and mental health may call for support programs rather than paternalism, and happiness interventions might push people to experiment rather than mandate specific behaviors.

Forms of paternalism include hard paternalism (forcing choices, significant price changes, mandates, bans, taxes) and soft paternalism. Soft paternalism has two variants: libertarian paternalism (influencing behavior while preserving freedom of choice) and asymmetric paternalism (helping those who make mistakes while minimally interfering with those who behave optimally).

Arguments against paternalism include: the government may not know better due to informational issues and heterogeneity; government may not be benevolent, leading to corruption or regulatory capture; freedom of choice may matter intrinsically; people dislike hard paternalism; and practical problems of choosing and implementing policies exist. Arguments in favor note that people make mistakes and can be helped, some prefer not to make complex choices themselves, and soft paternalism with opt-out provisions addresses many criticisms.

Examples of popular paternalism include Social Security, Medicare, investment menu restrictions, consumer safety regulations, mandatory education, cigarette and sin taxes, and bans on prostitution or polygamy. Soft paternalism examples include banning junk food in school vending machines, calorie disclosure laws, and default 401(k) enrollment. Cigarette and alcohol taxes vary widely across states. Unpopular paternalism includes helmet and seatbelt laws, where there is often no externality and disagreement over risk-reward tradeoffs. Mask mandates involve externalities and thus differ. Some policies, like drug prohibition, may be inefficient, and shifting public sentiment is leading to legalization.

Nudges can have large effects: automatic enrollment dramatically increases retirement plan participation, and text message reminders reduce failures to appear in court. However, not all interventions work; a clinical trial providing multiple supports after heart attacks showed no effect. A recent study comparing academic nudge studies with nudge unit interventions finds smaller effects in the latter, possibly due to publication bias or implementation challenges.

Not everyone wants to be nudged. In an energy report study, some people were willing to pay not to receive social comparison reports, indicating they were made worse off. Asymmetric paternalism would respect such preferences and allow opt-out.

Determining the form of paternalism is difficult because many options exist, and even a “no default” choice acts as a form of paternalism since defaults influence behavior. The discussion should therefore focus on optimal soft paternalism.

The Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) plan is presented as an example of libertarian paternalism. Employees were asked before a pay raise to commit to increasing retirement contributions starting after the raise, with automatic increases at each subsequent raise, and could opt out anytime. The plan uses behavioral principles: present bias (committing future self), loss aversion (reducing future raises rather than current pay), and defaults (procrastination keeps people enrolled). It significantly increased savings among participants.

On market solutions, the argument that markets will provide self-control goods is countered by the fact that firms also exploit consumers, target naive individuals, and naive people do not seek help. Thus, the market may not solve self-control problems, and government regulation (e.g., Consumer Financial Protection Bureau) may be needed.

Finally, “sludges” are nudges used to harm, such as mail-in rebates designed to be forgotten or voter registration barriers. Identifying and eliminating sludges can be as important as implementing helpful nudges.

The lecture concludes that soft paternalism can improve welfare, but nudges can backfire, some people dislike being nudged and their preferences should be respected, the market does not solve everything, and reducing sludges is valuable. The broader class summary emphasizes that psychological considerations are important in economic choices, understanding one’s own biases can improve decision-making, small changes can have large effects, and these insights apply to personal choices, helping others, and designing products and teams.

New research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science determined dinosaur incubation periods by counting daily growth lines in fossilized teeth of Protoceratops and Hypacrosaurus embryos. The small Protoceratops incubated for nearly three months, the larger Hypacrosaurus for six months. These periods are longer than bird incubation (11–85 days) and similar to primitive reptiles, indicating birds evolved rapid incubation later. Long incubation exposed eggs to prolonged risks from predators, starvation, and flooding, and combined with slow maturation, may have disadvantaged non-avian dinosaurs during the Cretaceous extinction, while birds with shorter incubation could reproduce faster and survive. Andrew Sabo appealed his conviction for cocaine possession with intent to deliver and felon in possession of a firearm, arguing that evidence seized from his residence should have been suppressed. He contended the search warrant affidavit lacked probable cause because it relied on an unproven citizen informant, that he was entitled to a Franks-Mann hearing due to alleged false statements in the affidavit, and that the informant’s identity should have been disclosed.

The trial court found the informant credible based on specific details provided—seeing Sabo load a black semi-automatic pistol and process cocaine for distribution—and because police independently corroborated Sabo’s identity, criminal record, and presence at the address. The court denied suppression and disclosure of the informant’s identity. It also denied a Franks-Mann hearing, finding Sabo failed to make a substantial preliminary showing that the affidavit contained deliberately false or recklessly made statements. Sabo’s renewed motion, which alleged the information came from a 911 caller who later claimed to have lied, was rejected because the caller was deemed not credible.

The Court of Appeals affirmed. It held the warrant affidavit established probable cause under the relaxed reliability test for citizen informants, the trial court’s factual findings were not clearly erroneous, and the denial of a Franks-Mann hearing and refusal to compel informant disclosure were proper exercises of discretion.

A method for selecting an ingress edge region of an Internet-based overlay network is described. The overlay network has an authoritative DNS. A customer router performs a DNS lookup for a service hostname, which is resolved by the authoritative DNS. The DNS response may return an edge region based on the DNS resolver's location rather than the router's location. The router establishes an IKEv2 session to that first overlay network edge. Upon tunnel establishment, the first edge performs a secondary DNS lookup for the router's IP address to determine if it is the appropriate ingress region. If the first edge determines it is not the best choice, it issues an IKEv2 redirect to a second overlay network edge. The router then establishes a new tunnel to the second edge. The second edge may also perform periodic lookups; if it determines it is no longer a valid choice for the router, it intentionally drops liveness probes (IP-SLA probes) sent by the router over the tunnel. This triggers the router to initiate another service hostname lookup to find a new edge region.

The lecture examines exact solutions of the inviscid Burgers' equation. Starting from a delta function initial condition, the solution consists of a fan (u = x/t) followed by a shock. The shock position is determined by mass conservation, yielding X = √(2t). The shock speed satisfies the jump condition (average of u left and right) and the entropy condition (u_left > shock speed > u_right). A general solution formula involving minimization of an expression with the initial function is presented. The viscous Burgers' equation is introduced and transformed into the heat equation by first integrating u and then applying a nonlinear change of variables. The solution is expressed via convolution with the heat kernel; as viscosity tends to zero, the dominant contribution comes from the minimum of an exponent, recovering the inviscid formula. The Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation is mentioned as a dispersive nonlinear PDE. Numerical experiments showed that solitary waves (solitons) interact and emerge unchanged, leading to the discovery of infinite conserved quantities and complete integrability. Other integrable equations include the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The Navier-Stokes equations are not integrable; a Clay prize problem concerns their global existence, and a recent numerical experiment refuted a specific blow-up conjecture. Future topics include finite differences, the level set method, financial mathematics PDEs, and solving large linear systems.

SOS Pressure Defense is presented as a response to the increasing offensive power in modern basketball. It emphasizes that tough pressure defense will be increasingly employed by successful teams as an equalizer. The system offers fundamentals and teaching techniques that can enhance any defensive scheme. Six keys are outlined: 1) Fundamental defensive skills are taught in a logical simple-to-complex progression, from one-on-one to five-on-five, with daily reinforcement. 2) Specific SOS key words identify and trigger defensive actions: on-ball words are SET, ON, SMOTHER; off-ball words are SNUGGLE, OFF, STRIKE. These provide a common court language. 3) Defenders pressure opponents to specific checkpoint areas in "no-man's-land" 18 feet or more from the hoop to reduce shooting percentage. 4) Two-on-two switching is encouraged as an option to stifle screens, eliminating hesitation and frustrating screening teams. 5) Stopping the break begins in the backcourt immediately after a rebound, with each player applying pressure through specific assignments like denying passing lanes or pushing the ballhandler to checkpoints. 6) Each defender has a clear-cut specific role, working together to dictate offensive action and create turnovers. Well-executed SOS defense acts as an equalizer, helping teams outclassed offensively, giving an edge to equally skilled teams, and providing a winning edge on poor shooting nights.

The paper proposes NeuroAdapter, an end-to-end framework that conditions a latent diffusion model directly on fMRI brain activity, bypassing intermediate feature spaces used in typical two-stage decoding pipelines. fMRI data are processed using Schaefer parcellation into parcel-wise embeddings, which are integrated into Stable Diffusion via cross-attention. Training employs fMRI token dropout and min-SNR loss weighting, and a brain encoder selects the best decoded image from multiple candidates. Evaluated on the Natural Scene Dataset (NSD), NeuroAdapter achieves competitive performance, particularly on high-level semantic metrics, and generalizes to NSD-Imagery and Deeprecon datasets. The authors also introduce IBBI, a bi-directional interpretability framework that leverages cross-attention dynamics across diffusion steps. The brain-directed view yields parcel contribution vectors showing relative influence of brain parcels, while the image-directed view produces ROI attention maps highlighting where specific brain regions attend in the reconstructed image. Causal perturbation analysis indicates that masking high-level ROIs alters semantic content. The discussion notes that current decoding benchmarks may be saturating and emphasizes the need for interpretability frameworks to understand the neural–generative interface.

The Put-Call ratio is a sentiment indicator that divides the volume or open interest of put options by call options for a given instrument or asset class. It can be calculated by dividing the number of traded put options by the number of traded call options. Volume is what is traded within a certain time frame, while open interest is the total number of option contracts still open at the end of the trading day. There are many types of Put-Call ratios, such as those on indices and on stocks.

A call gives the right to buy shares at a predetermined price within a timeframe; a put gives the right to sell. Put options work like insurance against a drop in market prices. The logic behind the ratio is that traders buy puts for protection when uncertainty is high, making it a contrarian signal because the stock market is susceptible to mean reversion. Extreme readings are often used as contrarian signals to fade the market. Generally, high readings signal fear and low readings signal complacency, but there are no universal rules for what is a good or bad ratio; relative readings must be considered.

The author’s backtests reveal that the Put-Call ratio is not among the best sentiment indicators, and the VIX indicator is cited as better. A backtest using an index Put-Call ratio produced unimpressive trading performance metrics. The author has never used the Put-Call ratio for trading strategies, finding it inferior to VIX strategies. The ratio is available on many trading and investing websites and apps, and can be calculated from exchange data, but free downloadable sources are not easy to find.

The PGA848 linear operating input voltage range extends within 3V of either power supply, with excellent common-mode rejection. The valid common-mode range depends on input common-mode voltage, differential voltage, gain, and reference input voltage. A typical application drives a single-ended input SAR ADC (ADS8860). The circuit accepts single-ended or differential inputs, using ±15V supplies for the input stage and a 5.3V supply for the output stage, which matches the ADC supply. The REF6250 provides a 5V reference; the PGA848 REF pin is set to ADC midscale (2.5V) via a precision 10kΩ-to-10kΩ resistive divider (±0.05% tolerance, ±5ppm/°C drift) buffered by an OPA192 in a dual-feedback configuration (RISO=20Ω, RF=2kΩ, CF=2nF) providing 86° phase margin. The noninverting input has a 1kΩ, 10nF low-pass filter. Three filters are used: an input EMI/RFI filter, a CFB capacitor (75pF) in parallel with the internal 6.67kΩ feedback resistors giving a nominal 318kHz cutoff (277kHz at high tolerance), and a charge reservoir filter at the ADC inputs. The overall bandwidth is 318kHz with –0.1dB flatness to 41kHz. Power supply recommendations: nominal performance with ±15V supplies, VICM and VREF at mid-supply; output-stage supplies are clamped to input-stage levels. Supply voltages above 40V (±20V) cause permanent damage. Layout guidelines include symmetrical input paths, 0.1µF ceramic bypass capacitors between each supply pin and ground, keeping input traces away from supply/output traces, minimizing leakage and parasitic capacitance on DA_IN+ and DA_IN– pins, using keep-out areas in ground planes below input pins, minimizing thermal junctions, and keeping distance from heat sources. The large N expansion of gauge theory and string scattering amplitudes share the same mathematical structure, with the string coupling identified as 1/N. Both expansions are organized by topology: worldsheet topology for strings and Feynman diagram topology for gauge theory. Summing Feynman diagrams of a given genus can be viewed as a discrete sum over triangulations of surfaces, analogous to a continuum sum over surfaces in string theory. If the weight of each Feynman diagram could be identified with a string action, large N gauge theory would be equivalent to string theory, with the large N limit corresponding to classical string theory and single-trace operators mapping to string states.

However, making this identification is difficult. Feynman diagram amplitudes are products of propagators and look nothing like a string action. The choice of target space and worldsheet degrees of freedom is vast, and string theory is formulated in the continuum while Feynman diagrams provide only a discrete version. A geometric picture is expected to emerge only at strong coupling, where complicated diagrams with many vertices dominate and provide a fine triangulation. For simple systems like matrix integrals or matrix quantum mechanics, this philosophy can be shown to work, but not for higher-dimensional field theories.

Generalizations include adding fields in the fundamental representation (quarks), which leads to Feynman diagrams classified by surfaces with boundaries, corresponding to open strings. Using gauge groups like SO(N) or Sp(N) instead of U(N) yields unorientable surfaces and non-orientable strings.

Attempting to guess a string theory description for large N QCD in 3+1 Minkowski spacetime fails. A string theory in that spacetime is mathematically inconsistent except in 26 or 10 dimensions. Even with extra compact dimensions to preserve Poincaré symmetry, string theory always contains gravity and gives a massless spin-2 particle, which QCD lacks according to the Weinberg-Witten theorem. Hints from the holographic principle (gravity describable by a lower-dimensional boundary theory) and from string theory consistency (anomalies dynamically generating an extra dimension) suggest a five-dimensional (4+1) uncompact spacetime.

If the field theory is scale invariant (a CFT), the metric of the corresponding string theory must be anti-de Sitter spacetime. Requiring the metric to have Poincaré and scaling symmetries fixes it to the AdS form with a curvature radius R. Thus, a large N CFT in D dimensions, if described by a string theory, should be a string theory in AdS_{D+1}.

Historically, string theory was initially developed for strong interactions but was abandoned after QCD was established. In 1974, 't Hooft noted the large N expansion resembles string theory, and others realized string theory contains gravity. That year also saw Hawking radiation, experimental observation of charmonium, and Wilson's lattice QCD showing quark confinement via strings. In the late '80s and early '90s, matrix models were connected to lower-dimensional string theory. The holographic principle was proposed in 1993-94. In 1997, Polyakov argued for a five-dimensional string theory, and later that year Maldacena provided explicit examples of large N CFTs equivalent to string theory in AdS, using D-branes. Witten subsequently connected this to the holographic principle.

To derive this relation, the lecture turns to string theory details: the Nambu-Goto action describes a string's worldsheet area using the induced metric. It can be rewritten in polynomial form as the Polyakov action, introducing an auxiliary worldsheet metric gamma_{ab}. Eliminating gamma_{ab} recovers the Nambu-Goto action. The Polyakov action is a two-dimensional nonlinear sigma model coupled to gravity, so quantizing the string becomes quantizing 2D gravity coupled to D scalar fields.

In a study of 45 patients aged 50–74 with CSF biomarker-confirmed mild Alzheimer disease (AD), the impact of BCHE-K variant on age-at-diagnosis was examined in APOE4 carriers. Among APOE4 carriers (n=33), BCHE-K carriers (n=11) had a mean age-at-diagnosis 6.4 years earlier than noncarriers (n=22, P<.001). No similar effect was seen in APOE4 noncarriers. In APOE4 carriers with BCHE-K, baseline age was over 6 years earlier and accompanied by slightly higher amyloid and tau accumulations. APOE4 homozygotes with BCHE-K exemplified a predominant amyloid, limited tau pathophysiology, and limbic-amnestic phenotype. Multiple regression showed amyloid accumulation associated with APOE4 carrier status, larger ventricular volume, less synaptic injury, and less tau; tau pathophysiology associated with more neuroaxonal damage, synaptic injury, and glial activation. The findings suggest BCHE-K carrier status reduces age-at-diagnosis in APOE4 carriers, potentially through effects on glial activation.

The lecture focuses on finite impulse response (FIR) systems and structures that exploit their properties. The general FIR system function is a finite sum, and the difference equation corresponds to convolution. Direct form, transposed, and cascade form realizations are possible; a parallel form is not generally possible for FIR systems, though a parallel-like structure exists. For linear phase FIR systems, the impulse response satisfies h(n)=h(N-1-n). This symmetry allows the transfer function to be expressed with half the number of multiplications by grouping symmetric terms. A structure for even N uses a chain of delays, summing symmetric outputs and multiplying by shared coefficients, reducing multipliers by half. The frequency sampling structure is derived by expressing the system function in terms of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) coefficients H(k), which are samples of the frequency response. The resulting structure cascades a comb filter (1-z^{-N}) with a parallel bank of first-order recursive sections, each having a pole at W_N^{-k} and a gain H(k). The poles cancel zeros of the comb filter, so the overall system remains FIR. Advantages include reduced complexity when many frequency samples are zero, and suitability for filter banks because the comb filter and pole sections can be shared, with only the H(k) multipliers differing. A disadvantage is the need for pole-zero cancellation on the unit circle, which causes sensitivity to finite register length effects. The lecture concludes by discussing finite register length effects, specifically parameter quantization. The sensitivity of pole locations to coefficient errors increases with polynomial order, making direct form structures more sensitive than cascade or parallel forms. Even within second-order sections, different structures yield different quantized pole grids: a direct form second-order section quantizes r² and 2r cosθ, resulting in a grid of realizable poles along circles and vertical lines; a coupled form quantizes r cosθ and r sinθ, yielding a rectangular grid.

This study investigated the relationship between cancer mortality and COVID-19 using US vital statistics from 2014–2020, analyzing both underlying cause (UC) and multiple cause (MC) death data for six cancer types and other chronic conditions. Observational studies have provided conflicting evidence on cancer as a COVID-19 mortality risk factor. Nationally, UC cancer deaths showed a non-significant decline in spring 2020, while MC cancer mortality (any mention of cancer) increased significantly during all three pandemic waves, resulting in 12,000 excess deaths—a statistically significant 2% elevation over baseline. The largest relative increase was for hematological cancers (5%, 3,100 excess deaths). No excess MC mortality was seen for pancreatic or lung cancers. In contrast, diabetes and Alzheimer’s deaths exhibited large, statistically significant excesses (MC elevations of 39% and 31%, respectively) that were temporally synchronous with COVID-19 waves.

State-level analyses in New York, California, and Texas showed modest, non-significant MC cancer mortality increases, with the largest in New York’s spring wave (8% overall, up to 15% for breast cancer). A demographic model projected expected excess mortality under the null hypothesis that a condition itself does not confer additional COVID-19 risk, accounting only for age distribution, population size, and baseline mortality. Under this null, projected elevations were 7% for all cancers, 1–2% for pancreatic and lung cancers, and 6–14% for colorectal and breast cancers, broadly consistent with observed MC excesses. For diabetes and Alzheimer’s, projected elevations were 28% and 46%, respectively, also aligning with observations. The model illustrates that competing risks—where high baseline cancer mortality overshadows COVID-19 mortality risk—explain the limited excess cancer deaths, especially for cancers with low survival.

The findings rule out the immune incompetence rescue hypothesis, as hematological cancers showed the highest relative excess mortality. The authors conclude that there is at most a modest elevation in cancer mortality during the pandemic, reflecting competing mortality risk from cancer itself rather than immunosuppressive protection. They note limitations including uncertainty in attack rates, potential shielding by cancer patients, and the need for longer-term data on care disruptions and vaccination effects.

The article discusses ultralight backpacking, tracing its origin to a 1994 article by Mark Jenkins about shedding gear to travel farther, faster, and lighter. Ultralight is defined as a base weight of 10 pounds or less (all gear minus worn items and consumables), with "super ultralight" at 5 pounds or less and "lightweight" at 15 pounds or less. The author notes that ultralight backpackers are now common. The key to reducing weight is bringing less stuff, evaluating each item by whether it is truly needed for warmth, comfort, food, or safety, as per Mike Clelland's guidelines. Eliminating unnecessary items like excess stuff sacks can shed weight without cost. The heaviest items are the backpack, sleep system, and shelter; upgrading these yields significant weight savings. The author suggests starting with shelter and sleep system, and encourages trying cowboy camping or using a tarp, though personal experience with Lyme disease made him more selective. He also switched from sleeping bags to quilts after experimenting, emphasizing openness to new approaches. Ultralight backpacking is described as a philosophy focused on staying comfortable and safe with minimal gear, not just a weight limit. Practical tips include not eating where you camp to avoid attracting animals and enjoying early-morning hiking. Lighter gear makes breaking camp easier, allowing more spontaneous stops. Beginners may not achieve the 10-pound goal immediately, and occasional overages are acceptable. Over time, refining what you truly need leads to a lighter pack and a more enjoyable experience, removing barriers to appreciating the outdoors.

The passage discusses environmental education (EE) and sustainable development in the context of global environmental crises such as global warming and natural disasters. It traces international cooperation from the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment and the 1992 Earth Summit, which adopted Agenda 21, emphasizing the need for EE to address pollution and resource depletion. EE is defined as an interdisciplinary process to cultivate awareness, knowledge, skills, attitudes, and participation for solving environmental problems. The Belgrade Charter sets six objectives: awareness, knowledge, attitude, skills, participation, and evaluation ability. Guiding principles include considering natural and man-made environments, lifelong learning, an interdisciplinary approach, participation, a global perspective with regional differences, and attention to current and future situations.

The environment is classified into natural (biotic and abiotic) and man-made (physical and social). Environmental knowledge is structured into natural resources, social environment, environmental technology, and waste/pollution. Environmental properties include uniqueness, interdependence, chain reactions, and temporal changes. EE is delivered through formal and non-formal education, with learning outside the classroom shown to benefit all students, including those with special needs.

Sustainable development is defined as meeting present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet their own needs, balancing economic growth, social equity, and environmental quality. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) highlight interconnectedness, with climate action as critical. Achieving sustainable environmental development involves reducing energy consumption, minimizing waste, conserving natural resources, and using clean technologies. Environmental management employs tools like ISO 14000. Examples of projects integrating EE include the Huai Sai Royal Initiative Project and Thailand’s Natural Capital Accounting project. The United States experienced an unusually early, severe surge in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in autumn 2022. RSV-A genomes belonged to at least 10 distinct lineages with most recent common ancestor times between 2014 and 2017. RSV-B genomes had a tMRCA estimate of 2019. Genomes from Washington state also revealed multiple lineages, with four shared with Massachusetts. The genetic divergence was consistent with normal evolutionary rates, unlike accelerated evolution in SARS-CoV-2 variants. The surge consisted of numerous pre-existing viral lineages, many shared geographically, inconsistent with a single highly transmissible lineage. Non-viral factors, such as immunity changes from altered RSV dynamics during the COVID-19 pandemic, should be investigated.

The Go Top trap deploys the high Helpside I defender to double team when the post turns to the middle. The Go Wing trap sends the wing defender to double team when the post defender is caught behind. The TPS7H500x-SP controllers use a transconductance error amplifier that compares the VSENSE pin voltage to the lower of the SS pin voltage or a 0.613-V internal reference. The output voltage is set via a resistor divider from VOUT to VSENSE, dividing the output down to 0.613 V. During soft start, the error amplifier uses the SS pin voltage as its reference until it rises above VREF; a capacitor between SS and AVSS controls the soft-start time.

The device has three switching frequency modes: internal oscillator mode, set by a resistor from RT to AVSS with a 100-kHz to 2-MHz range; external synchronization mode, with RT floating and a clock applied to SYNC at twice the desired switching frequency; and primary-secondary mode, where one controller's SYNC output clocks a secondary controller. Primary switching outputs (OUTA/OUTB) and synchronous rectifier outputs (SRA/SRB) are available, with some outputs only active under a 50% duty cycle limit. Dead times and leading edge blank time are programmable via external resistors for certain devices.

Peak current mode control turns on primary outputs via an internal clock and turns them off when the sensed peak current reaches the COMP/2 pin voltage. A resistor from CS_ILIM to AVSS sets the current limit threshold at 1.05 V, triggering cycle-by-cycle limiting and hiccup mode. The HICC pin capacitor controls delay and restart times. The FAULT pin allows external fault protection, and slope compensation is set via the RSC pin. Frequency compensation components are connected between the COMP pin and AVSS. Thermal shutdown occurs if the junction temperature exceeds 175°C.

The product incorporates almost ten architectural, reliability, and feature improvements over the unsupported Cisco RSM, with Cisco product engineering involvement. Silent monitoring allows supervisors to listen to live agent-customer calls unheard; coaching lets supervisors assist agents without the customer hearing. UniRSM™ enables remote monitoring and coaching by dialing from any phone without a network connection. Features include a new architecture eliminating RTSP audio delays, Whisper Coaching, multiple call monitoring per session, monitoring from call start, full HA failover, support for Cisco VVB and VXML gateways, web-based reporting and administration, and Windows/Linux support.

Sergeant Marlon Appollis, the investigating officer, testified in the Western Cape High Court that no suicide note or sign of suicide was found near Susan Rohde's body in a Spier hotel room in July 2016. This study reports genomic sequencing and characterization of twelve SARS-CoV-2 samples collected from Esteio, Rio Grande do Sul (RS), Brazil, between April 9 and June 29, 2021. All twelve genomes belonged to the Gamma variant clade, with ten assigned to P.1 lineage and two to P.1.17 sublineage. Sixty-eight nucleotide substitutions were identified, including 36 non-synonymous changes. The most common missense substitutions (in at least 75% of sequences) were NSP12:P323L, S:K417T, S:T1027I, ORF8:E92K, N:P80R, 5'UTR:C241T, NSP3:K977Q, and H655Y. Mutations S:E484K and S:N501Y were present in only two samples. Several mutations were described for the first time in RS, including ORF3a:A72S, NSP3:P1103L, NSP3:D1208A (also first in Brazil), NSP4:D144G, NSP13:L325F, and NSP12:I136V, the latter not previously described on GISAID.

A dataset of 4,706 RS genomes from GISAID (March 2020 to May 2022) showed that sequencing efforts correlated with COVID-19 waves. Lineage B.1.1.33 predominated in 2020, followed by Zeta (P.2) and B.1.1.28/P.7 from November 2020 to January 2021. Gamma (P.1 and derivatives) became prevalent from February to July 2021, coinciding with the second wave. Delta lineages (mainly AY.99.2 and AY.101) were dominant from August to the end of 2021, and Omicron (BA.1.1 and BA.2) emerged in December 2021, exceeding 90% of sequenced genomes from January to April 2022. In the RS genome set, the most prevalent missense variant was NSP12:P323L (98.70%), and other frequent mutations included C241T, NSP3:F106F, S:D614G, N:R203K/G204R, S:N501Y, and S:H655Y.

Phylogenomic analysis of RS genomes recovered monophyletic groups for Alpha, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron VOCs, with supported subclades for P.1.2, P.1.17, P.1.7, AY.101, and AY.9.2. The twelve Esteio genomes clustered within the Gamma clade. Global phylogenomic searches using AudacityInstant found that four Esteio genomes were most closely related to sequences from Brazil, while four others were closer to genomes from Chile, Mexico, USA, and Canada; four genomes had no related sequences due to low sequencing quality.

Molecular evolution analyses of structural proteins E, M, and N were performed using FUBAR, FEL, and SLAC methods. For the E protein, no positively selected sites were identified; two sites (25 and 63) were under negative selection. In the M protein, two sites (94 and 125) were under positive selection, and twelve sites were under purifying selection. In the N protein, fourteen sites were identified as positively selected (including codons 9, 34, 63, 151, 182, 192, 208, 215, 238, 265, 289, 362, 366, and 391), and forty-six sites were under negative selection.

DynaMut2 predictions of stability changes for positively selected sites showed that in the M protein, mutation S94G was destabilizing while S94I, H125L/Q/Y were stabilizing. In the N protein N-terminal domain, D63G and D63Y were stabilizing, whereas P151L and P151S were destabilizing. In the C-terminal domain, most mutations were destabilizing, except Q289L which was stabilizing. The study notes that some samples had low sequencing coverage, and further research is needed to understand the impact of structural changes on host-pathogen interactions.

This study protocol describes a three-arm randomized controlled trial evaluating a digital mindfulness psychoeducation programme (Digital-MindCAN) for cancer survivors. The programme delivers cancer-specific education, mindfulness principles, and mindfulness practice in real-time via videotelephony. Eligible participants are adults who completed curative cancer treatments between two weeks and two years prior. They will be randomly assigned to Digital-MindCAN with standard care, an active control (Palouse Mindfulness programme with standard care), or a wait-list control group. A convenience sample of 150 participants (50 per group) will be recruited from a tertiary hospital in Singapore. Primary outcomes are objective stress (peripheral skin temperature, heart rate, oxygen saturation) and subjective stress. Secondary outcomes include psychological well-being, perceived relaxation, mindfulness, resilience, depression, and anxiety. Data collection uses self-administered questionnaires, physiological measures, and focus group interviews. Quantitative analyses will employ descriptive statistics, analysis of covariance, and repeated measures analysis of variance; qualitative data will be analyzed using a realist evaluation method. The trial aims to test whether Digital-MindCAN is superior to wait-list control and non-inferior to Palouse Mindfulness in improving psychological outcomes. Positive findings could inform clinical practice by offering the programme as part of standard care for cancer survivors in Singapore. Anticipated challenges include low recruitment and attrition, with strategies such as social media advertising and honorariums to address them.

This study aimed to examine preschool teachers' views on sensory education and their classroom practices. Using a phenomenological design, data were collected via semi-structured interviews from 20 preschool teachers selected through maximum diversity sampling. Content analysis identified three main themes. Regarding importance, all teachers emphasized sensory education is crucial in early childhood, contributes to all developmental areas, and should be supported through planned activities, enriched environments, and family cooperation. Concerning the preschool education program, teachers stated sensory education is not sufficiently or clearly included, though they incorporate sensory activities like visual, auditory, music, and touch studies into daily routines, evaluating them primarily through observation. For challenges and limitations, teachers reported insufficient materials, unfavorable physical conditions in schools, and inadequate self-efficacy, with nearly all desiring further training on sensory integration.

Stanford researchers developed biofilm lithography, using engineered E. coli that secrete a sticky protein in response to blue light to pattern bacterial communities at 25-micrometer resolution. The technique, described in PNAS, creates intricate designs overnight. It offers speed, simplicity, higher resolution, and compatibility with surfaces including microfluidic devices. The method could clarify biofilm growth, enable novel biomaterials, and create synthetic microbial communities for applications like microfluidic chips or biofilm-based circuits. Testing revealed sharp patterns, suggesting bacteria are weakly surface-bound and continuously attach and detach, supporting a biofilm formation hypothesis. The resolution parallels early silicon photolithography. Researchers aim to grow multi-species communities to study antibiotic resistance sharing, with clinical implications.

The passage examines higher education projects (HEPs) created in exile by Russian academics after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent state repression. It situates these initiatives within research on academic exile, collective institutional relocation, and education in emergencies. The study focuses on four HEPs that vary in formalisation, legitimacy, and autonomy. Using interviews and discourse analysis, it identifies three self-conceptualisations: HEPs as “safe havens” offering infrastructure and intellectual freedom for fleeing scholars and students; as spaces for preserving and partially reconceptualising academic heritage, including schools of thought and the Russian academic language, though reconceptualisation remains limited; and as “hope-making praxis,” where active, future-oriented work generates hope for a democratic Russia despite uncertain return. The passage notes that HEPs’ roles reveal gaps in international education frameworks and calls for further scrutiny of preserved biases, colonial approaches, and discrepancies between stated missions and everyday practice.

This study developed a Markov model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style nutritional intervention for household contacts of persons with TB in India. The intervention provided a food basket (750 Kcal, 23g protein, multi-micronutrient) for 6 months to household contacts, and nutritional support for those developing TB during treatment. Model parameters were based on the RATIONS trial, which showed a 40% reduction in TB incidence and a 35% reduction in mortality. Over a lifetime, per 100,000 household contacts, the intervention reduced TB cases from 7718 to 6749 and TB deaths from 1529 to 906, averting 13,775 DALYs. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was $229 per DALY averted from a healthcare perspective and $184 from a societal perspective, both below India’s willingness-to-pay threshold of $550. Sensitivity analyses showed the intervention remained cost-effective under a wide range of assumptions, with cost-effectiveness most sensitive to the cost of supplementation and the risk ratio of TB incidence. The authors conclude that RATIONS-style nutritional support is cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in settings with high undernutrition.

The lecture examines the gravity dual of a CFT on a sphere at finite temperature. Because the sphere introduces a scale, physics depends on the dimensionless product rT, leading to richer behavior than in flat space. In global AdS, making Euclidean time periodic yields a well-defined thermal AdS solution, as the proper size of the time circle is bounded below. A black hole solution also exists, with horizon radius r0. The Hawking temperature as a function of r0 has a maximum, so there is a minimum temperature T_min. Above T_min, two black hole solutions appear: a small black hole with negative specific heat (resembling flat-space Schwarzschild) and a big black hole with positive specific heat. Together with thermal AdS, three gravity solutions exist at a given temperature, interpreted as three possible phases of the CFT.

To find the stable phase, one compares Euclidean actions. In the large-N limit, actions scale as N². Thermal AdS has classical action zero (same as pure AdS), with fluctuations of order N⁰. The big black hole always has larger Euclidean action than the small black hole, so the small black hole never dominates. A critical temperature Tc > T_min exists. For T < T_min, only thermal AdS is present. For T_min < T < Tc, thermal AdS dominates. For T > Tc, the big black hole dominates. At Tc the free energies are equal, marking a first-order phase transition (Hawking-Page transition). The black hole free energy vanishes at r0 = R, giving Tc = (d–1)/(2πR).

The field theory interpretation is illustrated by a toy model of N² harmonic oscillators with an SU(N) singlet condition. The density of states is of order one for energies of order one, but becomes exponential in N² for energies of order N². At low temperatures (large β), only O(1) energy states contribute, yielding free energy O(1). At high temperatures (small β), the large entropy of O(N²) states overcomes thermal suppression, making the free energy O(N²). This behavior depends only on large N and the density of states, capturing the essence of the Hawking-Page transition.

In Coxheath, Cape Breton, Dale Capstick has seen about three dozen giant house spiders (Eratigena atrica) since August. The palm-sized spiders are fast and frightening. Robertson discusses indexing options, including model portfolios and robo-advisors, and co-created AutoInvest.ca, a tool to compare robo-advisor costs (the site receives affiliate commissions). He also offers an online course, *Practical Index Investing for Canadians*, with tutorials for Tangerine, TD Direct Investing, and Questrade.

The lecture discusses dynamic optimality: whether a single binary search tree (BST) can perform as well as any other BST on any access sequence. The BST model allows following left, right, and parent pointers and performing rotations; only successful searches are considered, with no insertions or deletions. Worst-case cost is Ω(log n), but some sequences allow faster access. Several amortized properties are defined: sequential access (accessing keys in order costs constant amortized), dynamic finger (cost log of key distance from previous access), entropy bound (cost based on access frequencies), working set (cost log of number of distinct keys since last access of that key), and the unified property (combines dynamic finger and working set: cost log of spatial plus temporal distance to a recently accessed close key). It is unknown if any BST achieves the unified property; the best known adds an additive log log n. Dynamic optimality asks for an online BST whose total cost is within a constant factor of the offline optimal BST. This remains open. Splay trees are conjectured dynamically optimal; they satisfy sequential access, working set, and dynamic finger, but unified and dynamic optimality are unproven.

A geometric view maps an access sequence to points (key, time). A BST execution corresponds to the set of touched nodes, forming a point set. A point set is a valid BST execution if and only if it is arborally satisfied: every rectangle spanned by two points not on the same horizontal or vertical line contains another point. The cost equals the number of touched points. Thus, offline optimal BST is equivalent to finding a minimum arborally satisfied superset of the input points. The complexity of this problem is unknown; no constant-factor approximation is known, but an O(log log n)-approximation exists.

The greedy algorithm processes points sweep-line by time, adding points on the current row to satisfy unsatisfied rectangles. In tree terms, this corresponds to rearranging touched nodes into a treap ordered by next access time. This offline algorithm can be made online using split trees: touched nodes are stored in a split tree that supports moving an accessed item to the root and splitting in constant amortized time, simulating the treap without knowing future accesses. The resulting online BST is conjectured optimal but not proven. Next lecture will cover lower bounds.

HPE announced the Edgeline Services Platform, Data Aggregation App, and Address Translation App at Discover 2017 to help manage IoT device inventories and integrate IT with Operational Technology (OT). These Software Defined OT offerings build on Edgeline Converged Edge systems. The platform runs IoT apps at equipment locations outside data centers. The Data Aggregation App combines data from OT devices into a single collection. The Address Translation App transfers network address translations from larger to subset networks and uses software-defined configuration for remote management. Analyst Mike Krell noted HPE's single-vendor approach relieves OT customers from navigating many new vendors and technologies.

Researchers from UCL and Imperial College London used high-resolution imaging to show how polymyxin antibiotics disrupt Gram-negative bacteria. Polymyxin B caused bumps and rapid shedding of the outer armor within minutes, forcing cells to overproduce and shed it, which left gaps that allowed the antibiotic to enter and kill the cell. This process only occurred in active cells; dormant bacteria, with armor production switched off, were unaffected. Dormant cells could be killed after being awakened with sugar, with a 15-minute delay. The findings suggest combining polymyxins with treatments that wake dormant bacteria could improve effectiveness, and that bacterial state must be considered when assessing antibiotics.

The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia answered certified questions from the Circuit Court of Mercer County in a case where three at-will employees (cleaning maids) of a Holiday Inn were terminated after refusing to take a polygraph test. The employees had signed agreements in 1981 to submit to polygraph testing if required, and in 1982 the employer notified them testing would begin. They refused and were discharged. The circuit court found the termination violated a substantial public policy and denied the employer’s motion to dismiss, certifying two questions.

The Supreme Court held that the determination of whether a substantial public policy exists is a question of law for the court, not a question of fact for a jury. On the main question, the court held that it is contrary to the public policy of West Virginia for an employer to require or request an employee to submit to a polygraph test or similar test as a condition of employment. This public policy is not absolute; under certain circumstances such testing may be permitted, as contemplated by a later-enacted statute (W.Va. Code 21-5-5b). The court grounded this policy in the state’s recognition of an individual’s interest in privacy, citing prior decisions (Sutherland v. Kroger Company, Roach v. Harper, Golden v. Board of Education) that protected privacy rights. The court noted that the later statute, though not applicable to this case, embodied a recognized facet of public policy. The circuit court’s ruling that the termination violated public policy was affirmed, and the case was remanded.

Justice Miller dissented, arguing that at the time of the plaintiffs’ termination there was no established public policy prohibiting discharge for refusing a polygraph test. The relevant statute did not become effective until months later. He contended that the privacy tort cases relied upon did not establish such a policy, and that courts elsewhere require a preexisting constitutional, statutory, or judicial expression of public policy. Justice Neely also dissented, emphasizing the ex post facto effect and stating that the legislature’s enactment of a statute indicated no prior common law public policy existed. He argued the decision should not apply retroactively under the criteria set forth in Bradley v. Appalachian Power Co.

The card initialization and identification process begins after bus activation. The host issues ACMD41 with the HCS bit in the OCR: HCS=1 indicates support for SDHC or SDXC cards, while HCS=0 indicates no such support. CMD8 expands ACMD41 functionality; HCS is ignored by cards not responding to CMD8, and the host should set HCS to 0 if no response is received. Standard Capacity SD cards ignore HCS. If HCS=0, SDHC and SDXC cards never return ready (busy bit remains 0). The busy bit in the OCR signals initialization completion: 0 means initializing, 1 means complete. Initialization must finish within 1 second from the first ACMD41; the host repeats ACMD41 for at least 1 second or until busy=1. The card checks operational conditions and HCS only at the first ACMD41 with a voltage window set. While repeating ACMD41, only CMD0 may be issued. If the card responded to CMD8, the ACMD41 response includes the CCS field, valid when ready. CCS=0 indicates SDSC, CCS=1 indicates SDHC or SDXC. Incompatible cards are sent to Inactive State. The host then issues CMD2 to each card to obtain its unique CID; the card enters Identification State. Next, CMD3 asks the card to publish an RCA, after which the card enters Stand-by State. The host may assign another RCA by sending another CMD3; the last published RCA is the actual one. The identification process (CMD2 and CMD3) repeats for each card.

For UHS-I, the host sets S18R=1 in ACMD41 to request 1.8V signaling. The card responds with S18A=1 (in 3.3V mode) to allow voltage switch; then the host issues CMD11 to invoke the voltage switch sequence. Completion is detected by a high level on DAT[3:0]. After switching, appropriate driver strength and UHS-I mode are selected via CMD6 Function Groups 3 and 1. For SDR50 and SDR104 modes, tuning may be performed by repeatedly issuing CMD19. CMD11 can be executed in ready state and does not change state; if no response is detected, a power cycle is needed. CMD19 is used for tuning, with a fixed block length, and a sequence of up to 40 executions must complete within 150ms.

During card identification mode, the host remains at fOD frequency. In data transfer mode, the host may operate at fPP. The host issues CMD9 to obtain CSD, and CMD4 (SET_DSR) to configure driver stages. CMD7 selects one card into Transfer State; only one card can be in that state at a time. Deselection occurs automatically if another card is selected with a common CMD line. All data communication is point-to-point. Data read commands (block read, multiple block read, etc.) can be aborted by CMD12, returning the card to Transfer State. Data write commands can also be aborted by CMD12 before deselecting the card. After data transfer, the card moves to Programming State (if successful) or Transfer State (if failed). If a block write is stopped with a valid last block, data is programmed. The card may buffer block writes; when buffers are full, DAT0 is held low (BUSY). No buffering exists for write CSD, write protection, or erase. Parameter set and read commands are not allowed while programming. Moving another card to Transfer State does not terminate erase/programming; the card enters Disconnect State and releases DAT. Resetting a card (CMD0 or CMD15) terminates any pending programming and may destroy data. Wide bus (4-bit) mode is selected/deselected via ACMD6, with default 1-bit after power-up or CMD0; a locked card rejects ACMD6.

Erase operations use CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38. If an out-of-sequence command is received, ERASE_SEQ_ERROR is set and the sequence resets. Write-protected sectors are skipped. The card indicates erase in progress by holding DAT0 low. Discard is similar to erase but the content becomes 'don't care'. It uses the same address setting commands and CMD38 with argument 00000001h. Discard is supported only for SDHC/SDXC, not via SPI. Busy timeout is 250ms. Full User Area Logical Erase (FULE) uses CMD32 with argument 0, CMD33 with end of user area, and CMD38 with argument 00000002h. FULE is supported only for SDHC/SDXC, with a 1-second busy timeout. If the card does not support Discard or FULE, it executes ERASE.

Password protection uses 128-bit PWD and 8-bit PWD_LEN registers. Locked cards accept basic commands, ACMD41, CMD16, and lock card commands. CMD42 performs lock/unlock, set/clear password, and force erase. Card Ownership Protection (COP) adds FEP and FEP_LEN registers. COP cards require COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]) after power-on if FEP is set, to enable COP functions. FEP management includes set, replace, and reset. Force Erase (CMD42[08h]) erases all content and PWD, but is disabled when FEP=set. FEP Force Erase (CMD42[18h] with FEP) erases all content and PWD while keeping FEP. COP cards have different command sequences and error handling compared to non-COP cards.

Switch function command (CMD6) is used to switch or expand functions. Four function groups are defined: Access Mode, Command System, Driver Strength, and Power Limit. Mode 0 queries support and maximum current/power; Mode 1 sets the function. The default function is 0. Power Limit settings range from 0.72W to 1.80W, with corresponding current limits. UHS-I cards operate up to 1.44W; UHS-II cards may use higher power. Busy status bits indicate when a function cannot be switched.

High-Speed mode (25 MB/sec) is achieved by switching to the High-Speed function via CMD6, increasing clock to 50 MHz. It requires a 1-to-1 connection between host and card. CMD8 is used before ACMD41 for cards compliant to Version 2.00 or later, checking voltage compatibility. The card echoes back the voltage and check pattern in R7 response.

SDSC cards use byte address format and variable block length set by CMD16. SDHC and SDXC cards use block address format with fixed 512-byte block length, disable partial and misalign access, and do not support write-protected groups. CMD42 block length can be set up to 512 bytes.

The device supports single-ended and differential inputs with bipolar and unipolar ranges, outputting in straight-binary format. The full-scale range is the difference between positive and negative full-scale input voltage, and the LSB size equals FSR / 2^16. The device features an active-high alarm output on the ALARM/SDO-1/GPO pin when configured for alarm functionality. Two alarm types exist: an input alarm with user-programmable high and low thresholds, and an AVDD alarm with fixed thresholds of 4.7V (low) and 5.3V (high). Both alarms are enabled by default when alarm functionality is on and can be selectively disabled. Each alarm has an active flag, cleared at the end of a conversion if the condition is gone, and a tripped flag, cleared only after the ALARM_REG register is read. Alarm flags can be read via the ALARM pin, internal registers, or appended to the data output. The input high alarm triggers when the digital output exceeds the high threshold and resets when it is less than or equal to the high threshold minus hysteresis minus 1. The input low alarm triggers when the digital output falls below the low threshold and resets when it is greater than or equal to the low threshold plus hysteresis plus 1.

The device uses a multiSPI digital interface. The device has three functional states: RESET, ACQ, and CONV, determined by the CONVST/CS and RST pins. The RST pin can issue an application reset (resets configuration registers) or a power-on reset (resets all internal circuitry). A data transfer frame begins on the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends on the rising edge. A frame with 32 SCLKs is optimal; a short frame invalidates a write operation, and a long frame uses the last 32 bits as the command. Input commands include NOP, CLEAR_HWORD, READ_HWORD, READ_BYTE, WRITE_HWORD, WRITE_MSBYTE, WRITE_LSBYTE, and SET_HWORD. The output data word for a frame is determined by the previous frame's command and the DATA_VAL bits, and can include appended flags like device address, input range, alarm flags, and parity bits. Data transfer protocols include legacy SPI-compatible protocols with single or dual SDO-x, and source-synchronous protocols where the RVS pin provides an output clock. The device has nine configuration registers, including DEVICE_ID_REG, RST_PWRCTL_REG, SDI_CTL_REG, SDO_CTL_REG, DATAOUT_CTL_REG, RANGE_SEL_REG, ALARM_REG, ALARM_H_TH_REG, and ALARM_L_TH_REG. The device is a fully integrated 16-bit SAR ADC-based data acquisition system with an integrated analog front-end and reference. An example application is an 8-channel analog input module using the ADS8681W with an external multiplexer. The device offers NAP and power-down low-power modes. Power supply decoupling and specific PCB layout guidelines are provided.

The lecture introduces ordinary differential equation initial value problems (ODE-IVPs), defined as systems where all differentials are with respect to a single variable and all initial conditions are given at one time point. Higher-order ODEs can be converted into a first-order vector form dy/dt = f(y) (or f(t,y) for Matlab). The desired output is typically a vector of time points and a matrix of corresponding y-values for plotting.

The Forward Euler method updates using y_new = y_old + Δt f(y_old), analogous to the rectangle rule for integration. Its local error per step is O(Δt²), leading to a global error of O(Δt). More accurate integration rules like the trapezoid rule (average of f at endpoints) and midpoint rule (f at half-step) reduce global error to O(Δt²). For ODEs where f depends on y, direct application is not possible because future y-values are unknown. The second-order Runge-Kutta method (RK2) approximates the midpoint rule by using a Forward Euler estimate for the midpoint y-value.

Error propagation analysis shows that errors from previous steps are multiplied at each step by a factor of (I + Δt * dg/dy), where g is the update formula. For numerical stability, the norm of this matrix must be ≤ 1; otherwise, small errors amplify and the solution may become meaningless. Even for intrinsically stable systems (where the Jacobian df/dy has negative eigenvalues), a poor choice of method or step size can cause instability. An example with dy/dt = -2y solved via Forward Euler with Δt=1 yields an oscillating, non-physical solution, while the true solution decays smoothly. The lecture notes that homework will involve writing an ODE solver, and the next class will cover implicit solvers.

The passage discusses business process modeling in the context of extended enterprises, where multiple organizations share common goals. It proposes a Model Driven Architecture-based business process model comprising three components: a static domain model (entities, actors, resources), a workflow model (process activities), and a value model (value exchanges between parties). For static modeling, controlled natural languages like Attempto Controlled English and SBVR are used, translated into logic-based formalisms (Discourse Representation Structures, OWL DL, SWRL) to enable automated reasoning. The chapter highlights the need for hybrid reasoning combining open-world (e.g., Semantic Web) and closed-world (e.g., Horn rules) assumptions, and addresses modal interpretations (alethic and deontic) of business rules. Workflow modeling employs graphical notations such as BPMN and UML Activity Diagrams, with declarative representations supporting consistency checking, data export, and annotation. Value modeling is presented through graphical (e3-value) and logic-based (Prolog-style FOL) techniques to estimate profitability. Relations between the three models are examined, including static consistency (matching value and message exchanges), semi-dynamic consistency (forecast feasibility), and dynamic consistency (monitoring runtime execution against models). The chapter concludes that multi-faceted business process models require different formalisms and hybrid reasoning, and identifies open issues like critical areas detection and representing stakeholder pragmatics.

This passage presents a qualitative document analysis of digital storytelling (DST) in African higher education. The study analyzed 15 scientific articles selected via a PRISMA protocol from databases such as Google Scholar, ERIC, and JSTOR, focusing on studies from 2000 onward in education and social sciences. The research questions addressed the skills promoted by DST and the contexts of its integration.

The literature defines DST as storytelling using digital tools like text, graphics, sound, and video, typically involving a short narrative with seven elements: point of view, dramatic question, emotional content, voice, soundtrack, economy, and pacing. The creation process includes pre-production, production, and post-production phases. Benefits include improved digital literacy, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, motivation, and engagement.

Findings from the selected studies indicate that DST promotes empowerment, cultural enrichment, and transformative learning experiences. Specific skills developed include identity expression, reflective capabilities, higher-order thinking, oral performance, and map reading. DST fosters community building among pre-service teachers and students, and serves as a tool for social activism by giving voice to marginalized groups.

Contexts of integration include pre-service teacher training, geography education, language learning, postgraduate research, and multicultural classrooms. DST modernizes traditional oral narrative customs and preserves indigenous knowledge. Challenges such as resource shortages, lack of self-confidence, time constraints, insufficient digital equipment, inconsistent electricity, and low technological proficiency hinder implementation. Educators sometimes prioritize administrative tasks over student digital literacy activities, though solutions like group work using smartphones are noted.

The study concludes that DST is a transformative force in African higher education, enhancing skills and cultural understanding, but requires emphasis on narrative content over technology in assessments.

In 1946, the mother left Edward, age 2, with the father and went to Nevada, obtaining a divorce decree that awarded her custody of their daughter and purported to award the father custody of Edward. The father had exclusive custody of Edward from 1946 until a 1949 visit, after which the mother refused to return him and sought custody. The trial court ordered Edward returned to the father pending trial and later denied the mother's application, confirming custody in the father. On appeal, the mother argued both parents were equally fit with suitable homes, so under Civil Code section 138, the child of tender years should be with her. The appellate court affirmed, holding the trial court had discretion to consider the child's best interests, including the stability of his established home with the father from age 2 to 6 and the disruption a change would cause. No abuse of discretion was found.

The professor introduces AMO physics as defined by its community and building blocks: atoms, molecules, photons, and electromagnetic fields. Historically focused on individual particles and collisions in gases, the field now emphasizes few-body and many-body physics, entanglement, and overlap with condensed matter, including quantum dots, NV centers, and optical control of mechanical oscillators. AMO physics is characterized as low-energy quantum physics, distinct from biophysics and solid-state unless laser methods are used. Key paradigmatic systems are the hydrogen atom, two-level system, and harmonic oscillator.

The field evolved from observing nature to controlling it. Control progressed from internal states via optical pumping to external motion through laser cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation, and to single quantum systems. Current frontiers involve creating complexity and entanglement in many-body systems, moving from high-entropy hot gases to zero-entropy, highly correlated wave functions.

Technological advances drove these developments: proliferation of solid-state lasers, short-pulse high-intensity lasers, frequency combs enabling precision metrology, and high-finesse cavities for single-photon physics. Historical paradigms include atomic structure, laser spectroscopy, magneto-optical traps, Bose-Einstein condensation, ultracold fermions, and emerging topics like quantum computation, topological states, and ground-state cooling of mechanical oscillators.

The course 8.422, part of a two-course cycle, can be taken out of sequence. It covers light-atom interactions from first principles (QED), including excitation, stimulated emission, spontaneous emission, open systems, density matrix, master equation, mechanical forces of light, trapping and cooling, single photons, quantum information building blocks, and many-body physics of quantum gases. It excludes topics above 10 eV, high-energy collisions, advanced atomic structure, and high-intensity lasers. Requirements include problem sets, a term paper, and no exams.

As an appetizer, the professor discusses atoms in an optical lattice formed by interfering laser beams. The standing wave creates a periodic potential. When spontaneous emission is non-negligible, it leads to Sisyphus cooling. When negligible, deep lattices isolate atoms for atomic clocks using magic wavelengths, achieving high accuracy. Shallow lattices allow tunneling, band structure, and Mott insulator transitions. Pulsing the lattice enables atom optics and interferometry for precision measurements, and when applied to interacting systems, probes the dynamic structure factor. The professor shares a personal example of switching an experiment between interferometry and many-body physics by adjusting a knob, illustrating the synergy of precision control and complex quantum systems.
